> Defendat quod quisque sentit: sunt enim judicia libera: nos institutum tenebimus, nullisque unius disciplinae legibus adstricti, quibus in Philosophia necessariò pareamus, quid sit in unaquaque re maximè probabile semper requiremus.

Let each man defend what he thinks, for judgments are free: we shall hold to our practice and, bound by the laws of no single school which we should be obliged to obey in Philosophy, we shall always seek what is most probable in each matter.

> CICERO TUSC. L. IV. C. III.

Cicero, Tusc. bk. IV, ch. III.

> *D. JOACHIMVS VELASQVEZ DE LEON, in Reg. Mexican. Curia Causarum Patronus, publicus antehac in Alma Academ. Matheseos Professor, & Regiae Societatis Cantabricae* de los Amigos del País *Socius Literatus, ita censuit.*

Don Joaquín Velázquez de León, Advocate of Causes in the Royal Audiencia of Mexico, formerly Public Professor of Mathematics in the Illustrious University, and Literary Member of the Royal Cantabrian Society of the Friends of the Country, gave this opinion.

> EXCELLENTISSIME DOMINE.

MOST EXCELLENT LORD.

> Volumina, quae jussu Vestro ad me adlata sunt, hunc inscripta titulum RECENTIORIS PHILOSOPHIAE ELEMENTA á P. Doct. D. *Johanne Benedicto Diaz de Gamarra & Davalos* Oratorii S. Philippi Nerii Presbytero Seculari quum evolverim, miratus sum Auctoris laborem, diligentiam, alacritatem, brevitatem. Vix enim credibile dictu est, quàm multa ipse, quàm eruditè, quàm ad Juventutem in Philosophia (quae verè philosophiae nomine adpellanda sit) erudiendam, strenuè operam navarit! Tantum verò abest, ut Scholares Institutiones ipsae hae aliquid, aut moribus quos incorruptos esse decet, aut sanctissimis legibus adversum atque inimicum obtrudant; ut me judice, (si quid cernere [PDF 10] mihi licet, non admodum mediocriter versato) via haec, & ratio tradendae Philosophiae, cum vera germanaque, saepè â praeclarissimis Viris cooptatâ, & qualem hac tempestate apud nostrates, jussu Regio, Hispanae Academiae jam pridem sectatae sunt, plurimum consentiat. Quae quum ita sint, Princeps Excellentissime, nihil causae subest, quamobrem horum Elementorum per typos evulgatiò prohibeatur. Ita equidem censeo. Dat. Mexici postrid. Non. Septemb. anno D. 1774.

The volumes which were brought to me by Your command, bearing this title, Elements of the Newer Philosophy, by the Rev. Father Dr. Don Juan Benito Díaz de Gamarra y Dávalos, Secular Priest of the Oratory of St. Philip Neri — when I had turned through them, I wondered at the Author’s labor, diligence, alacrity, brevity. For it is scarcely credible to say how much he himself, how learnedly, how vigorously he has labored to instruct Youth in Philosophy (in a philosophy that truly deserves to be called by the name of philosophy)! So far, indeed, are these School Institutions themselves from thrusting upon us anything adverse or hostile either to morals, which ought to be kept uncorrupted, or to the most holy laws, that in my judgment (if I may be permitted to discern anything, [PDF 10] being not altogether indifferently versed in these matters) this way and method of teaching Philosophy agrees very closely with the true and genuine one, often adopted by most distinguished Men, and such as the Spanish Universities among our countrymen have long since followed in these times by Royal command. This being so, Most Excellent Prince, there is no reason why the publication of these Elements in print should be forbidden. Such, at least, is my opinion. Given at Mexico, on the day after the Nones of September, in the year of the Lord 1774.

> *Joachimus Velasquez de Leon.*

Joaquín Velázquez de León.

> ¶ N. B. *Sigue la misma Aprobacion traducida por su Autor, de orden verbal, que para ello se sirviò dàr su Excelencia.*

¶ N. B. There follows the same Approbation, translated by its Author, by verbal order which His Excellency was pleased to give for the purpose.

[PDF 11]

> EXCMÔ. SR.

MOST EXCELLENT SIR.

> Haviendo visto los Libros, que por Superior mandato de V. Exciá. se me remitieron con este Titulo: RUDIMENTOS DE LA MODERNA FILOSOFIA, por el P. Dr. D. *Juan Benito Diaz de Gamarra y Davalos* Presbytero Secular de la Congregacion del Oratorio de San Felipe Neri: admiré el trabajo del Autor, su diligencia, la generalidad, y al mismo tiempo la concision con que escribe. En efecto, apenas puede creerse, quanta variedad de cosas el P. Dr. con quanta erudicion, y quan seriamente se haya tomado este trabajo para instruir á la Juventud en una Filosofia, que merece bien este nombre! Y están tan lexos estas Instituciones Escolares de incluir algo, que se oponga, ô â las Leyes del Reyno, ô â la integridad, y pureza de las costumbres; que antes bien en mi dictamen (si puedo darlo en estos asuntos, en que no dejo de estár algo versado) este metodo de enseñar Filosofia conviene mucho con el verdadero, que han deseado siempre los Autores de mejor [PDF 12] doctrina y gusto, y que en este tiempo se ha comenzado yá â poner en practica en las Universidades de nuestra España de orden del Rey Nuestro Señor. Por lo qual, nada hallo, Señor Excelentissimo, que impida la impresion, y publicacion de esta Obra. Asì lo juzgo. Mexico, y Septiembre 6. de 1774.

Having seen the Books which, by superior command of Your Excellency, were sent to me with this Title: Rudiments of the Modern Philosophy, by the Rev. Father Dr. Don Juan Benito Díaz de Gamarra y Dávalos, Secular Priest of the Congregation of the Oratory of St. Philip Neri, I admired the labor of the Author, his diligence, his comprehensiveness, and at the same time the concision with which he writes. Indeed, it can scarcely be believed what a variety of things the Father Doctor has taken up, with how much erudition, and how earnestly he has undertaken this labor in order to instruct Youth in a Philosophy that well deserves this name! And these School Institutions are so far from including anything opposed either to the Laws of the Kingdom or to the integrity and purity of morals, that, on the contrary, in my opinion (if I may give one in these subjects, in which I am not without some experience) this method of teaching Philosophy agrees closely with the true one, which has always been desired by the Authors of better doctrine [PDF 12] and taste, and which at this time has already begun to be put into practice in the Universities of our Spain by order of the King Our Lord. Wherefore I find nothing, Most Excellent Sir, to hinder the printing and publication of this Work. So I judge it. Mexico, September 6, 1774.

> EXCMÓ. SR.

Most Excellent Sir.

> *Joachin Velasquez de Leon.*

Joaquín Velázquez de León.

## DOMINE JUDEX AMPLISSIME. — MOST HONORABLE LORD JUDGE.

> Vetus illud Sapientis, nescio cujus, responsum (quaerenti *quid pueris esset addiscendum*) id denique oportere *quod Viris usui foret*: ipsum equidem omninò mihi usurpatum volo, sanctèque profiteor; postquam RECENTIORIS PHILOSOPHIAE ELEMENTA haec â P. Doct. D. *Johanne Benedicto Diaz Gamarra & Davalos*, Oratorii S. Philippi Nerii Presbytero Seculari in usus Scholaris Juventutis Americanae congesta, perlegi, ac penè syllabatim sum persecutus. Quare quum Auctor multò diligentissimus pleraque omnia, Juventutis ergò rectè instituendae, ex optimis quibusque excerpserit, composuerit, breviterque exararit; nihil autem ipse ego offenderim, quod absonet â fide ortodoxa, [PDF 14] vel sit Christiano Philosopho alienum: aequissimum censeo, atque utile futurum, ut chartae istae Typis mandentur. Dabam Mexici prid. Id. Septembres 1774.

That old answer of some Sage, I know not whose (to one asking what boys ought to learn), that they ought, in short, to learn what would be of use to them as Men: this I wish wholly to make my own, and I solemnly profess it, now that I have read through these Elements of the Newer Philosophy, compiled by the Rev. Father Dr. Don Juan Benito Díaz de Gamarra y Dávalos, Secular Priest of the Oratory of St. Philip Neri, for the use of the American Youth of the Schools, and have followed them almost syllable by syllable. Wherefore, since the Author, a man diligent above most, has excerpted nearly everything from all the best writers for the sake of instructing Youth rightly, has composed it and written it out briefly, while I myself have come upon nothing that is out of harmony with the orthodox faith, [PDF 14] or that is foreign to a Christian Philosopher, I judge it most equitable, and that it will be useful, that these pages be committed to the Press. Given at Mexico on the day before the Ides of September, 1774.

> *Dr. Josephus Ignatius Bartolache.*

Dr. José Ignacio Bartolache.

> Jussu Congregationis Michaelopolitanae, summâ ope nisus sum, ut volumina haec duo, quibus titulo est *Elementa Recentioris Philosophiae*, quantâ maximè potui adtentione perlegerem. Verebar autem, ne praejudicio magis, & Clariss. Auctoris (quo cum conjunctissimè vivere jam pridem coeperam) existimatione, quàm jure meritò de hoc opere sentirem. At ingenuè fateor, me in eo totum fuisse, ut superciliosi censoris, non putidi efrontisque laudatoris personam agerem. Itaque postquam diu multumque cogitavi, quid tandem mihi eamobrem scribendum esset, & ad Conscriptos Familiae nostrae Patres deferendum: en pauca haec animo ocurrebant, quae censurae loco erunt. Primùm quidem, Patrem Doctorem nostratemD *Johann. Benedictum* rem acu tetigisse, dum Philosophiae nomine, non inanem fallaciam, decipiendo; sed doctrinam apprimè utilem, docendo, in Juvenum gratiam contulisse. Nam Elementa [PDF 16] haec Recentioris Philosophiae mira brevitate, perspicuitate, miro item ordine complecti mihi videntur, quidquid Angli, Galli, Hollandi, Itali, Hispani, per longas annorum decadas seriò in rem philosophicam intenti, perquisivêre. Comperiet utique tyro Juvenis quamplurima hìc, ritè tractata, quae frustrà alibi requirat; nisi adolescentior factus, in reliqua vita [quod paucis admodùm contingit] strenuam Philosophiae, ac libris, quorum non multa nobis copia fit, operam dabit. Quod si quaestiunculas illas, toties agitari solitas, De *Praescissionibus*, De *Ente rationis*. De *Materiae appetitu*, De *Infinito cathegorematico*, aliasve multò vaniores, quas Auctor sciens prudensque praetermisit, cum disceptationibus à se breviter exaratis De *Deo Vno existente*, De *Animorum immortalitate*; De *Virtute*, De *Officiis*, deque multis id genus aliis, quisquam compararit: is mehercule sentiet, utrae magis ad rectam puerorum institutionem, tùm ad Sacram Theologiam viam sternere, ac complanare queant. Profectò verò res ita se habet. Non enim recta puerorum Institutio, non vitae civilis officia, non scientia rerum naturae corporeae, non artes optimae (imò ne sutoria [PDF 17] quidem, quum illiberalissima omnium haberi soleat), non denique Sacra Theologia, ipsis iis nugis, quas supra commemoravimus, juvari augerive possunt. Desinant ergo Viri, alioquin gravissimi, totos dies noctesque consepultis *Summulis*, *Cathegorijs*, atque praecisae *Arbori Porphyrianae* illachrymari, quasi actum porrhò esset de republica, de se quoque liberisque suis, de aris atque focis. Quod perridiculum est, nec multâ tamen bile, sed pituitâ magis, hoc est, risu excipiendum. Quare ita censeo: nihil morari Patres Congregationis nostrae debere, ut volumina haec typis mandari sinant, quum & sanam, & utilem doctrinam Auctor diligentissimè undique excerptam, congesserit, explanárit: quod Juvenibus, qui apud nos Philosophiae operam dabunt, commodo atque emolumento fore, nullus equidem dubito. Dabam Michaelopoli X. Kal. Majas Ann. MDCCLXXIV.

At the bidding of the Congregation of San Miguel I have striven with all my might to read through, with the greatest attention I could, these two volumes whose title is Elements of the Newer Philosophy. I feared, however, lest I should judge of this work more from prejudice and from my esteem for its most distinguished Author (with whom I had long since begun to live in the closest intimacy) than by right and deservedly. But I frankly confess that I gave myself wholly to playing the part of a supercilious censor, not of a fulsome and shameless praiser. And so, after I had long and much considered what in the end I ought to write on this account and lay before the Conscript Fathers of our Family, behold, these few things came to mind, which will serve in place of a censure. First, indeed, that our countryman, Father Doctor Don Juan Benito, has hit the nail on the head, in that under the name of Philosophy he has brought together for the benefit of the young not an empty fallacy, by deceiving, but a doctrine of the first utility, by teaching. For these Elements [PDF 16] of the Newer Philosophy seem to me to embrace, with wonderful brevity and clarity, and likewise in wonderful order, whatever the English, the French, the Dutch, the Italians and the Spaniards, earnestly intent upon philosophical matters through long decades of years, have searched out. The young beginner will certainly find here a great many things duly treated which he would seek elsewhere in vain; unless, having grown older, he devotes himself strenuously for the rest of his life (which happens to very few indeed) to Philosophy and to books, of which we have no great supply. But if anyone should compare those little questions so often debated, On Prescissions, On the Being of Reason, On the Appetite of Matter, On the Categorematic Infinite, or others far emptier still, which the Author knowingly and prudently passed over, with the disquisitions he has briefly written out On God, One and Existing, On the Immortality of Souls, On Virtue, On Duties, and on many others of that kind: he will, by Hercules, perceive which of them are better able to pave and smooth the way both to the right instruction of boys and to Sacred Theology. And truly, so the matter stands. For neither the right Instruction of boys, nor the duties of civil life, nor the science of corporeal nature, nor the best arts (nay, not even the cobbler’s, [PDF 17] although it is commonly held the most illiberal of all), nor finally Sacred Theology, can be helped or increased by those very trifles which we have mentioned above. Let men, then, otherwise most grave, cease to weep whole days and nights over the burial of the Summulae and the Categories, and over the felled Porphyrian Tree, as though it were all over with the commonwealth, with themselves too and their children, with altars and hearths. This is most ridiculous, and is to be met not with much bile but rather with phlegm, that is, with laughter. Wherefore my opinion is this: that the Fathers of our Congregation ought in no way to hinder these volumes from being committed to the press, since the Author has most diligently excerpted from every side, compiled and explained a doctrine both sound and useful; and that it will be of advantage and profit to the young men who will apply themselves to Philosophy among us, I for my part in no way doubt. Given at San Miguel el Grande, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, in the Year mdcclxxiv.

> *Josephus Henriquez de Rivera.*

José Henríquez de Rivera.

> *PRAEPOSITVS, ET PRAESBYTERI DEPVTATI Congregationis Oratorii S. Philippi Nerii Municipii S. Michaëlis Michchuacanensis Dioeceseos in Nova Hispania.*

The Provost and the Deputy Priests of the Congregation of the Oratory of St. Philip Neri of the Town of San Miguel, of the Diocese of Michoacán, in New Spain.

> Quum ELEMENTA RECENTIORIS PHILOSOPHIAE ad usum Collegii Salesiani á P. D. D. *Johanne Benedicto Diaz de Gamarra & Davalos* nostrae Congregationis Presbytero Deputato, ac ejusdem Collegii Moderatore elaborata jussu nostro recognita sint, nihilque in illis reperiatur rectis moribus absonum, aut Fidei, Religioni, Regiisque sanctionibus adversum; quin potius regendis moribus, Fidei, & Religioni tuendae, ac demum Juventuti salubri utilique Philosophia erudiendae aptissima censeantur, facultatem concedimus, ut typis mandentur, si ita iis ad quos reliquum spectat, videbitur. In quorum fidem praesentes literas manu nostra subscriptas, & Sigillo nostrae Congregationis munitas jussimus expedire Michaëlopoli ex AEdibus Congregationis VI. Kal. Junii A. R. S. MDCCLXXIV.

Whereas the Elements of the Newer Philosophy, prepared for the use of the Salesian College by Father Don Juan Benito Díaz de Gamarra y Dávalos, Deputy Priest of our Congregation and Rector of the same College, have been examined by our order, and nothing is found in them out of harmony with right morals, or contrary to the Faith, to Religion and to the Royal Ordinances, but rather they are judged most apt for governing morals, for defending the Faith and Religion, and finally for instructing Youth in a wholesome and useful Philosophy, we grant permission that they be committed to the press, if it shall so seem good to those to whom the rest pertains. In witness whereof we have ordered these present letters, signed by our hand and fortified with the Seal of our Congregation, to be dispatched at San Miguel el Grande from the House of the Congregation, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, in the Year of Restored Salvation mdcclxxiv.

> CENSURA DOCTORUM ALMAE MEXICANAE ACADEMIAE, ET PATRUM GRAVISSIMORUM, QUI PHILOSOPHIAM, ET SACRAM THEOLOGIAM IN URBE MEXICO PROFITENTUR.

of   the    Illustrious       University      of Mexico, and of the Most Grave Fathers who profess Philosophy and Sacred Theology in the City of Mexico.

> Nos RECTOR, & infrascripti Doctores Patresque, Sacrae Theologiae, & Philosophiae Professores, fidem facimus, & adtestamur, haec RECENTIORIS PHILOSOPHIAE ELEMENTA á P. Doct. D. *Johanne Benedicto Diaz de Gamarra et Davalos* Congregationis Oratorii S. Philippi Nerii Presbytero Seculari, in usum Americanae nostrae Juventutis conscripta; non modò saniorem doctrinam, & ad mores informandos aptissimam, sed etiam selectiorem ex omnibus recentioris aevi Philosophis, complecti: ideoque post maturam rei cognitionem, judicavimus ê re Scholastica fore, ut [PDF 20] typis editum volumen Tyronibus in Philosophiae curriculo praestò sit, ad ea perdiscenda, quae hoc jam temporis ignorari, & controverti, sine dedecore & ignominia nequeunt. In quorum fidem & adtestationem propria quisque manu chartam signavimus.

We, the Rector and the undersigned Doctors and Fathers, Professors of Sacred Theology and of Philosophy, certify and attest that these Elements of the Newer Philosophy, written by the Rev. Father Dr. Don Juan Benito Díaz de Gamarra y Dávalos, Secular Priest of the Congregation of the Oratory of St. Philip Neri, for the use of our American Youth, contain not only a sounder doctrine, and one most apt for forming morals, but also a more select one, drawn from all the Philosophers of the more recent age; and therefore, after mature examination of the matter, we have judged that it will be to the advantage of the Schools that the volume, once printed, [PDF 20] be at hand for Beginners in the course of Philosophy, for thoroughly learning those things which at this time cannot be unknown, or disputed, without disgrace and ignominy. In faith and attestation whereof each of us has signed this paper with his own hand.

> ¶ N. B. Sapientissimorum Doctorum, Patrumque nomina eo demùm ordine conscripta sunt, quem Alma Mexican. Academia hactenus servavit, ut (salvâ Facultatum ac Scientiarum praecedentiâ) qui prior tempore fuerit, sit quoque jure & loco potior. Quod verò adtinet ad Sacras Ordinum Familias, idem omninò moris, quod in Disputationibus Academicis publicè servatur, retentum est. Fatemur interim, nonnullos praeclarissimos Viros, ob dignitatem, atque honoris decoramenta, alia aliis praestantiora, fortè aliter fuisse recensendos: quod nostrum non erat, nec verò temerè faciendum.

¶ N. B. The names of the most learned Doctors and Fathers have been written down in precisely that order which the Illustrious University of Mexico has hitherto observed, so that (saving the precedence of the Faculties and Sciences) he who is prior in time is also prior in right and in place. As for the Sacred Families of the Orders, exactly the same custom has been retained as is publicly observed in Academic Disputations. We acknowledge, meanwhile, that some most distinguished Men, on account of their dignity and their ornaments of honor, some more eminent than others, ought perhaps to have been listed otherwise: which was not ours to do, nor indeed a thing to be done rashly.

[PDF 24]

## JUVENTUTI AMERICANAE — To the Youth of America

> *Jo. Bened. Diaz Gamarra* S. vigiliasque.

Juan Benito Díaz de Gamarra sends greetings and his lucubrations.

> Vestra omnium res agitur, Juvenes ingenio praestantissimi, & praeter ceteras gentes ad Scientias comparati. Vestra nunc res agitur. Neque enim doctis ego Viris, qui se Philosophiam, qualem illam cunque biennii labore (nec admodùm improbo) adsequutos esse arbitrantur; neque verò iis haec conscripta volui, & nuncupata, qui totos dies ê suggestu Scholari tanquam ex trípode, de rebus multò difficillimis, non item multò sibi compertissimis [^PDF24-s1], pronunciant. Sed vobis, Juvenes, qui sacra haec primùm adoriemini, humanae Philosophiae, quî nihil jucundius esse potest, arcem, ubi aliquando tandem liceat, ingressuri.

Your cause, all of you, is at stake, young men of most excellent talent, fitted beyond other nations for the Sciences. It is your cause that is now at stake. For I did not wish these pages to be written for, or dedicated to, learned Men who think they have attained Philosophy, such as it is, by the labor of two years (and not very strenuous labor at that); nor to those who all day long pronounce from the School’s lectern, as from a tripod, on matters exceedingly difficult and not equally well known to themselves (*). But to you, young men, who are now for the first time approaching these sacred rites, and who are about to enter, when at length it may be allowed, the citadel of human Philosophy, than which nothing can be more delightful.

> [^PDF24-s1]: Cl. Melch. Cano Lib. VIII. de Loc. Theolog.

[^PDF24-s1]: The renowned Melchor Cano, bk. VIII of De locis theologicis.

> Vobis, magna Patriae spes, Recentioris Philosophiae Institutiones, brevissimè quidem hinc inde excerptas subjicio, longè alia daturus, benè multa, nisi adeò breve curriculum Scholae esset, quod de more vobis est percurrendum. Age verò, & quoniam [PDF 25] vestri gratiâ hoc muneris ac laboris susceptum est, quid scribendo praestiterim, aut saltem conatus fuerim, paucis accipite.

To you, great hope of our Country, I submit these Institutions of the Newer Philosophy, excerpted, very briefly indeed, from here and there; and I would give you far other things, and a good many of them, were the course of the Schools not so short, which by custom you must run through. But come, and since it was for your [PDF 25] sake that this task and labor were undertaken, hear in a few words what I have accomplished in writing, or at least have attempted.

> Principio enim, Philosophiae quam adgredimini, *Historiam*, breviusculè exaratam in ipso Institutionum limine, etiam atque etiam vobis commendo. Ipsam perlegite, volvite, meditamini, ac reputate cum animis vestris, quanti momenti futura sit ad Philosophiam ipsam rectè atque ordine perdiscendam. Nam ubi nescias, quid Philosophia sit, sub quibus Auctoribus nata, quousque apud majores nostros, & quo tandem in pretio habita, quae fata, qui progressus, quae via ratioque docendi; omninò fieri non potest quin passim turpiter erres. Cujus erroris genus non aliud magis, meâ quidem sententiâ, cavendum vitandumque est; quàm eorum, quibus hoc unum ad veram philosophiam refertur, quod pueri imberbesque ipsi didicerint; cetera pro nihilo ducunt, quasi vana fingentis aegri somnia essent. Quocirca meritò ridentur.

First of all, then, I commend to you again and again the History of the Philosophy you are entering upon, set down rather briefly at the very threshold of the Institutions. Read it through, turn it over, meditate on it, and weigh in your minds how important it will be for learning Philosophy itself thoroughly, correctly and in due order. For if you do not know what Philosophy is, under what Authors it was born, how far and in what esteem it was held among our forebears, what its fortunes were, what its progress, what its way and method of teaching, it cannot possibly be that you will not err shamefully at every turn. And no kind of error, in my opinion at least, is more to be guarded against and avoided than that of those for whom this alone counts as true philosophy, what they themselves learned as beardless boys; everything else they hold as nothing, as though it were the empty dreams of a sick man’s fancy. For which reason they are deservedly laughed at.

> Alios autem, & quidem plurimos hac tempestate, cùm Aristoteles, tùm vero quae [PDF 26] tanti Viri nomine (nam ultro fatemur, summum utique virum fuisse) vulgò in Scholis venditantur, adeò delectant, ut seriò adfirment, non aliud aptius commodiusve ad exacuenda puerorum ingeniola, & ad Sacram Theologiam dissertè atque eruditè tradendam inveniri unquam posse, quàm exercitamenta illa sempiterna, concertationes, logomachias *De Universalibus*, *De Ente rationis*, *De Formis substantialibus*; *De Unione*, *& toto Composito*, & sexcentis id genus aliis, quibus ingenia torquentur quidem, adteruntur; at timeo nè nihilo acutiora fiant ad sapientiae studium, & optimas disciplinas, quò nostra omnis vis ac cogitatio, tanquam ad scopum, collimare debet. ¿Ecquid autem, amabo, vanissima illa Mahumedanorum *Avicennae*, *Averrois*, *Alpharabii*, & reliquae Arabum turbae interpretamenta, ad veram religionem, ad Christi Ecclesiam, ad Sacram denique Theologiam emolumenti adferre poterunt? Scilicet venerandi Ecclesiae Patres, majores nostri, nunc apud Caelites Conscripti, *Dionysius Areopagita*, *Ephremus*; *Irenaeus*, *Cyprianus*, *Athanasius*, *Epiphanius*, *uterque Gregorius*, [PDF 27] *Chrysostomus*, *Basilius*, *Leo*, *Hilarius*, *Prosper*, *Ambrosius*, *Hieronymus*, *Augustinus*, non ipsi quoque aut Ecclesiam tutati sunt, aut de rebus Theologicis disseruere, aut prophanos novatores Haereticos profligârunt. Imo verò maximè: id enim aurea volumina testantur. Atqui frustra quisquam ibi Aristotelem requirat. Non quòd summi viri dialecticen & syllogismos ignorârint, aut penitus exulare jusserint, dum esset de rebus multò gravissimis agendum, disceptandumvè: id quod omninò temerè atque oscitanter factum (nec tamen ab iis factum) nos haudquaquam imitaremur, quippè quibus syllogismorum acumina non adeò displicent. Sed, ut ego arbitror, Pauli effato commonefacti, dum ait: *Videte, ne quis vos decipiat per philosophiam, & inanem fallaciam*, Sanctissimi Viri sanctè sibi tractanda omnia voluerunt, quae ad vitae sanctimoniam, & sempiternam beatitudinem, Deo revelante, pertinerent: à quibus profectò parum abest, quin tota Ethnicorum Philosophia abhorreat. Desinant ergo nobis aures obtundere, maledictis etiam nos nostraque lacerare, qui se non antè Sacram Theologiam [PDF 28] adgredi posse putant, quàm integras quaestiuncularum centurias in discrimen vocaverint. Nisi fortean ii (quod vehementer equidem suspicor, doleoque) non Sacram denique Theologiam, quae divina prorsus scientia est; sed Theologiae fumum atque umbram consectantur; nubem pro Junone amplexati, quod est in proverbio.

Others, however, and indeed very many in these times, are so delighted both by Aristotle and, above all, by what, under the name of so great [PDF 26] a Man (for we freely admit that he was certainly a very great man), is commonly peddled in the Schools, that they seriously affirm that nothing fitter or more convenient could ever be found for sharpening the little wits of boys, and for teaching Sacred Theology eloquently and learnedly, than those everlasting exercises, the disputes and logomachies On Universals, On the Being of Reason, On Substantial Forms, On the Union and the Whole Composite, and six hundred others of that kind, by which minds are indeed tortured and worn down; but I fear they grow no sharper for the pursuit of wisdom and for the best disciplines, at which all our strength and thought ought to aim, as at a target. And what profit, pray, will those utterly empty interpretations of the Mahometans Avicenna, Averroes, Alfarabi, and the rest of the Arab throng be able to bring to the true religion, to the Church of Christ, and finally to Sacred Theology? No doubt the venerable Fathers of the Church, our forebears, now Fathers Conscript among the dwellers in heaven, Dionysius the Areopagite, Ephrem, Irenaeus, Cyprian, Athanasius, Epiphanius, both Gregories, Chrysostom, [PDF 27] Basil, Leo, Hilary, Prosper, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, did not themselves also either defend the Church, or discourse on Theological matters, or rout the profane innovators, the Heretics. On the contrary, they did so above all: for their golden volumes bear witness to it. And yet one would look for Aristotle there in vain. Not that these very great men were ignorant of dialectic and syllogisms, or ordered them banished altogether when matters of the very gravest weight were to be treated or debated: a thing which, had it been done, would have been done quite rashly and heedlessly (yet it was not done by them), and which we would by no means imitate, since the subtleties of syllogisms do not so greatly displease us. But, as I judge, admonished by the saying of Paul, where he says: Beware lest any man cheat you by philosophy, and vain deceit, these most Holy Men resolved, in holiness, to treat all those things which pertain, by God’s revelation, to holiness of life and to everlasting beatitude: from which, assuredly, the whole Philosophy of the Heathen is all but alien. Let them cease, therefore, to deafen our ears, and even to tear us and ours to pieces with abuse, who think they cannot approach Sacred Theology [PDF 28] until they have called whole hundreds of petty questions into contest. Unless perhaps these men (as I strongly suspect, and grieve) are pursuing not, after all, Sacred Theology, which is an altogether divine science, but the smoke and shadow of Theology, having embraced a cloud for Juno, as the proverb has it.

> At enimvero, inquies, Divum Albertum cognomento Magnum, Divum Thomam Aquinatem, (ut nihil interim de Div. Johanne Damasceno) Divum quoque Bonamventuram, ceterosque recentioris aevi Theologos, Sapientissimos Viros, consilio, maturitate, moribus spectabiles, Petrum Lombardum, Scotum, Halesium, multos in disceptando fuisse, non operosas quaestiones, non syllogismos, non Aristotelem dedignatos: cui Philosopho auctoritatem plurimam quòd saepè tribuerint, non ideò tamen quasi inferioris subsellii Philosophos, ac minimè dissertos Theologos, tantos Viros jure quisquam reprehendat. ¿Nonnè compertissima haec sunt, & posita ante omnium oculos, meridie ipso clariora? Ajo. Sed quoniam ejus rei [PDF 29] tio incidit, circunspecto autem maturèque dicto opus est: rem, si placet, ordine persequamur.

But surely, you will say, St. Albert, surnamed the Great, St. Thomas Aquinas (to say nothing for the moment of St. John Damascene), St. Bonaventure too, and the other Theologians of the more recent age, Most Wise Men, admirable for counsel, maturity and character, Peter Lombard, Scotus, Alexander of Hales, were much given to disputation, and did not disdain laborious questions, nor syllogisms, nor Aristotle: and because they often attributed very great authority to this Philosopher, no one could rightly reproach such great Men on that account, as though they were Philosophers of a lower bench and Theologians of little eloquence. Are not these things most certain, and set before the eyes of all, clearer than noonday itself ? I grant it. But since mention of this matter [PDF 29] has come up, and it calls for circumspect and well-considered speech, let us, if you please, pursue the matter in order.

> Ad Divum Thomam quod adtinet, (nam de ceteris omnibus posteà dicendum) nemo unquam mortalium plura, nemo solertiùs, eruditiùs, temperatiùs, nemo breviùs omnia complexus est, quae ad Sacram Theologiam spectare, aut quoquo pacto referri posse viderentur. ¡Deus immortalis! quale Viro ingenium! quanta disceptandi copia! quàm adsidua, quàm multa in evolvendis Sacrae Paginae voluminibus diligentia! quàm fuit ille veritus Sanctos Ecclesiae Patres! quàm incredibile ac penè divinum ejus, cernendo difficillima, acumen illud mentis prorsùs Angelicae! quis in scribendo candor, quae docendo méthodus, severitas in judicando! Verè utique dixeris (id quod in re satis absimili Cicero prior dixerat) Divi Thomae Aquinatis libros, ac praesertim Summam illam Theologicam, omnium Theologorum bibliothecas, fremant omnes licet, & maximarum rerum ubertate, & auctoritatis róbore longè multumque superare. Plura enim Div. [PDF 30] Thomas immortali suâ & plusquàm Sallustianâ brevitate in rem Theologicam invexit, adprimè erudita, ac scitu dignissima, quàm plerique ceteri concupiverunt. Haec autem Divum Thomam *Theologum* egregia laus manet, manebitque quandiù scientiae honos erit. Quòd si interdum (nam eò, unde discesseram, redeo) Aristoteli auctoritatem tribuere disceptando solet, invitus quidem fecit, ubi de Sacra Doctrina ageretur. Nisi velis, summum Virum adeò hebetem ingenio, adeò etiam ineptum atque oscitantem fuisse, ut quae consultò in superioribus, *Art.* nimirum *VIII. Quaest.* I. statuerat, de minuenda omnium auctoritate praeterquam divinae revelationis, Apostolis & Prophetis factae, qui Canonicos Libros scripserunt; eadem postèa exemplo suo ipsemet, datâ operâ infirmaret. Sin verò de Divo Thoma, non Theologo, sed planè *Philosopho*, quaeritur, mementote, non jam Thomam illum Aquinatem Ecclesiae lumen atque ornamentum; sed Ethnicum (ex impio pium recens factum) Philosophum, nomine *Aristotelem*, negotium vobis facéssere, quod propemodùm [PDF 31] nullum erit. ¿Nam quotusquisque nescit, Angelicum Doctorem repurgâsse quidem Peripateticam Philosophiam, sexcentis passim erroribus commaculatam, ceterùm quod reliquum erat, non idcircò firmum, ratum, sanctum denique fore voluisse, nisi quod invicta ratio suadéret? ¿Ubinam ergo sunt, qui nos de oppugnato laesove Divo Thoma toties postulârunt? praepósteri homines, quibus satiùs multò fuisset strenuam operam in legendo Divum Thomam navâsse, quod minimè isti faciunt; quàm sedentibus otiosisque, per summam ignaviam, quae nè adtigére quidem, aut certe non adsequuntur, ludibrio, joco esse. Sed haec hactenus.

As for St. Thomas (for of all the others I must speak afterwards), no mortal ever embraced more, none more skillfully, more learnedly, more temperately, none more briefly, all the things that seemed to bear upon Sacred Theology, or could in any way be referred to it. Immortal God! what genius the Man had! what abundance in disputation! how constant, how great his diligence in unrolling the volumes of the Sacred Page! how he revered the Holy Fathers of the Church! how incredible and almost divine that acumen of his altogether Angelic mind in discerning the most difficult things! what candor in writing, what method in teaching, what severity in judging! You might truly say (as Cicero had said before, in a matter not very unlike) that the books of St. Thomas Aquinas, and especially that Theological Summa, though all should roar against it, far and greatly surpass the libraries of all the Theologians, both in the abundance of the greatest matters and in the strength of authority. For St. Thomas [PDF 30] brought into Theology, with his immortal and more than Sallustian brevity, more things, exceedingly learned and most worth knowing, than most others even desired. And this outstanding praise of St. Thomas as a Theologian remains, and will remain as long as learning is held in honor. But if at times (for I return to the point from which I had digressed) he is wont in disputing to attribute authority to Aristotle, he did so unwillingly indeed, where Sacred Doctrine was in question. Unless you would have it that so great a Man was so dull of wit, so inept too and heedless, that what he had deliberately laid down in the preceding pages, namely in Art. VIII of Quest. I, about diminishing the authority of all save that of divine revelation, made to the Apostles and Prophets who wrote the Canonical Books, he himself afterwards weakened on purpose by his own example. But if the question concerns St. Thomas not as Theologian but plainly as Philosopher, remember that it is not now that Thomas Aquinas, the light and ornament of the Church, but a Heathen Philosopher (lately made pious from impious), Aristotle by name, who is making trouble for you, a trouble which will amount to next to nothing. [PDF 31] For how few do not know that the Angelic Doctor did indeed purge the Peripatetic Philosophy, stained everywhere with six hundred errors, but that he did not on that account wish what remained to be firm, ratified, and in a word sacrosanct, except what unconquered reason urged? Where, then, are those who have so often arraigned us for attacking or injuring St. Thomas? Perverse men, for whom it would have been far better to have spent strenuous effort in reading St. Thomas, which is the last thing they do, than, sitting idle, out of utter sloth, to make a mockery and a jest of things they do not even touch, or at least do not grasp. But enough of this.

> Venio nunc ad reliqua: nimirùm Divi *Jo. Damascenus*, *Antoninus*, *Albertus*, *Bonaventura*: Doctores post hominum memoriam praeclarissimi, *Scotus*, *Halesius*, (nam Episcopo Parisiensi alia mens fuerat) neque quaestiones, hoc est, ancipites illas controversias multùm in Scholis agitari sólitas, neque syllogismos, neque Aristotelem aspernantur. ¿An verò nos aspernamur, aut disceptationibus Scholae bellum indicimus? [PDF 32] Profectò res ipsa loquitur: & nos quoque seculo nostro, Magistrisque, quorum magna apud nostrates existimatio est, morem gessimus, quaestiones, syllogismos, postremò Aristotelem ipsum, ubi rectè sápere visus erat, complexi; omnia tamen, pro viribus atque inertia nostra, sobriè, prudenter, temperatè. Nam vel ipsum brevitatis studium, quod omninò curae cordique esse debuit, nos, tametsi aliter, aut multò plura scribendi operae pretium foret, perstringere tamen calamum coëgisset, nè Juvenes tyrones nostros obrueremus.

I come now to the rest: namely Sts. John Damascene, Antoninus, Albert, Bonaventure, Doctors most illustrious within the memory of man, Scotus, Hales (for the Bishop of Paris had been of another mind), do not spurn questions, that is, those doubtful controversies much agitated in the Schools, nor syllogisms, nor Aristotle. And do we, then, spurn them, or declare war on the disputations of the School? Assuredly [PDF 32] the thing speaks for itself: we too have humored our age, and our Masters, who are held in great esteem among our countrymen, embracing questions, syllogisms, and finally Aristotle himself, where he seemed to judge rightly; but all of it, as far as our strength and our want of skill allowed, soberly, prudently, temperately. For the very pursuit of brevity, which ought to have been our whole care and concern, would have compelled us to restrain the pen, even had it otherwise been worth the trouble to write much more, lest we overwhelm our young recruits.

> Et quoniam satis multa hucusque praemisimus, tanquam vindicias nostras, ne quis (ut ferè fit) silentium in conscientiam duceret: superest, ut nonnihil de instituto operis nostri breviter subjungamus. Et primùm quidem philosophiam, non vulgarem, stylo paullulùm limatiori quàm vulgò traditur, exaratam, vobis exhibemus, eamque cùm arctissimè quàm fieri potuit, tùm etiam apertissimè, atque omnibus numeris absolutam: ut prodigio simile quiddam factum mihi, persuasum haberem, nisi pleraque omnia ex [PDF 33] optimis quibusque recentioris aevi Philosophis, magno labore, summâ item fide decerpsissem. *Quod unum* mihi jure tribuo, ratus, non mediocri vel ad id ipsum diligentiâ opus esse: proindè aliquammultam vos olim, Juvenes, gratiam, sin minus vivo, at saltim extincto relaturos. ¿Quid enim? Plus centum volumina, nec oscitanter tamen, evolvi, priusquam ad haec Elementa conscribenda manum admovérem. Oculis omnia circunspexi, diu noctuque chartis impallescere in animum induxi, quò Juventuti nostrae consúlerem. ¿Quid plura? Otium ego meum, [si quid reliqui D. O. M. facit adsiduè pro Christo Jesu laborantibus] dulcis Patriae domicilium; aes, grande satis, quod impensum mihi est; &, quod mortales pluris habere solent, famam, nominisque existimationem (quippè qui eversae Philosophiae, & avítae maiorum religionis reus apud imperitum vulgus agor); cuncta haec tanti profectò feci, ut maioris quidem, aut certè multò maximi, vestram institutionem ac disciplinam mihi faciendam putarem.

And since we have set forth enough so far, by way of our defense, lest anyone (as usually happens) should take our silence for a bad conscience, it remains for us to add briefly something about the plan of our work. And first, we present to you a philosophy that is not the common one, set down in a style a little more polished than that in which it is commonly taught, and that both as concisely as could be done and also as plainly as possible, and complete in every respect: so that I would be persuaded that I had done something like a marvel, had not nearly everything come from all the best [PDF 33] Philosophers of the newer age, culled with great labor and likewise with the utmost fidelity. This alone I rightly claim for myself, judging that no ordinary diligence was needed even for that very task: and therefore that you, young men, will one day render me no small thanks, if not while I live, then at least when I am dead. For what? I turned over more than a hundred volumes, and not carelessly either, before I set my hand to writing these Elements. I surveyed everything with my own eyes; I resolved to grow pale over papers day and night, so as to provide for our Youth. What more? My leisure [if God, Best and Greatest, leaves any to those who labor without rest for Christ Jesus], my home in my sweet Country; money, a sum large enough, which I have spent; and, what mortals are wont to hold dearer, my reputation and the good opinion of my name (since I am arraigned before the ignorant crowd as guilty of overthrowing Philosophy and the ancestral religion of our forefathers): all these I have valued, to be sure, but only so far as to judge that your instruction and training were to be held of greater worth, or rather by far the greatest.

> Verum enimverò recentiorem ipse [PDF 34] philosophiam adfero. ¿Quidni adferrem? At tota *haeretica est*, inquiunt, & ex imis Erebi Orcique sedibus dudùm excitata, nimirum qualem apud exteras gentes

But in truth, it is a newer philosophy that I myself [PDF 34] bring forward. And why should I not bring it forward? But it is wholly heretical, they say, and was long ago raised up from the lowest seats of Erebus and Orcus, such, namely, as is found among foreign nations, where

> *Ambubajárum collegia, pharmacopólae,*

The guilds of flute-girls, the quack-druggists,

> *Mendíci, mimae, balatrónes, hoc genus omne*, dum ingenio suo nimiùm indulgent, dum Christi Ecclesiam funditùs evertere moliuntur, quasi aliud quiddam agentes, cum *Schola Peripatetica* fidem ipsi ii orthodoxam, Christianam religionem, sanctissimos tot jam secula mores, corrumpunt, pessumdant, perditum eunt.

Beggars, actresses, buffoons, all that breed, while they indulge their own wit too freely, while they strive to overturn the Church of Christ from its foundations, as though about some other business, these very men, together with the Peripatetic School, corrupt, ruin and go about to destroy the orthodox faith, the Christian religion, and the morals held most holy for so many centuries now.

> ¿Itanè verò? O praeclaros, vigilantes, egregios Ecclesiae custodes! Scilicet, quem vos pro deo philosophiae colitis, *Aristóteles* [?], is denique orthodoxus erat, is pietate ac religione insignis. ¿Sed quid adtinet nunc de his plura? Suam quisque ferè tuetur philosophiam, à maioribus acceptam, tanquam deos aliquos penates, quos oppugnari, vinci, diripi, acerbissimè doleat.

Is it so indeed? O splendid, watchful, excellent guardians of the Church! Of course Aristotle, whom you worship as the god of philosophy, was orthodox after all, he was outstanding in piety and religion. But what is the point of saying more about these things now? Each man, as a rule, defends his own philosophy, received from his forebears, as if it were some household gods, and would grieve most bitterly to see them attacked, conquered, plundered.

> Vos igitur, Juvenes, moneo obtestorque, ne quis vestrûm ab incoepto harum Institutionum & recentioris Philosophiae [PDF 35] curriculo pedem referre velit, neu patiatur sibi fucum ab imperitis fieri, qui rectam docendi discendique viam cane peius & angue perhorrescunt, fugiunt, aversantur, nè latum unguem à prisca Scholae consuetudine discedere ausi: quasi religio iis esset cum antiquioribus praejudicatò errare malle quàm cum aliis vera sentire [^PDF35-s1], aut denique verosimillimis [PDF 36] adquiescere, ubi veriora praestò non erunt. Cujus farinae obtrectatores, quaerulos, difficiles, leviores etiam quàm sibi fingere quisquam posset subacti ingenii viros, quos neque in arundine equitare, neque nuces, & par impar delectet: hos, inquam, ne auditóte. Putidi enim vanique sunt.

I warn and adjure you, therefore, young men, that none of you, from the course once begun of these Institutions and of the newer Philosophy, [PDF 35] be willing to draw back his foot, nor let himself be imposed upon by the ignorant, who dread the right way of teaching and learning worse than a dog or a snake, shun it, turn away from it, not daring to depart a nail’s breadth from the ancient custom of the School: as though it were a point of religion with them to prefer erring, by prejudgment, with the ancients to thinking the truth with others [*], or, in short, to acquiesce in the most probable [PDF 36] where truer things will not be at hand. Detractors of this stamp, querulous, difficult, more frivolous even than anyone could imagine men of mature mind to be, whom riding on a reed, and nuts, and odd-and-even no longer delight: these, I say, do not listen to. For they are tiresome and empty.

> [^PDF35-s1]: Praeclariss. Doctor nostras trienniò antè in lucem edidit Librum, cui titulum fecerat La Logica de D. Andres Piquer, ubi adeò multus est in reprehendendo (acerbè satis, ne dicam jejunè atque ineptè) quoscunque unquàm legerit Recentiores, ut propè fúrere ipsum dixeris, non ratiocinari. Verulamium, Arnaldum, Cartesium, Gassendum, Mallebranchium, Lockium, Heineccium, Wolffium, Genuensem, Verneyum, sus deque habet, quasi rem Logicam ipsi non auxerint, sed perfunctoriè modo tractaverint. Unus Aristoteles magnus & clarus existimatur, post quem unus Piquerus Logices praecepta tradidit; ceteri meras nugas, & quae ad rem minimè pertinebant, saepius inculcavere. Tanta profectò erat Clariss. viri philautia, (ipse autem more suo dicat, quae sit Latinè, Graecè, Hispanè, ejus vocabuli potestas) & praeconcepta vetustatis opinio, ut venerandum illum Senem, aevi nunc senescentis atque Hispaniae nostrae ornamentum, fato suo recens functum excitârit, P. Bened. Hieronymum Feijoó, quem eo nomine tráducit, quòd Recentiores ex antè nominatis quosdam sine discrimine laudâsset.

[^PDF35-s1]: A most distinguished Doctor, a countryman of ours, three years ago brought to light a Book to which he had given the title La Lógica de D. Andrés Piquer, in which he is so prolix in censuring (harshly enough, not to say jejunely and ineptly) whatever Moderns he has ever read, that you would almost say he raves rather than reasons. Bacon, Arnauld, Descartes, Gassendi, Malebranche, Locke, Heineccius, Wolff, Genovesi, Verney he holds of no account, as if they had not advanced Logic themselves but only treated it perfunctorily. Aristotle alone is esteemed great and famous, after whom Piquer alone handed down the precepts of Logic; the rest have all too often inculcated mere trifles, and things not at all to the point. So great indeed was the most distinguished man’s philautia (let him tell us himself, in his usual way, what the force of that word is in Latin, Greek and Spanish), and his preconceived opinion in favor of antiquity, that he has roused that venerable Old Man, the ornament of our now aging century and of our Spain, lately gone to his fate, Fr. Benito Jerónimo Feijóo, whom he holds up to ridicule on the ground that he had praised some of the Moderns named above without discrimination.

> Quòd si postremo id loco nobis objecerint, frustrà in lucem haec decerpta nostra edi in gratiam Juventutis, quum aliae Institutiones non desint, antehac typis evulgatae: ostendant ij, quaeso, ubinam tandem reperire sit (quod diu multumque quaesivimus) doctrinam recentiorem, more ab Scholis omninò non abhorrente, & cùm brevissimè traditam tùm planam illam satis, apertam, ordine congestam, adornatam, atque (id quod maximum est) utilem futuram in reliqua vita [^PDF36-s1].

But if, finally, they object to us that it is useless for these extracts of ours to be published for the benefit of Youth, since other Institutions, already made public in print, are not lacking: let them show, I beg, where at length one may find (what we have long and much sought) a newer doctrine, in a manner not at all at odds with the Schools, and both very briefly delivered and also sufficiently plain, open, arranged in order, adorned, and (what matters most) likely to be useful in the rest of life (*).

> [^PDF36-s1]: Agitur enim hîc de Dei Existentia, de Animorum immortalitate: refelluntur religionis hostes infensissimi Materialistae, Deistae, Fatalistae &c: traduntur Geometrica, Ethica, Psychologica: postremò nihil deesse videtur, quod jure quisquam requirat, ex iis, quae ad Juvenum institutionem pertinebunt.

[^PDF36-s1]: For here the subjects treated are the Existence of God and the Immortality of Souls; the most bitter enemies of religion, the Materialists, Deists, Fatalists, etc., are refuted; Geometry, Ethics, Psychology are taught: in short, nothing seems to be lacking that anyone could rightly require, of the things that will pertain to the instruction of Youth.

[PDF 37]

> Dolendum verò mihi est, hasce meas Institutiones, minutioribus, neque tamen paribus & concinnis typis editum iri: quod ob typographicae rei inopiam in hoc terrarum orbe, & temporis angustias, invito ac reluctanti contigerit. Vos autem facilè ignoscetis, non culpae quidem, sed quòd deforme quiddam atque absurdum volumina praeseferant; accuratiora, emendatiora, pulchriora in dies, si Superis placet, expectantes, quae polliceor equidem vobis.

It grieves me, though, that these Institutions of mine are to be printed in type that is smaller, and yet neither uniform nor elegant: a thing that has befallen me against my will and to my reluctance, owing to the poverty of the printing trade in this part of the world and to the shortness of time. But you will readily forgive, not a fault indeed, but the fact that the volumes display something unsightly and awkward, looking forward to more accurate, more correct, more handsome ones from day to day, if it please the Powers above, which I for my part promise you.

> Pergite verò, Juvenes, ut coepistis, & ampliss. Domino Praesuli nostro Michchuacanensi D. Ludovico Ferdinando de Hoyos et Mier grates quàm potestis maximas unà mecum rependite: quòd munificentissimâ erga nos benivolentiâ singulari studiorum rationem in hoc Perillustri Colleg. Salesiano etiam atque etiam diligenter habendam, in animum suspiciendus Vir suum, celsum quidem, & ad optima quaevis paratissimum, induxerit: quòd recentioris philosophiae Institutiones, vobis jam pridem â me traditas é suggestu Academico nostro, non probârit modò, verum etiam laudando concelebraverit: quodque [PDF 38] humanissimè exceptos me vosque clientes, ac dulciori vocabulo filios, paternâ caritate, & semper summopere expetendâ benedictione prosequatur. Faxit Deus O. M. ut Ecclesiae nostrae bono atque ornamento quàm diutissimè praesit. Dabam Mexici, ubi edendis per typos Institutionibus totus incumbebam, a. d. Calend. Septembres, anno Domini

Go on, then, young men, as you have begun, and together with me render the greatest thanks you can to our most illustrious Lord Prelate of Michoacán, Don Luis Fernando de Hoyos y Mier: because, with most munificent benevolence toward us, he, a Man to be looked up to, brought his mind, lofty indeed and most ready for every good thing, to take singular and ever more diligent care of the order of studies in this Most Illustrious College of St. Francis de Sales; because he not only approved the Institutions of the newer philosophy, long since delivered to you by me from our Academic chair, but even celebrated them with praise; and because, most kindly [PDF 38] received me and you as his clients, or, by a sweeter name, his sons, he attends us with fatherly charity and with a blessing ever most earnestly to be sought. May God, Best and Greatest, grant that he preside over our Church, for its good and its ornament, as long as may be. Given at Mexico, where I was wholly taken up with seeing the Institutions through the press, on the —— day before the Kalends of September, in the year of the Lord

> CIↃ IↃ CCLXXIV.

ciↄ iↄ cclxxiv.

> ¶ *N. B. Orthographicam rationem eam ferè secuti sumus, quàm viri Eruditissimi* Heineccius, Verneyusque *cùm praeceptionibus saepè tùm saepius exemplis magis probavére. Quod ideò animadversum volumus, nè quis arbitretur, novandi studio id praestitum á nobis fuisse. Typographicos aerores (si qui supersunt) posteriores curae, quum recudendi operis copia erit, emendabunt.* [PDF 39] ## HISTORIAE

¶ N. B. We have for the most part followed that system of spelling which the most Learned men Heineccius and Verney commended, often by precepts and more often still by examples. We wished this to be noted so that no one may think it was done by us out of a love of novelty. Typographical errors (if any remain) later care will correct, when there is opportunity to reprint the work.                              HISTORY [PDF 39]

## HISTORIAE — HISTORY

## PHILOSOPHIAE — OF PHILOSOPHY

## EPITOME. — IN EPITOME

> §. I.

§. I.

> *Philosophiae origo & progressus á mundo condito usque ad Christi D. adventum.*

The origin and progress of Philosophy from the creation of the world to the coming of Christ our Lord.

> 1 Philosophia idem sonat ac Studium, seu amor sapientiae. „Sapientia autem est (uti ex veterum sententia loquitur Tullius [^1-s1]), „rerum divinarum, & humanarum, causarumque, quibus hae res continentur scientia. In Philosophia namque, res cùm ad Deum, tùm ad alia extra Deum posita, pertinentes, rationis naturalis adminiculo scilicèt, exiguntur, causae quoque earundem ex principiis aut certis omninò, aut verosimilimis admodùm concinna, atque suis è legibus perfecta consecutione ducuntur. Ipsam hanc qui expetunt, *Philosophi* nominantur, adpellatione jam inde à Pithagorae modesto responsò studiosiùs retenta, ut postea dicemus.

hilosophy means the same as Study, or Love of Wisdom. “Wisdom, 1 P moreover, is (as Tully says, following the opinion of the ancients (a)) the knowledge of things divine and human, and of the causes by which these things are held together.” For in Philosophy, things pertaining both to God and to other things placed outside God are examined, namely with the help of natural reason, and their causes are derived, by a well-ordered consequence complete according to its own laws, from principles either altogether certain or highly probable. Those who seek it are named Philosophers, a name retained all the more carefully ever since the modest answer of Pythagoras, as we shall say later.

> [^1-s1]: Lib. 2. de Offic.

[^1-s1]: Bk. 2 of On Duties.

> 2 Philosophiam ab Omnipotenti Deo numeris omnibus absolutam sine ullo labore accepisse dicitur primus hominum parens Adamus. Sed quum ob violatam Dei legem (ait Purchotius [^1-s2]) [p. 2] ab eo, in quo positus erat, deliciarum horto fuisset expulsus, inter ceteras peccati poenas, quibus obnoxius esse coepit, ignorantiae tenebris traditus, in eas posteritatem secum traxit omnem. Quare nulla propemodùm excellentis illius, caelestisque doni in hominum animis vestigia supererant, quum nonnulli, excussâ ceterorum socordiâ, rerum pulcherrimarum admiratione commoti, & frequenti effectuum singularium observatione, quae *experientia* dicitur, edocti, eam à fundamentis instaurare omni ope ac studio sunt adgressi.

2 Adam, the first parent of mankind, is said to have received from Almighty God, without any labor, a Philosophy complete in every respect. But when, as Purchot says (b), for violating the law of God he [p. 2] had been expelled from the garden of delights in which he had been placed, then, given over to the darkness of ignorance among the other penalties of sin to which he became subject, he dragged all his posterity with him into that darkness. Hence almost no traces of that excellent and heavenly gift remained in men’s minds, when some, shaking off the sloth of the rest, moved by admiration of the most beautiful things and taught by frequent observation of particular effects, which is called experience, set about restoring it from its foundations with every effort and zeal.

> [^1-s2]: In Praef. ad suas Instit. Philos. ex qua nonnulla quae ad hanc primam Hist. Philosoph. partem spectant, paucis immutatis excerpsimus, uti & reliqua ex operibus Brukerii, Stanlei, Klausi, aliorumque.

[^1-s2]: In the Preface to his Institutiones Philosophicae, from which we have excerpted, with a few changes, some things that pertain to this first part of the History of Philosophy, as also the rest from the works of Brucker, Stanley, Klausius and others.

> 3 Id autem ferè apud omnes constat, scientiae naturalis, liberaliumque artium studium in Graecia potissimùm viguisse, sed quod ait Diogenes Laertius in Proemio ad vitas Philosophorum, Philosophiam in Graecia natam esse, non secùs ac homines ipsos, à vero prorsùs est alienum. Nam ut omittam quod ait Josephus [^2-s1] Sethi nepotes Caelorum ordinem, ac siderum cursus observasse: „neve inventa sua ex hominum notitia dilaberentur, quum Adamus generalem Mundi interitum, unum incendio, diluvio alterum praedixisset, duas excitasse columnas, alteram lateritiam, alteram lapideam, & utrique sua inventa insculpsisse, ut si lateritia diluvio periret, superstes esset lapidea, quae hominibus discendi copiam faceret“: Ut haec; inquam, omittam; quae vulgò nota sunt: (quamquam Ethnicis magna ex parte fuerint ignota) nemo sanè inficias ibit, Hebraeorum Patriarchas ac duces, ut Abrahamum, Mosen, & alios, rerum naturalium scientiâ fuisse informatos, non secus ac Salomonem Judaeorum Regem, qui, ut testantur Sacrae Literae [^2-s2], „disputavit super lignis à cedro, quae est in libano, usque ad hyssopum, quae egreditur de pariete, & disseruit de jumentis, & volucribus, & reptilibus, & piscibus.“ Illud insuper ipsorum Ethnicorum testimonio certum est, Assyrios, & Chaldaeos in Astronomia cum laude fuisse versatos, invitante scilicèt eos plana patentique regione, quam incolebant, ex qua siderum cursus liberè observare poterant. Hinc Tullius [^2-s3] Chaldaeos cognitione astrorum, solertiâque ingeniorum antecelluisse memorat.

3 It is agreed among nearly all, moreover, that the study of natural science and of the liberal arts flourished above all in Greece; but what Diogenes Laertius says in the Proem to the Lives of the Philosophers, that Philosophy was born in Greece just as men themselves were, is altogether foreign to the truth. For, to pass over what Josephus says (c), that the grandsons of Seth observed the order of the Heavens and the courses of the stars, “and, lest their discoveries should slip out of men’s knowledge, since Adam had foretold a general destruction of the World, the one by fire, the other by flood, set up two columns, one of brick, the other of stone, and carved their discoveries on both, so that if the brick one should perish in the flood, the stone one would survive and give men the means of learning”: to pass over these things, I say, which are commonly known (although they were for the most part unknown to the Heathen), no one will indeed deny that the Patriarchs and leaders of the Hebrews, such as Abraham, Moses and others, were instructed in the science of natural things, just like Solomon, King of the Jews, who, as the Sacred Scriptures testify (d), “treated about trees from the cedar that is in Libanus, unto the hyssop that cometh out of the wall: and he discoursed of beasts, and of fowls, and of creeping things, and of fishes.” This moreover is certain from the testimony of the Heathen themselves, that the Assyrians and Chaldeans were laudably versed in Astronomy, invited, namely, by the flat and open region they inhabited, from which they could freely observe the courses of the stars. Hence Tully (e) records that the Chaldeans excelled in the knowledge of the stars and in the shrewdness of their minds.

> [^2-s1]: Lib. 1. Antiq. Judaic. c. 3.

[^2-s1]: Bk. 1 of the Jewish Antiquities, ch. 3.

> [^2-s2]: Lib. III. Reg. cap. 4.

[^2-s2]: Bk. III of Kings, ch. 4.

> [^2-s3]: De Divinat. Lib. 1.

[^2-s3]: On Divination, bk. 1.

> 4 Ab Assyriis, autem, & Chaldaeis, teste Josepho [^2-s4] Arithmetica per Abrahamum translata est ad AEgyptios, qui necessitate compulsi Geometriae pariter studuerunt: quoniam per anniversariam Nili inundationem, ut Proclus refert, agrorum termini apud illos sic turbarentur, ut discerni postea sine Geometria non possent.

4 From the Assyrians and Chaldeans, moreover, as Josephus witnesses (f), Arithmetic was carried by Abraham to the Egyptians, who, compelled by necessity, likewise studied Geometry: since, as Proclus reports, the boundaries of their fields were so confounded by the annual flooding of the Nile that they could not afterwards be distinguished without Geometry.

> [^2-s4]: Antiquit. Judaicar. cap. 9.

[^2-s4]: Jewish Antiquities, ch. 9.

> 5 Tandem ab AEgyptiis ad Phoenices simul, & ad Graecos [p. 3] trajecto mari, delata est Geometria; quam videlicet in AEgypto didicit Thales Milesius, & in Graeciam intulit, ut narrat ipse Diogenes Laertius in ejus vita.

5 Finally, from the Egyptians, at once to the Phoenicians and to the Greeks across the [p. 3] the sea, Geometry was carried; which Thales of Miletus, namely, learned in Egypt and brought into Greece, as Diogenes Laertius himself narrates in his life.

> 6 Itaque non Graecis solis acceptam referre debemus Philosophiam; sed quemadmodum apud eos extitére viri ingenio, & rerum naturalium cognitione praecellentes qui *Sapientes* primùm, postea *Philosophi* sunt adpellati: ita ceteris quoque nationibus sui fuerunt veritatis interpretes, ac doctores; Hebraeis quidem *Rabbini*, Babylonis, & Assyriis *Chaldaei*; Persis *Magi*; Indis *Brachmanes*, seu *Gymnosophistae*; imò & in extremis Orientis oris apud *Sinas* fuere disciplinarum humanarum, & liberalium Artium cultores, in quibus maximè celebratur *Confucius*, qui ideò *Sinensis Philosophus* adpellatur. Item apud AEgyptios *Hierophantae*, apud Gallos *Druidae* floruerunt.

6 Therefore we must not credit Philosophy to the Greeks alone: but just as among them there arose men excelling in ingenuity and in the knowledge of natural things, who were first called Wise Men, afterwards Philosophers, so the other nations too had their own interpreters and teachers of truth: among the Hebrews, indeed, the Rabbis; of Babylon and Assyria, the Chaldeans; among the Persians, the Magi; among the Indians, the Brahmans, or Gymnosophists; nay, even on the shores of the farthest East, among the Chinese, there were cultivators of the human disciplines and of the liberal Arts, among whom Confucius is most celebrated, who is therefore called the Chinese Philosopher. Likewise among the Egyptians the Hierophants flourished, and among the Gauls the Druids.

> 7 Praecipua autem Philosophiae gloria Graecis ideo tribuitur, quòd ii diligentiùs incubuerint in singulas illius partes, eamque in quoddam veluti corpus digestam Scriptis suis ad posteros transmiserint. Quamobrem illustriores Philosophorum sectae, de quibus mentio fit in Scholis, á Graecis sunt repetendae.

7 The chief glory of Philosophy, however, is attributed to the Greeks because they applied themselves more diligently to each of its parts, and, having arranged it as it were into a kind of body, handed it down to posterity in their Writings. Wherefore the more illustrious sects of Philosophers, of which mention is made in the Schools, are to be traced back to the Greeks.

> §. II.

§. II.

> *Illustriores Philosophorum Sectae.*

The More Illustrious Sects of Philosophers. 8

> 8 Secta autem est quaedam hominum multitudo quae ab aliis quodammodò *secta* & divisa certum doctrinae genus sub aliquo Duce *sectatur*. Hinc vel à *secando*, vel à *sectando* nominata est *secta*.

A sect, moreover, is a certain multitude of men which, in some way cut off and divided from others, follows a certain kind of doctrine under some Leader. Hence it was named secta either from secando [cutting] or from sectando [following].

> 9 Porrhò primi Graecorum Philosophi in duas sectas dividuntur, scilicet in *Dogmaticam*, & *Academicam*.

9 Further, the first Philosophers of the Greeks are divided into two sects, namely the Dogmatic and the Academic.

> 10 Secta Dogmatica eos comprehendit Philosophos, qui veritatem adsecutos esse se, saltem in pluribus, contendunt: quae iterum duplex est, *Jonica*, & *Italica*.

10 The Dogmatic sect comprises those Philosophers who contend that they have attained the truth, at least in most things; and it is in turn twofold, the Ionic and the Italic.

> 11 Ionicae sectae dux fuit Thales, dictus Milesius, sive quia Miletum, quae Urbs est Ioniae caput, patriam habuit; sive quia quum ex Phaenicia oriundus esset, inter Cives Milesios, ut quidam tradunt, fuit adscriptus. Ipsum anno primo Olympiadis 35. natum esse memorat Apollodorus apud Diogenem Laertium in ejus vita, mortuum verò anno aetatis septuagesimo. Annus autem ille primus Olympiadis 35. est 639. ante aeram vulgarem Christianorum, & à mundo condito 3365. [^3-s1] Thaletem sectati sunt Anaximander, [p. 4] Anaximenes, Anaxagoras, Xenophanes, Heraclítus, Demócritus, & alii, qui omnes praeceptoris sui Philosophiam illustrarunt, & ad Socratem usque, ac Platonem perduxerunt.

11 The leader of the Ionic sect was Thales, called the Milesian, either because he had as his native city Miletus, which is the capital City of Ionia, or because, although he was of Phoenician origin, he was enrolled, as some relate, among the Citizens of Miletus. Apollodorus, in Diogenes Laertius’s life of him, records that he was born in the first year of the 35th Olympiad, and died in the seventieth year of his age. That first year of the 35th Olympiad, moreover, is the year 639 before the common era of the Christians, and 3365 from the founding of the world. (*) Thales was followed by Anaximander, [p. 4] Anaximenes, Anaxagoras, Xenophanes, Heraclitus, Democritus, and others, all of whom made the Philosophy of their master illustrious, and carried it down as far as Socrates and Plato.

> [^3-s1]: Olympias spatium est quatuor annorum. Olympias prima celebrata est anno mundi 3250.

[^3-s1]: An Olympiad is a space of four years. The first Olympiad was celebrated in the year of the world 3250.

> 12 Italicae princeps fuit Pythagoras Samius, qui quum Pherecydis Syri fuisset discipulus, ac AEgyptum & Babyloniam doctrinae comparandae gratia perlustrasset, tandem recepit se in Italiam, tempore Servii Tullii Romanorum Regis; & Crotone non longe à Tarento Philosophiae per annos circiter viginti operam navavit; indeque postea Metapontum profectus, testante Justino [^4-s1], diem ibi supremum obit anno 4 Olympiadis 70. Ab eo primùm Philosophi nomen usurpatum est. Quippe quum per Peloponnesum transiens interrogatus esset à Leonte *Sicyoniorum*, vel *Phliasiorum* Tyranno (erant autem *Sicyon*, & *Phlius* urbes Peloponnesi) quem se profiteretur: respondit se Philosophum esse, hoc est, Sapientiae studiosum; modestiore scilicet, adpellatione usus, inquit Diogenes Laertius in Proemio ad vitas Philosophorum, ut retunderet fastum ac superbiam Graecorum, qui se *Sapientes* praedicabant: quia solus Deus vere Sapiens dici potest; homines verò potius Sapientiae amatores sunt nominandi, quàm Sapientes.

12 The chief of the Italic sect was Pythagoras of Samos, who, having been a disciple of Pherecydes the Syrian, and having traveled through Egypt and Babylonia for the sake of acquiring learning, at length betook himself to Italy, in the time of Servius Tullius, King of the Romans; and at Croton, not far from Tarentum, he devoted himself to Philosophy for about twenty years; and having afterwards gone from there to Metapontum, as Justin testifies (g), he died there in the 4th year of the 70th Olympiad. By him the name of Philosopher was first used. For when, passing through the Peloponnese, he was asked by Leon, Tyrant of the Sicyonians, or of the Phliasians (Sicyon and Phlius, moreover, were cities of the Peloponnese), what he professed himself to be, he answered that he was a Philosopher, that is, one devoted to Wisdom; using, namely, a more modest appellation, says Diogenes Laertius in the Proem to the Lives of the Philosophers, in order to beat down the arrogance and pride of the Greeks, who proclaimed themselves Wise Men: because God alone can truly be called Wise, whereas men are rather to be named lovers of Wisdom than Wise.

> [^4-s1]: Lib. XX. Historiar. cap. 4.

[^4-s1]: Bk. XX of the Histories, ch. 4.

> 13 Pythagorae dogmata inter ceteros amplexi sunt *Timaeus* Locrensis, *Archytas* Tarentinus, *Philolaus* Crotoniata, *Parmenides*, & *Zeno* ambo Eleatae, quorum hic Dialecticae auctor dicitur á Diogene Laertio, ac *Melissus* Samius: qui omnes Physicae seu naturali scientiae praecipuam dederunt operam ad institutionem usque veteris Academiae, cujus Princeps fuit Socrates: quo tempore Philosophi animum á rebus Physicis ad morum scientiam Socratis exemplo converterunt.

13 Among others, the doctrines of Pythagoras were embraced by Timaeus of Locri, Archytas of Tarentum, Philolaus of Croton, Parmenides and Zeno, both of Elea, the latter of whom is called the author of Dialectic by Diogenes Laertius, and Melissus of Samos: all of whom gave their chief attention to Physics, or natural science, right up to the institution of the old Academy, whose Chief was Socrates; at which time the Philosophers, following the example of Socrates, turned their minds from Physical things to the science of morals.

> 14 Secta Academica nomen suum desumpsit ab *Academia* hoc est a loco nemoroso in suburbio Athenarum sito, quem heros nobilis, *Academus* nomine, Philosophorum exercitationibus consecrarat. Hujus sectae Philosophi adsensum omnem cohibebant: nihil omnino adfirmabant: ipsaque rursus in veterem, mediam, & novam Academiam fuit divisa.

14 The Academic sect took its name from the Academy, that is, from a wooded place situated in a suburb of Athens, which a noble hero, Academus by name, had consecrated to the exercises of the Philosophers. The Philosophers of this sect withheld all assent; they affirmed nothing whatever: and the sect itself was in turn divided into the old, the middle, and the new Academy.

> 15 Veteris Academiae Principes fuere *Socrates*, & ejus discipulus *Plato*. Unde veteres Academici, iidem Platonici dicti sunt, ut & *Sceptici* seu Inquisitores: quod licet ignotam esse veritatem arbitrarentur, de ea tamen invenienda non desperarent; ideoque ejus inquisitioni constanter vacarent. *Pyrrhonici* quoque vocati sunt, à *Pyrrhone* Academico.

15 The Chiefs of the old Academy were Socrates and his disciple Plato. Hence the old Academics were called by the same token Platonists, and also Sceptics, or Inquirers: because, although they judged truth to be unknown, they nevertheless did not despair of finding it, and therefore devoted themselves constantly to the inquiry after it. They were also called Pyrrhonists, from Pyrrho, an Academic.

> 16 Socrates in Attica natus est anno 4. Olympiadis 77. Secundum Diogenem Laertium in ejus vita: hoc est anno mundi juxta calculum Usserianum 3536. Mortuus verò ann. 1 Olympiadis 95. aetatis septuagesimo. „Primus ille à rebus occultis, (*ut ait Cic.*) [^4-s2] & ab ipsa natura involutis, in quibus omnes ante eum [p. 5] Philosophi occupati fuerant, avocavit Philosophiam, & ad vitam communem adduxit, ut de virtutibus, & vitiis, omninoque de bonis rebus, & malis quaereret: caelestia autem vel procul esse á nostra cognitione censeret, vel si maximè cognita essent, nihil tamen ad benè vivendum conferre. Hic in omnibus ferè sermonibus, qui ab iis, qui illum audierunt, perscripti varie, & copiosè sunt, ita disputabat, ut nihil adfirmaret ipse, refelleret alios, nihil se scire diceret, nisi id ipsum.

16 Socrates was born in Attica in the 4th year of the 77th Olympiad, according to Diogenes Laertius in his life; that is, in the year of the world 3536 according to Ussher’s calculation. He died, however, in the 1st year of the 95th Olympiad, in the seventieth year of his age. “It was he who first, from things hidden (as Tully says (h)) and wrapped up by nature herself, in which, before him, all [p. 5] the Philosophers had been occupied, called Philosophy away and brought it to common life, so that it should inquire about virtues and vices, and in general about good and evil things; and he held that heavenly things were either far removed from our knowledge, or, even if they were known as fully as possible, still contributed nothing to living well. In nearly all the discourses which were written down, variously and copiously, by those who heard him, he disputed in such a way that he affirmed nothing himself, refuted others, and said that he knew nothing, except that very thing.”

> [^4-s2]: Academic. quaest. Lib. 1.

[^4-s2]: Academic Questions, bk. 1.

> 17 Operam Socrati dedere Crito, Aristippus, Cebes, Xenophon, Euclides, &c. Sed inter eos omnes eminebat Plato Atheniensis, qui & Socrati in Academia successit, ejusque methodo insistens nihil adfirmabat, sed, ut ait idem Tullius[^5-s1] ,, multa in ejus libris in utramque partem disseruntur, de omnibus quaeritur, nihil certi dicitur ,,. Plato autem discipulum inter ceteros habuit Aristotelem Peripateticae sectae postea Principem, & sibi adversarium.

17 Crito, Aristippus, Cebes, Xenophon, Euclid and others were followers of Socrates. But among them all Plato the Athenian was eminent, who also succeeded Socrates in the Academy and, keeping to his method, affirmed nothing, but, as the same Tully says (i), “in his books many things are argued on both sides, everything is inquired into, nothing certain is said.” Plato, moreover, had among his other disciples Aristotle, afterwards the Chief of the Peripatetic sect, and his own adversary.

> [^5-s1]: Loco sup. citat.

> 18 Post mortem Platonis, & Speusippi, ceteri Socratis successores in Academia timidam illam Philosophandi methodum abjecere; & in Dogmaticorum partes translati triplicem constituere Sectam, *Peripateticorum*, *Stoicorum*, & *Epicureorum*.

18 After the death of Plato and of Speusippus, the other successors of Socrates in the Academy cast off that timid method of philosophizing; and, having passed over to the party of the Dogmatics, they established a threefold Sect, that of the Peripatetics, of the Stoics, and of the Epicureans.

> 19 Peripatetici praeceptore gloriantur Aristotele. Hic natus Stagyrae opido Macedoniae circa annum mundi 3621 scilicet anno primo Olympiadis 99, patre Nicomacho, matre Phaestide, septimum decimum annum agens Platonem audivit. Philosophicis disciplinis ipsos viginti annos excultus, magistro é vivis sublato, ad Hermiam Aternensium in Mysia tyrannum se contulit Aristoteles, apud quem triennio ubi versatus fuisset, in Macedoniam ad erudiendum Alexandrum profectus, exactis cum eo annis octo, Athenas rediit: hic Xenocratem Speusippi successorem in Acedemia quum reperisset, *Lyceum* (in suburbio locus fuerat à Pericle conditus, ut lectum recens militem ipse in eo bellicis artibus instrueret) sibi delegit: qua in statione, quoniam de rebus philosophicis inambulando disseruit, factum iccircò, ut Schola ab inambulandi consuetudine PERIPATETICA vocaretur.

19 The Peripatetics glory in Aristotle as their master. He was born at Stagira, a town of Macedonia, about the year of the world 3621, namely in the first year of the 99th Olympiad, his father being Nicomachus and his mother Phaestis, and in his seventeenth year he heard Plato. When he had been trained in the Philosophical disciplines for full twenty years and his master had been taken from among the living, Aristotle betook himself to Hermias, tyrant of the Atarneans in Mysia; and having stayed with him for three years, he set out for Macedonia to instruct Alexander, and, after spending eight years with him, returned to Athens. Here, since he found Xenocrates, the successor of Speusippus, in the Academy, he chose for himself the Lyceum (a place in the suburb, which had been built by Pericles so that he himself might train newly levied soldiers in it in the arts of war); and since in that station he discoursed on philosophical matters while walking about, it came about that the School was called Peripatetic, from its custom of walking about.

> 20 Auctor est Strabo[^5-s2] & in eo mirè consentiunt Historiae Philosophiae Scriptores, Aristotelem scripta sua & Bibliothecam discipulo suo Theophrasto tradidisse, cui & Scholam reliquit. Theophrastum pariter & suos, & Aristotelis libros testamento legasse *Neleo* Scepsio, qui fuerat illius, & Aristotelis Auditor, ut testatur Diogenes Laertius[^5-s3]. Igitur Neleus Bibliothecam illam in oppidum *Scepsin* transtulit, eamque haeredibus ineruditis hominibus moriens reliquit. Illi autem ubi Attalicorum Regum, quibus Scepsis [p. 6] parebat in libris undequaque ad instruendam Pergami Bibliothecam conquirendis studium intellexissent: suos ne auferrentur in terram defoderunt. ubi diù relicti ac quodammodo sepulti jacuere. Tandem ab illorum successoribus éruti sunt, humore & blattis vitiati & corrossi, ac *Apelliconi* Tejo, librorum magis quam scientiae studioso magnâ pecuniâ venditi. Apellicon verò, facta imperita exesarum partium instauratione, in nova libros transtulit exempla, quae tamen mendis adhuc plurimis, & plurimis etiam relictis lacunis, scatebant.

20 Strabo is our authority (k), and the Writers of the History of Philosophy agree wonderfully with him on this, that Aristotle handed over his writings and his Library to his disciple Theophrastus, to whom he also left his School; and that Theophrastus likewise bequeathed by will both his own books and Aristotle’s to Neleus of Scepsis, who had been a hearer of him and of Aristotle, as Diogenes Laertius testifies (l). Neleus, therefore, carried that Library over to the town of Scepsis, and at his death left it to his heirs, unlearned men. But they, when they learned of the zeal of the Attalid Kings, to whom Scepsis [p. 6] was subject, in seeking out books from every quarter to furnish the Library of Pergamum, buried their own in the ground lest they be carried off; and there they lay a long time, abandoned and, as it were, entombed. At length, dug up by the successors of those men, damaged and gnawed by damp and by moths, they were sold for a great sum of money to Apellicon of Teos, a man more devoted to books than to learning. Apellicon, for his part, after an unskilled restoration of the eaten-away parts, transcribed the books into new copies, which nevertheless still teemed with very many faults, and with very many gaps also left unfilled.
