> 21 At statim post mortem Appelliconis bibliotheca illius, quae erat in Piraeo à L Sulla, ut Plutarchus in ejus vita commemorat, subducta est, ac Romam asportata, ubi Grammaticus quiddam *Tyrannio*, Aristotelicorum librorum usum sibi permitti petiit: eaque facultate obtentâ, plurima in iis intervertit ipse, & cum Andronico quodam Rhodio exempla communicavit, à quo similiter interpolata, tandem in lucem emissa sunt. Ex quo satis superque constat Aristotelis libros miserè foedatos esse, multisque locis hiulcos, ita ut nullus pro certo adfirmare possit qualia sint verba ipsiusmet Aristotelis; quid suppleverit Appellicon, quid Tyrannio & Andronicus. Qui de hoc plura velit legat *Stanleyum*[^6-s1]. Nos ad reliqua gradum facimus.

21 But immediately after the death of Apellicon his library, which was at Piraeus, was carried off by L. Sulla, as Plutarch records in his life, and taken to Rome, where a certain Grammarian, Tyrannio, asked to be allowed the use of the Aristotelian books; and, having obtained this permission, he himself corrupted a great many things in them, and shared copies with a certain Andronicus of Rhodes, by whom, after they had been likewise interpolated, they were at length brought out into the light. From this it is more than sufficiently clear that the books of Aristotle were wretchedly defiled and full of gaps in many places, so that no one can affirm for certain which are the words of Aristotle himself, and what Apellicon supplied, what Tyrannio and Andronicus. Whoever wishes to know more of this, let him read Stanley (m). We pass on to the rest.

> 22 Stoicorum Dux fuit *Zeno* Cittieus, sive è Cittio Cypri oppido oriundus, qui Athenis in Porticu severioris Philosophiae dogmata magna cum nominis celebritate tradebat circa Olympiadem 130.

22 The Leader of the Stoics was Zeno of Citium, that is, a native of Citium, a town of Cyprus, who at Athens, in the Portico, taught the doctrines of a severer Philosophy, with great celebrity of name, about the 130th Olympiad.

> 23 Epicurei ità vocati sunt ab *Epicuro* hujus sectae Patrono; qui in hortis, ubi suos agebat conventus, Demócriti placita, quae propria fecerat, explicabat. Obiit annó secundo Olympiadis 127, post mund. condit. 3735, quum vixisset annos 72. Epicuri Philosophiam latinis carminibus in sex libros distributis scripsit *Lucretius* Cicerone duodecim annis minor. Reprehenditur Epicurus à Tullio[^6-s2] quod Logicam contempserit, multò autem maximè, quod ,, ex animis hominum extraxerit radicitùs Religionem cum Diis immortalibus :::::: re tollens, oratione relinquens Deos ,,. Unum hoc adnectimus: Epicuri Scholam serie continua & rara consensione ad Augusti aetatem usque pertinuisse quatuordecim Magistris spatium annorum 237 explentibus.

23 The Epicureans were so called from Epicurus, the Patron of this sect, who in the gardens where he held his gatherings expounded the tenets of Democritus, which he had made his own. He died in the second year of the 127th Olympiad, in the year 3735 after the founding of the world, having lived 72 years. Lucretius, twelve years younger than Cicero, wrote out the Philosophy of Epicurus in Latin verses divided into six books. Epicurus is censured by Tully (n) for having despised Logic, but far most of all because “he tore Religion up by the roots from the minds of men, abolishing it, together with the immortal Gods, in reality, while leaving the Gods in words.” We add this one thing: that the School of Epicurus lasted, in a continuous succession and with a rare agreement, down to the age of Augustus, fourteen Masters filling a space of 237 years.

> 24 Interea verò Socratis methodus ab Arcesila revocata fuerat circa Olympiadem 120; unde ipse secundae, seu mediae Academiae Princeps nominatur. Is autem Socratis opinioni hoc addidit, ut non modò nihil sciri adfirmaret cum Socrate, sed ne posse quidem rem ullam sciri contenderet. Hinc novi Academici, iidem *Acataleptici* sunt vocati, quasi diceres, qui nihil omninò comprehendere se posse profiterentur.

24 Meanwhile, however, the method of Socrates had been revived by Arcesilaus about the 120th Olympiad, whence he himself is named the Chief of the second, or middle, Academy. He, moreover, added this to the opinion of Socrates: that he not only affirmed with Socrates that nothing is known, but contended that nothing whatever can even be known. Hence the new Academics were also called Acataleptics, as if you were to say, men who professed that they could comprehend nothing at all.

> 25 Arcesilae suffragati sunt Lacydes, novae, seu tertiae Academiae Auctor, Evander, & praecipuè Carneades, qui Romae magna cum eloquentia novorum Academicorum doctrinam explicuit, ibique discipulos habuit Clitomachum, Philonem, & Antiochum, à quibus eruditus est M. T. Cicero, qui & ipse Academicus fuit, ac Platonicae methodi strenuus adsertor.

25 Arcesilaus was supported by Lacydes, the Author of the new, or third, Academy, by Evander, and above all by Carneades, who at Rome expounded the doctrine of the new Academics with great eloquence, and there had as disciples Clitomachus, Philo and Antiochus, by whom M. T. Cicero was taught, who himself also was an Academic and a vigorous champion of the Platonic method.

## §. III. — §. III

> *De Eclectica Philosophia, deque Philosophia post Christum natum.*

On the Eclectic Philosophy, and on Philosophy after the Birth of Christ.

> 26 Quae Philosophia Graecis *Eclectica*, Latinis *Electiva* dicitur. Hanc philosophandi rationem Clemens Alexandrinus explicat, dum, ubi multa in laudem Philosophiae disseruisset, addit, se omnia haec in Philosophiam non Stoicam, nec Platonicam, nec Epicuream, aut Aristotelicam pronunciasse; sed quaecumque ab his sectis rectè dicta sunt, quae docent justitiam cum pia scientia, hoc totum electum, Philosophiam se adpellare ait[^7-s1]. Quasi (ut subdit *Stanleyus*[^7-s2] ,, ne nomine quidem Philosophiae dignum censeret studium eorum, qui superstitiosè in unius verba magistri jurare non dubitant ,,. Eclectici nempè apes imitantur, quae (Senecae sunt verba[^7-s3] ,, vagantur, & flores ad mel faciendum idoneos carpunt, deinde quidquid attullere disponunt, ac per favos digerunt, utque Virgilius ait:

26 This Philosophy is called Eclectic by the Greeks, Elective by the Latins. This manner of philosophizing is explained by Clement of Alexandria when, after discoursing at length in praise of Philosophy, he adds that he had declared all this not of the Stoic Philosophy, nor of the Platonic, nor of the Epicurean or the Aristotelian; but whatever things have been rightly said by these sects, which teach justice together with pious knowledge, this whole selection, he says, he calls Philosophy (o). As if (as Stanley adds (p)) “he judged the study of those who do not hesitate superstitiously to swear by the words of a single master not worthy even of the name of Philosophy.” The Eclectics, namely, imitate the bees, which (these are Seneca’s words (q)) “wander about and pluck the flowers fit for making honey, then arrange whatever they have brought in, and distribute it through the combs, and, as Virgil says:

> 27 Hujus Philosophiae Princeps *Potamon* Alexandrinus fuit, illustresque fama nactos auditores habuit haec philosophandi ratio (neque enim *Sectae* nomine isthaec philosophandi methodus venire potest). Viri etiam Sanctimonia inclyti Eclecticam philosophiam studiosiùs propugnare contenderunt, cum primis quidem Clemens Alexandrinus, & Gregorius Thaumaturgus, non alia videlicet causâ eam professi ,, nisi, ut veritatem, quae in una secta reperiri non poterat, ex pluribus derivarent ,, quod innuit Lactantius, adfirmans unà ,, eos omnes sapientiam sibi adimere, qui sine ullo judicio inventa majorum probant, & ab aliis pecudum more [p. 8] dicuntur; nec putant fieri posse, ut aut ipsi plus sapiant, quia minores vocantur, aut illi desipuerint, quia majores nominantur[^8-s1].

27 The Chief of this Philosophy was Potamon of Alexandria, and this manner of philosophizing (for this method of philosophizing cannot come under the name of a Sect) had hearers who had won illustrious fame. Men renowned for Holiness also strove to defend the Eclectic philosophy with especial zeal, foremost among them Clement of Alexandria and Gregory Thaumaturgus, having professed it, namely, for no other reason “than that they might draw from many sects the truth which could not be found in one”; which Lactantius intimates, affirming at the same time that “all those deprive themselves of wisdom who without any judgment approve the discoveries of their forefathers, and, like cattle, by others are [p. 8] are led; nor do they think it possible either that they themselves should be wiser, because they are called the younger, or that those others should have been foolish, because they are named the elders (r).”

> 28 Sequentibus temporibus post Christi adventum doctrina Platonis ad octavum circiter Ecclesiae seculum primas semper obtinuit, eique plurimi SS. Patres studium, & vigilias suas consecrarunt. Eandem inter Latinos Patres diligentissimè excoluit S. Augustinus, qui ut erat acerrimo ingenio, multis eam partibus illustravit, & ad refellendos Ethnicorum errores, adserendamque Religionis Christianae veritatem feliciter adhibuit.

28 In the following ages after the coming of Christ, the doctrine of Plato always held first place until about the eighth century of the Church, and very many of the Holy Fathers consecrated their study and their vigils to it. Among the Latin Fathers it was most diligently cultivated by St. Augustine, who, being of a most penetrating wit, illustrated it in many parts and happily employed it to refute the errors of the Heathen and to assert the truth of the Christian Religion.

> 29 Quod verò Philosophiam Aristotelicam adtinet, certum est, illam primis Ecclesiae seculis nullum unquam obtinuisse dominatum, quinimo SS. Patres innumeris conviciis eam derisere. Illos legere est apud Cl. Petavium[^8-s2] Eorum agmen ducit S. Justinus Martyr (sive quis alius Christianus Doctor, qui librum inscripsit: *Quorundam Aristotelicarum dogmatum eversio*) Clemens Alexandr. sequitur ita scribens.[^8-s3] ,, Sed nec molestum fuerit meminisse etiam Peripateticorum, cujus quidem sectae qui pater est, nihil de eo Patre qui est Supremus intelligens errores plurimos docet ,,. Iraeneus Lugdunensis Episcopus[^8-s4] duo ab Aristotele refutat accepta nimirùm minutiloquium, & subtilitatem, quibus Christianae Fidei simplicitas, & candor corrumpitur. Hoc ipsum in Aristotele reprehendunt Origenes[^8-s5], Lactantius Firmianus[^8-s6], Eusebius Caesariensis[^8-s7], Athanasius Alexandr. Episcopus[^8-s8] Basilius[^8-s9], Gregorius Nicenus[^8-s10], Ambrosius[^8-s11], Johann. Chrisostomus[^8-s12], Augustinus[^8-s13], Hieronymus[^8-s14] qui testatur quod Ariana haeresis argumentationum rivos de fontibus Aristotelis mutuatur, quod & confirmat S. Ambrosius[^8-s15] inquiens: ,, Sic enim Arianos in perfidiam ruisse cognovimus, relinquunt Apostolum, [p. 9] sequuntur Aristotelem ,,. Gregorius quoque Nazianzenus[^9-s1] dolet irrepsisse in Ecclesiam captiones sophisticas & pravum artificium Aristoteleae artis velut AEgyptiacas quasdam plagas. S. Augustinus ita Pelagianos compellat[^9-s2] ,, Ad hoc redacta est haeresis vestra, ut gemant Sectatores vestri non inveniri Dialecticos Judices in Ecclesia de Scholis Peripateticorum à quibus possitis absolvi ,,. S. Vincentius Ferrerius quaerulus exclamat[^9-s3], Aristotelem & Averroem fuisse phialas irae Dei projectas super aquas sapientiae Christianae, unde factae sunt amarae, ut absynthium. Plura qui velit, legat Cl. Guidonem Grandi. Historiam sequamur.

29 As for the Aristotelian Philosophy, it is certain that in the first ages of the Church it never held any dominion; nay rather, the Holy Fathers derided it with countless reproaches. These may be read in the celebrated Petavius (s). Their file is led by St. Justin Martyr (or whatever other Christian Doctor wrote the book entitled The Overthrow of Certain Aristotelian Doctrines). Clement of Alexandria follows, writing thus (t): “But it will not be irksome to recall also the Peripatetics, the father of whose sect, understanding nothing about that Father who is Supreme, teaches very many errors.” Irenaeus, Bishop of Lyons (u), refutes two things received from Aristotle, namely hair-splitting talk and subtlety, by which the simplicity and candor of the Christian Faith are corrupted. This very thing is censured in Aristotle by Origen (x), Lactantius Firmianus (y), Eusebius of Caesarea (z), Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria (a), Basil (b), Gregory of Nyssa (c), Ambrose (d), John Chrysostom (e), Augustine (f), and Jerome (g), who testifies that the Arian heresy borrows the streams of its argumentations from the fountains of Aristotle; which St. Ambrose (h) also confirms, saying: “For thus we know that the Arians rushed headlong into perfidy: they abandon the Apostle, [p. 9] they follow Aristotle.” Gregory Nazianzen too (i) laments that the captious arguments of the sophists and the depraved artifice of the Aristotelian art had crept into the Church like certain Egyptian plagues. St. Augustine addresses the Pelagians thus (k): “Your heresy has been brought to this, that your followers groan that no Dialectician Judges from the Schools of the Peripatetics are to be found in the Church by whom you might be acquitted.” St. Vincent Ferrer exclaims querulously (l) that Aristotle and Averroes were vials of the wrath of God poured out upon the waters of Christian wisdom, whence they were made bitter as wormwood. Whoever wishes more, let him read the celebrated Guido Grandi. Let us follow our History.

> [^8-s2]: Theolog. Dogmat. Tom. 1. Proleg. Cap. 3.

[^8-s2]: Theologica Dogmata, vol. 1, Proleg., ch. 3.

[^9-s3]: In the celebrated Grandi, in the Diacrisis against the Philosophia Novo-Antiqua.

> 30 Occidentales interea Provincias haud paulò alia rerum facies habuit. Arabes namque sub finem octavi seculi, & noni principium subactis antea amplissimis regionibus per Africam latè & Hispaniam dominationem adepti, Aristotelis doctrinam ex Graeco Arabicè,& ex Arabico Latinè redditam, commentariisque illustratam exsuscitarunt, atque in scholas publicas invexére; quae quidem ratio ipsos penè quingentos annos tenuit, linguarum Graecae ac Latinae intelligentia ferè consepultâ. Haec philosophandi methodus per Arabes in Hispaniam invecta ad Anglos & Gallos transmigravit, latèque diffussa est, Platonis tùm facundus & uberior in sermone stylus negligi, acumen dialecticum vigére coepit, Aristotelis interpretibus subtile, minutum, contentiosum, nimiùm loquax disserendi genus studiosè consectantibus: quos inter praecipui numerantur *Avicenna*, *Alpharabius*, *Alchindus*, omnium autem facile princeps *Averroes*, Cordubensis, nuncupatione singulari *Commentator* adpellatus. Hinc nata Philosophia *disputatrix*, *& contentiosa*, quae sermonis barbariem secum in Scholas invexit, & *Scholastica* vocata est, eo quod in Scholis ad nostra usque tempora sit usurpata: quamvis tamen variam diversis temporibus fortunam experta sit, de qua si longiùs orationem protrahere mens foret exscribenda mihi essent integra volumina Bruckerii, aliorumque; aliqua tamen capita delibabimus.

30 The Western Provinces, meanwhile, presented a far different face of things. For the Arabs, toward the end of the eighth century and the beginning of the ninth, having previously subdued very extensive regions and obtained dominion far and wide through Africa and Spain, revived the doctrine of Aristotle, rendered from Greek into Arabic and from Arabic into Latin and illustrated with commentaries, and brought it into the public schools; and this system indeed held them for nearly five hundred years, the understanding of the Greek and Latin languages being almost buried along with it. This method of philosophizing, brought by the Arabs into Spain, migrated to the English and the French and was spread far and wide; then the eloquent and richer style of Plato’s discourse began to be neglected and dialectical acumen to flourish, the interpreters of Aristotle zealously pursuing a subtle, minute, contentious, excessively talkative manner of discoursing: among whom are reckoned as chief Avicenna, Alfarabi, Alkindi, but easily the prince of all Averroes of Córdoba, called by the singular title of the Commentator. Hence was born the disputatious and contentious Philosophy, which brought barbarism of speech with it into the Schools, and was called Scholastic, because it has been in use in the Schools down to our own times; although it has met with varied fortune at different times, and if I had a mind to draw out my discourse on it at greater length, whole volumes of Brucker and others would have to be copied out by me; we shall, however, touch on some chief points.

> 31 Anno 1209. Parisiensis Concilii Decreto praecipui Aristotelis libri combusti sunt, & eorum lectio interdicta. Anno 1591 Franciscus Patricius Gregorio XIV. suadet ut é Scholis Christianorum Aristotelis Philosophia tollatur. Postea vero Petrus Ramus Parisis defendit Theses contra Aristotelis doctrinam Dein Johann. Picus Mirandulanus Philosophiam Pythagoricam restituere conatus est. Besarion & Marcilius Ficinus Platonicam, Gaspar *Sciopius* Stoicam, Bernardinus Telesius illam quae Parmenidis adpellatur.

31 In the year 1209, by Decree of the Council of Paris, the principal books of Aristotle were burned and the reading of them forbidden. In the year 1591 Francesco Patrizi urges Gregory XIV to remove the Philosophy of Aristotle from the Schools of Christians. Afterwards Peter Ramus defended Theses at Paris against the doctrine of Aristotle. Then John Pico della Mirandola attempted to restore the Pythagorean Philosophy, Bessarion and Marsilio Ficino the Platonic, Caspar Scioppius the Stoic, Bernardino Telesio that which is called the Parmenidean.

> 32 Scholasticae Philosophiae Principem alii *Lanfrancum* Archiepiscopum Cantuariensem statuunt. Nonnulli, inter quos *Naudaeus* à D. Johann. Damasceno primam originem repetunt, á quo ad [p. 10] Latinos Petrum Abaelardum, hujusque discipulum Petrum Lombardum fuerit derivata. Tres in aetates dividitur, quarum prima initium sumpsit quorundam ex sententia sub medium seculi undecimi ad medium duodecimi perducta; Effloruere id temporis Abaelardus, Lombardus dictus *Magister Sententiarum* propterea quod sententias ex antiquis Patribus collectas exposuerit. Gilbertus Porretanus, Petrus Comestor, & Johann. Sarisberiensis. Secunda periodus ad ann. circitèr 1330 excurrit, hanc illustrarunt ingenia Alberti Magni, D. THOMAE AQUINATIS, & D. Bonaventurae. Tertia tenuit dum literae artesque repararentur, qua quidem aetate claruerunt Durandus, Ochamus, Petrus de Alliaco Cardinalis.

32 Some establish Lanfranc, Archbishop of Canterbury, as the Founder of the Scholastic Philosophy. Others, among them Naudé, trace its first origin back to St. John Damascene, from whom it came down to the Latins, [p. 10] Peter Abelard and his disciple Peter Lombard. It is divided into three ages, of which the first, in the opinion of some, began about the middle of the eleventh century and was carried down to the middle of the twelfth. At that time there flourished Abelard; Lombard, called the Master of the Sentences because he expounded the sentences collected from the ancient Fathers; Gilbert de la Porrée, Peter Comestor, and John of Salisbury. The second period runs to about the year 1330; it was made illustrious by the geniuses of Albert the Great, St. Thomas Aquinas, and St. Bonaventure. The third lasted until letters and the arts were restored; in which age Durandus, Ockham, and Cardinal Pierre d’Ailly were renowned.

> 33 Inter Scholasticos verò seu novos Peripateticos tres numerantur illustriores sectae: *Thomistarum* nempè, *Scotistarum*, & *Nominalium*. Primi ducem sequuntur D. THOMAM natum ann. 1224 in Castro Aquino, Regulam Ordinis Praedicatorum subinde professum, atque ob morum nitorem, doctrinaeque praestantiam *Doctoris Angelici* nuncupatione jure merito insignitum. Celebrantur Thomistas inter Dominicus de Flandria, Franciscus Victoria, Illustrissim. Melchior Cano, Dominicus Soto, Medina aliique plurimi, quos longum esset recensere.

33 Among the Scholastics, or new Peripatetics, three more illustrious sects are reckoned: namely those of the Thomists, the Scotists, and the Nominalists. The first follow as their leader St. Thomas, born in the year 1224 in the Castle of Aquino, who afterwards professed the Rule of the Order of Preachers, and on account of the purity of his morals and the excellence of his doctrine was justly and deservedly distinguished with the title of the Angelic Doctor. Among the Thomists are celebrated Dominic of Flanders, Francisco de Vitoria, the Most Illustrious Melchor Cano, Domingo de Soto, Medina and very many others, whom it would take long to recount.

> 34 Altera Schola principem agnoscit Johannem Duns, qui seu patriâ *Scotus* fuerit, quod cognomentum & ipsi tribuitur etiamnum, & in sectam ab eo constitutam derivatur, seu Dunstonae in Nortumbria, aut é vico Duns in Ultonia (neque enim de eo inter Scriptores convenit) ortus, Ordinem Minorum ingressus sub exordia quartidecimi seculi potissimum claruit. Ingenium subtile, & respondens ei Sapientia *Doctoris Subtilis* peperit nomenclationem: utrumque effecit, ut dum Cathedram Theologicam moderaretur Oxonii, ejus audiendi gratiâ, triginta & amplius Scholarium millia confluxerint. Scoti adseclae eminuerunt Franciscus Mayronius, qui adhuc dum superstitis Magistri doctrinam exceperat, Johann. Ponzius, Barthol. Mastrius, Martinus Meurisse, & Claud. Frassen, celeber Scotista anno seculi hujus undecimo, è vivis sublatus[^10-s1].

34 The second School acknowledges as its chief John Duns, who, whether he was a Scot by country (a surname that is still given to him even now and is carried over to the sect founded by him), or was born at Dunstan in Northumberland, or in the village of Duns in Ulster (for the Writers are not agreed about this), entered the Order of Minors and flourished chiefly at the beginning of the fourteenth century. His subtle wit, and the Wisdom answering to it, brought forth the title of Subtle Doctor; and both together brought it about that, while he held the Theological Chair at Oxford, thirty thousand Scholars and more flocked together to hear him. Among the followers of Scotus there excelled Francis of Meyronnes, who had received the doctrine while his Master was still living, John Punch, Bartholomew Mastrius, Martin Meurisse, and Claude Frassen, a celebrated Scotist, who was taken from among the living in the eleventh year of this century (m).

> [^10-s1]: Wadingus in Bibliotheca Minorum.

[^10-s1]: Wadding, in the Bibliotheca Minorum.

> 35 Tertia secta est Nominalium, qui *nomina* & *voces* objectum esse Logicae contendebant, quorum Doctor fuit Guillelmus Ochamus, natione Anglus, Ordin. Fratrum Minor., & Scoti discipulus. Dispecuntur etiam Scholastici in *Reales* & *Nominales*. Argumentum porrhò hujus discrepantiae, *universalium* tractatio praebuit, quum primi, naturas universales reapse velut existere contederent, postremi non nisi in vocibus eas constitutas adfirmarent.

35 The third sect is that of the Nominalists, who contended that names and words are the object of Logic, and whose Doctor was William of Ockham, English by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, and a disciple of Scotus. The Scholastics are also divided into Realists and Nominalists. The matter of this disagreement, moreover, was furnished by the treatment of universals, since the former contended that universal natures exist, as it were, in reality, while the latter affirmed that they are constituted only in words.

[p. 11]

> §. IV.

§ . I V.

> *Novatores in Philosophia, qui doctrinam veterem suscitarunt.*

Innovators in Philosophy who Revived the Ancient Doctrine.

> 36 Circa medium decimiseptimi seculi Gallilaeus Magni Ducis Hetruriae Mathematicus egregius[^11-s1] excusso inveteratae in Scholis consuetudinis jugo, novas vias tentavit. Hujus vestigiis inhaerentes plurimi doctrinâ praestantes Viri *Mechanicam* philosophiam instaurarunt.

36 About the middle of the seventeenth century Galileo, the excellent Mathematician of the Grand Duke of Tuscany (n), shook off the yoke of the custom grown inveterate in the Schools and tried new paths. Following in his footsteps, very many Men outstanding in learning restored the Mechanical philosophy.

> [^11-s1]: Ortus Pisis ann. 1564.

[^11-s1]: Born at Pisa in the year 1564.

> 37 Petrus Gassendus Regius in Academia Paris. Matheseos Professor natus est ann. 1562. Is Epicureae Philosophiae systema concinnavit, iis repudiatis, quae cum Religione minus conciliari potuere. Ac profectò emendata per ipsum Epicuri placita Eruditis sese probarunt tantopere, ut à praecellenti hoc restitutore *Gassendistica* secta fuerit exorta.

37 Pierre Gassendi, Royal Professor of Mathematics in the Academy of Paris, was born in the year 1562. He put together a system of the Epicurean Philosophy, rejecting those things which could not well be reconciled with Religion. And indeed the tenets of Epicurus as emended by him so commended themselves to the Learned that from this eminent restorer the Gassendist sect arose.

> 38 Quidam novum Philosophiae genus excogitarunt, *Christianorum* compellatum. Horum è numero est Thomas Burnet in *Theoria Telluris Sacra*, ubi Mosen interpretari satagit, verum contorquet miserrimè narrationem Mosaicam. Huic adjungenda Wistoni *Theoria*, quae tamen utraque à Viris doctis confutata fuit. Eodem pertinet Edmundus Dikinsonus in *Physica veteri, & nova*, Johannes Comenius in *Physica ad lumen divinum reformata*. Ejus hypotheses potissimùm retinuit Johann. Bayerus in Op. inscript. *Ostium, & atrium naturae*.

38 Certain men devised a new kind of Philosophy, called the Philosophy of the Christians. Of their number is Thomas Burnet in the Sacred Theory of the Earth, where he busies himself with interpreting Moses, but most wretchedly distorts the Mosaic narrative. To him must be joined the Theory of Whiston; both of these, however, were refuted by learned Men. To the same class belong Edmund Dickinson in his Physica vetus et nova, and John Comenius in his Physica ad lumen divinum reformata. His hypotheses were for the most part retained by Johann Bayer in the Work entitled Ostium et atrium naturae.

> 39 Hoc jam loco inferenda est mentio restitutae *Chemicorum* Philosophiae eorumque qui illam à cineribus velut eruerunt, excoluerunt, & disciplinam hanc *Experimentalem* reddiderunt, naturam operosè perscrutando, tentaminibus corporeas res subjiciendo, & sterilibus aliorum speculationibus utilem experientiam sufficiendo. Vetustissimam esse Chemiae metallurgicae originem inter alios ostendit Cl. Boerhaave[^11-s2]. Fertur Paracelsum artem Chemicam praecipuè apud Germanos suscitasse, unde & *Chimicarum Pater* dictus est. Eam disciplinae hujus partem, quae metallurgiam complectitur excoluerunt post Georg. Agricolam, Lazarus Erckern, Joach. Becher, Joahann. Kunckel. Chemiam Medicinae, Physicaeque utilem tradiderunt Boyle, Slare, Homberg. Geoffroy, Le Mery Junior, Hoffmannus, & hos aliosque proferens Cl. Hermannus Boerhaave.

39 At this point mention must now be made of the restored Philosophy of the Chemists, and of those who as it were dug it out of the ashes, cultivated it, and rendered this discipline Experimental, by laboriously scrutinizing nature, subjecting bodily things to trials, and putting useful experience in place of the sterile speculations of others. That the origin of metallurgical Chemistry is most ancient is shown, among others, by the celebrated Boerhaave (o). Paracelsus is said to have revived the Chemical art, chiefly among the Germans, whence he is also called the Father of the Chemists. That part of this discipline which comprises metallurgy was cultivated, after Georg Agricola, by Lazarus Ercker, Joachim Becher and Johann Kunckel. Chemistry was made useful to Medicine and Physics by Boyle, Slare, Homberg, Geoffroy, Lémery the Younger, Hoffmann, and the celebrated Hermann Boerhaave, who brings forward these and others.

> [^11-s2]: Elem. Chem. Tom. 1. Pat. 1. de Histor. Artis.

[^11-s2]: Elements of Chemistry, vol. 1, pt. 1, On the History of the Art.

[p. 12]

> §. V.

§ . V.

> *Eclectica Recentior Philosophia Verulamio Auctore.*

The Newer Eclectic Philosophy, with Bacon of Verulam as its Author.

> 40 Eclecticae verò Recentioris Philosophiae, illius nempè, quae non adprobatores modò sed & cultores adepta est, parens habetur Franciscus Baconus de Verulamio ann. 1561 in Anglia natus. Viri hujus ductu incitati per Angliam alii, Philosophiam, ab illo adumbratam informatamque excoluerunt. Praecipui fuere Boyle, Wilkius, Wilis, Christoph. & Mathaeus Wrenii, á quibus Societas Regia Anglia originem duxit Regiis auspiciis condita ann. 1660. Atque Eclectica isthaec philosophandi ratio ad Newtoni tempora penè tenuit inter Anglos, cujus auctoritate in sectariam abiit.

40 Of the newer Eclectic Philosophy, namely of that which has gained not only approvers but also cultivators, the parent is held to be Francis Bacon of Verulam, born in England in the year 1561. Others throughout England, stirred by the lead of this Man, cultivated the Philosophy sketched and shaped by him. The chief were Boyle, Wilkins, Willis, Christopher and Matthew Wren, from whom the Royal Society of England took its origin, founded under Royal auspices in the year 1660. And this Eclectic manner of philosophizing held sway among the English almost until the times of Newton, by whose authority it passed into a sectarian one.

> 41 Idem in Gallia evenit; Cartesius quippe natus ann. 1569. ubi in Flexiano Collegio curriculum philosophicum emensus est, & exactis per diversas provincias itineribus elaboratum doctrinae suae systema vulgavit, reperit, uti adversarios longè acerrimos, ita adseclas, propugnatoresque strenuos, qui latè sparsi, sectam ab Auctoris nomine *Cartesianam* effecere. Hos inter praecipui habentur Franc. Bayle, Anton. Le Grand, Jac. Rohault, Nicol. Malebranche, D. de Molieres, Hartsoeker, Purchot aliique Illud tamen hic animadvertendum est, Cartesii ductu sive exemplo, seu consilio, philosophandi rationem commutatam fuisse, & *Mechanicam* sectam effloruisse.

41 The same thing happened in France: for Descartes, born in the year 1569, after he had passed through the philosophical course in the College of La Flèche and had completed journeys through various provinces, published the system of his doctrine that he had worked out, and found adversaries by far the fiercest, but also adherents and vigorous champions, who, spread far and wide, formed a sect named Cartesian from the name of its Author. Among these the chief are held to be François Bayle, Antoine Le Grand, Jacques Rohault, Nicolas Malebranche, D. de Molières, Hartsoeker, Purchot and others. This, however, must here be noted: that by the lead, or the example, or the counsel of Descartes the manner of philosophizing was changed, and the Mechanical sect flourished.

> 42 In Anglia, quo usque Cartesiana Philosophandi ratio penetraverat, aliam auspicatus est Philosophiam Isaacus Newtonus anno seculi superioris secundo supra quadragesimum editus in lucem, quae in sectariam deinceps abiit, & magnis hodie permultorum studiis propugnatur. Nempè Vir summus rejectis Cartesii hypothesibus, & conjecturis quibusvis, novas philosophandi regulas constituit, ratus, nihil admitti oportere in Philosophia, nisi quod aut experimenta, aut rationes invictè demonstrarent. Fundamenta doctrinae suae proposuit partim in eximio opere, quod inscripsit: *Principia Philosophiae Mathematica* Clarissim. le Seur & Jacquier Commentariis illustrata, partim in *Optica*. In his universè summa temperatione utitur, professus, res naturales ab se *mathematicè* spectari duntàxat, neque physicas earundem causas inquiri: quo circa generalia quaedam usurpavit vocabula, queis abstractas notiones Geometrarum more indigitavit.

42 In England, as far as the Cartesian manner of philosophizing had penetrated, another Philosophy was inaugurated by Isaac Newton, who was brought into the light in the forty-second year of the last century; and it afterwards passed into a sectarian one, and is today defended with great zeal by very many. That eminent Man, namely, rejecting the hypotheses of Descartes and conjectures of every kind, established new rules of philosophizing, holding that nothing ought to be admitted in Philosophy except what either experiments or reasons invincibly demonstrate. He set out the foundations of his doctrine partly in the excellent work which he entitled Mathematical Principles of Philosophy, illustrated with Commentaries by the most celebrated Le Seur and Jacquier, partly in the Opticks. In these he everywhere uses the greatest moderation, professing that natural things are considered by him only mathematically, and that their physical causes are not inquired into: wherefore he made use of certain general terms, by which he designated abstract notions after the manner of Geometers.

> 43 Celebres secta haec Viros censet, atque ab experimentandi, [p. 13] calculosque ineundi peritiâ cumprimis illustres: ut iccircò ipsa Auctoris nomine *Newtoniana*; ob tractandi methodum verò *Mathematica* vocitetur. Libet honoris causâ speciatim nominare: Keilium, Rogerum Cotes, S'Gravessandum, Musschenbroekium, Clarkium, Mac-Laurin, Jurin, Desagullierium, Krafftium; atque, ut alios taceamus, Astronomis recentioribus theoria Newtoni planè adridet.

43 This sect numbers celebrated Men, men who for their skill in experimenting [p. 13] and in making calculations are especially illustrious: so that it is for this reason called Newtonian from the name of its Author, but Mathematical on account of its method of treatment. It is pleasing, for honor’s sake, to name in particular Keill, Roger Cotes, ’s Gravesande, Musschenbroek, Clarke, MacLaurin, Jurin, Desaguliers, Krafft; and, to say nothing of others, the theory of Newton finds plain favor with the more recent Astronomers.

> 44 In Germania *Eclectico-Exoticum* Philosophiae genus sese explicuit per Gotofred. Guilielm. Leibnitzium anno 1646 Lipsiae prognatum. Is Scholasticorum philosophandi rationem laudavit; eorundemque labefactatam hactenùs, & tantum non conculcatam, postliminio restituere auctoritatem adgressus, quae ad Philosophiam rationalem, ac moralem pertinet, etiam adtigit suis in operibus; verum ampliora praestitit in Mathési sublimiore.

44 In Germany an Eclectic-Exotic kind of Philosophy unfolded itself through Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, born at Leipzig in the year 1646. He praised the Scholastics’ manner of philosophizing; and, having undertaken to restore to its former standing their authority, hitherto shaken and all but trampled underfoot, he also touches in his works on what pertains to rational and moral Philosophy; but he accomplished greater things in the higher Mathematics.

> 45 Philosophiam naturalem mixtam Cartesii principiis vulgavit, *hypothesim physicam novam*, & *Theoriam motus abstracti*, geminis libellis complexus: primus adhaec, posita virium in *vivas*, & *mortuas* distinctione, has, multo alia ratione, atque illas, aestimari oportere docuit. In Metaphycisis exoticum se se praebuit quammaximè, *principium rationis sufficientis* invehendo; *monades*, *harmoniam praestabilitam* adserendo; *mundi perfectionem*, nimio plus propugnando. Leibnitzii principia excoluit Christianus Wolffius, clarus hoc aevo nostro editis voluminibus, quibus Mathesim universam, Logicam, Metaphysicam, Ethicam, Physicamque comprehendit. Hujus utriusque adseclas referre haud lubet; ut, qui scriptis neque magnopere inclaruerunt, neque doctrinam latius propagarunt.

45 He published a natural Philosophy mixed with the principles of Descartes, comprising it in two little books, a New Physical Hypothesis and a Theory of Abstract Motion; he was, moreover, the first to lay down the distinction of forces into living and dead, and to teach that the former must be estimated in a far different way from the latter. In Metaphysics he showed himself exotic in the highest degree, by introducing the principle of sufficient reason, asserting monads and a pre-established harmony, and defending the perfection of the world far too much. The principles of Leibniz were cultivated by Christian Wolff, famous in this our age for the volumes he has published, in which he comprised universal Mathematics, Logic, Metaphysics, Ethics and Physics. I do not care to list the adherents of either of the two, since they have neither greatly distinguished themselves by their writings nor propagated the doctrine more widely.

> §. VI.

§. VI.

> *Recentiorum conatus in excolendis Philosophiae partibus.*

The Efforts of the Moderns in Cultivating the Parts of Philosophy.

> 46 Reliquum est, ut eorum jam pertexamus historiam, qui post instaurata literarum studia, seu privatos inter parietes, seu consociata plurium opera, peculiares Philosophiae partes emendarunt atque illustrarunt. Id agendo, Recentiorum maximè proferentur nomina Auctorum illorum etiam, quos nulli adhuc inseruimus sectae; unà tamen animum in eorum quoque memoriam revocare oportebit, quorum antehac jam conatus patuere.

46 It remains for us now to weave together the history of those who, after the restoration of the study of letters, whether within private walls or by the combined labors of many, emended and illustrated particular parts of Philosophy. In doing this, the names chiefly of the Moderns will be brought forward, including those Authors whom we have so far placed in no sect; at the same time, however, it will be necessary to recall to mind those also whose efforts have already been made plain before.

> 47 Philosophiam rationalem, praeter Laurentium Valla, Rudolph. Agricola, Ludov. Vives, Verulamium, Cartesium, Gassendum, Hobbesium, quorum alios diversa aetas amplius, minus alios dispescit, Petrus Ramus, in Gallia anno 1515. natus, emendandam sumpsit, eo successu, ut *Dialectica Ramaea* multis adprimè [p. 14] commendarit sese hoc nomine, quod rejectis inanibus subtilitatibus, disciplinam illam ad usum fori, & vitae, atque inprimis ad lectionem veterum Scriptorum retulerit. Factum iccircò, ut & discipulos frequentes, & fautores nancisceretur viros egregios: in Gallia Audomarum Talaeum, in Germania Franc. Fabricium, Sturmium, Chytraeum.

47 Rational Philosophy, besides Lorenzo Valla, Rudolph Agricola, Juan Luis Vives, Bacon, Descartes, Gassendi and Hobbes, whom their differing periods set apart, some more widely, others less, was taken up for emendation by Peter Ramus, born in France in the year 1515, with such success that the Ramist Dialectic commended itself exceedingly to many [p. 14] on this account, that, rejecting empty subtleties, it referred that discipline to the use of the courts and of life, and above all to the reading of the ancient Writers. Hence it came about that it gained both numerous disciples and eminent men as patrons: in France, Omer Talon; in Germany, Franz Fabricius, Sturm, Chytraeus.

> 48 Inter Cartesianos Logicae Scriptores eminent: Auctor *Artis cogitandi* (*L' Art de penser*) seu Arnaldus, sive alius quispiam fuerit;[^14-s1] & Malebranckius, artem *inquirendi veritatem* diffuse persequutus. Fuerunt quoque, qui è principiis Mathematicis, Logicae praecepta deduxerunt, hujus generis opus vulgavit Erhard. Weigelius, inscriptum hac formâ: *Analysis Aristotelica ex Euclide restituta* &c. Item Waltherus à Tschirnhausen in libro, cui titulus: *Medicina mentis*. Eodem pertinet Christiani Wolffi Logica, quam methodo Mathematicâ, exemplis illustratam sublimioribus, concinnavit. Qui Eclecticorum nuncupatione donandi videntur Logicae Scriptores, hi fere censentur: Johann. Lokius; Christ. Thomasius; Mariottus, Poiretus; Johann. Clericus; Johann. de Crousaz. Andr. Rudigerus; Fortun. à Brixia; Anton. Genovesi, Cl. Aloysius Antonius Verney, qui etiam *Methodum Studendi* sub ementito nomine P. Barbadiño Valentiae edidit, Honor. Fabri, Dominicus Buffier, Natalis Regnault, Cochet, aliique.

48 Among the Cartesian Writers on Logic there stand out the Author of the Art of Thinking (L’Art de penser), whether he was Arnauld or someone else (p), and Malebranche, who treated at length the art of seeking the truth. There were also those who deduced the precepts of Logic from Mathematical principles; a work of this kind was published by Erhard Weigel, entitled in this form: Analysis Aristotelica ex Euclide restituta, etc. Likewise Walther von Tschirnhaus, in the book whose title is Medicina mentis. To the same class belongs the Logic of Christian Wolff, which he composed by the Mathematical method, illustrated with higher examples. Those Writers on Logic who seem to deserve the name of Eclectics are generally reckoned to be these: John Locke; Christian Thomasius; Mariotte; Poiret; Jean Le Clerc; Jean- Pierre de Crousaz; Andreas Rüdiger; Fortunato da Brescia; Antonio Genovesi; the celebrated Luís António Verney, who also published at Valencia a Method of Studying under the feigned name of Father Barbadiño; Honoré Fabri, Dominique Buffier, Noël Regnault, Cochet, and others.

> [^14-s1]: Aliis Auctor hujus operis est Nicolius, aliis D. de Trigny, aliis plures é Portu Regio.

[^14-s1]: Some say the Author of this work is Nicole, others D. de Trigny, others several men of Port- Royal.

> 49 Metaphysica, & Logica, quoniam mutuas sibi operas tradunt, á plerisque indigitatis Logicae auctoribus consociatae fuerunt. Morhofius Metaphysicae reformatores Cartesium & Honor. Fabri ait; Henrici Moore *Enchiridion Methaphysicae*, ac Thomae Angli *Euclidem Metaphysicum* subinde profert, in hoc methodum reprehendit. Ad extremum Ludovici Vives de *prima Philosophia* libellum commendat. Quod ad alios adtinet, numerare est complures, qui disciplinae hujus partes tractarunt. *Ontologiam*, *Cosmologiam*, *Psychologiam*, *& Theologiam naturalem* amplis voluminibus, Leibnitzii secutus doctrinam, exposuit Wolffius. Neque aliorum defuere studia; quamvis argumenta haec singula modo paulùm discrepante, minus etiam exserte sint persecuti. Ceteros inter claruerunt: Claubergius, Hamelius, le Grand. Regis, Buddeus, Clericus, Purchotius, Corsinus, Cudworthus, Clarkius Niewentitius, Derhaamus, iique omnes, qui adversum Atheos pugnando, de Theologia naturali optimè meruerunt. Horum nectendus numero recentior. Cl. Ant. Genovesi. Doctrinam verò *primarum veritatum*, velut partem Methaphysices peculiarem, quam nervose, tam nitide ac solerter evolvit Cl. Verney, & P. Buffier.

49 Metaphysics and Logic, since they lend each other mutual service, have been joined together by most of the authors of Logic just indicated. Morhof says that Descartes and Honoré Fabri were reformers of Metaphysics; he then brings forward Henry More’s Enchiridion Metaphysicum and Thomas White’s Euclides Metaphysicus, and in the latter he censures the method. Finally, he commends the little book of Juan Luis Vives On First Philosophy. As for others, a great many may be counted who treated parts of this discipline. Ontology, Cosmology, Psychology and natural Theology were expounded in ample volumes by Wolff, following the doctrine of Leibniz. Nor were the studies of others lacking, although they pursued these several subjects in a somewhat different way, and also less expressly. Among the rest there were renowned Clauberg, Du Hamel, Le Grand, Régis, Buddeus, Le Clerc, Purchot, Corsini, Cudworth, Clarke, Nieuwentyt, Derham, and all those who, by fighting against the Atheists, deserved best of natural Theology. To their number must be joined, more recently, the celebrated Antonio Genovesi. The doctrine, moreover, of first truths, as a particular part of Metaphysics, was unfolded as vigorously as it was elegantly and skillfully by the celebrated Verney and by Father Buffier.

> 50 Verum abusi fuere nonnulli praecellenti hac, utilissimâque Philosophiae parte dum vel animae, atque ideis largiti nimiùm, in [p. 15] *Idealismum*, *Egoïsmum*, ceu fanatici, & enthusiastae proruerunt; vel dum ex adverso, mentem à corporis adfectione non secernentes, nobilissimi entis praestantiam perperám elevando, *Materialismi* foedo errore semet involverunt. Impudentissimè unà, atque imperitissimè omnium hac in materia versatus est Benedictus Spinosa; quem dicere est, erronem Philosophiae abortivum, & quiddam homine viliùs compellare.

50 But some have abused this most excellent and most useful part of Philosophy, while either, granting too much to the soul and to ideas, they rushed headlong into [p. 15] Idealism and Egoism, like fanatics and enthusiasts; or while, on the opposite side, not separating the mind from the affection of the body, and wrongly disparaging the excellence of the noblest being, they entangled themselves in the foul error of Materialism. Most impudently, and at the same time most unskillfully of all, this matter was handled by Benedict Spinoza, whom one may call an abortive vagabond of Philosophy, and something viler than a man.

> 51 Philosophiam Moralem dum scriptis auxere suis permulti, non perinde omnes pro dignitate promoverunt. Contaminarunt enim verò doctrinam hanc plenis veneni principiis Hobbesius, & Spinosa. De ceteris, nempè Montano, Grotio, Puffendorffio, Buddeo, Seldeno, Heineccio, Cumberlandio, Wolfio, atque aliis, ecquid sentiendnm sit, à suis hac in disciplina magistris tirones condiscant, necesse est. Egregiam hic rursum operam praestitit doctissimus Buffierius, tractatum de *Societate Civili* quatuor libris complexus, quibus suas adjecit animadversiones in Aristotelis, Ciceronis, Gassendi, Puffendorffii, Silvani Regis, Petri Charron, & Scholasticorum moralem doctrinam. Reliquorum, ut Hamelii, Purchotii, Corsini Ethica praecepta in omnium alioqui manibus versantur. Cl. item Genovesi Moralem complexus est in Opere inscript. *Diceosina: owero Filosofia dell Giusto, e del' Onesto.*

51 Many increased moral Philosophy by their writings, but not all advanced it equally as its dignity deserved. For Hobbes and Spinoza indeed contaminated this doctrine with principles full of poison. As for the rest, namely Montaigne, Grotius, Pufendorf, Buddeus, Selden, Heineccius, Cumberland, Wolff and others, what is to be thought of them beginners must necessarily learn from their own masters in this discipline. Here again the most learned Buffier performed excellent service, comprising a treatise On Civil Society in four books, to which he added his remarks on the moral doctrine of Aristotle, Cicero, Gassendi, Pufendorf, Silvain Régis, Pierre Charron and the Scholastics. The Ethical precepts of the rest, such as Du Hamel, Purchot and Corsini, are in any case in everyone’s hands. Likewise the celebrated Genovesi comprised Moral philosophy in the Work entitled Diceosina: ovvero Filosofia del Giusto, e dell’Onesto.

> 52 Mathematicas disciplinas, & Physicae intima consensione illigatas, & ad vitam societatemque hominum oportunas longè plurimi Recentiorum excoluerunt. Nobis praestitutum haud quaquam est, recensere singulos, quando novimus id inter alios à Cl. Wolffio exactum fuisse[^15-s1]. Praecipuos duntaxat, atque eos, qui à Philosopho ignorari haud possunt proferemus.

52 The Mathematical disciplines, bound to Physics by an intimate agreement and serviceable to the life and society of men, have been cultivated by a great many of the Moderns. It is by no means our purpose to review them one by one, since we know that this has been done, among others, by the celebrated Wolff (r). We shall bring forward only the chief ones, and those who cannot be unknown to a Philosopher.

> [^15-s1]: Elem. Mathem. Tom. V.

[^15-s1]: Elem. of Mathematics, vol. V.

> 53 Et Astronomiae quidem, seculo Christi quinto decimo instauratores eminuerunt: Georg. Peubarchius; Johann. Regiomantanus; Copernicus; Tycho Brahe, systematis mundani conformatione clarus; Keplerus, Galilaeus; Hugenius; Hevelius; de la Hire; Newtonus; Cassini, &c. Longum foret eos omnes, qui diversas Matheseos partes evolverunt, consociare. Inter alios locum sibi hic quoque vindicant. Christoph. Clavius, Paulus Guldinus, Scheinerus, Grimaldus, Claud. Milliet de Chales, Ricciolus, D. de la Caille, D. Clairaut, Guido Grandi, P. Cametti Abbas Vallumbrosanus, D. La Lande, qui postremus omnium, sed suprà omnes de rebus Astronomicis tractavit.

53 And of Astronomy, indeed, there were eminent restorers in the fifteenth century of Christ: Georg Peurbach; Johann Regiomontanus; Copernicus; Tycho Brahe, famed for his arrangement of the world system; Kepler, Galileo; Huygens; Hevelius; de la Hire; Newton; Cassini, etc. It would take long to bring together all those who developed the various parts of Mathematics. Among others, these too claim a place here: Christopher Clavius, Paul Guldin, Scheiner, Grimaldi, Claude Milliet de Chales, Riccioli, D. de la Caille, D. Clairaut, Guido Grandi, Father Cametti, Abbot of Vallombrosa, and D. La Lande, who last of all, but above all, has treated of Astronomical matters.

> 54 Philosophiam denique naturalem quantis locupletarint accessionibus Studiosi Naturae scrutatores, definire paucis nequit. ¿ Quis enim inventa multiplicia, quis additam veterum inventis perfectionem, quis experimentorum numerum, modum venustatem; in iis, adcurationem, adtentionem, delectum, pagina comprehendat? Strictim nos, & Physicae restitutores, & novam disciplinae hujus formam adumbramus.

54 Finally, with how great accessions the Studious searchers of Nature have enriched natural Philosophy cannot be defined in a few words. For who could comprise in a page the manifold discoveries, the perfection added to the discoveries of the ancients, the number, manner and elegance of the experiments, and in them the accuracy, the attention, the selection? We shall briefly sketch both the restorers of Physics and the new form of this discipline.

[p. 16]

> 55 Excepere scilicet jam antehac nominatos Verulamium, Gassendum, Cartesium, Viri adprime illustres: Galilaeus Florentinus, Is doctrinam de motu, methodo perspicua tractandam suscepit aëris gravitatem commonstravit, vel ad eam detegendam lumen praetulit ceteris: tribuitur eidem inventio telescopii Astronomici, macularum solarium, & Jovis Satellitum quamvis illas à Patre Scheinero, hos á Simone Mario jam antea detectos alii velint.

55 After those already named before, namely Bacon, Gassendi and Descartes, there followed exceedingly illustrious Men: Galileo of Florence. He undertook to treat the doctrine of motion by a clear method; he demonstrated the weight of the air, or held up a light to the others for discovering it; to him is also attributed the discovery of the Astronomical telescope, of the sunspots, and of the Satellites of Jupiter, although others will have it that the former were detected earlier by Father Scheiner, the latter by Simon Marius.

> 56 Suum hunc magistrum in promovenda Physica consectatus est Evangelista Torricelli á quo tuborum ad mensurandam aëris gravitatem aptatorum usus traxit originem. Quid de reliquis inventoribus atque inventis dicam? Andr. Caesalpinus, Clementis VIII. P M. Archiater, Physicam illustravit, deprehensâ, aut explanatâ sanguinis circulatione, quanquam id Angli Harvaeo tribuant, alii Gomezio Pereyra Hispano, alii aliis.

56 This master of his was followed in advancing Physics by Evangelista Torricelli, from whom the use of tubes adapted to measuring the weight of the air took its origin. What shall I say of the remaining discoverers and discoveries? Andrea Cesalpino, Chief Physician to Clement VIII, Supreme Pontiff, illustrated Physics by having detected, or explained, the circulation of the blood, although the English attribute this to Harvey, others to the Spaniard Gómez Pereira, others to others.

> 57 Pequetus primum seculo superiore deprehendit, receptaculum Chyli. ¿ Quantum verò alii in diversis scientiae naturalis partibus desudarunt? Boyle, Digbaeus, Hombergius, Le Mery, Boerhaave in Chemia; Grewius, Sam. Morlandus, Camerarius, Vaillantius, Morisonius, Hermannus, Raius, Rivinus, Tournefortius, Linaeus, in Botanica? Profectò Mariotte, ope tentaminum, de motu, de plantis, aquis, coloribus &c. factorum: Paschal investigando aëris gravitatem, aequilibrium liquorum expendendo: Newtonus observationibus opticis, traductione Geometriae ad scientiam naturalem: Otto Guericke inventione Machinae pneumaticae; magnam Physicae lucem, par sibi, in republica literaria nomen conciliarunt. Ut jam nihil dicamus de Richerii, Cassini utriusque, Picardi, Maraldi, Malapertii, ac Sociorum conatibus; de Hookii; Lewenhoekii, Poweri, Hartsoekeri &c. microscopicis arcanis; Jallaberti, Watzoni, Waitzii, Boesi, Noletti, Musschembroekii, Franklini, Beccariae, Pauliani, Electricis experimentis; de Hauksbei, Fermatii, Carrei, Petitii, Sauveurii, Maiezieui, Ramazzini, Dodardi, Sanctorii, Fevilleei, Halesii, Cotesii, Ozanami, Desagullierii, Borelli, Malpighii, Rhedi, utriusque Bernoullii, Varignonii, Hermanni, Bulfingeri, Poleni, Euleri, Grandi, Teychemayeri, Krafftii, Verdriesii, Sturmii, Wolffi, & aliorum quam plurimorum diversis studiis, quorum in Physica persaepe recurret memoria.

57 Pecquet, in the last century, first detected the receptacle of the Chyle. And how much did others toil in the various parts of natural science? Boyle, Digby, Homberg, Lémery, Boerhaave in Chemistry; Grew, Sam. Morland, Camerarius, Vaillant, Morison, Hermann, Ray, Rivinus, Tournefort, Linnaeus in Botany? Indeed Mariotte, by means of trials made on motion, on plants, waters, colors, etc.; Pascal, by investigating the weight of the air and weighing the equilibrium of liquids; Newton, by his optical observations and the bringing of Geometry over to natural science; Otto Guericke, by the invention of the air pump, won great light for Physics and for themselves a matching name in the republic of letters. To say nothing now of the efforts of Richer, of both Cassinis, of Picard, Maraldi, Maupertuis and his Companions; of the microscopical secrets of Hooke, Leeuwenhoek, Power, Hartsoeker, etc.; of the Electrical experiments of Jallabert, Watson, Waitz, Bose, Nollet, Musschenbroek, Franklin, Beccaria, Paulian; of the various studies of Hauksbee, Fermat, Carré, Petit, Sauveur, Malézieu, Ramazzini, Dodart, Santorio, Feuillée, Hales, Cotes, Ozanam, Desaguliers, Borelli, Malpighi, Redi, both Bernoullis, Varignon, Hermann, Bülfinger, Poleni, Euler, Grandi, Teichmeyer, Krafft, Verdries, Sturm, Wolff, and very many others, whose memory will very often recur in the Physics.

## §. VII. — §. VII

> *Constitutae vtiliter Academiae Scientiarum.*

The Academies of Sciences, Usefully Established.

> 58 Porrhò quantas debeat Philosophia naturalis accessiones Academiis Scientiarum, literatorum nemo unus ignorat; [p. 17] Neque tamen has dum repraesentamus, animus nobis est, Gymnasia omnia, Scholasque publicas inde á Carolo Magno diversis in locis constitutas, referre: minus verò libet privata pauculorum conciliabula, aevi brevioris nempe, & ad publicam utilitatem vix quidem comparata, enumerare. Academiae nuncupatio Paulo II. P. M. Ecclesiam gubernante indita fuit Collegio eorum qui Romae commorati, colapsae priscae doctrinae restitutionem aliquam instituerunt.

58 Further, how great are the accessions that natural Philosophy owes to the Academies of Sciences, not one of the learned is unaware. Nor [p. 17] is it our intention, however, while we present these, to list all the Gymnasia and public Schools established in various places from Charlemagne onward; still less does it please us to enumerate the private little gatherings of a few, which were, namely, of short life and hardly fitted for the public utility. The name of Academy was given, while Paul II, Supreme Pontiff, governed the Church, to the College of those residing at Rome who had undertaken some restoration of the fallen ancient learning.

> 59 Eadem deinceps in urbe celebres Academiae patuerunt, videlicèt: *Humoristarum*, Auctore Paulo Mancino, nobili Romano, sic dictorum à pluvia è nubibus desidua, quod eis Symbolum cum lemmate: *Redit agmine dulci*, fuit Altera *Lynceorum*, ii hoc nomen ob Lyncis visu praecellentis dotem sumpserunt, ut perspicacitatem in scrutandis naturae operibus innuerent; quae seu à Federico Caesio, seu ab Angelo, Federici filio instituta, praecipuè Chemiam excoluit, virosque claros Gallilaeum à Gallilaeis, Fabium Columnam, atque alios dedit. Plura fuere item Collegia Romae, ut: *Ordinatorum*, *Delficorum*, *Incitatorum*, *Partheniorum*, *Renovatorum*, &c.[^17-s1] Venetiis Academia *Veneta*; alia etiam *Incognitorum* floruit. Patavii à Scipione Gonzaga *AEthereorum* Academia ortum duxit; altera Academicos *Animosos* comprehendit. Nec ceteris Italiae partibus suae deerant Academiae: Neapoli, Senae, Ravennae, Ferrariae, Veronae, Mediolani, Bononiae &c.

59 In the same city celebrated Academies afterwards opened, namely: that of the Humorists, founded by Paolo Mancini, a Roman nobleman, so called from the rain falling from the clouds, because this was their Emblem, with the motto Redit agmine dulci [it returns in a sweet stream]. The other was that of the Lynxes; they took this name from the gift of the Lynx, which excels in sight, so as to intimate their perspicacity in scrutinizing the works of nature; and this Academy, founded either by Federico Cesi or by Angelo, son of Federico, cultivated chiefly Chemistry, and produced illustrious men, Galileo Galilei, Fabio Colonna, and others. There were likewise several Colleges at Rome, such as those of the Ordinati, the Delfici, the Incitati, the Partenii, the Rinnovati, etc. (s); at Venice the Veneta Academy flourished, and also another, of the Incogniti. At Padua the Academy of the Eterei took its origin from Scipione Gonzaga; another comprised the Animosi Academicians. Nor did the other parts of Italy lack their Academies: at Naples, Siena, Ravenna, Ferrara, Verona, Milan, Bologna, etc.

> [^17-s1]: Johann. Ferro in Theatr. Emblemat.

[^17-s1]: Giovanni Ferro, in the Theater of Emblems.

> 60 In Hetruria, Florentiae, praeter Academiam *Furfurariorum*, seu *della Crusca* (ita nuncupatam, quod disceptationibus suis farinam puriorem, animorum cibum scilicèt, à furfuribus, hoc est: erroribus, secernerent Academici, praecipua tamen in id cura intenti, ut linguae Italicae nitorem impertirent) enituit Academia *Experimentalis*, seu del *Cimento*, Magni Hetruriae Ducis Leopoldi munificentia: qua effectum, ut & praecellentes in eam consociarentur Philosophi, & ad instituenda experimenta animus, adjumenta, oportunitas, Academicis adjicerentur. Secuta exemplum Britannia, quando sub annum circiter 1663. Caroli III. Regis auctoritate Londini erecta est *Societas Regia Angliae*. Gallia Academiarum Italiae, & Angliae exortu incitata; laetis etiam successibus suarummet: (Academiae nimirum *Gallicae* (Academie Françoise) anno 1637 instjtutae á Ludovico XIII. procurante Cardinale Richelieu, alterius item Academiae *Sculturae & Picturae*, quae 1664 sese explicuit, commota;) regiis, Ludovici XIV. auspiciis enatam conspexit Academiam *Scientiarum* anno 1666, quae anno 1699. novam Regis voluntate normam accepit. In Germania, quamvis initium anno 1652. factum fuerit Collegii Germanici *Naturae Curiosorum*, fatendum tamen, illud diu in infantia haesisse, ob Collegarum distantiam, patronorum defectum &c.

60 In Tuscany, at Florence, besides the Academy of the Bran-Sifters, or della Crusca (so named because in their disputations the Academicians separated the purer flour, namely the food of minds, from the bran, that is, from errors, being nevertheless intent with their chief care on imparting elegance to the Italian language), there shone forth the Experimental Academy, or del Cimento, by the munificence of Leopold, Grand Duke of Tuscany: by which it came about both that outstanding Philosophers were associated in it, and that spirit, aids and opportunities for setting up experiments were furnished to the Academicians. Britain followed the example when, about the year 1663, the Royal Society of England was erected at London by the authority of King Charles II. France, stirred by the rise of the Academies of Italy and England, and moved also by the happy successes of her own (namely of the French Academy (Académie Françoise), instituted in the year 1637 by Louis XIII through the agency of Cardinal Richelieu, and likewise of the other Academy, of Sculpture and Painting, which unfolded itself in 1664), saw the Academy of Sciences born under the auspices of King Louis XIV in the year 1666, which in the year 1699 received a new rule by the King’s will. In Germany, although a beginning of the German College of the Curious of Nature was made in the year 1652, it must nevertheless be confessed that it long remained stuck in its infancy, on account of the distance between its Colleagues, the lack of patrons, etc.

[p. 18]

> 61 Iccirco Leopoldus M. Imperator 1670. stimulos addidit Academicis, patrocinii spe ipsis oblata, suos ut conatus in promovendum hocce negotium conferrent. Et profectò votis tanti Principis responderunt studia Academiae Naturae Curiosorum; eodem quippe anno videlicet 1690 evulgare coeperunt *Miscellanea Curiose*. Anno 1690. Bononiae informata est Academia Philosophorum, qui scientias ad Mathésin, & Physicam pertinentes inter se partirentur; aliam exinde anno 1712 faciem indepta favore ac donis, Comitis Marsigli, nuncupataque: *Institutum Bononiense Scientiarum & Artium*. Fridericus Rex Borussiae, *Berolinensem*; Petrus Imperator Moscoviae, *Petropolitanam* Academias constituerunt. In nostra verò Hispania praeter Regiam Hispalensem Academiam, & Cantabricam, non desunt aliae pro Scientiarum, & Artium cultu atque incremento. Jam, quae ac quanta ex Academiis, favore, largitate, curâ Principum stabilitis in Physicam praecipuè, dimanarint emolumenta, & post haec sint exspectanda, facilè cernitur. Loquuntur illud Physicorum libri; hoc Academicorum industria, sagacitas, ardor, pollicentur.

61 For this reason the Emperor Leopold the Great in 1670 added spurs to the Academicians, holding out to them the hope of his patronage, so that they might devote their efforts to promoting this business. And indeed the studies of the Academy of the Curious of Nature answered the wishes of so great a Prince; for in that same year, namely 1670, they began to publish the Miscellanea Curiosa. In the year 1690 an Academy of Philosophers was formed at Bologna, who were to share among themselves the sciences pertaining to Mathematics and Physics; it afterwards, in the year 1712, took on another face through the favor and gifts of Count Marsigli, and was named the Institute of Sciences and Arts of Bologna. Frederick, King of Prussia, established the Academy of Berlin; Peter, Emperor of Muscovy, that of Petersburg. In our own Spain, moreover, besides the Royal Academy of Seville and the Cantabrian, there is no lack of others for the cultivation and increase of the Sciences and Arts. Now, what and how great advantages have flowed, chiefly into Physics, from the Academies established by the favor, liberality and care of Princes, and what are to be expected hereafter, is easily seen. The former the books of the Physicists declare; the latter the industry, sagacity and ardor of the Academicians promise.

## §. VIII. — §. VIII

> *Ephemeridum Literariarum institutio.*

The Institution of Literary Journals.

> 62 Ecquid ad extremum, arbitramur illud esse, quod Physica recentior Ephemeridum seu literariorum actorum institutioni debet? Anno seculi superioris sexagessimoquinto (antehac namque his adjumentis orbis eruditus caruit) vir magnae mentis, promovendarumque literarum perstudiosus, Dominus Sallo, Supremae Parisiis Curiae Senator, consilium suscepit adornandi Ephemerides universales, quod & exsecutus est ipse primum, inscripsitque opus: *Diarium Eruditorum* (Journal des Scavans). Excepit anno 1666. auctoris laborem Cl. Gallois ad annum 1674. continenter in hebdomadas singulas Diarium operosè complexus; quod exinde persecutus est Cl. de la Roque. Regiae Scientiarum Academiae Historia, & Commentarii (Histoire & Memoires de l' Academie des Sciences) quotannis cum orbe erudito communicantur.

62 What, finally, do we judge it to be that the newer Physics owes to the institution of Journals, or literary acts? In the sixty-fifth year of the last century (for before this the learned world lacked these aids) a man of great mind and most zealous for the promotion of letters, Monsieur Sallo, Senator of the Supreme Court at Paris, formed the plan of preparing universal Journals; this he himself also first carried out, and he entitled the work Diarium Eruditorum (Journal des Sçavans). In the year 1666 the celebrated Gallois took over the author’s labor, laboriously compiling the Journal continuously week by week up to the year 1674; and it was afterwards carried on by the celebrated de la Roque. The History and Memoirs of the Royal Academy of Sciences (Histoire & Mémoires de l’Académie des Sciences) are communicated annually to the learned world.

> 63 Anno de hinc seculi hujus primo, Ducis Coenomanensis auspiciis, prodire coeperunt Acta Trivoltiensia (Memoires de Trevoux, pour servir a l' Histoire des Sciences, & des beaux Arts). Italia quoque anno 1668. eruditas Ephemerides (Giornale de Literati) vulgavit. In Germania literati quidam è Saxoniae Electoratu, conjuncto labore, sub annum 1682. (Acta Eruditorum Lipsiae) seu Ephemerides, dederunt. Hollandia suam isthic desiderari industriam haud passa, anno 1684. Amstelaedami *excerpta Reipublicae Literariae* (Nouvelles de la Reipublique des lettres) procúdit.

63 Next, in the first year of this century, under the auspices of the Duke of Maine, the Acta Trivoltiensia (Mémoires de Trévoux, pour servir à l’Histoire des Sciences, & des beaux Arts) began to appear. Italy too, in the year 1668, published learned Journals (Giornale de’ Letterati). In Germany certain men of letters from the Electorate of Saxony, with joint labor, produced about the year 1682 the Acta Eruditorum of Leipzig, or Journals. Holland, not suffering its own industry to be found wanting here, brought out at Amsterdam in the year 1684 the Excerpta Reipublicae Literariae (Nouvelles de la République des lettres).

[p. 19]

> 64 Seculi jam hujus anno tertio decimo Hagae Comitum *Dirium Literarium* (Journal Litteraire à la Haye) pluribus operas suas jungentibus, prodiit. Praetermitto commentarios Societatis Anglicanae (Transactions Philosophiques) inde ab anno 1665. editos: sub primordia hujus seculi Ephemerides Literarias Magnae Britanniae: anno 1720 vulgatam *Bibliothecam Germanicam*, seu Hstoriam literariam Germaniae Regionumque. Anno 1737 in Hispania nostra in lucem edi coepit *el Diario de los Literatos*, egregium quidem opus, atque utinam in hanc usque diem protractum.

64 In the thirteenth year of this present century the Diarium Literarium (Journal Litteraire à la Haye) appeared at The Hague, several men joining their labors. I pass over the transactions of the English Society (Transactions Philosophiques), published from the year 1665; the Literary Journals of Great Britain at the beginning of this century; the Bibliotheca Germanica, published in the year 1720, or the literary History of Germany and its Regions. In the year 1737 there began to be brought out in our Spain el Diario de los Literatos, an excellent work indeed; and would that it had been carried on down to this day.

> 65 Nec memoro *Acta Instituti Bononiensis*, *Petropolitana*, *Suecica*, *Mercurios Eruditos* (les Mercures Sçavans) &c. Hanc in classem inserenda monumenta eorum, qui Historiam naturae collegerunt, viam praeeuntibus (Aristotelis aliorumque vetustiorum exemplo) Caio Plinio secundo, seu seniore, qui aetate Vespasiani, ac Titi clarus, septem supra triginta Historiae naturalis libros congessit; quem secuti Solinus, Dioscorides: item Claudio AEliano, septemdecim librorum Historiae animalium auctore, Hadriani Imp. tempore, his, inquam, praeeuntibus, argumentum isthoc tractarunt: Conradus Gesnerus, anno 1516. in Helvetia prognatus, insignis Physicus, & Philologus, iccircò *Plinii Germanici* cognomento donatus, praeter alia, *Historiam animalium* quatuor voluminibus complexus; Rembertus Dodonaeus, in Brabantia 1517. ortus, Caesarum Maximiliani II, & Rudolphi II. Medicus, editis stirpium, florum &c. *Historiis* clarus; Ulysses Aldrovandus, *Dendrologia naturali*, *Musaeo metallico*, *historia Monstrorum*, *Serpentum*, item, ac *Draconum* conscriptis celeber.

65 Nor do I mention the Acta of the Institute of Bologna, the Petersburg and the Swedish, the Learned Mercuries (les Mercures Sçavans), etc. In this class must be placed the monuments of those who have collected the History of nature; the way being led (after the example of Aristotle and other more ancient writers) by Gaius Plinius Secundus, or the Elder, who, famous in the age of Vespasian and Titus, compiled thirty-seven books of natural History; he was followed by Solinus and Dioscorides; likewise by Claudius Aelian, author of seventeen books of the History of animals, in the time of the Emperor Hadrian. With these, I say, leading the way, the following treated this subject: Conrad Gesner, born in Switzerland in the year 1516, a distinguished Physicist and Philologist, and for this reason given the surname of the German Pliny, who, besides other things, comprised a History of animals in four volumes; Rembert Dodoens, born in Brabant in 1517, Physician to the Emperors Maximilian II and Rudolph II, famous for the Histories he published of plants, flowers, etc.; Ulisse Aldrovandi, celebrated for having written a natural Dendrology, a Museum metallicum, a history of Monsters, of Serpents, and also of Dragons.

> 66 Quibus addenda Verulamii *Silva silvarum* seu *Historiae naturalis centuriae decem:* D. de Buffon Opera Histor. Natur. (Description du Cabinet du Roy). Quid his etiam adjumentis, Physica praecipuè, debeat, referre non vacat singillatim. Quot enimverò scientiae hujus capita in examen vocata? Quot naturae phaenomena detecta? Quot errores ex animis abstersi, evulsa dubia, opiniones emendatae? Pluribus ista persequitur Regnault diffusè commonstrans, Physicam parte omni seculis quidem hisce postremis redditam fuisse perfectiorem. I. Conjecturas veterum in examen ducendo. II. Ipsam naturam scrutando. III. Disciplinam è legibus methodi tractando. IV. Observationes exigendo, iterando experimenta, instrumenta utilia inveniendo. V. Stabiliendo Academias. VI. Ephemerides constituendo.

66 To these must be added Bacon’s Sylva sylvarum, or Ten Centuries of natural History, and the Works on Natural History of M. de Buffon (Description du Cabinet du Roy). What Physics in particular owes to these aids too, there is no leisure to relate one by one. For how many heads of this science have been called into examination? How many phenomena of nature discovered? How many errors wiped from minds, doubts uprooted, opinions emended? These things are treated at greater length by Regnault, who shows diffusely that Physics has in these last centuries been rendered more perfect in every part: I. By bringing the conjectures of the ancients to examination. II. By scrutinizing nature itself. III. By treating the discipline according to the laws of method. IV. By requiring observations, repeating experiments, inventing useful instruments. V. By establishing Academies. VI. By instituting Journals.

> 67 Atque his definire libuit *Historiam Philosophiae*: quam quidem, si cum prolixis Laertii, Gassendi, Hornii, Stanleii, Jonsii, Vosii, Bruckeri operibns conferas, haud esse aliud intelliges, atque *Epitomen*; ea tamen lege adornatam comperies, ut praecipua hujus argumenti capita sint pertractata, delibata cétera, nihil denique eorum, quae ad primam Philosophorum institutionem pertinent, ac sufficiunt, praetermissum.

67 And with this it has pleased us to conclude the History of Philosophy: which indeed, if you compare it with the lengthy works of Laertius, Gassendi, Horn, Stanley, Jonsius, Vossius and Brucker, you will understand to be nothing other than an Epitome; you will find it, however, arranged on this principle, that the chief heads of this subject have been treated thoroughly, the rest touched upon, and, finally, nothing omitted of those things which pertain to, and suffice for, the first instruction of Philosophers.
