## EXERCITATIONES — SCHOLASTIC EXERCISES

## SCHOLASTICAE IN LOGICAM. — ON LOGIC

> EXERCITATIO I.

EXERCISE I .

> ¿An idea sive simplex rei perceptio possit esse falsa?

Whether an idea, or the simple perception of a thing, can be false?

> 190 Veritas Logica, ut dictum est supra, est convenientia idearum nostrarum cum objectó, & haec etiam dicitur veritas *cognitionis*, unde qualiscumque fuerit idea, sive simplex, sive complexa, illius veritas in sola consensione cum re percepta, citra adfirmationem, aut negationem consistit. Sed veritas *judicii*, quae *compositionis* dicitur in adfirmatione aut negatione sita est. Atque ita judicium censétur verum, quum dicit id esse, quod re vera est, vel negat esse, quod non est: falsum verò si adfirmet, esse, quod non est, vel negat esse quod est. His positis.

ogical truth, as was said above, is the agreement of our ideas with the 190 L object, and this is also called the truth of cognition; whence, whatever the idea may be, whether simple or complex, its truth consists solely in agreement with the thing perceived, apart from affirmation or negation. But the truth of judgment, which is called the truth of composition, lies in affirmation or negation. And so a judgment is deemed true when it says that that is which really is, or denies that that is which is not; but false if it affirms that that is which is not, or denies that that is which is. These things being posited,

> 191 Dico I. perceptio aut idea sive simplex, sive complexa potest esse vera. Prob.: tunc perceptio dicitur vera, quum est objectó suo consentánea; sed perceptio sive simplex, sive complexa, potest esse objecto suo consentánea: ergo. Prob. min.: percéptió *montis*, quae est simplex, & perceptio *montis praerupti*, quae est complexa consentíre possunt cum objectis suis, seu rebus perceptis, ut omnes intelligunt: ergo.

191 I say I. A perception or idea, whether simple or complex, can be true. Proof: a perception is called true when it agrees with its object; but a perception, whether simple or complex, can agree with its object: therefore. Proof of the minor: the perception of a mountain, which is simple, and the perception of a steep mountain, which is complex, can agree with their objects, or the things perceived, as all understand: therefore.

> 192 Dico 2: perceptio sive simplex, sive complexa propriè loquendó falsa nunquam dici potest. Prob.: perceptio falsa propriè loquendo dicenda foret ea, quae objecto percepto esset dissentánea, sed perceptio sive simplex sive complexa non potest dici objecto dissentánea; nam si repraesentat rem praesentem sicuti est, ex. gr. aurum praesente auro, tunc objecto consentánea est, ut nemo diffitetur. Quòd si objectum praesens non repraesentet, sed aliquod aliud, ex. gr. si praesente [p. 63] *orichalco* aurum exhibeat, vera quidem est auri perceptio, minimè *orichalci*, adeòque non est falsa orichalci perceptio, sed nulla, seu minimè est orichalci perceptio: ergo perceptio sive simplex, sive complexa proprie loquendo dici non potest falsa.

192 I say 2: a perception, whether simple or complex, can never, properly speaking, be called false. Proof: that perception would, properly speaking, have to be called false which disagreed with the object perceived; but a perception, whether simple or complex, cannot be said to disagree with its object; for if it represents a present thing as it is, e.g. gold when gold is present, then it agrees with its object, as no one denies. But if it does not represent the present object, but something else, e.g. if, when brass is present, [p. 63] it presents gold, it is indeed a true perception of gold, but by no means of brass, and so it is not a false perception of brass, but none, or rather it is no perception of brass at all: therefore a perception, whether simple or complex, cannot, properly speaking, be called false.

> 193 Dico 3.: perceptio sive simplex, sive complexa dici potest falsa *materialiter*, ut ajunt, & occasione subsequentis judicii. Prob.: ut perceptio vel idea ita dici possit falsa, satis est eam esse posse materiam & occasionem judicii falsi; sed perceptio maximè complexa potest esse materia & occasio subsequentis judicii falsi: ergo. Prob. min: perceptio auri praesente orichalco, esse potest occasio cur judicet aliquis aurum esse id quod tantùm est orichalcum: ergo.

193 I say 3: a perception, whether simple or complex, can be called false materially, as they say, and by occasion of the subsequent judgment. Proof: for a perception or idea to be capable of being called false in this way, it is enough that it can be the matter and the occasion of a false judgment; but a perception, especially a complex one, can be the matter and the occasion of a subsequent false judgment: therefore. Proof of the minor: the perception of gold when brass is present can be the occasion for someone’s judging that to be gold which is only brass: therefore.

> Argumenta solvuntur.

THE ARGUMENTS ARE ANSWERED.

> 194 Opp. 1. contra 1. perceptio sive simplex sive complexa nihil adfirmat vel negat: ergo non potest esse vera. Dist. conseq. non potest esse vera veritate compositionis, quae ad judicium pertinet, conc.: veritate simplici aut complexa, quae est veritas cognitionis cum objecto percepto convenientis, nego. *Secundo*: eadem ratio datur ut perceptio simplex falsa esse nequeat, quàm ut possit esse vera; sed per nos potest esse vera: ergo & falsa. Nego maj. argumenti: nam tùm perceptio esset falsa, quum objecto repraesentato & percepto non conveniret, quod utique nunquàm dici potest, imò ideo est vera; quia semper est objecto repraesentato consentánea, si autem idea non sit objecto repraesentando consentánea non erit falsa, sed *nulla* ut diximus.

194 Obj. 1, against I. A perception, whether simple or complex, affirms or denies nothing: therefore it cannot be true. Dist. the consequent: it cannot be true with the truth of composition, which belongs to judgment, I grant; with simple or complex truth, which is the truth of a cognition agreeing with the object perceived, I deny. Secondly: the same reason holds for a simple perception’s being unable to be false as for its being able to be true; but on our view it can be true: therefore also false. I deny the major of the argument: for a perception would be false only when it did not agree with the object represented and perceived, which certainly can never be said; nay, it is true precisely because it always agrees with the object represented; and if an idea does not agree with the object that was to be represented, it will not be false, but none, as we have said.

> 195 Opp. 2: idea quae non repraesentat objectum sicuti est, est falsa ratione sui, sed idea auri praesente orichalco non repraesentat objectum sicuti est: ergo. Dist. min.: non repraesentat sicuti est objectum, quod est praesens, & quod repraesentandum foret, conc.: non repraesentat objectum perceptum sicuti est, nego & conseq. *Dices*: perceptio complexa est verùm judicium, judicio enim aequivalet, sed judicium potest esse falsum: ergo & perceptio complexa. Nego maj.: perceptio enim sive simplex sit sive complexa nihil adfirmat vel negat, unde non potest ipsa esse judicium, quamvis dicatur ipsi judicio aequivalére. *Instabis*: perceptio complexa ex. gr. *montis aurei*, vel *baculi fracti* tribuit aliquid monti, nempè esse aureum, & détrahit baculo integritatem; sed cogitatio quae aliquid alicui subjecto tribuit, aut ab eo détrahit aequívalet judicio, seu est verùm judicium: ergo.

195 Obj. 2: an idea which does not represent the object as it is, is false in itself; but the idea of gold when brass is present does not represent the object as it is: therefore. Dist. the minor: it does not represent as it is the object which is present and which ought to have been represented, I grant; it does not represent the perceived object as it is, I deny; and I deny the consequent. You will say: a complex perception is a true judgment, for it is equivalent to a judgment; but a judgment can be false: therefore a complex perception can be too. I deny the major: for a perception, whether it be simple or complex, affirms or denies nothing, whence it cannot itself be a judgment, although it is said to be equivalent to a judgment. You will insist: a complex perception, e.g. of a golden mountain, or of a broken stick, attributes something to the mountain, namely that it is golden, and takes away from the stick its integrity; but a cognition which attributes something to some subject, or takes something away from it, is equivalent to a judgment, or is a true judgment: therefore.

[p. 64]

> 196 Dist. min.: cogitatio quae aliquid alicui subjecto tribuit, aut ab eo détrahit per adfirmationem, aut negationem est verum judicium, conc. per conceptionem tantum subjecti simul cum adtributo sine adfirmatione, aut negatione: nego. *Dices*: perceptio *Dei injusti* est falsa: ergo aliqua dari potest perceptio falsa. Respondeo negando hypóthesim, videlicèt dari posse notionem Dei injusti; vel enim nomine Dei intelligitur id quod necessariò debet intelligi, nimirùm ens summè perfectum, vel non? Si primum, nulla est, vel esse potest perceptio Dei injusti, quia évidens daretur contradictio; si secundum nihil ad rem facit, quum falsa non sit illa idea quae enti imperfecto injustitiam adtribuit. Id ipsum dicimus de iis perceptionibus, quae *chymaericae* dicuntur; etenim vel nullae sunt si contradictoria involvant, vel sunt verae si nulla in illis contradictio habeatur, quia congruunt his rebus, quae percipiuntur, etsi res illae non existant in rerum natura.

196 Dist. the minor: a cognition which attributes something to some subject, or takes something away from it, by affirmation or negation, is a true judgment, I grant; by a mere conception of the subject together with the attribute, without affirmation or negation, I deny. You will say: the perception of an unjust God is false: therefore some false perception can be given. I reply by denying the hypothesis, namely that there can be a notion of an unjust God; for either by the name of God is understood what must necessarily be understood, namely a supremely perfect being, or not? If the first, there is not, nor can there be, any perception of an unjust God, because there would be an evident contradiction; if the second, it is nothing to the purpose, since that idea is not false which attributes injustice to an imperfect being. We say the very same of those perceptions which are called chimerical: for either they are none, if they involve contradictories, or they are true, if no contradiction is found in them, because they agree with the things that are perceived, even though those things do not exist in the nature of things.

> 197 Opp. demum: idea debet exprímere id à quo excitatur; sed idea auri quae in nobis excitatur praesente orichalco non exprímit orichalcum: ergo id non exprímit quod debet exprímere: ergo est falsa. Dist. maj.: omnis idea, nego; major pars earum, concedo. Plurima enim sunt corpora natura diversa, sed planè similia quoad aliquas sensibiles qualitates. Certum est, autem ex símilibus motionibus in organis sensuum factis, easdem ideas in mente necessariò excitari: ergo impedire nequímus, quin corpora dissimilia similes quandoquè ideas in nobis éxcitent, ac proinde quin aliqua idea rem interdum menti exhibeat, omninò diversam ab ea, à qua excitatur.

197 Obj., finally: an idea must express that by which it is excited; but the idea of gold which is excited in us when brass is present does not express brass: therefore it does not express what it ought to express: therefore it is false. Dist. the major: every idea, I deny; the greater part of them, I grant. For there are very many bodies different in nature, but quite similar as to certain sensible qualities. It is certain, moreover, that from similar motions made in the organs of the senses the same ideas are necessarily excited in the mind: therefore we cannot prevent dissimilar bodies from sometimes exciting similar ideas in us, nor, accordingly, some idea from sometimes presenting to the mind a thing altogether different from that by which it is excited.

> EXERCITATIO II.

EXERCISE II .

> ¿ An omnes ideae originem ducant à sensibus? Philosophorum opiniones exponuntur, & refutantur, nostraque sententia stabilitur.

Whether all ideas take their origin from the senses? The opinions of the Philosophers are set forth and refuted, and our own view is established.

> 198 Perceptionum duae species distinguuntur. Prima est *intellectio pura*, per quam mens citra phantasmatis, aut speciei corporeae subsidium quidpiam cognoscit, ex. gr. quum percipit se, suas cogitationes, & adfectiones, puta gaudium, tristitiam, &c. Ubi observandum, eam [p. 65] perceptionem *conscientiam* adpellari, quia suarum cogitationum aut adfectionum sibi conscia est, secumque quodammodò, scit, se cogitare. Altera perceptionis species, dicitur *imaginatio*, de qua jam dictum. (§. 12.)

wo species of perceptions are distinguished. The first is pure intellection, by 198 T which the mind knows something without the aid of a phantasm or of a corporeal species, e.g. when it perceives itself, its thoughts and affections, say joy, sadness, etc. Where it must be observed that this [p. 65] perception is called consciousness, because it is conscious to itself of its own thoughts or affections, and in a certain way knows within itself that it is thinking. The other species of perception is called imagination, of which we have already spoken (§. 12.)

> 199 Ideas omnes ab animo adquiri certissimum est, sed quomodo eas acquirat non satis convenit inter Philosophos: *Lucretius* [^65-s1] putat, ex ipsis rebus objectis, avolare simulacra quaedam, quae sensus ingrediuntur, & motus similes in cérebro faciunt, & hoc modo mentem ideas adquirere. Quod falsum omninò est: nam juxta ipsum, haec idóla sunt corpora, quumque continenter à superficiebus avolarent, hae demum raderentur, & perirent funditùs. Praeterea res abstractae, ut ratiocinationes, & volitiones, &c. intelligi non possent quia ex his simulacra ad sensus non veniunt: at haec experientiae répugnant.

199 That all ideas are acquired by the mind is most certain; but how it acquires them is not sufficiently agreed among the Philosophers. Lucretius (z) thinks that from the objects themselves certain images fly off, which enter the senses and make similar motions in the brain, and that in this way the mind acquires its ideas. Which is altogether false: for according to him these idols are bodies, and since they would be continually flying off from the surfaces, these would at length be worn away and perish utterly. Moreover, abstract things, such as reasonings and volitions, etc., could not be understood, because no images come from them to the senses; but these things are repugnant to experience.

> [^65-s1]: De Rerum nat. lib. 4. Init, & praesertim ℣. 703. & seqq.

[^65-s1]: On the Nature of Things, bk. 4, beginning, and especially v. 703 ff.

> 200 Aristotelici nullas admittunt ideas purè intellectuales, sed credunt à corporeis sensibus omnes rerum imagines animum acquirere. Hinc celeberrimum apud illos est effatum illud, [^65-s2] *nihil est in intellectu quod prius non fuerit in sensu*. Eandem sententiam tuetur Gassendus. *Mallebranchius* [^65-s3] putat mentem in Deo, cui est essentialiter conjuncta, tanquam in speculo omnia vidére, quod falsum est, nam mens non videt in Deo tanquam in speculo. Nam speculum omnibus intuentibus, eandem rem offert: tamen non omnia vident omnes. Indocti ea non vident, quae docti intelligunt. (Vide dicta §. 86.)

200 The Aristotelians admit no purely intellectual ideas, but believe that the mind acquires all the images of things from the bodily senses. Hence that most celebrated maxim among them (a): nothing is in the intellect which was not first in the sense. Gassendi defends the same opinion. Malebranche (b) thinks that the mind sees all things in God, to whom it is essentially joined, as in a mirror; which is false, for the mind does not see in God as in a mirror. For a mirror offers the same thing to all who look into it: yet not all men see all things. The unlearned do not see what the learned understand. (See what was said in §. 86.)

> [^65-s2]: Aristot. de anima lib. 3. cap. 5. & 8.

[^65-s2]: Aristotle, On the Soul, bk. 3, ch. 5 and 8.

> [^65-s3]: Recherche de la Verité lib. 1. cap. 2.

[^65-s3]: Recherche de la Verité, bk. 1, ch. 2.

> 201 Cartesiani volunt intellectum nostrum esse potentiam merè passivam, quae non producat ipse suas ideas, sed eas à Deo recipiat. Triplicis verò generis ideas distinguunt, *innatas*, *adventitias*, & *factitias*. *Innatas* vocant ideas, quae menti nostrae statim ab ortu divinitùs impraesae sunt, & à sola prima causa, sine corporis, aut cujuscumque causae secundae subsidio suam habent oríginem. *Adventitias* dicunt illas, quae occasione motuum in organis corporeis producuntur. Tales sunt sensationes *caloris*, *soni*, *odoris*, &c. *Factitias* denique vocant ideas, quae ex illis, quibus jam mens nostra informata est, componuntur, ut quum aliquis ex idea montis, & idea auri, montem aureum sibi fingit.

201 The Cartesians hold that our intellect is a merely passive power, which does not itself produce its ideas, but receives them from God. And they distinguish ideas of a threefold kind: innate, adventitious, and factitious. They call innate the ideas which were divinely impressed on our mind immediately from its birth, and which have their origin from the first cause alone, without the aid of the body or of any second cause whatsoever. They call adventitious those which are produced on the occasion of motions in the bodily organs. Such are the sensations of heat, sound, smell, etc. Factitious, finally, they call the ideas which are composed from those with which our mind has already been informed, as when someone, from the idea of a mountain and the idea of gold, makes up for himself a golden mountain.

> 202 De adventitiis, factitiisque ideis nulla potest esse dubitatio. Verùm quod ideas innatas spectat, quaestionis status non [p. 66] satis clarè exponi solet, ut optimè advertit Cl. *Jacquier*. Si enim hoc nomine intelligant *ideas menti perpetuò praesentes*, nulla potest esse controversia. ¿ Quis enim dixerit aliquam in nobis esse ideam, quam *indesinenter* contemplemur? Si autem significare voluerint ideas, quae ante omnem experientiam, omnemque ratiocinationem semper praestò sunt; nemo sane hujusmodi ideae meminit? de qua ante omnem experientiam, omnemque ratiocinationem mens cogitaverit.

202 About adventitious and factitious ideas there can be no doubt. But as regards innate ideas, the state of the question is not [p. 66] usually set out clearly enough, as the celebrated Jacquier excellently observes. For if by this name they understand ideas perpetually present to the mind, there can be no controversy. For who would say that there is some idea in us which we contemplate unceasingly? But if they mean ideas which are always at hand before all experience and all reasoning, no one surely remembers any idea of this kind which the mind thought of before all experience and all reasoning.

> 203 At si per ideas innatas intelligamus notiones illas, quae aliquàndò sine objectorum externorum occasione, & facili atque expedito rationis usu acquiruntur, *innatas* in hoc tantùm sensu ideas dicimus esse admittendas. Et re vera quidem, nihil aliud significari posse vocabulo idearum innatarum fatebitur is, qui gravissimam hanc quaestionem non ex disputationis aestu, aut definitionis ambiguitate, sed ex proprio conscientiae testimonio expendet. His explicatis sit conclusio contra Peripateticos, & Gassendum, & Lockium.

203 But if by innate ideas we understand those notions which are sometimes acquired without the occasion of external objects, and by an easy and ready use of reason, we say that ideas are to be admitted as innate in this sense only. And in truth nothing else can be signified by the term innate ideas, as he will confess who weighs this most weighty question, not from the heat of disputation or the ambiguity of a definition, but from the proper testimony of his own consciousness. These things explained, let the conclusion be against the Peripatetics, Gassendi, and Locke.

> 204 Plures habemus ideas purè intellectuales, quarum aliquas facili rationis usu acquirimus. Prob.: in iis quae ad animam pertinent, nulla tutior regula adhiberi debet, quam intimum conscientiae testimonium: atqui conscientiae testimonio experimur nos multa percipere per intellectionem puram absque ulla imagine corporea: ergo plures habemus ideas purè intellectuales. Prob. min.: plures menti nostrae obversantur ideae rerum, quae ab omni materia & sensibili qualitate prorsùs secretae sunt, quales sunt ideae *assensus* & *dissensus*, *justitiae*, *intelligentiae*, *Dei*, ergo. Prob. antec.: assensus & dissensus justitia, &c. & alia idearum nostrarum objecta nullam habent similitudinem cum rebus sensibilibus, nulla qualitate sensibili praedita sunt, nullaque proindè sensatione aut imaginatione repraesentari possunt.

204 We have many purely intellectual ideas, some of which we acquire by an easy use of reason. Proof: in those things which pertain to the mind, no safer rule ought to be applied than the inmost testimony of consciousness: but by the testimony of consciousness we experience that we perceive many things by pure intellection without any bodily image: therefore we have many purely intellectual ideas. Proof of the minor: many ideas of things present themselves to our mind which are entirely separated from all matter and sensible quality, such as are the ideas of assent and dissent, of justice, of intelligence, of God: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: assent and dissent, justice, etc., and other objects of our ideas have no likeness to sensible things, are endowed with no sensible quality, and accordingly can be represented by no sensation or imagination.

> 205 Confirmatur conclusio; illae ideae sunt purè intellectuales quarum objecta nec colorata sunt, nec sápida, nec sonóra, nec ulla sensibili qualitate adfecta, ut ait Sanctus Augustinus, [^66-s1] atqui multae sunt ideae quarum objecta nec colorata sunt, &c., cujusmodi sunt idea *entis generatim*, idea *Dei*, &c.: ergo dantur ideae purè intellectuales.

205 The conclusion is confirmed: those ideas are purely intellectual whose objects are neither colored, nor savory, nor sonorous, nor affected by any sensible quality, as St. Augustine says (c): but there are many ideas whose objects are neither colored, etc., such as are the idea of being in general, the idea of God, etc.: therefore purely intellectual ideas are given.

> [^66-s1]: Lib. 10. Confess. n. 17. alias cap. 10.

[^66-s1]: Bk. 10 of the Confessions, no. 17, otherwise ch. 10.

## Responsiones ad objecta. — REPLIES TO THE OB JECTIONS

> 206 Opp. 1: si qua sit idea purè intellectualis quae ortum non habeat à sensibus, maximè idea entis generatim, idea Dei, [p. 67] &c.: sed istae ideae ortum ducunt à sensibus: ergo. Nego min.: quia ens generatim nec coloratum est, nec sápidum, nec ulla sensibili qualitate praéditum. Sed probabis minorem: idea entis generatim formatur per abstractionem â singularibus, & individuis corporibus; sed singularia corpora sensibus percipiuntur: ergo talis idea ortum ducit à sensibus. Ad probationem dist. maj.: formatur per abstractionem à rebus corporeis & spiritualibus, conc. à rebus corporeis tantùm, nego maj. & conseq.

206 Obj. 1: if there is any purely intellectual idea which does not have its origin from the senses, it is above all the idea of being in general, the idea of God, [p. 67] etc.: but these ideas take their origin from the senses: therefore. I deny the minor: because being in general is neither colored, nor savory, nor endowed with any sensible quality. But you will prove the minor: the idea of being in general is formed by abstraction from singular and individual bodies; but singular bodies are perceived by the senses: therefore such an idea takes its origin from the senses. To the proof, I distinguish the major: it is formed by abstraction from corporeal and spiritual things, I grant; from corporeal things only, I deny the major and the consequent.

> 207 Ens generatim dicimus id quod potest existere, itaque etsi nulla esse corpora fingeretur, hanc entis ideam formare possémus ex íntima operationum mentis nostrae conscientia, et sine ulla ad corpus relatione. Praeterea si haec idea ortum tantum duceret à sensibus non omnia planè entis genera in sua extensione comprehenderet, sed tantùm entia corporea, quod tamen est falsum. *Instabis* 1: Nihil est in intellectu quod prius non fuerit in sensu; ergo ideae omnes ac proindè idea entis generatim pendet à sensibus Dist. antec. quod prius non fuerit in sensu externo vel interno, conc. in sensu tantùm externo, nego antec. & conseq.

207 We call being in general that which can exist; and so, even if it were supposed that there are no bodies, we could form this idea of being from the inmost consciousness of the operations of our mind, and without any relation to body. Moreover, if this idea took its origin only from the senses, it would not comprehend in its extension absolutely all the genera of being, but only corporeal beings; which, however, is false. You will insist 1: Nothing is in the intellect which was not first in the sense; therefore all ideas, and accordingly the idea of being in general, depend on the senses. Dist. the antecedent: which was not first in the external or the internal sense, I grant; in the external sense only, I deny the antecedent, and the consequent.

> 208 Duplicem esse idearum originem, fatémur, sensum externum, quo rerum corporearum ideas acquirimus, & sensum internum, quo per mentis adtentionem, ac reflexionem in proprias operationes rerum spiritualium idéas comparamus. *Instabis* 2: atqui nihil est in intellectu quod priùs non fuerit in sensu externo tantùm: ergo falsa est distinctio. Prob. subsumpta: illud priùs fuit in sensu externo, quod à nobis non cognoscitur nisi per comparationem cum rebus corporeis; sed res spirituales non cognoscimus, nisi per comparationem cum rebus corporeis: ergo. Prob. min.: Deus est substantia spiritualis; sed Dei nullam habemus ideam, nisi quia sub imagine Venerandi Senis illum nobis repraesentamus: ergo.

208 We confess that there is a twofold origin of ideas: the external sense, by which we acquire the ideas of corporeal things, and the internal sense, by which, through the mind’s attention and reflection upon its own operations, we procure the ideas of spiritual things. You will insist 2: but nothing is in the intellect which was not first in the external sense only: therefore the distinction is false. Proof of the subsumption: that was first in the external sense which is not known by us except by comparison with corporeal things; but we do not know spiritual things except by comparison with corporeal things: therefore. Proof of the minor: God is a spiritual substance; but we have no idea of God except insofar as we represent Him to ourselves under the image of a Venerable Old Man: therefore.

> 209 Respondeo negando minorem: verùm quidem est, mentem nostram sine summa cura & adtentione, ideas ab omni prorsùs labe corporea expurgare non posse, & hac de causa rudiores homines nihil nisi cum imagine percipiunt. At illae imagines Senis, ex. gr. & juvenis alati non sunt ipsae Dei, & Angelorum ideae, sed mera phantasmata, quae ideas illas comitantur. Nam si nullam aliam Dei ideam haberemus, praeter ideam Venerabilis Senis, omnia quae de Deo formamus judicia, nobis adparére deberent prorsùs falsa, utporè huic ideae contraria: illa enim judicia falsa esse credimus, quae contraria sunt ideis rerum quas in mente habemus; ideòque non possemus judicare, Deum esse incorporeum, invisibilem, siquidem haec omnia cum idea Venerabilis Senis nulla ratione convenire possunt.

209 I reply by denying the minor. It is true indeed that our mind cannot, without the utmost care and attention, entirely purge its ideas of every bodily taint, and that for this reason the ruder sort of men perceive nothing except with an image. But those images, e.g. of an Old Man and of a winged youth, are not themselves the ideas of God and of the Angels, but mere phantasms which accompany those ideas. For if we had no other idea of God than the idea of a Venerable Old Man, all the judgments that we form about God would have to appear to us entirely false, as being contrary to this idea; for we believe those judgments to be false which are contrary to the ideas of things that we have in our mind; and therefore we could not judge God to be incorporeal, invisible, since none of these can in any way agree with the idea of a Venerable Old Man.

[p. 68]

> 210 Instabis 3.: Apostolus ad Rom. cap. 1 scribit: *invisibilia Dei, per ea quae facta sunt intellecta conspiciuntur*: ergo Deus non cognoscitur â nobis nisi per comparationem cum rebus corporeis. Dist. antec.: quatenùs ex consideratione rerum corporearum, & spiritualium, rectè concludimus, existere supremum omnium Opíficem, conc., quatenùs idea Dei sit phantasma quoddam per comparationem cum rebus corporeis formatum, nego. *Cavendum ergo* est, *ne*, *ut* loquitur ibidem Sanctus Paulus, *mutetur gloria incorruptibilis Dei in similitudinem imaginis curruptibilis hominis*.

210 You will insist 3: The Apostle writes in Rom. ch. 1: the invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made: therefore God is not known by us except by comparison with corporeal things. Dist. the antecedent: insofar as from the consideration of corporeal and spiritual things we rightly conclude that the supreme Maker of all things exists, I grant; insofar as the idea of God is some phantasm formed by comparison with corporeal things, I deny. We must beware, therefore, lest, as St. Paul says in the same place, the glory of the incorruptible God be changed into the likeness of the image of a corruptible man.

> 211 Instabis 4: idea Dei formatur ex ideis perfectionum omnium creaturarum etiam corporearum: ergo idea Dei formatur per comparationem cum rebus corporeis. Dist. antec.: formatur ex ideis perfectionum creaturarum etiam corporearum *eminenter* sumptarum, conc.: *formaliter* sumptarum, nego & conseq. Adtributa corporea in idea Dei non includimus formaliter, id est prout sunt in corporibus, sed tantùm eminenter, hoc est, modo quodam nobiliori ac sublimiori sine ulla imperfectione, removendò à Deo omnes ideas materiae, divisionis, coloris & ceteras, quae formalitèr sumptae includunt necessariò quasdam imperfectiones, & Enti summo convenire non possunt nisi eminenter.

211 You will insist 4: the idea of God is formed from the ideas of the perfections of all creatures, even corporeal ones: therefore the idea of God is formed by comparison with corporeal things. Dist. the antecedent: it is formed from the ideas of the perfections of creatures, even corporeal ones, taken eminently, I grant; taken formally, I deny, and the consequent. We do not include corporeal attributes in the idea of God formally, that is, as they are in bodies, but only eminently, that is, in a certain nobler and more sublime manner, without any imperfection, removing from God all the ideas of matter, of division, of color, and the rest, which, taken formally, necessarily include certain imperfections, and cannot belong to the supreme Being except eminently.

> 212 Opp. 2.: si quis nasceretur omni sensu orbatus, ita ut neque videret, neque audiret, &c. is sanè nullas ideas haberet: ergo non dantur ideae purè intellectuales. Nego antec.: mens quippe in ea hypothesi viveret; vita autem mentis, in cogitatione consistit, hoc est in perceptione intellectus, & inclinatione voluntatis: ergo mens cogitaret. Non cogitaret autèm de rebus à se remotis, sed de eis quae praesentes sibi forent, & à quibus commoveretur. *Nihil autem menti magis praesto est, quam ipsa sibi*, ut docet Sanctus Augustinus [^68-s1]: ergo se ipsam per quamdam conscientiam cognosceret.

212 Obj. 2: if someone were born deprived of every sense, so that he neither saw nor heard, etc., he would surely have no ideas: therefore there are no purely intellectual ideas. I deny the antecedent: for in that hypothesis the mind would live; but the life of the mind consists in thinking, that is, in the perception of the intellect and the inclination of the will: therefore the mind would think. It would not, however, think of things remote from it, but of those which were present to it and by which it was moved. But nothing is more present to the mind than itself, as St. Augustine teaches: therefore it would know itself by a certain consciousness.

> [^68-s1]: Lib. 14 de Trinit.

[^68-s1]: Bk. 14 of On the Trinity.

> 213 Opp. 3. contra secundam conclusionis partem; si aliquae essent ideae, quae facili rationis usu acquirerentur, tales essent ideae Dei, & moralitatis actionum, sed istae non sunt; ergo. Prob. min.: experientia testatur homines nullam Dei, & moralitatis actionum ideam habere, nisi illam ab aliis hominibus quibuscum vivunt, accipiant: ergo tales non sunt ideae Dei, & moralitatis actionum, ut facili rationis usu acquirantur. Prob. antec.: ex duobus exemplis quae ab Academia Regia Parisiensi [p. 69] referuntur, patet hominem inter ursos educatum, & alterum, qui surdus & mutus fuerat usque ad 24 aetatis suae annum, nullam ideam Dei & moralitatis actionum habuisse, priusquàm sermonem cum aliis hominibus miscérent, & ab iis ideam illam recíperent: ergo.

213 Obj. 3, against the second part of the conclusion: if there were any ideas acquired by an easy use of reason, such would be the ideas of God and of the morality of actions; but these are not: therefore. Proof of the minor: experience testifies that men have no idea of God and of the morality of actions unless they receive it from other men with whom they live: therefore the ideas of God and of the morality of actions are not such as to be acquired by an easy use of reason. Proof of the antecedent: from two examples which are reported by the Royal Academy of Paris, [p. 69] it is plain that a man brought up among bears, and another who had been deaf and dumb up to the twenty-fourth year of his age, had no idea of God and of the morality of actions before they conversed with other men and received that idea from them: therefore.

> 214 Ad argumentum respondeo negando minorem, cujus probationem explicamus. Adlata exempla valent duntáxat adversùs eos, qui ante omnem adtentionem, ideas illas mentibus nostris praestò esse arbitrantur. At quum juxta nostram definitionem, ideae innatae non sine aliquo rationis usu percipiantur, tam crassae, ac ferè incredibilis ignorantiae causa haec adferri debet, quod nempè illi homines mentis suae facultates negléxerint, & ad primarum veritatum investigationem non adhibuerint.

214 To the argument I reply by denying the minor, whose proof we shall explain. The examples adduced hold good only against those who think that those ideas are present to our minds before all attention. But since, according to our definition, innate ideas are not perceived without some use of reason, the cause to be assigned for so gross and almost incredible an ignorance is this: that those men neglected the faculties of their mind and did not apply them to the investigation of the first truths.

> EXCERCITATIO III.

EXERCISE III .

> De praecipuis sensationum legibus.

On the principal laws of sensations.

> 215 Sit conclusio: lex sensationum est, ut quotiès ab objecto sensibili mutatio quaedam producitur in organo sensorio ritè constituto, totiès in anima oriatur sensatio quaedam particularis huic mutationi respondens. Prob.: illa sensatio mutationi respondet, quae ad arbitrium nostrum variari non potest; sed mutatio facta in organo sensorio ritè constituto non potest ad arbitrium nostrum variari: ergo. Prob. min. quotidiana experientia: si fragor ex. gr. tormenti bellici aurem ferit, illum necessariò percípimus, neque sensationem illam in sonum blandiorem mutare póssum: si faetor nares óccupat efficere nullomodo possumus ut ejus loco, vel odórem suavem, vel faetórem minus molestum percipiamus: ergo.

et the conclusion be: it is a law of sensations that as often as some 215 L change is produced by a sensible object in a duly constituted sense organ, so often there arises in the soul some particular sensation corresponding to this change. Proof: that sensation corresponds to the change which cannot be varied at our will; but the change made in a duly constituted sense organ cannot be varied at our will: therefore. Proof of the minor, from daily experience: if, e.g., the crash of a cannon strikes the ear, we necessarily perceive it, nor can we change that sensation into a gentler sound; if a stench fills the nostrils, we can in no way bring it about that in its place we perceive either a sweet odor or a less offensive stench: therefore.

> 216 Ex hac generali sensationum lege, quatuor regulae colliguntur. I. *Si mutatio in eodem organo, eadem est, sensatio quoque in anima eadem esse debet*. II. *Si contingat, à diversis objectis sensibilibus eamdem in eodem organo sensorio mutationem produci, objecta eadem adparere debent*. III. *Si mutatio in organo sensorio diversa est, sensatio quoque in anima diversa esse debet*. IV. *Hinc si contingat idem objectum diversam in eodem organo mutationem efficere, diversum quoque adparere debet objectum*. Ex his fluunt generalia visionis explicandae principia, & opticarum deceptionum fundamenta.

216 From this general law of sensations four rules are gathered. I. If the change in the same organ is the same, the sensation in the soul must also be the same. II. If it happens that the same change is produced in the same sense organ by different sensible objects, the objects must appear the same. III. If the change in the sense organ is different, the sensation in the soul must also be different. IV. Hence if it happens that the same object produces a different change in the same organ, the object too must appear different. From these flow the general principles for explaining vision, and the foundations of optical illusions.

[p. 70]

> Solvuntur argumenta.

THE ARGUMENTS ARE ANSWERED.

> 217 Opp. 1.: plures producuntùr in organo sensorio ritè constituto mutationes sine ulla animi sensatione: ergo. Prob. antec.: dum interdiù caelum intuemur singulae stellae luminis radios in oculum ritè constitutum immittunt, quibus stellarum imago in oculo delineatur, ac proindè mutationes in organo sensorio producunt: atqui tamen stellas anima non pércipit: ergo. Dist. antec.: plures producuntur sine sensatione mutationes *insufficientes*, conc. *sufficientes*, nego. Ad probationem conc. maj. dist. min.: anima stellas non percipit interdiù, id est, anima stellarum perceptiones debiliores ab aliis fortioribus non distinguit, conc., nullas habet stellarum perceptiones obscuras, nego, & conseq.

217 Obj. 1: many changes are produced in a duly constituted sense organ without any sensation of the soul: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: when by day we gaze at the sky, the single stars send rays of light into the duly constituted eye, by which the image of the stars is delineated in the eye, and accordingly they produce changes in the sense organ; and yet the soul does not perceive the stars: therefore. Dist. the antecedent: many changes are produced without sensation that are insufficient, I grant; sufficient ones, I deny. To the proof, I grant the major and distinguish the minor: the soul does not perceive the stars by day, that is, the soul does not distinguish the weaker perceptions of the stars from the other, stronger ones, I grant; it has no obscure perceptions of the stars, I deny; and I deny the consequent.

> 218 Non omnis mutatio facta in organo sensorio sufficit ut anima sentiat, sed requiritur, ut mutatio illa ad cérebrum usque transmittatur, & idcircò necessariam esse diximus mutationem factam ab *objecto sensibili*, hoc est, ab objecto quod mutationem sufficientem in organo sensorio ritè constituto producere possit. Sed instabis: eidem mutationi in eodem organo sensorio factae, non respondet eadem in anima sensatio: ergo. Prob. antec.: Sol & Luna dum vértici nostro imminent, minores videntur, quàm propè horizontem positi: atqui in utroque loco eandem mutationem in eodem oculo producunt: ergo.

218 Not every change made in the sense organ suffices for the soul to feel; but it is required that the change be transmitted all the way to the brain; and for this reason we said that the change must necessarily be made by a sensible object, that is, by an object which can produce a sufficient change in a duly constituted sense organ. But you will insist: the same sensation in the soul does not correspond to the same change made in the same sense organ: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: the Sun and the Moon, when they hang over our zenith, appear smaller than when placed near the horizon; and yet in both places they produce the same change in the same eye: therefore.

> 219 Nego antec., & ad probationem dist. min.: eamdem mutationem in oculo producunt conjunctam cum diversis mutationibus aliis in utroque loco, conc. secus nego, & conseq. Phaenomenon ita explicamus. Id enim circò Lunam & Solem in horizonte majores videri solent quam in meridiano, quia in horizonte simul cum earum imaginibus in oculo pinguntur interjecta corpora terraestria caelique fornix oblongus. At illa objectorum series, dùm Sol & Luna in vertice caeli conspiciuntur, oculum non adficiunt, atque inde est, quod si Solem & Lunam in horizonte per tubum angustum conspiciamus, haud majores videantur, quàm in caeli vertice. Dum ergo dicimus eidem mutationi in eodem organo factae eandem in anima sensationem respondere, propositio intelligenda est de mutationibus singulis seorsim consideratis.

219 I deny the antecedent, and to the proof I distinguish the minor: they produce the same change in the eye, joined with different other changes in each place, I grant; otherwise, I deny, and the consequent. We explain the phenomenon thus. The Moon and the Sun are usually seen larger on the horizon than at the meridian because on the horizon, together with their images, the intervening terrestrial bodies and the oblong vault of the sky are painted in the eye. This series of objects does not affect the eye when the Sun and Moon are seen at the top of the sky; and hence it is that if you look at the Sun and the Moon on the horizon through a narrow tube, they do not appear larger than at the top of the sky. When, therefore, we say that the same sensation in the soul corresponds to the same change made in the same organ, the proposition is to be understood of the changes each considered separately.

[p. 71]

> EXERCITATIO IV.

EXERCISE IV.

> De veri & falsi criterio.

On the criterion of the true and the false.

> 220 Saepe observamus tam luculentèr & perspicuè in pluribus casibus cògnitam nobis esse praedicati cum subjecto convenientiam, ut statim pateat, & adsensum extorqueat. Ex hac summa evidentia persuassum nobis est, nullam unquàm extitisse hominum sectam, qui de omnibus seriò dubitaverit. Quae quum ita sint, quaestionis statum non satis intellígere videntur ii, qui veritatis criterium investigantes, illud in evidentia reponunt, & evidentiam existere contra Scepticos prolixiùs demonstrant. Hi quidem sibi fingunt hostes quos feriant. Nos verò quaestionem hanc sequenti conclusione explicabimus.

e often observe that in many cases the agreement of the predi220 W cate with the subject is known to us so clearly and plainly that it is at once manifest and wrests our assent. By this supreme evidence we are persuaded that there has never been any sect of men that seriously doubted of all things. This being so, those seem not to understand sufficiently the state of the question who, in investigating the criterion of truth, place it in evidence, and demonstrate at length against the Sceptics that evidence exists. These, indeed, invent for themselves enemies to strike. We, however, shall explain this question by the following conclusion.

> 221 Conclusio: ad verum à falso distinguendum sufficiunt regulae Logicae, nec alio veritatis criterio opus est. Prob. 1. pars: is verum à falso discernit, qui *demonstrat* praedicatum subjecto convenire, atqui ad id demonstrandum sufficiunt regulae Logicae: ergo. Prob. min.: demonstratio constat ex syllogismorum nexu, quorum praemissae sunt definitiones, axiómata, & propositiones jam demonstratae, sed Logica tradit definitionum regulas, constituit discrimen inter axiómata, & propositiones demonstrabiles, delineat formam syllogismorum, ostendit deniquè modos conjungendi syllogismos &c.: ergo. Prob. 2. pars: si alio veritatis criterio praeter Logicae regulas opus est; regulae illae ad verum à falso discernendum non sufficerent; sed illas sufficere demonstravimus: ergo.

221 Conclusion: to distinguish the true from the false the rules of Logic suffice, and no other criterion of truth is needed. Proof of the 1st part: he discerns the true from the false who demonstrates that the predicate agrees with the subject; but the rules of Logic suffice for demonstrating this: therefore. Proof of the minor: a demonstration consists of a chain of syllogisms whose premises are definitions, axioms, and propositions already demonstrated; but Logic hands down the rules of definitions, establishes the distinction between axioms and demonstrable propositions, delineates the form of syllogisms, and shows, finally, the modes of joining syllogisms together, etc.: therefore. Proof of the 2nd part: if some other criterion of truth were needed besides the rules of Logic, those rules would not suffice for discerning the true from the false; but we have demonstrated that they suffice: therefore.

> 222 Veritatis criterium constituunt aliqui in ipsa evidentia. Verùm satis determinatum non est illud veritatis criterium: nam clara perceptio sive evidentia, in dato quolibet casu per regulas Logicae adplicari debet. ita nempè argumentadum est, *quidquid clare & distincte percipi potest, illud est verum; sed hoc clare & distincte percipi potest: ergo hoc est verum*, id autem fit per regulas Logicae; tradendae ergo sunt regulae, quarum ope judicari possit, adesse evidentiam aut veritatem, illae autem sunt regulae Logicae: quum dicitur ergo, evidentiam esse veri criterium, res perindè se habet, ac si diceretur, veritatem esse veritatis criterium, quod nugari est.

222 Some place the criterion of truth in evidence itself. But that criterion of truth is not sufficiently determined: for clear perception, or evidence, must in any given case be applied through the rules of Logic. One must, namely, argue thus: whatever can be clearly and distinctly perceived is true; but this can be clearly and distinctly perceived: therefore this is true; and this is done through the rules of Logic. Rules must therefore be handed down by whose help it may be judged that evidence, or truth, is present; and these are the rules of Logic. When it is said, therefore, that evidence is the criterion of the true, the matter stands just as if it were said that truth is the criterion of truth, which is to trifle.

[p. 72]

> Reffelluntur opposita.

CONTRARY VIEWS ARE REFUTED.

> 223 Opp. 1: illud est veritatis criterium quod verum à falso ita secernit, ut veritati adsensum negare non possímus, sed id praestat evidentia, seu quod idem est propositio ista, *quidquid clare & distincte percipitur verum est*: ergo. Dist. min.: & criterium illud non est satis determinatum per se, sed per regulas Logicae, conc., & determinatum est, ita ut Logicae regulis opus non sit, nego & conseq.: Solutio manet explicata. Instabis: illud non est veritatis criterium quod alio criterio índiget; sed Logicae regulae alio indigént veritatís criterio, nempè ad demonstrandas Logicae regulas opus est evidentiâ; ergo.

223 Obj. 1: that is the criterion of truth which so separates the true from the false that we cannot refuse assent to the truth; but evidence does this, or, what is the same, the proposition whatever is clearly and distinctly perceived is true: therefore. I distinguish the minor: and that criterion is not sufficiently determined by itself, but through the rules of Logic, I grant; and it is so determined that there is no need of the rules of Logic, I deny; and the consequence. The solution remains explained. You will insist: that is not the criterion of truth which needs another criterion; but the rules of Logic need another criterion of truth, for evidence is needed to demonstrate the rules of Logic: therefore.

> 224 Dist. min.: opus est evidentiâ, quae deinde per Logicae regulas adplicari debeat, conc., quae non indigeat, nego. Omnis dificultas evanescit si quaestionis status rectè intelligatur. Instabis 2: veritatis criterium potest esse principium illud: *impossibile est, idem simul esse, & non esse*: ergo praeter regulas Logicae saltem aliquod aliud esse poterit veritatis criterium. Dist. antec.: & propositio demonstranda ad principium illud per regulas Logicae redúci debet, conc. secùs nego. Ad objectionem eadem est, quae ad praecedentem responsio.

224 I distinguish the minor: evidence is needed, which must then be applied through the rules of Logic, I grant; evidence that does not need them, I deny. The whole difficulty vanishes if the state of the question is rightly understood. You will insist 2: the criterion of truth can be the principle it is impossible for the same thing at once to be and not to be: therefore, besides the rules of Logic, at least something else could be the criterion of truth. I distinguish the antecedent: and the proposition to be demonstrated must be reduced to that principle through the rules of Logic, I grant; otherwise, I deny. To this objection the reply is the same as to the preceding one.

> 225 Habetis jam, Adolescentes optimi, Logicae praecepta & quaestiones, quae vobis tanquam maxime utilia proponimus; quae si pro ingenio vestro, pro discendi cupiditate, uti par est, adripuéritis, non poenitendum opere praetium vos facturos esse confidimus. Pauca haec sunt, sed pro aetatis genio satis multa. Plura si vultis, ea legendis auctoribus, quos hactenus commendavimus facili negotio comparabitis.

225 You now have, excellent young men, the precepts and questions of Logic, which we put before you as the most useful; if you lay hold of them as befits your talent and your eagerness to learn, we are confident that you will have done work not to be regretted. These things are few, but for the character of your age many enough. If you want more, you will easily acquire it by reading the authors whom we have commended thus far.
