> ELEMENTA METAPHYSICES.

ELEMENTS OF METAPHYSICS.

## PRAEFATIO. — PREFACE

> 1 Post Logicam, non Physicam quemadmodùm Peripatetici faciunt, sed Metaphysicam tradunt Recentiores, & jure quidem; quum enim haec disciplina *prima Philosophia* adpelletur, & in vocabulorum significatione expendenda, & in principiis maximè genericis evolvendis prima sui parte versetur, hinc cum *facultate disserendi*, societatem ac foedus iníre debet. Ceterùm Metaphysicae nomen antiquis Philosophis planè incognitum ab Alexandro Aphrodisaeo, & Johanne Philopono, Aristotelis interpretibus, primò usurpatum fuisse traditur. Hoc autem nomine illa Aristotelis scripta inscripta fuere, quae Logicis, Ethicis, atque Physicis â Tyrannione Grammatico, & Andronico quodam Rhodio primùm in [p. 2] ordinem digestis, ad nullam certam classem visa sunt posse revocari [^2-s1-2]

fter Logic, not Physics, as the Peripatetics do, but Metaphysics 1 A is what the Moderns teach, and rightly so; for since this discipline is called first Philosophy, and in its first part is occupied with weighing the meaning of words and with unfolding the most generic principles, it must therefore enter into partnership and alliance with the faculty of discoursing. The name of Metaphysics, moreover, altogether unknown to the ancient Philosophers, is said to have been first used by Alexander of Aphrodisias and John Philoponus, interpreters of Aristotle. By this name, however, were entitled those writings of Aristotle which, once the Logical, Ethical and Physical works had first been put in order by Tyrannio the Grammarian and a certain Andronicus of Rhodes, [p. 2] seemed unable to be referred to any definite class (a).

> [^2-s1-2]: *Aristotelis* scripta, quae Theophrasto primùm, dein *Neleo* relicta fuere, ab ejus haeredibus per aliquot secula sub humo abscóndita fuere, & consepulta. Indè quum extraherentur humore penitùs corrupta, véndita fuere *Apelliconi Tejo*, qui depraváta loca imperíte supplevit. Subactis Athénis â *L. Sulla*, Apellicónis bibliotheca ejus jussu Romam delata est, ubi *Tyrannio* primùm, deindè *Andronicus* Rhódius Aristotelis opera recensuerunt, & ordine posuerunt. Vide dicta in Hist. Philosoph.

[^2-s1-2]: The writings of Aristotle, which were left first to Theophrastus, then to Neleus, were hidden and buried under the earth by his heirs for some centuries. Then, when they were drawn out thoroughly corrupted by damp, they were sold to Apellicon of Teos, who unskillfully filled in the corrupted passages. When Athens had been subdued by L. Sulla, Apellicon’s library was carried to Rome by his order, where first Tyrannio, then Andronicus of Rhodes revised the works of Aristotle and put them in order. See what was said in the Hist. of Philos.

> 2 Nunc autem Metaphysicae nomine apud Philosophos ea disciplina in mentem venit, quae res sursum positas, id est supra corporum naturam constitutas, seu res spirituales, & à materiae commercio solutas prosequitur. Hinc illa â Philosophis omnibus optimè definiri solet: *Facultas quae generales omnes entis adfectiones, corporeis & incorporeis etiam entibus communes considerat; adeòque incorporeas etiam substantias, ipsarumque adfectiones solo rationis lumine nobis perspicuas contemplatur*. Tres sunt Metaphysicae partes principes. Illarum prima *Ontologia*, sive *Ontosophia*, hoc est *entis scientia* vocatur, adeòque de ente generatim sumpto disserit, ejusque adfectiones per mentem abstractas expendit. Altera spirituales substantias ita scrutatur, ut earum naturam, existentiam, atque operationes solo rationis lumine nobis exhibeat. Quoniam autèm duae potissimùm sunt substantiae spirituales, quae naturae luminae cognosci à nobis possunt, Deus, scilicèt, & mens humana, ideò *Pneumatologia*, seu *Spirituum scientia* in duas partes satis aptè dividi consuevit; illa quae agit de mente humana *Psychologia*, vel *Pneumatologia* vocatur, quae de Deo sola dirigente ratione disserit *Theologia Naturalis*.

2 Now, however, by the name of Metaphysics there comes to the mind of Philosophers that discipline which pursues things placed on high, that is, things established above the nature of bodies, or spiritual things freed from all commerce with matter. Hence it is commonly and very well defined by all Philosophers: The faculty which considers all the general affections of being that are common to corporeal and incorporeal beings alike, and which also contemplates incorporeal substances and their affections, as they are perceptible to us by the light of reason alone. There are three principal parts of Metaphysics. The first of them is called Ontology, or Ontosophy, that is, the science of being, and so it treats of being taken in general, and weighs its affections as abstracted by the mind. The second so scrutinizes spiritual substances as to set before us their nature, existence and operations by the light of reason alone. And since there are chiefly two spiritual substances that can be known by us through the light of nature, namely God and the human mind, Pneumatology, or the Science of Spirits, has customarily been divided, quite fittingly, into two parts: that which treats of the human mind is called Psychology, or Pneumatology; that which discourses of God, with reason alone as guide, Natural Theology.

> 3 Itaque tres nobis erunt partes Metaphysicae, quarum prima *Ontologiam*, secunda *Psychologiam*, postrema *Theologiam Naturalem* comprehendet. Peripatetici Philosophi tam perturbatè Metaphysicam tradiderunt, nihil ut obscuriùs cogitari possit. Nos verò, Adolescentes optimi, Metaphysicam vobis dabimus, non illam veterem, longam, intricatam, sed brevem, perexpedítam, quaeque ad reliquas disciplinas percipiendas, mentem acuat, viamque muniat.

3 Accordingly we shall have three parts of Metaphysics, of which the first will comprise Ontology, the second Psychology, the last Natural Theology. The Peripatetic Philosophers handed down Metaphysics in so confused a manner that nothing more obscure can be conceived. We, however, excellent young men, shall give you a Metaphysics, not that old, long and intricate one, but a brief and very expeditious one, such as may sharpen the mind and pave the way for grasping the remaining disciplines.

[p. 3]

## METAPHYSICES — METAPHYSICS

> PARS I.

PA RT I .

## ONTOLOGIA. — ONTOLOGY

## DISSERTATIO UNICA. — SINGLE DISSERTATION

> De Ente, ejusque speciebus, & proprietatibus.

On Being, its species, and its properties.

> 4 Scientia quae ens in genere vel in communi, hoc est, â circunstantiis & accidentibus omnibus separatum cognoscit, ut ab universali ipsius contemplatione clarior deindè cujuslibet particularis entis cognitio oriatur, vocatur *Ontologia* sive *scientia de ente*. Scientiam hanc clariori, & adcuratiori quo fieri poterit ordine complectemur; quumque obscuritas maxima, ex innumeris prorsusque inutilibus quaestionibus oriatur, quibus illam Arabes & vulgares Peripatetici miserrimè deturparunt, quaestiones illas veluti innutiles omittemus, atque ens ipsum, ejusque species, & proprietates omnes contemplabimur.

he science which knows being in general, or in common, that is, 4 T separated from all circumstances and accidents, so that from the contemplation of it as universal a clearer knowledge of any particular being may afterwards arise, is called Ontology, or the science of being. We shall embrace this science in the clearest and most accurate order possible; and since its greatest obscurity arises from the countless and altogether useless questions with which the Arabs and the common Peripatetics have most wretchedly disfigured it, we shall omit those questions as useless, and shall contemplate being itself, its species, and all its properties.

## CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

> De Ente in communi ejusque divisione.

On Being in common, and its division. 5

> 5 Ens est *id quod est, aut esse potest*, unde quidquid ab intellectu nostro concipitur *Ens* adpellatur, nihilque intelligi, effingi, adfirmari, sive negari poterit, cui generalis, & universalissima haec *Entis* idea, conceptus aut nomen non conveniat. *Ens* universaliter sumptum dividitur in *substantiam*, & [p. 4] *accidens*, sive in *ens propriè & rigorosè sumptum, & modum entis*. *Substantia* vel *res* dicitur illud ens, quod per se existit, vel existere aut perfectè concipi potest independenter ab alio ente ut *lapis*, *homo* &c.: accidens verò vel modus entis, est illud ens quod existere debet in alio, neque potest esse, vel concipi, nisi veluti alteri inhaerens, atque conjunctum, ut *albedo*, *rotunditas*, *motus* &c.

Being is that which is, or can be; hence whatever is conceived by our intellect is called Being, and nothing can be understood, imagined, affirmed or denied to which this general and most universal idea, concept or name of Being does not apply. Being taken universally is divided into substance and [p. 4] accident, or into being properly and strictly taken, and a mode of being. Substance, or thing, is the name given to that being which exists by itself, or can exist or be perfectly conceived independently of another being, as a stone, a man, etc.: an accident, on the other hand, or mode of being, is that being which must exist in another, and can neither be nor be conceived except as inhering in and joined to another, as whiteness, roundness, motion, etc.

> 6 *Substantia* verò vel *res* dividitur in *creatam*, & *increatam*; *increata* dicitur illa, quae à nullo recipit esse quod habet, ut est solus Deus, *creata* verò quae liberè, contingenter, ab alio, id est, à Deo producta est, ut *homines*, *sidera* &c. Creatae substantiae in *corporeas* & in *incorporeas* dividuntur. *Accidentia* verò dividuntur praecipuè in *extrinseca*, & *intrinseca*. *Intrinseca* dicuntur illa, quae rem, substantiam aut subjectum ipsum, in quo reperiuntur, intrinsecè ac realiter adficiunt, ut in corpore *motus*, *figura*: *extrinseca* verò quae nihil intrinsecè, verè ac realiter ponunt in re, sed in illa solum ab intellectu nostro concipiuntur, à nobis tamèn veluti entia considerantur, cujusmodi sunt, *relationes* omnes, *privationes*, & *denominationes extrinsecae*.

6 Substance, or thing, is divided into created and uncreated: that is called uncreated which receives from no one the being that it has, as God alone is; created, that which has been produced freely, contingently, by another, that is, by God, as men, stars, etc. Created substances are divided into corporeal and incorporeal. Accidents are divided chiefly into extrinsic and intrinsic. Those are called intrinsic which affect intrinsically and really the thing, the substance or subject itself in which they are found, as motion and figure in a body; extrinsic, those which posit nothing intrinsically, truly and really in the thing, but are only conceived in it by our intellect, and yet are considered by us as beings, of which kind are all relations, privations, and extrinsic denominations.

> 7 Substantia itaque definiri potest: *essentia separata á suis modis*. Est autem *modus* id, quo substantia hoc, vel illo modo est, eamque quodammodo vestit, & ut sensibus percipiatur facit. Hinc fit manifestum, substantiam esse ideam relatam ad modos, á quibus fingitur separata, ideòque esse ideam abstractam: nulla enim existit *substantia* carens omnibus *modis*. Quare qui de substantia sine modis sumpta disputant, non de re aliqua, quae extra mentem sit, disputant; sed de abstracta idea, quae tantum in eorum mente existit. *Substantiae* enim, nullam aliam ideam habemus, nisi concipientes *cumulum modorum*, & *proprietatum*, adjungendo iis ideam obscuram naturae nobis incognitae; id est complexionis ex. gr. partium materiae nobis non cognitae, quam putamus tales res continere. (§§. 29. 30. Log.)

7 Substance, therefore, can be defined: an essence separated from its modes. A mode, moreover, is that by which a substance is in this or that way, and which in a manner clothes it and makes it perceived by the senses. Hence it becomes manifest that substance is an idea related to the modes from which it is imagined as separated, and therefore that it is an abstract idea: for no substance exists lacking all modes. Therefore those who dispute about substance taken without modes are disputing not about some thing that is outside the mind, but about an abstract idea that exists only in their mind. For we have no other idea of substance than by conceiving a cluster of modes and properties, and adding to them the obscure idea of a nature unknown to us, that is, of a combination, e.g., of parts of matter not known to us, which we think such things contain. (§§. 29, 30, Log.)

> 8 *Accidentia* sive *modi interni* ita in substantia intrinsecùs inhaerent, ut ab ea nec esse, nec intelligi possint existere separati: veluti *figura* & *motus*: ¿ ubi enim est figura sine corpore? motus sine mobili? *Externi* verò non reapse in substantia existunt, sed á mente nostra concipiuntur veluti aliquid, quod eam adficit, cujusmodi sunt, ut jam diximus *relationes* omnes.

8 Accidents, or internal modes, so inhere intrinsically in substance that they can neither be, nor be understood to exist, separated from it: as figure and motion: for where is there figure without a body? motion without a movable thing? External modes, however, do not really exist in the substance, but are conceived by our mind as something that affects it, of which kind are, as we have already said, all relations.

> 9 Ergo substantia *physicè* & reapse sumpta aliquot modos internos habeat necesse est. Quamobrèm ineptum est quaérere, *an sine modis esse possit*: quia & si substantia sine ullo vel altero *modo* interdùm sit, tamen in hoc rerum ordine omnibus modis spoliata esse non potest. *Metaphysicè* vero sumta, sine modis esse posse perspicuum est. Quare ineptum etiam est quaerere *an sine modis possit esse*; quia id ipsum significat substantia metaphysicè sumta, nempè *naturam sejunctam à modis*. Tamen quum idea abstracta *substantiae*, ut *essentiae*, non eadem in omnibus sit, sed pro varietate [p. 5] rerum varia & ipsa; talis interdum est, quae aliquos modos complectitur: qui propterea non amplius vocandi sunt modi sed *essentia* & *substantia* rei. Sed haec aliquo exemplo commodè declarabimus.

9 Therefore substance taken physically and really must have some internal modes. Hence it is inept to ask whether it can be without modes: because even if a substance is at times without this or that mode, yet in this order of things it cannot be stripped of all modes. Taken metaphysically, however, it is plain that it can be without modes. Therefore it is also inept to ask whether it can be without modes; because substance taken metaphysically signifies precisely this, namely a nature separated from modes. Yet since the abstract idea of substance, as of essence, is not the same in all things, but according to the variety [p. 5] of things is itself also various, it is at times such as to comprise some modes: which for that reason are no longer to be called modes, but the essence and substance of the thing. But we shall conveniently explain these things by an example.

> 10 Ex. gr. *Pluma* quam in praesentia manu moveo ut haec scribam, potest non movéri, si consistam: propterea *motu* privari potest, & *quiéscere*, quin désinat esse pluma. Non tamen privari potest simul & *motu* & *quiete*, sed altérutrum habeat necesse est. Item non potest privari omni magnitudine, figurâ, ceterisque: sed unum vel aliud necessario habet. Contrà *horologium* ex. gr. praeter artificium partium complectitur motum earum. Ideòque etsi *motus* generatim sumtus sit *modus* corporis, tamen essentia seu substantia est horologii. Item *fulmen* praeter materiam inflammatam, includit motum pernicíssimum. Qua de causa hic motus non ampliùs est modus, sed essentia fulminis. Quare ut de *modis* rectè judicemus, oportet primò constituamus, in quo sita sit natura rei, ne inscîe vocemus *modum*, id quod naturam constituit.

10 E.g., the pen that I am at present moving with my hand in order to write these things can be not moved, if I stop: therefore it can be deprived of motion, and be at rest, without ceasing to be a pen. It cannot, however, be deprived at once of motion and of rest, but must necessarily have one or the other. Likewise it cannot be deprived of all magnitude, figure, and the rest: but it necessarily has one or another. A clock, on the contrary, e.g., comprises, besides the artful construction of its parts, their motion. And therefore, although motion taken in general is a mode of body, it is nevertheless the essence or substance of the clock. Likewise a thunderbolt, besides the inflamed matter, includes a most violent motion. For this reason this motion is no longer a mode, but the essence of the thunderbolt. Therefore, that we may judge rightly of modes, we must first establish in what the nature of the thing consists, lest we unwittingly call a mode that which constitutes its nature.

> 11 Hinc *modi interni* re ipsa nihil aliud sunt quam substantia, quae hoc vel illo modo se habet: propterea ab ea separari non possunt. Sed incredibile dictu est quot *logomachiae* de natura *modorum* seu *accidentium* audiantur in Scholis quorundam Philosophorum, qui decepti abstractis ideis, quibus propriam naturam, & existentiam tribuere solent, acritèr contendunt, modos entia quaedam esse, quae à substantia existere seorsum possunt. Sed si rem libero judicio considerarent, planè cognóscerent ejusmodi entia nulla esse, nec aliud esse *rotunditatem* vel *magnitudinem* globi aurei ex. gr., quám aurum hoc modo figuratum, & hac magnitudine constans. Possum quidem *rotunditatem* abstractè considerare, sed intelligere existentem sine materia, cui insit, non possum. Si negant Peripatetici, ostendant *rotunditatem* & *motum*, sine subjecto, & habebimus illis gratiam de tam mirabili explicatione phaenomeni. Sed de his oportunius in Physica.

11 Hence internal modes are in reality nothing other than the substance, which is in this or that way: therefore they cannot be separated from it. But it is incredible to say how many logomachies about the nature of modes or accidents are heard in the Schools of certain Philosophers, who, deceived by abstract ideas, to which they are wont to attribute a nature and existence of their own, sharply contend that modes are certain beings which can exist apart from substance. But if they considered the matter with a free judgment, they would plainly recognize that there are no such beings, and that the roundness or magnitude of a golden globe, e.g., is nothing other than gold shaped in this way and having this magnitude. I can indeed consider roundness abstractly, but I cannot understand it as existing without the matter in which it is. If the Peripatetics deny this, let them show us roundness and motion without a subject, and we shall be grateful to them for so wonderful an explanation of the phenomenon. But of these things more fittingly in the Physics.

> 12 *Privatio* est carentia perfectionis in subjecto, quod aptum, & capax sit ad formam illam, vel perfectionem recipiendam, ut *tenebrae* in aëre, *caecitas* in homine &c. itaque à *negatione* distinguitur, quae est privatio sive carentia formae in subjecto, quod alioquin incapax est ejusdem formae, ut tenebrae in corpore opaco, caecitas in lapide &c. Itaque *caecitas*, & *tenebrae* ita concipiuntur ab intellectu nostro, ac si modus aliquis forent, quum tamen sint purum nihil.

12 Privation is the lack of a perfection in a subject that is apt and capable of receiving that form or perfection, as darkness in the air, blindness in a man, etc.; and so it is distinguished from negation, which is the privation or lack of a form in a subject that is otherwise incapable of that form, as darkness in an opaque body, blindness in a stone, etc. And so blindness and darkness are conceived by our intellect as if they were some mode, although they are pure nothing.

> 13 *Relatio* verò est ordo quidam, habitudo, sive respectus unius rei ad aliam, qui nempè concipitur in aliqua re, ex eo quod ipsa res ordinetur, vel referatur ad aliam, ut ex. gr. si *Alexarder* referatur ad *Philippum*, dicitur *filius*, quum tamen hoc esse filii in intellectu solum reperiatur. *Denominatio* denique *extrinseca*, est purum nomen quod alicui rei tribuitur, licèt concipiatur ab intellectu veluti ens aliquod, perfectio vel modus alteri inhaerens, ut qui [p. 6] *judex*, *eques*, *nobilis* constituitur, qui *laudatur*, aut *vituperatur* exteriorem quidem hanc vocem, sive denominationem solum recipit, aliquid tamen à nobis concipitur, quod *Judici*, *equiti*, *nobili*, *laudato*, *vituperato* veluti intrinsecè inhaereat.

13 Relation, on the other hand, is a certain order, habitude, or respect of one thing to another, which is conceived in some thing because that thing is ordered or referred to another, as, e.g., if Alexander is referred to Philip, he is called son, although this being a son is found only in the intellect. An extrinsic denomination, finally, is a pure name that is attributed to some thing, although it is conceived by the intellect as some being, perfection or mode inhering in another, as when one is made a judge, [p. 6] a knight, a nobleman, or is praised or blamed: he receives indeed only this outward word, or denomination, yet something is conceived by us that inheres, as it were intrinsically, in the judge, the knight, the nobleman, the man praised or blamed.

> 14 Hinc alia entis divisio desumitur in *ens reale*, & *ens rationis*. *Ens reale* dicitur illud, quod verè, & realiter est, independenter ab intellectu, sive quod etiamsi intellectus nihil consideret, esse debet, ut *rosa*, *homo*, *lapis*: *ens rationis* illud est, quod solum concipitur, efficitur, & dependet ab intellectu cogitante, ideòque si intellectus nihil consideret *ens rationis* esse non poterit. Hìc quaestionem movent Peripatetici utrum nempè ens ipsum generaliter sumtum, sive conceptus entis univocus sit respectu Dei & creaturarum, quemadmodùm etiam respectu substantiae & accidentis, denique respectu entis realis, & rationis: utrum nempè conceptus entis eodem modo illis conveniat, & aequaliter omnia sint ens, etsi variis deinde proprietatibus ac differentiis distinguantur?

14 Hence another division of being is drawn, into real being and being of reason. Real being is said to be that which truly and really is, independently of the intellect, or which must be even if the intellect considers nothing, as a rose, a man, a stone: a being of reason is that which is only conceived, is made by and depends on the thinking intellect, and therefore, if the intellect considers nothing, a being of reason cannot be. Here the Peripatetics raise the question whether being itself taken generally, or the concept of being, is univocal with respect to God and creatures; as also with respect to substance and accident, and finally with respect to real being and being of reason: whether, namely, the concept of being applies to them in the same way, and all things are equally being, although they are afterwards distinguished by various properties and differences?

> 15 Sed videtis jam ex sola ipsius quaestionis expositione eam inutilem prorsùs esse, nihiloque nos doctiores efficere posse. Verumenimverò ne prorsùs ignoretis celebriores Peripati quaestiones aliqua cum Corsinio dicere decrevi. Itaque si Deus ipse cum creaturis sive substantia cum accidente comparetur, verisimilior opiniomihi videtur illa, quae putat conceptum entis aequaliter illis & univocè convenire. Quum enim communis ac generalissimus conceptus *entis* nihil prorsùs significet, ut antea diximus, nisi id *quod est*, vel id quod habet esse, Deus autem & creaturae habeant esse, sub hoc communi entis genere aequaliter continebuntur, ut tuentur *Scotistae*.

15 But you see already, from the mere exposition of the question itself, that it is altogether useless and can make us none the more learned. But truly, lest you be altogether ignorant of the more celebrated questions of the Peripatetics, I have decided to say something about them with Corsini. Accordingly, if God himself is compared with creatures, or substance with accident, the more probable opinion seems to me to be that which holds that the concept of being applies to them equally and univocally. For since the common and most general concept of being signifies nothing at all, as we said before, but that which is, or that which has being, and God and creatures have being, they will be contained equally under this common genus of being, as the Scotists maintain.

> 16 Quod si dicatur Deum longè diversa ratione existere quam creaturae, Deum nempè infinito perfectissimoque modo, essentialiter, *necessariò*, independenter ab alio ut ipse de se proinde dixerit [^6-s1-3] *Ego sum qui sum*; creaturas verò finito modo, contingenter, & dependenter, à libera Dei voluntate, ut omnes ut ait Isaías [^6-s2-2] *ut omnes gentes, quasi non sint, sic sunt coram eo, & quasi nihilum & inane reputatae sunt ei*, facilè poterit responderi: infinitum ejusmodi intervallum quo Deus Opt Max. à creaturis distinguitur non ab ipsa entis idea oriri, sed ab infinitis illis perfectionibus, quae reperiuntur in Deo, quemadmodum communis idea *animae* univocè *animae rationali, & vegetativae* tribuitur, quamvis illae miro discrimine distinguantur.

16 But if it be said that God exists in a far different manner from creatures, God namely in an infinite and most perfect manner, essentially, necessarily, independently of another, so that he accordingly said of himself (b) I am who am; but creatures in a finite manner, contingently and dependently, on the free will of God, so that all, as Isaiah says (c), all nations are before him as if they had no being at all, and are counted to him as nothing, and vanity, it can easily be answered: such an infinite interval, by which God, the Best and Greatest, is distinguished from creatures, arises not from the idea of being itself, but from those infinite perfections which are found in God; just as the common idea of soul is attributed univocally to the rational and to the vegetative soul, although these are distinguished by a wonderful difference.

> [^6-s1-3]: Exodi cap. 3. ℣. 14.

[^6-s1-3]: Exodus, ch. 3, v. 14.

> [^6-s2-2]: Cap. 40. ℣. 17.

[^6-s2-2]: Ch. 40, v. 17.

> 17 Et sanè si conceptus aut idea entis adcuratissimè concipiatur, videbitur esse simplicissima, ac prorsus indivisibilis, quod verificari non poterit si aliqua entis idea creaturis, altera verò Deo conveniret. Deindè idea Dei, & creaturae distingui debent ope rationis alicujus, aut differentiae, quae utrique conceptui, vel enti [p. 7] conjungitur, ideoque semper admitti debet universalis ille, & communis conceptus entis, cui rationes illae, vel differentiae superaddantur. Iterum igitur inquiri potest, an communis ille conceptus, cui differentiae non superadduntur sit unus, & idem, & univocus, an potius à differentiis illis distinguatur? Si primum, erit ille univocus respectu inferiorum. Si secundum poterit á differentiis abstrahi, & unus, simplex, indistinctus, ac indivisibilis, ideoque univocus etiam reddi. Quae dicta sunt intelligi etiam debent de *substantia* respectu *accidentis*.

17 And indeed, if the concept or idea of being is conceived most accurately, it will be seen to be most simple and altogether indivisible, which could not be verified if one idea of being applied to creatures and another to God. Then, the ideas of God and of the creature must be distinguished by means of some character, or difference, which is joined to either concept, or to being; [p. 7] and therefore that universal and common concept of being, to which those characters or differences are superadded, must always be admitted. Again, then, it can be asked whether that common concept, to which the differences are not superadded, is one and the same and univocal, or is rather distinguished by those differences? If the first, it will be univocal with respect to its inferiors. If the second, it can be abstracted from the differences, and so be rendered one, simple, undistinguished and indivisible, and therefore univocal as well. What has been said must also be understood of substance with respect to accident.

## CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

> De essentia, existentia, & subsistentia.

On essence, existence, and subsistence.

> 18 Quamvis conceptus entis omninò simplex, & incompositus videatur, plura tamen adtributa, ac véluti partes in illo distingui debent, quae véluti proprietates entis haberi, vocarique solent. Ejusmodi sunt *essentia*, *existentia*, *subsistentia*, ex quibus deinde rerum discrimen *hypóstasis*, & *personarum* nomina deducuntur, aliaque id genus plurima quae apud Theologos, & Philosophos Peripateticos pertractantur. Nos verò haec omnia quàmbrevissimè exponemus, quòd ex recepta jam Scholarum consuetudine haec ipsa rerum, sive vocum discrimina ignorare, nefas propemodùm videatur.

lthough the concept of being seems altogether simple and uncom18 A pounded, several attributes, and as it were parts, must nevertheless be distinguished in it, which are commonly held and called, as it were, properties of being. Such are essence, existence, subsistence, from which are then derived the distinction of things and the names of hypostasis and of persons, and very many other things of the kind which are treated at length among the Theologians and the Peripatetic Philosophers. We, however, shall set forth all these things as briefly as possible, because, by the now accepted custom of the Schools, to be ignorant of these very distinctions of things, or of words, would seem almost a crime.

> 19 Itaque *essentia* ut ab illa exordiamur nihil est aliud quam primum adtributum, quod in re concipitur, & ex quo cetera omnia veluti ex radice proveniunt. In Scholis vulgò definitur id per quod ens est, vel esse concipitur, sive id quod intrinsecè rem componit, sive quod intrinsecè dat esse rei. Ejusmodi principium quod dat esse rei vocatur *essentia*, *natura*, *constitutivum* ejusdem rei, hoc uno discrimine, quod ubi concipitur tanquam fons, & origo proprietatum, vocatur *essentia*; ubi verò concipitur tanquam fons & origo operationum, quae à tali re producuntur, dicitur *natura*, plerumque tamen, *natura*, & *essentia* promiscuè usurpantur.

19 Accordingly essence, to begin with it, is nothing other than the first attribute that is conceived in a thing, and from which all the rest proceed as from a root. In the Schools it is commonly defined: that through which a being is, or is conceived to be; or that which intrinsically composes a thing; or that which intrinsically gives being to a thing. Such a principle, which gives being to a thing, is called the essence, the nature, the constitutive of that same thing, with this one difference, that where it is conceived as the source and origin of properties it is called essence, but where it is conceived as the source and origin of the operations which are produced by such a thing it is called nature; most often, however, nature and essence are used indiscriminately.

> 20 Hinc dirimi breviter poterunt celeberrimae quaestiones illae, quae tanto adparatu in Scholis agitari solent; utrum nempè essentiae rerum sint aeternae ac invariabiles, utrum Deus contradictoria efficere possit? Quamvis enim plurimi existiment rerum essentias ita, reluctante licet intellectu nostro, à Deo variari posse, ut circulus in figura angulis praedita, sive quadrata redduci possit, ut Deus efficere possit bis duo non esse quatuor &c, longè tamen verisimilius videtur rerum essentias ita certas ac invariabiles esse, ut nec à Deo variari possint.

20 Hence those most celebrated questions which are wont to be agitated in the Schools with so much apparatus can be briefly settled: namely, whether the essences of things are eternal and invariable, and whether God can bring about contradictories? For although very many think that the essences of things can be varied by God, even against the resistance of our intellect, in such a way that a circle could be turned into a figure endowed with angles, or into a square one, and that God could bring it about that twice two is not four, etc., yet it seems far more probable that the essences of things are so certain and invariable that they cannot be varied even by God.

[p. 8]

> 21 Quum enim essentiae nomine nihil aliud intelligatur, nisi adtributum illud, aut illa perfectio, quae dat esse rei, impossibile est certe ut principium illud varietur quin ipsa quoque res, quae recipit esse variari debeat, ut ex. gr. si radiorum aequalitas, & angulorum privatio auferatur, circulus etiam auferri debebit, sive circulus amplius concipi vel haberi non poterit. Et certè ejusmodi rerum essentiae nihil aliud sunt quam archétypae rerum ideae, vel imagines illae, quae ab aeterno Deus in mente habuit, & ad quarum similitudinem res in tempore creavit, ideòque sicuti imagines illae, vel divinae ideae immutabiles sunt, sic ipsae rerum essentiae invariabiles etiam censeri debent.

21 For since by the name of essence nothing else is understood but that attribute, or that perfection, which gives being to a thing, it is certainly impossible for that principle to be varied without the thing itself, which receives its being, having to be varied as well; as, e.g., if the equality of the radii and the privation of angles are taken away, the circle too will have to be taken away, or a circle can no longer be conceived or had. And certainly such essences of things are nothing other than the archetypal ideas of things, or those images which God had in his mind from eternity, and in whose likeness he created things in time; and therefore, just as those images, or divine ideas, are immutable, so the essences of things themselves must also be deemed invariable.

> 22 *Existentia* communiter definitur: positio entis aut essentiae extra nihil & omnes causas; ideòque inter essentiam & existentiam discrimen illud reperitur, quod essentia possibilibus etiam rebus conveniat, quae in causae primae, sive secundae potentia continentur, existentia vero iis solum rebus conveniat, quae extra causam primam sive secundam positae sunt. Quandoquidem verò essentia & existentia aequaliter substantiis omnibus, & accidentibus convenit, ut accidentia non minus quàm substantiae, si possibilia fuerint, habeant *esse*, si producta fuerint habeant *existere*, & accidentia tamen seu modi á substantiis maximè distinguuntur, in subtantiis ipsis praeter essentiam, & existentiam accidentibus quoque communem concipi, vel admitti debet alia perfectio, quae accidentibus convenire non possit, ut illae proinde substantiae ab accidentibus veluti constanti, clarissimoque discrimine distinguantur.

22 Existence is commonly defined: the placing of a being or essence outside nothing and all causes; and therefore between essence and existence there is found this difference, that essence applies also to possible things, which are contained in the power of the first or of a second cause, whereas existence applies only to those things which have been placed outside the first or second cause. Since, however, essence and existence apply equally to all substances and to accidents, so that accidents no less than substances, if they are possible, have being, and, if they have been produced, have existing, and since accidents or modes are nonetheless very greatly distinguished from substances, in substances themselves, besides essence and existence, which are common to accidents as well, another perfection must be conceived or admitted which cannot apply to accidents, so that those substances may accordingly be distinguished from accidents as by a constant and most clear difference.

> 23 Haec nova perfectio substantiis solum conveniens dicitur *hypostasis*, vel *subsistentia*, ultima nempè perfectio, forma, vel actus, quo res, aut natura, vel essentia ita perficitur, terminatur, completur, vel redditur sui juris non modò, ut non indigeat alio ad essendum, & operandum, sed etiam ut sibi tribuantur operationes suae, sive ut sit ac operetur independenter ab alio, quod soli certae substantiae convenire potest, quae per se subsistit, & substat, sive subjicitur accidentibus. Subjectum verò, substantia, sive compositum quod hac ultima perfectione donatur, sive quod per se subsistit ac operatur dicitur *suppositum*, & si spiritualis & incorporeae cognitionis capax sit ut in Deo, Angelis, & hominibus vocatur *persona*, quae proinde à Boethio definitur: *rationalis naturae individua substantia.*

23 This new perfection, which applies to substances alone, is called hypostasis, or subsistence: namely the ultimate perfection, form or act by which a thing, or nature, or essence, is so perfected, terminated, completed, or made its own master, not only so that it does not need another for being and operating, but also so that its operations are attributed to it, or so that it is and operates independently of another; which can belong only to a certain substance, which subsists by itself, and stands under, or is subjected to, accidents. The subject, moreover, the substance or composite, that is endowed with this ultimate perfection, or that subsists and operates by itself, is called a suppositum; and if it is spiritual and capable of incorporeal knowledge, as in God, the Angels and men, it is called a person, which is accordingly defined by Boethius: an individual substance of a rational nature.

> 24 Hinc in divinis tres *hypostases*, vel subsistentiae reperiuntur, ideòque etiam tres *personae*: quumque subsistentia Divini Verbi, subsistentiae creatae, vel humanae vices in Christo Domino suppleverit, sive terminaverit naturam humanam, quae propria creata, vel humana subsistentia terminari debebat, clarissimè adparet quod in Christo Domino *duplex* quidem *natura*: divina, scilicèt, ac humana, ideoque duplex voluntas ut à VI Synodo contra [p. 9] Monothelitas definitum est, reperitur: unica tamen *hypostasis*, vel subsistentia divina, ideòque unica *persona* divina in illo reperiebatur.

24 Hence in divine things three hypostases, or subsistences, are found, and therefore also three persons: and since the subsistence of the Divine Word took the place of the created, or human, subsistence in Christ the Lord, or terminated the human nature, which ought to have been terminated by its own created or human subsistence, it appears most clearly that in Christ the Lord there is found a twofold nature, divine, namely, and human, and therefore a twofold will, as the Sixth Synod against the Monothelites [p. 9] defined; but only one hypostasis, or divine subsistence, and therefore only one divine person, was found in him.

> 25 Quumque non natura, sed persona sit illa, quae aliquid operari vel pati dicitur, juxta commune principium illud: *operationes sunt suppositorum*, operationes aut merita Christi D. infiniti valoris, ac dignitatis, ideoque infinitis hominibus à scelerum culpa, vel poena redimendis pares esse debebant, quippè quae ab infinita persona, sive Supposito divino producebantur. Sed haec Theologis pro rei dignitate explicanda relinquimus, ne nos falcem in alienam messem immitamus.

25 And since it is not the nature but the person that is said to operate or to suffer something, according to that common principle, operations belong to supposita, the operations or merits of Christ the Lord had to be of infinite value and dignity, and therefore equal to redeeming infinite men from the guilt or the punishment of their crimes: since they were produced by an infinite person, or divine Suppositum. But these things we leave to the Theologians, to be explained according to the dignity of the matter, lest we put our sickle into another’s harvest.

## CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

> De aliis proprietatibus vel adtributis Entis, sive de Unitate, Veritate, & Bonitate.

On the other properties or attributes of Being, or on Unity, Truth, and Goodness.

> 26 Proprietates illae vel adtributa entis, quae sup. cap. sunt explicatae, non cuilibet enti, sed singulis entis generibus convenire possunt, sed essentia quidem in entibus omnibus etiam possibilibus, existentia verò in iis rebus, quae extra omnem causam positae sunt, subsistentia denique in substantiis tantummodò reperitur. Alia tamen sunt adtributa quae sic universaliter enti conveniunt, ut omnes entium fines vel terminos *transcendant*, vel excedant, unde transcendentalia vocantur, ideòque non aliqua solum, sed singula prorsùs entium genera complectuntur, solentque tria praesertim à Philosophis enumerari *Vnitas*, nempè, *Veritas*, & *Bonitas*.

he properties or attributes of being which were explained in the chap26 T ter above can apply not to every being, but to the individual genera of being: essence, indeed, is found in all beings, even possible ones, existence in those things which have been placed outside every cause, and subsistence, finally, in substances only. There are, however, other attributes which apply to being so universally that they transcend, or exceed, all the bounds or limits of beings, whence they are called transcendentals; and therefore they embrace not some only, but absolutely all the genera of beings; and three in particular are commonly enumerated by the Philosophers: namely Unity, Truth and Goodness.

> 27 *Vnitas* nihil est aliud quàm carentia sive privatio divisionis, nec alia de causa conceptus entis unicus, & simplex est, nisi quod ille varias in partes dividi non potest. Quoniam ergo unitas divisioni opponitur, totidem unitatis genera distingui possunt, quot sunt divisiones ipsae, vel distinctiones quae inter entia reperiuntur. Distinctio verò sive divisio triplex â Philosophis numeratur; *generica* nempè, *specifica*, & *numerica*. Distinctio *generica*, dicitur illa, quae reperitur inter entia, quae sub diverso genere, sive cathegoria continentur, ut inter *circulum*, & *lineam rectam*, circulus enim sub *figurae curvilinae*, *linea* verò *recta*, neque ad curvilineum genus, neque ad quodvis aliud genus figurae pertinet.

27 Unity is nothing other than the lack or privation of division, and for no other reason is the concept of being one and simple except that it cannot be divided into various parts. Since, therefore, unity is opposed to division, as many kinds of unity can be distinguished as there are divisions themselves, or distinctions, found among beings. Distinction or division is reckoned threefold by the Philosophers: namely generic, specific and numerical. Generic distinction is said to be that which is found between beings that are contained under a different genus or category, as between a circle and a straight line; for the circle is contained under the genus of curvilinear figure, whereas the straight line belongs neither to the curvilinear genus nor to any other genus of figure.

> 28 *Specifica* reperitur inter entia, quae quum sub eodem genere contineantur diversae tamen speciei sunt, ut inter *circulum* & *triangulum*, qui sub eodem figurae genere collocantur, ad varias tamen figurae species pertinent. *Numerica* denique est illa, quae reperitur [p. 10] inter individua ejusdem speciei, vel inter illa quae sub eadem specie continentur, & solis circunstantiis & conditionibus individuantibus distinguuntur, ut circulus A, circulus B. Distinctio generica atque specifica desumi concipitur à forma, natura, vel essentia rerum, unde illa quae specificè sive genericè differunt diversam essentiam habere debent.

28 Specific distinction is found between beings which, though they are contained under the same genus, are yet of a different species, as between a circle and a triangle, which, though placed under the same genus of figure, yet belong to different species of figure. Numerical distinction, finally, is that which is found [p. 10] between individuals of the same species, or between those that are contained under the same species and are distinguished only by individuating circumstances and conditions, as circle A, circle B. Generic and specific distinction is conceived to be drawn from the form, nature, or essence of things; whence those things that differ specifically or generically must have a different essence.

> 29 Distinctio verò numerica quae *materialis* etiam vocari solet, ut plurimi existimant à sola materia, quae proindè *principium individuationis* vocatur, vel à circunstantiis materialibus desumi debet; unde *Thomistae* arbitrantur in Angelis quia materia carent, hanc numericam distinctionem admitti, sive plures Angelos in unica specie reperiri non posse, sed potius Angelos singulos specificè inter se differre. Quemadmodùm tamèn rationales animae, etsi incorporeae sint, numericè inter se distinguuntur ex ordine, vel habitudine qua singulae ad proprium corpus diriguntur; ita quoque Angeli numericè distingui possunt ex accidentibus vel circunstantiis spiritualibus quibus adfecti sunt, aut certè ex varia actione Dei qua creati fuerint, vel conserventur.

29 Numerical distinction, on the other hand, which is also commonly called material, must, as very many think, be drawn from matter alone, which is accordingly called the principle of individuation, or from material circumstances; whence the Thomists hold that in Angels, because they lack matter, this numerical distinction is not admitted, or that several Angels cannot be found in a single species, but rather that individual Angels differ specifically from one another. Yet just as rational souls, though they are incorporeal, are numerically distinguished from one another by the order or habitude by which each is directed to its own body, so too Angels can be numerically distinguished by the spiritual accidents or circumstances with which they are affected, or at any rate by the varied action of God by which they were created or are conserved.

> 30 Distinctio *realis* est illa quae reperitur in re independenter ab intellectu. Distinctio *rationis* est illa quae pendet ab intellectu. Distinctio realis dividitur in *entitativam*, *modalem*, *& virtualem*. Realis *entitativa* quae etiam *major* vocari solet, dicitur illa quae reperitur inter varias res, quarum entitates ita distinctae sunt, ut una ab alia separari, vel saltem una sine alia perfectè concipi possit, ut inter Lunam & Solem, aurum, & argentum &c. Realis *minor* seu *modalis* dicitur illa quae datur inter rem & modum rei, qui modus ab ipsa re separari, vel sine ipsa perfecte concipi non potest, ut inter *figuram & corpus figuratum*. *Virtualis* denique, quam potius fundamentum distinctionis, quàm distinctionem dixeris, quae reperitur in re, quae quamvis unica & simplex sit, pluribus tamen aequívalet, ideòque occasionem praebet intellectui, ut plures in illa partes concipiat, ut in Deo, ejusque adtributis & perfectionibus, adtributa ipsa veluti distincta cóncipimus, ut Justitiam à Misericordia.

30 Real distinction is that which is found in the thing independently of the intellect. Distinction of reason is that which depends on the intellect. Real distinction is divided into entitative, modal and virtual. Real entitative distinction, which is also commonly called major, is said to be that which is found between various things whose entities are so distinct that one can be separated from the other, or at least one can be perfectly conceived without the other, as between the Moon and the Sun, gold and silver, etc. Real minor, or modal, distinction is said to be that which obtains between a thing and a mode of the thing, which mode cannot be separated from the thing itself, or perfectly conceived without it, as between figure and the figured body. Virtual distinction, finally, which you might rather call the foundation of a distinction than a distinction, is that which is found in a thing which, although it is one and simple, is yet equivalent to several, and therefore gives the intellect occasion to conceive several parts in it; as in God and in his attributes and perfections we conceive the attributes themselves as distinct, e.g., Justice from Mercy.

> 31 Praeter haec distinctionis genera Scotus distinctionem aliam admittit, quam dicit esse *formalem*, *actualem ex natura rei*, *formalem* quia non reperitur inter rem & rem, sive inter rem & modum entis, sed inter varias *formalitates* seu perfectiones ejusdem rei, ut inter adtributa Dei, inter animalitatem & rationalitatem hominis &c. *actualem* verò *& ex natura rei*, quia *actualiter de facto* independenter ab intellectu reperitur in rebus. Hinc gravissima exorta est quaestio inter *Thomistas*, *& Scotistas*, quo nimirùm distinctionis genere distinguantur *gradus metaphysici* ejusdem rei, ut ex. gr *animalitas & rationalitas* quae reperiuntur in homine, gradus *vegetandi & sentiendi* qui reperitur in brutis, atque universaliter *genus & differentia*, quae in singulis rebus, sive speciebus continentur.

31 Besides these kinds of distinction Scotus admits another distinction, which he says is formal, actual, and from the nature of the thing: formal, because it is found not between thing and thing, or between a thing and a mode of being, but between various formalities or perfections of the same thing, as between the attributes of God, between the animality and rationality of man, etc.; actual, and from the nature of the thing, because it is found in things actually and in fact, independently of the intellect. Hence arose a most weighty question between the Thomists and the Scotists: by what kind of distinction, namely, the metaphysical grades of the same thing are distinguished, as, e.g., the animality and rationality that are found in man, the grade of vegetating and of sensing that is found in brutes, and universally the genus and difference that are contained in individual things or species.

[p. 11]

> 32 *Thomistae* existimant inter haec omnia distinctionem solum *virtualem* sufficere. *Scotistae* praeter hanc virtualem, *formalem* etiam admittunt, qua gradus ipsi non veluti duae res aut modi (alioquin distinctio foret realis) sed veluti duae formalitates concipiantur, ideòque formalis illa distinctio minor est reali, major autem virtuali, sive inter utramque media. Sed haec Scholastici viderint. Distinctio rationis in *majorem*, *minorem*; ac *minimam* dividi solet. Prima vocatur illa, qua in unica, eadémque re varii conceptus distinguuntur, quorum unus non continetur in alio, ut *justitia* & *misericordia* quae distinguutur in Deo. Distinctio rationis minor quando conceptus ipsi impliciter mutuò includuntur, ut *unum*, *bonum*, *verum*, quae concipiuntur in ente.

32 The Thomists think that among all these only a virtual distinction suffices. The Scotists, besides this virtual one, admit also a formal one, by which the grades themselves are conceived not as two things or modes (otherwise the distinction would be real) but as two formalities; and therefore that formal distinction is less than the real, but greater than the virtual, or midway between the two. But let the Scholastics see to these things. Distinction of reason is commonly divided into major, minor and minimal. The first is the name given to that by which, in one and the same thing, various concepts are distinguished, of which one is not contained in the other, as justice and mercy, which are distinguished in God. Distinction of reason is minor when the concepts themselves mutually include each other implicitly, as one, good, true, which are conceived in being.

> 33 Distinctio denique rationis minima vocatur illa, quae sine ullo fundamento, & ex solo intellectus arbitrio, sive potius infirmitate aut prava consuetudine unum ab alio distinguit ut ex. gr. Deum à Divinitate hominem ab humanitate &c. Unde haec distinctio vocatur *rationis ratiocinantis*, quòd nempè à sola ratione dependeat, quum distinctio rationis *major*, aut *minor* nomine *rationis ratiocinatae* vocari soleat, quasi nimirùm ratio quaedam aut fundamentum distinctionis in ipsa re reperiatur. Sed haec aliaque id genus, quae fusè à Peripateticis explicantur tanti certè non sunt, ut uberiùs exponi debeant. Innuenda tamen hic fuerant, quòd frequentissimus illorum usus in Theologiam ipsam irrepserit; ideòque plura intelligi nequeant, nisi haec vocum significatio explicetur.

33 Minimal distinction of reason, finally, is the name given to that which, without any foundation, and by the mere choice of the intellect, or rather by its weakness or by a bad habit, distinguishes one thing from another, as, e.g., God from the Divinity, man from humanity, etc. Hence this distinction is called a distinction of reasoning reason, because, namely, it depends on reason alone, whereas the major or minor distinction of reason is commonly called by the name of reasoned reason, as if, namely, some ground or foundation of the distinction were found in the thing itself. But these and other things of the kind, which are explained at length by the Peripatetics, are certainly not of such worth that they should be set forth more fully. They had to be hinted at here, however, because the very frequent use of them has crept into Theology itself; and therefore many things cannot be understood unless this meaning of the words is explained.

> 34 Altera proprietas entis est *Veritas*, aptitudo nempè ut ens ipsum ab intellectu cognoscatur. Distinguitur in *transcendentalem* & *formalem*. Prima, est entitas ipsa rei, quatenùs ab intellectu praesertim Divino concipitur, quum nempè entitas ipsa & essentiae rerum in Deo vel archétypis ipsius ideis & imaginibus expraessa contineatur, potest à Deo cognosci, ideòque concipi velut objectum aut terminus Divinae cognitionis, quae ipsi rei vel ideae cognitae perfectissimè respondet, ideòque veritatem ab illa sortítur, & vicissim illi communicat, ut idea vera, vel vera cognitio dicatur. *Veritas* autem *formalis* est eadem conformatio intellectus cognoscentis cum re cognita.

34 The second property of being is Truth, namely the aptitude of being itself to be known by the intellect. It is divided into transcendental and formal. The first is the very entity of the thing, insofar as it is conceived by an intellect, especially the Divine one: for since the very entity and essences of things are contained, expressed, in God, or in his archetypal ideas and images, it can be known by God, and therefore conceived as the object or term of the Divine knowledge, which corresponds most perfectly to the thing itself, or to the idea known, and therefore derives its truth from it, and in turn communicates it to it, so that it is called a true idea, or true knowledge. Formal truth, however, is that same conformity of the knowing intellect with the thing known.

> 35 Quae denique de *veritate* jam diximus, de ultima quoque centis adfectione de *Bonitate* nimirum intelligi facilè poterunt, nisi quod veritas ad intellectum, bonitas autem ad voluntatem refertur. Bonitas autem transcendentalis est ipsum ens, quatenus adpeti vel amari potest à voluntate; bonitas formalis quae *moralis* etiam vocatur, est conformatio objecti *vóliti & amáti* cum legibus morum, praeceptis nimirùm, & archétypa boni imagine quae in Deo reperiuntur. Et haec quae ex Cl. Corsinio excerpta sunt dicta sufficiant.

35 What we have said, finally, about truth can easily be understood also of the last affection of being, namely of Goodness, except that truth is referred to the intellect, and goodness to the will. Transcendental goodness, then, is being itself, insofar as it can be desired or loved by the will; formal goodness, which is also called moral, is the conformity of the object willed and loved with the laws of morals, namely with the precepts and with the archetypal image of the good, which are found in God. And let these things, which have been excerpted from the distinguished Corsini, suffice as said.

[p. 12]

## METAPHYSICES — METAPHYSICS

> PARS ALTERA.

SECOND PART.

> PSYCHOLOGIA,

PSYCHOLOGY,

> sive

OR

> De Anima rationali.

On the Rational Soul.

> 36 Quid prodesse nobis possunt sublimiores scientiae, Adolescentes optimi, si nos metipsos ignoremus? Si nesciamus quid sit anima nostra, an spiritualis, & immortalis, quodnam inter ipsam & corpus commercium intercedat? Hae autem cognitiones omnes, ¿quid nobis prosunt, si animam ipsam perdamus, si ejusdem facultatibus ad veram immortalitatem, aeternam scilicet beatitudinem consequendam non utamur? In duas ergo Dissertationes alteram hanc Metaphysices partem dividemus. Prima erit de origine, spiritualitate, & immortalitate mentis humanae. Secunda de admirabili commercio quod inter ipsam mentem, & corpus est.

hat can the loftier sciences profit us, excellent young men, if we are 36 W ignorant of ourselves? If we do not know what our soul is, whether it is spiritual and immortal, and what commerce intervenes between it and the body? And all these cognitions, what do they profit us, if we lose the soul itself, if we do not use its faculties to attain true immortality, namely eternal beatitude? We shall therefore divide this second part of Metaphysics into two Dissertations. The first will be on the origin, spirituality and immortality of the human mind; the second on the admirable commerce that exists between the mind itself and the body.

## DISSERTATIO I. — DISSERTATION I

> De Origine, spiritualitate, & immortalitate mentis humanae.

On the Origin, spirituality, and immortality of the human mind.

## CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

> De Animae origine, & quo tempore corpori infundatur.

On the origin of the Soul, and at what time it is infused into the body. 37

> 37 *Ut vera creationis habeatur notio*, (ait celebr. Clarkius [^12-s1]) *non oportet eam sibi effingere tanquam generationem alicujus rei erutae ex nihilo considerato ut materia, Creare est* [p. 13] *existentiam dare rei, quae prius illam non habeat, hoc est, efficere, ut existat res quae prius non existebat.* Omnes Philosophi admittunt, quod nullum agens creatum potest quidquam eorum efficere, quae non nisi per creationem esse possunt. Soli quippe Deo convenit creandi virtus. *Neque enim fas est*, inquit S. Augustinus [^13-s1], *ullius naturae, quamlibèt minimae, mortalisque, creatorem, nisi Deum, credere ac dicere.* His positis.

That a true notion of creation may be had (says the celebrated Clarke (d)), one must not picture it to oneself as the generation of some thing drawn out of nothing considered as matter. To create is to give existence [p. 13] to a thing that did not have it before; that is, to bring it about that a thing exists which did not exist before. All Philosophers admit that no created agent can bring about any of those things which cannot be except through creation. For the power of creating belongs to God alone: For it is not lawful, says St. Augustine (e), to believe or to say that the creator of any nature, however small and mortal, is anyone but God. These things being laid down,

> [^12-s1]: De l' Existence de Dieu tom. 1. c. 11.

[^12-s1]: De l’Existence de Dieu, vol. 1, ch. 11.

> [^13-s1]: Lib. 12. de Civit. Dei. c. 24.

[^13-s1]: Bk. 12, City of God, ch. 24.

> 38 Dico 1: rationalis anima à Deo solo creatur, quum corpusculo infunditur. Prob.: creare est efficere ut existat res quae prius non existebat; sed Deus facit ut anima existat, quae prius non existebat: ergo. Prob. 2: creare est aliquid efficere, nullo quod ad ipsum intrinsecùs pertineat, priùs existente; sed ita facit Deus animam: ergo. Prob. min.: mens humana est substantia simplex, carens partibus, compositionis, & divisibilitatis expers: ut in sequentibus videbimus: ergo efficitur sine ulla partium successione nulloque quod ad ipsam intrinsecùs pertineat priùs existente: ergo sola creatione fit; sed creatio soli Deo competit, ut dictum est jam: ergo anima rationalis â Deo Creatore conditur.

38 I say 1: the rational soul is created by God alone when it is infused into the little body. It is proved: to create is to bring it about that a thing exists which did not exist before; but God brings it about that the soul exists, which did not exist before: therefore. It is proved 2: to create is to make something when nothing that intrinsically pertains to it exists beforehand; but it is thus that God makes the soul: therefore. Proof of the minor: the human mind is a simple substance, lacking parts, devoid of composition and divisibility, as we shall see in what follows: therefore it is made without any succession of parts, and with nothing that intrinsically pertains to it existing beforehand: therefore it comes to be by creation alone; but creation belongs to God alone, as has already been said: therefore the rational soul is made by God the Creator.

> 39 Prob. 3: anima rationalis non est generabilis, sed quod non est generabile per creationem fit: ergo. Prob. maj.: quod generabile est, est corruptibile, ut omnes fatentur; sed anima rationalis est incorruptibilis quia est immortalis, ut posteriùs Cap. III. ostendetur: ergo. Prob. 4: natura non extenditur nisi ad generandum, *sed quod non est, non generatur, non enim est unde generetur*, ut optimè ait Hippócrates [^13-s2] ergo creatio excedit naturae potentiam: ergo nequit fieri nisi â Deo.

39 It is proved 3: the rational soul is not generable; but what is not generable comes to be by creation: therefore. Proof of the major: what is generable is corruptible, as all admit; but the rational soul is incorruptible, because it is immortal, as will be shown later in Ch. III: therefore. It is proved 4: nature extends only to generating; but what is not is not generated, for there is nothing from which it might be generated, as Hippocrates says very well (f); therefore creation exceeds the power of nature: therefore it cannot be done except by God.

> [^13-s2]: Lib. 1. de Diaeta num. 5.

[^13-s2]: Bk. 1, On Regimen, no. 5.

> 40 Christianus Wolff [^13-s3] celebris nostri seculi philosophus fatetur quidem animam rationalem à solo Deo per creationem fieri, verùm Libnitzium sequutus contendit animas omnium hominum, initio simul conditas a Deo fuisse, easque singulas suis inclusas corpusculis. *Animae*, inquit, *praeexistunt in corpusculis organicis praeexistentibus ex quibus fetus in utero formatur.*

40 Christian Wolff (g), a celebrated philosopher of our age, admits indeed that the rational soul comes to be by creation from God alone; but, following Leibniz, he contends that the souls of all men were made by God together at the beginning, and each of them enclosed in its own little body. Souls, he says, pre-exist in pre-existing organic corpuscles, from which the fetus is formed in the womb.

> [^13-s3]: Psycholog. Rat. §. 704. & seq.

[^13-s3]: Psychologia Rationalis, §. 704 ff.

> 41 Dico 2: contra Leibnitzium, & Wolfium: animae rationales non fuerunt omnes simul initio temporis à Deo creatae, iisque organicis corpusculis inclusae, quae tunc itidèm à Deo condita in útero matris delitescunt. Prob. 1: ex Concilio Lateranensi V. [^13-s4] ubi expraessè definitum fuit, *animam rationalem pro corporum, quibus infunditur multitudine singulariter esse multiplicabilem, multiplicatam, & multiplicandam*: ergo animae omnium hominum, qui ad finem usque mundi nascituri sunt non fuere initio temporis à Deo creatae, quia tunc licet sint *multiplicatae*, non sunt tamen [p. 14] *multiplicandae*: ergo animarum praexistentia apertè refragatur Concilio Lateranensi, ac proindè propugnari minimè potest.

41 I say 2, against Leibniz and Wolff: rational souls were not all created together by God at the beginning of time and enclosed in those organic corpuscles which, likewise made by God at that time, lie hidden in the mother’s womb. It is proved 1: from the Fifth Lateran Council (h), where it was expressly defined that the rational soul, according to the multitude of the bodies into which it is infused, is singly multipliable, multiplied, and to be multiplied: therefore the souls of all men who are to be born until the end of the world were not created by God at the beginning of time, because at that time, although they are multiplied, they are not, however, to be multiplied: [p. 14] therefore the pre-existence of souls is openly contrary to the Lateran Council, and consequently can by no means be defended.

> [^13-s4]: Sub Leone X. Sess. 8. Tom. 19. Collect. Concil. Labb.

[^13-s4]: Under Leo X, Sess. 8, vol. 19 of Labbe’s Collection of the Councils.

> 42 Probatur 2. ab absurdo: hac opinione positâ non posset indiscriminatim singulis feminis Virginitas suadéri, quippe quum non constet quae feminae animatis corpusculis praeditae sint, nequit virginitas singulis feminis suaderi, quin verum sit, optionem in nobis esse, ut tot pereant animae, quot animata corpuscula illae complectuntur. Eandem quoque ob causàm nulli feminae licèret perpetuo se virginitatis voto obstríngere, nisi certò ei primò constiterit corpuscula animata suo in sinu minimè contineri, quae omnia, quum non minus falsa, quàm absurda sint sequitur, Wolffianam opinionem penitùs à Viro Catholico rejiciendam esse.

42 It is proved 2. from absurdity: once this opinion is granted, Virginity could not be urged upon all women indiscriminately; for since it is not known which women are endowed with animated corpuscles, virginity cannot be urged upon individual women without its being true that it lies in our choice that as many souls should perish as those animated corpuscles contain. For the same reason, too, no woman would be permitted to bind herself by a perpetual vow of virginity unless it were first certainly established for her that no animated corpuscles are contained in her womb; and since all these things are no less false than absurd, it follows that the Wolffian opinion is to be utterly rejected by a Catholic man.

> 43 Pro secunda quaestionis parte sciendum est, in hoc convenire antiquos omnes Philosophos, nempè, animam rationalem non illicò à conceptione infundi, sed post aliquod tempus. Communissima opinio defendit animam rationalem post quadraginta dies fetum informare, quia tunc, & non antea perfectè organizatum est corpusculum. Ita Galenus [^14-s1-3]. Hippocrates [^14-s2] sive quisquis Auctor est libri de *Natura pueri*, differentiam docens inter fetus masculos, & femineos illos triginta, hos duobus supra quadraginta diebus dearticulari dixit, hoc est, perfectè organizari. Multò autem breviorem terminum ad hujusmodi perfectionem adsignavit idem Hippocrates lib. de Carnibus, num. 10. inquiens *in septem diebus habet quaecumque, corpus habere debet*, atque hoc pacto si corpus in septem diebus absolutum est, in septimo animari, ex sententia Hippocratis videtur consentaneum. Alii adserunt fetum humanum triduo perfici, ac tertia die rationalem animam recipere. Aristoteles [^14-s3] adseruit hominem vivere vita plantae, vita animalis, & hominis, adeoque animam rationalem post aliquot tempus fetui advenire, licet illud tempus non definierit. His positis.

43 For the second part of the question, it should be known that all the ancient Philosophers agree in this, namely that the rational soul is not infused immediately upon conception, but after some time. The most common opinion holds that the rational soul informs the fetus after forty days, because then, and not before, the little body is perfectly organized. So Galen (i). Hippocrates (j), or whoever is the author of the book On the Nature of the Child, teaching a difference between male and female fetuses, said that the former are articulated in thirty days, the latter in forty-two, that is, perfectly organized. But the same Hippocrates, in the book On Flesh, no. 10, assigned a much shorter term for perfection of this kind, saying in seven days it has whatever the body ought to have; and in this way, if the body is complete in seven days, it seems consistent with the opinion of Hippocrates that it is animated on the seventh. Others assert that the human fetus is completed in three days, and receives the rational soul on the third day. Aristotle (k) asserts that man lives the life of a plant, the life of an animal, and that of a man, and hence that the rational soul comes to the fetus after some time, although he did not define that time. These things being laid down,
