Sed mirabilius est, quod jam dudum nobis communicavit praeclarissimus Carolus Drelincurtius, quodque observaverat in virgine circiter 20 ann, quae postquam dira cephalaea [^49-s2] semestri discruciata fuisset, ac tandem occaecata, ac deincèps sensibus orbata, in mediis planctibus mortem obierat; ipsi scilicet pinealis glandula non tantum saxea fuit, sed etiam ad ovi gallinacei amplitudinem excreverat, qua sua mole nervorum opticorum thalamos [^49-s3] nec non reliquos tandem nervos compressit [^49-s4].

154 But neither does the pineal gland seem to be established as a fit seat for the mind. Let us hear the Anatomists (f). “Frederik once saw this gland (the pineal) petrified, and found three stones in it. But more wonderful is what the most distinguished Charles Drelincourt long ago communicated to us, and what he had observed in a virgin of about 20 years, who, after she had been tormented for six months by a dreadful cephalaea (g), and at length blinded, and thereafter deprived of her senses, had met her death amid lamentations: in her, namely, the pineal gland was not only stony, but had even grown to the size of a hen’s egg, and by its bulk had compressed the thalami (h) of the optic nerves and finally the remaining nerves as well (i).”

> [^49-s1]: Ruysch. in Thes. Anat.

[^49-s1]: Ruysch, in the Thes. Anat.

> [^49-s2]: Cephalaea est capitis dolor inveteratus, aegrè cedens, contumax & pertinax.

[^49-s2]: Cephalaea is an inveterate pain of the head, yielding with difficulty, stubborn and persistent.

> [^49-s3]: Locum è quo nervi optici egrediuntur Galenus *thalamus* vocavit.

[^49-s3]: The place from which the optic nerves issue Galen called the thalamus.

> [^49-s4]: Vid. Theatr. Anatom. Boneti tom. 2. p. 309.

[^49-s4]: See Bonet, Theatr. Anatom., vol. 2, p. 309.

[p. 50]

> 155 Recentiùs D. Dela Peyronie [^50-s1] sedem animae *corpus callosum* [^50-s2] constituit. Ostendit namque laesis reliquis cérebri partibus, solo illaeso corpore calloso, usum sensuum & rationis in diversis perstitisse integrum, laeso verò corpore calloso, unà sensationes, & rationis usum subtractum fuisse. His verò non obstantibus adserendum mihi videtur animam sedem propriam habere in solo cérebro, licet certò statui non possit in qua praecisè cerebri parte resideat. In ea enim sola corporis parte dicendum est animam residere, quae sola est in qua anima immediatè operetur; animum verò in solum cerebrum immediatè operari, apertissimè constat: etenim vitiato solo cérebro, sensuum omnium usus amittitur; hinc Apoplexia correpti, veluti fulmine percussi, omni sensu privantur, ita ut nihil sentiant. Corporis etiam adfectiones, quae non transmittuntur ad cérebrum, mentem prorsùs latent, ut in parálysi accidit. (*Vide Phys.* §. 560, *& seq.*)

155 More recently M. de La Peyronie (k) has placed the seat of the soul in the corpus callosum (l). For he showed that when the other parts of the brain were injured and the corpus callosum alone was unharmed, the use of the senses and of reason remained whole in various persons; but when the corpus callosum was injured, sensations and the use of reason were taken away together. Notwithstanding these things, however, it seems to me that it must be asserted that the soul has its proper seat in the brain alone, although it cannot be settled with certainty in precisely which part of the brain it resides. For the soul must be said to reside in that part of the body alone which is the only one in which the soul operates immediately; but that the mind operates immediately on the brain alone is most plainly evident: for when the brain alone is impaired, the use of all the senses is lost; hence those seized by Apoplexy, as if struck by lightning, are deprived of all sense, so that they feel nothing. The affections of the body, too, which are not transmitted to the brain, remain wholly hidden from the mind, as happens in paralysis. (See Phys. §. 560 ff.)

> [^50-s1]: Ann. 1741.

[^50-s1]: In the year 1741.

> [^50-s2]: *Corticalis substantia cerebri*, dicitur exterior substantia illius cinerei coloris ad differentiam interioris candidioris, quae medullaris, & *callosum corpus* dicitur.

[^50-s2]: The cortical substance of the brain is the name given to its outer substance, of an ashen color, as distinguished from the inner, whiter substance, which is called the medullary substance and the corpus callosum.

> 156 Peripatetici verò saltem ab XIII. Christiani nominis seculo, animum in toto corpore esse contendunt. Moventur talibus argumentis. Primo, quia quamcumque corporis partem tangamus, animus sentit, quod signum est, eum ibi esse. Deinde quia intelligi non potest, quo pacto animus sit *forma substantialis* corporis humani, ut definitum est in Concilio Viennensi [^50-s3], id est, sit id, quod corpus regit, nisi totum corpus occupet. Verum opus non est hujusmodi rationes ad Lydium lapidem revocare.

156 The Peripatetics, however, at least from the thirteenth century of the Christian name, contend that the mind is in the whole body. They are moved by arguments such as these. First, because whatever part of the body we touch, the mind feels, which is a sign that it is there. Next, because it cannot be understood how the mind is the substantial form of the human body, as was defined at the Council of Vienne (m), that is, is that which governs the body, unless it occupies the whole body. But there is no need to bring reasons of this kind to the Lydian touchstone.

> [^50-s3]: Sub Clem. V. Ann. 1311.

[^50-s3]: Under Clement V, in the year 1311.

> 157 Et ad primam quod adtinet dico cum Cl. Jacquiero, animam percipere impressionem factam in qualibet corporis parte, quia impressio illa ad cerebrum propagatur ope nervorum, qui à qualibet corporis parte ad cerebrum usque pertingunt; nimirùm à qualibet parte corporis, tensi sunt nervi usque ad cerebrum, unde quum nervi extremitas, quae est in pede ex. gr. vel in manu vellitur, pariter vellitur, seu movetur altera extremitas, quae est in cerebro, & vi istius motus in cerebro excitati admonetur anima, doloremque sentit, si impressio facta vehemens fuerit. Illud verò multis experimentis confirmatur. I. Si arctissimè stringatur pars aliqua corporis, cerébrum inter, & partem aliam corporis resecandam, aut pungendam, nullus, aut ferè nullus sentitur dolor: quia scilicèt nullus, aut ferè nullus pérvenit motus ad extremitatem nervi, quae est in cérebro. II. Si quis, ut aliquandò evenit, altè defixus sit in aliquam cogitationem, ut plurimùm, non percipit objecta externa, quae tamen feriunt sensus illius externos; quia nimirùm tunc nervi ita sunt tensi, ut non admittant alium motum, quo mens determinetur ad percipienda objecta externa.

157 And as regards the first, I say with the distinguished Jacquier that the soul perceives an impression made on any part of the body because that impression is propagated to the brain by means of the nerves, which reach from any part of the body all the way to the brain; namely, from any part of the body nerves are stretched as far as the brain, so that when the extremity of a nerve which is, e.g., in the foot or in the hand is plucked, the other extremity, which is in the brain, is likewise plucked or moved, and by the force of this motion excited in the brain the soul is alerted, and feels pain if the impression made was vehement. This is moreover confirmed by many experiments. I. If some part of the body is bound very tightly, between the brain and another part of the body that is to be cut off or pricked, no pain, or almost none, is felt; because, namely, no motion, or almost none, reaches the extremity of the nerve which is in the brain. II. If someone, as sometimes happens, is deeply fixed on some thought, he very often does not perceive external objects, which nevertheless strike his external senses; because, namely, the nerves are then so stretched that they do not admit another motion by which the mind might be determined to perceive external objects.

[p. 51]

> 158 Sed *instant*. Quaecumque pars corporis laedatur, anima percipit dolorem, veluti existentem in illa ipsâ parte corporis, quae laeditur: ergo mens proximè praesens est parti cuilibet corporis. Nego conseq. Quamvis enim percipiatur ab anima dolor, velut existens in quacumque laesa corporis parte, non tamen anima dolorem percipit in illa ipsa corporis parte, quae laeditur.

158 But you will insist. Whatever part of the body is injured, the soul perceives the pain as existing in that very part of the body which is injured: therefore the mind is immediately present to every part of the body. I deny the consequence. For although the pain is perceived by the soul as existing in whatever part of the body is injured, the soul nevertheless does not perceive the pain in that very part of the body which is injured.

> 159 Et quidem caecus baculo explorans objecta externa, proprietates eorundem, liquiditatem ex. gr. vel duritiem percipit extremo baculo, ac extremo in baculo velut existentem quodammodò. Nemo tamen dixerit, animam hominis caeci residere in extremitate baculi. Sic etiam quamvis anima percipiat sensationem aliquam ex. gr. caloris, aut frigoris velut existentem in extremo digito, aut quâlibet alterâ corporis parte, non iccircò dicendum est animam agere in extremum digitum, & in eo proximè percipere sensationem, quâ adficitur; motus nimirùm extremo digito primùm communicatus, postmodùm per nervos ad cérebrum diffusus pervenit ad animae sedem, ubi fit sensatio, quam tamen anima naturaliter refert ad alteram extremitatem nervorum, ubi facta fuit prima impulsio.

159 And indeed a blind man exploring external objects with a stick perceives their properties, e.g. fluidity or hardness, at the end of the stick, and as it were existing in a certain manner at the end of the stick. Yet no one would say that the blind man’s soul resides at the extremity of the stick. So too, although the soul perceives some sensation, e.g. of heat or of cold, as existing in the tip of the finger or in any other part of the body, it must not therefore be said that the soul acts upon the tip of the finger and immediately perceives in it the sensation by which it is affected; namely, the motion first communicated to the tip of the finger, then spread through the nerves to the brain, reaches the seat of the soul, where the sensation takes place, which the soul nevertheless naturally refers to the other extremity of the nerves, where the first impulse was made.

> 160 Ad secundam objectionem quod spectat, dico animam esse posse veram corporis formam, (ut reverâ est) nempè principium á quo actiones humanae oriuntur, licet negemus eam in toto corpore esse diffussam. Quod quidem ut illustrius exponatur audiamus locum insignem ex Angelico Magistro S. Thoma [^51-s1] *Spiritus* (inquit S. Doct.) *possunt alligari corpori, vel per modum formae, sicut anima corpori humano alligatur ut* DET EI VITAM: *vel etiam absque hoc, quod sit ejus forma, sicut Necromántici virtute daemonum spiritus alligatur imaginibus.*

160 As regards the second objection, I say that the soul can be the true form of the body (as indeed it is), namely the principle from which human actions arise, although we deny that it is diffused through the whole body. That this may be set forth more clearly, let us hear a notable passage from the Angelic Master St. Thomas (n): Spirits (says the holy Doctor) can be bound to a body either by way of form, as the soul is bound to the human body to give it life; or else without this, that it be its form, as Necromancers by the power of demons bind spirits to images.

> [^51-s1]: IV. Cont. Gent. cap. 90.

[^51-s1]: IV Contra Gentiles, ch. 90.

> 161 Porrò advertamus, quo tempore Clemens V. Synodum Viennensem coëgit, extitisse, qui docerent, animas nostras non aliâ ratione corporibus humanis uti, ac daemones iis corporibus, quae obsident [^51-s2]. Haec satis docent, quid & Veteres Theologi, & Patres Viennenses sibi voluerint, quum docuere animas esse formas substantiales, nempè mentes humanas non obsidere humana corpora, velut quandoque daemones, sed *informare*, id est, *vitam eis dare*. Duae igitur sunt hìc secernendae quaestiones: prima: *informet anima corpus*, id est, *ei vitam det*, *necne*. Hoc dogma esse vult Synodus Viennensis, idque nos etiam docemus. Altera: *si ut eum informet ac vivum reddat nécessum sit ut per totum corpus sit diffusa?* Hoc Philosophiae juris est. Dicta sufficiant.

161 Let us note, moreover, that at the time when Clement V convened the Synod of Vienne there were those who taught that our souls make use of human bodies in no other way than demons make use of the bodies which they possess (o). These things show well enough what both the Ancient Theologians and the Fathers of Vienne meant when they taught that souls are substantial forms, namely that human minds do not possess human bodies, as demons sometimes do, but inform them, that is, give them life. There are therefore two questions to be distinguished here: the first, whether the soul informs the body, that is, gives it life, or not. The Synod of Vienne wills this to be dogma, and we too teach it. The other: if it informs it and renders it living, is it necessary that it be diffused through the whole body? This is a matter of Philosophy’s jurisdiction. Let what has been said suffice.

> [^51-s2]: Abregè d' Histoire Ecclesiastique. Paris. A. 1751. ad ann. 1312.

[^51-s2]: Abregé d’Histoire Ecclesiastique, Paris, 1751, under the year 1312.

[p. 52]

## METAPHYSICES — METAPHYSICS

> PARS POSTREMA.

FINAL PART.

> THEOLOGIA NATURALIS.

NATURAL THEOLOGY.

## DISSERTATIO UNICA. — SINGLE DISSERTATION

> Omni argumentorum genere, Existentia Supremi Numinis invictissimè demonstratur.

By every kind of argument the Existence of the Supreme Deity is most invincibly demonstrated.

> 162 De Deo quantum ad Metaphysicam spectat acturi, expendemus, an ratione naturali possit illius existentia ostendi; tempus enim non fert, ut in exponendis Divinae Essentiae adtributis immoremur, hoc enim, quum Sacrae Theologiae studio animum adplicueritis, oportunius expendetis.

f God, being about to treat of him so far as concerns Metaphysics, we 162 O shall weigh whether his existence can be shown by natural reason; for time does not allow us to dwell on setting forth the attributes of the Divine Essence; these, indeed, you will weigh more opportunely when you have applied your mind to the study of Sacred Theology.

> 163 *Atheus* [^52-s1] dicitur, qui Supremi Numinis existentiam inficiatur. Dei nomine intelligitur ,, ens à se, atque adeò necessariò existens, plenum rationis atque consilii, à quo adspectabilis mundus, quaeque in illo sunt, condita fuerint, & facta regantur ,,. Haec definitio nominalis est. In ea tamen consentire omnes, (ut ait Cl. à Brixia), arbitror inficiari posse neminem, ut enim habet Cicero [^52-s2] ,, Deus qui intelligitur à nobis, non alio modo intelligi potest, nisi mens soluta quaedam & libera, [p. 53] segregata ab omni concretione mortali, omnia sentiens, & movens, ipsaque praedita motu sempiterno ,,. His positis inquirendum est, an sit evidens evidentiâ physica, Deum existere? Loquimur de physicâ evidentiâ, nempè de ea, quae sufficit ad extorquendum adsensum constantem, atque firmum, non à protervo, deque omnibus dubitante, sed à viro veritatis amatore ingenuo, Rem quippè cum his agere, in animo mihi non est hoc loci, qui adeò inficiantur omnia, ut ne ipsa quidem prima cognitionis principia, etsi evidentissima sint, pro veris sine dubitatione admittant. Sat erit horum sophismata, & cavillationes convellere.

163 He is called an Atheist (p) who denies the existence of the Supreme Deity. By the name of God is understood “a being from itself, and hence necessarily existing, full of reason and counsel, by whom the visible world and the things that are in it were founded and, having been made, are ruled.” This definition is a nominal one. Yet that all agree in it, no one, I think (as the distinguished Fortunato da Brescia says), can deny; for as Cicero has it (q): “God, who is understood by us, cannot be understood in any other way than as a certain mind, unfettered and free, separated from [p. 53] from all mortal admixture, perceiving and moving all things, and itself endowed with everlasting motion.” These things laid down, we must inquire whether it is evident with physical evidence that God exists. We speak of physical evidence, namely of that which suffices to extort a constant and firm assent, not from a wanton man who doubts of everything, but from an ingenuous lover of truth. For it is not in my mind in this place to deal with those who so deny everything that they do not admit as true without doubting even the first principles of knowledge themselves, most evident though they are. It will be enough to pull up their sophisms and cavils.

> [^52-s1]: Sint re verâ Athei, an non, magna quaestio est. Nullos extitisse Atheos, aliqui Viri docti putarunt, maximè verò antiquos Philosophos nullomodo Atheos dici posse, contendit Johann. Christophorus Wolffius in libro de *Atheismi falsò suspectis*, & alii post eum. E contrariò Veteres plures Atheos fuisse, defendit post alios Johan. Henricus Poppius. *De Atheismo Philosophorum Gentilium celebriorum*, & Buddeus de *Spinosismo ante Spinosam*.

[^52-s1]: Whether there really are Atheists or not is a great question. Some learned men have thought that no Atheists have existed, and Johann Christoph Wolf, in his book De Atheismi falso suspectis, and others after him, contend that the ancient Philosophers in particular can in no way be called Atheists. On the contrary, Johann Heinrich Poppius, after others, maintains that many of the Ancients were Atheists, in De Atheismo Philosophorum Gentilium celebriorum; and so does Buddeus in De Spinozismo ante Spinozam.

> [^52-s2]: Tusc. Lib. 1. cap. 27.

[^52-s2]: Tusculan Disputations, bk. 1, ch. 27.

> 164 Dico igitur: evidens est, evidentiâ physicâ Deum existere. Prob. 1. ex perpetuo, constantique omnium nationum, populorumque consensu: qod enim natura universaliter confitetur, necesse est, verum esse. Naturam enim universaliter mentiri, impossibile est. Omnes porrò gentes, nationes omnes quantumvis feras, ac barbaras in id perpetuò consentire, ut supremum aliquod Numen admitterent, adeò apertum est, ut negari ab eo tantum possit, qui in Historiis planè hospes fuerit. ,, Nulla gens est ,, (*inquit Tullius*) [^53-s1], ,, neque tam immansueta, neque tam fera, quae non etiam si ignoret, qualem habere Deum deceat, tamen habendum sciat ,,.

164 I say, therefore: it is evident with physical evidence that God exists. Proof 1, from the perpetual and constant consent of all nations and peoples: for what nature universally confesses must necessarily be true. For it is impossible for nature universally to lie. Now that all races, all nations, however wild and barbarous, have perpetually agreed in this, that they admit some supreme Deity, is so plain that it could be denied only by one who is an utter stranger to History. “There is no race” (says Cicero (r)) “so untamed, nor so wild, that, even if it does not know what sort of God it ought to have, does not yet know that it ought to have one.”

> [^53-s1]: Lib. 1. de Legib. Cap. 8.

[^53-s1]: Bk. 1 of On the Laws, ch. 8.

> 165 Et sanè nisi id cognitum, comprehensumque animis haberemus inquit laudat. Cicero [^53-s2] ,, non tam stabilis opinio permanéret, nec confirmaretur diuturnitate temporis, nec unà seculis, aetatibusque hominum inveterari potuisset. Etenim videmus ceteras opiniones fictas atque vanas diuturnitate extabuisse. ¿Quis enim hyppocentaurum fuisse, aut chimaeram putat? ...... ......Opinionum *enim* commenta delet dies, naturae judicia confirmat ,,. Sed licet jam, ut cum eodem *Tullio* loquar, [^53-s3] (& haec erit secunda probatio) licet inquam ,, remota subtilitate disputandi, oculis quodammodò contemplari pulchritudinem rerum earum, quas Divinâ Providentiâ dicimus constitutas ,,.

165 “And surely, unless we had this known and grasped in our minds,” says the praised Cicero (s), “so stable an opinion would not have remained, nor would it have been confirmed by length of time, nor could it have grown old together with the centuries and ages of men. For we see that other opinions, feigned and empty, have wasted away with length of time. For who thinks that the hippocentaur existed, or the chimera? …… For time blots out the fictions of opinion, but confirms the judgments of nature.” But it is now permitted, to speak with the same Cicero (t) (and this will be the second proof), it is permitted, I say, “setting aside subtlety of disputation, to contemplate in a manner with our eyes the beauty of those things which we say were established by Divine Providence.”

> [^53-s2]: Lib. 2. de Nat. Deor.

[^53-s2]: Bk. 2 of On the Nature of the Gods.

> [^53-s3]: Lib. 2. de Nat. Deor. Cap. 39.

[^53-s3]: Bk. 2 of On the Nature of the Gods, ch. 39.

> 166 ,, At principiò terra universa cernatur, locata in media mundi sede, solida & globosa, & undique ipsa sese nutibus suis conglobata, vestita floribus, herbis, arboribus, frugibus; quorum omnium incredibilis multitudo insatiabili varietate distinguitur. Adde hùc fontium gelidas perennitates, liquores perlucidos amnium, riparum vestitus viridissimos, speluncarum concavas altitudines, saxorum asperitates, impendentium montium altitudines, immensitatesque camporum. Adde etiam reconditas auri, argentique venas. ¿Quae verò, & quàm varia genera bestiarum vel cicurum, vel ferarum? ¿qui volucrum lapsus, atque cantus¿ ¿qui pecudum pastus? ¿quae vita silvestrium?

166 “And first let the whole earth be beheld, set in the middle seat of the world, solid and globular, and on every side gathered into a globe by its own tendencies, clothed with flowers, grasses, trees, crops: the incredible multitude of all of which is distinguished by an insatiable variety. Add to this the cool perennial flowings of springs, the transparent waters of rivers, the greenest clothing of the banks, the hollow depths of caverns, the roughness of rocks, the heights of overhanging mountains, and the immensities of the plains. Add also the hidden veins of gold and silver. And what kinds of beasts, and how varied, whether tame or wild! What flights and songs of birds! What pasturings of cattle! What life of the creatures of the woods!

[p. 54]

> 167 ,, Quid jam de hominum genere dicam, qui quasi cultores terrae constituti, non patiuntur eam, nec immanitate belluarum efferari, nec stirpium asperitate vastari, quorumque operibus agri, insulae, litoraque collúcent distincta testis, & urbibus; quae si, ut animis, sic oculis vidére possémus, nemo, cunctam intuens terram, de divina ratione dubitaret. At verò ¿quanta maris est pulchritudo? ¿Quae species universi? ¿Quae multitudo, & varietas insularum? ¿Quae amaenitates orarum & litorum, quot genera, quámque disparia partim summersarum, partim fluitantium, & innatantium belluarum, partim ad saxa nativis testis inhaerentium? Ipsum autem mare sic terram adpetens, litoribus eludit, ut una ex duabus naturis conflata videatur ,,.

167 “What shall I now say of the race of men, who, set up as it were as cultivators of the earth, suffer it neither to grow wild with the savagery of beasts nor to be laid waste by the roughness of thickets, and by whose works the fields, the islands and the shores shine, studded with houses and cities? If we could see these things with our eyes as we can with our minds, no one, gazing upon the whole earth, would doubt of the divine reason. And truly, how great is the beauty of the sea! What an aspect of the whole! What a multitude and variety of islands! What delights of coasts and shores! How many kinds, and how unlike, of creatures, partly submerged, partly floating and swimming, partly clinging to the rocks with their native shells! And the sea itself, so making for the land, sports upon the shores that the two natures seem fused into one.

> 168 ,, Exindè mari finitimus aër die, & nocte distinguitur, isque tum fusus, & extenuatus sublime fertur, tùm autèm concretus in nubes cogitur, humoremque colligens terram auget imbribus, tum effluens hùc & illùc, ventus efficit. Idem annuas frigorum, & calorum facit varietates, idemque & volatum alitum sustinet, & spiritu ductus alit, & sustentat animantes Restat ultimus, & á domiciliis nostris altissimus, omnia cingens & coercens caeli complexus: qui idem aether vocatur, extrema ora, & determinatio mundi in quo cum admirabilitate maxima igneae formae cursus ordinatos definiunt ,,.

168 “Next, the air bordering on the sea is divided by day and night, and it is now borne aloft, spread out and thinned, and now, condensed, is gathered into clouds, and, collecting moisture, enriches the earth with rains, and now, flowing this way and that, makes wind. It too produces the yearly variations of cold and heat, and it also sustains the flight of birds, and, drawn in by breathing, nourishes and sustains living creatures. There remains the last and, from our dwellings, the highest, the embrace of heaven, girding and confining all things: which is also called the ether, the outermost border and boundary of the world, in which the fiery forms trace out their ordered courses with the greatest wonder.

> 169 ,, E quibus Sol cujus magnitudine multis partibus terra superatur, circum eam ipsam volvitur, isque oriens, & occidens diem, noctemque conficit; & modò accedens, tùm autèm recedens binas in singulis annis reversiones ab extremo contrarias facit, quarum intervallo, tùm quasi tristitiâ quadam contrahit terram, tùm vicissim laetificat, ut cum caelo hilarata videatur? Luna autèm quae est, ut ostendunt Mathematici, major quàm dimidia pars terrae, iisdemque spatiis vagatur, quibus Sol; sed tùm congrediens cum Sole, tùm digrediens, & eam lucem, quam à Sole accepit mittit in terras, & varias ipsa mutationes lucis habet; atque etiam tùm subjecta & opposita Soli radios ejus & lumen obscurat; tùm ipsa incidens in umbram terrae, quum est è regione Solis, interpositu interjectuque terrae, repentè deficit, iisdemque spatiis hae stellae, quas vagas dicimus, circum terram feruntur, eodemque modo oriuntur, & occidunt; quarum motus, tùm incitantur, tùm retardantur, saepè etiam insistunt. Quo spectaculo nihil potest admirabiliùs esse, nihil pulchriùs ,,. Hactenùs Romanae eloquentiae Princeps.

169 “Of these the Sun, by whose magnitude the earth is surpassed many times over, revolves around that very earth, and by rising and setting it makes day and night; and now approaching, now receding, it makes each year two returns from opposite extremes, in the interval of which it now as it were contracts the earth with a kind of sadness, now in turn gladdens it, so that it seems to be made joyful together with the sky. The Moon, moreover, which is, as the Mathematicians show, larger than half the earth, wanders through the same spaces as the Sun; but now coming together with the Sun, now parting from it, it both sends to the earth the light which it has received from the Sun and itself undergoes various changes of light; and sometimes, placed beneath the Sun and over against it, it darkens its rays and light; sometimes, falling itself into the shadow of the earth, when it is opposite the Sun, it suddenly fails, through the interposition and intervention of the earth; and through the same spaces those stars which we call wandering are borne around the earth, and in the same way they rise and set; and their motions are now quickened, now retarded, often they even stand still. Than which spectacle nothing can be more wonderful, nothing more beautiful.” Thus far the Prince of Roman eloquence.

> 170 Haec igitur, qui seriò animadverterit, adtentoque fuerit animo comtemplatus, non dubito, quin eò tandèm veniat, ut nobiscum fateatur, eximiam mundi machinam, quaeque in illo sunt corpora, sine ratione atque consilio fieri minimè potuisse. ,, An cum machinatióne quâdam, (*inquit laudat. Elegantissim. Cicero*) [p. 55] ,, [^55-s1-2] moveri aliquid videmus, ut sphaeram, ut horas, ut alia permulta non dubitamus, quin illa opera sint rationis; quum autem impetum caeli admirabili cum celeritate moveri, vertique videamus constantissimè conficientem vicissitudines anniversarias, cum summa salute, & conservatione rerum omnium, dubitamus, quin ea non solùm ratione fiant, sed etiam excelenti quâdam, divinâque ratione?

170 Whoever, then, has seriously attended to these things and contemplated them with an attentive mind will, I do not doubt, at last come to confess with us that the excellent machine of the world, and the bodies that are in it, could by no means have come to be without reason and counsel. “Or when, by some contrivance,” (says the praised, most elegant Cicero) we [p. 55] “(u) we see something being moved, as a sphere, as clocks, as very many other things, we do not doubt that those are works of reason; but when we see the onrush of the heaven moved with wonderful swiftness and turned round, most constantly bringing about the yearly alternations with the utmost safety and preservation of all things, do we doubt that these things are done not only by reason, but by a reason that is excellent and divine?”

> [^55-s1-2]: Loc. citat.

[^55-s1-2]: In the place cited.

> 171 Lubet itaque argumentum ita paucis conficere. Si est aliquid in rerum naturâ, quod hominis mens, quod ratio, quod vis, quod potestas humana efficere non possit, est certè quod illud efficit, homine meliùs. Atqui res caelestes, omnesque eae quarum est ordo sempiternus ab homine confici non possunt. Est igitur id, quo illa conficiuntur, homine meliùs. Id autem quòd potiùs dixeris quam Deum? Etenim si Deus non est, quid esse potest in rerum naturâ homine meliùs? In eo enim sola ratio est; quâ nihil potest esse praestantius. Esse autem hominem qui nihil in mundo melius esse, quam se, putet, desipientis adrogantiae est, ne dicam amentiae. Ergo est aliquid homine melius. Est igitur Deus.

171 It pleases me, therefore, to complete the argument thus in a few words. If there is something in the nature of things which the mind of man, which reason, which human force, which human power cannot bring about, that which brings it about is certainly better than man. But the heavenly things, and all those whose order is everlasting, cannot be brought about by man. That, therefore, by which they are brought about is better than man. And what would you call this rather than God? For if God does not exist, what can there be in the nature of things better than man? For in him alone is reason, than which nothing can be more excellent. But for a man to think that there is nothing in the world better than himself is the arrogance of a fool, not to say of a madman. Therefore there is something better than man. Therefore God exists.

> 172 Prob. 3: ex humani corporis structurâ, quae adeó mirabilis est, tamque stupenda, ut supremi opificis existentia planè ad evidentiam per eam, si considerata diligenter fuerit, optimèque perspecta contra Atheum evincatur. Age, circunspice humani corporis opificium, cujus admonitione perdisce, quis tam pulchrae imaginis conditor, quis oculorum pictor, quis nares, auresque tornavit, quis labia distendit oris, quis nervos tetendit, atque ligavit, quis irrigavit venas, quis ossa congesit solida, quis carnem pellicula tenui circumtexit, quis digitos, articulósque discrevit, quis fundamenta pedis extendit, quis perforavit poros, atque meatus aperuit, quis pulmonum exculpsit fistula?

172 Proof 3: from the structure of the human body, which is so wonderful and so astounding that by it, if it has been diligently considered and thoroughly examined, the existence of the supreme maker is plainly established against the Atheist to the point of evidence. Come, look around at the workmanship of the human body, and by its prompting learn thoroughly who is the founder of so beautiful an image, who the painter of the eyes, who turned the nostrils and the ears, who stretched the lips of the mouth, who drew taut the nerves and bound them, who watered the veins, who piled up the solid bones, who wove the flesh round with a thin skin, who parted the fingers and the joints, who laid out the foundation of the foot, who pierced the pores and opened the passages, who carved out the pipes of the lungs?

> 173 Vide quot Divinae Artis opera in unâ materiâ demonstrantur, singulaque pulchra, recteque dimensa, nec non propriis invicèm officiis differentia. ¿Quisnam singula finxit? ¿Nonnè haec solus ipse Deus cuncta, propria voluntate molitus est? Et quum statuam, & imaginem absque fabro, & pictore fieri, nullus adserere audeat, miram hominis fabricationem sine conditore constitisse putabimus? Ipsa demum humana mens, ejusque vires atque operationes, nonnè ostendunt, & quidem ad evidentiam usque Supremum extare Numen à quo cóndita tam sublimis substantia fuerit, in corpore posita eique ineffabiliter copulata? Certè animum, mentemque hominis, rationem, consilium, prudentiam, qui non divinâ curâ perfecta esse perspicit, his ipsis rebus mihi videtur prorsùs carére.

173 See how many works of Divine Art are displayed in a single matter, each of them beautiful and rightly measured, and also differing from one another in their proper functions. Who, then, fashioned each of them? Did not God himself alone contrive all these things by his own will? And when no one would dare assert that a statue and an image come to be without a sculptor and a painter, shall we think that the wonderful fabric of man came to stand without a founder? Finally, does not the human mind itself, with its powers and operations, show, and indeed to the point of evidence, that there exists a Supreme Deity by whom so sublime a substance was founded, placed in a body and ineffably coupled with it? Surely whoever does not perceive that the mind and intellect of man, his reason, counsel and prudence were perfected by divine care seems to me to be wholly lacking in these very things.

> 174 Prob. 4, & ab Atheis quaero cum Tullio [^55-s2], cur si [p. 56] volunt, naturalia quaeque composita, ipsumque mundum ornatissimum atque pulcherrimum ex témerè concursantibus átomis non tantùm fieri potuísse, sed factum esse re ipsâ; cur, inquam, ipsi quoque non dicant, si innumerabiles unius & viginti formae literarum aliquò conjiciantur posse ex his Annales Ennii ut deincèps legi possint effici? Id certè minus quàm unum vile animalculum, ne dicam quàm tota ipsa mundi machina operosum est. Cur non Annales Enni, sed unus tantùm Virgilii versus nunquam hac ratione effectus est? Praeterea, (ut egregiè idem Cicero argumentatur [^56-s1], si mundum efficere potest concursus atomorum, cur porticum, cur templum, cur domum, cur urbem non potest, quae sunt minus operosa. & multò quidem faciliora? Certè ita témerè Athei de mundo effutiunt, ut mihi quidem nunquam admirabilem hunc Caeli ornatum suspexisse videantur.

174 Proof 4. And I ask of the Atheists with Cicero (x) why, if they maintain that [p. 56] that all natural composites, and the most adorned and most beautiful world itself, not only could have come to be from atoms running together at random, but were in fact so made, why, I say, do they not also say that if innumerable forms of the one-and-twenty letters were thrown together somewhere, the Annals of Ennius could be produced from them, so that they could afterwards be read? That is certainly less laborious than a single paltry animalcule, not to say than the whole machine of the world itself. Why has not the Annals of Ennius, but even a single verse of Virgil, never been produced in this way? Moreover (as the same Cicero excellently argues (y)), if a concourse of atoms can make a world, why can it not make a portico, a temple, a house, a city, which are less laborious and indeed much easier? Surely the Atheists babble so rashly about the world that they seem to me never to have looked up at this wonderful adornment of the Heaven.

> [^55-s2]: Loco citat. cap. 47.

[^55-s2]: In the place cited, ch. 47.

> [^56-s1]: Loco citat. cap. 37.

[^56-s1]: In the place cited, ch. 37.

> 175 Adde cum Lactantio [^56-s2]. Si fortuitis atomorum concursionibus nascuntur omnia, cur nunquàm fortuitò accidit, sic coire illa principia, ut efficerent animal ejusmodi, quod naribus potiùs audiret, odoraret oculis, auribus cérneret? Ceterùm eâ ipsâ quam usurpant ratione jugulantur Athei. Dicunt non repugnare ut mundus fieret ex atomorum concursione fortuitâ, & si non repugnat, nullam esse rationem cur hoc modo re ipsâ factum non fuerit. At contra ipsos ita hoc idem urgetur argumentum. Non repugnat ut existat causa plena rationis, quae ad eam combinationem, quae nunc habetur primigenias atomos determinaverit: ergo causa istiusmodi re ipsá existit.

175 Add, with Lactantius (z): If all things arise from chance concurrences of atoms, why has it never happened by chance that those principles came together so as to make an animal of such a kind that it would hear with its nostrils rather, smell with its eyes, see with its ears? Moreover, the Atheists have their throats cut by the very reasoning they employ. They say that it is not repugnant that the world should be made from a chance concurrence of atoms, and that if it is not repugnant, there is no reason why it should not in fact have been made in this way. But against them this same argument is urged thus: It is not repugnant that there should exist a cause full of reason which determined the primordial atoms to that combination which is now found: therefore a cause of this kind in fact exists.

> [^56-s2]: De Opificio Dei cap. 6.

[^56-s2]: On the Workmanship of God, ch. 6.

> 176 Prob. 5. Ipsa namque rerum contingentia invictissimum omnium judicio argumentum est Deum existere. Hinc etenim fit, ut admittere, vel inviti cogamur Ens aliquod a se, & necessariò existens, à quo res quae existunt contingenter, suum deindè esse receperint. Certum est itaque repugnare ad evidentiam, ut omne *ens* sit ab alio. Quum enim extra collectionem omnium entium, nullum habeatur ens, collectio omnium entium esset à nihilo tanquam ab efficiente causa, si omne ens haberet ab alio ut existeret. Igitur aliquod datur ens non ab alio. Quod autem est non ab alio, & est, à se ipso est, ut patet: ergo aliquod necessariò datur ens, quod à se existit.

176 Proof 5. For the very contingency of things is, in the judgment of all, a most invincible argument that God exists. For hence it comes about that we are compelled, even against our will, to admit some Being from itself, and necessarily existing, from which the things that exist contingently have afterwards received their being. It is therefore certain that it is evidently repugnant that every being should be from another. For since outside the collection of all beings no being is found, the collection of all beings would be from nothing as from an efficient cause, if every being had from another that it should exist. Therefore there is some being not from another. But what is not from another, and is, is from itself, as is plain: therefore there necessarily is some being which exists from itself.

> 177 Similiter repugnat ut tota collectio entium sit contingens. Si enim tota est contingens, tota ita existit, ut non esse ex aequo potuerit, & si ex aequo potuit non esse, nulla est ratio cur ad existendum potiùs, quàm ad non existendum fuerit determinata, nisi fortè placeat dicere, illam collectionem determinasse se ipsam ad existendum, quo certè, (ut ait Cl. *à Brixia*) nihil magis absurdum est, nihilque risu magis dignum. Datur ergo ens [p. 57] necessarium, & quidem tale, ut in eo contineatur ratio, cur contingentia entia existunt. Plurae aliae sunt hujus dignissimi argumenti invictissimae demonstrationes, quas videre potestis apud Cl. Thomam Mariam Cerboni [^57-s1]

177 Likewise it is repugnant that the whole collection of beings should be contingent. For if the whole is contingent, the whole so exists that it could equally have not been; and if it could equally have not been, there is no reason why it was determined to existing rather than to not existing, unless perhaps one is pleased to say that that collection determined itself to existing, than which surely (as the distinguished Fortunato da Brescia says) nothing is more absurd, and nothing more worthy of laughter. There is, therefore, a necessary being, [p. 57] and indeed such that in it is contained the reason why contingent beings exist. There are many other most invincible demonstrations of this most worthy argument, which you can see in the distinguished Tommaso Maria Cerboni (a).

> [^57-s1]: In Theologia Naturali, & Revelatâ.

[^57-s1]: In Theologia Naturalis et Revelata.

> Atheorum cavillationes refutantur.

The cavils of the Atheists are refuted.

> 178 Opp. 1. Existentia Dei est articulus fidei: ut enim habet *Apostolus* [^57-s2], *accedentem ad* Deum *oportet credere quid est*: ergo nequit ratione naturali demonstrari. Dist. antec.: est articulus fidei adeò nempè, ut nonnisi per revelationem cognosci possit, nego, hoc est, admitti debet per fidem, si per rationem non innotescat, conc, & nego conseq. Porrò nullam in eo esse repugnantiam ut existentia Dei per media cùm naturalia, tùm supernaturalia innotescere nobis possit, manifestum adeò est, ut demonstratione non indigeat. Praeterea, quum Fides Divina sit adsensus datus alicui propositioni ex revelatione Divinâ tanquam motivo, prius est hominem esse certum de existentiâ Dei, quam ipsum moveri ad adsentiendum ex auctoritate Dei revelantis. Hinc sensus testimonii supra laudati, hic est: quisquis accedit ad Deum, id est, quisquis vult amplecti veram Religionem, debet esse certus de existentiâ Dei.

bj. 1. The existence of God is an article of faith: for, as the Apostle has it 178 O            (b), he that cometh to God must believe that he is: therefore it cannot be demonstrated by natural reason. I distinguish the antecedent: it is an article of faith in such a way, namely, that it can be known only through revelation, I deny; that is, it must be admitted through faith if it does not become known through reason, I grant; and I deny the consequence. Moreover, that there is no repugnance in the existence of God becoming known to us through means both natural and supernatural is so manifest that it needs no demonstration. Besides, since Divine Faith is an assent given to some proposition on account of Divine revelation as its motive, a man must be certain of the existence of God before he is moved to assent on the authority of God revealing. Hence the sense of the testimony praised above is this: whoever cometh to God, that is, whoever wishes to embrace the true Religion, must be certain of the existence of God.

> [^57-s2]: Ad Heb. c. 11.

[^57-s2]: To the Hebrews, ch. 11.

> 179 Vel propter metum, vel propter ignorantiam causarum, vel propter fraudes imperantium, atque Legislatorum, vel demùm propter educationem factum fuisse ut omnes homines in aliquam Religionem consenserint Hobbesius [^57-s3], Spinosa [^57-s4], Bayle [^57-s5], Tolandus [^57-s6] & alii complures falsò & temerè contendunt.

179 That it came about either through fear, or through ignorance of causes, or through the frauds of rulers and Legislators, or finally through education, that all men have agreed in some Religion, is falsely and rashly contended by Hobbes (c), Spinoza (d), Bayle (e), Toland (f) and very many others.

> [^57-s3]: Leviath. cap. 12.

[^57-s3]: Leviathan, ch. 12.

> [^57-s4]: Tract. Theolog. Polit. cap. 19.

[^57-s4]: Tractatus Theologico-Politicus, ch. 19.

> [^57-s5]: Tom. 3. Op. P. 1. Pensèes sur la Comete §. 107, & seq.

[^57-s5]: Vol. 3 of the Works, pt. 1, Pensées sur la Comète, §. 107 ff.

> [^57-s6]: Pensées Philosophiques, & alibi.

[^57-s6]: Pensées Philosophiques, and elsewhere.

> 180 Opponunt itaque 2[?]: homines quia natura sua infirmi sunt & rerum futurarum expectatione solliciti, res formidolosas facilè sibi fingunt: ergo probabile est, metu inductos fuisse, ut aliquod Supremum Numen admitterent. Nego conseq. Nam sicut multi in metum, ita etiam plures in audaciam naturaliter inclinant: ergo metus non potest esse causa universalis ob quam omnes in rem aliquam unanimiter consentiant. Deindè homines libertatis & dominii amantes esse ex sua ipsorum natura Athei fatentur cum Hobbesio [^57-s7]; sed impossibile est apud omnes homines naturalem dominii, & libertatis cupiditatem ita obrutam esse inani metu, ut [p. 58] omnes convenerint in confingendo Supremo Numine: ergo Athei qui utrumque ponunt secum ipsis pugnant.

180 They object, therefore, 1: men, because they are weak by their nature and anxious with the expectation of things to come, easily feign fearful things for themselves: therefore it is probable that it was induced by fear that they admitted some Supreme Deity. I deny the consequence. For just as many incline naturally to fear, so also more incline to boldness: therefore fear cannot be the universal cause on account of which all agree unanimously in some thing. Next, the Atheists confess with Hobbes (g) that men are lovers of liberty and of dominion by their very nature; but it is impossible that among all men the natural desire for dominion and liberty should be so overwhelmed by empty fear that [p. 58] all should agree in feigning a Supreme Deity: therefore the Atheists, who posit both, contradict themselves.

> [^57-s7]: De Cive cap. 1. §. 4.

[^57-s7]: De Cive, ch. 1, §. 4.

> 181 Opp. 3: homines ab ipsa naturâ insitum habent investigare causas rerum: si autem veras adsequi non potuerint, supposititias sibi fingunt: hinc Deum existere, sibi falsò persuaserunt, ut primum principium rerum omnium se adsequutos esse gauderent: ergo ignorantia & error in causâ fuere cur Deus aliquis admitteretur ab hominibus. Nego antec. & conseq.: quae enim propter ignorantiam constituta sunt inanibus levibusque rationibus innituntur: ergo facilè refelli possunt: ergo impossibile est, ut peritissimi quique in eo consentiant. Quàm absurdum ergo est, & ab omni ratione alienum, cunctas nationes, easque inter se dissitas, nullamque invicem communicationem habentes convenire potuisse in uno eodemque errore, & genere fictionis.

181 Obj. 3: men have it implanted by nature itself to investigate the causes of things; but if they have been unable to attain the true ones, they feign supposititious ones for themselves: hence they have falsely persuaded themselves that God exists, so that they might rejoice at having attained the first principle of all things: therefore ignorance and error were the cause why some God was admitted by men. I deny the antecedent and the consequence: for things established on account of ignorance rest on empty and light reasons, and therefore can easily be refuted: therefore it is impossible that all the most skilled men should agree in them. How absurd, then, it is, and how foreign to all reason, that all nations, and those far removed from one another and having no communication with one another, should have been able to agree in one and the same error and kind of fiction!

> 182 Opp. 4. Quum intelligerent Legislatores fore ut cives in officio multò facilius continerentur si aliquod Supremum Numen existere crederent, à quo puniri possent dum malè agerent, eorum astutiâ factum est, ut Religio in populos introduceretur, atque propagaretur: ergo ab ipsis Legislatoribus, Religionis origo repetenda est. Nego antec. Opiniones namque, quae hominum calliditate disseminantur, praecipuè si indè fiat, ut haud leve gravamen omnibus imponatur, diutiùs non perdurare, experientiâ compertum est. Ergo quum haec consensio, quamvis homines propter eam pluribus legibus subjecti sint, semper perduraverit, suam ab astutiâ Legislatorum orginem habere non potuit. Deindè barbarae quoque gentes, quae nemini subjectae essent in aliquam Religionem semper consenserunt, ipsaque Religio unà cum humano genere suum ortum habuit.

182 Obj. 4. Since Legislators understood that citizens would be kept in their duty much more easily if they believed that there exists some Supreme Deity by whom they could be punished when they did wrong, it came about by their cunning that Religion was introduced among the peoples and propagated: therefore the origin of Religion must be sought from the Legislators themselves. I deny the antecedent. For it has been found by experience that opinions which are disseminated by the craft of men do not last very long, especially if it comes about from them that no light burden is laid upon all. Therefore, since this consent has always endured, although on account of it men are subjected to more laws, it cannot have had its origin from the cunning of Legislators. Next, barbarous nations too, which were subject to no one, have always agreed in some Religion, and Religion itself had its origin together with the human race.

> 183 Opp. 5. Saepissimè contingit, ut certissimum id habeamus, quod vanum atque inane in se est, cùm propter praejudicia, tùm etiam propter educationem, institutionemque, quam in pueritia habuimus: ergo etiam Religio ab hisce duobus principijs dimanassè potuit. Nego antec. Nam quod omninò diversum est, in unius, ejusdemque rei consensionem inducere non potest; sed educatio atque institutio apud gentes omninò diversa est, semperque fuit; indèque contigisse videmus, ut mores eorum, atque consuetudines diversae sint: ergo. Deindè educationis, atque institutionis praejudicia depelluntur si ad veritatem adsequendam animus seriò adjiciatur; sed licet omni aetate non defuerint, qui meditationi scientiarum operam dederint, nullus tamen fuit, (si unum aut alterum delirantem excipias) qui ab hac communi consensione recesserit: ergo.

183 Obj. 5. It very often happens that we hold as most certain what is vain and empty in itself, now on account of prejudices, now also on account of the education and instruction which we had in childhood: therefore Religion too could have flowed from these two principles. I deny the antecedent. For what is altogether diverse cannot lead to agreement in one and the same thing; but education and instruction among the nations is, and always was, altogether diverse; and hence we see it has come about that their morals and customs are diverse: therefore. Next, the prejudices of education and instruction are driven out if the mind is seriously applied to attaining the truth; but although in every age there have not been lacking those who devoted their effort to the study of the sciences, there was nevertheless no one (if you except one or another raving man) who departed from this common consent: therefore.

> 184 Dices: fuere Philosophi qui nullos Deos esse putarunt teste Tullio [^58-s1]. Quatuor autem Atheistarum sectas physicas [p. 59] Cudwortus [^59-s1] distinxit: ergo. Secundo: Deum nemo vidit unquam: ergo credimus Supremi Numinis existentiam ex praeceptorum institutione, & parentum educatione; Ad primum nego conseq. Ex eo namque quod nonnulli Philosophi contra hanc consensionem pugnaverint, majorem in ea vim inesse ad persuadendum rectè concluditur; ex hoc enim evincitur hanc universalem consensionem, non ab ignorantia, errore, educatione, aut aliquo praejudicio dimanasse, sed profluxisse ab interna voce naturae, ab ipsa ratione, quae unicuique congenita est, ab ipso naturali lumine, quod propter ineptias paucorum delirantium philosophorum nunquam obscurari potuit. Ad secundum dist. antec.; nemo vidit in se, conc., in ejus operibus, nego, & conseq. ¿Quis enim animum vidit unquam? Eum tamen agnosco ex ejus operibus, quia cogito, &c.

184 You will say: there were Philosophers who thought that there are no Gods, as Cicero witnesses (h). Moreover, four physical sects of Atheists were distinguished by Cudworth therefore [p. 59] (i): therefore. Second: no one has ever seen God: therefore we believe the existence of the Supreme Deity from the instruction of our teachers and the education given by our parents. To the first I deny the consequence. For from the fact that some Philosophers have fought against this consent, it is rightly concluded that a greater force for persuading is in it; for from this it is established that this universal consent did not flow from ignorance, error, education or some prejudice, but proceeded from the inner voice of nature, from the reason itself which is inborn in each man, from the natural light itself, which on account of the follies of a few raving philosophers could never be obscured. To the second I distinguish the antecedent: no one has seen him in himself, I grant; in his works, I deny; and I deny the consequence. For who has ever seen the mind? Yet I acknowledge it from its works, because I think, etc.

> [^58-s1]: De Nat. Deor.

[^58-s1]: On the Nature of the Gods.

> [^59-s1]: System. Intellect. cap. 3. §. 30.

[^59-s1]: Systema Intellectuale, ch. 3, §. 30.

> 185 Opp. 6. Gentium consensus si uti firmum ad suadendum argumentum admittatur, multa absurda consequuntur: ergo. Prob. antec. Polytheismus consensui gentium fuit constitutus; nam si Judaei excipiantur omnes in eum consenserunt. Secundo. Unaquaeque natio ob consensum majorum suorum Religionem suam Religioni alterius praeferri deberet. Tertio, Multos errores disseminatos, variasque superstitiones consensu gentium fuisse institutas, nullus ignorare potest: ergo. Respondeo cum distinctione: & in hisce omnibus consensus certus, atque universalis fuit, nego, inconstans, incertus, atque particularis, conc. Consensus ergo, ex quo ad rem aliquam suadendam firmissimum argumentum desumi posse contendimus, ejusmodi esse debet, ut omnes cunctarum nationum, omniumque temporum homines firmiter, constanterque, complectatur.

185 Obj. 6. If the consent of nations is admitted as a firm argument for persuading, many absurdities follow: therefore. Proof of the antecedent. Polytheism was established by the consent of nations; for, if the Jews are excepted, all agreed in it. Second. Each nation, on account of the consent of its forefathers, ought to prefer its own Religion to the Religion of another. Third. No one can be ignorant that many errors were disseminated and various superstitions instituted by the consent of nations: therefore. I reply with a distinction: that in all these things the consent was certain and universal, I deny; that it was inconstant, uncertain and particular, I grant. The consent, therefore, from which we contend that a most firm argument for persuading of some thing is drawn must be such that it embraces firmly and constantly all men of all nations and of all times.

> 186 Opp. 7. Oritur à praejudicio, quod dicamus aliquem esse ordinem in mundo, nimirùm, inquit Spinosa, ex eo, quod homines in se, & extra se multa invenerint sibi utilia ex. gr. oculos ad videndum, herbas, & alimenta ad nutritionem, Solem ad illuminandum, &c., indè factum est, ut statim judicaverint, ita omnia ab aliquo agente parata & disposita fuisse: ergo ex opificio, & ordine mundi non rectè probatur Deum existere. Neg. antec. Non magis enim praejudicio laborant homines dum judicant ex. gr. partes organicas oculorum ab opifice sapientissimo paratas, & dispositas fuisse, non autem fatali quadam necessitate coaluisse, quàm praejudicio laboraret ipse Spinosa (cujus est haec cavillatio) si vel considerando structuram aedificiorum, vel horologii fabricam, suspicaretur causas intelligentes, â quibus singulari industriâ fuerunt disposita; atqui praejudicio non laboraret Spinosa, si causas ejusmodi vel existere, vel extitisse suspicaretur: imò haberetur ut insanus, si haec omnia fatali quâdam necessitate disposita fuisse contenderet; quàm igitur potiori jure ex mirabili totius [p. 60] mundi dispositione sine praejudicio comperimus existere opificem summè intelligentem.

186 Obj. 7. It arises from prejudice that we say there is some order in the world; namely, says Spinoza, from the fact that men found within themselves and outside themselves many things useful to them, e.g. eyes for seeing, plants and foods for nourishment, the Sun for giving light, etc., it came about that they at once judged that all things had thus been prepared and disposed by some agent: therefore from the workmanship and order of the world it is not rightly proved that God exists. I deny the antecedent. For men do not labor under prejudice when they judge, e.g., that the organic parts of the eyes were prepared and disposed by a most wise maker, and did not grow together by some fatal necessity, any more than Spinoza himself (whose cavil this is) would labor under prejudice if, in considering either the structure of buildings or the construction of a clock, he were to suspect intelligent causes by which they were disposed with singular industry; but Spinoza would not labor under prejudice if he suspected that causes of this kind either exist or have existed; nay, he would be held a madman if he contended that all these things had been disposed by some fatal necessity; with how much better right, then, from the wonderful disposition of the whole world [p. 60] do we find, without prejudice, that there exists a supremely intelligent maker.

> 187 Non injocundum vobis fore existimo, si argumenta aliqua quae exponit P. Hieronymus Maria Buzzi in Accurata Synopsi Theologiae Cl. P. Joh. Laur. Berti totidem verbis exscripta vobis proponam: vel ex hoc namque cognoscetis quàm perspicuè omnia complectatur, quàm nitidè proponat, quamque utile Theologiae ejusmodi studium vobis postea futurum sit [^60-s1].

187 I think it will not be unpleasant for you if I set before you some arguments which Fr. Girolamo Maria Buzzi expounds in the Accurate Synopsis of the Theology of the distinguished Fr. Giovanni Lorenzo Berti, copied out in as many words; for even from this you will learn how clearly it embraces everything, how lucidly it sets things forth, and how useful a study of this kind will afterwards be to you in Theology (*).

> [^60-s1]: Hac Synopsi utimur in Colleg. Salesiano ad studium Sac. Theologiae.

[^60-s1]: We use this Synopsis in the Salesian College for the study of Sacred Theology.

> 188 Opp. 8. Mundum a Deo conditum non fuisse pluribus argumentis ostenditur: ergo ex ejus Opificio Dei existentia non probatur. Antec. prob. 1. Percipi enim nequit Deum Æternum mundum fecisse mortalem, idque repentè, quum tot seculis ante cessaverit. ¿Quam indè coeperit gloriam, aut gaudium, qui nunquam potuit gloria, aut felicitate carére? ¿Quibus instrumentis aut ministris sit usus? Si lucem postea creavit, quomodo non antea jacuerit in tenebris? Ergo Deus mundum non condidit. *Secundo*. Vel Sapientibus mundum Deus condidit, vel insipientibus; atqui neutris condidit, nam illi sunt pauci, isti prorsus indigni: ergo nulli condidit.

188 Obj. 8. It is shown by several arguments that the world was not founded by God: therefore the existence of God is not proved from his Workmanship. The antecedent is proved: 1. For it cannot be conceived that God, being Eternal, made a mortal world, and that suddenly, when he had rested for so many ages before. What glory or joy did he gain from it, who could never lack glory or happiness? What instruments or ministers did he use? If he created light afterwards, how did he not lie in darkness before? Therefore God did not found the world. Second. God founded the world either for the Wise or for the foolish; but he founded it for neither, for the former are few, the latter wholly unworthy: therefore he founded it for none.

> 189 *Tertio*. Nullus est ordo in ejus partibus, quarum aliae desertae, aliae belluis tantùm, aut volucribus aptae, ut aër, montes, mares, paludes. Agri verò non nisi labore improbo fruges emittunt, quae saepè grandine, aut illuvione pessumdantur: ergo à Deo Sapientissimo creatum non est. *Quarto*. Ferae péssimae, pestilentiae, fames, morbi, Dei Providentiam evertunt: ergo. *Quinto* Vagitus infantium, corporis nuditas, & calamitates innumerae, quibus homo quovis animalculo est miserior, satis probant mundum à Deo in ejus gratiam non fuisse constructum: ergo mundus à Deo non est conditus, ac proinde ex mundi Opificio non benè probatur Supremi Numinis existentia.

189 Third. There is no order in its parts, of which some are deserted, others suited only for beasts or for birds, as the air, the mountains, the seas, the marshes. The fields, moreover, put forth crops only with unremitting labor, and these are often ruined by hail or by flood: therefore it was not created by a most Wise God. Fourth. The most noxious wild beasts, pestilences, famines, diseases overthrow the Providence of God: therefore. Fifth. The wailing of infants, the nakedness of the body, and the innumerable calamities by which man is more wretched than any animalcule, prove sufficiently that the world was not built by God for his sake: therefore the world was not founded by God, and consequently the existence of the Supreme Deity is not well proved from the Workmanship of the world.

> 190 Respondeo neg. antec., & ad prim. prob. nego etiam antec., cui etiam Epicurei respondere debent, qui materiam aeternam statuunt licet mundo initium atque interitum tribuant. Porrò in aeternitate, ubi ait S. Augustinus [^60-s2] ,, nulla creatura est, cujus mutabilibus motibus tempora peragantur, tempora omninò esse non possunt, *&* *alibi* [^60-s3] ,,. Si ante Coelum & terram nullum erat tempus, cur quaeritur, quid tunc faciebas? ,, Neque Deus ministris, aut instrumentis indiguit, quae infirmitatem declarant artificis, neque in tenebris jacuit aliquando ille qui semper fuit lux vera. Ad 2. nego min. Deus enim primò propter se, deindè propter sapientes condidit universum. Quod verò alii sint [p. 61] mali, id non à Deo est, sed ab homine quem Deus posuit in manu consilii sui, melius esse ratus de malis benefacere, quàm mala nulla esse permittere.

190 I reply: I deny the antecedent; and to the first proof I deny the antecedent as well, to which the Epicureans too must reply, who posit eternal matter although they attribute to the world a beginning and an end. Moreover, in eternity, where, as St. Augustine says (k), “there is no creature by whose changeable motions times are carried on, times can by no means exist,” and elsewhere (l): “If before Heaven and earth there was no time, why is it asked what thou wast doing then?” Nor did God need ministers or instruments, which betray the weakness of a craftsman; nor did he who always was the true light ever lie in darkness. To the 2nd I deny the minor. For God founded the universe first for his own sake, then for the sake of the wise. But that others are [p. 61] wicked is not from God, but from man, whom God placed in the hand of his own counsel, judging it better to do good with evils than to permit no evils to exist.

> [^60-s2]: Lib. XII. de Civit. Dei Cap. 15.

[^60-s2]: Bk. XII of The City of God, ch. 15.

> [^60-s3]: Lib. XI. Confess. cap. 13.

[^60-s3]: Bk. XI of the Confessions, ch. 13.

> 191 Ad 3. neg. antec. Nulla enim est orbis pars, unde homini commodum non accedat. Montes puriorem aërem, saltus pascua, rupes metalla & marmora suppeditant. Flumina pisces alunt, hortos irrigant, urbes ornant, & muniunt. Mare nubes & imbres agrorum feracitati confert, mercesque è remotissimis oris transvehit. Calor & frigus etiam prosunt, is enim tellurem gravidat, ille fruges matúrat: ergo &c. Ad 4. & 5. nego antec. Ærumnae etenim & mors ipsa sunt originalis peccati stipendia. Sed quia haec Atheus irridet. Respondeo 2.: ex his induci homines ad terrenarum rerum contemptum, industriamque laudabilem: monéri ut parce vivant, nec nimia venere ac vino sibimortem accelerent. Ferarum verò nulla est, quae aut opem nobis, aut victum, voluptatem, aut medelam non praebeat. Ad ult. neg. antec. Melior est enim cum imbecillitate sapientia, quàm sine ratione, vel maxima fortitudo. Hactenùs P. Buzzi.

191 To the 3rd I deny the antecedent. For there is no part of the globe from which some advantage does not come to man. The mountains supply purer air, the woodlands pastures, the rocks metals and marbles. Rivers feed fish, water gardens, adorn and fortify cities. The sea contributes clouds and rains to the fertility of the fields, and carries goods across from the remotest shores. Heat and cold too are of use, for the latter makes the earth pregnant, the former ripens the crops: therefore, etc. To the 4th and 5th I deny the antecedent. For hardships, and death itself, are the wages of original sin. But since the Atheist mocks these things, I reply 2.: by these things men are led to contempt of earthly things and to praiseworthy industry; they are warned to live sparingly and not to hasten death upon themselves by excessive venery and wine. Of wild beasts, moreover, there is none which does not furnish us either help, or food, pleasure or remedy. To the last I deny the antecedent. For wisdom with weakness is better than even the greatest strength without reason. Thus far Fr. Buzzi.

> 192 Opp. 9. Non est certum adspectabilem mundum existere: ergo Dei quoque existentia incerta erit. Resp. 1. neg. antec. Non enim unum est argumentum, quo corporum existentia contra Idealistas evincitur. Resp. 2. neg. conseq. Demonstratur enim Supremi Numinis existentia ex eo etiam quod existat ens contingens, ipsa nimirùm humana mens, cujus existentiam inficiari nequit Idealista, quin velit neminem, ne quidem de propria existentia habere certitudinem posse, quod quàm falsum sit, ne dicam ampliùs, non est, cur longo sermone ostendam.

192 Obj. 9. It is not certain that the visible world exists: therefore the existence of God too will be uncertain. Reply 1: I deny the antecedent. For there is more than one argument by which the existence of bodies is established against the Idealists. Reply 2: I deny the consequence. For the existence of the Supreme Deity is demonstrated also from the fact that a contingent being exists, namely the human mind itself, whose existence the Idealist cannot deny without holding that no one can have certainty even of his own existence; and how false this is, not to say more, there is no reason for me to show at length.

> 193 Opp. 10. Ex eo quod existat ens contingens colligi certò nequit extare ens necessarium: ergo. Prob. antec.: potest existere ens necessarium, quin existat ens contingens: ergo vicissim potest existere ens contingens, quin existat ens necessarium. Resp. cum Cl. à Brixia neg. antec. ad cujus probationem permitto antec. & nego conseq. Ratio discriminis est evidens. Quum enim in ente contingente non detur ratio sufficiens cur ipsum existat potius, quàm non existat, nequit existere ens contingens quin detur etiam necessarium in quo sufficiens illius ratio contineatur. Contra verò res se habet loquendo de ente necessariò. Hoc enim tale est, ut rationem suae existentiae comprehendat.

193 Obj. 10. From the fact that a contingent being exists, it cannot be gathered with certainty that a necessary being exists: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: a necessary being can exist without a contingent being existing: therefore, in turn, a contingent being can exist without a necessary being existing. I reply with the distinguished Fortunato da Brescia: I deny the antecedent; to its proof I let the antecedent pass and deny the consequence. The reason for the difference is evident. For since in a contingent being there is no sufficient reason why it should exist rather than not exist, a contingent being cannot exist unless there is also a necessary being in which its sufficient reason is contained. The case is the contrary when we speak of the necessary being. For this is such that it comprises the reason of its own existence.

> 194 *Dices*: existentia entis contingentis non est necessariò connexa cum ente necessario, alioquin ens contingens necessariò existeret: ergo potest existere ens contingens quin existat ens necessarium. Dist. antec.: id est, non est hujusmodi ut haberi nequeat ens necessarium quin habeatur contingens, conc., hoc est potest extare ens contingens, quin existat necessarium, nego, & conseq. Verum est existentiam entis contingentis, non adeò esse connexam cum ente necessariò, ut extare nequeat ens necessarium; quin [p. 62] existat ens contingens. Non enim ens contingens necessariò producitur. At est falsum existentiam entis contingentis non ita connexam esse cum ente necessario, ut prorsus repugnet haberi ens contingens, quin necessarium habeatur. Quum enim ens necessarium rationem obtineat, cur existat contingens, contradictio est, ut existat ens contingens, quin existat necessarium; quemadmodùm evidens in eo est pugna, ut sit effectus, quin causa existat.

194 You will say: the existence of a contingent being is not necessarily connected with the necessary being; otherwise the contingent being would exist necessarily: therefore a contingent being can exist without a necessary being existing. I distinguish the antecedent: that is, it is not of such a kind that a necessary being cannot be had without a contingent one being had, I grant; that is, a contingent being can exist without a necessary one existing, I deny; and I deny the consequence. It is true that the existence of a contingent being is not so connected with the necessary being that the necessary being could not exist unless there existed [p. 62] a contingent being. For a contingent being is not produced necessarily. But it is false that the existence of a contingent being is not so connected with the necessary being that it is altogether repugnant that a contingent being be had without a necessary one being had. For since the necessary being holds the reason why the contingent exists, it is a contradiction that a contingent being should exist without a necessary one existing; just as the conflict is evident in this, that there should be an effect without a cause existing.

> 195 Opp. demum. Evidenter non repugnat processus in infinitum in causis efficientibus: ergo evidenter non constat admittendam esse causam, quae sit omnium prima. Omisso antec. neg. conseq. Existentia siquidem Dei demonstrata à nobis ex eo non est, quod infinita causarum series repugnet. Sive enim repugnet, sive non, semper verum est causam á se existentem admitti oportere; quum fieri nequeat ut tota entium collectio eâ ratione sit, ut non esse ex aequo potuerit. Esse itaque Deum O. M. indubium est. Si enim (verbis Ciceronis perorabo) ,, Si enim ratio mecum facit, si eventa, si populi, si nationes, si Graeci, si Barbari, si majores etiam nostri, si denique hoc semper ita putatum est, si summi Philosophi, si Poetae, si Sapientisimi Viri, qui Respublicas constituerunt, qui urbes condiderunt: an dum bestiae loquuntur, expectamus, hominum consentiente auctoritate contenti non sumus ,,? [^62-s1]. Atque haec de Theologia Naturali totaque Metaphysica dicta sufficiant.

195 Obj. finally. It is evidently not repugnant that there be a process to infinity in efficient causes: therefore it is evidently not established that a cause must be admitted which is the first of all. Passing over the antecedent, I deny the consequence. For the existence of God has not been demonstrated by us from the fact that an infinite series of causes is repugnant. For whether it is repugnant or not, it is always true that a cause existing from itself must be admitted, since it cannot be that the whole collection of beings should be in such a way that it could equally have not been. That God, the Best and Greatest, exists is therefore beyond doubt. For (I shall conclude in the words of Cicero): “For if reason is on my side, if events, if peoples, if nations, if Greeks, if Barbarians, if our forefathers too, if, finally, this has always been so thought, if the greatest Philosophers, if the Poets, if the Wisest Men, who established Commonwealths, who founded cities: are we waiting until the beasts speak, and are we not content with the agreeing authority of men?” (m). And let what has been said of Natural Theology and of the whole of Metaphysics suffice.

> [^62-s1]: De Divin. Lib. 1. Cap. 19.

[^62-s1]: On Divination, bk. 1, ch. 19.

OR

## PHILOSOPHIAE MORALIS — OF MORAL PHILOSOPHY

## ELEMENTA. — THE ELEMENTS

## PRAEFATIO. — PREFACE

> Ethicam, sive Moralem Philosophiam dirigendis, perficiendisque moribus institutam esse, ut virtutis amore, vitiorumque fugâ veram felicitatem, ac beatitudinem consequamur, nemo est qui nesciat. Hinc *ars bene vivendi*, *animi medicina*, *virtutis indagatrix*, *expultrixque vitiorum*, *ars vitae*, *morum magistra* meritò solet adpellari. Definiri ea potest, quamoptimè: *cognitio boni*, *vel scientia ostendens rationem ad summum bonum, ejusque fruitionem perveniendi*. Quum verò nos non modò Philosophos, sed Catholicos etiam esse sentiamus ac mirificè gloriemur, meritò Eruditorum reprehensionem incurrerem si animi medicinam nec summis, ut ajunt, labris Adolescentibus degustandam proponerem.

thics, or Moral Philosophy, has been instituted for directing E and perfecting morals, so that by love of virtue and flight from vices we may attain true felicity and beatitude: there is no one who does not know this. Hence it is deservedly wont to be called the art of living well, the medicine of the mind, the investigator of virtue and the expeller of vices, the art of life, the mistress of morals. It can be defined, and very well: the knowledge of the good, or the science showing the way to arrive at the highest good and at the enjoyment of it. But since we feel that we are not only Philosophers but Catholics too, and glory in this wonderfully, I would deservedly incur the reproach of the Learned if I set the medicine of the mind before Youths not even to be tasted, as they say, with the tips of the lips.

[p. 2]

> Innumera siquidem dicenda nobis occurrerent, si omnia complecti mens foret, quae à Veteribus, Recentioribusque Philosophis in adornanda Morum scientia explicari conspicimus: praecipua tamen, ac summa veluti capita seligémus, ut nobiliora morum praecepta breviori, clariorique ordine complectamur. Quum verò nemo possit ad summum bonum scilicèt Deum, ejusque fruitionem pervenire nisi officia erga Deum, erga seipsum, erga alios observet, si virtutem non colat, vitiaque detestetur, hinc omnis Ethica ad duo veluti supremà capita revocari optimè potest. Primò itaque de Officiis disseremus, tùm de virtute generatim ejusque causis & signis aliqua delibabimus. Longiùs enim orationem protahere praescripti *Elementorum* limites haud patiuntur. Sit itaque.

For countless things would present themselves for us to say, if we had a mind to embrace everything that we see explained by the Ancients and the Moderns in setting out the science of Morals; we shall, however, select the principal and, as it were, the chief heads, so as to embrace the nobler precepts of morals in a briefer and clearer order. Since, moreover, no one can attain the highest good, namely God, and the enjoyment of Him, unless he observes his duties toward God, toward himself and toward others, unless he cultivates virtue and detests vices, the whole of Ethics can very well be reduced to two, as it were, supreme heads. First, therefore, we shall discourse on Duties; then we shall touch on a few things concerning virtue in general and its causes and signs. For the prescribed limits of the Elements do not allow us to draw out the discussion any further. Let there be, then,

## CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

> De variis hominum officiis erga Deum, se ipsos, alios, & erga Rempublicam.

On the various duties of men toward God, toward themselves, toward others, and toward the Commonwealth. 1

> 1 „Quum multa sint in Philosophia gravia, & utilia, accuratè copiosèque à Philosophis disputata, latissimè patére videntur ea, quae de officiis tradita ab illis, & praecepta sunt. Nulla enim vitae pars, neque publicis, neque privatis, neque forensibus, nec domesticis in rebus, neque si tecum agas quid, neque si cum altero contrahas, vacare officio potest; in eoque edendo sita vitae est honestas omnis, & in negligendo turpitudo.„ ait Eloquentissimus Consularis Philosophus M. T. Cicero [^2-s1-3]. Et rectè quidem: quum enim homo exlex non sit, prosequatur officia quaedam oportet, ut fini suo optimè respondeat.

“Although there are many weighty and useful things in Philosophy, discussed accurately and copiously by Philosophers, those things which they have handed down and prescribed concerning duties seem to extend most widely. For no part of life, neither in public nor in private affairs, neither in the courts nor at home, neither if you transact anything with yourself nor if you contract with another, can be free of duty; and in discharging it lies all that is honorable in life, and in neglecting it all that is base,” says the most eloquent consular Philosopher M. T. Cicero (a). And rightly indeed: for since man is not without law, he must pursue certain duties in order to answer best to his end.

> [^2-s1-3]: De Officiis Lib. 1. cap. 1.

[^2-s1-3]: On Duties, bk. 1, ch. 1.

> 2 Hujusmodi officia & à ratione, & à Revelatione ducuntur. Est enim in praesenti rerum providentia lumen rationis obscurum, ac debile, cui proindè ne erret, alterius luminis praesidum necessarium est. Jam verò, quae ex ratione & Revelatione officia praestare homo debet, vel Deum respiciunt, & sunt Religionis, vel ad hominem prout sui custos est, referuntur, vel hominem spectant, prout ad alios refertur, & Societatis adpellantur, vel prout ad Rempublicam, & officia Civis nuncupantur.

2 Duties of this kind are derived both from reason and from Revelation. For in the present providence of things the light of reason is dim and weak, and therefore, lest it err, it needs the protection of another light. Now the duties which man must perform by reason and Revelation either regard God, and are those of Religion; or are referred to man inasmuch as he is his own guardian; or regard man inasmuch as he is related to others, and are called those of Society; or inasmuch as he is related to the Commonwealth, and are named the duties of the Citizen.

> 3 Quantum ad Deum adtinet, certum imprimis est non solùm interno, & spirituali, sed etiam externo, & sensibili Religionis [p. 3] cultu esse adorandum. Religionis nomine intelligimus cultum amoris, obsequii, & servitutis, ei praestandum cui debetur. Atque hinc vera Religio quae Catholica est, omnem *impietatem*, & *superstitionem* excludit. Impietatem voco, & neglectum Religionis, & contemptum, quorum utrumque directè cum rationis lumine pugnat: superstitio verò vel est cultus ortus ex erroneis de Deo opinionibus, vel exhibitus rei, cui non debetur, vel Deo quidem exhibitus, sed modis, & ritibus ejus perfectionibus non consentaneis. Hinc & Atheismus, & Pantheismus, & Polyteismus, & superstitio Mahumedana, & pervicacia Judaica, & omnis omninò secta ab Ecclesia Catholica proscripta, eliminatur.

3 As regards God, it is certain first of all that not only with an internal and spiritual, but also with an external and sensible worship of Religion [p. 3] He must be adored. By the name of Religion we understand the worship of love, of obedience and of service, to be rendered to Him to whom it is due. And hence the true Religion, which is the Catholic one, excludes all impiety and superstition. I call impiety both the neglect and the contempt of Religion, each of which directly conflicts with the light of reason; superstition, on the other hand, is either a worship arising from erroneous opinions about God, or one shown to a thing to which it is not due, or one shown indeed to God, but in ways and rites not consonant with His perfections. Hence Atheism, and Pantheism, and Polytheism, and the Mahometan superstition, and Jewish obstinacy, and every sect whatever proscribed by the Catholic Church, are excluded.

> 4 Atque ex hoc conficitur summam esse obligationem amplectendi Religionem Catholicam, utpotè quae sola est vera Religio Revelata.
