In ea enim signa credibilitatis deprehenduntur, qualia sunt praecipua, sanctitas & unitas doctrinae, tum etiam vitae probitas praecipuorum, maximè primorum praedicatorum, ac propagatorum, signa quae loquentem Deum testantur, uti miracula, & prophetiae opere completae, Martyrum testimonium, continua succesivo Religionis Interpretum, ac controversiarum Judicum. Hujusmodi Religio nefariis perditissimorum hominum adgressionibus nequaquam victa, à primordio rerum usque ad haec quibus vivimus tempora, immobilis restitit, constansque: est ergo ipsa Dei opus.

4 And from this it follows that there is the highest obligation to embrace the Catholic Religion, inasmuch as it alone is the true revealed Religion. For in it are found the signs of credibility, of which the chief are: the holiness and unity of its doctrine; then also the probity of life of its principal, and above all of its first, preachers and propagators; the signs that testify that God is speaking, such as miracles and prophecies fulfilled in deed; the testimony of the Martyrs; the continual succession of the Interpreters of Religion and of the Judges of controversies. Such a Religion, in no way overcome by the wicked assaults of the most abandoned men, has stood immovable and constant from the beginning of things down to these times in which we live: it is therefore the work of God Himself.

> 5 Quis tamen induxisset animum ut hoc crederet, Ornatissimi Adolescentes, nisi res ipsa maximo cum nostrorum temporum dedécore id ipsum demonstrasset? Turba hominum emersit, qui statuerunt non antiquas superstitiones revocare, sed superstitioni oppositam impietatem disseminantes, post secula tot ex terrarum orbe eliminare Religionem, Deumque ipsum ejus auctorem é Caelo detrudere. Hujus consilii Hobbesius, Spinosa, Tolandus, Bayle recensentur inter insigniores duces. Hos veluti conductitia gens, sequuntur Collinius, Wolstonus, Marchio Argensis, Voltaire, Rouseau, Helvetius, aliique plurimi qui prae pudore non audentes nomen adponere suum pestiferis liberculis *Epistolarum*, *Speciminum*, *Tractatuum*, *Cogitationum*, *Examinum*, *Ephemeridum* [^3-s1-2], [p. 4] pluribusque aliis hujus farinae operibus, quibus Europa scatèt, descenderunt in aciem.

5 Yet who would have brought his mind to believe this, most accomplished Young Men, had not the thing itself demonstrated it, to the very great disgrace of our times? A crowd of men has arisen who have resolved, not to call back the ancient superstitions, but, by disseminating the impiety that is the opposite of superstition, to eliminate Religion from the face of the earth after so many centuries, and to thrust God Himself, its author, down from Heaven. Among the more notable leaders of this design are counted Hobbes, Spinoza, Toland, Bayle. These are followed, like a hired band, by Collins, Woolston, the Marquis d’Argens, Voltaire, Rousseau, Helvétius, and very many others, who, not daring for shame to put their names to their pestilential little books of Letters, Specimens, Treatises, Thoughts, Examinations, Ephemerides (b), and to many [p. 4] other works of this stamp, with which Europe teems, have come down into the battle line.

> [^3-s1-2]: En Liberculorum inscriptiones. La Philosophie du Bon Sens (vulgò Marchio Argensis). Epitres Persanes (vulgò D. de Montesquieu). Lettres sur la Religion essentielle àl' homme. Pensès Philosophiques. Les Oracles de la Raison. Examen de *la* Religion. Code de la Nature, ou le veritable sprit de ses loix. Le Christianisme aussi ancien que le monde. Les Mœurs. Tolerance des Religions. Epitres Turces. Epitres Chinoises, Epitres Cabalistes. Epitres Peruvienes. L' Esprit. Dictionnaire Philosophique. Dictionnaire Raisonné des Sciences, ds Arts, & des Métiers, ou Dictionnaire Encyclopédique. A Neufchatel 1751. 17. vol. in fol. (Negari nequit Physicam, Mathematicas, uno verbo Scientias & Artes optimè in hoc opere exponi, quum ea quae de illis traduntur nec directè neque indirectè Religionem moresque spectant. Quae autem sunt Religionis, quae Principis auctoritatem respiciunt, quae denique ad bonos adtinent mores pessumdantur, deprimuntur, irridentur. His omnibus sublatis Opus denuò recognitum & expurgatum prodit nunc *Lucae*, & *Livurni* in Hetruria, Eruditorum plausu, & maximo totius Reipublicae Literariae bono & emolumento.) Rousseau L' Emille, ou traité d' Education. Voltaire in suis variis opusculis. Validissimis rationibus Libertinos hosce, aliosque plures, perstrinxerunt Viri Clarissimi Thomas Maria Cerbonni O. P. Op inscript. De Theologia Naturali, & Revelata. Anton. Valsechi O. P Op inscript. Dei Fondamenti della Religione, ê de i fonti dell' Empietá. P. Muniglia O. P. Dissertazzione contro i Fatalisti. Auctor Op. inscript. La Pretessa Filosofia degli moderni increduli. Abb. Nonnott Op. inscript. Les Erreurs de Voltaire. Abb. Gauchat [?], Op. inscript. Lettres Critiques, ou analyse & refutation des ecrits modernes contre la Religion, aliique.

[^3-s1-2]: Here are the titles of the little books. La Philosophie du Bon Sens (commonly the Marquis d’Argens). Epitres Persanes (commonly M. de Montesquieu). Lettres sur la Religion essentielle à l’homme. Pensés Philosophiques. Les Oracles de la Raison. Examen de la Religion. Code de la Nature, ou le veritable esprit de ses loix. Le Christianisme aussi ancien que le monde. Les Mœurs. Tolerance des Religions. Epitres Turces. Epitres Chinoises, Epitres Cabalistes. Epitres Peruvienes. L’Esprit. Dictionnaire Philosophique. Dictionnaire Raisonné des Sciences, des Arts, & des Metiers, ou Dictionnaire Encyclopédique. At some Neufchatel 1751. 17 vols. in fol. (It cannot be denied that Physics, Mathematics, in a word the Sciences and Arts, are set forth excellently in this work, since what is handed down about them regards Religion and morals neither directly nor indirectly. But the things that belong to Religion, that regard the authority of the Prince, and finally that pertain to good morals, are ruined, debased, derided. With all these removed, the Work, revised anew and expurgated, is now coming out at Lucca and at Livorno in Tuscany, to the applause of the learned and to the very great good and profit of the whole Republic of Letters.) Rousseau, L’Emille, ou traité d’Education. Voltaire in his various little works. With most valid reasons these Libertines, and many others besides, have been censured by most distinguished men: Tommaso Maria Cerboni O.P., in the work entitled De Theologia Naturali, & Revelata; Anton. Valsecchi O.P., in the work entitled Dei Fondamenti della Religione, e de i fonti dell’Empietà; P. Muniglia O.P., Dissertazzione contro i Fatalisti; the author of the work entitled La Pretessa Filosofia degli moderni increduli; Abbé Nonnotte, in the work entitled Les Erreurs de Voltaire; Abbé Gauchat, in the work entitled Lettres Critiques, ou analyse & refutation des ecrits modernes contre la Religion; and others.

> 6 Equidem dijudicare non aussim, (verbis utor Clariss. Valsechi), quinam potius in homine sapienti turbam hanc intuente excitari sensus debeat, num indignationis, an contemptus, an verò misericordiae. ¡Heu miseros! ¿Tantùmne vobis virium esse putatis, ut aliquot pagellis in lucem éditis, tot seculorum consensum vos refellere, erroris coarguere universum hominum genus, vocem naturae comprimere, Supremoque Numini bellum inferre posse arbitramini? ¿An Religionem illam, quam non tunc dominans idololatria, non Tyrannorum crudelitas, armis totius Romani imperii instructa, non acumen tot Philosophorum in disputandi artibus omnibus exercitatorum opprimere potuerunt, avaritia, voluptas, mos, gestus cupiditatibus omnibus orbis corrupti, effeminatique domabunt? Fabulae.

6 For my part I would not dare to decide (I use the words of the most distinguished Valsecchi) which feeling ought rather to be aroused in a wise man beholding this crowd, whether that of indignation, or of contempt, or rather of pity. Ah, wretched men! Do you think you have so much strength that you judge yourselves able, by bringing out a few little pages, to refute the consensus of so many centuries, to convict the whole human race of error, to stifle the voice of nature, and to wage war on the Supreme Deity? Will that Religion which neither idolatry, then dominant, nor the cruelty of Tyrants equipped with the arms of the whole Roman empire, nor the acumen of so many Philosophers practiced in all the arts of disputation could overwhelm, be subdued by avarice, pleasure, the manners and bearing of a world corrupted by every desire and made effeminate? Fables.

> 7 Quinimò ipsa omnium óbicum victrix, cordium triumphàtrix, ingeniorumque, multiplicavit victorias suas certaminibus, suosque adversarios post pugnam, propugnatores suos acerrimos est experta. ¿An Religionem, inquam, istam prosternet, delebitque omninò, infamis quaedam satyra, Libertinarum fabellarum collectio; delectus aliquot ambiguorum verborum, pueriliumque sophismatum? Nisi haec est summa audacia, imò insignis vesania nescio quaenam unquam possit esse. Et re vera satis est, vel obiter legere horum Magistrorum scriptiuncula, ut statim dignoscantur indicia levium, & delirantium. Ne, quaeso, putetis, vos in iis [p. 5] reperire posse systema aliquod deductum benè, ut prima imis, media, & imis, & primis respondeant, & aptè inter se cohaereant, quo & Religioni, & Deo O. M. bellum inferatur.

7 Nay rather, Religion itself, victorious over all obstacles, triumphant over hearts and minds, has multiplied its victories by its contests, and has found its adversaries, after the battle, to be its keenest champions. Shall that Religion, I say, be laid low and utterly destroyed by some infamous satire, a collection of libertine little tales, a selection of a few ambiguous words and puerile sophisms? If this is not the height of audacity, nay, a signal madness, I do not know what ever could be. And in truth it is enough to read even in passing the little writings of these Masters for the marks of light-minded and raving men to be recognized at once. Do not, I beg you, think that in them you can find [p. 5] some well-deduced system, in which the first things answer to the last, the middle ones both to the last and to the first, and all cohere aptly with one another, by which war might be waged both on Religion and on God, the Best and Greatest.

> 8 Nil nisi confusae audiuntur declamationes, & voces; veluti audiebantur in terra Senaar inter ingentis turris opifices, qui ne ipsi quidem mutuos sermones suos intelligébant. Evomit unusquisque infanda, & falsa, sed tam varia, tam contraria, ut non solum idem significent, sed haec, illa destruant.

8 Nothing is heard but confused declamations and voices, as they were heard in the land of Sennaar among the builders of the huge tower, who did not even understand one another’s speech. Each one spews out unspeakable and false things, but so various, so contrary, that not only do they not mean the same thing, but these destroy those.

> 9 Negat *Atheus* Deum esse: *Deista* [^5-s1-2] ait, esse, sed res humanas non curare. *Naturalista* contra utrumque pugnat, defenditque summa ope & Providentiam, & Deum. Hic autem quum nolit in Deo recognoscere, nisi quod ipse ingenio suo tam hebeti capere potest, & Athei, & Deistae telis se praebet confodiendum. Dat *Helvetius* homini animam ejusmodi, quàm equi, lupique habent, illamque libertate quàvis spoliat. *Rousseau* eam liberam facit, & spiritualem: at primaeva originalis conditio hominis, sententiâ ejus, nihil differt ab origine luporum, & equorum.

9 The Atheist denies that God exists; the Deist (c) says that He exists, but does not care for human affairs. The Naturalist fights against both, and defends with all his might both Providence and God. But this man, since he will recognize nothing in God except what he himself can grasp with so dull a wit, offers himself to be pierced by the weapons both of the Atheist and of the Deist. Helvétius gives man a soul of the same kind as horses and wolves have, and strips it of all freedom. Rousseau makes it free and spiritual: but the primeval, original condition of man, in his opinion, differs in nothing from the origin of wolves and horses.

> [^5-s1-2]: *Deista*, sive *Theista* adpellatur, qui Deum existere quidem concedit, sed Religionem nullam, cultum nullum profitetur. Religionem omnem, Divinamque Revelationem tanquam meras fabulas fastidiosè traducunt Deistae, satisque esse garriunt; si Deus in naturae, cordisque simplicitate adoretur.

[^5-s1-2]: A Deist, or Theist, is the name given to one who indeed grants that God exists, but professes no Religion, no worship. The Deists disdainfully decry all Religion and divine Revelation as mere fables, and prattle that it is enough if God is adored in the simplicity of nature and of the heart.

> 10 Adserunt ii hominem totum perire, pereunte vitâ: alii putant, eum futurum immortalem. Inter hos tamen quidam sentiunt eum in altera vita nullis puniendum suppliciis; alii haec supplicia futura volunt, quae necessariò lex praescribit; irrídent alii has leges, has poenas tanquàm pura putaque Poetarum, & Regum commenta. Si hos audis, ab aeterno fuit mundus, si illos, initium habuit, ut placet unis à Deo, ut alteris à casu & fortuito concursu atomorum aeternarum, & errantium.

10 These assert that the whole man perishes when life perishes; others think that he will be immortal. Among the latter, however, some hold that in the other life he is to be punished with no torments; others will have it that there will be those torments which the law necessarily prescribes; others laugh at these laws, these penalties, as the pure and simple fictions of Poets and of Kings. If you listen to these, the world has been from eternity; if to those, it had a beginning: from God, as some hold; from chance and the fortuitous concourse of eternal and wandering atoms, as others do.

> 11 Quod tamen est non minus verum, quam mirandum, illud est, unumquemque eorum bello irrequieto in se saevíre, & semeptisum suis se armis confodere. Quot sint in Hobbesii operibus, quorum haec evertunt illa, ii unùm ignorant, qui ea non legerunt. Tota Spinosae *Ethica* innititur definitioni, quae duobus modis intelligi potest, quorum unus, qui verus est, alterum evertit; hic autem eversus librum totum, qui ex *definitione* pendet à principio ad finem usque, Geometricè destruit [^5-s2-2] Libertinorum grex [p. 6] hoc in capite duces suos praeclaros religiosè imitatur, à quibus quum mendacium didicerit etiam illud didicit, ut respuat, quod adprobavit sibique semper contradicat.

11 What, however, is no less true than astonishing is this: that each of them rages against himself in a restless war, and very often pierces himself with his own weapons. How many things there are in the works of Hobbes of which some overturn others, only those are ignorant who have not read them. The whole Ethics of Spinoza rests on a definition which can be understood in two ways, of which the one, which is true, overturns the other; and this other, once overturned, destroys geometrically the whole book, which depends on the definition from beginning to end (d). The herd of Libertines [p. 6] religiously imitates its illustrious leaders in this point: having learned lying from them, it has also learned this, to reject what it has approved and always to contradict itself.

> [^5-s2-2]: Definitio cui innititur Spinosae systema est definitio *substantiae* his concepta verbis. *Per substantiam intelligo id, quod in se est, & per se concipitur: hoc est, id, cujus conceptus non indiget conceptu alterius rei, à quo formari debeat* (Ethic. P. 1. Def 3). Jam verò haec verba id *quod in se est* duplicem significationem habere possunt. I. *quod est in se*, hoc est, quod est *ex se*, exclusâ causâ, quae illud producat. II. *id quod est in se*, id est, *quod est per se ipsum* excluso *subjecto*, quod illud sustentet. *Modi* ut ex. gr. *motus*, *figura* &c. non existunt *ex se*, quoniam indigent causâ à qua producantur, sed neque existunt *per se*; requirunt enim subjectum, quo inhaereant, ut pila ex. gr. Ens autèm perfectissimum existit *per se*, & *ex se*. Non enim indiget subjecto, à quo sustentetur, sed ne habere quidem causam potest, á qua producatur. Equus *per se* existit, quum nullo subjecto *inhaereat*; at non existit *ex se*, quum habuerit causam à qua fuit productus. *Spinosa* usus est ambigua dictione *existit in se*, vultque proprium esse substantiae *existere ex se ipsâ*, exclusâ causa quae illam producat; sed hoc est, quod omnes negant, & quod nusquam in libro suo probavit *Recutitus* ille philosophus. Transeamus ad alias definitionis partes, & praeunte adlatae distinctionis face, illius fraudem detegemus. *Per substantiam intelligo id*, *quod in se est*, additque, *& per se concipitur*. Si credit *Spinosa* substantiae conceptum esse tam absolutum, ut nullam importet relationem cum subjecto, quod eam sustineat, ut *motus* eam importat ad *mobile*, verè sentit, sed hoc nihil *Pantheismo* opitulatur. ¿Quid ergo vult? Hoc nempè: conceptum substantiae ita esse absolutum, ut à se removeat quamcumque relationem ad causam, quae illam producat, sed hoc falsum omninò est, & hoc nunquam probaturus est. Idem dicendum de aliis verbis, quae sequuntur, quae impius *Appella* addit explicaturus adlatam substantiae definitionem, hoc est, *substantia est id*, *cujus conceptus non indiget conceptu alterius rei*, *à quo formari debeat*. Si enim significare vult conceptum substantiae debere à se excludere relationem ad aliam substantiam, ad quam ipsa referatur, veluti effectus ad causam, id negamus, neque ille unquam id probabit. Vafer tamen Haebreus hoc intelligebat; ex hoc enim uno falso principio derivavit totum suum *Pantheisticum* systema, volebatque in ea definitione includere tanquam fundamentum id, quod erat totius controversiae caput; hoc est, esse de essentia substantiae, ut existat *ex se*, exclusâ quacumque causâ, neque posse unquam concipi in substantia unâ relationem effectus ad aliam substantiam, tanquam ad causam ipsius procreatricem.

[^5-s2-2]: The definition on which Spinoza’s system rests is the definition of substance conceived in these words: By substance I understand that which is in itself and is conceived through itself: that is, that whose concept does not need the concept of another thing from which it must be formed (Ethics, Pt. 1, Def. 3). Now these words, that which is in itself, can have a twofold meaning. I. That which is in itself, that is, which is from itself, excluding a cause that produces it. II. That which is in itself, to that is, which is through itself, excluding a subject that sustains it. Modes, e.g. motion, shape, etc., do not exist from themselves, because they need a cause by which they are produced; but neither do they exist through themselves, for they require a subject in which to inhere, e.g. a ball. But the most perfect Being exists through itself and from itself. For it does not need a subject by which to be sustained, nor can it even have a cause by which it is produced. A horse exists through itself, since it inheres in no subject; but it does not exist from itself, since it has had a cause by which it was produced. Spinoza used the ambiguous expression exists in itself, and will have it proper to substance to exist from itself, excluding a cause that produces it; but this is what everyone denies, and what that circumcised philosopher nowhere proved in his book. Let us pass to the other parts of the definition and, with the torch of the distinction just given going before us, uncover his fraud. By substance I understand that which is in itself, and he adds, and is conceived through itself. If Spinoza believes that the concept of substance is so absolute that it implies no relation to a subject that sustains it, as motion implies one to the movable, he thinks truly, but this helps Pantheism not at all. What then does he mean? This, namely: that the concept of substance is so absolute that it removes from itself every relation to a cause that produces it; but this is altogether false, and this he will never prove. The same must be said of the other words that follow, which the impious Apella adds to explain the definition of substance just given, that is, substance is that whose concept does not need the concept of another thing from which it must be formed. For if he means that the concept of substance must exclude from itself a relation to another substance to which it is referred, as an effect to a cause, we deny it, nor will he ever prove it. The crafty Hebrew, however, understood this; for from this one false principle he derived his whole Pantheistic system, and he wished to include in that definition, as its foundation, that which was the head of the whole controversy: namely, that it is of the essence of substance that it exist from itself, excluding any cause whatever, and that there can never be conceived in a substance a relation of effect to another substance as to the cause that procreates it.

> 12 Adhaec. Reperietis in hujusmodi libellulis *Polyantheam* universam, sive rudem indigestamque collectionem declamationum, & eruditionis. De Jurisprudentia, de Politica, de Astronomia, de Commercio, de Ethica, de Bello disputatur in illis. Dialectica una, sive Ars Cogitandi omninò desideratur. Volatur Athenis Spartam, [p. 7] Hierosolyma Romam, ab Augusti seculo ad Ludovici aetatem. A Caraibis Antillarum fit transitus ad Ottentotos Africae; ab his ad Groelandos Boreales; inde ad homines sylvestres aliarum regionum remotiorum. Hinc orbis plagarum adeò inter se dissitarum modò examinantur leges, modo conferuntur inter se mores, nunc enarrantur turpitudines, nunc plausibus celebratur irreligio. Antiquitates Sinenses majus pondus, quàm Sacra Genesis penès eos habent. Diodorus, Strabo, & Tacitus citantur Judaicarum antiquitatum Moyse ipso peritiores. Horatius, Petronius, Manilius, Lucretius, Poppius sapientiae incomparabiles praeceptores adferuntur.

12 Besides this, you will find in little books of this sort a whole Polyanthea, or a rude and undigested collection of declamations and of erudition. They dispute in them about Jurisprudence, about Politics, about Astronomy, about Commerce, about Ethics, about War; Dialectic alone, or the Art of Thinking, is wholly lacking. They fly from Athens to Sparta, from Jerusalem [p. 7] to Rome, from the age of Augustus to the age of Louis. A passage is made from the Caribs of the Antilles to the Hottentots of Africa; from these to the northern Greenlanders; thence to the wild men of other remote regions. Hence the laws of regions of the world so unlike one another are now examined, now their customs are compared with one another, now their turpitudes are recounted, now irreligion is celebrated with applause. Chinese antiquities carry greater weight with them than sacred Genesis. Diodorus, Strabo and Tacitus are cited as more expert in Jewish antiquities than Moses himself. Horace, Petronius, Manilius, Lucretius, Poppius are brought forward as incomparable teachers of wisdom.

> 13 Totum tamèn id saepius fit, quin auctorum loca percenseant; ut plurimùm infideliter loca adferunt; semper autem sine arte Critica, satis namque est ut enuncientur voce impávidâ, censoria, quae sola potest, ut opinantur, dare pondus fabulis, & mendaciis.

13 Yet all this is mostly done without the passages of the authors being examined; for the most part they bring in those passages unfaithfully, and always without the art of Criticism; for it is enough that they be pronounced in a fearless, censorious voice, which alone, as they suppose, can give weight to fables and lies.

> 14 Haerent in obtutu Libertini juvenes tantae eruditionis congeriem, tantam rerum varietatem, tantam decidendi confidentiam legentes. Admirantur hujusmodi Philosophos velut sapientiae oracula. Religio, cujus neque fundamenta, neque systema meditati sunt unquam, in eorum mentibus vacillat. Praeceptores autem isti existimant re ipsâ se, quod intendebant fuisse consequutos, & rapidâ, turbulentaque loquacitate reverâ ostendisse Religionem Catholicam fictionem esse, Evangelium jocum, lymphatos ejus Martyres, Sanctos Patres nihil omninò scire, omnesque veros Catholicos gregem stolidorum, inutiles, imò Societati, & Reipublicae perniciosos esse.

14 Libertine youths stand fixed in their gaze as they read such a heap of erudition, such a variety of matters, such confidence in deciding. They admire Philosophers of this kind as oracles of wisdom. Religion, whose foundations and whose system they have never meditated, wavers in their minds. These teachers, for their part, think that they have in fact achieved what they intended, and by their rapid and turbulent loquacity have really shown that the Catholic Religion is a fiction, the Gospel a jest, its Martyrs madmen, that the Holy Fathers know nothing at all, and that all true Catholics are a herd of fools, useless, nay pernicious to Society and to the Commonwealth.

> 15 Quod si in farragine tantâ rerum inutilium & absurdarum, sophismata quaedam sunt intermixta, quae Religionem Naturalem & Revelatam adgrediantur, hoc tamen certissimum est, non semel, sed saepissimè à nostris Doctoribus & praecipuè ab Angelico Mag. D. Thoma Aquinate ea fuisse dissoluta, imò, ut ita dicam, in cinerem redacta & difflata.

15 But if in so great a farrago of useless and absurd things certain sophisms are mixed in which attack natural and revealed Religion, this nevertheless is most certain: that these have been resolved, not once but very often, by our Doctors, and especially by the Angelic Master St. Thomas Aquinas, nay, so to speak, reduced to ashes and blown away.

> 16 Intelligetis jam non sine gravi causâ me à principio dixisse, nullos alios quàm indignationis, contemptus miserationis sensus in homine prudenti excitari posse, quotiescumque hos intuetur Scriptores, qui artibus tam puerilibus se posse Religionem evertere confidunt; eam Religionem dico, cujus Divina origo, dógmatum veritas sanctitas praeceptorum, eximia virtus, & protectionis vis, quâ munitur, effecerunt, ut per tot seculorum cursus, post tot casus neque ferro vinceretur, neque scriptis concuteretur; neque superaretur superstitione, & impietate: uno verbo ut retunderet omnes hominum, daemonisque impetus.

16 You will now understand that it was not without grave cause that I said at the beginning that no other feelings than those of indignation, contempt and pity can be aroused in a prudent man whenever he looks upon these Writers, who trust that with such puerile arts they can overturn Religion: that Religion, I say, whose divine origin, the truth of its dogmas, the holiness of its precepts, and the eminent virtue and force of the protection by which it is defended, have brought it about that through the course of so many centuries, after so many vicissitudes, it has been neither conquered by the sword, nor shaken by writings, nor overcome by superstition and impiety: in a word, that it has beaten back all the assaults of men and of demons.

> 17 *In tanta* ergo *pestilentissimorum colluvie librorum*, *quibus*, (ut sapientissimè loquitur felic. record. Clemens Papa XIII. [^7-s1-3] [p. 8] *homines corrupti, & reprobi circa Fidem impudentissimâ licentiâ cum impunitate conjuncta absurdissimas, impiasque opiniones in imperitorum animos conantur infundere*; necessarium omninò duxi commonere vos, ut ab hujusmodi librorum lectione, si (quod Deus non sinat) in manus fortassè vestras aliquandò inciderint omnino abstineatis, *ne vos decipiant per philosophiam, & inanem fallaciam secundum traditionem hominum, & non secundum Christum*, ut loquitur S. Paulus [^8-s1-3]. Sed unde egressa fuit oratio revertatur.

17 In so great a cesspool, then, of most pestilential books, by which (as Pope Clement XIII of happy memory most wisely says (e)) men [p. 8] corrupt and reprobate concerning the Faith, with a most impudent license joined with impunity, try to pour most absurd and impious opinions into the minds of the unlearned, I have thought it altogether necessary to warn you that, should books of this kind (which God forbid) perhaps at some time fall into your hands, you abstain altogether from reading them, lest they cheat you by philosophy, and vain deceit; according to the tradition of men, and not according to Christ, as St. Paul says (f). But let our discourse return to the point from which it set out.

> [^7-s1-3]: Litt. in forma Brevis dat. ad P. Anton. Valsechi die 21. Mart. Ann. 1767.

[^7-s1-3]: Letter in the form of a Brief, given to Fr. Anton. Valsecchi on 21 March, in the year 1767.

> [^8-s1-3]: Ad Coloss. Cap. 2. ℣. 8.

[^8-s1-3]: To the Colossians, ch. 2, v. 8.

> 18 Quantum ad Deum adtinet, quum praestantissimus ille sit, summumque jus, summamque auctoritatem in omnia jure ac meritò sibi vindicet, quisque intelligit, illum tanto obsequio ac veneratione prosequendum, quantum Optimo rerum Conditori, & Amantissimo Conservatori debeatur. Multa sunt quibus nostrum erga alios obsequium testificamur, & quidem amor, obsequii nostri praecipuum argumentum est. Fit enim illo, ut mirum in modum eos studio ac pietate colamus, quos benevolentiâ nostra dignos esse censemus. Dubium ergo esse non potest, quin Deus O. M. qui jure dominii à nobis colendus est, prae reliquis & amandus sit, & summoperè diligendus. Nec certè una tantum ratio est, qua ad id praestandum adigamur. Est namque Deus summum illud bonum, quod si oculis cerneretur, mirabiles, amores (ut de Sapientia ait Plato) excitaret sui. Quippè quidquid nobis in hac vita bene est, ab eo uno proficisci intelligimus, aeternam beatitudinem in altera ex ejus fruitione recepturi.

18 As regards God, since He is most excellent and rightly and deservedly claims for Himself the supreme right and the supreme authority over all things, everyone understands that He is to be honored with as great a homage and veneration as is owed to the Best Founder and the most Loving Preserver of things. There are many things by which we testify our homage toward others, and indeed love is the chief proof of our homage. For by it it comes about that we cultivate in a wonderful way, with zeal and devotion, those whom we judge worthy of our benevolence. There can therefore be no doubt that God, the Best and Greatest, who by right of dominion is to be worshipped by us, is to be loved above all else and cherished supremely. Nor indeed is there only one reason by which we are driven to do this. For God is that highest good which, if it were seen with the eyes, would arouse (as Plato says of Wisdom) wondrous loves of itself. For whatever is good for us in this life we understand to proceed from Him alone, and we are to receive eternal beatitude in the other life from the enjoyment of Him.

> 19 Hinc à Sacris Literis erùdimur *Deum ex toto corde*, *ex tota anima*, *& totis viribus diligendum esse*, [^8-s2-2] ut si cor nostrum perenni, ac irrequietâ veluti flammâ incensum, amoris victima consumi posset, vix, ac ne vix quidem amor ille par foret, ut aliquas amantissimi Patris amori vices rependeret. Omnibus itaque animi viribus nobis est enitendum, ut Deum super omnia diligamus, & quandoquidem *Deus charitas*, *& ignis est*, *ignem venit mittere in terram*, *nec aliud vult nisi ut accendatur* [^8-s3-2] ipsum lacrymis, effusisque votis rogare debemus, ut vehementius ille divinae charitatis ardor in nostris cordibus accendatur, adfectus omnes consumat, nosque demum placabilem, Deoque placentem hostiam efficiat.

19 Hence we are taught by Sacred Scripture that God is to be loved with the whole heart, with the whole soul, and with all one’s strength (g), so that, if our heart, kindled as it were by a perpetual and restless flame, could be consumed as a victim of love, that love would scarcely, nay not even scarcely, be equal to repaying in some measure the love of a most loving Father. With all the powers of the mind, therefore, we must strive to love God above all things; and since God is charity, and is a fire, and came to cast fire on the earth, and wills nothing else but that it be kindled (h), we ought to ask Him Himself with tears and outpoured prayers that the ardor of divine charity may be kindled more vehemently in our hearts, consume all our affections, and at last make us a victim acceptable and pleasing to God.

> [^8-s2-2]: Math. Cap. 22. ℣. 37.

[^8-s2-2]: Matthew, ch. 22, v. 37.

> [^8-s3-2]: Luc. 12. ℣. 29.

[^8-s3-2]: Luke 12, v. 29.

> 20 Supremum verò numen non amore solum, sed etiam timore veneramur. Quoniam autem, ut Scholae loquuntur, duplex est timor Dei, *filialis*, nimirum, ac *servilis*, praestat utrumque ad illud colendum adhibere. Primus ab ejus amore nascitur, nec potest ab hoc dulci vinculo separari. Alter oritur à poena, nec potest à servitute sejungi. Huic enim, & timori certissima quoque fides addenda est. ¿Quis enim non fidat ei, quem nec decipi, nec decipere posse certo sciat? Est [p. 9] quidem Deus ipsa ratio suprema, ipsa bonitas, ipsaque veritas. De ejus ergo promissis, dictisque, ubi constet, dixisse, & promisisse, nemini licet dubitare. Ex fide necessariò consequitur Spes, qua & praemium virtuti constitutum expectare debemus, & auxilia etiam illa, quae cum virium nostrarum imbecillitatem adjuvent, sunt proinde ad illud consequendum omninò necessaria.

20 We venerate the Supreme Deity, however, not with love alone but also with fear. And since, as the Schools say, the fear of God is twofold, namely filial and servile, it is best to employ both in worshipping Him. The first is born of love for Him and cannot be separated from this sweet bond. The other arises from punishment and cannot be disjoined from servitude. To this love, moreover, and to fear, a most certain faith must also be added. For who would not trust Him whom he knows for certain can neither be deceived nor deceive? God is indeed [p. 9] supreme reason itself, goodness itself, and truth itself. Concerning His promises and words, therefore, once it is established that He has spoken and promised, no one may doubt. From faith there necessarily follows Hope, by which we ought to expect both the reward appointed for virtue and also those helps which, since they assist the weakness of our powers, are therefore altogether necessary for attaining it.

> 21 Amor itaque ille *filialis*, quo Deum, veluti Patrem diligimus, excitare nos debet, ut ab illo bona cuncta nobis profutura certò sperare possimus: ideoque ab illo nobis opem, in adversis rebus auxilium petere, atque exorare debemus, ut Redemptor ipse saepissimè nos ad orandum, atque petendum invitat: *petite*, *& accipietis*, *quaerite*, *& invenietis*; *pulsate*, *& aperietur vobis* Divino tamen consilio nos admonet, ut in Christi ipsius nomine petamus *Siquid petieritis Patrem in nomine meo dabit vobis*.

21 That filial love, therefore, by which we love God as a Father, ought to rouse us to hope with certainty from Him for all the goods that will profit us; and therefore we ought to ask and entreat of Him help, and aid in adversity, as the Redeemer Himself very often invites us to pray and to ask: Ask, and you shall receive; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. By divine counsel, however, He admonishes us to ask in the name of Christ Himself: If you ask the Father any thing in my name, he will give it you.

> 22 Verum ne ab ipsa quidem invocatione Dei precibusque, velit nolit *Rousseau*, abstinere possumus. Haec enim officii nostri prima pars est, cui certè deesse non possumus, quin maxima nobis incommoda, & detrimenta importemus. Quippe quum tot, tantisque malis adflictemur, in iis recreari Supremi tantum Numinis potestate, ac sapientiâ datum est. Immortales quoque Deo non habendae solum, sed etiam agendae sunt gratiae. ¿Quis namque innumeris beneficiis cumulatus se ab hoc officio praestando immunem esse arbitretur? Quod si vel uno creationis, & conservationis adfecti beneficio Deo plurimum deberemus, quid de ea vitae conditione statuendum in qua nobis longè plura sunt impertita?

22 But not even from the invocation of God and from prayer can we abstain, whether Rousseau will or no. For this is the first part of our duty, in which we certainly cannot fail without bringing on ourselves the greatest inconveniences and losses. For since we are afflicted by so many and such great evils, it is granted to us to be refreshed in them only by the power and wisdom of the Supreme Deity. Immortal thanks, too, are not only to be felt toward God, but also to be rendered to Him. For who, heaped with innumerable benefits, would think himself exempt from performing this duty? And if, endowed with the single benefit of creation and conservation alone, we would owe God very much, what must we judge of that condition of life in which far more has been imparted to us?

> 23 At haec interna sunt Religionis officia. De externis autem haec veluti summatim nobis videntur statuenda. Deus non modò interno, & spirituali, sed etiam externo, & sensibili Religionis cultu est adorandus, ut supra diximus. Et sanè nihil est in nobis, quod Dei munus non sit, illique propterea omni ex parte subjectum. Igitur externa quoque corporis membra illi serviant oportet. Cui argumento alterum quoque accedit, & illud quidem gravissimum ex ipsa naturae nostrae conditione desumptum. Si enim agnitio numinis, Societatis naturalis, ac status civilis vinculum est necessarium, ejusdem quoque cultus utrique hominum conditioni erit summopere commendatus. Certum est autem nec Societatem, nec Civilem hanc formam absque sensibili operatione posse subsistere, quamobrem ad eam statuendam cultus etiam externus, ac sensibilis accedat necesse est. Ex lege externi cultus praestandi alia consequuntur officia. Primum est, ut de Deo, deque rebus Divinis, non nisi honorificentissimè colloquamur. Secundum, ut omnibus externis argumentis, interna officia ad aliorum exemplum manifestemus. Tertium, ut Divinorum etiam scientiam aliis explicemus, ut sic vicissim alter alteri prosit. Tandem, ut Dei gloriam omni pietate, & studio promoveamus.

23 But these are the internal duties of Religion. Concerning the external ones, the following seem to us to be laid down, as it were in summary. God is to be adored not only with an internal and spiritual, but also with an external and sensible worship of Religion, as we said above. And indeed there is nothing in us that is not the gift of God, and therefore subject to Him in every respect. Therefore the external members of the body too must serve Him. To this argument another is added, and that a very weighty one, taken from the very condition of our nature. For if the acknowledgment of the Deity is the necessary bond of natural Society and of the civil state, the worship of that same Deity will also be supremely commended to both conditions of men. But it is certain that neither Society nor this Civil form can subsist without sensible operation; wherefore, in order to establish it, an external and sensible worship must also be added. From the law of rendering external worship other duties follow. The first is that we speak of God and of Divine things only in the most honorable way. The second, that by all external signs we manifest our internal duties for the example of others. The third, that we also explain the knowledge of Divine things to others, so that in turn one may profit another. Finally, that we promote the glory of God with all piety and zeal.

> 24 Sed de officiis pertractemus, quae homini erga se ipsum sunt [p. 10] excolenda. Quae ad genus hoc officiorum pertinent, ea cùm animi; tùm corporis custodiâ, & culturâ continentur. Sed quamvis ad utrumque adigamur, eò tamen major, adcuratiorque animi perfectio esse debet, quò mens ipsa corpore praestantior est, atque nobilior. Jam vero animi cura, intellectus, & voluntatis emendatione perficitur. Quidquid igitur hanc emendationem spectare videatur, id maximè Christiano viro omni studio, ac diligentia praestandum est. Et quoniam vitia intellectus, studio disciplinarum removentur faciliùs, ut voluntatis errores tutiùs emendantur exercitatione virtutum, ad utramque, nobis erit confugiendum. Nihil autem ad animi culturam, relatis adjumentis, procurandam aptius dari & excogitari potest, quàm adtenta, ac vigil adfectuum nostrorum moderatio.

24 But let us treat fully of the duties which are to be [p. 10] cultivated by man toward himself. The things that pertain to this kind of duties are contained in the custody and cultivation both of the mind and of the body. But although we are bound to both, the perfecting of the mind must nevertheless be greater and more careful, by as much as the mind itself is more excellent and nobler than the body. Now the care of the mind is perfected by the amendment of the intellect and of the will. Whatever, therefore, seems to regard this amendment must be performed by a Christian man above all, with all zeal and diligence. And since the vices of the intellect are more easily removed by the study of the disciplines, as the errors of the will are more safely amended by the exercise of the virtues, we shall have to take refuge in both. Nothing, however, among the aids just mentioned, can be offered or devised that is more apt for procuring the cultivation of the mind than an attentive and vigilant moderation of our affections.

> 25 Adfectus principes sunt, Amor, Odium, Desiderium, Laetitia, Spes, Tristitia, Diffidentia, Audacia, Desperatio, Voluptas, Ambitio, Avaritia, Ira, Pudor, Taedium. Invidia, Irrisio, Zelotypia, Immodicus sui amor, Aemulatio, quibus humanos animos allici, moveri, vel excitari conspicimus, ut exinde virtutes omnes, vel vitia, veluti ex uberrimis fontibus oriantur. [*Vid. dict. in Log. Lib.* 2. *cap.* 5.]. Hinc in omni vitae genere illud praeceptum nobis est, ut motus animi rationi non obtemperantes corrigamus. De corpore autem, quum nemo propriae vitae sit Dominus, quidquid effutiat Voltaire, nullum quoque absolutum ejus dominium potest in illud excercere. Et quidem tanta corporis custodia retinenda, quanta nec ad illud perimendum, nec ad illud labefactandum, requiritur. Quae tamen omnia, salvo semper Religionis negotio, intelligenda, & praestanda sunt.

25 The principal affections are Love, Hatred, Desire, Joy, Hope, Sadness, Distrust, Boldness, Despair, Pleasure, Ambition, Avarice, Anger, Shame, Weariness, Envy, Derision, Jealousy, immoderate Love of self, Emulation, by which we see human minds enticed, moved or excited, so that from them all the virtues or vices arise as from most abundant springs. [See what was said in the Logic, bk. 2, ch. 5.] Hence in every kind of life we have this precept: that we correct the motions of the mind that do not obey reason. As for the body, since no one is Lord of his own life, whatever Voltaire may blurt out, neither can anyone exercise an absolute dominion over it. And indeed such custody of the body must be kept as is required in order neither to destroy it nor to impair it. All of which, however, is to be understood and performed always without prejudice to the business of Religion.

> 26 Non defuere qui putarunt ad grave damnum evitandum & potissimum ad ignominiam ipsâ morte turpiorem effugiendam, licere sibi mortem consciscere. Sed haec nec cum juris naturae praescriptionibus, nec cum Christianis legibus ullomodo consentire certum est. Nulla enim est naturae necessitas, quamobrem, quod solius Dei proprium est, & Principum, Dei vices gerentium in terris, illud etiam imperium invito ipsomet domino nobis vindicemus. Accedit: in Providentiam injurios esse, ac nimis de Divina Bonitate diffidere, qui in summis rerum angustijs, se ab amantissimo luminum Patre dessertos esse conqueruntur, ut ne quid de virtute *Fortitudinis* dicam, quae certè in adversis, tantò magis elucescit, quantò fortius mala tolerantur.

26 There have not been lacking those who thought that, in order to avoid grave harm, and above all to escape an ignominy more shameful than death itself, it was lawful for them to inflict death on themselves. But it is certain that this in no way agrees either with the prescriptions of the law of nature or with Christian laws. For there is no necessity of nature why we should claim for ourselves, against the will of its very master, that dominion too which is proper to God alone, and to Princes, who act in God’s stead on earth. Add that those are injurious to Providence and distrust the Divine Goodness too much who, in the extreme straits of affairs, complain that they have been deserted by the most loving Father of lights; not to speak of the virtue of Fortitude, which certainly shines out in adversity the more, the more bravely evils are endured.

> 27 Reliqua hominis erga hominem officia servanda haec sunt. Hominum genus ad mutuam Societatem generari, quidquid in oppositum sentiat vivens adhuc hominum fabula *Rousseau*, compertum est apud omnes. ¿Quid enim aut organa ad loquendum apta proficiant, aut cuinam usui adfectus ad alios adjuvandos inserviant, nisi ab ipsa natura, nimirùm à Deo Sapientissimo naturae auctore ad magnam veluti Societatem ineundam destinemur? Mutuo ergo [p. 11] amicitiae & benevolentiae vinculo conjungimur. Et quemadmodum in eo observando omnis honestas, ita in eo frangendo, violandoque deformitas, ac turpitudo omnis sita est.

27 The remaining duties to be observed by man toward man are these. That the human race is generated for mutual Society, whatever Rousseau, still living and the talk of men, may think to the contrary, is ascertained among all. For what would organs fit for speaking profit, or to what use would affections for helping others serve, unless we were destined by nature itself, namely by God, the most wise author of nature, to enter as it were into one great Society? We are therefore joined by a mutual bond of friendship [p. 11] and benevolence. And just as all that is honorable lies in observing it, so all deformity and baseness lies in breaking and violating it.

> 28 Ex hac autem amicitia duo officiorum genera deducuntur. Primum ut ne quem verbo, facto ve offendamus; alterum, ut nostri similibus, quoad possumus, beneficentiâ opitulemur. Et quidem aliorum laesio, quae naturali illa lege prohibetur: *quod tibi non vis*, *alteri ne feceris*, patére quamlatissime potest. Quum enim vel animi, vel corporis, vel fortunae bona sint; hinc tribus modis aliis detrimento esse quimus.

28 From this friendship, moreover, two kinds of duties are derived. The first, that we offend no one by word or deed; the second, that we help our fellows with beneficence as far as we can. And indeed the injury of others, which is forbidden by that natural law, what you would not have done to you, do not do to another, can extend very widely. For since there are goods of the mind, of the body and of fortune, we can be harmful to others in three ways.

> 29 Itaque ea honestatis praecipua pars est, neminem, aut pravis opinionibus, aut exemplis ad malum perpetrandum impellere. Aeque enim dictis, aut factis dociles labefactantur animi, & in eo qui peccant, non unius tantum criminis, sed plurium, sed multiplicium sed planè innumerabilium summa aequitate reprehenduntur.

29 Thus the chief part of what is honorable is to impel no one to commit evil, either by depraved opinions or by examples. For impressionable minds are undermined equally by words and by deeds, and those who sin in this are reproved with the greatest justice for the sum, not of one crime only, but of many, nay of manifold, nay plainly of innumerable ones.

> 30 Hinc multò majorem curam adhibere debent Parentes, Tutores, Curatores, Pedagogi, bonarum artium Magistri, aut quicunque tandem sint, quibus precipuè incumbit Adolescentûm educatio, ut in iis instituendis eam teneant disciplinae rationem, quae ad probitatis normam sit exactè composita. In hoc autem officio excolendo puerorum naturam, & conditionem sequendam esse, nemo est qui non videat.

30 Hence much greater care must be applied by Parents, Guardians, Curators, Pedagogues, Masters of the liberal arts, or whoever at length they may be on whom the education of youth chiefly falls, that in instructing the young they keep to that method of discipline which is exactly conformed to the norm of probity. In discharging this duty, moreover, there is no one who does not see that the nature and condition of the children must be followed.

> 31 In his autem, quae ad fortunae bona referuntur, paucis multa sic explico. Quaecumque in aliorum facultate sunt posita, & extrinsecus ad eos conservandos, nobilitandosque accersita, ea violari non nisi cum *juris naturae* transgressione possunt. Etsi enim nulla sint privatâ naturâ, veteri tamen occupatione, victoria, bello, pactione, conditione, sorte, fiunt hujusmodi.

31 As for those things that are referred to the goods of fortune, I explain much in few words thus. Whatever things are placed in the possession of others, and procured from outside for their preservation and advancement, cannot be violated except with a transgression of the law of nature. For although no things are private by nature, they nevertheless become so by ancient occupation, victory, war, compact, condition, lot.

> 32 Optimum ergo illud nomen, quod cuique virtutum exercitatione obtigit, nec privatim, nec publicè laedi ab altero potest. Qua quidem in re si falsò aliorum dicta, seu facta criminemur, & sumus calumniae rei, & contra justitiam peccamus. Sin vero, quod in altero vitii, peccatique est, quod quidem verum sit, sed occultum, manifestemus alteri, jam mutuae benevolentiae adversamur. Sed nihil turpius, faedius nihil in hominum Societate dictorum, pactorumque inconstantiâ. Quum enim praecipuum *Justitiae* fundamentum sit *Fides*, hac virtute sublata, Justitia quoque, & unâ simul cum illa *Socialitas* corruat oportet. Quamobrem si nemini data fides est violanda, pari ratione alterum quoque decipiendi mendacio facultas omnis erepta est. Quod quidem de omni mendacii genere ita intelligimus, ut sive cum alterius detrimento id fiat, sive ad tui aliorumque mentiaris utilitatem, utriusque juris, perfecti nimirum, & imperfecti laesor existimeris. De beneficentia, ac liberalitate existimo, universa, quae ex hoc capite derivantur officia, ea principio illo contineri: *quodcumque ab aliis tibi fieri vis*, *& aliis facito*. Itaque istorum omissio non ad injustitiam, sed ad [p. 12] inhumanitatem, & turpitudinem referenda est. In beneficiis conferendis multae cautiones adhibendae sunt, & imprimis videndum cum Tullio: *ne obsit benignitas & iis ipsis, quibus benignè videbitur fieri, & ceteris; deinde, ne major benignitas sit, quàm facultas; tum, ut pro dignitate cuique tribuatur*. Sed aliqua de officio hominis erga Rempublicam dicere necessum existimo.

32 That excellent name, therefore, which has fallen to each man through the exercise of the virtues, can be injured by another neither privately nor publicly. In this matter, if we falsely charge the words or deeds of others as crimes, we are both guilty of calumny and sin against justice. If, on the other hand, we make manifest to another what is a vice and a sin in someone else, which is indeed true but hidden, we are already acting against mutual benevolence. But nothing is more shameful, nothing fouler in the Society of men, than inconstancy in words and compacts. For since the chief foundation of Justice is Faith, once this virtue is removed, Justice too, and together with it sociability, must collapse. Wherefore, if the faith given to anyone must not be violated, by the same reasoning every license of deceiving another by a lie has also been taken away. This indeed we understand of every kind of lie, so that whether it is done to the detriment of another, or you lie for the advantage of yourself and of others, you will be judged a violator of both rights, namely the perfect and the imperfect. Concerning beneficence and liberality, I think that all the duties derived from this head are contained in that principle: whatever you would have done to you by others, do also to others. Thus the omission of these is to be referred not to injustice, but to inhumanity [p. 12] and baseness. In conferring benefits many cautions must be applied, and first of all we must see to it, with Tully, that the kindness not harm the very persons to whom it will seem to be done kindly, nor others; next, that the kindness not be greater than one’s means; then, that to each be given according to his worth. But I judge it necessary to say something about the duty of man toward the Commonwealth.

> 33 Prudentis itaque & honesti Civis officium erit Patriam, & Principem ipsum sincero amore complecti, ipsius imperio, legibus, ministris humiliter parére, omnium animos eximia charitate, munificentiâ, morum suavitate, justitiâ, virtutibus omnibus promereri; ingenio, solertiâ, liberalibus artibus, fide, prudentia, familiae curâ, solicita liberorum educatione, pietate, religione ceteris praefulgere; a publicis honoribus, ac dignitatibus, quibus se quenquam imparem esse noverit, abhorrere, promeritas tamen, ac ultrò oblatas sedulò, diligenter, fideliter gerere; communi denique Civium, & Principis saluti, libertati, vel incolumitati, in secundis adversisque rebus consilio, viribus, opibus diligenter consulere; atque ubi injuncti muneris debitum, vel gravis calamitas postulaverit honores, fortunas, liberos, vitamque ipsam dulci ac decora morte constanter effundere. Haec atque alia principia non laxismum sapiunt, neque ê putidis *Laxismi* fontibus hausta sunt.

33 It will therefore be the duty of a prudent and honorable Citizen to embrace his Country and the Prince himself with sincere love; humbly to obey his rule, his laws and his ministers; to win over the minds of all by eminent charity, munificence, sweetness of manners, justice, and all the virtues; to outshine others in talent, skill, the liberal arts, good faith, prudence, care of the household, solicitous education of children, piety and religion; to shrink from public honors and dignities for which he knows himself to be unequal, but to administer those he has merited, and those offered of their own accord, sedulously, diligently and faithfully; finally, to provide diligently, by counsel, strength and resources, in prosperity and adversity, for the common welfare, liberty or safety of the Citizens and of the Prince; and, where the debt of the office laid upon him or a grave calamity shall have demanded it, steadfastly to pour out honors, fortunes, children, and life itself in a sweet and becoming death. These and other such principles do not savor of laxism, nor are they drawn from the putrid springs of Laxism.

## CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

> De Virtute generatim, ejusque causis, & signis.

On Virtue in general, and its causes and signs.

> 34 „Omnis summa Philosophiae (inquit Tullius [^12-s1-2]) ad beatè vivendum refertur, idque unum expetentes homines, se ad hoc studium contulerunt„. Virtutem necessariam esse ad benè beatèque vivendum agnoscunt omnes: eaque propter, quae ad virtutem generatim pertinent, ejusque effectrices causas tractare tantò lubentiùs suscepi, quantò res est quae naturae nostrae magis interest.

34 “The whole sum of Philosophy,” says Tully (i), “is referred to living happily, and men, seeking this one thing, have devoted themselves to this study.” All acknowledge that virtue is necessary for living well and happily; and on that account I have undertaken to treat the things that pertain to virtue in general, and its efficient causes, the more gladly as the matter is one that concerns our nature the more.

> [^12-s1-2]: De Finib. 2.

[^12-s1-2]: On Ends, 2.

> 35 *Virtus* verò est, (inquit Clariss. Genovesi [^12-s2]) quidquid naturam perficit, atque ad finem suum consequendum habiliorem reddit: ut contra *vitium* est, quod impeditiorem efficit ad finem suum, aut ab eo distrahit. Quoniam autem *adfectus* naturae humanae sunt quidam vehementiores impetus, à quibus in finem impellimur, tota natura virtutis, ejusque officium in hoc praesertim posita sunt, [p. 13] ut eos témporet, modificet, ac ad summum naturae nostrae bonum regat.

35 Virtue, moreover, is (says the most distinguished Genovesi (k)) whatever perfects nature and renders it more apt for attaining its end; as, on the contrary, vice is what makes it more hindered with respect to its end, or draws it away from it. But since the affections of human nature are certain more vehement impulses by which we are driven toward our end, the whole nature of virtue and its function are placed chiefly in this, that [p. 13] that it temper them, modify them, and direct them to the highest good of our nature.

> [^12-s2]: Dissert. de Virtute, quam paucis immutatis hìc damus.

[^12-s2]: Dissert. on Virtue, which we give here with a few changes.

> 36 Fines porrò naturae nostrae, aut praesentem tantùm vitam spectant, aut futuram quoque. Quae homines perficiunt ad vitae futurae beatitudinem, atque ad eam regunt, *virtutes Theologicae* dicuntur, de quibus disserere Theologorum est: quae verò eumdem hominem ad societatem sanctè colendam servandamque instituunt, & societatis tranquillitatem securitatemque pariunt dicuntur *virtutes Civiles*: quaecumque demùm hominem perficiunt ad tranquillitatem vitae privatae aut solitariae *virtutes Monasticae*, & *Ethicae* adpellantur.

36 Now the ends of our nature regard either the present life only, or the future one as well. The virtues that perfect men for the happiness of the future life and direct them toward it are called Theological virtues, about which it is for Theologians to discourse; those, on the other hand, that train the same man for holily cultivating and preserving society, and produce the tranquillity and security of society, are called Civil virtues; and finally whatever virtues perfect man for the tranquillity of a private or solitary life are named Monastic and Ethical virtues.

> 37 Sed gravis hoc in loco vetusque nobis exoritur quaestio, acquiri ne possit virtus? Sunt enim qui existimant virtutem à natura totam esse, non ab arte quoque, disciplinâ, & exercitio. Nam natura nostra temperamentis necessariò agitur, ut ea nec extirpare possímus nec immutare. Sunt quidam, qui sanguineo temperamento praediti, in jocos, scurrilitatem, amores, aliasque corporis voluptates quasi inviti rapiuntur, quos qui fraenare velit, is totam eorum naturam immutet necesse est. Alii temperamento sunt praediti melancholico, ut idcircò perpetuò inquieti sint, minimè sibi satisfacientes, turbidi, truces, immanes. Eos qui cícures efficere velit, fibras, vasa, fluida, structuram omnem humani corporis, & naturae constitutionem pervertere debet. Sunt quidam naturâ timidi, & pusillamines, iracundi alii; quidam molles, & inertes: alii avari: alii naturâ ambitiosi: quidam súbdoli & fraudulenti. Hos ubi ad virtutem compónere velímus, á primis naturae Elementis exordiri oportet. Accedit, quod naturae humanae constitutiones diversae á climatibus, si non integrae nascuntur, at plurimum tamen pendeant. Ita isti concludere sibi videntur, virtutem, nisi á natura sit, acquiri nullo pacto posse, aut naturae esse dissimulationem.

37 But here a grave and ancient question arises for us: can virtue be acquired? For there are those who think that virtue comes wholly from nature, and not also from art, discipline and exercise. For our nature, they say, is necessarily driven by the temperaments, so that we can neither root them out nor change them. There are some who, endowed with a sanguine temperament, are carried away as if against their will into jests, buffoonery, love affairs and the other pleasures of the body; whoever would curb them must change their whole nature. Others are endowed with a melancholic temperament, so that on that account they are perpetually restless, least of all satisfied with themselves, turbid, grim, savage. He who would make them tame must overturn the fibers, the vessels, the fluids, the whole structure of the human body, and the constitution of nature. Some are by nature timid and pusillanimous, others irascible; some soft and inert; others avaricious; others by nature ambitious; some sly and fraudulent. When we wish to compose these to virtue, we must begin from the first Elements of nature. Add that the constitutions of human nature, so diverse according to climate, if they are not wholly born of it, yet depend on it very greatly. Thus these men think they conclude that virtue, unless it be from nature, can in no way be acquired, or else is a dissimulation of nature.

> 38 Falluntur tamen, eaque naturae humanae faciunt indomabilia, quorum nihil est non patiens fraeni. Principiò enim temperamenta magis vim habent ad excipiendum, quam ad moraliter agendum. Ratione, sensu, & phantasiâ naturam commovent, faciliùs quidem & promtiùs, aut tardiùs & difficilius, quàm si abessent: imperium rationis non semper elúdunt. Ac ut mollitudo aut durities in cera facilitas est, aut difficultas ad literas excipiendas, non vis scalpens; eodem modo temperamenta efficiunt, ut promtiùs & faciliùs, aut difficiliùs & tardiùs quibusdam rerum imaginibus agitemur, non autem ut perpetuò inviti impellamur. Deinde vim habeant physicè agendi: vim certè habere non possunt ad necessariò moraliter agendum: libertatem enim ad *malitiam moralem* non necessariò trahunt, etsi saepè non leviter adliciant.

38 They are mistaken, however, and they feign to be untamable those things in human nature of which none is not patient of the rein. For in the first place, the temperaments have more force for receiving than for acting morally. They move nature by reason, sense and imagination, more easily indeed and more promptly, or more slowly and with more difficulty, than if they were absent; they do not always elude the command of reason. And just as softness or hardness in wax is an ease or a difficulty in receiving letters, not the force that carves them, in the same way the temperaments bring it about that we are stirred more promptly and easily, or with more difficulty and more slowly, by certain images of things, but not that we are perpetually impelled against our will. Next, let them have the force of acting physically: they certainly cannot have the force of acting by moral necessity; for they do not necessarily drag freedom to moral malice, even though they often entice it not lightly.

> 39 Quamobrem si rationem emendare, si phantasiam purgare studeamus, si rerum bonitatem aut malitiam exactè dimetiamur, si veras rerum cum natura & finibus nostris relationes [p. 14] dispiciamus, poterimus quidem ab illis aut paulò vehementiùs commoveri erga vitia, aut retardari aliquantùm à virtute concipienda, nullo autem modò inviti ad illa adigi, aut ab his retrahi. Nec ullum majus argumentum esse potest evádere illa posse instrumenta virtutis, quàm quod experientia docet, plures sibi illa & rationi submisisse, ut sentirent quidem se aut vehementiùs agitari, aut impediri vi magna, interea vel fraenarent, vel stimulis agerent. Neminem esse ego ajo quamtumvis depravatum, qui, si ingenuus esse velit, se invítum ad vitia rapi fateatur: neminem scelestissimum, qui ad honestatem & virtutem flecti nequeat. Hinc eleganter admodùm, & praeclarè dixit Horatius [^14-s1-4], quod

39 Wherefore, if we strive to amend reason, to purge the imagination, if we measure exactly the goodness or malice of things, if we discern the true relations of things to our nature and our ends, [p. 14] we shall indeed be able to be stirred by them somewhat more vehemently toward vices, or to be held back somewhat from conceiving virtue, but in no way to be driven to the former, or drawn back from the latter, against our will. Nor can there be any greater argument that those things can become instruments of virtue than what experience teaches: that very many have so subjected them to themselves and to reason that, while they felt themselves either more vehemently agitated or hindered by a great force, they meanwhile either curbed them or drove them on with goads. I say that there is no one, however depraved, who, if he would be candid, would confess that he is carried to vices against his will; no one so very wicked that he cannot be bent to what is honorable and to virtue. Hence Horace said very elegantly and admirably (l) that

> [^14-s1-4]: Epistolar. 1. Ep. 1. Vid. etiam Cicer. Tusc. 4. cap. 37.

[^14-s1-4]: Epistles 1, Ep. 1. See also Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 4, ch. 37.

> *Invidus, iracundus, iners, vinosus, amator,*

The envious man, the wrathful, the sluggard, the drunkard, the lover,

> *Nemo adeò ferus est, qui non mitescere possit,*

No one is so savage that he cannot grow gentle,

> *Si modò culturae patientem accommodet aurem.*

If only he lend a patient ear to cultivation.

> 40 Non equidem negaverim climata aliquid in temperamenta & mores influere; sed necessariò agere, id ego esse falsum adfirmo. D. *de Montesquieu* [^14-s2-2] probare nititur diversitatem climatis plus in nos posse, quam *moralem*, imò istam nihil ferè supra nos posse, & opinionem de *metempsychosi* climati Indorum eodem modo proportionatam esse, quo est proporcionata Hispanis Religio, quam profitentur. Alibi [^14-s3-2] adfirmat: per se adparere si humano more loqui velimus, à diversitate climatis terminos praescriptos esse Religioni cùm Christianae, tùm Mahometanae. In hoc opere clima idem praestat, ac motus in hac universitate rerum, estque causa eorum, quae á nobis fiunt. Tale verò quum sit fundamentum hujus Operis, qualia esse oportet, quae ex ea deducuntur?

40 I would not indeed deny that climates have some influence on temperaments and manners; but that they act necessarily, that I affirm to be false. M. de Montesquieu (m) strives to prove that the diversity of climate has more power over us than moral diversity, nay that the latter has almost no power over us, and that the opinion of metempsychosis is proportioned to the climate of the Indians in the same way as the Religion they profess is proportioned to the Spaniards. Elsewhere (n) he affirms that it appears of itself, if we wish to speak in human fashion, that limits have been prescribed by the diversity of climate both to the Christian Religion and to the Mahometan. In this Work climate performs the same office as motion in this universe of things, and it is the cause of the things that are done by us. Since such is the foundation of this Work, what must the things be that are deduced from it?

> [^14-s2-2]: L' Esprit des Loix. Lib. 24. cap. 24.

[^14-s2-2]: L’Esprit des Loix, bk. 24, ch. 24.

> [^14-s3-2]: Cap. 25.

[^14-s3-2]: Ch. 25.

> 41 Verùm per diversitatem climatum nullam ut supra dixi, voluntati necessitatem inferri posse, experientiâ compertum est. ¿Quam enim diversa climata sunt, in quibus vel una eademque Religio servatur, vel modò una, modò altera Religio, vel subitò vera, abjectâ antiquâ & patria, aut è contrario in pretio fuit? ¿Nonne in uno eodemque climate *Londini* verbi causâ omnino inter se diversas Religiones homines constantissimè profitentur? ¿Quidquod non eosdem mores in eadem gente diversis temporibus reperimus? Nisi quis dicere velit Graecorum ac Romanorum, qui fuerunt olim, mores & studia, eadem nunc esse, iidem populi, qui olim barbarie, aut immanitate efferabantur, nunc humani sunt, ac virtuosi: contra aut immanes, qui humani fuere, aut molles, qui fortes, aut injusti, qui juris olim tenacissimi, aut impii, qui fuere pii. Atque haec dicta sufficiant.

41 But that no necessity can be brought upon the will by the diversity of climates, as I said above, has been found by experience. For how diverse are the climates in which either one and the same Religion is kept, or now one Religion, now another; or in which the true one has suddenly come into esteem, the ancient and ancestral one being cast aside, or the contrary? Do not men in one and the same climate, in London for example, most constantly profess Religions altogether different from one another? And what of the fact that we do not find the same manners in the same nation at different times? Unless someone wishes to say that the manners and pursuits of the Greeks and Romans who once were are the same now; that the same peoples who once ran wild in barbarism or savagery are now humane and virtuous; or, on the contrary, that those are savage who were humane, or soft who were brave, or unjust who once held most tenaciously to right, or impious who were pious. And let what has been said suffice.

[p. 15]

> 42 Sed quoniam virtutes non innascuntur nobiscum, ut perspicuum est, jure hoc in loco à nobis quaeretur, quae sint causae effectrices virtutum moralium? Ac videntur esse omninò quinque, Deus, ingenium seu temperamentum, educatio, exercitatio, praecepta. Ac principio verae & perfectae virtutis fons primus sola esse potest prima rerum omnium causa: à qua enim sunt essentia, & natura nostra, ab eadem & conservantur & perficiuntur, & ad fines suos potentissimè & sapientissimè ducuntur. Praeterea nemo adcuratissimè noscere potest praeter Deum, naturarum rationalium fines, media ad fines, mediorum cum fine proportionem, & vires ad id necessarias. Deus ergò tantùm verae perfectaeque virtutis dator primus esse potest.

42 But since the virtues are not born with us, as is evident, it will rightly be asked at this point: what are the efficient causes of the moral virtues? And there seem to be five in all: God, talent or temperament, education, exercise, precepts. And in the first place, the first source of true and perfect virtue can only be the first cause of all things: for from Him our essence and nature are, by the same they are both preserved and perfected, and they are led to their ends most powerfully and most wisely. Moreover, no one but God can know most accurately the ends of rational natures, the means to the ends, the proportion of the means to the end, and the powers necessary for this. God alone, therefore, can be the first giver of true and perfect virtue.

> 43 Ingenium, seu natura & temperies ad virtutem moralem duo potissimum confert. Primùm facultatem seu aptitudinem ad virtutem excipiendam, aliàs enim virtutem nunquam adsequeremur. Secundum impetum, & inclinationem erga virtutem, quae aptitudinis illius naturalis quaedam perfectio est. Tertia & quarta virtutis causae sunt educatio, & exercitatio; educatione enim, & exercitatione, ut tenellae plantae continuatâ culturâ ad fruges, ita natura nostra ad habitus virtuosos tandem inflectitur. Qui dixit hominem civilem nihil esse aliud, nisi habituum congeriem educatione, & exercitatione contractorum, dignum philosopho verbum pronunciavit. Scilicet homo *Naturae* tam differt à *Civili*, quàm animal, ut ita dicam ab homine.

43 Talent, or nature and temperament, contributes chiefly two things to moral virtue. First, the faculty or aptitude for receiving virtue, for otherwise we should never attain virtue. Second, the impulse and inclination toward virtue, which is a certain perfection of that natural aptitude. The third and fourth causes of virtue are education and exercise; for by education and exercise our nature is at length bent toward virtuous habits, as tender plants are brought to bear fruit by continued cultivation. He who said that the civil man is nothing other than a heap of habits contracted by education and exercise pronounced a word worthy of a philosopher. The man of Nature, namely, differs as much from the Civil man as an animal, so to speak, from a man.

> 44 Sed ad educationem & exercitationem conferunt plurimum praecepta doctrinae, quae quinta sunt virtutis causa. Ea enim praecepta si adtentè excipiantur, & recolantur saepissimè ita, ut in succum & sanguinem convertantur, tantam vim obtinent ad naturam reficiendam, ut altera esse videantur natura. Sed de his nunc adcuratiùs edisseramus. Praecepta ei observanda, qui se ad virtutem excitare, & exercere vult, duorum sunt generum, alia generalia, alia specialia. De his cap. superiori egimus. Generalia hìc proponemus.

44 But the precepts of doctrine, which are the fifth cause of virtue, contribute very greatly to education and exercise. For if those precepts are attentively received and very often gone over again, so that they are turned into sap and blood, they acquire such force for refashioning nature that they seem to be a second nature. But of these let us now discourse more accurately. The precepts to be observed by one who wishes to rouse and exercise himself to virtue are of two kinds, some general, others special. Of these we treated in the preceding chapter. The general ones we shall set forth here.

> 45 *Primum* praeceptum est, ut divinum auxilium, quo ad virtutem colendam vires recipiamus, adsiduis praecibus imploremus. Nam & prima causa virtutis effectrix est Deus, & *timor Dei initium Sapientiae* in divinis Scripturis adpellatur. *Secundum* praeceptum est, ut virtutis insignis pulchritudo, ac uberrimi fructus continenter ob oculos habeantur. Socrates dicere solebat, quod si honestas, & virtus vultum suum sine velo ostenderet, incredibiles in nobis amoris flammas accenderet. Inter fructus verò virtutis praecipui sunt. I. Animi tranquillitas, quae à sola virtute proficiscitur. II. Vera laus, & gloria, quae non à vitiis, sed à sola virtute expectari potest, etiam in hac morum pravitate, qua plerique omnes sumus. III. Vera utilitas, quandoquidem vitia utilitatem mentiri possunt, veram praestare nequeunt. IV. Vera nobilitas; [p. 16] nobilitas enim ex virtute primum nata est, & in virtute posita est *essentialiter*, ut qui avita nobilitate gloriantur, ipsi omni virtute vacui, nobilium magis filii, quam nobiles dicendi sunt. V. tandem virtus magnum hoc beneficium secum adfert, ut amorem etiam à barbaris extundat: hinc praeclarum illud Tullii, *virtus etiam in hoste diligitur*.

45 The first precept is that we implore with assiduous prayers the divine help by which we may receive strength for cultivating virtue. For God is also the first efficient cause of virtue, and in the divine Scriptures the fear of God is called the beginning of Wisdom. The second precept is that the signal beauty of virtue and its most abundant fruits be kept continually before our eyes. Socrates used to say that if honorableness and virtue showed their face without a veil, they would kindle incredible flames of love in us. Among the fruits of virtue, moreover, the chief are: I. Tranquillity of mind, which proceeds from virtue alone. II. True praise and glory, which can be expected not from vices but from virtue alone, even in this depravity of morals in which nearly all of us live. III. True utility, since vices can feign utility, but cannot furnish the true kind. IV. True nobility; for nobility [p. 16] was first born of virtue, and is placed essentially in virtue, so that those who glory in ancestral nobility, while themselves wholly void of virtue, are to be called sons of nobles rather than nobles. V. Finally, virtue brings with it this great benefit, that it wrings love even from barbarians; hence that admirable saying of Tully: virtue is loved even in an enemy.

> 46 *Tertium* praeceptum est, ut non mediocria tantùm, aut factu faciliora, in virtute tibi proponas sequenda, sed ad summum ejus fastigium, ac virtutem, quae dicitur heroica semper adspires; quod ni feceris, vix in extrema ejus parte haerebis. *Quartum* praeceptum est, ut vitia omnia vivis coloribus perpetuò menti depingamus, atque adsuescamus exhorrére. Dici enim vix potest, quantam vim conferat ad virtutem constabiliendam horror vitiorum. *Quintum* praeceptum est, ut perpendamus, in quod vitium simus, aut ob temperamentum, aut ob educationem, aut ob seculi mores procliviores, ut ab eo nos longius abducamus. Atque in hoc praesertim homini virtutis amanti danda est opera. Eleganter Horatius [^16-s1-2]

46 The third precept is that you set before yourself, to be pursued in virtue, not only middling things or things easier to do, but that you always aspire to its highest summit, and to the virtue that is called heroic; for unless you do this, you will scarcely cling to its lowest part. The fourth precept is that we perpetually paint all the vices to the mind in vivid colors, and accustom ourselves to shudder at them. For it can scarcely be told how much force the horror of vices contributes to establishing virtue. The fifth precept is that we weigh to which vice we are more prone, whether because of temperament, or of education, or of the manners of the age, so that we may draw ourselves farther away from it. And to this above all the man who loves virtue must give his effort. Elegantly Horace (o):

> [^16-s1-2]: Satyr. Lib. 1. Satyr. 3. à V. 34.

[^16-s1-2]: Satires, bk. 1, Sat. 3, from v. 34.

> *……………………… Denique te ipsum*

……………………… Finally, shake out

> *Concute, num qua tibi vitiorum inseverit olim*

Yourself, whether nature, or else bad habit, has at some time

> *Natura aut etiam consuetudo mala: namque*

Sown in you any vices; for in neglected fields

> *Neglectis urenda filix innascitur agris.*

Springs up the fern that must be burned.

> 47 *Sextum* praeceptum est ex superiori ductum. Nempè quoniam sunt quaedam vitia, quae aetatum sunt propria, ut in adolescentibus ac juvenibus intemperantia, & praecipitantia: in viris aetate maturis ambitio, in senibus avaritia, querimonia: haec in primis coercenda sunt, & vitanda, ne si nos semel invadant totam vitam moralem conturbent. *Septimum* praeceptum est, ut otium cane pejus & angue fugias: est enim ut vitiorum omnium sentina, ita praecipuè virtutis inimicum. Quocirca labori incumbendum est viro virtutis amanti. Quumque duplices sint labores, animi, & corporis; corporis quidem labores pro cujusque conditione suscipiendi: sed animus nunquam, aut rarò á seriis occupationibus removendus est. Homines ipsi literarum studio dediti operae pretium facient, si artem aliquam honestam illam, & ingenuis dignam discant, atque in ea subcisivis horis se exerceant. Egregios superioris aetatis philosophos cum voluptate exercuisse aut sculpturam, aut picturam, aut artem perspiciliorum, vel horologiorum ex eorum Vitis scimus. Inter animi autem labores studia sunt literarum, quibus qui seriò vacant, tempus, quod impendant in vitia, non habent. Fama est rogatum Newtonum, an amationibus unquam operam dedisset, respondisse, nullum sibi reliquum fuisse tempus à meditationibus philosophicis, quo ea de re cogitaret.

47 The sixth precept is derived from the preceding one. Namely, since there are certain vices proper to the ages of life, as intemperance and rashness in adolescents and youths, ambition in men of mature age, avarice and querulousness in the old, these must above all be restrained and avoided, lest, once they invade us, they throw our whole moral life into confusion. The seventh precept is that you flee idleness worse than a dog and a snake: for it is, as it were, the sink of all the vices, and so the especial enemy of virtue. Wherefore the man who loves virtue must apply himself to labor. And since labors are twofold, of the mind and of the body, the labors of the body are indeed to be undertaken according to each one’s condition; but the mind is never, or rarely, to be removed from serious occupations. Men devoted to the study of letters will themselves do something worth the effort if they learn some honorable art, worthy of the freeborn, and exercise themselves in it in their spare hours. We know from their Lives that excellent philosophers of the last age practiced with pleasure either sculpture, or painting, or the art of optical glasses, or of clocks. Among the labors of the mind, moreover, are the studies of letters; those who seriously give themselves to these have no time to spend on vices. It is reported that Newton, when asked whether he had ever given his attention to love affairs, answered that no time had been left him from his philosophical meditations in which to think about that matter.

[p. 17]
