For the Triangles ABC and BCD are equal, from the preceding Theor.; therefore if from them we subtract the Triangle HBE, equal to the Triangle EBI, and also the Triangle FEC, for the same reason equal to the Triangle ECG, the complements that remain, AE and ED, are equal. (b)

> [^17-s2-2]: Prop. 43.

[^17-s2-2]: Prop. 43.

> *THEOREMA VII.* (Fig. 7.)

Theorem VII. (Fig. 7.)

> *Parallelogramma, in eadem Basi constituta, & inter easdem Parallelas, sunt aequalia,* [^17-s3-2]

Parallelograms constituted on the same Base and between the same Parallels are equal. (c)

> [^17-s3-2]: Eucl. lib. I. Prop. 35.

[^17-s3-2]: Eucl. bk. I, Prop. 35.

> Dem. Quoniam A G, & G F sunt Parallelogramma, constituta in eadem Basi C G, huic opposita latera A E, & F B erunt aequalia: *ex antec. Theor.* additâ communi linea E F, erunt latera A F, & E B aequalia, & latus C F est aequale lateri G B, & angulus externus A E C aequalis interiori opposito A B C; *ex Theor. II.* ergo Triangula A F C, & E B G sunt aequalia: ergo sublato communi Triangulo E L F, remanet Trapezium A E C L, aequale trapezio L G F B: ergo addito communi Triangulo L C G; fit Parallelogrammum A G aequale Parallelogrammo G F.

Dem. Since AG and GF are Parallelograms constituted on the same Base CG, the sides opposite it, AE and FB, will be equal, from the preceding Theor.; adding the common line EF, the sides AF and EB will be equal; and the side CF is equal to the side GB, and the exterior angle AEC equal to the interior opposite angle ABC, from Theor. II; therefore the Triangles AFC and EBG are equal: therefore, taking away the common Triangle ELF, there remains the Trapezium AECL, equal to the trapezium LGFB: therefore, adding the common Triangle LCG, the Parallelogram AG becomes equal to the Parallelogram GF.

> Coroll. I. Etiam Parallelogramma A G, & E D, constituta in aequalibus Basibus, & inter easdem Parallelas, sunt aequalia inter se; nam ambo sunt aequalia eidem Parallelogrammo F G. [^17-s4]

Cor. I. Parallelograms AG and ED constituted on equal Bases and between the same Parallels are also equal to each other; for both are equal to the same Parallelogram FG. (d)

> [^17-s4]: Prop. 36.

[^17-s4]: Prop. 36.

> II. Quoniam verò distantiam inter Parallelas A B, C D metitur perpendicularis A C; *ex Theor. V. coroll. ult.* Superficies Parallelogrammorum generantur ex ductu basis in perpendicularem: *juxtà def. V.* ita, ut si latus A C sit 9. palmorum ex. gr.; & G C 4; erit superficies, facta à motu lineae C G in lineam A C, & Parallelogrammum A G, vel huic aequale G F, 36. palmorum.

II. But since the distance between the Parallels AB, CD is measured by the perpendicular AC, from Theor. V, last cor., the Surfaces of Parallelograms are generated by drawing the base into the perpendicular, according to Def. V; so that if the side AC is, e.g., 9 palms, and GC 4, the surface made by the motion of the line CG along the line AC, and the Parallelogram AG, or GF equal to it, will be 36 palms.

[p. 18]

> III. Hinc si Parallelogramma sint aequalia super eadem, vel aequali Basi, manifestum est, etiam habere eandem perpendicularem altitudinem, seu esse inter easdem Parallelas.

III. Hence if Parallelograms on the same or an equal Base are equal, it is manifest that they also have the same perpendicular altitude, or are between the same Parallels.

## *THEOREMA VIII.* (Fig. 8.) — Theorem VIII. (Fig. 8.)

> *Parallelogrammi dimidium est Triangulum constitutum in eadem Basi, & inter easdem Parallelas.* [^18-s1]

A Triangle constituted on the same Base and between the same Parallels is half of the Parallelogram. (a)

> [^18-s1]: Eucl. lib. I. prop. 41.

[^18-s1]: Eucl. bk. I, prop. 41.

> Dem. Triangulum B C G est dimidium Parallelogrammi F G: *ex Theor. VI.* sed Parallelogrammum F G est aequale Parallelogrammo A G: *ex antecedenti*; ergo Triangulum B C G etiam est dimidium Parallelogrammi A G, constituti in eadem Basi C G, & inter easdem Parallelas.

Dem. The Triangle BCG is half of the Parallelogram FG, from Theor. VI; but the Parallelogram FG is equal to the Parallelogram AG, from the preceding; therefore the Triangle BCG is also half of the Parallelogram AG, constituted on the same Base CG and between the same Parallels.

> Coroll. I. Patet, etiam Triangulum B H D, constitutum in aequali basi, & inter easdem Parallelas, esse dimidium Parallelogrammi A G, quum sit dimidium aequalis Parallelogrammi F D.

Cor. I. It is plain that the Triangle BHD also, constituted on an equal base and between the same Parallels, is half of the Parallelogram AG, since it is half of the equal Parallelogram FD.

> II. Manifestum quoque est, Triangula, quae sunt in basibus iisdem, aut aequalibus, & inter easdem Parallelas, esse inter se aequalia; quum sint dimidia aequalium Parallelogrammorum [^18-s2].

II. It is also manifest that Triangles which are on the same or equal bases and between the same Parallels are equal to each other, since they are halves of equal Parallelograms (b).

> [^18-s2]: Eucl. lib. I. prop. 37, 38.

[^18-s2]: Eucl. bk. I, prop. 37, 38.

> III. Quum autem dimidium Parallelogrammi A G fiat ex ductu dimidiae basis in Perpendicularem A C; superficies Triangulorum, quae est aequalis dimidio Parallelogrammo, *ex Theorem. VI.* etiam cognoscitur ex ductu dimidiae basis in eandem Perpendicularem altitudinem; unde si basis Trianguli B C G sit 4. palmorum; Perpendicularis altitudo B D, vel A C sit 9. palmorum, erit tota Trianguli B C G. Superficies 18. palmorum.

III. But since half of the Parallelogram AG is made by drawing half the base into the Perpendicular AC, the surface of the Triangle, which is equal to half the Parallelogram, from Theorem VI, is likewise known by drawing half the base into the same Perpendicular altitude; whence if the base of the Triangle BCG is 4 palms, and the Perpendicular altitude BD, or AC, 9 palms, the whole Surface of the Triangle BCG will be 18 palms.

> IV. Triangula igitur aequalia super eadem, aut aequali basi, habent aequalem perpendicularem altitudinem, seu sunt inter easdem Parallelas [^18-s3].

IV. Equal triangles, therefore, on the same or an equal base, have an equal perpendicular altitude, or are between the same Parallels (c).

> [^18-s3]: Prop. 39. 40.

[^18-s3]: Prop. 39, 40.

> *THEOREMA IX.* (Fig. 9.)

Theorem IX. (Fig. 9.)

> *In Triangulo rectangulo Quadratum lateris, A C, subtendentis angulum rectum, B, est aequale duobus simul Quadratis laterum, A B, B C, continentium angulum rectum* [^18-s4].

In a right-angled Triangle the Square of the side AC, subtending the right angle B, is equal to the two Squares together of the sides AB, BC, which contain the right angle (d).

> [^18-s4]: Eucl. lib. I. prop. 47. valdè celebris.

[^18-s4]: Eucl. bk. I, prop. 47, very celebrated.

> Praep. Constructis octo Triangulis aequalibus, quae designantur numeris 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8; intelligatur Quadratum H O supra lineam H I aequalem lineae A B; Quadratum D M lateris B C; & Quadratum A E lateris A C.

Prep. Eight equal Triangles having been constructed, which are marked by the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, let there be understood the Square HO upon the line HI, equal to the line AB; the Square DM of the side BC; and the Square AE of the side AC.

[p. 19]

> Dem. Duo simul Quadrata H O, & M B componuntur ex Quadrato L O, & quatuor aequalibus Triangulis 1, 8, 4, 5; Similiter Quadratum A E componitur ex eodem Quadrato L O, & quatuor Triangulis aequalibus 5, 3, 7, 8; ergo Quadratum A E est aequale duobus simul Quadratis H O, & B M, quum constent ex partibus aequalibus.

Dem. The two Squares HO and MB together are composed of the Square LO and four equal Triangles 1, 8, 4, 5. Likewise the Square AE is composed of the same Square LO and four equal Triangles 5, 3, 7, 8; therefore the Square AE is equal to the two Squares HO and BM together, since they consist of equal parts.

> Coroll. In Quadrato quum Diameter opponatur angulo recto, erit Quadratum Diametri aequale duobus quadratis laterum aequalium, ac proinde duplum unius Quadrati.

Cor. In a Square, since the Diameter is opposite a right angle, the Square of the Diameter will be equal to the two squares of the equal sides, and consequently double one Square.

> *THEOREMA X.* (Fig. 10.)

Theorem X. (Fig. 10.)

> *Si recta linea, A B, secetur utcumque in F, erit totum Quadratum lineae, A B, aequale duobus simul Quadratis partium, & duobus Rectangulis, quae fiunt ex iisdem partibus* [^19-s1-3].

If the straight line AB is cut anyhow at F, the whole Square of the line AB will be equal to the two Squares of the parts together, and the two Rectangles which are made from the same parts (a).

> [^19-s1-3]: Eucl. lib. II. prop. 4.

[^19-s1-3]: Eucl. bk. II, prop. 4.

> Praeparat. Ducatur Perpendicularis F I Parallela lineae A C; secetur A H aequalis A F, & ducatur Perpendicularis H E Parallela lineae A B: ex quo omnes lineae in quadrato A D erunt ad angulos rectos, & oppositae fient aequales. *ex Theor. VI. cor. 1. & 2.*

Prep. Let the Perpendicular FI be drawn Parallel to the line AC; let AH be cut equal to AF, and let the Perpendicular HE be drawn Parallel to the line AB: from which all the lines in the square AD will be at right angles, and the opposite ones will be equal, from Theor. VI, cor. 1 & 2.

> Dem. Quadratum A G super partem A F, Quadratum G D super G E aequalem lineae F B, duo Rectangula C G, & G B ex partibus lineae A B, sunt omnes partes totius Quadrati A D: ergo sunt illi aequalia.

Dem. The Square AG upon the part AF, the Square GD upon GE, equal to the line FB, and the two Rectangles CG and GB from the parts of the line AB, are all the parts of the whole Square AD: therefore they are equal to it.

> Coroll. I. Si recta linea A B secetur utcumque in F, iisdem constructis, Rectangulum A I, cujus unum latus est aequale toti lineae A B, alterum parti A F; necnon Rectangulum F D, cujus unum latus est aequale toti A B, alterum alteri parti F B, sunt simul aequalia toti Quadrato A D, cujus sunt partes [^19-s2-2].

Cor. I. If the straight line AB is cut anyhow at F, with the same construction, the Rectangle AI, one side of which is equal to the whole line AB, the other to the part AF, and the Rectangle FD, one side of which is equal to the whole AB, the other to the other part FB, are together equal to the whole Square AD, of which they are the parts (b).

> [^19-s2-2]: Eucl. lib. II. prop. 2.

[^19-s2-2]: Eucl. bk. II, prop. 2.

> II. Si eadem linea secetur utcumque in F, similiter Quadratum A G ex ejus parte A F, & Rectangulum F E ex duabus partibus F B, & A F, seu aequali F G, sunt aequalia toti Rectangulo E A ex tota linea A B, & ejus segmento A F, quum illa duo sint partes omnes Rectanguli A E [^19-s3-2].

II. If the same line is cut anyhow at F, the Square AG from its part AF, and the Rectangle FE from the two parts FB and AF, or the equal FG, are likewise equal to the whole Rectangle EA from the whole line AB and its segment AF, since those two are all the parts of the Rectangle AE (c).

> [^19-s3-2]: Prop. 3.

[^19-s3-2]: Prop. 3.

> *THEOREMA XI.* (Fig. 11.)

Theorem XI. (Fig. 11.)

> *In Triangulis Obtusangulis Quadratum lineae, C A, quae opponitur Angulo Obtuso, C B A, continet, praeter Quadrata duorum laterum, C B, B A, duo rectangula, quae* [p. 20] *fiunt ex latere, C B, & segmento, B D, ulteriùs producto usque ad Perpendicularem A D* [^20-s1-2]

In Obtuse-angled Triangles the Square of the line CA, which is opposite the Obtuse Angle CBA, contains, besides the Squares of the two sides CB, BA, two rectangles which [p. 20] made from the side CB and the segment BD, produced further as far as the Perpendicular AD (a).

> [^20-s1-2]: Prop. 12.

[^20-s1-2]: Prop. 12.

> Praeparatio. Producatur alterutrum latus C B usque ad perpendicularem A D; tum fiant Quadratum C L totius lineae C D; Quadratum D F segmenti B D; Quadratum D O Perpendicularis D A: & producantur C F, F I, quae constituent Quadratum G I ex lateribus aequalibus lineae C B, *ex Theor. VI. cor. 1 & 2.*

Prep. Let the side CB be produced on one side as far as the perpendicular AD; then let there be made the Square CL of the whole line CD, the Square DF of the segment BD, and the Square DO of the Perpendicular DA; and let CF, FI be produced, which will constitute the Square GI from sides equal to the line CB, from Theor. VI, cor. 1 & 2.

> Dem. Quadratum lateris C A est aequale duobus simul quadratis laterum C D, & D A, comprehendentium Angulum rectum D: *ex Theor. IX* & ex eadem ratione Quadratum lateris A B est aequale duobus simul Quadratis laterum A D, B D, cujus Quadratum E B continetur in toto Quadrato C L: sed Quadratum C L, praeter Quadratum B E, & Quadratum G I, continet duo rectangula C F, F L quae fiunt ex lineis C B, & B D; ergo Quadratum lateris C A continet, praeter quadrata laterum CB, B A, duo Rectangula, quae fiunt ex latere C B, & segmento B D, producto usque ad Perpendicularem A D.

Dem. The Square of the side CA is equal to the two squares together of the sides CD and DA, which comprehend the right Angle D, from Theor. IX; and by the same reasoning the Square of the side AB is equal to the two Squares together of the sides AD, BD, whose Square EB is contained in the whole Square CL: but the Square CL, besides the Square BE and the Square GI, contains two rectangles CF, FL, which are made from the lines CB and BD; therefore the Square of the side CA contains, besides the squares of the sides CB, BA, two Rectangles which are made from the side CB and the segment BD, produced as far as the Perpendicular AD.

> THEOREMA XII. (Fig. 12.)

Theorem XII. (Fig. 12.)

> *In quocumque Triangulo Quadratum lateris, A C, oppositi angulo Acuto, A B C, superant Quadrata laterum A B, B C, duobus Rectangulis totius lateris, C B, & ejus segmenti, D B, quod est inter angulum acutum, B, & Perpendicularem, A D* [^20-s2].

In any Triangle whatever, the Squares of the sides AB, BC exceed the Square of the side AC, opposite the Acute angle ABC, by two Rectangles of the whole side CB and its segment DB, which lies between the acute angle B and the Perpendicular AD (b).

> [^20-s2]: Eucl. lib. II. prop. 13.

[^20-s2]: Eucl. bk. II, prop. 13.

> Praepar. Ducatur ab Angulo A Perpendicularis A D, cujus fiat Quadratum D O, & segmenti D B Quadratum D N; & secta I E aequali D B, ducantur etiam ad angulos rectos F E, D L, quarum singula latera opposita erunt aequalia, *ex Theor. VI. cor. 2.*

Prep. From the Angle A let the Perpendicular AD be drawn, of which let the Square DO be made, and of the segment DB the Square DN; and, IE having been cut equal to DB, let FE, DL also be drawn at right angles, the opposite sides of which will each be equal, from Theor. VI, cor. 2.

> Dem. Quadratum lateris C B, hoc est totum Quadratum C I, continet, praeter Quadrata C G, & G I, duo rectangula H G, G B; & Quadratum lateris A B est aequale Quadrato D O perpendicularis A D, & insuper alteri quadrato D N lateris D B, propter angulum rectum D: *ex Theor. IX* Sed, ex eodem, Quadratum lateris C A est solùm aequale Quadratis G C, D O: ergo Quadratum lateris C A superant duo Quadrata laterum C B, B A duplici Rectangulo H G, & duplici Quadrato G I: quae simul sunt aequalia duobus Rectangulis E I ex toto latere C B, & ejus segmento B D, *ex Theor. X. cor. 2.*

Dem. The Square of the side CB, that is, the whole Square CI, contains, besides the Squares CG and GI, two rectangles HG, GB; and the Square of the side AB is equal to the Square DO of the perpendicular AD together with the other square DN of the side DB, on account of the right angle D, from Theor. IX. But, by the same, the Square of the side CA is equal only to the Squares GC, DO: therefore the Squares of the sides CB, BA exceed the Square of the side CA by the double Rectangle HG and the double Square GI, which together are equal to the two Rectangles EI from the whole side CB and its segment BD, from Theor. X, cor. 2.

[p. 21]

> Coroll. Hinc manifestum fit, quòd in Triangulis, si Quadrata laterum sint majora Quadrato Basis, angulus huic oppositus, erit Acutus: si sint minora, Obtusus; si sint aequalia, Rectus.

Cor. Hence it becomes manifest that in Triangles, if the Squares of the sides are greater than the Square of the Base, the angle opposite it will be Acute; if they are less, Obtuse; if they are equal, Right.

> Quatuor proximè demonstrata Theoremata optimè numeris explicantur, quos habes apud Clavium, aliosque. Ex iis verò duo ultima, quamvis valde utilia ad practicam Geometriam, non sunt tamen necessaria ad sequentes Propositiones, post quas repeti possunt, si cui difficiliora videantur. In Demonstrationibus autem, quae sequuntur, quum Liber non indicatur, intelligitur is, in quo fit sermo.

The four Theorems just demonstrated are very well explained by numbers, which you have in Clavius and others. Of these, however, the last two, although very useful for practical Geometry, are nevertheless not necessary for the following Propositions, after which they can be gone over again, if they seem rather difficult to anyone. In the Demonstrations that follow, moreover, when the Book is not indicated, the one under discussion is understood.

## LIBER II. — BOOK II

> *De Figuris curvilineis.*

On Curvilinear Figures.

> Inter figuras, quae curvâ lineâ continentur, primum habet in Geometria locum, Circulus, qui solus uno, ac certo Circini ductu perficitur. Ejus tres praecipuè mirabiles proprietates considerat Aristoteles *cap. 2. Mechanicarum quaestionum*: Prima est, quòd circulus fit ex linea mota, & quiescente: dum enim linea tota circumducitur ad circulum efficiendum, ejus extremum in puncto centri quiescit.

Among the figures that are contained by a curved line, the first place in Geometry is held by the Circle, which alone is completed by one sure sweep of the Compass. Aristotle, in ch. 2 of the Mechanical Questions, considers three especially wonderful properties of it. The first is that the circle is made from a line that is moving and at rest: for while the whole line is carried round to make the circle, its end rests in the point of the center.

> Secunda est, quòd singula lineae puncta, quamvis continua, dum linea circumagitur, inaequali velocitate moventur: majus enim spatium percurrit punctum, quod magis â centro removetur.

The second is that the single points of the line, although continuous, are moved with unequal velocity while the line is carried round: for the point that is farther removed from the center runs through a greater space.

> Tertia est, quòd Peripheria, circulum ambiens, constat quodammodo ex contrariis, & extremis sine medio: ex concavo nimirum, & convexo; inter quae Rectum ita medium est, ut AEquale inter magnum, & parvum. Nam quemadmodum linea, ut ex magna fiat parva, priùs debet fieri aequalis; ita, ut ex concava fiat convexa, priùs debet fieri recta. Idque eò mirabilius est, quòd ea contraria insunt lineae, nullam latitudinem habenti, qualis est Circuli Peripheria.

The third is that the Periphery that surrounds the circle consists in a certain manner of contraries, and of extremes without a middle: namely of the concave and the convex; between which the Straight is a middle, just as the Equal is between the great and the small. For just as a line, in order to become small from great, must first become equal, so, in order to become convex from concave, it must first become straight. And this is the more wonderful in that these contraries are found in a line having no breadth, such as the Periphery of the Circle.

> De Circulo igitur agit Euclides tertio, & quarto libro Elementorum: & nos hic tum Problemata, quae ad Circulos, & Figuras circulo inscribendas pertinent: tum Theoremata, ad eorum proprietates investigandas utiliora, praejactis principijs trademus.

Of the Circle, then, Euclid treats in the third and fourth books of the Elements; and here we, having laid down the principles, shall deliver both the Problems that pertain to Circles and to Figures to be inscribed in the circle, and the more useful Theorems for investigating their properties.

[p. 22]

## CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

> *Principia.*

Principles.

> Non alia in hoc Libro adhibentur Axiomata, & Postulata, quàm ea, quae in primo libro tradidimus. Supersunt solùm aliquae Definitiones explicandae, quarum.

No other Axioms and Postulates are employed in this Book than those which we delivered in the first book. There remain only some Definitions to be explained, of which:

> I. Circuli aequales sunt, quorum Diametri sunt aequales.

I. Circles are equal whose Diameters are equal.

> II. Recta linea circulum tangere dicitur, quae ulteriùs producta, circulum non secat.

II. A straight line is said to touch a circle which, when produced further, does not cut the circle.

> III. Angulus, qui fit ex linea tangente, & circumferentia, dicitur Angulus contingentiae.

III. The angle that is made by a tangent line and the circumference is called the Angle of contingence.

> IV. In Circulo lineae aequè distant à centro, quum Perpendiculares à centro ad eas ductae, sunt aequales.

IV. In a Circle, lines are equally distant from the center when the Perpendiculars drawn from the center to them are equal.

> V. Segmenta Circuli sunt partes Circuli, quae ab aliqua linea recta secantur.

V. Segments of a Circle are the parts of the Circle that are cut off by some straight line.

> VI. Angulus dicitur esse in Segmento circuli, â quo lineae, angulum in circumferentia constituentes, circumdantur.

VI. An angle is said to be in the Segment of the circle by which the lines constituting the angle at the circumference are surrounded.

> Ut in Figura I. Theorem. Icon. III. Angulum B A C circumdat Semicirculus; Angulum B A G pars Circuli major; Angulum B A E pars Circuli minor.

As in Figure I, Theorems, Pl. III: a Semicircle surrounds the Angle BAC; the greater part of the Circle the Angle BAG; the lesser part of the Circle the Angle BAE.

> VII. Angulus insistere dicitur Segmento, quod angulo opponitur, eumque claudit.

VII. An angle is said to stand upon the Segment that is opposite the angle and closes it.

> Ut in eadem Figura Angulum B A C claudit semicirculus; Angulum B A E pars Circuli major; Angulum B A G pars Circuli minor.

As in the same Figure, a semicircle closes the Angle BAC; the greater part of the Circle the Angle BAE; the lesser part of the Circle the Angle BAG.

> VIII. Angulus Segmenti dicitur, qui est mixtus ex linea recta, & parte Circumferentiae intra circulum. Quòd si recta linea sit Diameter, dicitur angulus semicirculi.

VIII. The angle of a Segment is that which is mixed of a straight line and a part of the Circumference within the circle. But if the straight line is a Diameter, it is called the angle of the semicircle.

> Ut in eadem Figura, est angulus, compositus ex diametro C B, & circumferentia B A.

As in the same Figure, the angle composed of the diameter CB and the circumference BA.

> IX. Sector Circuli dicitur Portio Circuli, comprehensa duabus semidiametris.

IX. A Sector of a Circle is the Portion of the Circle comprehended by two semidiameters.

> X. Figura circulo inscribi dicitur, quum omnium Angulorum vertices in circumferentia sunt. Ut ibidem Triangulum B A C.

X. A Figure is said to be inscribed in a circle when the vertices of all its Angles are in the circumference. As, in the same place, the Triangle BAC.

[p. 23]

## CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

> *Problemata.*

Problems.

> PROBLEMA I. (Icon. III. Fig. 1.)

Problem I. (Pl. III. Fig. 1.)

> *Dati arcus Centrum invenire, et Circulum perficere.*

To find the Center of a given arc, and to complete the Circle.

> Sit data circuli portio A B C, cujus Centrum oportet invenire, & Circulum perficere. Ex duobus punctis, pro libito sumptis, A, & B, aequali radio, fiant duo arcus extra, & intra circulum, se secantes in O, & E. Similiter ex punctis B, & C, ad libitum sumptis, fiant duo arcus se secantes in F, & G. Deinde per puncta sectionum ducantur lineae O E, & F G, quae arcus bifariam secabunt, & se contingent in H: ubi est Centrum circuli perficiendi. *Dem. ex Theor. III. Cor. 1. ductis lineis A B, B C.*

Let ABC be the given portion of a circle, whose Center must be found and the Circle completed. From two points taken at pleasure, A and B, with an equal radius, let two arcs be made outside and inside the circle, cutting each other at O and E. Likewise from the points B and C, taken at pleasure, let two arcs be made cutting each other at F and G. Then through the points of the sections let the lines OE and FG be drawn, which will bisect the arcs and will meet each other at H, where the Center of the circle to be completed is. Dem. from Theor. III, Cor. 1, with the lines AB, BC drawn.

> Eodem modo fit Circulus, qui transeat per tria puncta A, B, C, quae non sint in directum posita.

In the same way a Circle is made that passes through three points A, B, C which are not placed in a straight line.

> PROBLEMA II. (Fig. 2.)

Problem II. (Fig. 2.)

> *Tangentem ducere.*

To draw a Tangent.

> Primò, si Tangens ducenda sit ad datum Punctum in Circumferentia, ut A; Ducatur semidiameter A D, ad cujus extremitatem A excitetur perpendicularis hoc modo. Semidiametri A D intervallo secetur circulus ex A in B, & per B ducatur linea indefinita D F, quae ex B eodem semidiametri intervallo secetur in F. Juncta F A, erit perpendicularis Tangens circulum. *Ex Theor. I. & V.*

First, if a Tangent is to be drawn to a given Point in the Circumference, as A: let the semidiameter AD be drawn, at whose extremity A let a perpendicular be raised in this way. With the interval of the Semidiameter AD let the circle be cut from A at B, and through B let the indefinite line DF be drawn, which from B, with the same interval of the semidiameter, is to be cut at F. When FA is joined, the perpendicular will be Tangent to the circle. From Theor. I & V.

> Secundò. Si ex Puncto extra circulum F ducenda sit recta, Tangens circulum: Ducatur linea F D ad centrum Circuli, quae dividatur bifariam, ut in B: deinde ex B, intervallo dimidiae, velut F B, secetur Peripheria in A. (Facto, ad demonstrandum, semicirculo F A D.) Linea F A erit Tangens circulum. *Ex eod.*

Second, if from a Point F outside the circle a straight line Tangent to the circle is to be drawn: let the line FD be drawn to the center of the Circle, and let it be bisected, as at B; then from B, with the interval of the half, namely FB, let the Periphery be cut at A. (Having made, for the demonstration, the semicircle FAD.) The line FA will be Tangent to the circle. From the same.

> PROBLEMA III. (Fig. 3.)

Problem III. (Fig. 3.)

> *Triangulum Rectangulum, Obtusangulum, Acutangulum in Circulo constituere.*

To construct a Right-angled, Obtuse-angled, and Acute-angled Triangle in a Circle.

> Ducatur in Circulo quaecumque Diameter A B: si fiat supra Diametrum Triangulum, cujus vertex C tangat in quovis [p. 24] puncto Circumferentiam; Erit B C A Rectangulum: si vertex D cadet extra Circumferentiam, erit B D A Acutangulum: si cadit intra Circulum, veluti in E; erit B E A Triangulum Obtusangulum. *Ex Theor. I. hujus, & Coroll. Theor. IV. Lib. 1.*

Let any Diameter AB whatever be drawn in the Circle: if upon the Diameter a Triangle is made whose vertex C touches at any point [p. 24] the Circumference, BCA will be Right-angled: if the vertex D falls outside the Circumference, BDA will be Acute-angled: if it falls inside the Circle, as at E, BEA will be an Obtuse-angled Triangle. From Theor. I of this book, & Cor. of Theor. IV, Bk. I.

## PROBLEMA IV. (Fig. 4.) — Problem IV. (Fig. 4.)

> *Triangulum alteri dato AEquiangulum circulo inscribere.*

To inscribe in a circle a Triangle Equiangular to another given one.

> Sit datum Triangulum quodcumque P H O, cui AEquiangulum in circulo D B E inscribendum sit. Ducatur tangens quaecumque A C: deinde fiat Angulus A B D, aequalis angulo O; & angulus C B E aequalis angulo P: tum ducatur D E. Erit angulus D aequalis angulo P, & angulus E aequalis angulo O, *ex Theor. VI. hujus lib.* & Triangulum B D E aequiangulum Triangulo P H O.

Let there be given any Triangle PHO, to which an Equiangular one is to be inscribed in the circle DBE. Let any tangent AC be drawn: then let the Angle ABD be made equal to the angle O, and the angle CBE equal to the angle P: then let DE be drawn. The angle D will be equal to the angle P, and the angle E equal to the angle O, from Theor. VI of this book; and the Triangle BDE equiangular to the Triangle PHO.

> Quòd si data sit recta D E, supra quam describendum sit segmentum circuli, capiens angulum datum H. Fiat angulus D aequalis angulo P, & angulus E aequalis angulo O: ac producantur D B, E B, donec se intersecent: tum per tria puncta D, B, E ducatur Circulus, *juxtà Probl. I.* Erit segmentum D B E illud, quod petebatur: in quo angulus B erit aequalis angulo H. *ex Theor. III. lib. I.*

But if a straight line DE is given, upon which a segment of a circle is to be described that contains the given angle H: let the angle D be made equal to the angle P, and the angle E equal to the angle O, and let DB, EB be produced until they intersect; then through the three points D, B, E let a Circle be drawn, according to Probl. I. The segment DBE will be the one that was sought, in which the angle B will be equal to the angle H, from Theor. III, bk. I.

> PROBLEMA V. (Fig. 5.)

Problem V. (Fig. 5.)

> *Quadratum*, *Hexagonum*, *Trigonum Circulo inscribere.*

To inscribe a Square, a Hexagon, a Trigon in a Circle.

> Primò. Quadratum circulo inscribitur, si ducantur duae Diametri A B, C D ad angulos rectos; nam lineae, ductae per earum extrema puncta, constituent Quadratum A C B D. *ex Theor. I. & IV. cor. 2.*

First. A Square is inscribed in a circle if two Diameters AB, CD are drawn at right angles; for the lines drawn through their extreme points will constitute the Square ACBD, from Theor. I & IV, cor. 2.

> Octagonum verò circulo inscribitur, si quilibet arcus, subtendens latus Quadrati, bifariam secetur: lineae quippe, ductae per octo circumferentiae puncta, constituent Octagonum regulare; cujus scilicet omnia latera, & Anguli sunt aequales.

An Octagon, moreover, is inscribed in a circle if each arc subtending a side of the Square is bisected: for the lines drawn through the eight points of the circumference will constitute a regular Octagon, that is, one all of whose sides and Angles are equal.

> Secundò. Hexagonum circulo inscribitur, si semidiameter sexies in circulo ducatur; nam lineae, ductae per ea circumferentiae puncta, constituent Hexagonum A E M B N G. *ex Theor. III. cor. 2.* Dodecagonum circulo inscribitur, si arcus Hexagoni, ut A E, bifariam secentur.

Second. A Hexagon is inscribed in a circle if the semidiameter is carried round six times in the circle; for the lines drawn through those points of the circumference will constitute the Hexagon AEMBNG, from Theor. III, cor. 2. A Dodecagon is inscribed in a circle if the arcs of the Hexagon, as AE, are bisected.

> Tertiò, si per tria puncta Hexagoni, intermedio omisso, ducantur lineae, constituent Trigonum aequilaterum in circulo, ut A M N. *ex Theor. V. cor. 2.*

Third, if through three points of the Hexagon, omitting the intermediate one, lines are drawn, they will constitute an equilateral Trigon in the circle, as AMN, from Theor. V, cor. 2.

> Dimidium lateris Trigoni dat latus Heptagoni in eodem circulo, non Geometricè, & perfectè, sed proximè.

Half the side of the Trigon gives the side of the Heptagon in the same circle, not Geometrically and perfectly, but very nearly.

[p. 25]

## PROBLEMA VI. (Fig. 6.) — Problem VI. (Fig. 6.)

> *Pentagonum Circulo inscribere.*

To inscribe a Pentagon in a Circle.

> Pentagonum circulo inscribitur, ductis duabus diametris ad angulos rectos A B, C D: deinde semidiameter E B dividatur bifariam in F: intervallum F C transferatur ex F in G: eritque C G, latus Pentagoni. *ex Theor. XI. lib. III.* Latus autem Decagoni erit linea G E. *ex Theor. X. lib. III.* Quòd si arcus Decagoni bifariam dividantur, habebitur latus Icosagoni, seu Figurae regularis viginti laterum.

A      Pentagon is inscribed in a circle when two diameters AB, CD have been drawn at right angles: then let the semidiameter EB be bisected at F: let the interval FC be transferred from F to G: and CG will be the side of the Pentagon, from Theor. XI, bk. III. The side of the Decagon, moreover, will be the line GE, from Theor. X, bk. III. But if the arcs of the Decagon are bisected, one will have the side of the Icosagon, or regular Figure of twenty sides.

> Si in circulo, cui est inscriptum Pentagonum, inscribatur etiam Trigonum regulare; ita, ut vertex Trigoni congruat cuilibet vertici Pentagoni, distantia minima inter angulum Pentagoni, & Trigoni erit latus Quindecagoni.

If in a circle in which a Pentagon is inscribed a regular Trigon is also inscribed, in such a way that a vertex of the Trigon coincides with some vertex of the Pentagon, the least distance between an angle of the Pentagon and one of the Trigon will be the side of the Quindecagon.

> Figurae verò omnes Circulis circumscribuntur, si priùs inscribatur Circulo Figura quaesita: & deinde per vertices angulorum ejusdem Figurae, Circulo inscriptae, ducantur Tangentes, quae similem Figuram circa circulum constituent.

All Figures, moreover, are circumscribed about Circles if the Figure sought is first inscribed in the Circle; and then through the vertices of the angles of that same Figure, inscribed in the Circle, Tangents are drawn, which will constitute a similar Figure about the circle.

> Possunt quoque istae, aliaeque omnes Figurae Circulo inscribi, Circuli Quadrante diviso in gradus 90. Sumantur enim in Quadrante tot gradus, quot conveniunt quaesitae Figurae; si secundùm eos circulus dividatur, dabuntur arcus, quos ejus Figurae latera subtendunt, & ejusdem Anguli ad Centrum comprehendunt.

These and all other Figures can also be inscribed in a Circle when a Quadrant of the Circle has been divided into 90 degrees. For let as many degrees be taken in the Quadrant as belong to the Figure sought; if the circle is divided according to them, there will be given the arcs which the sides of that Figure subtend and which its Angles at the Center comprehend.

> Ut autem cognoscatur, quot gradus conveniant singulis Figuris dividantur 360. gradus circuli per numerum laterum Figurae construendae; & Quotiens dabit gradus quaesitos. Ex. gr. Trigono conveniunt 120 gradus circuli; quia 360, divisa per 3, dant 120.

But in order to know how many degrees belong to each Figure, let the 360 degrees of the circle be divided by the number of the sides of the Figure to be constructed; and the Quotient will give the degrees sought. E.g., 120 degrees of the circle belong to the Trigon, because 360 divided by 3 gives 120.

> Possunt etiam similes Figurae sine circulo construi supra datam lineam, inveniendo angulum, quem duo latera Figurae construendae comprehendunt: qui dici solet Angulus ad Circumferentiam.

Similar Figures can also be constructed without a circle upon a given line, by finding the angle that two sides of the Figure to be constructed comprehend; which is usually called the Angle at the Circumference.

> Is autem invenitur, subtrahendo ex 180 gradibus circuli angulum ad centrum. Ex. gr. Si quaeratur Trigoni angulus ad circumferentiam: quum ejus angulus ad centrum inventus sit graduum 120; his subtractis ex 180, remanent 60 gradus pro angulo Trigoni ad circumferentiam; quem scilicet ejus Figurae latera comprehendunt: ut videre est in adposita Tabella.

This, moreover, is found by subtracting the angle at the center from 180 degrees of the circle. E.g., if the angle of the Trigon at the circumference is sought: since its angle at the center has been found to be of 120 degrees, when these are subtracted from 180, there remain 60 degrees for the angle of the Trigon at the circumference, which, that is, the sides of that Figure comprehend: as may be seen in the adjoining Little Table.

[p. 26]

## CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

> *Theoremata.*

Theorems.

> Hic primò lineas, & angulos intra circulum; deinde lineas circulum contingentes, considerabimus: nonnullis in tertium Proportionum librum rejectis, ubi clariùs ostendentur.

Here we shall consider first the lines and angles within the circle; then the lines touching the circle; some having been put off to the third book, on Proportions, where they will be shown more clearly.

> THEOREMA I. (Ic. III. Fig. I. Theor.)

Theorem I. (Pl. III. Fig. I. Theor.)

> *Angulus in Semicirculo Rectus est.* [^26-s1]

The Angle in a Semicircle is Right. (a)

> [^26-s1]: Eucl. lib. III. prop 31.

[^26-s1]: Eucl. bk. III, prop. 31.

> Praepar. Ducatur, ad demonstrandum, semidiameter A D.

Prep. For the demonstration, let the semidiameter AD be drawn.

> Dem. Angulus C A D est aequalis angulo A C D; & angulus A B D est aequalis angulo D A B; quum sint oppositi aequalibus semidiametris: *ex Theor. V. libri primi.* Ergo totus angulus B A C est aequalis duobus simul B, & C: ergo est dimidium duorum rectorum, seu Rectus est. *ex Theor. III lib. 1. & Axiom. VI*

Dem. The angle CAD is equal to the angle ACD; and the angle ABD is equal to the angle DAB, since they are opposite equal semidiameters, from Theor. V of the first book. Therefore the whole angle BAC is equal to the two B and C together; therefore it is half of two right angles, or is Right, from Theor. III, bk. 1, & Axiom VI.

> Coroll. Ductâ lineâ A E, patet, quòd angulus B A E, habens pro basi arcum majorem semicirculo, est Obtusus: & angulus G A B, insistens arcui minori semicirculo, est Acutus.

Cor. When the line AE is drawn, it is plain that the angle BAE, having for its base an arc greater than a semicircle, is Obtuse; and the angle GAB, standing upon an arc less than a semicircle, is Acute.

[p. 27]

> THEOREMA II. (Fig. 2.)

Theorem II. (Fig. 2.)

> *Angulus in Centro, ut B D C, est Duplus anguli in Circumferentia B A C, si eidem arcui insistant.* [^27-s1]

The Angle at the Center, as BDC, is Double the angle at the Circumference BAC, if they stand upon the same arc. (a)

> [^27-s1]: Eucl. lib. III. prop. 20.

[^27-s1]: Eucl. bk. III, prop. 20.

> Praepar. Ducatur, ad demonstrandum, Diameter A E.

Prep. For the demonstration, let the Diameter AE be drawn.

> Dem. Anguli D A B, & D B A sunt aequales, utpotè oppositi aequalibus semidiametris; *ex Theor. V. lib. I.* ergo angulus exterior B D E est duplus anguli D A B. *ex Theor. III. lib. I.* Similiter anguli D A C, & D C A sunt aequales, utpotè oppositi etiam aequalibus semidiametris: ergo etiam angulus exterior C D E est duplus anguli C A D: ergo totus angulus B D C ad centrum est duplus totius anguli A ad circumferentiam.

Dem. The angles DAB and DBA are equal, as being opposite equal semidiameters, from Theor. V, bk. I; therefore the exterior angle BDE is double the angle DAB, from Theor. III, bk. I. Likewise the angles DAC and DCA are equal, as being opposite equal semidiameters too: therefore the exterior angle CDE is also double the angle CAD: therefore the whole angle BDC at the center is double the whole angle A at the circumference.

> Coroll. I. Anguli in circumferentia, ut G, A, F, si habent pro basi eandem circuli portionem, sunt aequales inter se; nam singulorum duplus est angulus ad centrum B D C, utpotè exterior. *ex Theor. III. lib. I.* [^27-s2]

Cor. I. Angles at the circumference, as G, A, F, if they have for base the same portion of the circle, are equal to each other: for the angle BDC at the center, as exterior, is double each of them, from Theor. III, bk. I. (b)

> [^27-s2]: Eclud. lib. III. prop. 21.

[^27-s2]: Eucl. bk. III, prop. 21.

> II. Angulus in circumferentia habet pro mensura dimidium arcus, cui insistit; quum sit dimidius anguli ad centrum, cujus Mensura est totus arcus, cui insistit. *Ex defin. anguli not. I. lib. I.*

II. The angle at the circumference has for its measure half the arc upon which it stands, since it is half the angle at the center, whose Measure is the whole arc upon which it stands. From the def. of angle, note 1, bk. 1.

> THEOREMA III. (Fig. 3.)

Theorem III. (Fig. 3.)

> *Si Diameter secet in Circulo aliam lineam rectam bifariam, erit ad illam Perpendicularis; & si sit Perpendicularis, illam bifariam secabit.* [^27-s3]

If a Diameter in a Circle bisects another straight line, it will be Perpendicular to it; and if it is Perpendicular, it will bisect it. (c)

> [^27-s3]: Prop. 3.

[^27-s3]: Prop. 3.

> Praepar. Ad demonstrandum, ducantur semidiametri F B, F C,

Prep. For the demonstration, let the semidiameters FB, FC be drawn.

> Dem. Triangulum F B C est Isosceles; ergo si linea F A secet bifariam lineam B C, est ad illam perpendicularis: si est perpendicularis, illam bifariam secat. *Ex Theor. V. lib. I. cor. 4.*

Dem. The Triangle FBC is Isosceles: therefore if the line FA bisects the line BC, it is perpendicular to it: if it is perpendicular, it bisects it. From Theor. V, bk. 1, cor. 4.

> Coroll. I Si perpendicularis aliquam lineam in circulo bifariam dividat, in medio perpendicularis centrum est; nam facilè demonstratur, solùm ex eo puncto lineas omnes ad circumferentiam esse aequales. [^27-s4]

Cor. I. If a perpendicular bisects some line in a circle, the center is in the middle of the perpendicular; for it is easily demonstrated that only from that point are all the lines to the circumference equal. (d)

> [^27-s4]: Eucl. lib. III. cor. prop. 1.

[^27-s4]: Eucl. bk. III, cor. prop. 1.

> II. Si B C sit latus Hexagoni, erit aequale semidiametro; nam quum arcus B C in Hexagono sit sexta pars circuli, erit angulus B F C 60. graduum: & propter Triangulum Isosceles duo anguli aequales B, & C singuli erunt etiam graduum 60, dimidium [p. 28] graduum 120, Residui ad duos rectos: ergo singula latera trianguli F B C erunt aequalia, utpote opposita aequalibus angulis. *Ex Theor. V. lib. I. cor. II.* [^28-s1]

II. If BC is the side of a Hexagon, it will be equal to the semidiameter; for since the arc BC in the Hexagon is the sixth part of the circle, the angle BFC will be of 60 degrees: and on account of the Isosceles Triangle, the two equal angles B and C will each also be of 60 degrees, half of the degrees [p. 28] 120 that remain up to two right angles: therefore the single sides of the triangle FBC will be equal, as being opposite equal angles. From Theor. V, bk. I, cor. II. (a)

> [^28-s1]: Lib. IV prop. 15.

[^28-s1]: Bk. IV, prop. 15.

> III. Si Chorda B C secetur bifariam à diametro E D, ab eadem diametro etiam arcus B C secabitur bifariam in D, nam imposito puncto C in B, totus semicirculus E C D congruet semicirculo E B D, & arcus C D arcui B D; adeoque erunt aequales.

III. If the Chord BC is bisected by the diameter ED, the arc BC will also be bisected at D by the same diameter: for when the point C is laid upon B, the whole semicircle ECD will coincide with the semicircle EBD, and the arc CD with the arc BD; and so they will be equal.

> THEOREMA IV. (Fig. 4.)

Theorem IV. (Fig. 4.)

> *In Circulo aequales lineae aequaliter à Centro distant.* [^28-s2]

In a Circle, equal lines are equally distant from the Center. (b)

> [^28-s2]: Eucl. lib. III. prop. 14.

[^28-s2]: Eucl. bk. III, prop. 14.

> Praepar. Ex centro ducantur Perpendiculares A B, & A C: tum conjungantur A D, A E.

Prep. From the center let the Perpendiculars AB and AC be drawn: then let AD, AE be joined.

> Dem. Quoniam lineae A D, A E sunt aequales, earum Quadrata erunt aequalia. Rursum Quadratum lineae D A propter angulum rectum in B, est aequale duobus simul Quadratis linearum D B, B A: *ex Theor. IX. lib. I.* & Quadratum lineae A E est aequale quadratis linearum E C, C A: sed lineae D B, & E C sunt aequales, *ex antecedenti*; adeoque etiam eorum quadrata; ergo, sublatis aequalibus, remanent etiam aequalia quadrata linearum perpendicularium A B, A C; adeoque & ipse perpendiculares aequales: ergo D F, & E G equaliter à centro distant. *Ex definit. IV. hujus libri.*

Dem. Since the lines AD, AE are equal, their Squares will be equal. Again, the Square of the line DA, on account of the right angle at B, is equal to the two Squares together of the lines DB, BA, from Theor. IX, bk. I; and the Square of the line AE is equal to the squares of the lines EC, CA: but the lines DB and EC are equal, from the preceding; and so their squares are equal too; therefore, when the equals are taken away, the squares of the perpendicular lines AB, AC also remain equal; and so the perpendiculars themselves are equal: therefore DF and EG are equally distant from the center. From Def. IV of this book.

> Coroll. I. Lineae, quae aequaliter distant â centro, sunt inter se aequales: quod patet eadem demonstratione.

Cor. I. Lines that are equally distant from the center are equal to each other: which is plain from the same demonstration.

> II. Si chordae, seu lineae D F, E G, subtendentes arcum, sint aequales, etiam arcus erunt aequales; & è converso: quia si superponantur, congruent. [^28-s3]

II. If chords, or lines DF, EG, subtending an arc, are equal, the arcs will also be equal; and conversely: because if they are laid upon each other, they coincide. (c)

> [^28-s3]: Eucl. lib. III. pr. 28. 29.

[^28-s3]: Eucl. bk. III, pr. 28, 29.

> III. Hinc linearum in circulo maxima est Diameter; & lineae, quae magis â Diametro recedunt, minores sunt, quia subtendunt arcum minorem. [^28-s4]

III. Hence the greatest of the lines in a circle is the Diameter; and lines that recede farther from the Diameter are less, because they subtend a lesser arc. (d)

> [^28-s4]: Pr. 15.

[^28-s4]: Pr. 15.

> IV. Quaecumque demonstrata sunt de eodem Circulo, vera sunt etiam de Circulis aequalibus, qui superpositi omninò congruunt.

IV. Whatever has been demonstrated of the same Circle is true also of equal Circles, which, when laid upon each other, coincide entirely.

> THEOREMA V. (Fig. 5.)

Theorem V. (Fig. 5.)

> *Si linea ponatur extremitati Diametri Perpendicularis, circulum Tanget in uno puncto.* [^28-s5]

If a line is placed Perpendicular to the extremity of a Diameter, it will Touch the circle in one point. (e)

> [^28-s5]: Pr. 16.

[^28-s5]: Pr. 16.

> Dem. Semidiameter A D, perpendicularis ad lineam B C, est [p. 29] brevissima omnium linearum ex centro ad eandem lineam; ergo linea A C, & quaecumque alia ducta ad lineam B C est major, quàm semidiameter A D: & consequenter omnis alia linea ad lineam B C cadit ultra circulum; quia major semidiametro: ergo linea B in uno puncto D circulum tangit.

Dem. The Semidiameter AD, perpendicular to the line BC, is the shortest [p. 29] of all the lines from the center to the same line; therefore the line AC, and any other drawn to the line BC, is greater than the semidiameter AD: and consequently every other line to the line BC falls beyond the circle, because it is greater than the semidiameter: therefore the line BC touches the circle in one point D.

> Coroll. I. Nulla linea recta duci potest per punctum D inter Circumferentiam, & Tangentem: nam perpendicularis ex centro A, quae duci potest ad quamcumque lineam, ductam per punctum D, *juxtà Problema V. lib. 1.* debet esse brevior semidiametro A D, non perpendiculari ad lineam D E: *ex Theor. V. lib. 1. cor. ult.* adeoque linea D E, & quaecumque alia, quae ducatur per punctum D infra tangentem, non cadit extra, sed intra Circulum.

Cor. I. No straight line can be drawn through the point D between the Circumference and the Tangent: for the perpendicular from the center A, which can be drawn to any line drawn through the point D, according to Problem V, bk. 1, must be shorter than the semidiameter AD, which is not perpendicular to the line DE, from Theor. V, bk. 1, last cor.; and so the line DE, and any other that is drawn through the point D below the tangent, does not fall outside, but inside the Circle.

> II. Hinc, ajunt, nullus angulus acutus rectilineus fieri potest minor angulo contactus, & nullus major angulo semicirculi; quia per punctum contactus D nulla recta duci potest, inter Tangentem, & Circumferentiam, constituens angulum acutum cum linea contactus, aut cum semidiametro.

II. Hence, they say, no acute rectilinear angle can be made less than the angle of contact, and none greater than the angle of the semicircle; because through the point of contact D no straight line can be drawn between the Tangent and the Circumference that would constitute an acute angle with the line of contact or with the semidiameter.

> III. Ex centro nulla linea, nisi quae ad punctum contactus ducitur, est tangenti perpendicularis; nam sola semidiameter A D est brevissima omnium, quae duci possunt ex centro A ad tangentem B C. [^29-s1-3]

III. From the center no line is perpendicular to the tangent except the one that is drawn to the point of contact; for only the semidiameter AD is the shortest of all those that can be drawn from the center A to the tangent BC. (a)

> [^29-s1-3]: Eucl. lib 3. pr. 18.

[^29-s1-3]: Eucl. bk. 3, pr. 18.

> THEOREMA VI. (Fig. 6.)

Theorem VI. (Fig. 6.)

> *Angulus, qui fit ex linea tangente circulum, & secante quaelibet, ut A B C, est aequalis angulo, B D C, in circumferentia, qui habet pro basi eandem secantem B C.* [^29-s2-3]

The Angle that is made by a line tangent to the circle and any secant, as ABC, is equal to the angle BDC at the circumference, which has for its base the same secant BC. (b)

> [^29-s2-3]: Eucl. lib. 3. pr. 32.

[^29-s2-3]: Eucl. bk. 3, pr. 32.

> Praepar. Ducatur, ad demonstrandum, Diameter B E.

Prep. For the demonstration, let the Diameter BE be drawn.

> Dem. Angulus A B E, rectus [*ex antecedenti*] est aequalis angulo B D E, utpotè in semicirculo: sed anguli C B E, & C D E sunt aequales, utpote insistentes eidem arcui C E: *ex Theor II. Cor. 1.* ergo, iis sublatis, remanent aequales anguli ABC, & BDC.

Dem. The angle ABE, a right angle [from the preceding], is equal to the angle BDE, as being in a semicircle: but the angles CBE and CDE are equal, as standing upon the same arc CE, from Theor. II, Cor. 1; therefore, when these are taken away, the remaining angles ABC and BDC are equal.

> Similiter demonstratur, angulum F B D esse aequalem angulo B C D, qui habet pro basi eandem secantem, & arcum B D. Qui anguli dicuntur ab Euclide esse in alterno circuli segmento.

Likewise it is demonstrated that the angle FBD is equal to the angle BCD, which has for its base the same secant and the arc BD. These angles are said by Euclid to be in the alternate segment of the circle.

> Coroll. In quacumque Figura quadrilatera circulo inscripta duo anguli oppositi, & si recti non sint, sunt tamen aequales duobus rectis: nam ducta ad punctum anguli B tangente, & secante B E, duo anguli A B E, & F B E *ex Theor. I. lib. 1.* sunt aequales duobus rectis; sed angulus A B E est aequalis toti angulo D ex modò demonstratis: similiter angulus F B E est aequalis toti angulo C: ergo duo anguli C, & D sunt aequales duobus rectis [^29-s3]

Cor. In any quadrilateral Figure inscribed in a circle, the two opposite angles, even if they are not right, are nevertheless equal to two right angles: for when the tangent is drawn to the point of the angle B, and the secant BE, the two angles ABE and FBE, from Theor. I, bk. 1, are equal to two right angles; but the angle ABE is equal to the whole angle D, from what has just been demonstrated: likewise the angle FBE is equal to the whole angle C: therefore the two angles C and D are equal to two right angles (c)

> [^29-s3]: Eucl. lib. 3. pr. 22.

[^29-s3]: Eucl. bk. 3, pr. 22.

[p. 30]

## LIBER III. — BOOK III

> *De Figuris proportionalibus.*

On Proportional Figures.

## CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

> *Principia.*

Principles.

> Nomine Principiorum complectimur Definitiones, quae ad librum 5, & 6 Euclides spectant: Axiomata quaedam, & Proportionum Argumentationes, quae potiùs explicationem indigent, quàm demonstratione.

Under the Name of Principles we comprehend the Definitions which belong to Euclid’s books 5 and 6; certain Axioms; and the Arguments about Proportions, which need explanation rather than demonstration.

> §. I.

§. I.

> *Definitiones.*

Definitions.

> I. Pars est magnitudo minor, quae metitur majorem.

A    I. part is a lesser magnitude that measures a greater.

> Dividitur Pars in Aliquotam, & Aliquantam. Pars aliquota dicitur, quae aliquoties repetita adaequat suum totum: ut 4 adaequatè continetur in 8, 12, 16, &c. Pars aliquanta dicitur, quae aliquoties repetita non adaequat suum totum, sed vel ipsum excedit, vel ab eodem deficit: ut 4 in 6, 7, 9, &c. Definitur hic solùm pars aliquota, quae metitur, & adaequat totum; tum quia ejus praecipuus usus est in proportionibus demonstrandis: tum quia pars aliquanta propriè non dicitur pars, sed partes totius; nam numerus 4: ex. gr. dicitur duae tertiae numeri 6.

Part is divided into Aliquot and Aliquant. An aliquot part is so called which, repeated a number of times, exactly equals its whole: as 4 is exactly contained in 8, 12, 16, etc. An aliquant part is so called which, repeated a number of times, does not exactly equal its whole, but either exceeds it or falls short of it: as 4 in 6, 7, 9, etc. Only the aliquot part, which measures and exactly equals the whole, is defined here; both because its chief use is in demonstrating proportions, and because an aliquant part is not properly called a part, but parts of the whole; for the number 4, e.g., is called two thirds of the number 6.

> II. Multiplex magnitudo est, quam metitur minor.

II. A multiple magnitude is one that a lesser measures.

> Scilicet Magnitudo multiplex dicitur comparata cum sua parte aliquota, quam pluries adaequatè continet; ut 6 continet 2.

That is, a magnitude is called multiple when compared with its aliquot part, which it contains exactly several times; as 6 contains 2.

> III Ratio, seu (ut aliis placet) Proportio est Modus, quo una quantitas aliam ejusdem generis continet, vel ab ea continetur.

III. Ratio, or (as others prefer) Proportion, is the Mode in which one quantity contains another of the same kind, or is contained by it.

> Ejusdem autem generis dicuntur ea, quae multiplicata se possunt mutuò superare: hinc inter Deum, & Creaturam, Finitum, & Infinitum nulla proportio; quia non se possunt mutuò superare: similiter inter angulum contingentiae, & rectilineum; quia angulus contingentiae quantumvis auctus, non superat angulum rectilineum.

Those things, moreover, are said to be of the same kind which, when multiplied, can exceed each other: hence between God and the Creature, the Finite and the Infinite, there is no proportion, because they cannot exceed each other: likewise between the angle of contingence and a rectilinear one; because the angle of contingence, however much increased, does not exceed a rectilinear angle.

[p. 31]

> Dividitur 1. proportio in rationalem, & irrationalem. Rationalis dicitur, quae numeris exprimi potest: ut proportio dupla, tripla, &c. Irrationalis dicitur illa, quae numeris exprimi nequit: qualis est proportio diametri ad costam quadrati; nullo enim numero exprimi potest, quot partibus Diameter superat costam quadrati. (quod qui nesciat, ait Plato, non inter homines, sed inter bruta est connumerandus) Et quantitates quidem, quae proportionem habent inter se rationalem, dicuntur Commensurabiles: quae verò irrationalem, dicuntur Incommensurabiles.

Proportion is divided, 1, into rational and irrational. That is called rational which can be expressed by numbers: as double, triple proportion, etc. That is called irrational which cannot be expressed by numbers: such is the proportion of the diameter to the side of the square; for by no number can it be expressed by how many parts the Diameter exceeds the side of the square (whoever does not know this, says Plato, is to be counted not among men but among the brutes). And quantities that have a rational proportion to each other are called Commensurable; those that have an irrational one are called Incommensurable.

> Dividitur 2. Proportio in Proportionem AEqualitatis, quae intercedit inter aequalia; & inaequalitatis, quae intercedit inter inaequalia: ex iis verò quum major continet adaequatè minorem, dicitur proportio multiplex; ut in definitione 2. Quum continet minorem, & insuper aliquam ejus partem aliquotam, dicitur proportio supernaturalis, ut 6 ad 4. Quum est major aliqua parte aliquanta, dicitur proportio superpartiens: ut 8 ad 5. Si verò minor ad majorem referatur, praeponitur particula sub: ut 2 ad 4 est proportio subdupla.

Proportion is divided, 2, into the Proportion of Equality, which obtains between equal things, and of inequality, which obtains between unequal things: of these, when the greater contains the lesser exactly, it is called multiple proportion, as in definition 2. When it contains the lesser and, besides, some aliquot part of it, it is called superparticular proportion, as 6 to 4. When it is greater by some aliquant part, it is called superpartient proportion: as 8 to 5. But if the lesser is referred to the greater, the particle sub is prefixed: as 2 to 4 is subduple proportion.

> IV. Proportionalitas, quae & Proportio, & Analogia dici solet est Rationum, seu Proportionum Comparatio, & Similitudo.

IV. Proportionality, which is also usually called Proportion and Analogy, is the Comparison and Similitude of Ratios, or Proportions.

> Dividitur primò in Arithmeticam, & Geometriam. Arithmetica proportio est AEqualitas excessum inter plures quantitates: ut 1, 2, 3, 4; qui numeri omnes se excedunt unitate: vel 1, 3, 5, &c. aequaliter se excedunt binario.

It is divided first into Arithmetical and Geometrical. Arithmetical proportion is the Equality of the excesses among several quantities: as 1, 2, 3, 4, which numbers all exceed one another by unity; or 1, 3, 5, etc., which exceed one another equally by two.

> Geometrica proportio est similitudo excessuum inter plures terminos, qui eodem modo se continent: ut 1, 2, 4, 8, &c. qui similiter se excedunt in dupla ratione: vel 1, 3, 9, 27, &c. qui sunt in ratione tripla.

Geometrical proportion is the similitude of the excesses among several terms that contain one another in the same way: as 1, 2, 4, 8, etc., which likewise exceed one another in double ratio; or 1, 3, 9, 27, etc., which are in triple ratio.

> Est praeterea Proportio Harmonica, quae ad rem praesentem non pertinet.

There is, besides, Harmonic Proportion, which does not pertain to the present matter.

> Dividitur secundò proportio, seu proportionalitas in discretam, & continuam. Discreta est, quum inter terminos aliqua fit interruptio: ut si dicas; 8 ad 4 se habent, ut 6 ad 3; fit in mediis interruptio; quia 4 ad 6 non ita se habent, ut 8 ad 4.

Proportion, or proportionality, is divided secondly into discrete and continuous. It is discrete when there is some interruption between the terms: as if you say, 8 is to 4 as 6 to 3; there is an interruption in the middle terms, because 4 is not to 6 as 8 to 4.

> Proportio continua dicitur, quum nulla fit interruptio: ut si dicas; 1 ad 2, ut 2 ad 4, ut 4 ad 8, ut 8 ad 16, &c. in his enim terminis eodem modo priores ad posteriores referuntur, nulla facta interruptione. Quae proportio continua solet etiam dici progressio: & si fiat à minori ad majus, dicitur progressio crescens; si verò à majori ad minus, progressio decrescens.

Proportion is called continuous when there is no interruption: as if you say, 1 to 2, as 2 to 4, as 4 to 8, as 8 to 16, etc.; for in these terms the earlier are referred to the later in the same way, with no interruption made. This continuous proportion is also usually called a progression: and if it goes from the lesser to the greater, it is called an increasing progression; but if from the greater to the less, a decreasing progression.

> V. In eadem Proportione quatuor termini dicuntur, quando, quoties primus continet secundum, vel continetur à secundo, toties tertius continet quartum, vel continetur à quarto: & hujusmodi termini vocantur Proportionales.

V. Four terms are said to be in the same Proportion when the first contains the second, or is contained by the second, as many times as the third contains the fourth, or is contained by the fourth; and terms of this kind are called Proportionals.

> Ex iis verò primus, qui ad alium refertur, dicitur antecedens: posterior, ad quem primus refertur, dicitur consequens: & duo [p. 32] antecedentes dicuntur inter se homologi: sicut duo consequentes inter se: ex. gr. si dicatur: ut 4 ad 2, ita 6 ad 3: 4, & 6 dicuntur antecedentes, & homologi inter se: 2, & 3 etiam inter se homologi dicuntur consequentes.

Of these, moreover, the first, which is referred to another, is called the antecedent; the later, to which the first is referred, is called the consequent: and the two antecedents [p. 32] are called homologous to each other, just as the two consequents are to each other: e.g., if it is said, as 4 to 2, so 6 to 3: 4 and 6 are called antecedents and homologous to each other; 2 and 3 are also called consequents homologous to each other.

> VI. Proportio autem, seu Proportionalitas in tribus saltem terminis consistit:

VI. Proportion, moreover, or Proportionality, consists in at least three terms;

> Quia proportionalitas est comparatio duarum relationum, quarum singulae requirunt duos terminos. Si enim Proportio sit continua, sufficiunt tres termini; quia secundus bis repetitur: v. g. sicuti se habent 8 ad 4, ita 4 ad 2. At si Proportio sit discreta, requiruntur quatuor termini: v. g. sicuti se habent 8 ad 4, ita 6 ad 3.

Because proportionality is the comparison of two relations, each of which requires two terms. For if the Proportion is continuous, three terms suffice, because the second is repeated: e.g., as 8 is to 4, so 4 to 2. But if the Proportion is discrete, four terms are required: e.g., as 8 is to 4, so 6 to 3.

> VII. Proportio composita est, quae producitur ex multiplicatione proportionum.

VII. Compound Proportion is that which is produced by the multiplication of proportions.

> Ut Proportio duodecupla est, quae producitur ex proportione sextupla, & dupla, quia bis sex efficiunt 12.

As duodecuple Proportion is that which is produced from sextuple and duple proportion, because twice six make 12.

> Hinc Proportio extremorum dicitur composita ex proportione Mediorum: ut si sint 20, 10, 2, Proportio 20 ad 2 est decupla, composita ex proportione dupla 20 ad 10, & quintupla 10 ad 2.

Hence the Proportion of the extremes is said to be compounded of the proportion of the Means: as if there are 20, 10, 2, the Proportion of 20 to 2 is decuple, compounded of the duple proportion of 20 to 10 and the quintuple of 10 to 2.

> VIII. Quum verò Magnitudines sunt continuè proportionales, ut 27, 9, 3, 1, Prima dicitur habere ad tertiam rationem duplicatam ejus, quam habet ad secundam & triplicatam ad quartam, atque ita deinceps.

VIII. But when Magnitudes are continuously proportional, as 27, 9, 3, 1, the First is said to have to the third the duplicate ratio of that which it has to the second, and the triplicate to the fourth, and so on.

> Ratio dupla, & duplicata valde diversae sunt; nam Proportio dupla, vel tripla est, quum una quantitas bis, vel ter aliam continet. At Proportio duplicata, vel triplicata est, quum inter plures magnitudines intercedunt duae, vel tres continuae proportiones. Ita quia inter 27, 9, 3 intercedunt duae proportiones triplae; ideò dicitur 27 habere ad 3 duplicatam proportionem ejus, quam habet ad 9. Et quia inter 27, 9, 3, 1, intercedunt tres similes proportiones; ideò 27 ad 1 dicitur habere proportionem triplicatam ejus, quam habet ad 9.

Double and duplicate ratio are very different; for Proportion is double or triple when one quantity contains another twice or three times. But Proportion is duplicate or triplicate when between several magnitudes there intervene two or three continued proportions. Thus, because between 27, 9, 3 there intervene two triple proportions, 27 is therefore said to have to 3 the duplicate proportion of that which it has to 9. And because between 27, 9, 3, 1 there intervene three similar proportions, 27 is therefore said to have to 1 the triplicate proportion of that which it has to 9.

> IX. Similes Figurae sunt, quae angulos singulos singulis habent aequales, & latera circa aequales angulos proportionalia.

IX. Similar Figures are those that have their angles equal, each to each, and the sides about the equal angles proportional.

> In iis verò latera opposita aequalibus angulis dicuntur homologa: [*ut in Figura 6. Theor. Icon. V.*] latus G E homologum lateri N L; & latus E D homologum lateri L H.

In these, moreover, the sides opposite equal angles are called homologous: [as in Figure 6, Theor., Pl. V] the side GE homologous to the side NL, and the side ED homologous to the side LH.

> X. Reciprocae Figurae sunt, quae habent latera mutuò antecedentia, & consequentia.

X. Reciprocal Figures are those that have their sides mutually antecedent and consequent.

> Scilicet mutuò dupla, & dimidia; tripla, & subtripla, &c. *ut in Figura 1. Theorem. Icon. V.* sunt Rectangula X, & Y: nam Rectangulum Y habet latus G A duplum lateris A D rectanguli X, & reciprocè alterum latus A F dimidium lateris A B ejusdem rectanguli X.

That is, mutually double and half; triple and subtriple, etc., as in Figure 1, Theorems, Pl. V, are the Rectangles X and Y: for the Rectangle Y has the side GA double the side AD of the rectangle X, and reciprocally the other side AF half the side AB of the same rectangle X.

[p. 33]

> §. II.

§. II.

> *Axiomata.*

Axioms.

> Axiomatum loco pono plerasque Propositiones lib. 5. Euclidis, de quibus videtur loquutus Geminus illustris Mathematicus apud Proclum lib. 3. cap. 1. ubi ait: Alii indemonstrabilium quoque demonstrationes excogitarunt: ab ignotioribus Mediis ea, quae sunt omnibus nota, probare conati sunt.

In place of Axioms I put most of the Propositions of Euclid’s bk. 5, of which Geminus, the illustrious Mathematician, seems to have spoken in Proclus, bk. 3, ch. 1, where he says: Others have devised demonstrations even of indemonstrable things: they have tried to prove things that are known to all by less known Means.

> I. Si duae quantitates sint inter se aequales, eandem proportionem habebunt ad unum tertium, aut ad aequalia: *ut 8, & 8 eodem modo bis continent.* 4. [^33-s1-2]

I. If two quantities are equal to each other, they will have the same proportion to one third thing, or to equal things: as 8 and 8 contain 4 twice in the same way. (a)

> [^33-s1-2]: Eucl. lib. V. prop. 7.

[^33-s1-2]: Eucl. bk. V, prop. 7.

> II. Si duo eandem proportionem habeant ad idem tertium, aut ad aequalia, erunt inter se aequalia. Ut si numerus 4 bis contineatur à duobus numeris, erunt hi inter se aequales, nimirum 8, & 8. [^33-s2-2]

II. If two things have the same proportion to the same third thing, or to equal things, they will be equal to each other. As, if the number 4 is contained twice by two numbers, these will be equal to each other, namely 8 and 8. (b)

> [^33-s2-2]: Prop. 9.

[^33-s2-2]: Prop. 9.

> III. Ex quantitatibus inaequalibus, quae major est, majorem proportionem habet ad minorem, seu pluries continet minorem.

III. Of unequal quantities, the one that is greater has a greater proportion to the lesser, or contains the lesser more times.

> Ut numerus 8 pluries, quàm numerus 6, continet numerum 4. Et quae pluries continet eandem quantitatem, major est: & minor est, quae pluries continetur. [^33-s3-2]

As the number 8 contains the number 4 more times than the number 6 does. And that which contains the same quantity more times is greater: and that which is contained more times is less. (c)

> [^33-s3-2]: Eucl. lib. V. prop. 8. & 10.

[^33-s3-2]: Eucl. bk. V, prop. 8 & 10.

> IV. Proportiones, quae eidem sunt aequales, eaedem, similes, (idem diversa nomina significant) sunt aequales, eaedem, similes inter se. [^33-s4-2]

IV. Proportions that are equal, the same, similar to the same one (they signify the same thing by different names) are equal, the same, similar to each other. (d)

> [^33-s4-2]: 11.

[^33-s4-2]: 11.

> V. Si singulae magnitudines ad singulas habeant eandem proportionem, etiam omnes simul ad omnes habebunt eandem proportionem.

V. If single magnitudes have the same proportion to single magnitudes, all together will also have the same proportion to all together.

> Scilicet bis duplum, erit etiam duplum ad bis dimidium: ter duplum ad ter dimidium, &c.

That is, twice the double will also be double to twice the half; three times the double to three times the half, etc.

> Hinc omnes antecedentes simul ad omnes consequentes, ut singuli antecedentes ad singulos consequentes: ut si 4 ad 2 habeat eandem proportionem, quam 6 ad 3, scilicet duplam: etiam 4, & 6 simul habebunt duplam proportionem ad 2, & 3 simul. [^33-s5]

Hence all the antecedents together are to all the consequents as the single antecedents to the single consequents: as, if 4 has to 2 the same proportion as 6 to 3, namely double: 4 and 6 together will also have a double proportion to 2 and 3 together. (e)

> [^33-s5]: 12.

[^33-s5]: 12.

> VI. Partes similes, quae scilicet aequaliter continentur, sunt inter se, ut tota continentia. Hoc est, ut 2 ad 3, ita bis 2 ad bis 3; ter 2 ad ter 3.

VI. Similar parts, that is, those that are contained equally, are to each other as the wholes containing them. That is, as 2 to 3, so twice 2 to twice 3; three times 2 to three times 3.

> Hinc si similibus totis similes partes addantur, vel auferantur, quae supersunt, similia sunt. [^33-s6]

Hence if similar parts are added to or taken from similar wholes, what remains is similar. (f)

> [^33-s6]: 15.

[^33-s6]: 15.

> VII. Si ut totum ad totum, ita ablatum ad ablatum, etiam totum ad totum erit ut reliquum ad reliquum. [^33-s7]

VII. If, as the whole to the whole, so the part taken away to the part taken away, the whole will also be to the whole as the remainder to the remainder. (g)

> [^33-s7]: Eucl. lib. V. Prop. 19.

[^33-s7]: Eucl. bk. V, Prop. 19.

[p. 34]

> Ut si ex ter 4, & ter 2 in proportione dupla auferas semel 4, & 2 in proportione dupla; remanent bis 4, & bis 2, hoc est 8, & 4, etiam in proportione dupla.

As, if from three times 4 and three times 2, in double proportion, you take away once 4 and 2, in double proportion, there remain twice 4 and twice 2, that is, 8 and 4, also in double proportion.

> VIII. Si aequalibus proportionibus aequales addantur, totae erunt aequales.

VIII. If equals are added to equal proportions, the wholes will be equal.

> Ut si duobus numeris 4, & 4 in proportione dupla ad 2, addantur singulis 6; qui numerus est in proportione tripla ad idem 2; erunt 10, & 10 in aequali proportione quintupla ad 2.

As, if to the two numbers 4 and 4, in double proportion to 2, there is added to each 6, which number is in triple proportion to the same 2, there will be 10 and 10 in equal, quintuple proportion to 2.

> Hinc quum multiplicatio sit multiplex additio, si aequales proportiones per aequales multiplicentur, totae erunt aequales: ut si duae proportiones duplae, singulae multiplicentur per triplam proportionem, ambae erunt sextuplae.

Hence, since multiplication is multiple addition, if equal proportions are multiplied by equals, the wholes will be equal: as, if two double proportions are each multiplied by a triple proportion, both will be sextuple.

## §. III. — §. III

> *Proportionum Argumentationes.*

Arguments about Proportions.

> Mathematici, nec non Philosophi omnes ad proportiones inferendas, sex modis arguendi utuntur, quorum veritas, vel ex se, vel ex positis Principijs facilè patet.

Mathematicians, and also all Philosophers, use six modes of arguing for inferring proportions, the truth of which is readily plain either of itself or from the Principles laid down.

> I. Ratio inversa, seu conversa est Mutatio antecedentis in consequens, & consequentis in antecedens: ex. gr. ut antecedens 9 ad consequens 3, ita antecedens 6 ad consequens 2: ergo convertendo, ut 3 ad 9, ita 2 ad 6.

I. Inverse, or converse, Ratio is the Change of the antecedent into the consequent, and of the consequent into the antecedent: e.g., as the antecedent 9 to the consequent 3, so the antecedent 6 to the consequent 2; therefore, by converting, as 3 to 9, so 2 to 6.

> Patet ex se: quia si antecedentes aequaliter praecontinent consequentes, etiam consequentes aequaliter praecontinentur ab antecedentibus.

It is plain of itself: because if the antecedents contain the consequents equally, the consequents are also equally contained by the antecedents.

> II. Ratio alterna, seu permutata est comparatio antecedentis cum antecedente, & consequentis cum consequenti: ex. gr. ut 9 ad 3, ita 6 ad 2: ergo alternando, seu permutando, seu vicissim, ut 9. ad 6, ita 3 ad 2. [^34-s1-3]

II. Alternate, or permuted, Ratio is the comparison of antecedent with antecedent and of consequent with consequent: e.g., as 9 to 3, so 6 to 2: therefore, by alternating, or by permuting, or conversely, as 9 to 6, so 3 to 2. (a)

> [^34-s1-3]: Eucl. lib. V. prop. 16.

[^34-s1-3]: Eucl. bk. V, prop. 16.

> Patet ex Axiom. VI.: quia partes similes sunt inter se, ut tota; & tota, ut partes similes.

It is plain from Axiom VI: because similar parts are to each other as the wholes, and the wholes as the similar parts.

> In proportione tamen alterna debent esse quatuor termini ejusdem generis; nam si duo primi fuerint diversi generis à duobus secundis, non valet alternando; quia inter res diversi generis, nulla est proportio. *Ex definitione III.*

In alternate proportion, however, the four terms must be of the same kind; for if the first two are of a different kind from the second two, the argument by alternation is not valid: because between things of a different kind there is no proportion. From definition III.

> III. Ratio composita, seu conjuncta est Comparatio antecedentis, & consequentis instar unius ad consequentem: v. g. ut 9 ad 3, ita 6 ad 2: ergo componendo, ut 9, & 3 (scilicet 12) ad 3; ita 6, & 2 (scilicet 8) ad 2. [^34-s2-2]

III. Compound, or conjoined, Ratio is the Comparison of the antecedent and the consequent, as of one thing, to the consequent: e.g., as 9 to 3, so 6 to 2: therefore, by composition, as 9 and 3 (that is, 12) to 3, so 6 and 2 (that is, 8) to 2. (b)

> [^34-s2-2]: Eucl. lib. V. prop. 18.

[^34-s2-2]: Eucl. bk. V, prop. 18.

> Patet ex VI. Axiomate: quia ex similibus partibus additis, [p. 35] similia etiam fiunt tota; Termini autem proportionales sunt, quorum excessus sunt similes partes.

It is plain from Axiom VI: because when similar parts are added, similar [p. 35] wholes also result. And proportional terms are those whose excesses are similar parts.

> IV. Divisio rationis est Comparatio excessus antecedentis supra consequentem ad ipsum consequentem: v. g. ut 9 ad 3, ita 6 ad 2; ergo dividendo, ut 6 (quo numero 9 excedunt 3) ad 3; ita 4 (quo numero 6 excedunt 2) ad 2. [^35-s1-2]

IV. Division of ratio is the comparison of the excess of the antecedent over the consequent to the consequent itself: e.g., as 9 to 3, so 6 to 2; therefore, by division, as 6 (the number by which 9 exceeds 3) to 3, so 4 (the number by which 6 exceeds 2) to 2. (a)

> [^35-s1-2]: Prop. 17.

[^35-s1-2]: Prop. 17.

> Patet ex VI. Axiomate: quia similibus partibus ablatis, quae remanent, sunt similia.

This is plain from Axiom VI: because when similar parts are taken away, what remains is similar.

> V. Ratio eversa, seu Conversio rationis est Comparatio antecedentis ad differentiam terminorum, velut ad consequentem: v. g. ut 9 ad 3: ita 6 ad 2: ergo evertendo, ut 9 ad 6; (quae est differentia inter 9, & 3) ita 6 ad 4: quae est differentia inter 6, & 2. [^35-s2]

V. Ratio reversed, or conversion of ratio, is the comparison of the antecedent to the difference of the terms, as to a consequent: e.g., as 9 to 3, so 6 to 2; therefore, by conversion, as 9 to 6 (which is the difference between 9 and 3), so 6 to 4, which is the difference between 6 and 2. (b)

> [^35-s2]: Coroll. prop. 19.

[^35-s2]: Cor. prop. 19.

> Patet ex eodem Axiomate.

This is plain from the same Axiom.

> VI. AEqua ratio est Ilatio ad proportiones aequales extremorum ex aequalibus proportionibus intermediis: ut si ponantur.

VI. Equal ratio is the inference to equal proportions of the extremes from equal intermediate proportions: as if there are set down

> Ex una parte 27, 9, 3:

On the one side 27, 9, 3;

> Ex altera 18, 6, 2:

On the other 18, 6, 2.

> Ita arguitur: ut 27 ad 9 ex una parte; ita 18 ad 6 ex alterà: & ut 9 ad 3 ex una parte; ita 6 ad 2 ex altera: ergo ex aequo, ut 27 ad 3: ita 18 ad 2. [^35-s3]

The argument runs thus: as 27 to 9 on the one side, so 18 to 6 on the other; and as 9 to 3 on the one side, so 6 to 2 on the other: therefore, from equality, as 27 to 3, so 18 to 2. (c)

> [^35-s3]: Eucl. lib. V. prop. 22.

[^35-s3]: Eucl. bk. V, prop. 22.

> Et haec quidem Ratio ordinata dicitur; quia proportio primi cum secundo, & secundi cum tertio ex utraque parte ordinatim comparantur. Quòd si hic ordo non servetur, dicitur Ratio perturbata: ut si ponantur. [^35-s4]

And this indeed is called an ordered ratio, because the proportion of the first with the second, and of the second with the third, is compared in order on each side. But if this order is not kept, it is called a disturbed ratio: as if there are set down (d)

> [^35-s4]: Prop. 23.

[^35-s4]: Prop. 23.

> Ex una parte 12, 6, 2:

On the one side 12, 6, 2;

> Ex altera 24, 8, 4;

On the other 24, 8, 4.

> Ita arguitur: ut 12 ad 6 ex una parte; ita 8 ad 4, ex altera: & ut 6 ad 2 ex una parte; ita 24 ad 8 ex altera: ergo ex aequo perturbatim, ut 12 ad 2; ita 24 ad 4. Dicitur ratio perturbata, quia ex una parte comparatur proportio primi cum secundo: ex altera secundi cum tertio.

The argument runs thus: as 12 to 6 on the one side, so 8 to 4 on the other; and as 6 to 2 on the one side, so 24 to 8 on the other: therefore, from equality in disturbed order, as 12 to 2, so 24 to 4. It is called a disturbed ratio because on the one side the proportion of the first with the second is compared, on the other that of the second with the third.

> Patet utraque Argumentatio ex ipsa definitione, & Axiomate 8; quia utrobique Proportio extremorum fit ex aequalibus intermediis proportionibus, sive istae ordine sumantur, sive perturbatim.

Each argument is plain from the definition itself and from Axiom 8, because in both cases the proportion of the extremes arises from equal intermediate proportions, whether these are taken in order or in disturbed order.

> „ Quoniam verò quae de Proportionibus ab Auctore Cl. dicta sunt difficultatem adferre solent Adolescentibus, iccirco opportunum duxi haec iterum clarius fortasse proponere & explicare.

“Since, however, what has been said about proportions by the celebrated Author is apt to cause difficulty to young men, I have therefore thought it opportune to set these things forth and explain them again, perhaps more clearly.

> Si una quantitas ad aliam referatur ex. gr. numerus ad numerum, & adtendatur modus quo prior continet alterum, vel in altero continetur, relatio illa unius ad alium dicitur *Ratio Geometrica*, numerus qui refertur dicitur *antecedens*, numerus ad quem refertur *consequens* rationis adpellatur. At vero si dividatur [p. 36] antecedens per consequentem, *quotus* dicitur exponens rationis. Est autem Quotus sive Quotiens numerus qui denotat quoties aliquis numerus in alio contineatur. Sic in ratione 8 ad 2, numerus 8 est antecedens, 2 consequens, quotus 4 est exponens rationis: 4 autem est quotiens quia 2 quater continetur in 8.
