If one quantity is referred to another, e.g., a number to a number, and attention is paid to the manner in which the former contains the other, or is contained in the other, that relation of the one to the other is called a Geometric Ratio; the number which is referred is called the antecedent, and the number to which it is referred is called the consequent of the ratio. But if the antecedent is divided [p. 36] by the consequent, the quotient is called the exponent of the ratio. Now the Quotient, or Quotient number, is that which denotes how many times some number is contained in another. Thus in the ratio 8 to 2 the number 8 is the antecedent, 2 the consequent, and the quotient 4 is the exponent of the ratio; and 4 is the quotient because 2 is contained four times in 8.

> Si antecedens aequet consequentem ratio est aequalitatis ut 4 ad 4.

If the antecedent equals the consequent, the ratio is one of equality, as 4 to 4.

> Si prima quantitas secundam bis contineat, dicitur primam esse ad secundam in ratione dupla, si ter, in ratione tripla &c. & quae continetur dicitur esse in ratione subdupla, subtripla &c. Sic ex. gr. linea 8 pedum est ad aliam 4 pedum in ratione dupla, & linea 4 pedum ad lineam 8 pedum in ratione subdupla.

If the first quantity contains the second twice, the first is said to be to the second in double ratio; if three times, in triple ratio, etc.; and the one that is contained is said to be in subdouble, subtriple ratio, etc. Thus, e.g., a line of 8 feet is to another of 4 feet in double ratio, and the line of 4 feet to the line of 8 feet in subdouble ratio.

> Rationum aequalitas seu similitudo dicitur Proportio, & exprimitur hoc modo 8: 4:: 6: 3. vel 8: 4 = 6: 3. hoc est, 8 est ad 4, ut 6 ad 3, sive linea ex. gr. 8 pedum est ad lineam 4 pedum, ut linea 6 pedum ad lineam 3 pedum. Hi quatuor termini seu numeri sunt proportionales, & haec proportio vocatur Geometrica quia est rationum aequalitas. Sequens verò est Arithmetica 4 est ad 3, ut 2 ad 1 quia idem est excessus primi antecedentis respectu primi consequentis, qui secundi antecedentis respectu secundi consequentis.

The equality or likeness of ratios is called Proportion, and it is expressed in this way: 8 : 4 :: 6 : 3, or 8 : 4 = 6 : 3; that is, 8 is to 4 as 6 is to 3, or, e.g., a line of 8 feet is to a line of 4 feet as a line of 6 feet is to a line of 3 feet. These four terms, or numbers, are proportional, and this proportion is called Geometric because it is an equality of ratios. The following, however, is Arithmetic: 4 is to 3 as 2 to 1, because the excess of the first antecedent with respect to the first consequent is the same as that of the second antecedent with respect to the second consequent.

> Duae igitur rationes aequales sunt inter se, quum antecedens primae toties continet suum consequentem, quoties antecedens secundae suum continet, vel quum antecedens primae toties continetur in suo consequenti, quoties antecedens secundae in suo continetur. Sic ratio 12 ad 6 aequalis est rationi 48 ad 24, & ratio 3 ad 6 aequalis est rationi 50 ad 100. Duae igitur rationes aequales proportionem Geometricam componunt.

Two ratios, then, are equal to each other when the antecedent of the first contains its consequent as many times as the antecedent of the second contains its own, or when the antecedent of the first is contained in its consequent as many times as the antecedent of the second is contained in its own. Thus the ratio 12 to 6 is equal to the ratio 48 to 24, and the ratio 3 to 6 is equal to the ratio 50 to 100. Two equal ratios, then, make up a Geometric proportion.

> Duae quantitates dicuntur esse in ratione directa quum primus & tertius terminus proportionis Geometricae pertinent ad unam quantitatem, & secundus, & quartus terminus ejusdem proportionis ad aliam spectant. Supponamus ex. gr. Petrum habere 100 sapientiae, & 100 studii, Paulum verò non habere nisi 50 Sapientiae, & 50 studii. Petrus & Paulus habebunt Sapientiam in ratione directa sui studii: dicam ergo Sapientiam Petri esse ad scientiam Pauli, ut est studium Petri ad studium Pauli. In hac proportione primus & tertius terminus pertinent ad Petrum: secundus verò & quartus ad Paulum spectant, ut est perspicuum. Haec proinde ratio dicitur directa.

Two quantities are said to be in direct ratio when the first and third terms of a Geometric proportion belong to one quantity, and the second and fourth terms of the same proportion relate to another. Let us suppose, e.g., that Peter has 100 of wisdom and 100 of study, but that Paul has only 50 of Wisdom and 50 of study. Peter and Paul will have Wisdom in the direct ratio of their study: I shall say, therefore, that the Wisdom of Peter is to the knowledge of Paul as the study of Peter is to the study of Paul. In this proportion the first and third terms belong to Peter, while the second and fourth relate to Paul, as is evident. This ratio is therefore called direct.

> Duae quantitates sunt in ratione inversa, seu reciproca quum primus & quartus terminus proportionis Geometricae pertinent ad unam quantitatem, secundus verò & tertius ad aliam spectant. Si Petrus ex. gr. habeat 100 scientiae & 50 studii, & Paulus habeat 50 scientiae & 100 laboris, scientia Petri & scientia Pauli erunt in ratione inversa, seu reciproca. Dicam ergo scientiam Petri esse ad scientiam Pauli, ut labor Pauli est ad laborem Petri. Primus & [p. 37] quartus terminus hujus proportionis pertinent ad Petrum, secundus & tertius ad Paulum spectant, ut per se patet.

Two quantities are in inverse, or reciprocal, ratio when the first and fourth terms of a Geometric proportion belong to one quantity, while the second and third relate to another. If Peter, e.g., has 100 of knowledge and 50 of study, and Paul has 50 of knowledge and 100 of labor, the knowledge of Peter and the knowledge of Paul will be in inverse, or reciprocal, ratio. I shall say, therefore, that the knowledge of Peter is to the knowledge of Paul as the labor of Paul is to the labor of Peter. The first and fourth [p. 37] terms of this proportion belong to Peter, the second and third relate to Paul, as is self-evident.

> Ratio illa quae oritur ex multiplicatione plurium rationum inter se, dicitur Ratio composita. Sic si fuerit ratio 8 ad 4 & 3 ad 5 multiplices autem antec. 8 per antec. 3. & conseq. 4 per conseq. 5, ratio producti 24 ex antecedentibus ad productum 20 ex consequentibus, dicitur composita ex rationibus 8 ad 4 & 3 ad 5.

The ratio which arises from the multiplication of several ratios with one another is called a compound Ratio. Thus, if there are the ratios 8 to 4 and 3 to 5, and you multiply the antec. 8 by the antec. 3, and the conseq. 4 by the conseq. 5, the ratio of the product 24 from the antecedents to the product 20 from the consequents is said to be compounded of the ratios 8 to 4 and 3 to 5.

> Si plures sint quantitates, quarum prima eandem habeat rationem ad secundam, ac secunda ad tertiam, & tertia ad quartam: tum dicitur primam habere ad tertiam rationem duplicatam illius quam habet ad secundam. Item dicitur, ad quartam habere rationem triplicatam illius quae habet ad secundam. Ut si ex. gr. sint quatuor lineae, quarum prima sit 16 pedum, secunda 8 pedum, tertia 4 ped. & quarta 2 ped, & quaeras rationem primae ad secundam, dicam eam esse duplam, sive ut 2 ad 1. Si verò rationem primae 16 ped. ad tertiam 4 ped. dicam eam bis duplam esse quia composita est ex ratione primae lineae 16 ped. ad secundam 8, quae dupla est, & ex ratione secundae nempè 8 ad tertiam 4, quae iterum dupla est, unde ratio primae ad tertiam est duplicatae rationis primae ad secundam, sive est bis dupla, aut uno verbo quadrupla. Ratio verò primae ad quartam, seu 16 ad 2 est triplicatae rationis primae ad secundam. Adeoque componi debet ex ratione dupla, quae est primae ad secundam, & ex ratione quadrupla, quae est ejusdem primae ad tertiam, sicque est bis quadrupla, aut uno verbo, octupla. „

If there are several quantities, of which the first has the same ratio to the second as the second to the third, and the third to the fourth, then the first is said to have to the third the duplicate ratio of that which it has to the second. Likewise it is said to have to the fourth the triplicate ratio of that which it has to the second. Thus if, e.g., there are four lines, of which the first is of 16 feet, the second of 8 feet, the third of 4 ft. and the fourth of 2 ft., and you ask the ratio of the first to the second, I shall say that it is double, or as 2 to 1. But if you ask the ratio of the first, of 16 ft., to the third, of 4 ft., I shall say that it is twice double, because it is compounded of the ratio of the first line, of 16 ft., to the second, 8, which is double, and of the ratio of the second, namely 8, to the third, 4, which again is double; whence the ratio of the first to the third is the duplicate of the ratio of the first to the second, or is twice double, or in a word quadruple. And the ratio of the first to the fourth, or 16 to 2, is the triplicate of the ratio of the first to the second. And so it must be compounded of the double ratio, which is that of the first to the second, and of the quadruple ratio, which is that of the same first to the third; and thus it is twice quadruple, or, in a word, octuple.”

## CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

> *Problemata.*

Problems.

> Hic praeter selecta ex Euclidis libro VI. Problemata, adponimus ea, quae tradunt modum valdè utilem augendi, vel minuendi Figuras in qualibet Proportione.

Here, besides the Problems selected from Book VI of Euclid, we add those which teach a very useful way of enlarging or diminishing Figures in any Proportion whatever.

> PROBLEMA I. (Ic. IV. Fig. 1)

Problem I. (Plate IV. Fig. 1.)

> *Lineam in data Proportione dividere.*

To divide a line in a given Proportion.

> Sit linea A B dividenda in quinque partes, sicut linea A C divisa est. Conjungantur ita, ut faciant angulum quemcumque in A, & ducatur C B. Deinde per puncta, quibus secta est linea A C, ipsi C B fiant parallelae D E, F G, &c. secantes lineam A B. Istae [p. 38] divident lineam A B in eadem proportione, ac divisa est linea A C. *Ex Theor. II. hujus lib.*

Let the line AB be divided into five parts, just as the line AC is divided. Let them be joined so as to make any angle whatever at A, and let CB be drawn. Then through the points at which the line AC has been cut let DE, FG, etc. be made parallel to CB, cutting the line AB. These divisions [p. 38] will divide the line AB in the same proportion as the line AC is divided. From Theor. II of this book.

> Faciliùs tamen dividitur quaelibet linea, ut A B, si sit dividenda in partes aequales. Nam conjungatur ei ad quemcumque angulum linea indefinita A C, & in altero extremo ad aequalem angulum linea B I: (quae *ex Theor. II. lib. I.* erit parallela lineae A C propter angulos alternos aequales) deinde ex A in C, & ex B in I quocumque circini intervallo secentur quot volueris partes aequales. Lineae D L, F M, aliaeque ductae per puncta sectionis opposita, divident etiam lineam A B in partes aequales quaesitas. *Ex eodem.*

Any line, however, such as AB, is divided more easily if it is to be divided into equal parts. For let an indefinite line AC be joined to it at any angle whatever, and at the other end, at an equal angle, the line BI (which by Theor. II, bk. I will be parallel to the line AC, because of the equal alternate angles); then from A toward C, and from B toward I, with any opening of the compass, let as many equal parts be cut off as you wish. The lines DL, FM, and the others drawn through the opposite points of section, will also divide the line AB into the equal parts sought. From the same.

> PROBLEMA II. (Fig. 2.)

Problem II. (Fig. 2.)

> *Mediam proportionalem invenire.*

To find a mean proportional.

> Sint duae lineae A B, B C, inter quas media proportionalis sit invenienda. Jungantur in unam lineam A B C: deinde intervallo dimidiae A C, ut ex puncto E, fiat semicirculus: tum ad punctum B, quod duas lineas conjungit, erigatur perpendicularis B D, producta usque ad circumferentiam; quae erit media proportionalis quaesita: & quadratum ex linea B D erit aequale rectangulo ex lineis A B, & B C. *Ex Theor. IV. ac I. hujus lib. cor. II.*

Let there be two lines AB, BC, between which a mean proportional is to be found. Let them be joined into one line ABC; then, with the interval of half of AC, as from the point E, let a semicircle be made; then at the point B, which joins the two lines, let a perpendicular BD be erected, produced as far as the circumference; this will be the mean proportional sought. And the square on the line BD will be equal to the rectangle of the lines AB and BC. From Theor. IV and I of this book, cor. II.

> PROBLEMA III. (Fig. 3.)

Problem III. (Fig. 3.)

> *Datis duobus rectis tertiam continuam proportionalem invenire*

Given two straight lines, to find a third continued proportional.

> Sint duae lineae B D, & D A, quibus invenienda sit tertia continuè proportionalis. Constituantur ad angulum rectum D, & conjungantur per rectam B A: tum ducatur A C perpendicularis ad lineam B A, & producatur B D, donec ocurrat in C lineae A C. Erit linea D C tertia proportionalis quaesita: & rectangulum effectum ex lineis B D, D C erit aequale quadrato ex linea D A: *ex I. Theor. cor. 2.*

Let there be two lines BD and DA, for which a third continued proportional is to be found. Let them be placed at the right angle D, and joined by the straight line BA; then let AC be drawn perpendicular to the line BA, and let BD be produced until it meets the line AC at C. The line DC will be the third proportional sought; and the rectangle made of the lines BD, DC will be equal to the square on the line DA: from Theor. I, cor. 2.

> Similiter secundâ, & tertiâ ad angulum rectum dispositis, invenitur quarta continuè proportionalis, &c.

Similarly, by placing the second and third at a right angle, a fourth continued proportional is found, etc.

> PROBLEMA IV. (Fig. 4.)

Problem IV. (Fig. 4.)

> *Quartam etiam non continuè proportionalem invenire.*

To find a fourth proportional, even one not continued.

> Sint tres lineae A B, B C, A D, quibus sit invenienda quarta etiam non continuè proportionalis. Disponantur primae duae A [p. 39] B, B C in unam rectam: tertia verò A D cum prima A B faciat angulum quemcumque: deinde ducatur D B, cui per C parallela ponatur C E, occurrens rectae A D, productae in E. Erit D E quarta proportionalis. *Ex Theor. II. hujus libri.*

Let there be three lines AB, BC, AD, for which a fourth proportional, even one not continued, is to be found. Let the first two, AB, [p. 39] BC, be set out in one straight line, and let the third, AD, make any angle whatever with the first, AB; then let DB be drawn, and through C let CE be placed parallel to it, meeting the straight line AD, produced, at E. DE will be the fourth proportional. From Theor. II of this book.

## PROBLEMA V. (Fig. 5) — Problem V. (Fig. 5.)

> *Lineam extrema, ac media ratione dividere.*

To divide a line in extreme and mean ratio.

> Sit linea A B secanda extrema, ac media ratione, inveniendo scilicet in eadem linea mediam, & extremas proportionales. Ponatur ad A perpendicularis A C aequalis dimidiae totius AB: tum ducatur C B; ex qua secetur C D, aequalis lineae C A: reliqua verò D B transferatur ex A in E: eritque linea A B secta proportionaliter in E; ita, ut major pars A E sit media proportionalis inter totam A B, & minorem ejus partem E B. Nec non quadratum ex linea A E erit aequale rectangulo ex tota A B, & minori ejus parte E B. Quae propter eximios usus dicta est ab antiquis Divina proportio. *Ex Theor. VIII. hujus cor. I.*

Let the line AB be cut in extreme and mean ratio, that is, by finding in the same line the mean and the extreme proportionals. At A let a perpendicular AC be placed, equal to half of the whole AB; then let CB be drawn, and from it let CD be cut off, equal to the line CA; and let the remainder DB be transferred from A to E; and the line AB will be cut proportionally at E, so that the greater part AE is a mean proportional between the whole AB and its smaller part EB. Moreover, the square on the line AE will be equal to the rectangle of the whole AB and its smaller part EB. Because of its outstanding uses this was called by the ancients the Divine proportion. From Theor. VIII of this book, cor. I.

## PROBLEMA VI. (Fig. 6.) — Problem VI. (Fig. 6.)

> *Rectilineum efficere alteri simile, & proportionale.*

To make a Rectilinear figure similar and proportional to another.

> Dividatur Rectilineum A B C D in Triangula, ducta lineâ ad angulos oppositos A, B: tum fiat Triangulum E G F, habens aequales angulos Triangulo A C B: *juxtà Probl. XI. lib. 1.* & similiter fiat Triangulum E H F, habens aequales angulos Triangulo A D B. Et erit totum Rectilineum E G F H simile, ac proportionale Rectilineo A C B D. *Ex definit. IX. & Theor. III.*

Let the Rectilinear figure ABCD be divided into Triangles by drawing a line to the opposite angles A, B; then let a Triangle EGF be made having angles equal to the Triangle ACB, according to Probl. XI, bk. I; and similarly let a Triangle EHF be made having angles equal to the Triangle ADB. And the whole Rectilinear figure EGFH will be similar and proportional to the Rectilinear figure ACBD. From def. IX and Theor. III.

> PROBLEMA VII. (Fig. 7.)

Problem VII. (Fig. 7.)

> *Figuras similes addere, vel multiplicare.*

To add, or to multiply, similar figures.

> Dentur tres figurae circulares, aut rectilineae, quarum diametri, aut latera homologa sint A B, B C, D E. Constituantur ad angulum rectum A B, B C, quae producantur indefinitè; & ducatur A C: tum transferatur A C in B F, & D E in B G. Linea F G erit diameter, aut latus homologum figurae similis, & aequalis tribus simul super lineas A B, B C, D E. Si lineae A B, B C ponantur aequales, fiet figura super A C dupla figurae similis A B, vel B C: & translata A C in B F, erit figura super F C (quae hic intelligitur ducta) tripla: & translata F C in B H, erit similiter figura super H C (quae duceretur) quadrupla figurae super A B: atque ita in infinitum. *Ex Theor. VI. cor. 3.*

Let there be given three figures, circular or rectilinear, whose diameters or homologous sides are AB, BC, DE. Let AB, BC be set at a right angle and produced indefinitely, and let AC be drawn; then let AC be transferred to BF, and DE to BG. The line FG will be the diameter, or homologous side, of a figure similar and equal to the three together upon the lines AB, BC, DE. If the lines AB, BC are taken as equal, the figure upon AC will be double the similar figure upon AB or BC; and when AC is transferred to BF, the figure upon FC (which is here understood to be drawn) will be triple; and when FC is transferred to BH, the figure upon HC (were it drawn) will similarly be quadruple the figure upon AB; and so on to infinity. From Theor. VI, cor. 3.

[p. 40]

## PROBLEMA VIII. (Fig. 8.) — Problem VIII. (Fig. 8.)

> *Figuram similem ab alia subtrahere, vel minuere, vel in qualibet proportione augere.*

To subtract a similar figure from another, or to diminish it, or to enlarge it in any proportion whatever.

> Sint duae figurae similes rectilineae, aut circulares, quarum diametri, aut latera homologa sint A B, C B. Fiat super majorem lineam B C semicirculus, cui adplicetur altera aequalis lineae A B; deinde ducatur recta A C, quae erit latus figurae quaesitae: qua figurâ figuram, super A B descriptam, superat similis figura super B C. *Ex Theor. eodem.*

Let there be two similar figures, rectilinear or circular, whose diameters or homologous sides are AB, CB. Upon the greater line BC let a semicircle be made, within which let another line be fitted equal to the line AB; then let the straight line AC be drawn, which will be the side of the figure sought: the figure by which the similar figure upon BC exceeds the figure described upon AB. From the same Theor.

> Hinc patet, quomodo quaelibet figura minuenda sit ad datam proportionem: ex. gr. sit auferenda ex figura descripta super B C tertia pars. Facto semicirculo, dividatur B C in tres partes, & deinde ad intersectionem unius tertiae D C, erigatur perpendicularis D A: demum ducatur A C. Erit figura super A C tertia pars similis figurae super B C; & figura super B A duae tertiae ejusdem, *Ex eodem.*

Hence it is plain how any figure whatever is to be diminished to a given proportion: e.g., let a third part be taken away from the figure described upon BC. Having made the semicircle, let BC be divided into three parts, and then at the intersection of one third, DC, let a perpendicular DA be erected; finally let AC be drawn. The figure upon AC will be the third part of the similar figure upon BC, and the figure upon BA two thirds of the same. From the same.

> Patet etiam, quomodo figurae in qualibet proportione augeantur. Sit enim constituenda figura sesquialtera figurae similis descriptae super B D. Addatur lineae ejus medietas D C; & super totam B C descripto semicirculo, & erecta, perpendiculari A D, ducatur A B in semicirculo; super quam figura descripta, erit sesquialtera figurae similis, descriptae super lineam B D. *Ex eodem.*

It is plain also how figures are enlarged in any proportion whatever. For let a figure be constructed one and a half times a similar figure described upon BD. Let half of the line, DC, be added to it; and when a semicircle has been described upon the whole BC, and the perpendicular AD erected, let AB be drawn in the semicircle; the figure described upon it will be one and a half times the similar figure described upon the line BD. From the same.

> PROBLEMA IX. (Fig. 9.)

Problem IX. (Fig. 9.)

> *Parallelogramma aequalia efficere in data linea.*

To make equal parallelograms upon a given line.

> Sit parallelogrammum A C, cui aequale constituendum est in data linea C H. Ponatur C H in directum lineae D C, & compleatur parallelogrammum C I. Deinde ducatur diameter I C E indefinita. Producatur A D, donec occurrat diametro: per punctum concursus E fiat E G parallela, & aequalis lineae D H. Et erit parallelogrammum C G, constitutum super data linea C H, aequale dato parallelogrammo A C. *Ex Theor. VI. lib. I. cor. 3.*

Let there be a parallelogram AC, to which an equal one is to be constructed upon the given line CH. Let CH be placed in a straight line with the line DC, and let the parallelogram CI be completed. Then let the diameter ICE be drawn indefinitely. Let AD be produced until it meets the diameter; through the point of meeting E let EG be made parallel and equal to the line DH. And the parallelogram CG, constructed upon the given line CH, will be equal to the given parallelogram AC. From Theor. VI, bk. I, cor. 3.

> PROBLEMA X. (Fig. 10.)

Problem X. (Fig. 10.)

> *Quamcumque Figuram in aequale Rectangulum convertere.*

To convert any Figure whatever into an equal Rectangle.

> Trapezium in Rectangulum, aut quodcumque parallelogrammum convertere docuimus *lib. I. Prob. ult.* Quodcumque verò rectilineum in rectangulum, aut aliud parallelogrammum convertere, [p. 41] hic opportuniùs docemus. Sit igitur rectilineum quodcumque B A C, cui aequale rectangulum sit constituendum. Primò, ductis lineis ad vertices anguli, resolve totum rectilineum in Triangula, quae semper erunt duo minus, quàm latera figurae. Tum ad datam rectam quamcumque fac rectangulum D G, aequale triangulo B; & producta D N indefinitè, super rectam F G fiat rectangulum F I, aequale triangulo A; & super rectam H I rectangulum H M, aequale triangulo C. Erit totum rectangulum D M aequale rectilineo B A C: *Ex Theor. VIII. lib. 1.*

We taught in bk. I, last Prob., how to convert a Trapezium into a Rectangle, or into any parallelogram whatever. How to convert any rectilinear figure whatever into a rectangle, or another parallelogram, [p. 41] we teach here more conveniently. Let there be, then, any rectilinear figure BAC whatever, to which an equal rectangle is to be constructed. First, by drawing lines to the vertices of the angles, resolve the whole rectilinear figure into Triangles, which will always be two fewer than the sides of the figure. Then upon any given straight line make a rectangle DG equal to the triangle B; and, DN being produced indefinitely, upon the straight line FG let a rectangle FI be made equal to the triangle A; and upon the straight line HI a rectangle HM equal to the triangle C. The whole rectangle DM will be equal to the rectilinear figure BAC: From Theor. VIII, bk. I.

## PROBLEMA XI. (Fig. 11.) — Problem XI. (Fig. 11.)

> *Dissimilium figurarum Proportionem cognoscere.*

To know the Proportion of dissimilar figures.

> Sint duae figurae dissimiles A, & B, quarum proportio mutua est cognoscenda. Reducantur, juxta antecedens Problema, in duo Rectangula iis aequalia, C, & D, ejusdem altitudinis. Tum, quae proportio erit basis G F ad basim F H, eadem erit figurae A ad figuram B. *Ex Theor. I. hujus lib.*

Let there be two dissimilar figures A and B, whose mutual proportion is to be known. Let them be reduced, according to the preceding Problem, to two Rectangles equal to them, C and D, of the same height. Then the proportion of the base GF to the base FH will be the same as that of the figure A to the figure B. From Theor. I of this book.

## PROBLEMA XII. (Fig. 12.) — Problem XII. (Fig. 12.)

> *Figuram uni aequalem, alteri similem efficere.*

To make a figure equal to one and similar to another.

> Sit Poligono A efficienda aequalis figura, quae tamen similis sit Poligono B: Fiat super D C Poligoni B, cui constituenda est similis figura, rectangulum C E, aequale eidem Poligono B: rursum supra D E fiat rectangulum DG, aequale Poligono A, cui aequalis constituenda est figura. Tum inter C D, & D F inveniatur *juxt. Prob. II.* Media Proportionalis, ut I L, supra quam fiat figura H, similis figurae B; quae erit aequalis figurae A. *Ex Theor. VI. cor. 4.*

Let a figure be made equal to the Polygon A which shall nevertheless be similar to the Polygon B. Upon DC of the Polygon B, to which a similar figure is to be constructed, let a rectangle CE be made equal to the same Polygon B; again, upon DE let a rectangle DG be made equal to the Polygon A, to which an equal figure is to be constructed. Then between CD and DF let a Mean Proportional, such as IL, be found according to Prob. II, upon which let a figure H be made similar to the figure B; it will be equal to the figure A. From Theor. VI, cor. 4.

## CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

> *Theoremata.*

Theorems.

> Duodecim hoc capite Theoremata complectimur, praesertim ex sexto Euclidis libro selecta; quibus primò Rectilinearum Figurarum, deinde Linearum, ac Figurarum in circulo, necnon eorumdem circulorum Proportiones demonstrantur; [p. 42] nonnullis, quae huc spectant, ex libro Euclidis 3. 11. & 13. accersitis.

welve Theorems are comprised in this chapter, selected chiefly from the T sixth book of Euclid, in which are demonstrated first the Proportions of Rectilinear Figures, then of Lines and of Figures in the circle, and also of the circles themselves, [p. 42] some things that bear on this having been brought in from Euclid’s books 3, 11 and 13.

> THEOREMA I. (Icon. V. Fig. 1.)

Theorem I. (Plate V. Fig. 1.)

> *Parallelogramma, & Triangula, quorum eadem est Altitudo, seu quae sunt inter easdem Parallelas, sunt inter se, ut eorum Bases.* [^42-s1]

Parallelograms and Triangles that have the same Height, or that are between the same Parallels, are to each other as their Bases. (a)

> [^42-s1]: Eucl. lib. VI. prop. 1.

[^42-s1]: Eucl. bk. VI, prop. 1.

> Dem. Si basis B A Parallelogrammi X fuerit bis, vel ter aequalis basi A F Parallelogrammi Z; erit Parallelogrammum X bis, aut ter aequale, hoc est duplum, vel triplum Parallelogrammi Z, atque ita in infinitum: quum Parallelogramma aequalium basium inter easdem Parallelas sint aequalia: *ex lib. I. Theor. VII.* ergo Parallelogramma ejusdem altitudinis sunt inter se, ut eorum bases.

Dem. If the base BA of the Parallelogram X is twice or three times equal to the base AF of the Parallelogram Z, the Parallelogram X will be twice or three times equal, that is, double or triple, of the Parallelogram Z, and so on to infinity, since Parallelograms of equal bases between the same Parallels are equal, from bk. I, Theor. VII: therefore Parallelograms of the same height are to each other as their bases.

> Similiter triangulum X, dimidium parallelogrammi X, erit duplum, aut triplum trianguli Z, juxtà eorum bases.

Similarly the triangle X, half of the parallelogram X, will be double or triple the triangle Z, according to their bases.

> Coroll. I. Si basis B A fuerit dupla, aut tripla basis A F, & basis G A fuerit similiter dupla, aut tripla basis A D, erunt tota rectangula X, & Y, aut eorum dimidia triangula reciproca, & aequalia, quia similiter dupla, aut tripla ejusdem rectanguli, vel dimidii trianguli Z, ex modò demonstratis. Quod similiter patet de aliis Parallelogrammis. [^42-s2]

Cor. I. If the base BA is double or triple the base AF, and the base GA is likewise double or triple the base AD, the whole rectangles X and Y, or their halves, the triangles, will be reciprocal and equal, because they are likewise double or triple the same rectangle, or of the half, the triangle Z, from what has just been demonstrated. And this is likewise plain of other Parallelograms. (b)

> [^42-s2]: Eucl. lib. VI. Prop. 14. 15.

[^42-s2]: Eucl. bk. VI, Prop. 14, 15.

> II. Hinc patet, quòd si quatuor lineae sint proportionales, ut G A, A D, A B, A F, erit Rectangulum Y, quod fit ex extremis lineis G A, A F, aequale Rectangulo X, quod fit ex mediis A D, A B. [^42-s3]

II. Hence it is plain that if four lines are proportional, as GA, AD, AB, AF, the Rectangle Y, which is made of the extremes GA, AF, will be equal to the Rectangle X, which is made of the means AD, AB. (c)

> [^42-s3]: Prop. 16.

[^42-s3]: Prop. 16.

> III. Et si tres lineae sint continuè proportionales, hoc est duae mediae sint inter se aequales, ut A D, A B, Quadratum X ex media erit aequale rectangulo Y, quod fit ex extremis lineis A C, A F. [^42-s4]

III. And if three lines are continued proportionals, that is, if the two means are equal to each other, as AD, AB, the Square X of the mean will be equal to the rectangle Y, which is made of the extreme lines AC, AF. (d)

> [^42-s4]: Prop. 17.

[^42-s4]: Prop. 17.

> IV. Rectangula proportionalium basium, & altitudinum, ut O, & Z, sunt in duplicata ratione laterum: nam si basis G A sit dupla basis A D, & similiter basis B A sit dupla basis A F, erit rectangulum O duplum rectanguli X, aut Y: sed rectangulum X, aut Y est duplum rectanguli Z; ergo rectangulum O erit quadruplum rectanguli Z.

IV. Rectangles of proportional bases and heights, as O and Z, are in the duplicate ratio of their sides: for if the base GA is double the base AD, and similarly the base BA is double the base AF, the rectangle O will be double the rectangle X or Y; but the rectangle X or Y is double the rectangle Z; therefore the rectangle O will be quadruple the rectangle Z.

> Similiter, si eaedem bases fuerint triplae, erit rectangulum X, aut Y, triplum rectanguli Z; & ejusdem nonuplum erit rectangulum O: atque ita deinceps semper in duplicata ratione.

Similarly, if the same bases are triple, the rectangle X or Y will be triple the rectangle Z, and the rectangle O will be ninefold of the same; and so on successively, always in duplicate ratio.

> V. Hinc rectangulorum dimidia triangula O, & Z, quae habent proportionales bases, & altitudines, etiam habent basium, & altitudinum duplicatam rationem.

V. Hence the triangles O and Z, halves of rectangles, which have proportional bases and heights, also have the duplicate ratio of the bases and heights.

[p. 43]

> VI. Et si basis B A fuerit dupla basis A F, & basis G A tripla basis A D, habebit rectangulum O ad rectangulum Z rationem productam, seu compositam ex tripla, & dupla eorundem laterum: hoc est rectangulum O erit sextuplum rectanguli Z, quia triplum rectanguli X, aut Y, quod est duplum rectanguli Z. Quae similiter demonstrantur de omnibus similibus Parallelogrammis. [^43-s1-3]

VI. And if the base BA is double the base AF, and the base GA triple the base AD, the rectangle O will have to the rectangle Z the ratio produced, or compounded, of the triple and the double of the same sides: that is, the rectangle O will be sextuple the rectangle Z, because it is triple the rectangle X or Y, which is double the rectangle Z. These things are demonstrated in like manner of all similar Parallelograms. (a)

> [^43-s1-3]: Eucl. lib. VI. prop. 23.

[^43-s1-3]: Eucl. bk. VI, prop. 23.

## THEOREMA II. (Fig. 2.) — Theorem II. (Fig. 2.)

> *Si ponatur Parallela lateri alicujus Trianguli, haec secabit reliqua duo latera proportionaliter.* [^43-s2-2]

If a Parallel is placed to a side of any Triangle, it will cut the two remaining sides proportionally. (b)

> [^43-s2-2]: Prop. 2.

[^43-s2-2]: Prop. 2.

> Praepar. Ducantur, ad demonstrandum E D, B C.

Prep. For the demonstration, let ED, BC be drawn.

> Dem. Triangula E D B, & B C E sunt aequalia, quùm sint in eadem basi B E, & Parallela D C; ergo, *ex II. Axiom. hujus lib.* habent eandem proportionem ad Triangulum A B E: sed Triangula A B E, B D E habent eundem verticem E; adeoque eandem altitudinem. Similiter Triangula A E B, & C E B habent eundem verticem B; ergo basis B D habet eandem proportionem ad basim B A, ac basis C E ad basim E A. *Ex antec.*

Dem. The Triangles EDB and BCE are equal, since they are on the same base BE and between the same Parallel DC; therefore, by Axiom II of this book, they have the same proportion to the Triangle ABE. But the Triangles ABE, BDE have the same vertex E, and therefore the same height. Similarly the Triangles AEB and CEB have the same vertex B: therefore the base BD has the same proportion to the base BA as the base CE to the base EA. From the preceding.

> Coroll. I. Ergo alternando, ut B D ad C E, ita B A ad E A.

Cor. I. Therefore, by alternation, as BD to CE, so BA to EA.

> II. Ergo componendo, ut D A ad A B, ita C A ád E A.

II. Therefore, by composition, as DA to AB, so CA to EA.

> III. Et si linea B E secet latera Trianguli proportionaliter, erit Parallela reliquo lateri: nam similiter erunt aequalia inter se duo Triangula E D B, & E B C, quum habeant eandem proportionem ad Triangulum A B E sicut eorum bases: *ex antec. Theor.* ergo quum habeant eandem basim B E, erunt inter easdem Parallelas B E, D C, *ex Theor. VI. lib. I. cor. ult.*

III. And if the line BE cuts the sides of the Triangle proportionally, it will be Parallel to the remaining side: for similarly the two Triangles EDB and EBC will be equal to each other, since they have the same proportion to the Triangle ABE as their bases, from the preceding Theor.; therefore, since they have the same base BE, they will be between the same Parallels BE, DC, from Theor. VI, bk. I, last cor.

> THEOREMA III. (Fig. 3.)

Theorem III. (Fig. 3.)

> *Triangula Aequiangula habent latera circa aequales angulos Proportionalia.* [^43-s3-2]

Equiangular Triangles have their sides about the equal angles Proportional. (c)

> [^43-s3-2]: Eucl. lib. VI. prop. 4.

[^43-s3-2]: Eucl. bk. VI, prop. 4.

> Praepar. Ducatur linea G H; ita, ut latus D G sit aequale lateri A B, & latus D H sit aequale lateri A C.

Prep. Let the line GH be drawn, so that the side DG is equal to the side AB, and the side DH is equal to the side AC.

[p. 44]

> Dem. Si Trianguli A B C angulus A imponatur angulo D, basis B C cadet super G H; (supponuntur enim angulus, & latera aequalia) sed anguli B, & C supponuntur aequales angulis E, & F; ergo *ex II. Theor. lib. 1. in cor.* linea B C, seu G H erit Parallela basi E F: ergo *ex antecedente Theor.* ut latus D E ad latus A B, ita latus D F ad latus A C.

Dem. If the angle A of the Triangle ABC is placed upon the angle D, the base BC will fall upon GH (for the angles and sides are supposed equal); but the angles B and C are supposed equal to the angles E and F: therefore, by Theor. II, bk. I, in the cor., the line BC, or GH, will be Parallel to the base EF: therefore, by the preceding Theor., as the side DE to the side AB, so the side DF to the side AC.

> Quòd si angulus B imponatur angulo E, etiam basis A C fiet parallela lineae D F: ergo ut D E ad E F, ita A B ad B C. Idem ostendetur, si angulus C imponatur angulo F.

But if the angle B is placed upon the angle E, the base AC will also become parallel to the line DF: therefore, as DE to EF, so AB to BC. The same will be shown if the angle C is placed upon the angle F.

> Coroll. I. Parallela, ad unum latus trianguli ducta, ut G H ad E F, aufert triangulum minus omnino proportionale majori.

Cor. I. A Parallel drawn to one side of a triangle, as GH to EF, cuts off a smaller triangle wholly proportional to the larger.

> II. Si anguli A, & D sint aequales, & circa eos angulos latera proportionalia, erunt duo triangula A B C, & D E F omninò aequiangula; nam erit G H parallela lateri E F, *ex cor. 3. Theor. antecedente*, & triangulum D G H sicut triangulum A B C. [^44-s1]

II. If the angles A and D are equal, and the sides about those angles proportional, the two triangles ABC and DEF will be wholly equiangular; for GH will be parallel to the side EF, by cor. 3 of the preceding Theor., and the triangle DGH will be as the triangle ABC. (a)

> [^44-s1]: Eucl. lib. VI. prop. 6.

[^44-s1]: Eucl. bk. VI, prop. 6.

> THEOREMA IV. (Fig. 4.)

Theorem IV. (Fig. 4.)

> *In Triangulo Rectangulo Perpendicularis, ab angulo recto ad basim ducta, dividit totum Triangulum in duo triangula similia toti, & inter se.* [^44-s2]

In a Right-angled Triangle the Perpendicular drawn from the right angle to the base divides the whole Triangle into two triangles similar to the whole and to each other. (b)

> [^44-s2]: Eucl. lib. VI. prop. 8.

[^44-s2]: Eucl. bk. VI, prop. 8.

> Dem. I. Totum triangulum A B C, & ejus pars Triangulum A D C habent duos angulos C A B, & C D A rectos; *ex suppositione*; adeoque aequales: Sed angulus C est communis utrique; ergo reliquus angulus C A D est aequalis angulo B *ex Theor. III. lib. I.* ergo *ex antecd. Theor.* haec duo triangula aequiangula habent latera circa aequales angulos proportionalia.

Dem. I. The whole triangle ABC and its part, the Triangle ADC, have two right angles, CAB and CDA, by supposition, and therefore equal; but the angle C is common to both; therefore the remaining angle CAD is equal to the angle B, by Theor. III, bk. I; therefore, by the preceding Theor., these two equiangular triangles have the sides about the equal angles proportional.

> Coroll. I. Ergo linea A C est media proportionalis inter totam basim B C, & ejus segmentum D C. Nam ut in toto triangulo est C B ad C A, ita in triangulo A D C est eadem C A ad C D.

Cor. I. Therefore the line AC is a mean proportional between the whole base BC and its segment DC. For as in the whole triangle is CB to CA, so in the triangle ADC is the same CA to CD.

> Dem. II. Totum triangulum B A C, & ejus altera pars A B D habent angulos B A C, & B D A rectos: *ex suppositione*: sed angulus B est communis utrique; ergo reliquus angulus B A D est aequalis angulo C: adeoque sunt omnino similia.

Dem. II. The whole triangle BAC and its other part ABD have right angles BAC and BDA, by supposition; but the angle B is common to both; therefore the remaining angle BAD is equal to the angle C: and so they are wholly similar.

> Coroll. II. Ergo A B est media proportionalis inter totam basim B C, & ejus alterum segmentum B D. Nam ut in toto triangulo est B C ad B A; ita in triangulo B D A est eadem B A ad BD.

Cor. II. Therefore AB is a mean proportional between the whole base BC and its other segment BD. For as in the whole triangle is BC to BA, so in the triangle BDA is the same BA to BD.

> Dem. III. Duo triangula A B D, & A C D habent angulos ad D ambos rectos: sed angulus B A D est aequalis angulo C, & angulus C A D aequalis angulo B. *ex modo demonstratis*; ergo haec duo triangula sunt omninò similia.

Dem. III. The two triangles ABD and ACD both have right angles at D; but the angle BAD is equal to the angle C, and the angle CAD equal to the angle B, from what has just been demonstrated; therefore these two triangles are wholly similar.

[p. 45]

> Coroll. III. Ergo A D est media proportionalis inter duo segmenta basis B D, & D C. Nam, ut B D ad D A, ita in altero triangulo est A D ad D C.

Cor. III. Therefore AD is a mean proportional between the two segments of the base, BD and DC. For as BD to DA, so in the other triangle is AD to DC.

## THEOREMA V. (Fig. 5.) — Theorem V. (Fig. 5.)

> *Quaecumque Triangula similia habent duplicatam proportionem laterum homologorum.* [^45-s1]

Any similar Triangles whatever have the duplicate proportion of their homologous sides. (a)

> [^45-s1]: Eucl. lib. VI. prop. 19.

[^45-s1]: Eucl. bk. VI, prop. 19.

> Praepar. Ex aequalibus angulis ad bases ducantur Perpendiculares A G, D H.

Prep. From the equal angles let Perpendiculars AG, DH be drawn to the bases.

> Dem. Quoniam angulus B est aequalis angulo E, *ex suppositione*. Anguli ad G, & H recti, *ex constructione*; erit triangulum A B G aequiangulum, & proportionale Triangulo D E H: *Ex Theor. III.* ergo erit triangulum rectangulum A B G ad triangulum rectangulum D E H in duplicata ratione laterum. *Ex Theor. I. cor. 5.*

Dem. Since the angle B is equal to the angle E, by supposition, and the angles at G and H are right, by construction, the triangle ABG will be equiangular and proportional to the Triangle DEH, by Theor. III; therefore the right-angled triangle ABG will be to the right-angled triangle DEH in the duplicate ratio of the sides. By Theor. I, cor. 5.

> Similiter demonstratur de triangulis A C G, & D F H: ergo totum triangulum A B C est ad triangulum simile D E F in duplicata ratione laterum.

The same is demonstrated, similarly, of the triangles ACG and DFH: therefore the whole triangle ABC is to the similar triangle DEF in the duplicate ratio of the sides.

## THEOREMA VI. (Fig. 6.) — Theorem VI. (Fig. 6.)

> *Similia Poligona dividuntur in totidem Triangula similia, & proportionalia.* [^45-s2]

Similar Polygons are divided into as many similar and proportional Triangles. (b)

> [^45-s2]: Eucl. lib. VI. propr. 20.

[^45-s2]: Eucl. bk. VI, prop. 20.

> Praepar. Ducantur ab angulis ad angulos lineae, dividentes Poligonum A, & B in Triangula.

Prep. Let lines be drawn from angles to angles, dividing the Polygons A and B into Triangles.

> Dem. Angulus E est aequalis angulo L, & latera circa eos proportionalia; *ex definitione figurae similis*: ergo Triangulum G E D est simile, & proportionale Triangulo N L H. *Ex Theor. III. cor. 2.* Ex eadem ratione Triangulum G F C est aequiangulum, & proportionale triangulo N M I; ergo quum ex totis angulis G D C, qui ex suppositione sunt aequales angulis N, H, I, ablati sint hinc inde anguli aequales, remanent etiam triangula A, & B aequiangula, & proportionalia.

Dem. The angle E is equal to the angle L, and the sides about them are proportional, by the definition of a similar figure: therefore the Triangle GED is similar and proportional to the Triangle NLH. By Theor. III, cor. 2. By the same reasoning the Triangle GFC is equiangular and proportional to the triangle NMI: therefore, since from the whole angles G, D, C, which by supposition are equal to the angles N, H, I, equal angles have been taken away on either side, the triangles A and B that remain are also equiangular and proportional.

> Coroll. I. Totum Poligonum A ad Poligonum B habet duplicatam rationem laterum quùm componatur ex totidem triangulis proportionalibus, quae habent duplicatam proportionem laterum. *Ex Theor. ant.*

Cor. I. The whole Polygon A has to the Polygon B the duplicate ratio of the sides, since it is composed of as many proportional triangles, which have the duplicate proportion of the sides. From the preceding Theor.

> II. Ergo omnia Poligona similia sunt inter se, ut Quadrata, [p. 46] aliaque rectangula proportionalia, quae similiter habent duplicatam proportionem laterum. *ex Theor. I. cor. 4.*

II. Therefore all similar Polygons are to each other as the Squares and the other proportional [p. 46] rectangles proportional, which likewise have the duplicate proportion of the sides. By Theor. I, cor. 4.

> III. Ergo sicut in triangulo rectangulo quadratum basis est aequale duobus quadratis ex lateribus, continentibus angulum rectum; ità quaelibet figurae similes descriptae supra basim trianguli rectanguli, erunt aequales duabus simul figuris similiter descriptis supra latera, continentia angulum rectum, quum sint similiter in duplicata ratione laterum. [^46-s1-2]

III. Therefore, just as in a right-angled triangle the square of the base is equal to the two squares of the sides containing the right angle, so any similar figures whatever described upon the base of a right-angled triangle will be equal to the two figures together similarly described upon the sides containing the right angle, since they are likewise in the duplicate ratio of the sides. (a)

> [^46-s1-2]: Eucl. lib. VI. prop. 31.

[^46-s1-2]: Eucl. bk. VI, prop. 31.

> IV. Si sint tres lineae continuè proportionales, ut D C, H I, O P, ut prima ad tertiam, ita se habet rectilineum A, descriptum super primam, ad simile rectilineum B, descriptum supra secundam; nimirum in eadem duplicata proportione.

IV. If there are three continued proportional lines, as DC, HI, OP, then as the first is to the third, so is the rectilinear figure A, described upon the first, to the similar rectilinear figure B, described upon the second: namely, in the same duplicate proportion.

> THEOREMA VII. (Fig. 7.)

Theorem VII. (Fig. 7.)

> *Si duae lineae in circulo se secent, Rectangulum ex partibus unius, est aequale Rectangulo ex partibus alterius.* [^46-s2]

If two lines cut each other in a circle, the Rectangle of the parts of the one is equal to the Rectangle of the parts of the other. (b)

> [^46-s2]: Eucl. lib. VI. prop. 35.

[^46-s2]: Eucl. bk. VI, prop. 35.

> Praepar. Ducantur, ad demonstrandum, B C, E D.

Prep. For the demonstration, let BC, ED be drawn.

> Dem. Triangula E A D, & B A C sunt aequiangula: nam anguli ad verticem A sunt in utroque aequales. Anguli C, & D sunt aequales, quum insistant eidem arcui E B; *ex Theor. II. lib. 2.* & reliquus angulus reliquo aequalis: ergo *ex Theor. III.* habent latera circa aequales angulos proportionalia: nimirum A D est ad A E, sicut A C ad A B: ergo *ex Theor. I. cor. 2.* rectangulum ex extremis A D, A B est aequale rectangulo ex mediis A E, A C.

Dem. The Triangles EAD and BAC are equiangular: for the vertical angles at A are equal in both. The angles C and D are equal, since they stand on the same arc EB, by Theor. II, bk. 2; and the remaining angle is equal to the remaining angle: therefore, by Theor. III, they have the sides about the equal angles proportional: namely, AD is to AE as AC to AB: therefore, by Theor. I, cor. 2, the rectangle of the extremes AD, AB is equal to the rectangle of the means AE, AC.

> THEOREMA VIII. (Fig. 8.)

Theorem VIII. (Fig. 8.)

> *Si duarum rectarum ab eodem puncto, C, altera circulum secet, altera tangat, erit Quadratum tangentis, C B, aequale Rectangulo ex tota secante, C A, & ejus parte extra circulum, C D.* [^46-s3]

If, of two straight lines drawn from the same point C, one cuts the circle and the other touches it, the Square of the tangent CB will be equal to the Rectangle of the whole secant CA and of its part outside the circle, CD. (c)

> [^46-s3]: Eucl. lib. III. prop. 36.

[^46-s3]: Eucl. bk. III, prop. 36.

> Praep. Ducatur ex centro Perpendicularis E B, & nectantur A B, D B.

Prep. From the center let a Perpendicular EB be drawn, and let AB, DB be joined.

> Dem. Triangula A C B, & D C B sunt aequiangula; habent enim angulum C communem, & angulum C B D aequalem angulo A in alterno circuli segmento: *ex Theor. VI. lib. 2.* ergo ut A C ad C B in toto triangulo, ita eadem C B ad C D in triangulo [p. 47] minori C B D: ergo *ex Theor. I. cor. 3.* quadratum mediae C B est aequale rectangulo ex prima, & ultima C A, & C D.

Dem. The Triangles ACB and DCB are equiangular; for they have the angle C in common, and the angle CBD equal to the angle A in the alternate segment of the circle, by Theor. VI, bk. 2: therefore, as AC to CB in the whole triangle, so is the same CB to CD in the smaller triangle [p. 47] CBD: therefore, by Theor. I, cor. 3, the square of the mean CB is equal to the rectangle of the first and the last, CA and CD.

> Coroll. I. Si circuli diameter sit aequalis tangenti B C; erit A C secta in D extremâ, ac media ratione; nam quadratum lineae A D, aequalis lineae B C, ex supositione, erit aequale rectangulo lineae A C, & D C, ex modò demonstratis. [^47-s1]

Cor. I. If the diameter of the circle is equal to the tangent BC, AC will be cut at D in extreme and mean ratio; for the square of the line AD, which is equal to the line BC by supposition, will be equal to the rectangle of the lines AC and DC, from what has just been demonstrated. (a)

> [^47-s1]: Prop. 30.

[^47-s1]: Prop. 30.

> II. Et si ex linea B C, aequali circuli diametro secetur C F, aequalis lineae C D; erit etiam linea C B divisa extremâ, ac mediâ ratione in F: *juxta Probl. V.* Nam ex demonstratis, ut tota A C ad totam C B, ita pars A D ad partem C F, aequalem lineae C D: ergo *ex Axiom VII.* ita etiam erit reliqua D C (seu aequalis C F) ad reliquam F B.

II. And if from the line BC, equal to the diameter of the circle, CF is cut off equal to the line CD, the line CB will also be divided in extreme and mean ratio at F, according to Probl. V. For from what has been demonstrated, as the whole AC to the whole CB, so the part AD to the part CF, equal to the line CD: therefore, by Axiom VII, so also will the remainder DC (or its equal CF) be to the remainder FB.

> THEOREMA IX. (Fig. 9.)

Theorem IX. (Fig. 9.)

> *Quadratum lateris Trigoni, circulo inscripti, est triplum Quadrati ex semidiametro, seu latere Hexagoni.* [^47-s2]

The Square of the side of the Trigon inscribed in a circle is triple the Square of the semidiameter, or of the side of the Hexagon. (b)

> [^47-s2]: Eucl. lib. XIII. prop. 13.

[^47-s2]: Eucl. bk. XIII, prop. 13.

> Dem. Quadratum Diametri est quadruplum quadrati ex semidiametro, seu latere hexagoni; quum quadrata sint in duplicata ratione laterum. Est etiam aequale quadratis laterum A M, M B propter angulum M in semicirculo rectum: ergo sublato quadrato lateris M B uno, remanet quadratum A M triplum.

Dem. The Square of the Diameter is quadruple the square of the semidiameter, or of the side of the hexagon, since squares are in the duplicate ratio of their sides. It is also equal to the squares of the sides AM, MB, because the angle M in the semicircle is right: therefore, when the one square of the side MB is taken away, there remains the square AM, triple.

> Coroll. Quoniam verò quadratum A C B D, circulo inscriptum, est duplum quadrati ex semidiametro, propter angulum rectum in centro E; erit quadratum lateris trigoni ad quadratum, eidem circulo inscriptum, ut 3 ad 2, seu sexquialterum.

Cor. Since, moreover, the square ACBD inscribed in the circle is double the square of the semidiameter, because of the right angle at the center E, the square of the side of the trigon will be to the square inscribed in the same circle as 3 to 2, or sesquialteral.

> THEOREMA X. (Fig. 10.)

Theorem X. (Fig. 10.)

> *Si ejusdem circuli latus Decagoni, A B, & Hexagoni, A E, seu semidiametri in unam lineam, E B, componantur; erit tota linea, B E, secta in, A, extremâ, ac mediâ ratione.* [^47-s3]

If the side of the Decagon, AB, and of the Hexagon, AE, or of the semidiameter, of the same circle, are put together into one line, EB, the whole line BE will be cut at A in extreme and mean ratio. (c)

> [^47-s3]: Eucl. lib. XIII. prop. 9.

[^47-s3]: Eucl. bk. XIII, prop. 9.

> Praepar. Ducatur C A: eruntque tres lineae C B, C A, A E, ex suppositione aequales; & triangula E A C, B C A Isoscelia.

Prep. Let CA be drawn; and the three lines CB, CA, AE will be equal, by supposition; and the triangles EAC, BCA isosceles.

> Dem. Quum arcus D A sit quadruplus, *ex suppositione*, arcus B A Decagoni, quintae semicirculi partis; & mensura anguli B in circumferentia sit medietas totius arcus D A, cui insistit; *ex Theor. II.* [p. 48] *lib. 2. cor. 2.* erit angulus B, vel ei aequalis G A B, duplus anguli B C A, cujus mensura est quinta pars semicirculi; sed idem angulus C A B externus est duplus anguli E: ergo anguli E, & B C A sunt aequales: habent insuper Triangula E C B, & B C A angulum B communem; ergo aequianguli sunt, & proportionalia: ergo ut in toto triangulo E C B, est E B ad B C; ita eadem B C ad A B in triangulo minori A C B; sed A E facta est aequalis C B; ergo ut tota E B ad majus segmentum E A; ita eadem E A ad minus segmentum A B.

Dem. Since the arc DA is quadruple, by supposition, of the arc BA of the Decagon, the fifth part of the semicircle; and the measure of the angle B at the circumference is half of the whole arc DA on which it stands, by Theor. II, [p. 48] bk. 2, cor. 2, the angle B, or the angle GAB equal to it, will be double the angle BCA, whose measure is the fifth part of the semicircle; but the same external angle CAB is double the angle E; therefore the angles E and BCA are equal; the Triangles ECB and BCA have, moreover, the angle B in common; therefore they are equiangular and proportional: therefore, as in the whole triangle ECB is EB to BC, so is the same BC to AB in the smaller triangle ACB; but AE was made equal to CB; therefore, as the whole EB to the greater segment EA, so is the same EA to the smaller segment AB.

> Coroll. Patet, quòd triangulum E C B etiam est Isosceles, & ejus ad basim anguli dupli sunt anguli ad verticem: quod triangulum si in circulo constituatur, & anguli ad basim bifariam dividantur, erit totus circulus in quinque partes aequales divisus, ad Pentagonum inscribendum.

Cor. It is plain that the triangle ECB is also isosceles, and that its angles at the base are double the angle at the vertex: if this triangle is constructed in a circle and the angles at the base are bisected, the whole circle will be divided into five equal parts, for inscribing a Pentagon.

> THEOREMA XI. (Fig. 11.)

Theorem XI. (Fig. 11.)

> *Quadratum lateris Pentagoni, A C, est aequale duobus simul Quadratis lateris, A B, Decagoni, & Hexagoni, F C.* [^48-s1]

The Square of the side of the Pentagon, AC, is equal to the two Squares together of the side AB of the Decagon and of the side FC of the Hexagon. (a)

> [^48-s1]: Eucl. lib. XIII. prop. 10.

[^48-s1]: Eucl. bk. XIII, prop. 10.

> Praepar. Secetur arcus A C Pentagoni graduum 72 bifariam in B; ex quo arcus A B, B C Decagoni erunt singuli graduum 36. Tum ducatur perpendicularis F D, quae secet bifariam lineam, & arcum A B in D: ex quo arcus A D, B D erunt singuli graduum 18, & totus arcus C D graduum 54.

Prep. Let the arc AC of the Pentagon, of 72 degrees, be bisected at B; whence the arcs AB, BC of the Decagon will each be of 36 degrees. Then let a perpendicular FD be drawn which bisects the line and the arc AB at D; whence the arcs AD, BD will each be of 18 degrees, and the whole arc CD of 54 degrees.

> Dem. Quum totus angulus F Pentagoni sit graduum 72, & anguli F C A, F A C aequales dimidii graduum 108; residui ad duos rectos, erunt singuli graduum 54: quemadmodum etiam angulus E F C, cujus arcus D C est graduum 54: ergo quum duo Triangula A F C, & E F C habeant angulos E F C, & C A F aequales, necnon angulum C communem; erunt aequiangula, & proportionalia: ergo ut in majori triangulo est C A ad C F, ita in minori C E F est eadem C F ad C E; ergo Rectangulum, quod fit ex extremis C A C E est aequale Quadrato, quod fit ex media C F semidiametro, seu latere Hexagoni. *Ex Theor. I. cor. 3.*

Dem. Since the whole angle F of the Pentagon is of 72 degrees, and the equal angles FCA, FAC are each of half of 108 degrees, the remainder to two right angles, they will each be of 54 degrees, as is also the angle EFC, whose arc DC is of 54 degrees: therefore, since the two Triangles AFC and EFC have the angles EFC and CAF equal, and also the angle C in common, they will be equiangular and proportional: therefore, as in the larger triangle is CA to CF, so in the smaller, CEF, is the same CF to CE; therefore the Rectangle made of the extremes CA, CE is equal to the Square made of the mean CF, the semidiameter, or side of the Hexagon. By Theor. I, cor. 3.

> Rursum quum D F sit perpendicularis ad A B, quam bifariam dividit, erunt *ex Theor. IV. lib. 1.* latera A E, E B aequalia, & angulus A B E aequalis angulo E A B, cui etiam, propter triangulum Isosceles A B C, est aequalis angulus B C A: ergo duo triangula A B C, & A E B etiam sunt aequiangula, & proportionalia: ergo ut tota A C ad A B, ita eadem A B ad A E: ergo rectangulum factum ex extremis A C, A E est aequale quadrato lateris A B Decagoni.

Again, since DF is perpendicular to AB, which it bisects, the sides AE, EB will be equal, by Theor. IV, bk. 1, and the angle ABE equal to the angle EAB, to which the angle BCA is also equal, because of the isosceles triangle ABC: therefore the two triangles ABC and AEB are also equiangular and proportional: therefore, as the whole AC to AB, so the same AB to AE: therefore the rectangle made of the extremes AC, AE is equal to the square of the side AB of the Decagon.

[p. 49]

> Atqui duo rectangula ex tota A C, & singulis ejus partibus sunt aequalia quadrato totius A C: *ex Theor. X. lib. I. cor. 1.* ergo quadratum lateris Pentagoni A C est aequale quadratis laterum Hexagoni A F, & Decagoni A B.

But the two rectangles made of the whole AC and of each of its parts are equal to the square of the whole AC: by Theor. X, bk. I, cor. 1; therefore the square of the side AC of the Pentagon is equal to the squares of the sides AF of the Hexagon and AB of the Decagon.

> Coroll. Ex quo sequitur, quòd si disponantur ad angulum rectum latus Hexagoni, seu semidiameter, & latus Decagoni; linea subtendens angulum rectum, erit latus Pentagoni, eidem circulo inscribendi.

Cor. From which it follows that, if the side of the Hexagon, or semidiameter, and the side of the Decagon are placed at a right angle, the line subtending the right angle will be the side of the Pentagon to be inscribed in the same circle.

> THEOREMA XII. (Fig. 12.)

Theorem XII. (Fig. 12.)

> *Anguli, & sectores in eodem, aut aequalibus circulis, sunt inter se ut arcus, quibus insistunt.* [^49-s1-2]

Angles and sectors in the same or in equal circles are to one another as the arcs on which they stand. (a)

> [^49-s1-2]: Eucl. lib. VI. prop. 33.

[^49-s1-2]: Eucl. bk. VI, prop. 33.

> Dem. Si arcus C G est aequalis arcui G D, erit angulus C B G aequalis angulo G B D: *ex definit. anguli lib. 1.* ergo totus sector C B G, superpositus, congruet sectori G B D, eritque ei aequalis. Similiter si arcus C G est duplus arcus C P, erit angulus, & sector C B G duplus sectoris C B P, & ejusdem triplus C B M, & C B D quadruplus: ergo semper anguli, & sectores habent eandem rationem, ac arcus ejusdem, aut aequalium circulorum.

Dem. If the arc CG is equal to the arc GD, the angle CBG will be equal to the angle GBD: from the definition of an angle, bk. 1; therefore the whole sector CBG, superposed, will coincide with the sector GBD, and will be equal to it. Likewise, if the arc CG is double the arc CP, the angle and the sector CBG will be double the sector CBP, and CBM triple the same, and CBD quadruple: therefore angles and sectors always have the same ratio as the arcs of the same or of equal circles.

> Coroll. I. Etiam anguli ad circumferentiam in eodem, aut aequalibus circulis habent eamdem rationem, ac arcus, quibus insistunt; quia sunt dimidii angulorum ad centrum. *Ex Theor. II. lib. II. & hujus lib. Axiomate V.*

Cor. I. Angles at the circumference in the same or in equal circles also have the same ratio as the arcs on which they stand, because they are halves of the angles at the center. From Theor. II, bk. II, and Axiom V of this book.

> II. Circumferentiae, Chordae, & Arcus, sunt inter se, ut radii. Nam sint arcus C D, F E similes; ex. gr. sexta pars circuli: quum angulus B sit communis, & latera C B, D B aequalia, sicut etiam aequalia F B, E B, erunt similia triangula, F B E, C B D: ex Theor. [?] *III. cor. 2.* ergo chorda C D ad chordam F E erit, sicut radius C B ad radium F B; & dividendo aequaliter arcus in G, & H, erit C G ad F H, ut C B ab F B: & continuando bissectionem, erit C P ad F R, ut C B ad F B: sed aequalibus arcubus aequales chordae correspondent; *ex Theor. IV. lib. 2.* ergo arcus etiam habent eamdem rationem radiorum; & omnes simul, hoc est circumferentiae, se habent, ut radii.

II. Circumferences, Chords and Arcs are to one another as the radii. For let the arcs CD, FE be similar, e.g. a sixth part of a circle: since the angle B is common, and the sides CB, DB are equal, as are also FB, EB, the triangles FBE, CBD will be similar: by Theor. III, cor. 2; therefore the chord CD will be to the chord FE as the radius CB to the radius FB; and, dividing the arcs equally at G and H, CG will be to FH as CB to FB; and, continuing the bisection, CP will be to FR as CB to FB: but to equal arcs correspond equal chords, by Theor. IV, bk. 2; therefore the arcs also have the same ratio as the radii; and all of them together, that is, the circumferences, are to one another as the radii.

> III. Figurae similes, circulo inscriptae, habent inter se rationem duplicatam radiorum. Nam sint F E, C D latera homologa in similibus figuris, circulo inscriptis: istae habent rationem duplicatam laterum F E ad C D; ergo quum F E ad C D sit ut radius F B ad radium B C, *ex antecedente Coroll* habebunt singula Triangula, & totae figurae, circulo inscriptae, rationem duplicatam radiorum F B, C B. [^49-s2-2]

III. Similar figures inscribed in a circle have to one another the duplicate ratio of the radii. For let FE, CD be homologous sides in similar figures inscribed in a circle: these have the duplicate ratio of the sides FE to CD; therefore, since FE is to CD as the radius FB to the radius BC, by the preceding Cor., the single Triangles, and the whole figures inscribed in the circle, will have the duplicate ratio of the radii FB, CB. (b)

> [^49-s2-2]: Eucl. lib. XII. prop. 1.

[^49-s2-2]: Eucl. bk. XII, prop. 1.

[p. 50]

> IV. Etiam circuli habent duplicatam proportionem radiorum; nam Triangula B C D, & C F E habent duplicatam proportionem radiorum C B, & F B; *ex Coroll. antecedente.* Bissecentur arcus in G, & H. Etiam similia Triangula inscripta C B G, & F B H, habebunt duplicatam radiorum. Similiter facta iterum bissectione in P, & R, M, & N; omnia similia triangula, circulo inscripta, habebunt duplicatam proportionem radiorum: *ex antecedente Coroll.* sed circuli sunt aequales toti summae triangulorum, quae possunt iisdem inscribi: (nam si superesset in circulo spatium; facta bissectione arcus, posset aliud triangulum inscribi; adeoque non intelligeretur inscripta summa omnium triangulorum; contra hypothesim) ergo circuli sunt inter se in duplicata ratione suorum radiorum. *Unde quaecumque dicta sunt in Corollariis Theor. VI. de similibus rectilineis, etiam debent circulis adplicari.* [^50-s1-2]

IV. Circles also have the duplicate proportion of the radii; for the Triangles BCD and CFE have the duplicate proportion of the radii CB and FB, by the preceding Cor. Let the arcs be bisected at G and H. The similar Triangles inscribed, CBG and FBH, will also have the duplicate [proportion] of the radii. Likewise, the bisection being made again at P and R, M and N, all the similar triangles inscribed in the circle will have the duplicate proportion of the radii: by the preceding Cor. But the circles are equal to the whole sum of the triangles that can be inscribed in them (for if any space were left over in the circle, another triangle could be inscribed by bisecting the arc; and so the sum of all the triangles would not be understood to have been inscribed, contrary to the hypothesis); therefore circles are to one another in the duplicate ratio of their radii. Hence whatever was said in the Corollaries of Theor. VI on similar rectilinear figures must also be applied to circles. (a)

> [^50-s1-2]: Prop. 2.

[^50-s1-2]: Prop. 2.

> Quemadmodum autem Superficies, quae constant ex duplici dimensione, latitudine scilicet, & longitudine, si similes sint, habent duplicatam proportionem Diametrorum, seu laterum homologorum; ita eorumdem habent triplicatam proportionem corpora similia; ut duae integrae sphaerae; quum fiant ex triplici dimensione, latitudine nimirum, longitudine, & profunditate. Ex. gr. Si Diameter terrae sit quadrupla Diametri Lunaris, erit superficies Terrae quater quadrupla, hoc est sexdecupla superficiei Lunaris: & totum corpus Terraqueum erit quater sexdecuplum, hoc est sexagies, & quater, Majus corpore Lunari. Similiter quum Veneris diameter adpareat decima pars diametri Solaris, ejus circulus adparens erit centesima pars totius circuli Solaris; adeoque ubi Venus inter nos, & Solem interponatur, quasi macula in Sole adparebit. Atque haec qui noverit, aditum habet ad naturales omnes disciplinas apertissimum.

Moreover, just as Surfaces, which consist of a twofold dimension, namely breadth and length, have, if they are similar, the duplicate proportion of the Diameters, or of the homologous sides, so similar bodies, such as two whole spheres, have the triplicate proportion of the same, since they are made of a threefold dimension, namely breadth, length and depth. For example, if the Diameter of the earth is quadruple the Diameter of the Moon, the surface of the Earth will be four times quadruple, that is, sixteen times the surface of the Moon; and the whole terraqueous body will be four times sixteen, that is, sixty-four times, greater than the body of the Moon. Likewise, since the diameter of Venus appears as the tenth part of the diameter of the Sun, its apparent circle will be the hundredth part of the whole circle of the Sun; and so, when Venus comes between us and the Sun, it will appear like a spot on the Sun. And whoever knows these things has the most open access to all the natural disciplines.

PART IV.

## ELEMENTA PHYSICES. — ELEMENTS OF PHYSICS

## PROLEGÓMENA. — PROLEGOMENA

> §. I.

§. I.

> De Physica ejusque scópo.

On Physics and its scope.

> 1 Disciplinae illius tractationem ordimur, cujus munus est naturam ejusque ordinem, ac leges, vires item, atque effectus naturales inquírire, singulorum oríginem, causas investigáre, quae proinde *Physica* nuncupatur, eaque definiri potest: *Facultas, quae circa corpus naturale, quátenus naturale est, versatur.* Dicitur etiam *Scientia naturae*, cognitio scilicèt rerum earum quae sensibibilem mundi máchinam constituunt. Physicus namque totus in eo est, inquit Claris. *Gassendus*, [^1-s1-2] ut explóret tùm ipsum, rerum omnium complexum, tùm quamlibet speciatim rem, disquirendo quantum fas est; an, & ex quibus principiis constet, an, & â quibus producta causis, & ob [p. 2] quem finem effecta, an, & quibus viribus, proprietatibusque donata, ceteraque hujusmodi, quae si perspecta fuerint, tùm res, rerumque natura perspectae, censentur.

e begin the treatment of that discipline whose task is to in1 W quire into nature and its order and laws, and likewise its forces and natural effects, and to investigate the origin and causes of each single thing; which is therefore called Physics, and may be defined: The faculty which is concerned with natural body, insofar as it is natural. It is also called the Science of nature, namely the knowledge of those things which make up the sensible machine of the world. For the physicist, says the illustrious Gassendi (a), is wholly occupied in exploring both that complex of all things itself and each thing in particular, by inquiring, so far as is permitted, whether it exists, and of what principles it consists, whether, and by what causes it has been produced, and for [p. 2] what end it was made, whether, and with what forces and properties it is endowed, and other things of this kind; and once these have been seen through, then both the thing and the nature of things are deemed to be thoroughly known.

> [^1-s1-2]: In Proem. Physices.

[^1-s1-2]: In the Proem to the Physics.

> 2 Díximus in definitione, Physicam versari *circa corpus naturale prout naturale est*, nimirùm prout sensibilium adfectionum subjectum est, earumque omnium mutationum capax, quas in mundo fieri conspicimus: & per hoc distinguitur *corpus naturale* â *Mathemático*, ipsaque *Physica* â *Geometria*, quae itidem circa corpus versatur.

2 We said in the definition that Physics is concerned with natural body insofar as it is natural, namely insofar as it is the subject of sensible affections and capable of all those changes which we observe taking place in the world; and by this natural body is distinguished from the mathematical, and Physics itself from Geometry, which is likewise concerned with body.

> 3 Objecta Physicae sunt *Corpus*, *Spatium*, & *Motus*, quid verò per haec intelligitur paucis indicábo. Quamcumque rem oculis intueri, vel manu comprehéndere, & palpáre possumus, quaeque pressioni resistit, *Corpus* adpelamus. Extensionem universi, in quo corpora ponuntur, & liberè moventur, *Spatium*. Translationem corporis ex una in aliam spatii partem, vocamus *Motum*.

3 The objects of Physics are Body, Space and Motion; what is understood by these I shall indicate in a few words. Whatever thing we can behold with the eyes, or grasp and feel with the hand, and which resists pressure, we call Body. The extension of the universe, in which bodies are placed and move freely, we call Space. The transfer of a body from one part of space into another we call Motion.

> 4 Omnes situs, motus, mutationes, & actiones corporum, quae sensibus observantur, sive uno, sive pluribus, adpelantur *Phaenomena*. Omnia corpora secundum certas leges, vel regulas movéri constat. Lex autem naturae, est norma illa secundum quam Deus voluit certos motus semper, id est in omnibus occasionibus péragi, hinc ex. gr. quaelibet planta suum prodúcit semen, unde iterum similis, non diversi, renascitur planta; hinc unumquodque animal ex sese sui simile gignit. Corpus grave sibi liberè commissum spontè cadit deorsum. Ope harum legum intelligimus quid *naturalitèr*, quid *miraculosè* contingit. Nam naturalia sunt phaenómena, quae constanter eodem modo observantur, positis corporibus in similibus occasionibus; miracula autem sunt, quum phaenómena legibus istis contraria eveniunt.

4 All the positions, motions, changes and actions of bodies which are observed by the senses, whether by one or by several, are called Phenomena. It is agreed that all bodies are moved according to certain laws or rules. A law of nature, moreover, is that norm according to which God willed certain motions to be performed always, that is, on all occasions; hence, e.g., every plant produces its own seed, from which a like plant, not a different one, is born again; hence every animal begets from itself one like itself. A heavy body freely left to itself falls downward of its own accord. By means of these laws we understand what happens naturally and what miraculously. For those phenomena are natural which are observed constantly in the same manner when bodies are placed on similar occasions; but there are miracles when phenomena occur contrary to those laws.

> 5 Si verò aliquid évenit secundum naturae leges, sed praeter sólitum, seu contra id quod tali naturae debetur, vocatur *nonnaturale*. Ut febris, quae quidem ita palpitationem & cordis & arteriarum ágitat, ut dicantur esse in statu *nonnaturali*. Quod súperat naturae vires ac leges, *supernaturale* vocatur. Ita quod Sol ex. gr. dum est in meridie ad orientem retrò volvatur, est supernaturale, quia nullis naturae viribus id éffici potest, ut évidens est. Quaedam verò res sunt, quae etiamsi supra naturam sint, tamen nonnisi ab homine *bona Philosophia* exculto, benèque exercitato judicari potest, an naturalia sint, an praeter naturam. Hinc *de rebus insoléntibus cautè judicare debemus, ne ea pro miraculis habeamus, quae talia non sunt.* Utilissimum est hoc mónitum ut occurramus ineptae multitudini indoctórum, & verò etiam eorum, qui cétera docti, tamen, quòd *bonae Philosophiae* expertes sint, proni sunt, qui gárrulae cuivis muliérculae miraculum aliquod narranti fidem habeant.

5 But if something happens according to the laws of nature, yet beyond what is usual, or contrary to what is owed to such a nature, it is called nonnatural: as a fever, which so agitates the beating both of the heart and of the arteries that they are said to be in a nonnatural state. What surpasses the forces and laws of nature is called supernatural. Thus if the Sun, e.g., while it is at noon, were rolled back toward the east, this is supernatural, because it cannot be brought about by any forces of nature, as is evident. There are, however, certain things which, even though they are above nature, can nevertheless be judged only by a man cultivated in good Philosophy and well practiced, whether they are natural or beyond nature. Hence we must judge cautiously of unusual things, lest we take for miracles things which are not such. This warning is most useful, so that we may meet the foolish multitude of the unlearned, and indeed also of those who, though learned in other matters, yet, because they are without good Philosophy, are prone to give credence to any chattering little woman who tells of some miracle.

[p. 3]

> §. II.

§. II.

> Utilitas Physicae.

The usefulness of Physics. 6

> 6 Dignitas certè ac praestantia Physicae vel ex eo intelligi satis superque potest, quod disciplinae hujus studium tantumdem pateat, quantum ipsa natura. Et sanè ¿quis negèt longè dignissimum esse contemplari modò caelorum amplitudinem, corporum certa in iis lege decurrentium molem, jam in tellúris abdita se penetráre, metallorum, lápidum oríginem, plantarum, animalium varietatem penè infinitam scrutari, ipsam denique in hac rerum universitate relucentem Dei majestatem considerare? Unde *Seneca* [^3-s1-3] hanc tanti fecit contemplationem, ut dícere non dubitáverit: *nisi ad haec* (naturae secretiora) *admitterer, non fuerat opere pretium nasci.*

The dignity, certainly, and the excellence of Physics can be understood amply enough even from this alone, that the study of this discipline extends as far as nature itself. And indeed, who will deny that it is by far the worthiest thing now to contemplate the vastness of the heavens and the mass of the bodies running their courses in them by a fixed law, now to penetrate into the hidden recesses of the earth, to search out the origin of metals and stones and the almost infinite variety of plants and animals, and finally to consider the majesty of God shining forth in this universe of things? Hence Seneca (b) valued this contemplation so highly that he did not hesitate to say: unless I were admitted to these things (the more secret things of nature), it would not have been worth while to be born.

> [^3-s1-3]: Quaest. Nat. Lib. 1. Praefat.

[^3-s1-3]: Natural Questions, bk. 1, Preface.

> 7 Jocunditas deinde & suavissima voluptas hoc è naturae studio enascitur. ¿Quem enim non delectet scientia, in qua nunquam deest occasio, novos, eosque mirabiles effectus, velut tótidem summi rerum Conditoris testimonia luculenta & inveniendi & contemplandi? ¿Quis animalium innumerorum, terrestrium, aquatilium, volatilium, insectorum genera quàm diversissima, rerum ceterarum miram varietatem, pulchritudinem, ad certos usus habilitatem sine ingenua animi voluptate contueri possit? ¿Quid quod Physico jocundissimum praebeant spectaculum ea quoque, quae imperítos formídine complère solent? Ita dum vulgus rude inani metu eclipseos concútitur, Philosophi

7 Then delight and the sweetest pleasure spring from this study of nature. For whom would a science not delight in which there is never lacking the occasion both of discovering and of contemplating new and wonderful effects, as so many shining testimonies of the supreme Maker of things? Who could behold the most diverse kinds of innumerable animals, terrestrial, aquatic, flying, insects, the wondrous variety of the other things, their beauty and their fitness for definite uses, without a noble pleasure of mind? What of the fact that those very things which commonly fill the unskilled with dread afford the physicist a most delightful spectacle? Thus, while the rude multitude is shaken by an empty fear of eclipses, the Philosophers

> *Hunc solem & stellas; & decedentia certis Tempora momentis, sunt qui formidine nulla Imbúti spectent.* [^3-s2]

This sun, and the stars, and the seasons that pass at fixed Moments, there are some who, touched by no dread, Can behold. (c)

> [^3-s2]: Horat. Lib. 1. Ep. 6.

[^3-s2]: Horace, bk. 1, Ep. 6.

> 8 Quin gaudent amoénam tam sibi scenam aperiri [?], & occasionem parari, qua naturam caelestium corporum expendant. Physicus Cometarum facies aliis horríficas, tranquillo animo intuetur. *Omnium rerum*, (inquit *Tullius* [^3-s3]) *natura cognita, levamur superstitione, liberamur mortis metu, non conturbamur ignoratione rerum, è qua ipsa horribiles existunt saepè formídines.*

8 Nay, they rejoice that so pleasant a scene is opened to them, and an occasion afforded of weighing the nature of the heavenly bodies. The physicist beholds with a tranquil mind the faces of Comets, which to others are horrifying. By the knowledge of the nature of all things (says Tully (d)) we are relieved of superstition, freed from the fear of death, and not disturbed by ignorance of things, from which very ignorance horrible terrors often arise.

> [^3-s3]: Lib. 1. de Finib. cap. 19.

[^3-s3]: Bk. 1 On Ends, ch. 19.

> 9 His accedunt emolumenta plurima, quae è Physica per disciplinas reliquas omnemque vitae usum sese diffundunt. ¿Quae enim emolumenta in saluberrimam medendi artem è Physica profluunt? ¿quántas accessiones scientia nautica accepit usu acus magneticae, astrorum observatis motibus, rosae nauticae inventione? Praetereo [p. 4] utilitates, quas diversi generis horologia, tubi optici, microscopia perspicilla, aliaque innumera; quae Physicae in acceptis referenda sunt in vitam humanam praebent.

9 To these are added very many benefits, which spread from Physics through the remaining disciplines and every use of life. For what benefits flow from Physics into the most salutary art of healing? What great accessions has nautical science received from the use of the magnetic needle, from the observed motions of the stars, from the invention of the mariner’s compass card? I pass over the [p. 4] the advantages which clocks of various kinds, telescopes, microscopes, spectacles and innumerable other things, which must be credited to Physics, afford to human life.

## §. III. — §. III

> De Peripateticorum Physica.

On the Physics of the Peripatetics. 10

> 10 Hujusmodi verò & innumerae aliae utilitates, quae tacitus praetereo frustra in Peripateticorum Schola requiras, si adpelare possumus Physicam disciplinam illam in qua pléraque passím adversus naturae observationem, adversus perspicua experimenta tradi consueverunt. Sed audire juvat Mathematicum Physicumque egregium *Thomam Vincentium Tosca*, Hispaniae nostrae decus, ac Valentini Congregationis Oratorii ornamentum praeclarissimum. Hispánum hominem audiant ii, qui sputacílicis praejudiciis imbúti falsò putant Recentiorum Physicam ab *haereticis* tantum éxcoli, nefasque judicant studiosae juventúti propóni & commendari: genus hominum natum ad perniciem, interitumque bonarum artium.
