Beings, assuredly, are not to be multiplied beyond necessity; likewise, what can be done by fewer things ought not to be done by more, as all Philosophers agree. Wherefore neither the principles of things nor the causes of effects are to be multiplied, unless an undoubted reason demands it, as was said above [§. 20.]. Axiom III. That system is to be judged the better which unfolds the more of the things that must be taken into consideration among Physicists. For the whole of Physics is engaged in this: that the affections, effects, etc. of natural things be explained, as many of them as possible, and as well as possible.

[p. 20]

> 33 In adlata hujus axiomatis ratione fundatur Axioma IV. *Systema illud praeferendum est ceteris, quod non modò generalibus notionibus utitur ad explicanda rerum phaenómena, sed speciatim etiam naturam corporum, adfectiones, & causas effectuum quoad ejus fieri potest perspicuè, ac dilucide proponit.* Ideae enim generales pariunt duntaxat notitiam obscuram rerum particularium, resque naturales optimè non explicant, quod munus est Physicae. Hinc, si quaerenti ex. gr. ¿cur calor rarefaciat corpora, frigus adstringat? respondeatur: hanc esse caloris, hanc frigoris *naturam*, haud dignum Philosopho responsum datur. Similiter, interrogantem de variis naturae effectibus, generali *qualitatis* termino expedire, parvi est, atque humilis ingenii, ut Clariss. *Rohault* [^20-s1-3] loquitur. Hinc consequitur Axioma V. *Illa doctrina reliquis praestat, quae nihil adserit, vel ponit, quod cogitatione comprehendi, aut explicari satis nequeat.* Physica enim quantum fieri potest exhibére nobis debet naturam ad vires intelligentiae nostrae adcommodatam, & sublatis involúcris naturam rerum explicare.

33 On the reason given for this axiom is founded Axiom IV. That system is to be preferred to the rest which not only uses general notions to explain the phenomena of things, but also sets forth in particular the nature of bodies, their affections, and the causes of effects, as far as this can be done, perspicuously and lucidly. For general ideas produce only an obscure knowledge of particular things, and do not explain natural things in the best way, which is the task of Physics. Hence, if to someone asking, e.g., why does heat rarefy bodies and cold contract them? the answer is given that this is the nature of heat, and that the nature of cold, a response unworthy of a Philosopher is given. Similarly, to dispatch someone who asks about the various effects of nature with the general term quality is the mark of a small and lowly wit, as the most illustrious Rohault (u) says. Hence follows Axiom V. That doctrine excels the rest which asserts or posits nothing that cannot be sufficiently grasped in thought or explained. For Physics, as far as this can be done, ought to exhibit nature to us accommodated to the powers of our intelligence, and to explain the nature of things with its wrappings removed.

> [^20-s1-3]: In Phys. Praefat.

[^20-s1-3]: In the Preface to his Physics.

> 34 Axioma VI. *Systema illud in Physica obtineat necesse est, quod rerum naturalium doctrinam adcommodatè ad naturam ac rationem disciplinae hujus persequitur.* Hùc quoque ceu regulae quaedam aliae perquam utiles revocari possunt sequentes. I. *Non est recurrendum ad causam primam seu Deum, quando haberi potest causa secunda.* II. *Dum nobis ignotae sunt causae sensibiles effectuum, insensibilis quaedam, & perinde ignota haud quaquam adstruatur.* III. *In his quaestionibus, aut immorandum non est, aut ab iis tractandis omninò abstinendum, quarum solutio vel nunquam reperietur, vel si fortè reperiatur nihilo nos doctiores reddit.* IV. *Idem dicendum de iis controversiis, quae ab imperscrutabili Dei consilio pendent, & illi soli cognitae sunt, qui fecit omnia,* quae proinde rectè ait *Tertullianus*, *aut à Deo discenda esse, aut à nullo*. His constitutis.

34 Axiom VI. That system must prevail in Physics which pursues the doctrine of natural things in a manner suited to the nature and method of this discipline. To this may also be referred, as certain further rules, the following, which are extremely useful. I. One must not have recourse to the first cause, or God, when a second cause can be had. II. While the sensible causes of effects are unknown to us, let no insensible and equally unknown cause whatever be asserted. III. On those questions one must not dwell, or must altogether abstain from treating them, whose solution either will never be found, or, if perchance it is found, makes us none the more learned. IV. The same is to be said of those controversies which depend on the inscrutable counsel of God and are known to Him alone who made all things, and which therefore, as Tertullian rightly says, are to be learned either from God or from no one. These things being established,

> CAPUT V.

CHAPTER V.

> Refutatur Systéma metaphysicum Peripateticorum.

The metaphysical system of the Peripatetics is refuted.

> 35 Dico primo: principia corporis naturalis, prout ab Aristotele exponuntur, nihil ferè ad Philosophiam naturalem adipiscendam deserviunt. Veritas hujus adsertionis satis patebit, si consideremus corporis naturalis principia, materiam scilicet, & formam nonnisi [p. 21] metaphysicè & in abstracto fuisse ab Aristotele adsignata, & cuncta, quae de eisdem adserit, & determinat, solummodo esse metaphisicas quasdam praecisiones, quibus physicae res nunquam satis exponuntur, itaque ad cognitionem particularium corporum, diversorumque phaenomenorum explicationem nihil conferunt, proindeque nihil ferè ad Physicam adipiscendam deserviunt, nec in Physicae systemate locum habere possunt ex *Axiom. VI.*

say, first: the principles of natural body, as they are set forth by Aristotle, 35 I serve almost nothing toward acquiring natural Philosophy. The truth of this assertion will be sufficiently plain if we consider that the principles of natural body, namely matter and form, were only metaphysically and [p. 21] and in the abstract assigned by Aristotle, and that everything he asserts and determines about them is merely certain metaphysical abstractions, by which physical things are never sufficiently set forth; and so they contribute nothing to the knowledge of particular bodies or to the explanation of the various phenomena, and therefore serve almost nothing toward acquiring Physics, nor can they have a place in the system of Physics, by Axiom VI.

> 36 Quod ut clarius fiat hunc casum supponite. Quaerat aliquis ex. gr. ¿ex quibus, ceu intrinsecis principiis domus coalescat? Respondeam autem ego coalescere ex materia & forma domus: materiam autem esse id ex quo domus fit, formam verò esse actum, quo materia determinata est, ut domum componat. Hac certè responsione verum dixi, sed interrogantem doctiorem non feci, ideoque meritò rursum inquiret ¿quid nempè sit materia illa ex qua facta sit domus, quidve similiter sit actus ille, qui forma domus adpelatur. Non ergo ex Aristotelis Schola doctiores evadimus in iis, quae ad rerum naturalium primordia spectant, proindeque metaphysicum Peripateticorum systema nihil ferè ad Philosophiam naturalem adipiscendam deservit, non ex eo quod falsum sit, sed è contrario quod *nimis verum*, nihilque doceat praeter ea quae ignorari non possunt. ¿Quis enim unquam dubitare potest ex materia, & forma omnia composita esse? : at postquam haec didicimus nullius phaenomeni causam reddere possumus: nihil ergò deservit ad Physicam perdiscendam.

36 To make this clearer, suppose the following case. Let someone ask, e.g., from what, as from intrinsic principles, does a house come together? And let me answer that it comes together from the matter and the form of the house: that the matter, moreover, is that from which the house is made, and the form the act by which the matter is determined to compose a house. With this answer I have certainly spoken the truth, but I have not made the questioner more learned; and therefore he will rightly ask again what, namely, that matter is from which the house has been made, or likewise what that act is which is called the form of the house. We do not, therefore, come away from the school of Aristotle more learned in those things which pertain to the first beginnings of natural things; and therefore the metaphysical system of the Peripatetics serves almost nothing toward acquiring natural Philosophy, not because it is false, but on the contrary because it is too true, and teaches nothing beyond those things which cannot be unknown. For who can ever doubt that all composites are made of matter and form? But after we have learned these things we can give the cause of no phenomenon: therefore it serves nothing toward learning Physics thoroughly.

> 37 Dico secundo: Systema Peripateticum de principiis corporis naturalis negligendum omninò est in Physica. Prob: nam si in Philosophia naturali systema illud rectè negligitur, in quo res naturales, aut non explicantur, vel ignotum per aequè ignotum proponitur, Peripateticum certè systema locum in Physica habere non potest *ex Axiom. III. & IV.* ac proinde negligendum omnino est. Prima hujus propositionis pars, licet à nobis probata jam superiùs sit, plenius & ad evidentiam usque probatur. Pone etenim in quaestionem venire ¿cur ignis ex. gr. certis, quas experimur qualitatibus donetur, aqua ex adverso alias adfectiones sortiatur? Non alium responsum à Peripatetico excipies, quam hoc: videlicet eo ex capite, ista cónsequi, quod ignis aliam formam substantialem habeat, aqua aliam; quod si quis instet quaerendo ¿quid formae illae sint, qua lege diversos effectus producant, diversa exposcant accidentia? Reponunt hi philosophi continuò: *naturam* hanc esse formae ignis, ut tales exigat adfectiones, aliam contra esse *naturam* formae ipsius aquae, quod quidem est contra *Axiom. IV.*

37 I say secondly: the Peripatetic system of the principles of natural body is to be altogether neglected in Physics. Proof: for if in natural Philosophy that system is rightly neglected in which natural things either are not explained or the unknown is set forth through the equally unknown, the Peripatetic system certainly cannot have a place in Physics, by Axioms III and IV, and therefore it is to be altogether neglected. The first part of this proposition, although it has already been proved by us above, is proved more fully and to the point of evidence. For suppose the question arises why fire, e.g., is endowed with certain qualities which we experience, while water, on the other hand, obtains other affections? You will receive no other answer from a Peripatetic than this: namely, that these things follow from the fact that fire has one substantial form, water another; and if someone insists by asking what those forms are, by what law they produce diverse effects and demand diverse accidents? these philosophers reply at once that this is the nature of the form of fire, that it requires such affections, and that on the contrary the nature of the form of water itself is another; which is indeed against Axiom IV.

> 38 Secunda pars propositionis constat, nam dum â Peripatetico quaeritur ¿cur calor & frigus ex. gr. diversam sensationem producant? non aliam indigitant causam, quam *qualitates* has diversas, omninò esse *diversae naturae*. ¿Quis verò negabit his loquendi modulis rerum phaenomena neutiquam explicari, & [p. 22] ignotam controversiae materiam responso perinde ignoto expediri? ergo in Peripatetico systemate ignotum per aeque ignotum proponitur, generalibusque utitur notionibus ad explicanda rerum phaenomena contra *Axiom. IV.* ac proinde in Physica negligendum omnino est.

38 The second part of the proposition is evident; for when a Peripatetic is asked why heat and cold, e.g., produce a diverse sensation? they point to no other cause than that these qualities are diverse, of an altogether diverse nature. But who will deny that by these little ways of speaking the phenomena of things are by no means explained, and that the unknown [p. 22] matter of the controversy is dispatched with an answer just as unknown? Therefore in the Peripatetic system the unknown is set forth through the equally unknown, and it uses general notions to explain the phenomena of things, contrary to Axiom IV, and therefore it is to be altogether neglected in Physics.

> 39 Adhaec dum Peripatetici in eo sunt unicè ut formas substantiales interíre, atque generari propugnent ¿qua ratione novam formam substantialem ignis ex. gr. exoriri commonstrabunt, iisdem omnibus manentibus, quibus constitutis eadem forma destrui solet. *Eadem est candela*, (verbis utor Clariss. *Casati* [^22-s1-2]) *cum eodem ardente ellychnio flammam edens: insufflas, flamma perit: iterum insufflas, flamma reviviscit: ortus & interitus eadem est causa, scilicet idem flatus, aedem dispositiones, idem subjectum, quod flamma privatur, & flammam recipit*. Praetereo quam plurima argumenta adversus systema Peripateticum, speciatim ea, quibus *Henricus Wiber* materiam, & formam valide exagitat. [^22-s2] Systema hoc haudquaquam veluti ab Aristotele excogitatum spectamus, sed *Peripateticum vulgare* dicimus, quod fortasse aptiùs *Arabicum* ab Arábibus Stagyritae interpretibus nuncupari posset. Aristotelis quippe mentem longè aliam fuisse multis ostendunt *Gassendus*, [^22-s3] *Sturmius*, [^22-s4] *Stephanus Pace*, [^22-s5] alliique.

39 Moreover, while the Peripatetics are intent solely on maintaining that substantial forms perish and are generated, by what reasoning will they show that a new substantial form, e.g. of fire, arises while all the same things remain by which, once they are established, the same form is wont to be destroyed? The candle is the same (I use the words of the most illustrious Casati (x)), giving out flame with the same burning wick: you blow on it, the flame perishes; you blow again, the flame comes back to life: the cause of the arising and of the perishing is the same, namely the same breath, the same dispositions, the same subject, which is deprived of flame and receives flame. I pass over a great many arguments against the Peripatetic system, especially those by which Henricus Wiber vigorously assails matter and form (y). We by no means regard this system as devised by Aristotle, but call it the common Peripatetic system, which might perhaps more aptly be named Arabic, after the Arabs, the interpreters of the Stagirite. For that Aristotle’s mind was far different is shown at length by Gassendi (z), Sturm [a], Stephanus Pace (b), and others.

[^22-s1-2]: De igne, Diss. 9.

[^22-s2]: Princip. Philos. AntiPeripat.

[^22-s3]: Phys., bk. 7, sect. 1, ch. 3.

## CAPUT VI. — CHAPTER VI

> Systémata Artificiosa. Exponitur, & refutatur Atomistarum systéma.

Artificial Systems. The system of the Atomists is set forth and refuted.

> 40 *Petrus Gassendus* Vir célebris, & Philosophiae studiis mirificè commendatus, & cum eo tota *Atomistarum* Schola, censet unicum rerum principium esse atomos. *Atomus* autem juxta hos Philosophos est corpusculum inséctile, sive indivisíbile, figuratum tamen, trinèque mensurabile, extensum, solidum, & impenetrabile. Hae atomi sunt materia prima juxta ipsos. Figura in his, eaque diversissima est, ut aliquae habeant figuram *cubi*, *sphaerae*, *cylindri*, [p. 23] *pirámidis*, *prismatis*, &c. Phaenómena, & mutationes corporum naturalium per explicatas átomos exponunt. Hoc est antiquissimum *Epicúri* systema á Clariss. *Gassendo* renovatum. Sed plurima quae in Deum, Providentiam, Religionemque Epicúrus impiè congesserat expunxit, ceteraque uberrimè exornavit. Etenim Epicúrus posuit atomos aeternas, increatas, infinitas.

ierre Gassendi, a celebrated man, wonderfully commended for his studies 40 Pin Philosophy, and with him the whole school of the Atomists, holds that the only principle of things is atoms. An atom, moreover, according to these Philosophers, is a corpuscle that cannot be cut, or indivisible, yet having figure and measurable in three dimensions, extended, solid and impenetrable. These atoms are prime matter, according to them. There is figure in them, and that most diverse, so that some have the figure of a cube, a sphere, a cylinder, a pyramid, a [p. 23] a prism, etc. They set forth the phenomena and changes of natural bodies through the atoms thus explained. This is the most ancient system of Epicurus, renewed by the most illustrious Gassendi. But he expunged the very many things which Epicurus had impiously heaped up against God, Providence and Religion, and adorned the rest most richly. For Epicurus posited atoms eternal, uncreated, infinite.

> 41 Verúm *Gassendus*, & cum eo Atomistae Recentiores, Epicúrum errasse fatentur, dum átomos ipsas increatas, per se mobiles, admisit, atque illud etiam pérditae insaniae in Epicúro fuisse demonstrat, quod mundum ex fortuito atomórum concursu génitum fore, nulloque Divinae mentis consilio, vel Providentia regi credíderit; nam ut est á Cicerone observatum: nihil tam arcànum, admirabile, divinumque est, quod non apud istos atomorum turba conficiat. [^23-s1-2] Etsi itaque negari non possit plurima in Atomistarum sententia felicitèr, atque utilitèr esse excogitata, Atomistarum tamen systéma, sive hypothesis universè recipienda non videtur, quùm incertum prorsús sit, an ejusmodi corpuscula dari possint, quae extensa sint, simulque indivisibilia, proindeque est contra *Axiom. V.*

41 But Gassendi, and with him the more recent Atomists, acknowledge that Epicurus erred when he admitted the atoms themselves as uncreated and mobile of themselves; and he shows that this too was a mark of desperate madness in Epicurus, that he believed the world to have been generated from a fortuitous concourse of atoms and to be governed by no counsel of the Divine mind, or Providence; for, as Cicero observed, there is nothing so hidden, so admirable and divine, that among these men the throng of atoms does not accomplish it (c). Although, therefore, it cannot be denied that a great many things in the opinion of the Atomists have been devised happily and usefully, yet the system, or hypothesis, of the Atomists does not seem acceptable as a whole, since it is altogether uncertain whether there can be corpuscles of this kind which are extended and at the same time indivisible; and therefore it is contrary to Axiom V.

> [^23-s1-2]: Tusc. I. c. 2.

[^23-s1-2]: Tusculan Disputations I, ch. 2.

## CAPUT VII. — CHAPTER VII

> Exponitur Cartesii Systéma, & refutatur.

The system of Descartes is set forth and refuted.

> 42 Primò ponit *Cartesius* [^23-s2] creatam à Deo materiam simplicem, homogeneam, trine mensurabilem, & undìque extensam. Hanc materiam divisit Deus in particulas inter se quàmproximè aequales, cubicas, ita ut contactu immediato, ac omnem vacuum excludente se omni ex parte contingerent. Pártibus sic divisis Cónditor Deus impressit vehementissimum motum duplicem, unum quo singulae portiones circa proprium centrum, alterum quo plures simul circa commune centrum moverentur. Portionibus materiae ita in girum actis *Cartesius* à *vertendo* nomen *vórticum* adtribuit, atque hinc, *secundò* docet ex agitatione illa, motuque duplici materiae adtrítis particularum ángulis, *tria* diversi generis provenisse *elementa*, quorum *primum* minutissimas continet partes, *secundum* glóbulos, in quos quadrátae particulae ablatis ángulis sunt conformatae: *tertium* sunt partes crassiores, & variis ángulis irregulares

irst, Descartes (d) posits a matter created by God, simple, homogeneous, 42 F measurable in three dimensions, and extended everywhere. This matter God divided into particles as nearly equal to one another as possible, cubical, so that they touched one another on every side with an immediate contact excluding all void. On the parts thus divided God the Creator impressed a most vehement twofold motion: one by which the individual portions were moved about their own center, the other by which several together were moved about a common center. To the portions of matter thus driven round in a circle Descartes gave the name of vortices, from vertendo [turning]; and hence, secondly, he teaches that from that agitation and twofold motion of matter, the angles of the particles having been worn away, three elements of different kinds arose, of which the first contains the most minute parts; the second, globules, into which the square particles were shaped once their angles were removed; the third consists of the coarser parts, irregular, with various angles.

> [^23-s2]: Princip. part. 3. n. 45.

[^23-s2]: Principles, pt. 3, no. 45.

> 43 Quod ut ad vivum exhibeant Cartesii Intérpretes in [p. 24] *Tornatóris* Officinam animum advertunt, ubi ex cubo rapidissimè circumacto globus effingitur: ut enim ex ligni cúbici adtrítu trium specierum partes adpárent, aliae nimírum minutissimae, rursús quaedam majores, sed irregulares, nec figura, nec mole similes, ac tandem ipse globus efformatur; ita primum elementum minimis illis partibus, tertium majoribus, secundum globo ipsi cómparant.

43 To exhibit this to the life, the interpreters of Descartes turn their attention to the turner’s [p. 24] workshop, where a globe is shaped out of a cube turned round very rapidly: for just as, from the wearing of a cubic piece of wood, parts of three kinds appear — some, namely, most minute; others again larger, but irregular, alike neither in figure nor in bulk; and finally the globe itself is formed — so they compare the first element to those smallest parts, the third to the larger ones, the second to the globe itself.

> 44 *Tertiò* statuit tria haec elementa materiam esse, ex qua corpora omnia réliqua componuntur, ex primo quidem Sol, & Stellae fixae: ex secundo corpora diáphana, fluidaque omnia, ex tertio corpora opáca, ut sunt terra, aër, reliquaque corpora mixta. Tertium elementum vocant etiam *materiam striatam*, id est, crassiorem. Sed jam Cartesianos vortices, utpotè ad phaenomenorum explicationem ímpares, ineptosque paucis rejiciamus.

44 Thirdly, he lays down that these three elements are the matter of which all the remaining bodies are composed: from the first, indeed, the Sun and the fixed Stars; from the second, all diaphanous and fluid bodies; from the third, opaque bodies, such as earth, air, and the remaining mixed bodies. The third element they also call striated matter, that is, coarser matter. But let us now reject in a few words the Cartesian vortices, as unequal to the explanation of the phenomena, and unfit.

> 45 Dico igitur: Cosmogonia Cartesii (hoc est mundi efformatio á Cartesio excogitata) sive systéma vórticum locum in Physica habere nequit. Prob. etenim in hac hypothesi multa inter se parum cohaerent, atque adeò naturae phaenómena connexo ordine explicari in eo non possunt: ergo. Antec. constat. In primis namque systéma hoc in primo illo elementorum trium exortu deficit. Si enim vacuum nullum, ut vult Cartesius vel Divínitus est possíbile, quùm materia in partes cúbicas divisa fuit, earumque partium singulae, circa proprium axem, & universi centrum movebantur, cóncipi certè non potest, quomodo spatium aliquod vacuum inter ejusmodi partes, tunc non interciperetur, quod nulla scilicet subtíli materia tunc repleretur, quùm non dum haec ex angulorum adtritione prodiisset.

45 I say, therefore: the Cosmogony of Descartes (that is, the formation of the world devised by Descartes), or the system of vortices, cannot have a place in Physics. Proof: for in this hypothesis many things cohere poorly with one another, and so the phenomena of nature cannot be explained in it in a connected order: therefore. The antecedent is evident. For in the first place this system fails at that first origin of the three elements. For if no void is possible, as Descartes would have it, even by Divine power, then, when matter was divided into cubic parts and each of those parts was moving about its own axis and about the center of the universe, it certainly cannot be conceived how some empty space would not then be intercepted between parts of this kind, a space, namely, that would not then be filled by any subtle matter, since this had not yet come forth from the wearing of the angles.

> 46 Praeterea verò: omninò necessarium videtur, ut rapidissimo, jugique motu, & adtritu elementa haec á Cartesio excogitata suam naturam amítterent saltim post aliquot secula: ex. gr. globuli in materiam subtílem, & partes ramosae heterogenae tertii elementi in glóbulos tandem abirent. Ergo vel compensationem quandam fieri oportebat explicatu difficíllimam, & nusquam (quod víderim) á Cartesio aptis naturae legibus explicatam; vel mundi máchina corruisse post annos plus jam sex mille debuit. ¿Quid ad haec Cartesiani?

46 Moreover, it seems altogether necessary that, through so very rapid and continual a motion and wearing, these elements devised by Descartes should lose their nature, at least after some centuries: e.g., the globules would at length pass into subtle matter, and the branching heterogeneous parts of the third element into globules. Therefore either some compensation had to take place, most difficult to explain and nowhere (so far as I have seen) explained by Descartes by apt laws of nature; or the machine of the world must have collapsed after more than six thousand years by now. What do the Cartesians say to this?

## ADPENDICULUS. — APPENDIX

> Systéma Newtonianum leviter adtingitur.

The Newtonian system is touched upon lightly. 47

> 47 De Clariss. *Newtoni* systémate aliqua licet brevissimè exponere necessum est. A Cartesii elementis praeter alia in primigeniis corporum particulis differt, utpote quas Cartesius *friábiles*, Newtonus, *duras* ac solidas, ita ut nullis naturae viribus frangi possint adstruit. [^24-s1-2] Systématis Newtoniani [p. 25] praecipuum caput est *vis adtractrix*: per hanc íntelligunt virtutem, seu principium actionis illius, quae per vires corporum ordinarias, pressionem nempè, & percussionem explicari nequeat; actio autem illa propterquam corpora accedunt, *adtractio* iis dicitur. Hanc universalem esse, mutuamque tùm magnorum corporum, tùm minimarum materiae particularum volunt.

Of the system of the most illustrious Newton it is necessary to set forth some things, though very briefly. It differs from the elements of Descartes, besides other things, in the primordial particles of bodies, inasmuch as Descartes asserts them to be friable, Newton hard and solid, so that they cannot be broken by any forces of nature (e). Of the Newtonian system the principal head [p. 25] head is the attractive force: by this they understand the virtue, or principle, of that action which cannot be explained by the ordinary forces of bodies, namely pressure and impulse; and the action itself by which bodies approach one another is called by them attraction. This they hold to be universal and mutual, both of great bodies and of the smallest particles of matter.

> [^24-s1-2]: Optic. q. 31.

[^24-s1-2]: Opticks, Qu. 31.

> 48 Nonnulli Philosophi, Galli praesertim dicunt, quod quamvis Newtoni systema vagas, incertasque hypótheses ex Philosophia exturbatas velit [§ 20]: Newtonianorum tamen aliqui nihil minus praestant, vim adtractricem recipiendo Neque enim sciunt vim hujusmodi esse causam effectum, nec ope illius phaenomenorum rationem reddere possunt. Et ad primum quod adtinet Clariss. ipse *Newtonus* [^25-s1]: *quam ego*, inquit, *attractionem appello, fieri sanè potest ut ea[?] efficiatur impulsu, vel alio aliquo modo nobis ignoto. Hanc vocem attractionis ita hic áccipi velim, ut in universum solummodo vim aliquam significare intelligatur, qua corpora ad se mutuo tendant, cuicunque demum causae attribuenda sit illa vis.*

48 Some philosophers, the French especially, say that although Newton’s system would have vague and uncertain hypotheses driven out of Philosophy [§ 20], some of the Newtonians nevertheless do no less themselves, by admitting an attractive force. For they do not know whether a force of this kind is a cause or an effect, nor can they by its help give the reason of the phenomena. And as regards the first, the most illustrious Newton himself (f): “What I call Attraction may be perform’d by impulse, or by some other means unknown to me. I use that Word here to signify only in general any Force by which Bodies tend towards one another, whatsoever be the Cause.”

> [^25-s1]: Optic. p. 322.

[^25-s1]: Opticks, p. 322.

> 49 Et álibi [^25-s2] ita loquitur: *voces autem attractionis, impúlsus, vel propensionis cujuscunque in centrum indifferenter, & pro se mutuo promiscuè usurpo; has vires non physicè, sed mathematicè tantum considerando. Unde caveat Lector, ne per hujusmodi vires cógitet, me speciem, vel modum actionis, causamve, aut rationem physicam alicubi definire, vel centris, quae sunt puncta mathematica, vires verè, & physicè tribuere, si fortè aut centra trahere, aut vires centrorum esse dixero.* Ut ea propter dixerit *Nolletus* [^25-s3]: adtractionem, ubi è *Newtoni* manibus ad Sectatores transmissa est, simplicitate sua magnoperè fuisse expoliatam.

49 And elsewhere (g) he speaks thus: “I use the words attraction, impulse, or propensity of whatever kind toward a center indifferently and promiscuously for one another, considering these forces not physically but only mathematically. Hence let the Reader beware of thinking that by words of this kind I anywhere define the species or mode of action, or the physical cause or reason, or that I attribute forces truly and physically to centers, which are mathematical points, if perchance I should say that centers attract, or that there are forces of centers.” So that for this reason Nollet (h) said that attraction, once it passed from the hands of Newton to his followers, was greatly despoiled of its simplicity.

> [^25-s2]: Princip. Phil. Nat. Mathem Def. 8.

[^25-s2]: Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy, Def. 8.

> [^25-s3]: Leçons de Physique. Tom. 2. Append. art. 2.

[^25-s3]: Leçons de Physique, vol. 2, Append., art. 2.

> 50 Et ad secundum quod spectat, videlicet adtractionis ope phaenomenorum rationem reddi haud posse plurimis nititur osténdere D. *Pluche* [^25-s4]. Explicent, inquit, adtractionis ope; ¿eccur ingens moles aedificii cujusdam, quae comparatè ad plumam vi adtractrice penè infinita pollet, volitantem in aëre plúmulam ad sese non adducit? aut ¿cur lapis ponè turrim décidens potius à tellúre adtrahatur, quam à turri, quae vicinior est? Licet enim, (ut inquiunt Newtoniani) adtractionem quamvis aliam immensum quantum excedat vis adtractrix telluris, ¿quis tamen abnuat, si virtuti hujus augmentum adjiciatur, ipsam majori nisu acturam? Addatur ergò viribus adtrahentibus telluris vis adtractrix montis praerupti tanquam partis globo terraqüeo adnexae. ¿Ecquid causae fuerit, quod summa haec virium adtrahentium non accéleret motum lapidis juxta montem decidui, eumque non promoveat [p. 26] velocius, quam si eadem ex altitudine in plano aliquo nullis móntibus áspero delabatur?

50 And as regards the second, namely that by the help of attraction the reason of the phenomena cannot be given, M. Pluche (i) strives to show it by very many arguments. Let them explain, he says, by the help of attraction: why does the huge mass of some building, which compared with a feather possesses an almost infinite attractive force, not draw to itself a little feather fluttering in the air? or why is a stone falling beside a tower attracted by the earth rather than by the tower, which is nearer? For although (as the Newtonians say) the attractive force of the earth exceeds any other attraction by an immense amount, who will deny that, if an increase is added to this virtue, it will act with a greater effort? Let there be added, then, to the attracting forces of the earth the attractive force of a steep mountain, as of a part joined to the terraqueous globe. What cause could there be why this sum of attracting forces does not accelerate the motion of a stone falling beside the mountain, and does not drive it on faster [p. 26] than if it fell from the same height on some plain not rough with any mountains?

> [^25-s4]: Histoire du Ciel. Tom. 2. Cosmogon. §. 9.

[^25-s4]: Histoire du Ciel, vol. 2, Cosmogon., §. 9.

> 51 Nec refert vim adtractrícem montis, comparatè ad alteram telluris haud esse sensibilem, ut enim demus insensibilem illam haberi, si cum hac conferatur, ¿an tamen talis censenda, si relatè ad corpus in aëre péndulum, à cacúmine, atque adeo à parte globi terraquei haud remotum, si junctim cum tellure in eumdem motum deorsum conspírans spectétur? Deinde: si tellus ímpedit adtractionem aliam omnem, ¿qui fieri potest ut in harum virium praesentia aestuans mare â Luna adtrahatur? quùm tamen, & aquae telluri sint viciniores, quam etiam ceu pars terraquei componunt, & moles globi hujus, lunarem exsúperet? Sed dicta sufficiant, ut systema adtractionis Newtonianum summis, ut ajunt, labris degustétis. Neque enim mens fuit, (quod impossibile esset) paucis pagellis illud in universum expéndere: mysterium nempè est impervium iis, qui sublimiori mathési initiati haud sunt. Newtonii systéma jure, meritòque defendunt plurimi Clariss. gravissimique Philosophi, quos consúlere debetis, si bonae Philosophiae amatores estis.

51 Nor does it matter that the attractive force of the mountain is not sensible in comparison with the other force, that of the earth; for, granting that it is held insensible when compared with that, is it nevertheless to be reckoned such if it is regarded relative to a body hanging in the air from the summit, and hence not far from a part of the terraqueous globe; if it is regarded as conspiring jointly with the earth in the same downward motion? Then: if the earth impedes every other attraction, how can it happen that, in the presence of these forces, the surging sea is attracted by the Moon? when yet the waters are both nearer to the earth, and also compose it as a part of the terraqueous globe, and the mass of this globe exceeds that of the Moon. But let what has been said suffice for you to have tasted the Newtonian system of attraction, as they say, with the tips of your lips. For it was not my intention (which would be impossible) to weigh it in its entirety in a few little pages: it is indeed a mystery impenetrable to those who are not initiated in the higher mathematics. The system of Newton is defended rightly and deservedly by very many most illustrious and most weighty philosophers, whom you ought to consult if you are lovers of good Philosophy.

## CAPUT VIII. — CHAPTER VIII

> Systémata Physica elementria, seu sensibilia, & Chymicum systéma.

The elementary, or sensible, physical systems, and the chemical system.

> 52 *Elementarii*, Veteres quidam fuere, qui unum duntaxat elementum, dixerunt esse primum rerum naturalium principium. Ex his *Thales Milesius aquam*, sive *humidum* rerum principium esse censuit [^26-s1-2]. *Xenóphanes terram* [^26-s2]. *Anaxímenes*, *aërem* [^26-s3]. *Heraclitus*, *ignem* [^26-s4]. Alii duo statuerunt elementa. Inter Recentiores *Elérus* Academiae Berolinensis Sodális, *aquam* pro principio passivo ex quo aër, & terra fiant, *ignem* pro activo habet [^26-s5]. Praecipuum systéma Elementariorum cóndidit *Empédocles*. Is pro materia prima quatuor elementa vulgaria adsumpsit, *terram*, nimirum, *aquam*, [p. 27] *aërem*, & *ignem*, pro forma verò eorum combinationem [^27-s1-2]. Alii aliter opinabantur: *nihil enim*, (ut ait Cicero) *tam absurdum excogitari potest, quod non sit dictum ab aliquo Philosophorum.*

52 There were some of the Ancients, called Elementarians, who said that one element only was the first principle of natural things. Of these Thales of Miletus held water, or the moist, to be the principle of things (j); Xenophanes, earth (k); Anaximenes, air (l); Heraclitus, fire (m). Others laid down two elements. Among the Moderns, Eller, Fellow of the Berlin Academy, holds water as the passive principle, from which air and earth come to be, and fire as the active (n). The principal system of the Elementarians was founded by Empedocles. He took as prime matter the four common elements, namely earth, water, air, and [p. 27] and fire, but as their form, their combination [o]. Others held otherwise: for nothing (as Cicero says) can be thought up so absurd that it has not been said by some one of the philosophers.

> [^26-s1-2]: Apud Plutarch. de placit. Philosophor. Lib. 1. c. 3.

[^26-s1-2]: In Plutarch, On the Opinions of the Philosophers, bk. 1, ch. 3.

[^26-s2]: Sextus Empiricus, Against the Physicists, bk. 1, sect. 360.
