[^26-s3]: Plutarch, bk. 1, ch. 3.

> [^26-s4]: Plutarch. loc. cit.

[^26-s4]: Plutarch, loc. cit.

> [^26-s5]: Dissert. de Elem.

[^26-s5]: Dissertation on the Elements.

> [^27-s1-2]: Laert. Lib. 8. Sect. 76.

[^27-s1-2]: Diogenes Laertius, bk. 8, sect. 76.

> 53 *Chymia*, quae â Recentioribus etiam *Chemia* vocatur, id est ars resolvendi corpora, ab *Hérmete* dicitur inventa, ac propterea *Hermética* quoque dicitur. Eam non solum in ordine ad parandas medicínas, sed etiam ad explicanda rerum naturalium principia *Theophrastus Paracelsus* Pater Chymicorum dictus plurimùm inlustravit, *Chymici* itaque *Spargyrici*, aut *Empirici* sunt, qui in corporum analysi occupantur, nec aliud arte sua, & operationibus inquírunt, nisi ut conjuncta, & colligata in corporibus mixtis principia evolvant, evolúta sensibus ipsis subjiciant. Objectum artis hujus est corpus omne sensibile, dividitúrque in tres *classes*, seu *regna*, vel *familias*, ut ipsi loquuntur, nempè *animale*, *vegetabile*, & *minerale*. Quae autem ex his ope potissimum ignis, & per *menstrua*, seu dissolventia eliciunt, ea illis corporum principia sunt juxta axioma ipsorum: *quod ex iis partibus quodlibet constituatur, in quas resolvitur*. Principia eorum quinque numerantur videlicet, *Mercurius*, *Sulphur*, *Sal*, *Aqua*, & *Terra*. Priora tria, *activa* dicuntur, duo postrema, *passiva*.

53 Chymia, which by the Moderns is also called Chemia, that is, the art of resolving bodies, is said to have been invented by Hermes, and is therefore also called Hermetic. It was greatly illustrated, not only with a view to preparing medicines but also to explaining the principles of natural things, by Theophrastus Paracelsus, called the Father of the Chemists. The chemists, then, are the Spagyrists, or Empirics, who are occupied with the analysis of bodies and seek nothing else by their art and operations than to unfold the principles joined and bound together in mixed bodies and, once unfolded, to subject them to the senses themselves. The object of this art is every sensible body, and it is divided into three classes, or kingdoms, or families, as they themselves speak, namely the animal, the vegetable and the mineral. And what they draw out of these, chiefly by the help of fire and through menstrua, or dissolvents, those are for them the principles of bodies, according to their axiom: that anything is constituted of those parts into which it is resolved. Their principles are numbered five, namely Mercury, Sulphur, Salt, Water and Earth. The first three are called active, the last two passive.

> 54 *Mercurius*, sive *spiritus* est liqüor subtílis, penetrans, & volátilis, qui primus è corporibus adplicato igne exire solet, â quo etiam pro majore, vel minore dosi incrementum corporum, & corruptio pendet; & â quo mixtorum omnium motus immediatè proveniunt. Unde patet, mercurium Chymicorum longè aliam esse substantiam, quam sit *argentum vivum*, quod alias etiam *mercurius*, dicitur. *Sulphur* vocant substantiam quamdam pinguem, oleaginósam, per quam habent mixta, quae ea abundant, ut flammam concipiant. *Sal* est substantia sápida, [quia est sapórum origo], quae per aquam dilui, & igne liqüefieri potest. Dividitur in *fixum*, & *volátilem*, *ácidum*, & *álkali*; prior igne non ávolat, licet dissolvatur, & fundatur, alter calore ávolat, & dissipatur. Dicitur *ácidum*, quod linguae impositum eam certo quodam acrimoniae sensu omnibus noto adficit, ac véllicat. *Alkali*, quod rarioris texturae est, saporisque véluti urentis, multisque meatibus interruptum, unde si cum acido misceatur magnam ebullitionem efficit. *Alkálicum* idcirco vocatur illud omne corpus, quod miscéri cum *ácido* haud potest, quin magnam effervescentiam éxcitet.

54 Mercury, or spirit, is a subtle, penetrating and volatile liquor, which usually comes out of bodies first when fire is applied; on which, according to its greater or lesser dose, the growth and corruption of bodies depend; and from which the motions of all mixed bodies immediately proceed. Hence it is plain that the mercury of the chemists is a substance far different from quicksilver, which is otherwise also called mercury. Sulphur they call a certain fat, oily substance, through which mixed bodies that abound in it are able to catch flame. Salt is a savory substance [because it is the origin of savors], which can be diluted by water and liquefied by fire. It is divided into fixed and volatile, acid and alkali: the former does not fly off in the fire, though it is dissolved and melted; the latter flies off and is dissipated by heat. It is called acid because, placed on the tongue, it affects and twitches it with a certain sense of sharpness known to all. Alkali is that which is of a looser texture and of a taste as it were burning, and broken up by many passages; whence, if it is mixed with an acid, it produces a great ebullition. Therefore every body is called alkaline which cannot be mixed with an acid without exciting a great effervescence.

> 55 *Aqua*, quae etiam *phlegma* â Chymicis vocatur, est substantia fluida, maximè humida, inodóra insípida. *Terra* demum *damnata*, quae, & *caput mortuum* dicitur, non admodum curae est Chymicis, qui eam fere negligunt, estque substantia árida, fixa, insípida, sólida, ac pulvérea, quae post extractos liqüores dictos, & salia fixa rémanet. Haec sunt quinque Chymicorum elementa, quae [p. 28] ab ipsis tanquam principia corporum admittuntur. Hic óbitèr animadverto, negligendas minimè esse, neque verò floccifaciendas Chymicorum operationes. Fatendum namque est, ut ait *Hamelius* [^28-s1-2] Physicam ex Chymicorum laboribus, & experimentis magna incrementa cepisse. Hinc multae artes ad usum vitae perútiles manarunt. Quid verò de Elementariorum, & Chymicorum systémate statuendum sit, postea vidébimus.

55 Water, which is also called phlegm by the chemists, is a fluid substance, extremely moist, odorless, insipid. Earth, lastly, the damned earth, which is also called caput mortuum, is not much the concern of the chemists, who almost neglect it; it is a dry, fixed, insipid, solid and powdery substance, which remains after the said liquors and the fixed salts have been extracted. These are the five elements of the chemists, which [p. 28] are admitted by them as the principles of bodies. Here I note in passing that the operations of the chemists are by no means to be neglected, nor indeed to be held of no account. For it must be confessed, as Du Hamel says [p], that Physics has taken great increases from the labors and experiments of the chemists. Hence many arts very useful for life have flowed. What is to be determined about the system of the Elementarians and of the chemists we shall see later.

> [^28-s1-2]: Tract. 1. Phys. Gen. Diss. 3. c. 5.

[^28-s1-2]: [p] Tract. 1, General Physics, Diss. 3, ch. 5.

## CAPUT IX. — CHAPTER IX

> Expónitur nostra de principiis corporum internis doctrína.

Our doctrine on the internal principles of bodies is set forth. 56

> 56 Dico primo. Physica materiae natura in eo sita videtur, quod sit substantia impenetrabiliter extensa, constans partibus primigeniis exilissimis, iisdemque quoad substantiam homogeneis, quoad molem, figuram, motum, similesque adfectiones inaequalibus, ac diversis. Prob. per partes. In eo posita est physica natura materiae corporum naturalium, per quod habet, ut possit tanquam primum subjectum accedente forma compositum naturale constituere, & quod cognoscitur habere, tum ratione, tum quoad liceat sensuum experientia; sed hoc ipso quod materia sit substantia impenetrabiliter extensa habet, & habere intelligitur, quidquid requiritur, ut possit tanquam primum subjectum accedente forma compositum naturale constituere; ergo. Minor patet: hoc etenim constituto capax est motus, & quietis [?], variae dispositionis, compositionis, textúrae & aliarum ejusmodi adfectionum; ex quo resultat, ut deinceps patebit, forma substantialis cum qua compositum naturale constituit.

I say, first: The physical nature of matter seems to consist in this, that it is a substance impenetrably extended, consisting of primordial parts that are most minute, and these homogeneous as regards substance, but unequal and diverse as regards bulk, figure, motion and like affections. Proof, by parts. The physical nature of the matter of natural bodies is placed in that by which it has the capacity, as first subject, with a form supervening, to constitute a natural composite, and which it is known to have both by reason and, so far as is permitted, by the experience of the senses; but by this very fact, that matter is a substance impenetrably extended, it has, and is understood to have, whatever is required for it to be able, as first subject, with a form supervening, to constitute a natural composite: therefore. The minor is plain: for, this being established, it is capable of motion and rest, of varied disposition, composition, texture, and other affections of this kind; from which results, as will be plain hereafter, the substantial form with which it constitutes the natural composite.

> 57 Secunda pars propositionis constat: nam quoniam materia in compositione corporum esse intelligitur quiddam primum, uti est de ratione principii primi, idcirco primigeniis constare particulis rectè adfirmatur. Has particulas exilissimas esse stupenda corporum divisibilitas posthac perpendenda ad evidentiam commostrat: nunc verò in hujus rei confirmationem duo tantummodo experimenta adhibeamus.

57 The second part of the proposition is evident: for since matter in the composition of bodies is understood to be something first, as belongs to the notion of a first principle, it is therefore rightly asserted to consist of primordial particles. That these particles are most minute the stupendous divisibility of bodies, to be weighed hereafter, demonstrates to evidence; but now, in confirmation of this matter, we shall employ only two experiments.

> 58 Observat Clariss. *Boyle* [^28-s2-2], unum granum [^28-s3-2] cupri in [p. 29] spiritu salis ammoniaci dissolutum, tantam aquae copiam caerúleo colore, & quidem conspicuo, saturoque imbuisse, ut partes 256806. illi gránulo aequales comprehenderet. Doctiss. P. *Franciscus de Lanis* testatur [^29-s1-4] gumma lacca quae juglandis córtici implendo sufficiat, eam aquae copiam intenso colore tingi, quae satis est ad mille folia papyrácea ex utraque parte, eodem colore imbuenda. Cùm ergò in quolibet folio *mille milliones* punctorum coloratorum commodè designari possint, erunt in illis omnibus foliis 1,000,000,000,000 puncta visibilia colorata, ac inter se distincta. Haec certè probant exlissimas esse partes materiae. Deinde partes has minimas magnitudine sua inaequales, figura, motu, diversas esse ex eo manifestum fit, quod inaequalitas haec ac divérsitas exilissimarum partium adstrui debeat, ut sensibiles cujusvis naturalis corporis qualitates, & operationes rectè, & commodè explicentur.

58 The most illustrious Boyle observes [q] that one grain [*] of copper, dissolved in spirit [p. 29] spirit of sal ammoniac, imbued so great a quantity of water with a blue color, and that a conspicuous and saturated one, that it contained 256806 parts equal to that little grain. The most learned Fr. Francesco Lana testifies [r] that as much gum lac as would suffice to fill a walnut shell tinges with an intense color such a quantity of water as is enough to imbue a thousand paper leaves on both sides with the same color. Since, then, on any one leaf a thousand millions of colored points can conveniently be marked, there will be on all those leaves 1,000,000,000,000 visible colored points, distinct from one another. These things certainly prove that the parts of matter are most minute. Next, that these smallest parts are unequal in their magnitude, and diverse in figure and motion, is manifest from this, that this inequality and diversity of the most minute parts must be asserted in order that the sensible qualities and operations of any natural body may be rightly and conveniently explained.

> [^28-s2-2]: De mira subtilitat. effluvior. cap. 3.

[^28-s2-2]: [q] De mira subtilitate effluviorum, ch. 3.

> [^28-s3-2]: Uncia continet. 480 grana.

[^28-s3-2]: [*] An ounce contains 480 grains.

> [^29-s1-4]: Magist. Nat. & Art. Tom. 1. tract. 1. cap. 1. Obs. 3.

[^29-s1-4]: Magisterium naturae et artis, vol. 1, tract. 1, ch. 1, Obs. 3.

> 59 Hae demum exilissimae corporum partes homogeneae utique esse possunt, nec quoad substantiam diversae, quùm minimè requiratur, quod sint substantialiter diversae, ut ex illarum unione emergant corpora, quorum sensibiles *qualitates* diversae sint inter se, & *operationes* planè dissímiles. Possunt autem ex primigeniis illis partibus materiae fieri composita, quorum sensibiles qualitates, atque operationes planè diversae sint inter se, quamvis ipsae partes *quoad substantiam* minimè inter se differant: nam quùm sint inaequalis magnitudinis, & diversae figurae, possunt diversa ratione artificiosè disponi inter se, possunt denique earum aliquae secundum diversas directiones moveri in toto, quod constituunt, & aliae in illo quiescere, quod planè sufficit, ut ex illis componi queant corpora, quae dissimilibus qualitatibus praedita sint: ergo partes illae, homogeneae esse utique possunt.

59 These most minute parts of bodies, finally, can certainly be homogeneous, and not diverse as regards substance, since it is by no means required that they be substantially diverse in order that from their union bodies may emerge whose sensible qualities are diverse from one another, and whose operations are quite dissimilar. For composites can be made from those primordial parts of matter whose sensible qualities and operations are quite diverse from one another, although the parts themselves differ not at all from one another as regards substance: for since they are of unequal magnitude and diverse figure, they can be artfully disposed among themselves in diverse ways; finally, some of them can be moved in diverse directions within the whole that they constitute, and others be at rest in it, which quite suffices for bodies endowed with dissimilar qualities to be capable of being composed of them: therefore those parts can certainly be homogeneous.

> 60 Dico secundo: Forma essentialis, seu *substantialis* corporum naturalium vitae expertium, si physicé spectetur nihil diversum est â dispositione illa, convenientia & proportione illarum particularum ex quibus ipsa corpora intrinsecùs, & quoad essentiam componuntur. Prob: posita certâ dispositione, proportione, &c. partium materiae, & omni alio sublato, quamoptimé intelligitur ens corporeum, seu compositum substantiale ab aliis specifice distinctum; sed per formam substantialem nihil aliud intelligitur, quam ratio illa, quâ hoc compositum est *actu* tale ab aliis specificè diversum, & ratione cujus hos habet speciales effectus, & proprietates: ergo. Prob. maj. exemplo *plantae*: praecisè positâ in materiae particulis certâ dispositione, organisatione, &c. optimè habetur ratio, qua succus alimentitius exugatur, distribuatur, &c. & cur tale corpus végetans sit planta, non vero lapis &c. quin opus unquam sit ad aliquid aliud recúrrere, ut explicentur haec phaenómena, haec adtributa plantae: ergo.

60 I say, second: The essential, or substantial, form of natural bodies devoid of life, if it is regarded physically, is nothing different from that disposition, congruence and proportion of the particles of which the bodies themselves are composed intrinsically and as to their essence. Proof: given a certain disposition, proportion, etc., of the parts of matter, and everything else taken away, a corporeal being, or a substantial composite specifically distinct from others, is understood perfectly well: but by substantial form nothing else is understood than that ground by which this composite is actually such, specifically different from others, and by reason of which it has these special effects and properties: therefore. The major is proved by the example of a plant: given precisely a certain disposition, organization, etc., in the particles of matter, an excellent account is had of how the nutritive sap is sucked up, distributed, etc., and why such a vegetating body is a plant and not a stone, etc., without there ever being need to recur to anything else in order to explain these phenomena, these attributes of the plant: therefore.

[p. 30]

> 61 Eadem ratio obtinet in reliquis corporibus. Si enim, (ut rectè ait *Hamelius* [^30-s1-2] formam & speciem auri designáre velímus, proprietates ejus, adferemus, quod sit omnium maximè dúctile, quod in aqua forti non dissolvatur, ut argentum, &c. Ac perítus faber auratius quùm eas qualitates in corpus aliquod conveníre viderit, non dubitabit quin verum sit aurum, nec sollicitùs erit, an sit in eo forma quaedam auri absoluta. Nam eâ formâ detráctâ dum eae dótes permaneant, aurum purum futurum est: eademque est ratio omnium corporum: ergo forma essentialis, seu substantialis corporum vitae expertium nihil diversum est â certa congerie qualitatum sensibilium, quae ex certa partium materiae dispositione, motu, atque aliis adfectionibus consurgit. His accedit, posse ex substantia extensa, impenetrábili, mobili, divisibili, sibi tamen ubique similis, & uniformi, si variè configuretur, determinetur, modificetur res longè dissimilimas enásci.

61 The same reasoning holds in the remaining bodies. For if (as Du Hamel rightly says (s)) we wish to designate the form and species of gold, we shall adduce its properties: that it is the most ductile of all, that it is not dissolved in aqua fortis as silver is, etc. And a skilled goldsmith, when he has seen those qualities come together in some body, will not doubt that it is true gold, nor will he be anxious whether there is in it some absolute form of gold. For were that form withdrawn, so long as those endowments remained, it would be pure gold: and the same is the reasoning for all bodies; therefore the essential, or substantial, form of bodies devoid of life is nothing different from a certain aggregate of sensible qualities, which arises from a certain disposition, motion and other affections of the parts of matter. To these is added that, from a substance extended, impenetrable, mobile, divisible, yet everywhere like itself and uniform, things most dissimilar can spring up if it is variously configured, determined, modified.

> [^30-s1-2]: Phys. Gen. tract. 1. Diss. 1. c. 2. Concl. 2.

[^30-s1-2]: General Physics, tract. 1, Diss. 1, ch. 2, Concl. 2.

> 62 Prout enim ex vario ductu lineolarum nonnisi situ, positura, figura dissimilium omnes literae alphabeti prodeunt, quae variè collocatae innumerabilia verba conficiunt, atque ita semper permutari possunt, ut cálculo facto adfirmare non dubitet excéllens Geómetra Tacquet [^30-s2-2] mille milliones Scriptorum mille annorum millionibus non posse scribere omnes 24 literarum alphabeti permutationes, licet singuli quotidie absólverent 40. páginas: ita étiam partes materiae homogeneae, diverso modo, figura, situ dispositae, atque diverso ordine connexae, ac combinatae incomprehensibilem rerum varietatem, quam Infinitus Creator re ipsa exhibuit, & quam tot homines acutissimi, qui ab orbe cóndito vixerunt, nec cogitando ádsequi potuerunt, producunt.

62 For just as from the varied drawing of little lines, dissimilar only in situation, posture and figure, all the letters of the alphabet come forth, which, variously placed, make innumerable words, and can be permuted in such a way that, having made the calculation, the excellent geometer Tacquet (t) does not hesitate to affirm that a thousand millions of writers could not in a thousand millions of years write out all the permutations of the 24 letters of the alphabet, even if each of them finished 40 pages daily: so too the homogeneous parts of matter, disposed in diverse mode, figure and situation, and connected and combined in diverse order, produce that incomprehensible variety of things which the Infinite Creator has displayed in reality, and which so many most acute men who have lived since the founding of the world have not been able to attain even in thought.

> [^30-s2-2]: Apud Verdries, Phys. Gen. Tract. 1. §. 3.

[^30-s2-2]: In Verdries, General Physics, Tract. 1, §. 3.

> 63 His argumentis majus robur accedit ex analogia, quae inter modum operandi naturae, & artis intercédit; opera enim utriusque quantumvis magno discrimine sejungantur, in eo tamen mirè consentiunt, quod utrinque ratio vi cujus in certa rerum corporearum classe composita, & sint, & fiant, ad certas partium materiae modificationes, coordinationes, motus, texturas récidat, & in complexu ejusmodi qualitatum, adfectionumque consistat. Jam verò ex axiomátibus supra constitutis systema nostrum de physica materiae, & formae natura confirmari oportet.

63 To these arguments greater strength accrues from the analogy that exists between the mode of operating of nature and that of art; for the works of both, however great the difference that separates them, yet agree wonderfully in this, that in both the ground by virtue of which they are composites in a certain class of corporeal things, and both are and come to be, falls back on certain modifications, coordinations, motions and textures of the parts of matter, and consists in the complex of qualities and affections of this kind. Now, from the axioms established above, our system of the physical nature of matter and of form must be confirmed.

> 64 Systéma illud praeferendum est, quod simplicius est, & ex paucioribus principiis proprietates corporis naturalis explicat (*Axiom. II.*) Item quod plura, quae ad Physicam pertinent, evolvit; phaenomenòrumque rationes, non generalibus duntaxat notionibus éxprimit, verùm speciatim naturam corporum, adfectionesque ad captum proponit (*Axiom. III. & IV.*). In quo demùm nihil adséritur, vel adsúmitur, quod cogitatione comprehendi, vel [p. 31] explicari nunquam satis possit (*Axiom V.*). Hujusmodi autem est systema nostrum, utpotè quod multiplicitatem tot *semisubstantiarum* excludit, & homogeneam, spectata natura, materiam statuit: in quo (ut in decursu Physices patebit natura, & adfectiones corporum, causae effectuum, adcommodate ad intelligentiam nostram, distinctisque notionibus redduntur, quod ad extremum abstrúsa, & nunquam explicanda mysteria repudiat, uti ex discussione systématum, quisque intelliget: ergo systema nostrum in Physica obtineat necesse est.

64 That system is to be preferred which is simpler and explains the properties of a natural body from fewer principles (Axiom II). Likewise, that which unfolds more of the things pertaining to Physics, and expresses the reasons of the phenomena not merely by general notions, but sets forth the nature and affections of bodies specifically and to the capacity of the mind (Axiom III & IV). In which, finally, nothing is asserted or assumed that it would never be possible sufficiently to comprehend in thought or to explain [p. 31] (Axiom V). And such is our system, inasmuch as it excludes the multiplicity of so many semi-substances and, when nature is considered, lays down a homogeneous matter: in which (as will be plain in the course of the Physics) the nature and affections of bodies and the causes of effects are rendered in a way accommodated to our understanding, and by distinct notions; which, finally, repudiates abstruse mysteries never to be explained, as everyone will understand from the discussion of the systems: therefore it is necessary that our system should prevail in Physics.

> 65 Ex dictis *Inferes I.* In sententia nostra formam non esse entitatem absolutam, sed quid modale, & respectivum: etenim illa partium materiae textura, proportio, combinatio, &c. in qua consistit forma, sunt meri modi. *Inferes II*: quod si hoc nomen *substantia* sumatur pro *ente per se existente*, forma essentialis compositorum naturalium vitae expertium (de his enim tantùm loquimur) non est entitativè substantia, ut per se patet. *Inferes III*, quod praedicta forma propriè loquendo nec producitur, nec fit, nec generatur ut optimè ait *Angelicus Doctor* pluribus in locis, nam omne quod fit ait *S. Thomas* [^31-s1-3] semper *compositum* est, forma autem non est compositum. Nullátenus loquimur de anima rationali, quae verè & propriè est forma hominis, & á solo Deo creatur.

65 From what has been said you will infer I. That in our opinion form is not an absolute entity, but something modal and relative: for that texture, proportion, combination, etc., of the parts of matter, in which form consists, are mere modes. You will infer II: that if this name substance is taken for a being existing by itself, the essential form of natural composites devoid of life (for we are speaking only of these) is not entitatively a substance, as is self-evident. You will infer III, that the said form, properly speaking, is neither produced, nor made, nor generated, as the Angelic Doctor excellently says in very many places; for everything that is made, says St. Thomas (u), is always a composite, but form is not a composite. We are by no means speaking of the rational soul, which is truly and properly the form of man, and is created by God alone.

> [^31-s1-3]: Lib. 7. Metaph. Lect. 7. & 8. 1. p. q. 65. artic. 4. in corp. & aliis in locis.

[^31-s1-3]: Metaphysics, bk. 7, lect. 7 & 8; pt. 1, q. 65, art. 4, in the body of the article; and in other places.

> 66 Forma itaque materialis, sive essentialis non producitur, nec fit, nec generatur, sed compositum: quùm enim praedicta forma nihil aliud sit, quàm dispositio illa, proportio, textura, &c, & hae nihil aliud sint, quàm quid modale, forma fieri non potest, nisi impropriè, quatenus nempè sic denominatur â productione compositi, quùm enim partes materiae junguntur, variè disponuntur, &c, quod est componi seu generari compositum necessario eis insunt, praesentiae illae, dispositiones, &c, quas adpelamus formam, non ergò aliter forma fit, nisi quatenus fit, aut generatur compositum, quod optimè exponi potest in artefacto. *Inferes IV.* formam *contineri in potentia materiae* nihil aliud esse, quam partes materiae variè disponi, conformarique posse. Analogiam habes in statuta quae antequam ex ligno fiat, in illo ligno *potentia* continetur, quatenus nempe lignum in statuam formari potest

66 Material form, therefore, or essential form, is not produced, nor made, nor generated, but the composite is: for since the said form is nothing else than that disposition, proportion, texture, etc., and these are nothing else than something modal, form cannot be made except improperly, inasmuch, namely, as it is so denominated from the production of the composite; for when the parts of matter are joined, variously disposed, etc., which is for the composite to be composed or generated, there are necessarily in them those presences, dispositions, etc., which we call form; form, therefore, is not made otherwise than insofar as the composite is made or generated, which can best be set out in an artifact. You will infer IV. that for form to be contained in the potency of matter is nothing else than that the parts of matter can be variously disposed and conformed. You have an analogy in a statue, which, before it is made from wood, is contained in that wood in potency, inasmuch, namely, as the wood can be formed into a statue.

> 67 *Inferes V.* Materiam & formam realiter distingui, non quidem *entitativè*, quum forma non sit entitas, sed quid modale, ut diximus, nec distinctione reali *majori*, sed dictione reali *minori*, seu *modali*. Quùm idea unius rei *positivè*, & *completè* ideam alterius rei exclúdit, tunc dicimus eas distingui distinctione reali majori, ita distinguuntur corpus, & anima. Distinctio realis *minor*, sive *modalis* est illa quae datur inter rem, & modum ipsius rei, ut distinctio corporis â figura, quod & in *Ontologia* dictum est jam. Omne autem quod per se non [p. 32] subsistit, id propriè non est *ens*, sed *entis modus*, nam *per se subsistere*, nonminus substantiae, aut rei, sive *enti* cómpetit, quam *inhaerére accidenti*, aut *entis modo*.

67 You will infer V. That matter and form are really distinguished, not indeed entitatively, since form is not an entity but something modal, as we have said, nor by the major real distinction, but by the minor real distinction, or modal distinction. When the idea of one thing positively and completely excludes the idea of another thing, then we say that they are distinguished by a major real distinction; thus body and soul are distinguished. The minor, or modal, real distinction is that which is found between a thing and the mode of the thing itself, as the distinction of body from figure, which has already been stated in the Ontology too. But everything that does not subsist by itself [p. 32] is not properly a being, but a mode of a being, since to subsist by itself belongs no less to a substance, or thing, or being, than to inhere belongs to an accident, or mode of a being.

## CAPUT X. — CHAPTER X

> Ineluctabilibus argumentis ex *Tosca* [^32-s1-3] desumptis excluduntur ê Philosophiae albo formae substantiales, quae sint entitates absolutae, prout â Peripateticis communiter propugnantur.

By inescapable arguments drawn from Tosca (x), substantial forms that are absolute entities, as they are commonly defended by the Peripatetics, are struck from the roll of Philosophy.

> [^32-s1-3]: Philos. t. 3. Lib. 1. Tract. 3. Prop. 35.

[^32-s1-3]: Philos., vol. 3, bk. 1, tract. 3, prop. 35.

> 68 Dico primo: formae substantiales corporum vitae expertium, quae sint entitates absolutae, entitativè â materia distinctae, substantiaeque incompletae in sensu Peripatetico nullius usus in Physica sunt, nihilque prodesse possunt ad rerum naturalium causas explicandas, proindeque â Philosophia longè exulare debent. Prob. ¿Quodnam enim adsignabitur experimentum, quod ope illarum unquam explanatum sit? ¿Quid illae ad aëris impressiones, quid ad terrae, maris, aut ignis actiones agnoscendas contulére? ¿Quod naturae phaenomenon, ope earumdem formarum fuit unquam expósitum? Evolve, per me licet, Auctores, qui in abditis naturae arcanis detegendis insudarunt, nullumque reperies, qui ad id exequendum praedictarum formarum auxilium advocaverit: ergo.

68 I say, first: substantial forms of bodies devoid of life, such as are absolute entities, entitatively distinct from matter, and incomplete substances in the Peripatetic sense, are of no use in Physics, and can be of no help for explaining the causes of natural things, and accordingly ought to be banished far from Philosophy. Proof. For what experiment will be assigned that has ever been explained by their help? What have they contributed to understanding the impressions of the air, or the actions of earth, sea or fire? What phenomenon of nature has ever been set forth by the help of these same forms? Turn over, for all I care, the authors who have toiled at uncovering the hidden secrets of nature, and you will find none who has called in the help of the said forms to accomplish it: therefore.

> 69 Dico secundo: praedictae formae substantiales cum Philosophiae naturalis principiis praecipuè Aristotelicis, minimè congruunt. Prob. 1. Omnis entitas in rerum natura existens, & quae extra Deum est, producta est, sed tales formae substantiales si darentur, extra Deum in rerum natura existerent: ergo essent productae; sed non sunt productae: ergo non existunt. Min. subsumpta prob. 1. quia haec est expressa Aristotelis, & Angelici Praeceptoris doctrina. Primus enim 7. Metaph. cap. 8. text. 26. & 27. satis extensè probat formam nullomodo fieri, sed tantum compositum, cujus rei probationem ita concludit: *manifestum igitur est, quod nec species fit, aut quodcumque nominari oportet formam*, quod postea cap. 12. ejusdem libri text. 32. ad formas etiam accidentales extendit. [p. 33] Praeterea lib. 1. Phys. text. 64. ait: *Manifestum est ex dictis, quod omne quod fit, semper compositum est.* Id ipsum tuetur *Angelicus* locis citatis [§. 65.] Quidquod id ipsum loculentissimè ostenditur testimonio etiam *Ciceronis*, qui quum Graecae ad miraculum sciret, Aristotelemque Platonem, caeterosque quos adtente legerat, multò melius quam vel omnes vulgares Peripatetici in unum coacti intelligeret, non uno tantum loco ait, Peripateticos & Academicos nominibus differentes esse, re congruentes; quumque luce clarius sit Academicos nullomodo tales formas substantiales admisisse, dicere debemus, Aristotelem in exponendis rebus physicis nunquam ad tales formas confugere.

69 I say, second: the said substantial forms by no means agree with the principles of natural Philosophy, especially the Aristotelian. Proof 1. Every entity existing in the nature of things, and which is outside God, is produced; but such substantial forms, if they were given, would exist outside God in the nature of things: therefore they would be produced; but they are not produced: therefore they do not exist. The subsumed minor is proved, 1. because this is the express doctrine of Aristotle and of the Angelic Teacher. For the first, in bk. 7 of the Metaphysics, ch. 8, text 26 & 27, proves at sufficient length that the form is in no way made, but only the composite, and concludes the proof of this matter thus: it is manifest, therefore, that neither the species is made, nor whatever the form ought to be called; which afterwards, in ch. 12 of the same book, text 32, he extends to accidental forms as well. Moreover, in [p. 33] in bk. 1 of the Physics, text 64, he says: It is manifest from what has been said that everything that is made is always composite. The Angelic Doctor defends this very point in the places cited [§. 65]. Indeed, this very thing is shown most clearly also by the testimony of Cicero, who, since he knew Greek to a marvel, and understood Aristotle and Plato and the others, whom he had read attentively, much better than even all the common Peripatetics gathered into one, says in more than one place that the Peripatetics and the Academics differ in names but agree in substance; and since it is clearer than daylight that the Academics in no way admitted such substantial forms, we must say that Aristotle, in expounding physical things, never took refuge in such forms.

> 70 Prob. 2. quidquid extra Deum productum est, aut est productum per creationem, aut per generationem, sed formae substantiales, neque productae sunt per creationem, neque per generationem: ergo. Prob. min quoad secundam partem: si formae generarentur, fierent ex aliquo ipsis inexistente, hoc autem nihil aliud esse potest quam materia: ergo fierent ex materia inexistente ipsis formis; ergo formae ipsae ex materia & forma coaléscerent. Idem argumentum efformabo de forma formae, & sic in infinitum: ergo ut hujusmodi inconveniens vitetur, dicendum necessario est, formam non generari, nec fieri, & consequenter non esse entitatem absolutam, ut contendunt Peripatetici.

70 Proof 2. Whatever is produced outside God is produced either by creation or by generation; but substantial forms are produced neither by creation nor by generation: therefore. The minor is proved as to its second part: if forms were generated, they would be made out of something existing in them; but this can be nothing else than matter: therefore they would be made out of matter existing in the forms themselves: therefore the forms themselves would coalesce out of matter and form. I will frame the same argument about the form of the form, and so on to infinity: therefore, to avoid an inconvenience of this kind, it must necessarily be said that form is neither generated nor made, and consequently is not an absolute entity, as the Peripatetics contend.

> 71 Respondent: formam verè non fieri, quum compositum, cujus est forma generatur, sed *edúci ex potentia materiae*, ac propterea non *creari*. Sed contra: etenim edúci ex potentia materiae non convenit formae quae sit entitativè substantia: ergo vel illa forma non est entitativè substantia, vel creatur quum compositum producitur. Prob. ant. quod forma educatur de potentia materiae nihil est aliud, quàm eam ita fieri, ut necessarium saltem ordine naturali sit, subjectum existere in quo illa producatur, & conservetur: ergo forma quae de potentia subjecti educitur, necessariò ab illo dependet in fieri, esse, & conservari, quod perinde est ac dicere formam inhaerére subjecto, sed inhaerére subjecto tantummodo convenit accidenti physico, quia accidens physicum inhaeret subjecto, ab eoque saltem naturae viribus dependet in fieri, esse, & conservari: ergo sumpta substantia prout sumitur â Peripateticis nempè pro ente per se existente, forma quae hoc sensu sit substantia educi nequit de potentia materiae. Etenim existere per se, & inhaerére subjecto sunt modi existendi penitùs oppositi, ut perspicuum est.

71 They reply: the form is truly not made when the composite whose form it is is generated, but is educed from the potency of matter, and therefore is not created. But against this: for to be educed from the potency of matter does not befit a form that is entitatively a substance: therefore either that form is not entitatively a substance, or it is created when the composite is produced. The antecedent is proved: that a form is educed from the potency of matter is nothing other than that it is so made that it is necessary, at least in the natural order, that a subject exist in which it is produced and conserved: therefore a form which is educed from the potency of a subject necessarily depends on it in becoming, in being, and in being conserved, which is the same as saying that the form inheres in the subject; but to inhere in a subject befits only a physical accident, because a physical accident inheres in a subject and depends on it, at least by the forces of nature, in becoming, in being, and in being conserved: therefore, taking substance as it is taken by the Peripatetics, namely for a being existing by itself, a form that is a substance in this sense cannot be educed from the potency of matter. For to exist by itself and to inhere in a subject are wholly opposed modes of existing, as is evident.

> 72 Prob. 3. omnis entitas substantialis realiter ab aliis distincta potest propriè fieri, & generari, sed forma ex Aristotele & S. Thoma non potest propriè fieri & generari, [§§. 65, *&* 69] ergo non est entitas substantialis, sed tantùm modus modaliter â materia distinctus. Prob. 4. si darentur praedictae formae entitativae, anihilárentur in destructione compositi, sed non anihilantur: ergo. Prob. maj. entitas, quae desinit esse secundum totum suum esse, [p. 34] anihilatur, sed formae praedictae in destructione compositi desinunt esse secundum totum suum esse: ergo.

72 Proof 3. Every substantial entity really distinct from others can properly be made and generated; but form, according to Aristotle and St. Thomas, cannot properly be made and generated [§§ 65 & 69]: therefore it is not a substantial entity, but only a mode modally distinct from matter. Proof 4. If the said entitative forms were given, they would be annihilated in the destruction of the composite; but they are not annihilated: therefore. The major is proved: an entity which ceases to be according to its whole being is annihilated, [p. 34] but the said forms, in the destruction of the composite, cease to be according to their whole being: therefore.

> 73 Respondent: formas praedictas non anihilari licet destruatur compositum, quia remanet earum subjectum. Anihilatio enim est desitio rei nullo subjecto remanente; contra verò destructio, in qua semper subjectum remanet, ut ex definitionibus constat. Sed contra: nam hae ipsae definitiones arbitrariae sunt, & notionibus communibus minimè consentaneae. ¿Quis enim nisi Peripateticis praejudiciis mordicùs adhaerens, non capiat rem in nihilum abire, quando non ampliùs existit in rerum natura? ¿Quid verò adtinet, subjectum (nempè rem prorsùs aliam) remanére, ut non *anihilationis* quidem, sed *destructionis* vocabulo utamur? quasi verò re ipsa discrimen aliquod interesset, sive sic, seu aliter loquamur. Itaquè mera verba dabimus, neque latum unguem per has ambáges, & logomáchias Philosophia promovebit.

73 They reply that the said forms are not annihilated although the composite is destroyed, because their subject remains. For annihilation is the ceasing of a thing with no subject remaining; destruction, on the contrary, is that in which the subject always remains, as is clear from the definitions. But against this: for these very definitions are arbitrary, and by no means consonant with common notions. For who, unless he clings tooth and nail to Peripatetic prejudices, would not grasp that a thing goes into nothing when it no longer exists in the nature of things? And what does it matter that the subject (namely a wholly different thing) remains, so that we should use the word not of annihilation but of destruction? as though there were in reality some difference whether we speak in this way or otherwise. We shall therefore be offering mere words, and Philosophy will not be advanced a nail’s breadth by these circumlocutions and logomachies.

## Peripateticorum argumenta solvuntur. — THE ARGUMENTS OF THE PERIPATETICS ARE ANSWERED

> 74 Opp. 1. cont. 1. implicat partes materiae homogeneas esse sive ejusdem naturae, & quoad figuram, molem &c. inter se differre: ergo vel non differunt inter se, vel non sunt ejusdem naturae. N. ant. etenim licet partes materiae non differant quoad substantiam quum omnes sint homogeneae, differunt tamen penes artificiosas dispositiones, neque in hoc ulla repugnantia reperitur: omnes enim fatentur, posse per artem molèculas, seu partes auri quamplurimas ejusdem utique naturae differre in adfectionibus ejuscemodi, dum aliae pónuntur cubicae, aliae sphericae &c.

74 Obj. 1, against 1. It implies a contradiction that the parts of matter should be homogeneous, or of the same nature, and should differ from one another as to figure, bulk, etc.: therefore either they do not differ from one another, or they are not of the same nature. I deny the antecedent: for although the parts of matter do not differ as to substance, since all are homogeneous, they differ nevertheless in their artful dispositions, and no repugnance is found in this: for all admit that very many molecules, or parts, of gold, certainly of the same nature, can by art differ in affections of this kind, while some are made cubical, others spherical, etc.

> 75 Opp. 2. Si partes materiae quoad molem, figuram, &c. inter se differunt: ergo materia non est indifferens ad recipiendum omnes formas: ergo non erit *principium determinabile*. Ant. constat: corpus quippe unum, aër ex. gr. eo ipso quod dissimiles proprietates habeat, diversas quoque quibus constituatur particulas complecti debet, quam ignis. Resp. quod eo ipso quod exilissimae partes ad diversissimam combinationem inter se aptae sint nullamque prae altera exposcant, satis intelligitur materiam esse indifferentem. Quatuor & viginti, quibus utimur literae, figura, & magnitudine differunt, ¿quis tamen neget has ex se indifferentes esse, ut in definita cogantur vocabula, vel nullis illigentur, in voces ad metri leges stringantur, vel fluentem liberiùs orationem componant? Nullatenùs contendimus esse de ratione materiae, ut quae in uno inest composito, eadem ipsa praecisse mutatione nulla accedente quodvis aliud constituat.

75 Obj. 2. If the parts of matter differ from one another as to bulk, figure, etc., then matter is not indifferent to receiving all forms: therefore it will not be a determinable principle. The antecedent is evident: for one body, e.g. air, by the very fact that it has dissimilar properties, must also comprise particles, by which it is constituted, different from those of fire. Reply: by the very fact that the most minute parts are apt for a most diverse combination among themselves and demand none in preference to another, it is sufficiently understood that matter is indifferent. The four and twenty letters we use differ in figure and magnitude; yet who would deny that of themselves they are indifferent to being gathered into definite words, or to being bound by no laws, to being constrained into verses by the laws of meter, or to composing a more freely flowing speech? We by no means contend that it belongs to the notion of matter that the very same parts which are in one composite should, with no change at all supervening, constitute any other.

> 76 Opp. 3. materiae competit, ut sit subjectum primum omnium mutationum naturalium, & corporum incredibili varietate [p. 35] discrepantium; sed hoc non potest praestare materia, quae ejusdem ubique est generis, non diversae naturae: ergo. N. min. Varietas namque omnis â varia materiae dispositione, combinatione, &c. hoc est â forma duci debet. Sic ê terrae succis sola partium per arboris fibrillas transmissarum percolatione, cortex, flores, fructus nascuntur. Ex alimentis similiter chylus, sanguis, ossa, & caro, quae inter se magnoperè discrepant per solam partium transpositionem, novum ordinem &c. conformantur. Itaque varietas corporum quamaptissimè cohaeret cum materia quoad substantiam homogenea.

76 Obj. 3. It belongs to matter to be the first subject of all natural changes, and of bodies of incredible variety and discrepant [p. 35] from one another; but matter, which is everywhere of the same kind and not of diverse nature, cannot accomplish this: therefore. I deny the minor. For all variety must be derived from the varied disposition, combination, etc., of matter, that is, from form. Thus from the juices of the earth, by the mere percolation of their parts transmitted through the fibrils of a tree, bark, flowers and fruits are born. From foods likewise chyle, blood, bones and flesh, which differ greatly from one another, are formed by the mere transposition of parts, a new order, etc. Accordingly the variety of bodies coheres most aptly with a matter homogeneous as to substance.

> 77 Inst. si partes materiae ponuntur homogeneae ex earum additione, & conjunctione non resultaret nova aliqua essentia, sed totum quoddam integrale homogoneum, quod non esset diversae rationis ab una ejusdem parte, quemadmodum cum addimus aquam aquae non aliam essentiam efficimus, sed eamdem essentiam aquae, quae in qualibet gutta repéritur, extensivè augemus; sed hoc est contra experientiam: ergo. Confirmatur, si musicus duas voces inter se per omnia similes conjungeret, nullatenus faceret diapasón, ad hoc enim opus est, ut diversae rationis sint, inferior scilicet, superioris dupla: ergo idem dicendum est in nostro casu.

77 You will insist. If the parts of matter are supposed homogeneous, from their addition and conjunction there would not result some new essence, but a certain homogeneous integral whole, which would not be of a different nature from one part of it; just as, when we add water to water, we do not make another essence, but extensively increase the same essence of water that is found in any drop; but this is against experience: therefore. It is confirmed: if a musician joined two voices like each other in all respects, he would by no means make a diapason; for this it is necessary that they be of diverse nature, the lower, namely, double of the higher: therefore the same must be said in our case.

> 78 Ad. 1. neg. conseq. ad hoc enim ut producatur compositum specifice ab aliis diversum, sufficit partes materiae esse diversae rationis, non quidem substantialis, sed tantummodo modalis, hoc est, sufficit eas esse diversimodè figuratas, diversimodè extensas &c. quod longè diversum est in additione aquae ad aquam, quae enim additur, ejusdem omninò rationis est cum alia, ejusdem nempè figurae, ejusdem status, nempè fluiditatis: nullaque ex additione fit nova combinatio, nova textura, & consequenter nova aliqua forma, & essentia, sed tantum eadem aqua fit extensior.

78 To 1, I deny the consequence: for in order that a composite specifically different from others may be produced, it suffices that the parts of matter be of diverse nature, not indeed substantial, but only modal; that is, it suffices that they be diversely figured, diversely extended, etc.; which is very different in the addition of water to water: for what is added is of altogether the same nature as the other, namely of the same figure, of the same state, namely of fluidity; and from the addition no new combination is made, no new texture, and consequently no new form and essence, but only the same water becomes more extended.

> 79 Confirmatio autem argumenti nostram sententiam potius confirmat, nam voces, quae diapasón componunt, non differunt essentialiter, sed tantum accidentaliter, penes scilicet quantitatem, & motum, inferior enim major est, & tardiùs movetur, superior verò brevior, & concitatior, in hoc enim tantum stat diapasón, seu octava, quod nempe vox inferior dupló segnius moveatur, quam superior, ita ut haec duas perficiat vibrationes, interim dum inferior unam duntaxat conficit. Quemadmodum itaque species hujus consonantiae diapasón ex vocum combinatione coalescit, solo motu, & magnitudine diversis, ita ex materiae particulis magnitudine, figura, &c. diversis cunctae rerum species exurgere possunt.

79 The confirmation of the argument, however, rather confirms our opinion; for the voices that compose a diapason do not differ essentially, but only accidentally, namely in quantity and motion: for the lower is greater and moves more slowly, the higher shorter and quicker; for the diapason, or octave, consists in this alone, namely that the lower voice moves twice as sluggishly as the higher, so that the latter performs two vibrations in the time in which the lower completes only one. Just as, therefore, the species of this consonance, the diapason, coalesces from the combination of voices diverse only in motion and magnitude, so from particles of matter diverse in magnitude, figure, etc., all the species of things can arise.

> 80 Opp. 4. Si dicamus materiam esse substantiam, quae partibus mole, figura, &c. diversis constat, non explicatur â nobis essentia materiae, sed corpus ipsum: ergo. Prob. ant. natura materiae est, ut non sit completa, sed particulae ex quibus materia constat sunt completae: ergo. Dist. min: sunt completae in ratione materiae, conc. in ratione compositi naturalis, seu corporis sensibilis, nego. A nobis duntaxat exponitur essentia materiae physicè considerata: [p. 36] in ratione materiae est aliquid completum: in ratione verò corporis sensibilis non completur nisi per formam, quae ex certo complexu, ordine, proportione partium consurgit.

80 Obj. 4. If we say that matter is a substance consisting of parts diverse in bulk, figure, etc., it is not the essence of matter that is explained by us, but body itself: therefore. The antecedent is proved: it is the nature of matter that it is not complete; but the particles of which matter consists are complete: therefore. I distinguish the minor: they are complete in the character of matter, I grant; in the character of a natural composite, or sensible body, I deny. By us only the essence of matter physically considered is set forth: [p. 36] in the character of matter it is something complete; but in the character of sensible body it is not completed except by the form, which arises from a certain complex, order and proportion of the parts.

> Argumenta contra secundam Conclusionem.

ARGUMENTS AGAINST THE SECOND CONCLUSION .

> 81 Opp. 1. praecipuum Peripateticorum argumentum. In Sacramento Altaris rémanent accidentia panis, & vini, sed non manet forma substantialis panis, & vini: ergo forma substantialis est quiddam praeter certam accidentium congeriem. Dist. maj. rémanent accidentia, sensu Peripatetico sumpta, pro formis accidentalibus, seu qualitatibus absolutis, & inhaerentibus subjecto, nego maj.; sensu Theologico, & Dogmatico, sumpta pro *speciebus*, quae modo ineffabili, & planè miraculoso nos fallunt, conc. maj. Et rotundè concess. min. dist. conseq. forma substantialis est quiddam praeter certam accidentium Peripateticorum congeriem, permitto conseq.; praeter congeriem accidentium, quae talia Notéricis dicuntur, hoc est, praeter texturam, & combinationem molecularum materiae corporeae: subdist.: ubi revera datur talis textura, & combinatio, nego; ubi non datur revera, sensibus tamen ita adparet quasi verè daretur, conc.

81 Obj. 1, the principal argument of the Peripatetics. In the Sacrament of the Altar the accidents of bread and wine remain, but the substantial form of bread and wine does not remain: therefore the substantial form is something besides a certain aggregate of accidents. I distinguish the major: the accidents remain, taken in the Peripatetic sense, for accidental forms, or absolute qualities inhering in a subject, I deny the major; in the Theological and Dogmatic sense, taken for species, which in an ineffable and plainly miraculous way deceive us, I grant the major. And, having roundly granted the minor, I distinguish the consequent: the substantial form is something besides a certain aggregate of Peripatetic accidents, I let the consequent pass; besides the aggregate of accidents such as are so called by the Moderns, that is, besides the texture and combination of the molecules of corporeal matter, I subdistinguish: where such a texture and combination is really given, I deny; where it is not really given, but nevertheless so appears to the senses as if it were truly given, I grant.

> 82 Res eò redit, ut intelligamus, accidentia panis & vini in Sacrosancto Altaris Sacramento non veras qualitates corporeas esse, â corpore panis & vini abstractas & relictas sine subjecto sibi connaturaliter proprio; sed meras apparientias (ut ita loquar), seu *species* panis & vini, sub quibus verissimum Corpus, & verissimus Sanguis Christi Domini latent. Nos itaque per fidem Ortodoxam docti, negamus ibi substantiam panis & vini subesse post consecrationem, docti autèm per Philosophiam negabimus vera accidentia esse illa quae adparent.

82 The matter comes back to this, that we understand the accidents of bread and wine in the Most Holy Sacrament of the Altar not to be true corporeal qualities, abstracted from the body of the bread and wine and left without a subject connaturally proper to them, but mere appearances (if I may so speak), or species of bread and wine, under which the most true Body and the most true Blood of Christ the Lord lie hidden. We, therefore, taught by the Orthodox faith, deny that the substance of bread and wine lies beneath them after the consecration; but, taught by Philosophy, we shall deny that those things which appear are true accidents.

> 83 Est ergo Dogma Catholicae Fidei, quod in Venerabili Eucharistiae Sacramento existunt *verè*, *realitèr* & *substantialitèr* corpus, & sanguis Christi Domini. Ita expressè definitum est in Concilio Lateranensi [^36-s1-2] in Constantiensi [^36-s2] in Florentino [^36-s3] & in Tridentino [^36-s4] contra Berengarium, Calvinum, aliosque impios Novatores, non minùs falsò, quàm iniquè dogmatizantes, tantùm aut in *signo*, vel *figura*, aut *virtute* Christum Dominum in Eucharistia contineri. Est etiam Dogma Catholicum, quod vi Consecrationis fit realis conversio totius substantiae panis in corpus, & totius substantiae vini in sanguinem Christi Domini, quam conversionem mirabilem prorsùs ac singularem, Ecclesia Catholica [p. 37] *transubstantiationem* aptissimè adpélat. *Haec autem transubstantiatio*, ut optimè ait celeb. Theolog. *Honoratus Tournelly* [^37-s1-2] *nullum habet in natura exemplum, quia singularis, nec ab humana ratione comprehendi potest, quia mirabilis, hoc est tota in mysteriis recóndita.*

83 It is, therefore, a Dogma of the Catholic Faith that in the Venerable Sacrament of the Eucharist the body and blood of Christ the Lord exist truly, really and substantially. So it was expressly defined in the Council of the Lateran (y), in that of Constance (z), in that of Florence (a) and in that of Trent (b), against Berengar, Calvin and other impious Innovators, who dogmatize no less falsely than wickedly that Christ the Lord is contained in the Eucharist only in sign, or figure, or virtue. It is also a Catholic Dogma that by virtue of the Consecration there takes place a real conversion of the whole substance of the bread into the body, and of the whole substance of the wine into the blood, of Christ the Lord; which altogether wonderful and singular conversion the Catholic Church transubstantiation most [p. 37] most aptly calls. This transubstantiation, moreover, as the celebrated Theologian Honoré Tournely (c) excellently says, has no example in nature, because it is singular; nor can it be comprehended by human reason, because it is wonderful; it lies wholly hidden in the mysteries.

[^36-s1-2]: Under Innocent III, ch. 1.

[^36-s2]: Sess. 8.

[^36-s3]: In the Decree of Union.

[^36-s4]: Sess. 13, ch. 1, & Can. 1.

> [^37-s1-2]: Praelect. Theolog. de S. Eucharist. q. 3. art. 2.

[^37-s1-2]: Praelectiones Theologicae de S. Eucharistia, q. 3, art. 2.

> 84 Certissimum etiam omninò est Sacratissimum Christi Domini corpus, (quod etiam de ejusdem sanguine dicendum est) esse in Eucharistia *Sacramentalitèr*, nempè tali ratione, quam *etsi verbis*, (ut sapientèr monet Concil. Trident.) *exprimere vix possimus, possibilem tamen esse Deo constantissimè credere debemus*. [^37-s2] Ille quidem existendi modus nullum in rebus creatis exemplum habet, & miraculis plenus est, ac proinde meritò vocatur *Sacramentalis*, seu modus qui soli Sacramento conveniat. Haec dicta sufficiant, ut videant Peripatetici sarcta tectaque â nobis servari Sacratissima nostrae Religionis Dógmata.

84 It is also altogether most certain that the most Sacred body of Christ the Lord (and the same must be said of his blood) is in the Eucharist Sacramentally, namely in such a manner as, although we can scarcely express it in words (as the Council of Trent wisely admonishes), we must nevertheless most steadfastly believe to be possible to God (d). That mode of existing, indeed, has no example in created things, and is full of miracles, and is therefore deservedly called Sacramental, that is, a mode which belongs to the Sacrament alone. Let these things that have been said suffice for the Peripatetics to see that the most Sacred Dogmas of our Religion are kept safe and sound by us.

> [^37-s2]: Sess. 13. cap. 1.

[^37-s2]: Sess. 13, ch. 1.

> 85 Verùm quia ipsi nullum non movent lapidem ut Recentiorum Philosophorum de non substantialibus formis opinionem tanquam haereticam traducant, imperitisque persuadeant, Dogma Catholicum Transubstantiationis everti, posita opinione Recentiorum, opere pretium est, aliqua subjúngere, ut videant nullo jure posse ipsos existimare, nos esse reos violatae fidei. In primis enim plurimi â me essent numerandi Philosophi Catholici, qui opinionem de formis, ipsis verbis, quibus â nobis exposita, & probata est, constantissimè tuentur, quin eorumdem Opera ab Ecclesia unquàm proscripta, sint, imò summa cum laude â magnis Theologis adprobata. Sufficiat aliquos nominare. *Klaus*, *Macko*, *Regnault*, *Paulian*, *Scherffer*, *Lanis*, *Corsini Hamel*, *Purchot* formas substantiales Peripateticas explodunt omninò. Ex Minimorum familia *Maignan*, *Saguens & Jacquier*, ex inclyta Minorum familia Cl. *Fortunatus â Brixia*, qui pro mille sufficit, ex Congreg. Oratorii S. Philippi Nerii Vir Cl. *Thomas Vincentius Tosca*, aliique plurimi ex Oratorio Gallicano.

85 But since they leave no stone unturned to brand the opinion of the Modern Philosophers on non-substantial forms as heretical, and to persuade the unlearned that the Catholic Dogma of Transubstantiation is overthrown once the opinion of the Moderns is posited, it is worth the trouble to add some things, so that they may see that they have no right whatever to think us guilty of violating the faith. In the first place, then, I should have to count very many Catholic Philosophers who most steadfastly defend the opinion on forms in the very words in which it has been set forth and proved by us, without their Works ever having been proscribed by the Church; nay, they have been approved with the highest praise by great Theologians. Let it suffice to name some. Klaus, Macko, Regnault, Paulian, Scherffer, Lanis, Corsini, Hamel, Purchot utterly explode the substantial forms of the Peripatetics. From the family of the Minims, Maignan, Saguens and Jacquier; from the illustrious family of the Minors, the celebrated Fortunato da Brescia, who suffices for a thousand; from the Congregation of the Oratory of St. Philip Neri, the celebrated Tomás Vicente Tosca, and very many others from the French Oratory.

> 86 ¿Quidquod haec doctrina per totam Europam, & Romae praecipuè in Universitatibus, Collegiisque, publicè coràm ipso Rom. Pontifice propugnatur? Audiamus nunc Ill. Melch. Canum. *Puto*, (ait Vir Cl.) *Theologorum Scholasticorum etiam multorum testimonium, si alii contra pugnant Viri docti non plus valere ad faciendam fidem, quàm ratio ipsorum*, videlicet: *in Scholastica disputatione plurium auctoritatem óbruere Theologum non debére; sed si paucos Viros, modò graves secum habeat, posse sanè adversus plurimos stare* [^37-s3]. Ex Theologis verò sunt non pauci, qui expressè docent Recentiorum opinionem de forma non substantiali optimè componi cum iis quae Ecclesia tenet de Venerab. Euchar. Sacram. ac proindè posse salvâ [p. 38] Religione, tutâque Fide á Viro Catholico propugnari. Ita Cl. *Robertus Holchot* [^38-s1-2] ex inclyta PP. Praedicatorum familia. Ita Eminentiss S. R. E. Card. *Petrus de Alliaco*. [^38-s2]. Ita Doctiss Praesul. *Jac. Benign. Bossuet* [^38-s3] Ita Cl. *Ludovicus Anton. Muratori*. [^38-s4] Ita P. *Vanrroy*. [^38-s5] Ita lumen clariss. Augustinianae Relig. *Laurentius Berti*. [^38-s6] Ita Cl. *Natalis ab Alexandro*. [^38-s7].

86 What of the fact that this doctrine is publicly defended throughout all Europe, and at Rome especially, in the Universities and Colleges, before the Roman Pontiff himself? Let us now hear the illustrious Melchior Cano. I think (says the celebrated man) that the testimony even of many Scholastic Theologians, if other learned men contend against them, is of no more weight for producing belief than their reasoning; that is to say, that in a Scholastic disputation a Theologian ought not to be overwhelmed by the authority of the greater number, but that if he has a few Men with him, provided they are weighty ones, he can surely stand against very many (e). Among the Theologians, moreover, there are not a few who expressly teach that the opinion of the Moderns on non-substantial form agrees perfectly with what the Church holds concerning the Venerable Sacrament of the Eucharist, and that it can therefore, without harm [p. 38] to Religion and with the Faith secure, be defended by a Catholic man. So the celebrated Robert Holcot (f), of the illustrious family of the Preaching Fathers. So the most Eminent Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church Pierre d’Ailly (g). So the most learned Prelate Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet (h). So the celebrated Lodovico Antonio Muratori (i). So Father Vanrroy (j). So the most renowned light of the Augustinian Order, Lorenzo Berti (k). So the celebrated Noël Alexandre (l).

[^38-s7]: Vol. VI, Historia Ecclesiastica, Diss. 7, in the history of the 10th and 12th centuries, art. 6, in the Schol.

> 87 Sed praestat audire Theologum Doctiss ex Inclyta Praedicatorum familia *Hiacynthum Serry* [^38-s8] „¿Alia quid réferam, (*ait Vir Cl.*) Recentis Scholae systémata inconsideratis quorundam Theologorum censuris impeti sólita? Essentiam corporis physici in extensione quantitatis plerique nunc philosophi ponunt Cartesium secuti, ipsamque substantiam â quantitate minimè distingui, & quod certò novi ita illos philosophari permittit Ecclesia. ¿Quid tu ergo censuris illos inuris? Et quos communis Mater fovet, ut filios, tanquam ethnicos, & publicanos exsecraris, quod tibi fortè Sacrosanctae Eucharistiae fidem labefactare videantur? Studium, Zelumque pro Domo Dei laudo maximè, atque commendo: at secundum scientiam velim esse. Melior longè Theologus eris, si permissum ab Ecclesia systema cum Eucharistiae fidem conciliaveris.

87 But it is better to hear the most learned Theologian of the illustrious family of the Preachers, Hyacinthe Serry [m]: “Why should I relate other things” (says the celebrated man)? “Are the systems of the recent School to be subjected to the rash censures of certain Theologians? Most philosophers now, following Descartes, place the essence of physical body in the extension of quantity, and hold that substance itself is in no way distinguished from quantity; and the Church, as I know for certain, permits them to philosophize thus. Why then do you brand them with censures? And those whom the common Mother cherishes as sons, do you curse as heathens and publicans, because they seem to you perhaps to shake the faith of the most holy Eucharist? Your study and zeal for the House of God I praise highly and commend: but I would have it be according to knowledge. You will be by far a better Theologian if you reconcile the system permitted by the Church with the faith of the Eucharist.

> [^38-s8]: Tom. 1. Praelect. Theologic. Disp. de Opific. mund. Praelect. 1.

[^38-s8]: Vol. 1, Praelectiones Theologicae, Disp. on the making of the world, Lect. 1.

> 88 „Quod fortè non incommodè fiet, si díxeris, substantiae quidém panis conversionem in Eucharistiae Sacramento fieri sólitam, ab Ecclesia fuisse definitam, non ita tamen definítum esse mutationis modum; perindèque stare Mysterium, si mutata simul cum quantitate substantia, solae maneant sensationes externae nostris in sensibus factae, (quod Cartesius existimat) ac si sola mutata substantia, vera cum céteris accidentibus quantitas maneat, quod Peripatetici arbitrantur. Eaque de causa Tridentinos Patres, *specierum*, sublata substantia remanentium vocábulo fuisse usos, quum accidentia nominare potuissent: videlicèt, ut ea voce *specierum*, sensationes illas simplicitèr significarent, quas in sensibus nostris perindè fieri, & Cartesiani, & Peripatetici profitentur, seu cum substantia indistincta quantitas pereat, seu distincta non pereat. Id ni dicas, sed Cartesianos, donec in eos sententiam Ecclesia túlerit, violatae fidei pòstules, [p. 39] non Theologus és, sed audacissimus censor, non pro Fide, sed pro anteceptis opinionibus pugnas, non pro Ecclesia, sed pro Aristotelica Schola decertas„. Hácténùs Eloquentissimus Theologus. ¿Quid ad haec Peripatetici. Ipsi víderint.

88 “This will perhaps be done not unfittingly if you say that the conversion of the substance of bread which is wont to take place in the Sacrament of the Eucharist has been defined by the Church, but that the mode of the change has not been so defined; and that the Mystery stands just as well if, the substance being changed together with the quantity, only the external sensations produced in our senses remain (as Descartes thinks), as if, the substance alone being changed, the true quantity remains with the other accidents, as the Peripatetics judge. And that for this reason the Fathers of Trent used the word species for what remains when the substance has been taken away, when they could have named them accidents: namely, so that by the word species they might signify simply those sensations which both Cartesians and Peripatetics profess to be produced in our senses alike, whether the quantity, being undistinguished from the substance, perishes, or, being distinct, does not perish. If you do not say this, but charge the Cartesians with violating the faith until the Church passes sentence against them, [p. 39] you are not a Theologian but a most audacious censor; you fight not for the Faith but for preconceived opinions; you contend not for the Church but for the Aristotelian School.” Thus far the most Eloquent Theologian. What do the Peripatetics say to this? Let them see to it themselves.

> 89 „Neque enim, (*inquit Cl. Cano*) satis est ad sententiam de haéresi ferendam, haéresim ipsam suspicione attigisse, sed comprehensione quadam opus est, ut sine errore de erroribus judicemus„ [^39-s1]. „Désinant ergo Peripatetici [*verbis utor C. Muratori*] nullum non movére lápidem quò Recentiores Auctores novarum opinionum, licet nihil cum Sancta Religione habentium infáment, eorumque libros dílacerent, proscríbant, & Supremis Ecclesiae Tribunalibus configendos exhibeant„ [^39-s2].

89 “For it is not enough” (says the celebrated Cano) “for passing sentence of heresy to have touched upon the heresy itself by suspicion; but a certain comprehension is needed, so that we may judge of errors without error” (n). “Let the Peripatetics therefore cease” [I use the words of the celebrated Muratori] “to leave no stone unturned whereby they may defame the Modern Authors of new opinions, though these have nothing at odds with our Holy Religion, and tear their books to pieces, proscribe them, and present them to the Supreme Tribunals of the Church to be pierced through” (o).

> [^39-s1]: Lib. 12. de Locis Theolog. cap. 8.

[^39-s1]: Bk. 12 of De Locis Theologicis, ch. 8.

> [^39-s2]: De Moderamine ingen. Lib. 1. cap. 21.

[^39-s2]: De Moderamine Ingeniorum, bk. 1, ch. 21.

> 90 Praeterundum porrò non est silentio, eam quoque opinionem â Peripateticis pluribus censéri *haeréticam*, quae negat quantitatem â corporea substantia realitèr distingui. Haec igitur censura, ¿aut vera est, aut falsa? Si vera: ergo Em. S. R. E. Card. Petrus de Alliaco, Aureolus, Okamus, Bielus, Melchior Canus, qui realem illam quantitatis distinctionem inficiantur [^39-s3] *haeretici* sunt, quod profectò de tantis Viris nemo cordatus dicet: ergo *haeretici* paritèr sunt ii omnes Scholastici, praecipùe ex *Scotistarum* Schola, qui corporum quantitatem non in entitativa illorum extensione, sed in ipsorum impenetrabilitate statuendam censent, ob id potissimùm, quod *extensio* non sit accidens absolutum â corporea substantia realiter distinctum, sed substantia ipsa sit ex se, omni scilicèt accidente secluso entitativè extensa.

90 Further, it must not be passed over in silence that that opinion too is held by many Peripatetics to be heretical which denies that quantity is really distinguished from corporeal substance. This censure, then: is it true or false? If true: then the Most Eminent Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church Pierre d’Ailly, Auriol, Ockham, Biel, Melchior Cano, who deny that real distinction of quantity (p), are heretics, which surely no sensible person will say of such great Men: then likewise all those Scholastics are heretics, especially of the School of the Scotists, who think the quantity of bodies is to be placed not in their entitative extension but in their impenetrability, chiefly for this reason, that extension is not an absolute accident really distinct from corporeal substance, but substance itself is of itself entitatively extended, that is, with every accident excluded.

> [^39-s3]: Apud Cl. â Brix. In Dissert. de qualit. corp. sensibilib.

[^39-s3]: In the celebrated Fortunato da Brescia, in the Dissertation on the sensible qualities of bodies.

> 91 Ergo *haereticus* est *Doctor* ipse *Subtilis*, qui [^39-s4] constantèr tuetur (ut ait Cl. *Fortunat. â Brixia*) [^39-s5] quantitatem continuam permanentem in extensione consistere, hoc est in ordine partium in toto, ut ait P. *Hiquaeus* Scoti Commentator. Si autem illa censura sit falsa, (ut revera est): ergo ea quoque eodem jure penitùs falsa censenda est, quam de sententia negante accidentia absoluta iidem ipsi pronunciant. Nam quid *specierum* nomine intellexerit Ecclesia, vel quae demùm sit physica illarum natura, núllibì ab ea tráditum est, quemadmodùm núllibì quoque ab ea est definitum sub *specierum* nomine etiam *quantitatem* comprehendi.

91 Then the Subtle Doctor himself is a heretic, who (q) steadfastly maintains (as the celebrated Fortunato da Brescia says) [r] that continuous permanent quantity consists in extension, that is, in the order of the parts in the whole, as Father Hiquaeus, the Commentator of Scotus, says. But if that censure is false (as in truth it is): then that one too must by the same right be held entirely false which the very same men pronounce on the opinion that denies absolute accidents. For what the Church understood by the name of species, or what at length their physical nature may be, has nowhere been handed down by her, just as it has nowhere been defined by her either that quantity too is comprehended under the name of species.

> [^39-s4]: Dist. X. q 1. num. XIV.

[^39-s4]: Dist. X, q. 1, no. XIV.

> [^39-s5]: In citat. Dissertat.

[^39-s5]: In the dissertation cited.

> 92 Neque dicant Peripatetici Concilium Constantiense [^39-s6] contra *Wiclessum*, & *Johannem Hus* finivisse *formas accidentales esse in Eucharistia*. Id namque falsum est: nam, ut ait Cl. *Verney* [^39-s7] ex Historicis constat, *Wicleffum* nunquam dixisse, *non esse accidentia in Eucharistia*: sed *sub accidentibus esse substantiam panis, non verò* [p. 40] *Christum.* Hunc ergo errorem damnavit Concilium, non accidentium in sensu Peripatetico existentiam Dogma esse dixit.

92 Nor let the Peripatetics say that the Council of Constance (s) defined against Wycliffe and John Hus that there are accidental forms in the Eucharist. For that is false: for, as the celebrated Verney says [t], it is established from the Historians that Wycliffe never said that there are no accidents in the Eucharist, but that under the accidents is the substance of bread, and not Christ. [p. 40] This error, then, the Council condemned; it did not say that the existence of accidents in the Peripatetic sense is a Dogma.

> [^39-s6]: Celebrat. ann. Christ. MCCCCXIV. Sess. VIII. & XV.

[^39-s6]: Held in the year of Christ MCCCCXIV, Sess. VIII and XV.

> [^39-s7]: Synops. primi tentam. pro Literat. & Scient. instaur.

[^39-s7]: Synopsis primi tentaminis pro Literarum & Scientiarum instauratione.

> 93 Fide ergo sanctum est, *sub speciebus panis, & vini*, quae in Eucharistia se offerunt, non panis, & vini naturam, & substantiam, sed verum Christi D. Corpus contineri Sed quod praedictae *species*, accidentia *absoluta* sint, ut contendunt Peripatetici, nusquam definivit Ecclesia: nec unquam istiusmodi quaestio in Ecclesia mota est, imò verò [^40-s1] nusquam lego, de existentia *specierum* in Eucharistia dubitatum fuisse, quam nemo nisi caecus, aut demens negare potuisset. Atque hactenus de Ven. Eucharistiae Sacramento. Alia Peripateticorum momenta diluamus.

93 It is therefore established by Faith that under the species of bread and wine which present themselves in the Eucharist there is contained, not the nature and substance of bread and wine, but the true Body of Christ the Lord. But that the aforesaid species are absolute accidents, as the Peripatetics contend, the Church has nowhere defined: nor has any question of this kind ever been raised in the Church; nay rather (u), I nowhere read that the existence of the species in the Eucharist was doubted, which no one but a blind man or a madman could have denied. And so much on the Venerable Sacrament of the Eucharist. Let us dissolve the other arguments of the Peripatetics.

> [^40-s1]: Ita supra laud. Verney. *De Re Metaphysica.* Romae Typis Generosi Salomoni.

[^40-s1]: So the above-praised Verney, De Re Metaphysica. Rome, printed by Generoso Salomoni.

> 94 Opp. 2. si compositum naturale vita expers componerétur essentialiter ex particulis materiae penes mechanicas tantummodo adfectiones inter se diversis, non esset unum *per se*, sed unum *per accidens*, utpote minimè constans ex *per se actu*, & ex *per se potentia*; sed hoc est falsum, quemadmodum manifestè etiam falsum est, inter *naturalia*, & *artificialia* composita nullum penitùs discrimen haberi: ergo. Dist. maj. non esset unum per se, si hoc nomine intelligatur totum, quod fiat ex duplici semisubstantia, conc., si intelligatur totum quod primò & per se sit ab operante natura intentum, nego maj. & eod modo dist. min. nego conseq. In Recentiorum sententia, quae etiam nostra est, compositum naturale est unum per se, & ab artificiali satis superque distinguitur.

94 Obj. 2. If a natural composite devoid of life were composed essentially of particles of matter differing among themselves only in mechanical affections, it would not be one per se but one per accidens, as consisting by no means of an act per se and a potency per se: but this is false, just as it is also manifestly false that there is no difference whatever between natural and artificial composites: therefore. Dist. maj.: it would not be one per se, if by this name is understood a whole made of a double semi-substance, I grant; if a whole is understood which is primarily and per se intended by operating nature, I deny the maj.; and in the same way dist. the min.; I deny the conseq. In the opinion of the Moderns, which is also ours, the natural composite is one per se, and is more than sufficiently distinguished from the artificial one.

> 95 Est enim *unum*, quia indivisum in se, & divisum â quolibet alio. Est *unum per se*; quia particulae, quae illud constituunt simul uniuntur ex diversa intentione operantis naturae: at in composito artificiali ex directa intentione artificis simul copulantur partes, quae artificiale totum constituunt. Constat quoque ex *per se actu*, & ex *per se potentia*. Etenim *mechanicae adfectiones* sunt in materia ex directa intentione naturae, & ex eadem intentione materiam ipsam ad unum in *specie* compositum constituendum detérminant. Nec enim aliud nomine *potentiae & actus per se*, sine manifesta *petitione principii*, ut dicam infra, intelligi posse puto.

95 For it is one, because it is undivided in itself and divided from everything else. It is one per se, because the particles which constitute it are united together by the diverse intention of operating nature: whereas in an artificial composite the parts which constitute the artificial whole are coupled together by the direct intention of the artificer. It also consists of an act per se and a potency per se. For the mechanical affections are in matter by the direct intention of nature, and by the same intention they determine the matter itself to constitute a composite one in species. Nor do I think that anything else can be understood by the name of potency and act per se without a manifest begging of the question, as I shall say below.

> 96 Inst.: naturale quodcumque compositum est unum totum substantiale: ergo essentialis illius forma debet esse entitativè substantia, nam secùs â composito accidentali haud quaquam distingueretur. Dist. antec. est unum totum substantiale, hoc est per se intentum â natura, conc. alio sensu gratis â Peripateticis conficto, transeat, & nego conseq. Voco itaque totum substantiale, quod ab operante naturâ, qualiscumque demùm sit componentium partium essentia, *primò & per se*, quum agit respícitur; totum verò *accidentale*, quod vel non respicitur â naturâ, tanquam effectus â sua causa, sed tantùm ab arte; vel ab illa respicitur, *non primò*, sed [p. 41] *secundariò* duntaxat, ac veluti in gratiam alterius ab ipsa *directè voliti*. Sic domus ex. gr. quum non nisi per artem fiat, est totum accidentale. Ceterum hae, aliaeque id genus instantiae quae Scholasticorum scripta implent, principiis innituntur, quae neque ex ipsis terminis, nota sunt, neque ex aliis demonstrantur, sed quae secundum voluntarias hypotheses, primò excogitata fuere, mox potius crédita quam scita; cùm ab aliorum auctoritate in *axiomatum* album relata.

96 Inst.: every natural composite is one substantial whole: therefore its essential form must be entitatively a substance; for otherwise it would in no way be distinguished from an accidental composite.
