But let there be another body H G (Fig. II) whose line of direction Cd falls outside the base F G; it is understood that it will at once fall toward the side e, because, while the whole body is carried with a circular motion about F, its center of gravity C is continually descending: therefore it must needs fall [§. 144]. Moreover, the center of gravity C is not supported by the plane D E, since the line of direction Cd runs outside the base F G: therefore it is necessary that the body H G should tumble down [§. 144].

> 146 Hinc ratio adparet, cur aliquae turres inclinatae non cadant, cujusmodi sunt Bononiensis, & Pisana à me observatae dum Italiam anno 1767 peragrarem Bononiensis est turris quadrata altitudinis 130 pedum [^55-s1-3]. Pisana est turris rotunda altitudinis 138 pedum. Bononiensis turris perpendiculum distat à basi intervallo 9 pedum, perpendiculum verò turris Pisanae per spatium 15 pedum extra basim excurrit, Firmae tamen, & stabiles persevérant, quia utriusque linea directionis intra basim est, & ideò neutra ruere deorsum potest. Hinc etiam sequitur, exilia corpora, ut acus ex. gr. stare super cuspide sua minimè posse, nimis enim angusta ejus basis est, undè quaevis vel minima inclinatio, quivis vel minimus aëris impulsus súfficit, ut illius linea directionis extra basim excurrat.

146 Hence the reason appears why some leaning towers do not fall, such as those of Bologna and Pisa, observed by me while I was traveling through Italy in the year 1767. The Bologna tower is square, 130 feet high[^56-1]. The Pisa tower is round, 138 feet high. The plumb line of the Bologna tower stands off from the base by an interval of 9 feet, while the plumb line of the tower of Pisa runs outside the base over a space of 15 feet. Yet they remain firm and stable, because the line of direction of each is within the base, and therefore neither can tumble down. Hence it also follows that slender bodies, such as a needle, for example, can by no means stand upon their point, for its base is too narrow; whence any inclination, however slight, any impulse of the air, however small, suffices for its line of direction to run outside the base.

> [^55-s1-3]: Longitudo, & divisio mensurae linearum, non est eadem ubique gentium: aliquas celebrium mensurarum varietates expónet Tabula sequens in particulis istiusmodi, qualium Pes Regius Parisinus est 1440. Cóntinet is nempè 12 póllices, pollex verò 12 lineas, linea 10 particulas, seu puncta, adeòque pes ínteger Parisinus continebit particulas 1440. Pes Regius Parisinus ...1440 Vénetus... 1540. Hispánus... 1240. Bononiensis... 1691. Románus... 1320. Viennensis... 1399. Londinénsis... 1351. Holländicus... 1391.

[^55-s1-3]: [^56-1]: The length and division of the measure of lines is not the same among all nations: the following Table will set out some varieties of the well-known measures in particles of the kind of which the Royal Paris Foot is 1440. That foot, namely, contains 12 inches, the inch 12 lines, the line 10 particles, or points, and so the whole Paris foot will contain 1440 particles. Royal Paris Foot      1440.      Venetian       1540. Spanish               1240.      Bolognese      1691. Roman                 1320.      Viennese       1399. London                1351.      Dutch          1391.

> 147 Hinc etiam colligitur cur situla A (Fig. III.) aqua plena, baculo B C, è mensa cui imponitur suspensa, non cadat, dummodo alter baculus G D infra ansam, & prioris baculi extremum C in situlae fundo ad perpendiculum erigatur. Nam quum ambo baculi simul cum situla unum & idem corpus efficiant, cádere non potest situla, quin adtollatur pars extrema B baculi B C describendo [p. 56] nimitum arcum B L. Eadem autem adtolli non potest, quin simul centrum gravitatis *i*, quod est in situla describat arcum i M, quod describere nequit quin sursum ascendat contra gravium nissum (Axioma 3. §. 144.) ergo situla decidere non poterit, sed necessario è baculo immota dependet.

147 Hence it is also gathered why a bucket A (Fig. III) full of water, suspended from a rod B C laid on a table, does not fall, provided another rod G D is set upright below the handle and against the end C of the first rod, perpendicular to the bottom of the bucket. For since both rods together with the bucket make one and the same body, the bucket cannot fall without the end B of the rod B C being raised, describing, namely, [p. 56] the arc B L. But it cannot be raised without the center of gravity i, which is in the bucket, describing at the same time the arc i M, which it cannot describe without ascending upward against the tendency of heavy bodies (Axiom 3, §. 144): therefore the bucket will not be able to fall, but will necessarily hang motionless from the rod.

> 148 Ope motus centri gravitatis explicatur etiam, qui fieri possit, ut corpus aliquod ascendendo, adsiduè descendat, quod prima fronte Paradoxum videtur Tribus lignis triangulum A B C (Fig. IV.) construatur, cujus basis C B sit aequalis axibus duorum conorum, qui simul juncti sint per bases G F. Subjiciantur basi C B duo sustentacula C D, B E radio basis conorum G F breviora. Si coni illi duo ponantur super extremitatem A, videbuntur ascendere in C B ubi maxima est elevatio, centrum tamen gravitatis descendet.

148 By means of the motion of the center of gravity it is also explained how it can happen that a body, while ascending, continually descends, which at first sight seems a Paradox. Let a triangle A B C (Fig. IV) be constructed of three pieces of wood, whose base C B is equal to the axes of two cones joined together by their bases G F. Under the base C B let two supports C D, B E be placed, shorter than the radius of the base of the cones G F. If those two cones are set upon the extremity A, they will seem to ascend into C B, where the elevation is greatest; yet the center of gravity will descend.

> 149 Ut hoc planiùs intelligatur considerate planum A B b (Fig. V.) in quo centrum gravitatis *a* duorum conorum reperitur. Centrum hoc elevatum est supra horizontem quantum linea a b, quae aequalis est p F. Si conus incéderet super F D centrum gravitatis *a* describeret lineam a p horizonti F D parallelam. Conus autem in IV. figura ita movetur per duo plana B A, A C ut ejus vertex x x sit in B C, vel in C (Fig. V.) ergo in motu coni centrum gravitatis *a* describit *a* C, nempè adsiduè descendit, ita ut quando perveniat in C, centrum gravitatis ejusdem descenderit quantum notatur à p C, sed motus corporum determinatur à motu centri gravitatis ipsorum: ergo si centrum conorum descendit, ut est demonstratum, conus ascendere debet. Duplex itaque conus per duo plana IV. figurae ascendat necesse est.

149 That this may be understood more plainly, consider the plane A B b (Fig. V) in which the center of gravity a of the two cones is found. This center is raised above the horizon by as much as the line a b, which is equal to p F. If the cone advanced upon F D, the center of gravity a would describe the line a p parallel to the horizon F D. But the cone in the IV. figure moves along the two planes B A, A C in such a way that its vertex x x is in B C, or in C (Fig. V): therefore in the motion of the cone the center of gravity a describes a C, that is, it continually descends, so that when it arrives at C, its center of gravity will have descended by as much as is marked by p C; but the motion of bodies is determined by the motion of their center of gravity: therefore if the center of the cones descends, as has been demonstrated, the cone must ascend. It is necessary, then, that the double cone should ascend along the two planes of the IV. figure.

> 150 Cognitio centri gravitatis, & lineae directionis apta est aliis pluribus explicandis: Homo ex. gr. qui ita sedeat, ut cum femoribus crura angulum rectum constituant, fémora quoque cum trunco sint ad angulum rectum, súrgere non poterit, nisi priùs humeros inclinet aut pedem retróferat, ut linea directionis intra basim pedum décidat. Si humeris, & calcaneis parietem adtingens, ac pedum tantummodo extremitatibus terra innixus homo stet, infléctere se non poterit, nisi pedem anteferat, alias quum se inflectit, cadat necesse est, quia tunc linea directionis extra basim décidit.

150 The knowledge of the center of gravity and of the line of direction is suited to explaining many other things. A man, for example, who sits in such a way that his legs make a right angle with his thighs, and his thighs too are at a right angle with his trunk, will not be able to rise unless he first inclines his shoulders or draws his foot back, so that the line of direction may fall within the base of the feet. If a man stands touching a wall with his shoulders and heels, and resting on the ground only with the tips of his feet, he will not be able to bend himself unless he puts a foot forward; otherwise, when he bends, he must needs fall, because the line of direction then falls outside the base.

> 151 Verum haec leviter adtigisse satis est: nam si omnia, quae à figura & situ partium ducuntur, referre esset animus omnia ferè, & naturae, & artis phaénomena hùc essent congerenda: qualitates enim penè omnes à figura, & situ partium oriuntur.

151 But it is enough to have touched on these things lightly: for if it were my intention to report all the things that are derived from the figure and situation of the parts, almost all the phenomena both of nature and of art would have to be heaped together here: for nearly all qualities arise from the figure and situation of the parts.

[p. 57]

## CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

> De divisibilitate corporum.

On the divisibility of bodies.

> 152 Divisibilitatem esse adfectionem corporibus omnibus propriam; uti indubium est, ita in quaestionem hic venire minimè debet, id duntaxat Physici considerant ¿quorsum divisibilitas illa se extendat? Quae quidem comtemplatio summi in Physica est momenti, atque ea de causa Recentiores Physici experimenta plurima instituerunt, scriptisque editis argumentum hoc illustrarunt. ¿Num verò materia, corpus, sive continuum physicum dividi in infinitum queat, vel an tandem sit in partibus insectibilibus sistendum? Controversia est, quae ut ait P. Regnault [^57-s1-2] jam indè ab exortu Philosophiae célebris elegantissima citrà fructum torsit ingenia. Nos eo consilio rem adgrediemur, ut controversiae statu proposito, quod certum in illa videri possit ingenuè exponamus.

hat divisibility is an affection proper to all bodies, as it is beyond 152 T doubt, so it ought by no means to come into question here; the Physicists consider only this: how far does that divisibility extend? This contemplation is indeed of the highest moment in Physics, and for that reason the modern Physicists have instituted very many experiments and have illustrated this subject in published writings. But can matter, body, or the physical continuum be divided to infinity, or must one at last come to a stop at indivisible parts? It is a controversy which, as Fr. Regnault says (m), has from the very rise of Philosophy tormented famous and most elegant wits without fruit. We shall approach the matter with this design: that, having set forth the state of the controversy, we may candidly expound what can seem certain in it.

> [^57-s1-2]: Entret. Physiques. Entret. I.

[^57-s1-2]: Entret. Physiques. Entret. I.

> 153 *Continuum* ergo dicitur illud, quod resultat ex partibus ita conjunctis, ut illarum extrema sint unum, hoc est, quae ad eandem prorsus substantiam pertinent, ut sunt partes ligni, quae eandem, & unicam ligni substantiam componunt. Contiguum verò dicitur illud, cujus partes extremae sunt simul, ut quum manus, aut duo corpora sese tangunt Partes etiam alicujus compositi *deinceps positae*, vel *juxta positae* dicuntur, quum inter illas alterius corporis particulae ex. gr. aëris intérjacent, ut sunt grana in acervo tritici. Partes *aliquotae* dicuntur, quae aliquoties repetitae adaequant praecisse totum. Sic pes est pars aliquota *Hexapedae*, quia sexies repetitus Hexapedam pracisse adaequat.

153 That, then, is called a continuum which results from parts so joined that their extremities are one, that is, belong to altogether the same substance, as are the parts of wood, which compose the same single substance of the wood. That, however, is called contiguous whose extreme parts are together, as when hands, or two bodies, touch each other. The parts of some composite are also said to be placed in succession, or placed side by side, when particles of another body, e.g. of air, lie between them, as are the grains in a heap of wheat. Those parts are called aliquot which, repeated some number of times, exactly equal the whole. Thus the foot is an aliquot part of the fathom, because, repeated six times, it exactly equals the fathom.

> 154 Partes *aliquantae* dicuntur, quae nunquam aliquoties repetitae adaequant praecisse totum, sed vel excedunt, vel ab eo deficiunt: sic pars quatuor pedes extensa, est pars aliquanta hexapedae, quia si bis sumatur excedit hexapedam, semel verò sumpta non dum adaequat. Partes *proportionales* sunt, quae in continua proportione decrescunt, sic hexapeda dividi pótest in duas medietates, & quaelibet ex his in alias duas, & sic deinceps. Continui physici partes in infinitum divisibiles esse arbitrantur Peripatetici, & Cartesiani plurimi. Qui Epicurum, & Gassendum sequuntur contrariam tuentur sententiam.

154 Those parts are called aliquant which, repeated any number of times, never exactly equal the whole, but either exceed it or fall short of it: thus a part four feet long is an aliquant part of the fathom, because if it is taken twice it exceeds the fathom, while taken once it does not yet equal it. Proportional parts are those which decrease in continued proportion; thus the fathom can be divided into two halves, and either of these into two others, and so on. The Peripatetics and very many Cartesians judge the parts of the physical continuum to be divisible to infinity. Those who follow Epicurus and Gassendi defend the contrary opinion.

> 155 Primae sententiae defensores ita arguunt. Omne extensum est divisibile in partes; sed omne corpus quantumvis tenue [p. 58] semper extensum est: ergo omne corpus semper, & in infinitum est divisibile. Respondent Epicuréi disting. maj. omne extensum mathematicè sumptum, concedunt, physice sumptum, negant. Id *mathematicè* extensum dicitur, quod ratione suarum dimensionum duntaxàt consideratur, non inspecta subjecti extensi conditione, ac natura: *physice* verò extensum vocatur, quod tanquam substantia quaedam physica, certa natura ac conditione donata consideratur, quidquid extensum est, mathematicè, ac per mentem dividi potest; at non semper re ipsa, & physice, quum esse possit substantia quaedam simplex non ex partibus composita, scilicet *atomus*, quae primum est subjectum ex quo omnia corpora sensibilia constant, & ultimum in quod resolvuntur Hactenus Epicúrei, & Gassendistae.

155 The defenders of the first opinion argue thus. Everything extended is divisible into parts; but every body, however thin, is always [p. 58] extended: therefore every body is always, and to infinity, divisible. The Epicureans reply by distinguishing the major: everything extended taken mathematically, they grant; taken physically, they deny. That is said to be extended mathematically which is considered only by reason of its dimensions, without regard to the condition and nature of the extended subject; that, however, is called extended physically which is considered as a certain physical substance endowed with a definite nature and condition. Whatever is extended can be divided mathematically and by the mind, but not always in reality itself and physically, since there can be a certain simple substance not composed of parts, namely the atom, which is the first subject of which all sensible bodies consist, and the last into which they are resolved. Thus far the Epicureans and Gassendists.

> 156 Hi autèm contra Peripateticos sic arguunt: Si materia in infinitum esset divisibilis, corpus exiguum, ut granum tritici, infinitas actu partes in se continéret, nàm corpus in ea tantum quae continet divisibile cogitatur; sed hoc manifeste repugnat: ergo materia sive continuum non est in infinitum divisibile. Respondent Peripatetici disting. maj. si materia esset divisibilis secundum partes alíquotas, corpus exiguum haberet, &c. concedunt, si sit tantum divisibilis in partes proportionales quarum unaquaeque infinitas alias in se includit, negant. Habetis quaestionis statum.

156 These, moreover, argue thus against the Peripatetics: If matter were divisible to infinity, a tiny body, such as a grain of wheat, would contain within itself infinite parts in act, for a body is conceived as divisible only into those parts which it contains; but this is manifestly contradictory: therefore matter, or the continuum, is not divisible to infinity. The Peripatetics reply by distinguishing the major: if matter were divisible according to aliquot parts, a tiny body would have, etc., they grant; if it is divisible only into proportional parts, each of which includes infinitely many others within itself, they deny. You have the state of the question.

> 157 Sed haec omnia (ut optimè advertunt Purchot, & Klaus) [^58-s1-2] sunt hujusmodi, ut si rationes duntaxat, non responsiones ponderentur, demonstrationum vim obtinére ex utráque parte videantur. Ut iccircò unum hoc liceat pronunciare; incertum esse an corporea magnitudo dividi semper possit, an verò in insecabilibus partibus omnis tandèm illius divisio definiatur, quod quidem eò adserimus oportunius, quò certiùs novimus, ad incrementa Physicae perinde prorsùs esse, sive indivisibiles ponantur continui partes, sive divisibiles in infinitum, nam ad principia corporis naturalis, & ad phaenómena in universum explicanda commostrare sufficit corpora quaevis in partes adeò minutas dispésci posse, ut vel ipsa ratio obstupescat, quod sequenti propositione â nobis probandum quàmclarissime est.

157 But all these things (as Purchot and Klaus very well observe) (n) are of such a kind that, if only the reasons, and not the replies, are weighed, they seem on both sides to carry the force of demonstrations. So that it may therefore be permitted to pronounce this one thing: it is uncertain whether corporeal magnitude can always be divided, or whether all its division at last terminates in indivisible parts; which we assert all the more fittingly as we know the more certainly that for the advancement of Physics it is altogether the same whether the parts of the continuum are posited as indivisible or as divisible to infinity; for, for the principles of natural body and for explaining the phenomena in general, it suffices to show that any bodies whatever can be split into parts so minute that reason itself is astonished, which is to be proved by us as clearly as possible in the following proposition.

> [^58-s1-2]: Part. 2. Physic. Gener. num. 128.

[^58-s1-2]: Pt. 2, General Physics, no. 128.

> 158 Dico igitur: corpora in partes omnino exilissimas stupendum prorsùs in modum actu divisa sunt, dividique possunt. Primò quidem odoris diffusio subministrat argumentum summae subtilitatis, ad quam substantia odorifera pervenire potest. Ultrà ea quae diximus (§ 58.) exemplo sit càlculus exhalationum fumosarum, quem P. de Lanis [^58-s2] exequitur, & ab exiguo thuris grano egredientium, & singula cubiculi puncta occupantium. Laudatus igitur Pater posito cubiculo 20 pedes longo, totidem lato, & in altitudinem ad 15 pedes adtolli, càlculo facto adfirmat, forè [p. 59] particularum fumi in cubiculo reipsa contentarum 75,000,000,000,000, quae omnes uno exiguo thuris granulo conclusae antea, adhuc tamen tantae sunt, ut olfatum hominis adficere queant.

158 I say, therefore: bodies are actually divided, and can be divided, into utterly minute parts in an altogether stupendous manner. First, indeed, the diffusion of odor furnishes an argument of the extreme subtlety to which an odoriferous substance can attain. Beyond what we have said (§. 58), let an example be the calculation which Fr. Lana Terzi (o) carries out of the smoky exhalations that issue from a tiny grain of incense and occupy every point of a small room. The said Father therefore, supposing a room 20 feet long, as many wide, and rising to a height of 15 feet, affirms, having made the calculation, that the particles [p. 59] of smoke actually contained in the room will be 75,000,000,000,000, all of which, though previously shut up in one tiny grain of incense, are nevertheless still so many that they can affect a man’s sense of smell.

> [^58-s2]: Magist. Nat. & Art. Tract. 1. Lib. 1. cap. 1. Obs. 4.

[^58-s2]: Magist. Nat. & Art., Tract. 1, bk. 1, ch. 1, Obs. 4.

> 159 Reple Phialam A (Fig. VI.) colli recurvi quae Aeolypila dicitur, aqua rosarum, aut alia qualibet odóra, suppone ignem, vel thecam B, in qua sit spiritus vini cum ellychnio accenso, brevè evaporabit aqua per exíle collum, & odor per integrum, & si latum cubiculum diffundetur. Post duo, aut tria minuta rémove ab igne phialam, & obtúra, vix sensibilis erit aquae diminutio, ita ut minima ejus quantitas per totum aërem cubiculi dispersa sit. Jam verò calculo facto ab erudito P. Johanne de Turre [^59-s1-2] Viro in rimandis naturae arcanis perspicacissimo compertum est, quod illa minima aquae portio quae tempore trium minutorum evaporavit, resolvitur in particulas naribus sensibiles 3,583,180,800, quod sanè omnem superat captum.

159 Fill the vial A (Fig. VI) with a bent neck, which is called an Aeolipile, with rose water or any other fragrant water; put a fire under it, or the case B, in which there is spirit of wine with a lighted wick; the water will soon evaporate through the slender neck, and the odor will be diffused through the whole room, however large. After two or three minutes remove the vial from the fire and stop it up: the diminution of the water will scarcely be sensible, so that a very small quantity of it has been dispersed through the whole air of the room. Now, by a calculation made by the learned Fr. Giovanni della Torre (p), a man most perspicacious in searching out the secrets of nature, it has been ascertained that that very small portion of water which evaporated in the space of three minutes is resolved into 3,583,180,800 particles sensible to the nostrils, which truly surpasses all comprehension.

> [^59-s1-2]: Elem. Physic. Tom. 1. n. 135.

[^59-s1-2]: Elem. Physic., vol. 1, no. 135.

> 160 Odóres fragrantium camporum insulae Ceylán ad decem etiam leucarum distantiam versus navigia appropinquantia deferuntur. Exigua moschi particula odore ita imbuit alia corpora majora, vestes, chyrothécas, libros, ut per longissimum tempus odorem servent, & tamen continuò nunquam non partes odoriferas exibeant. Plura similia referuntur á Boyleo, Keilio, S'Graversandio, & aliis Physicis Quum verò tot perpetuò diffluentibus particulis odoratis, nullum sensibile substantiae dispendium in pluribus observari possit, incredibiliter subtilia, effluvia haec esse oportebit.

160 The odors of the fragrant fields of the island of Ceylon are carried toward approaching ships even at a distance of ten leagues. A tiny particle of musk so imbues other larger bodies — clothes, gloves, books — with its odor that they keep the odor for a very long time, and yet continually never cease to give off odoriferous parts. Many similar things are related by Boyle, Keill, ’s Gravesande, and other Physicists. Since, then, with so many odorous particles perpetually flowing off, no sensible loss of substance can be observed in many cases, these effluvia will have to be incredibly subtle.

> 161 Secundò ostenditur ex tincturis. Laudatus Boyle expertum se refert, quod si granum cupri dissolutum, & spiritu vini permixtum infundatur lampadi cujus ellychnium ex plumóso alúmine efformatum non consumitur, per semihoram integram flamma caeruleo colore tincta producitur, adeòque semper novae cupri particulae sibi succedunt, eundemque in flamma colorem efficiunt: ita ut mirari satis non possimus, qua ratione particula illa cupri tam minutim concídi potuerit, ut novum semper colorem, hoc est novas semper particulas suppéditet.

161 Secondly, it is shown from tinctures. The said Boyle relates that he found by experience that if a grain of copper, dissolved and mixed with spirit of wine, is poured into a lamp whose wick, made of plume alum, is not consumed, a flame tinged with a blue color is produced for a whole half hour; and so new particles of copper continually succeed one another and produce the same color in the flame: so that we cannot sufficiently wonder by what means that particle of copper could have been cut up so minutely as to supply always new color, that is, always new particles.

> 162 Tertiò idem evincitur ex *ductilitate* auri, nam ut celeberrimus Physicus Reaumurius [^59-s2] testatur: uncia auri cubica in tenuissima folia quadrata, plusquam quingenties centena millia à bracteatoribus contunditur, sed quod omnem prorsus imaginationis vim superat, si unum ex his foliis argenteo cylindro circumvolvatur, & totum illius superficiem ambiat, deindè cylindrus ejusmodi per plura foramina sensim, ac successivè angustiora trajiciatur, donec ad tenuissimi fili, vel capilli crassitiem redigatur, ubique tamen haec longissimi fili superficies inaurata adparebit, quod [p. 60] certè fieri non potest, ut inito cálculo demonstratur nisi unicum granum auri ad duas circiter leucas extendatur.

162 Thirdly, the same is proved from the ductility of gold; for, as the most celebrated Physicist Réaumur (q) testifies, a cubic ounce of gold is beaten out by the gold-beaters into more than five hundred times a hundred thousand square leaves of the utmost thinness; but, what altogether surpasses every power of the imagination, if one of these leaves is wrapped round a silver cylinder and covers its whole surface, and the cylinder is then drawn gradually through several successively narrower holes until it is reduced to the thickness of a very fine thread, or of a hair, the surface of this very long thread will nevertheless appear gilded everywhere, which [p. 60] certainly cannot happen, as is shown when the calculation is made, unless a single grain of gold is extended to about two leagues.

> [^59-s2]: Memoires de l' Academ. 1713.

[^59-s2]: Memoires de l’Academ., 1713.

> 163 Quartò ex observationibus microscopicis abyssus exilitatis materiae demonstratur. Observatum â se refert P. de Lanis [^60-s1-2], animalculum albissimum, quod oculis licèt perspicacissimis invisibile fuerat, microscopio viginti septem millionibus vicium augente objectum, grano triticeo videbatur aequale: velocissimo motu per duodecim minuta secunda temporis, vix grani triticei longitudinem confécit. ¿Quaenam ergo in ejusmodi animalculo passuum, quaenam pedum, quae oculorum, quae pupillae, quae sanguinis, quae spirituum animalium mira subtilitas esse debet! Idem dicendum de tenuissimis illis animalculis, qui in caseo, ope microscopii cernuntur. Quantula autèm est eorum animalculorum pupilla, per quam tamen longè tenuiores luminis radii transeunt? ¿Quantulae sunt eae partes quae spiritus animales possunt nominari? Haec si consideremus, fateamur necessè est, ampliùs quiddam, ac quod nostra nobis imaginandi facultas sistere queat, in minimis recondi.

163 Fourthly, an abyss of minuteness in matter is demonstrated from microscopic observations. Fr. Lana Terzi (r) relates that he observed a very white animalcule which had been invisible to even the most perspicacious eyes, and which, placed under a microscope magnifying twenty-seven million times, appeared equal to a grain of wheat: with a very swift motion it scarcely covered the length of a grain of wheat in twelve seconds of time. What, then, must be the wondrous subtlety of the steps, of the feet, of the eyes, of the pupil, of the blood, of the animal spirits in an animalcule of this kind! The same must be said of those very fine animalcules which are seen in cheese with the help of a microscope. How tiny, moreover, is the pupil of those animalcules, through which nevertheless far finer rays of light pass? How tiny are those parts which can be called animal spirits? If we consider these things, we must needs confess that something greater, and more than our faculty of imagining can present to us, lies hidden in the smallest things.

> [^60-s1-2]: Magist. Nat. & Art. Praefat.

[^60-s1-2]: Magist. Nat. & Art., Preface.

> 164 Solertissimus Naturae indagator Lewenhoek in aqua per aliquot dies adservata, exquisiti microscopii ope, minima observavit animalcula, quorum millia, vulgaris arenae globuli magnitúdinem non excedunt. Jam quum animalculum quodvis sit corpus organicum, perpendamus paulispèr; quàm delicatae, & subtiles debent esse partes ad ipsum constituendum, & ad vitalem actionem conservandam necessariae. Haud facilè concipitur, quo pacto in tam angusto spatiolo comprehendi possint cor, quod vitae fons est, músculi ad motum necessarii, glandulae, ventriculus, & intestina, aliaque membra innumera, sine quibus animal esse non potest. Praeterea, quum singula memorata membra sint etiam corpora organica, aliis carére non possunt partibus ad suas actiones necessariis. Constabunt ergo ex fibris, membránulis, túnicis, venis, arteriis, nervis, & his similibus canaliculis, quorum éxilitas imaginationis vires longè superat. At his infinitae propèmodum minores esse debent partes fluidi, quod per canaliculos decurrit, nempè sanguis, lympha, & spiritus animales. ¡Quanta in vilissimo animalculo portenta, Divinaeque Omnipotentiae argumenta!

164 That most skillful investigator of Nature, Leeuwenhoek, observed in water kept for some days, with the help of an exquisite microscope, very small animalcules, thousands of which do not exceed the size of a globule of common sand. Now since any animalcule whatever is an organic body, let us weigh for a little how delicate and subtle must be the parts necessary to constitute it and to preserve its vital action. It is not easily conceived how in so narrow a little space there can be comprised the heart, which is the fount of life, the muscles necessary for motion, the glands, the stomach and intestines, and innumerable other members without which an animal cannot exist. Moreover, since each of the members mentioned is also an organic body, they cannot lack other parts necessary for their actions. They will therefore consist of fibers, little membranes, tunics, veins, arteries, nerves, and similar little canals, whose minuteness far surpasses the powers of the imagination. But almost infinitely smaller than these must be the parts of the fluid which runs through the little canals, namely the blood, the lymph and the animal spirits. What prodigies in the meanest animalcule, and what proofs of the Divine Omnipotence!

> 165 Nec tantum naturae opera admirabilem materiae subtilitatem manifestò demonstrant, artis etiam opera celebratissima idem evincunt, admirationeque nos complére jure merito debent. Cl. Derham, [^60-s2-2] P. Klaus, [^60-s3-2] & Sigaud de la Fond [^60-s4] referunt, quod Oswaldus Nerlinger conformavit è grano píperis scyphum in quo inserti erant mille ducenti caliculi eburnei, quorum singuli [p. 61] sustentaculo instructi, & inaurato margine ornati erant, tanto adhuc relicto spatio, ut quatuor centum alii consimiles potuerint ímponi.

165 Nor do the works of nature alone manifestly demonstrate the admirable subtlety of matter: the most celebrated works of art also prove the same, and must with full justice fill us with admiration. The distinguished Derham (s), Fr. Klaus (t) and Sigaud de la Fond (u) relate that Oswald Nerlinger fashioned out of a peppercorn a cup in which were set twelve hundred little ivory cups, each of which was furnished with a stand [p. 61] and adorned with a gilded rim, so much space being still left over that four hundred others like them could have been put in.

> [^60-s2-2]: Thelogie Physique. Lib. 8. c. 4. not. 11.

[^60-s2-2]: Théologie Physique, bk. 8, ch. 4, note 11.

> [^60-s3-2]: Phys Gener. Part. 2. n. 127.

[^60-s3-2]: Phys. Gener., pt. 2, no. 127.

> [^60-s4]: Leçons de Physique. Tom. 1. pag. 64.

[^60-s4]: Leçons de Physique, vol. 1, p. 64.

> 166 Atque haec pauca è multis quae adjici possent ad commonstrandam summam continui divisibilitatem, exilitatemque materiae à nobis proposita, iis verbis concludimus, quibus suam de insectis tractationem ordítur Plinius [^61-s1]: *rerum*, scilicèt, *naturam nusquam magis, quàm in minimis sitam esse*. Àgnoscimus etiam, & cum Magno Augustino [^61-s2] profitemur: *Deum ita esse magnum in operibus magnis, ut minor non sit in minimis.*

166 And these few things, out of the many that could be added, which we have put forward to show the extreme divisibility of the continuum and the minuteness of matter, we conclude with those words with which Pliny (x) begins his treatment of insects: that the nature of things, namely, is nowhere more to be found than in the smallest things. We acknowledge also, and profess with the great Augustine (y), that God is so great in his great works that he is not less in the least.

> [^61-s1]: Hist. Nat. Lib. 11. cap. 2.

[^61-s1]: Natural History, bk. 11, ch. 2.

> [^61-s2]: Lib. 21. cont. Faust. cap. 5.
