## CAPUT VI. — CHAPTER VI

> De Rarefactione, & Condensatione corporum.

On the Rarefaction and Condensation of bodies.

> 198 Corpus *rarum* dicitur, *quod sub mognis dimensionibus parum continet materiae: densum* verò, *quod multum habet materiae sub parvis dimensionibus*, sic aqua medium implens vásculum, igni admota ebulliens, *rara* dicitur, quia pro tanta quam habet tunc extensione, re ipsa parum est materiae aqueae: contrà cera antea calefacta, postea frigescens, *densa* est, quia ad minus spatium contrahitur. Unde *rarefactio* est *motus, quo corpus eadem manente materiae quantitate ad majus spatium exiénditur.* Nam si aliquid ejusdem materiae adjiciatùr, ex. g: aqua, bullienti aquae, non *rarefactio*, sed *aumentatio* erit. *Condensatio* est *motus quo corpus ad minus spatium redigitur, quin aliquid de ejus materia dematur*, nam si de cèra ex. gr. quidquam auferatur, non *condensatio*, sed *diminutio* erit.

body is called rare which under great dimensions contains little matter; dense, 198 A however, which has much matter under small dimensions; thus water filling half a little vessel and boiling when brought near the fire is called rare, because for so great an extension as it then has there is in reality little aqueous matter; wax, on the contrary, first heated and afterwards cooling, is dense, because it contracts into a smaller space. Hence rarefaction is the motion by which a body, the same quantity of matter remaining, is extended into a greater space. For if something of the same matter is added, e.g. water to boiling water, it will not be rarefaction but augmentation. Condensation is the motion by which a body is reduced to a smaller space without anything of its matter being taken away; for if anything is taken away from wax, e.g., it will not be condensation but diminution.

> 199 Corpus *rarum*, & *tensum* in eo conveniunt, quod sub majori extensione parum materiae contineant, differunt tamen in eo, quod *tensum* ad minorem extensionem éxigit redúci: non verò *rarum*, precisè scilicet ob raritatis statum. Similiter corpus *densum*, & *compressum* in eo conveniunt, quod sub parva extensione multum habent materiae. *Compressum* verò majorem exigit extensionem, non verò *densum*, ratione nempè *densitatis*. Compressum majorem exigit extensionem: nam particulae illud componentes per causam extrinsecam ad minus spatium sunt reductae, *densum* verò ab aliqua causa intrinsecùs ita constituitur, ut majorem extensionem non éxigat, haec autem causa potest esse colligatio, novaque implexio, ac fixatio paticularum corpus illud componentium, qua pósita, etiam [p. 71] nullo repágulo extrinsecùs adhibito, pristinam extensionem non répetunt. His ita constitutis.

199 A rare and a stretched body agree in this, that under a greater extension they contain little matter; they differ, however, in this, that the stretched body requires to be brought back to a smaller extension, but not the rare body, precisely, that is, on account of its state of rarity. Similarly a dense and a compressed body agree in this, that under a small extension they have much matter. But the compressed body requires a greater extension, not, however, the dense, namely by reason of its density. The compressed body requires a greater extension: for the particles composing it have been reduced to a smaller space by an extrinsic cause; but the dense body is so constituted by some intrinsic cause that it does not require a greater extension; and this cause can be the binding together, the new interweaving and the fixing of the particles composing that body; and once this is in place, even with [p. 71] with no restraint applied from outside, they do not regain their former extension. These things being thus established,

> 200 Dico: rarefactio corporum in eo sita est, quod pori corporis dilatentur: condensatio autem in eo, quod ejusdem pori constringantur, ad quam dilatationem ingressus particularum, & corpusculorum insensibilium, uti ad constrictionem expulsio earumdem conséquitur. Prob.: corpus tum raréscere dicitur, si non aucta materia ejus volumen crescat, & majus spatium óccupet, densari verò, si non imminuta materia volúmen decrescat, & corpus spatio minori congruat [§. 198]; sed evidens est augeri volumen corporis, quin crescat materia illius, hoc ipso quod pori dilatentur in eo; decréscere autem volumen corporis, quin de materia quidpiam auferatur hoc ipso quod pori coarctentur; ergo. Quod verò in sensu physico esse non possit rarefactio sine ingressu corpusculorum insensibilium, igneorum, aethereorum, aut aliorum patet, quia quum ex dicendis nullum detur vacuum sensibile, adeòque sensibile quodvis spatium plenum sit materia aliqua subtilissima, cónsequens est, ut quando dilatantur pori, mole totius corporis sensibiliter aucta, haec materia utpotè subtilissima eos subeat, repleatque. Eodem proportionaliter modo de condensatione ratiocinandum est.

200 I say: the rarefaction of bodies consists in this, that the pores of the body are dilated; condensation, however, in this, that the same pores are constricted; upon which dilatation there follows an entry of particles and of insensible corpuscles, as upon the constriction their expulsion. Proof: a body is said to rarefy when, its matter not being increased, its volume grows and occupies a greater space; to be condensed when, its matter not being diminished, its volume decreases and the body fits a smaller space [§. 198]; but it is evident that the volume of a body is increased without its matter growing, by the very fact that the pores in it are dilated, and that the volume of a body decreases without anything being taken away from its matter, by the very fact that the pores are narrowed: therefore. That in the physical sense, moreover, there cannot be rarefaction without the entry of insensible corpuscles, fiery, ethereal or others, is plain; because, since (as will be said) there is no sensible void, and so every sensible space is full of some very subtle matter, it follows that when the pores are dilated, the bulk of the whole body being sensibly increased, this matter, being very subtle, enters and fills them. One must reason about condensation in the same way, proportionally.

> 201 Confirm.: Illa sententia in rebus physicis praeferenda est ceteris, quae captu est facilis, nec mysteria humanum intellectum ferè superantia invehit, & in qua facillimè redditur ratio phaenomenorum in motu rarefactionis, & condensationis occurrentium [*Axiom. III. IV. & V. §§. 32. & 33.*]; sed talis est nostra sententia: ergò. Min. tum ex hactenùs dictis, tum ex solutione objectionum elucéscet, & etiam inductione experimentorum, eorumdemque explicatione probatur. Explicatur enim cur aqua in glaciem concréta majus spatium occupet, quàm in statu suo naturali. Academici Florentini ut id exactè examinarent, tubum vitreum elegérunt, altera extremitate clausum, quem aqua ad medietatem implevérunt, tum nivi minutim contritae immerserunt, donec aqua in glaciem verteretur, quo fiebat, ut aqua dilatata adsúrgeret in tubo, & majus in illo spatium, quàm quum fluida esset occuparet.

201 Confirm.: In physical matters that opinion is to be preferred to the others which is easy to grasp, does not bring in mysteries almost surpassing the human intellect, and in which an account is most easily given of the phenomena occurring in the motion of rarefaction and condensation [Axiom. III, IV & V, §§. 32 & 33]; but such is our opinion: therefore. The minor will shine forth both from what has been said thus far and from the solution of the objections, and is also proved by induction from experiments and by their explanation. For it is explained why water congealed into ice occupies a greater space than in its natural state. The Florentine Academicians, to examine this exactly, chose a glass tube closed at one end, which they filled with water to half its height, then immersed it in finely crushed snow until the water was turned into ice; whereby it came about that the dilated water rose in the tube and occupied a greater space in it than when it was fluid.

> 202 Praeterea exactissima bilance examinarunt aquae pondus ante glaciationem; & ejusdem jam glaciatae, & repererunt, plus ponderasse non glaciatam, quàm post glaciationem. Horum autem ratio est, quia quum aquae particulae ex una parte invicem congelatione adhaereant, mutuoque strictiùs compléctantur, innumeros, eosque satis notabiles poros ex alia parte relinquunt, qui materia praecípuè aërea sunt repleti, quae quum per poros strictiores aquae quae glaciatur exire nequeat, dilatatur; quo fit, ut glacies quae quoddam adgregatum est ex aqua coagulata, & ex aëre sic dilatato in illis búllulis incluso extensior evadat, quàm erat ipsa aqua ante glaciationem.

202 Moreover, with a most exact balance they examined the weight of water before freezing, and of the same water once frozen, and found that the unfrozen water weighed more than after freezing. The reason of these things, moreover, is this: since the particles of water on one side adhere to one another by congelation and embrace one another more tightly, they leave on the other side innumerable and quite notable pores, which are filled chiefly with aerial matter; and since this cannot escape through the narrower pores of the water that is freezing, it is dilated; whence it comes about that ice, which is a kind of aggregate of coagulated water and of air thus dilated and enclosed in those little bubbles, becomes more extended than the water itself was before freezing.

[p. 72]

> 203 Dùm enim dilatatur aër, nec erumpit, totam aquae molem in qua continetur, augéri necesse est, & consequenter sub majori mole constituta, eandemque aquae materiam cóntinens, sed plurimis praesertim igneis particulis destitutam, levior evadit. Existimo tamen, aquam si â búllulis separata posset existere sub eodem volumine, post glaciationem reddendam fore graviorem; patet enim grándinem, in qua nullae adparent búllulae, esse graviorem aqua pluviali, in hac siquidem mérgitur, quum è contrario glacies vulgaris, & búllulis conspicuis plena eidem aquae supérnatet; fit enim ex aqua tantillum condensata, & ex aëre plurimum dilatato, quoddam adgregatum leviùs aqua antè glaciationem. Omitto plura alia, quae ex his nullo admodùm negotio exponuntur. Momenta nùnc à diversis phaenómenis petita paucis discutiamus.

203 For while the air is dilated and does not burst out, the whole bulk of the water in which it is contained must necessarily be increased; and consequently, being set under a greater bulk and containing the same matter of water, but deprived of very many particles, especially fiery ones, it becomes lighter. I think, however, that water, if it could exist separated from the little bubbles under the same volume, would be rendered heavier after freezing; for it is plain that hail, in which no little bubbles appear, is heavier than rain water, since it sinks in it, whereas, on the contrary, common ice, full of conspicuous little bubbles, floats on the same water: for out of water condensed a little and air very greatly dilated there is made an aggregate lighter than the water before freezing. I omit many other things which are set forth from these with no trouble at all. Let us now discuss in a few words the difficulties drawn from various phenomena.

> Argumenta solvuntur.

THE ARGUMENTS ARE ANSWERED.

> 204 Opp. 1. in nostra sententia non potest reddi congrua ratio phaenomenorum, quae observantur in vase, quod ex cupro conflatur formam, piri, vel pomi réferens, pro cáudiculo habens tubum exiguo forámine terminatum, quod vas *Aeolípila* nuncupatur. Haec spiritu vini ad certam quantitatem impleta, ignique superimposita, fontem ex spiritu vini salientem exhibebit, cui si candélam, admoveas liquor prosiliens inflammábitur (Fig. IX.). Similiter, si ad dimidium aqua repleatur, & carbonibus admoveatur, vapórem per canaliculum magna vehementia, & sónitu ejiciet (Fig. X.): imò vapor aquam in Aeolípila contentam ad altitudinem 20 pedum propellet. His autèm constitutis ita argumentum efformatur.

204 Obj. 1. On our opinion no fitting account can be given of the phenomena observed in a vessel which is made of copper, has the shape of a pear or an apple, and has for its little stem a tube ending in a tiny opening; this vessel is called an Aeolipile. Filled with spirit of wine to a certain quantity and set upon a fire, it will exhibit a fountain of spirit of wine leaping up, and if you bring a candle near it, the liquor springing out will be set alight (Fig. IX). Similarly, if it is filled to half with water and set near coals, it will throw out vapor through the little canal with great vehemence and noise (Fig. X): nay, the vapor will drive the water contained in the Aeolipile to a height of 20 feet. These things being established, the argument is formed thus.

> 205 Si rarefactio habetur per dilatationem pororum, tunc quando in aeolipilà rarescit aqua, vel spiritus vini, tantundem etiam rarefiat necesse est ipsum vasculum, quum propiùs sit igni, quàm liquor in eo contentus; sed hoc adversatur experientiae: ergo. Neque aptiùs complura alia explicantur, ut quod globus vitreus (Fig. XI.) gutta aquae, vel spiritu vini plenus, & undique clausus, igni aproximatus cum fragóre dissiliat; similiter castaneae non incisae prunis immissae sonitu rumpantur, praesertim quum dici non possit, quod aër externus, qui rarefácere aquam déberet, vitrei globuli poros permeet. Sed haec argumenta citra difficultatem explanari possunt. Equidèm aeolípila calore nonnihil dilatari, & rarefieri quoque ádsero, at quum solidior sit, magisque compacta materia constet, habet partes magis cohaerentes, sibique invicèm infixas, unde ut pori ejus tantoperè, ac liquor contentus rarefierent, major vis caloris requiritur, quam sit illa quae ad poros aquae, vel spiritus vini, corporum nempè liquidorum, ideoque minus sibi cohaerentium dilatandos sufficit.

205 If rarefaction takes place through the dilatation of the pores, then, when water or spirit of wine is rarefied in the aeolipile, the little vessel itself must necessarily be rarefied just as much, since it is nearer to the fire than the liquor contained in it; but this is contrary to experience: therefore. Nor are several other things explained more aptly: as that a glass globe (Fig. XI), full of a drop of water or of spirit of wine and closed on all sides, bursts with a crash when brought near the fire; similarly, that chestnuts not cut open, put into live coals, burst with a noise; especially since it cannot be said that the external air, which would have to rarefy the water, permeates the pores of the glass globule. But these arguments can be explained without difficulty. I indeed assert that the aeolipile is somewhat dilated, and also rarefied, by heat; but since it is more solid and consists of more compact matter, it has parts more cohering and fixed into one another; whence, for its pores to be rarefied as much as the liquor contained, a greater force of heat is required than that which suffices for dilating the pores of water or of spirit of wine, bodies, namely, that are liquid and therefore cohere less among themselves.

[p. 73]

> 206 Nec minus alia explicari queunt. Certè difractio globi vitrei ab aquae rarefactione, seu vapore oritur. Castanae in ignem injectae disruptio similiter ab humidis particulis intra córticem inclusis calore rarefactis, & exitum quaerentibus efficitur. Neque miremini vim á nobis tantam tribui vapori, quum constet vaporem rarefactum majori pollére vi, quam pulverem pyrium qui simili globulo vitreo, & ejusdem ponderis, cujus est gutta aquae inclusus globum quidem diffringit, sed fragóre longè minori; quumque insuper ex Nolleto [^73-s1] innotuerit aquam in vaporem conversam 14000 vicibus majus volumen formare.

206 Nor can the other phenomena be explained any less easily. Certainly the bursting of a glass globe arises from the rarefaction of water, or from vapor. The bursting of chestnuts thrown into the fire is likewise brought about by moist particles shut up within the shell, which are rarefied by the heat and seek an outlet. Nor should you wonder that so great a force is attributed by us to vapor, since it is established that rarefied vapor has a greater force than gunpowder, which, shut up in a like little glass globe and of the same weight as the drop of water, does indeed shatter the globe, but with a far smaller crash; and since, moreover, it is known from Nollet (n) that water converted into vapor forms a volume 14000 times greater.

> [^73-s1]: Leçons de Physique. Tom. 4. Lect. 12. Sect. 2. Exp. 7.

[^73-s1]: Leçons de Physique, vol. 4, lesson 12, sect. 2, exp. 7.

> 207 Opp. 2. in condensatione excluditur materia subtilis; ergo tunc non intromittitur aliqua subtilis materia. Nego conseq.: quum enim materia subtilis quae introducitur, partes corporis invicèm strictiùs conjungat, ac nectat, in causa est, ut pori constringantur: & consequenter alia materia subtilis, quae in ipsis continebatur, foras erumpat, quae autèm excluditur plus est, quàm quae de novo adjicitur, ideòque corpus densum minus spatium occupat, quàm antè condensationem occupabat. Alia argumenta quae Scholastici movére solent, distinguendo duplicem significatum raritatis, & densitatis; alterum quo *metaphysicè*, & insensibiliter, alterum quo *physicè*, & sensibiliter corporum gemina haec mutatio usurpatur facillimè diluuntur.

207 Obj. 2. In condensation subtle matter is excluded; therefore no subtle matter is then introduced. I deny the consequence: for since the subtle matter which is introduced joins and binds the parts of the body more tightly to one another, it is the cause of the pores being contracted, and consequently of the other subtle matter, which was contained in them, bursting out; but what is excluded is more than what is newly added, and therefore the dense body occupies less space than it occupied before condensation. The other arguments which the Scholastics are wont to raise are very easily dissolved by distinguishing a twofold signification of rarity and density: one in which this twin change of bodies is taken metaphysically and insensibly, the other in which it is taken physically and sensibly.

> 208 Opp. tandem: quum scintilla ignis in acervum pulveris, pyrij delapsa eum accendit, & rarefacit, motus ille aut rarefactio, nec à pororum dilatatione, nec á materia subtili proficisci potest. ¿Quid est enim quod eam impellat materiam, aut tanta vi agitet, ut vel solo contactu tantam pulveri pyrio agitationem impertiatur? ¿Unde illius vis ut arces ipsas disjiciat, ut in cuniculis videmus? Respondeo, eum effectum pororum dilatationi, & vi elasticae accensi pulveris potissimùm esse referendum, etenim accensus pulvis qui majorem locum postulat, omni ex parte parietibus innixus, qua parte minus obsistitur, ea erumpit: dilatatio successiva pulveris, vim percussionis auget. Vis etiam pulveris qua globum è tormento bellico propellit, particulis etiam igneis, adjuncta aëris, & nitri elasticitate tribuenda est, hi enim tot elatéres in omnem partem summa vi nituntur, quumque minor sit resistentia globi, quàm ex parte posteriori tormenti bellici, idcircò etiam globum aliquot librarum ad notabilem distantiam éjicit. Atque tantorum effectuum in pulvere, princeps causa est sal nitri ob suam elasticitatem, unde ut ait Kircherus, si tormentum pulvere, ex solo sulphure, & carbonibus citra nitrum confecto impleatur, pulvisque accendatur, is non ejiciet globum ex tormento, deficiente nempè elaterio.

208 Obj. finally: when a spark of fire falling on a heap of gunpowder kindles and rarefies it, that motion or rarefaction can proceed neither from the dilatation of the pores nor from subtle matter. For what is it that impels that matter, or agitates it with such force that by mere contact it imparts so great an agitation to the gunpowder? Whence comes its force, so that it throws down citadels themselves, as we see in mines? I reply that this effect is to be referred chiefly to the dilatation of the pores and to the elastic force of the kindled powder; for the kindled powder, which demands a greater place, pressing against the walls on every side, bursts out on the side where it is less resisted: the successive dilatation of the powder increases the force of the percussion. The force of the powder by which it propels a ball from a cannon is also to be attributed to the fiery particles, joined with the elasticity of the air and of the niter; for these so many springs strive in every direction with the utmost force, and since the resistance of the ball is less than that of the hinder part of the cannon, it therefore hurls even a ball of several pounds to a notable distance. And of such great effects in the powder the principal cause is saltpeter, on account of its elasticity; whence, as Kircher says, if a cannon is filled with powder made of sulphur and charcoal alone, without niter, and the powder is kindled, it will not expel the ball from the cannon, the spring, namely, being wanting.

[p. 74]

## DISSERTATIO IV. — DISSERTATION IV

> Aliae corporum proprietates brevitèr exponuntur, & principaliora phaenomena quamclarissimè explicantur.

OTHER PROPERTIES OF BODIES ARE BRIEFLY SET FORTH, AND THE PRINCIPAL PHENOMENA ARE EXPLAINED AS CLEARLY AS POSSIBLE

## CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

> De Fermentatione corporum.

On the Fermentation of bodies.

> 209 Nihil aliud videtur esse *fermentatio*, quàm motus intestínus mixti, quo subtiliores partes illius, magisque actuosae texturam laxant, crassiores particulas adtenuant, & exágitant ita, ut in toto mixto effervescentia quaedam, & ebullitio observetur. A duobus principiis répeti optimè potest fermentationis explicatio: à salibus nempè acidis, & alkalicis: quum enim acidi salis particulae ob suam rigiditatem non nisi cum violentia in poros salis alkalici, & materias alkalicas se intrudant, magnam partem impellente materia aetherea, igneasque, & aëreas particulas in poris latentes cómprimant, violentis his concussionibus, & accedente, tum ignis, tum aëris elaterio, fit, ut meatus in quos rapidè irruerunt effringantur, aëris rarefacti, ignisque adminiculo impellantur, & in omnem partem disjiciantur particulae alkalicae, quam disjectionem partium diversarum sequitur illa intumescentia in fermentationibus observata, quae si bullas vaporum instar efformet, *ebullitio*, si cum calore sensibili conjungatur, *effervescentia* dicitur.

ermentation seems to be nothing other than an intestine motion of a mixed 209 F body, by which its subtler and more active parts loosen its texture, attenu‐ ate the coarser particles, and agitate them in such a way that a certain effervescence and ebullition is observed in the whole mixture. The explanation of fermentation can best be derived from two principles, namely from acid and alkaline salts: for since the particles of an acid salt, on account of their rigidity, intrude themselves only with violence into the pores of an alkaline salt and into alkaline materials, the ethereal matter impelling a great part of them, and compress the fiery and airy particles lying hidden in the pores, it comes about through these violent concussions, with the spring both of the fire and of the air coming to their aid, that the passages into which they rapidly rushed are broken open, and that the alkaline particles are impelled by the help of the rarefied air and of the fire and are scattered in every direction; and this scattering of the diverse parts is followed by that swelling observed in fermentations which, if it forms something like bubbles of vapor, is called ebullition, and if it is joined with sensible heat, effervescence.

> 210 In universum dici potest: motum illum intestínum fermentationis, excitari à spirituosis particulis, quae intra crassiores, & solidiores contentae, & compressae, illis disjectis, & concissis, aperto velut cárcere erumpunt, sese liberiùs explicant, suoque motu alias partes ágitant, variè permiscent, ac perturbant. Sed ex P. [p. 75] Regnault [^75-s1] adnotare placet fermentationem pulveris fulminantis.

210 In general it can be said that that intestine motion of fermentation is excited by spirituous particles which, contained and compressed within coarser and more solid ones, burst out, when these are scattered and cut to pieces, as from an opened prison, unfold themselves more freely, and by their motion agitate the other parts, variously mix them together, and disturb them. But I am pleased to note, following Father Regnault (o) [p. 75] (o), the fermentation of fulminating powder.

> [^75-s1]: Entret. Physiq. 2. Entret. sur les fermentations Chymiques.

[^75-s1]: Entretiens physiques, Conversation 2, sur les fermentations chymiques.

> 211 Pulvis fulminans est mixtura composita ex tribus partibus nitri, duabus salis tártari, & una sulphuris, separatim in pulverem redactis, & commixtis. Haec in cochleari ferreo candelae sive prunis admota, & ad certum gradum calefacta, repentè cum horribili detonatione, dissipatur, & interdùm cochlear disrúmpit. Actio nempè igneorum corpusculorum se insinuantium defert spícula nitri in salem tartari, & dilatatio aëris interni violentam illam agitationem efficit, ex qua detonatio oritur. Disrupti cochlearis causam reddit P. Regnault, quod vis pulveris non modo in omnem partem feratur, sed illa insupèr in cochleare impellatur ab aëre superiore resistente, tantò potentius, quantò majori celeritate, & vehementia pulvis dissipatus aërem ímpetit, àc commovet. Ex quibus phaenomena fermentationis explicantur.

211 Fulminating powder is a mixture composed of three parts of niter, two of salt of tartar, and one of sulphur, each reduced separately to powder and then mixed together. This, put in an iron spoon over a candle or live coals and heated to a certain degree, is suddenly dissipated with a horrible detonation, and sometimes bursts the spoon. The action, namely, of the fiery corpuscles insinuating themselves carries the spicules of the niter into the salt of tartar, and the dilatation of the internal air brings about that violent agitation from which the detonation arises. Father Regnault gives as the cause of the bursting of the spoon that the force of the powder is not only borne in every direction, but is moreover driven into the spoon by the resisting upper air, the more powerfully the greater the speed and vehemence with which the dissipated powder strikes and moves the air. From these things the phenomena of fermentation are explained.

> 212 Primò: si spiritus nitri adfundatur mercurio stannovè, effervescentia, & ebullitio benè calida sequetur; acidae quippe spiritus nitri particulae aëris interni elaterio adjutae, rapidè irruunt in particulas alkalicas mercurij, aut stanni; hinc agitationem communicant in omnem partem, unde effervescentia, ebullitio, calor sensibilis. Secundò: si misceatur óleum tartari cum spiritu nitri in quo antea sint soluta ramenta ferri, fermentatio ignem concipiet; nam acidae particulae, alkalicis communicant motum & agitationem omnem in partem, qui motus major est eo, qui à simplici calore producitur, hic autèm motus in omnem partem producitur à spiritu nitri, qui in ramenta ferri offendit plurima obstacula, quae ab eo vinci debent. Aliae explicationes phaenomenorum videri possunt in Lexic. Physices, Gallicè edito à P. Paulian [^75-s2]

212 First: if spirit of niter is poured onto mercury or tin, an effervescence and a very hot ebullition will follow; for the acid particles of the spirit of niter, aided by the spring of the internal air, rush rapidly into the alkaline particles of the mercury or of the tin; hence they communicate agitation in every direction, whence effervescence, ebullition, sensible heat. Secondly: if oil of tartar is mixed with spirit of niter in which iron filings have previously been dissolved, the fermentation will take fire; for the acid particles communicate motion and agitation in every direction to the alkaline ones, and this motion is greater than that which is produced by simple heat; this motion in every direction, moreover, is produced by the spirit of niter, which meets in the iron filings a great many obstacles that must be overcome by it. Other explanations of the phenomena can be seen in the Dictionary of Physics published in French by Father Paulian (p).

> [^75-s2]: Dictionnaire de Physique, Tom. 2. verb. Fermentat.

[^75-s2]: Dictionnaire de Physique, vol. 2, s.v. Fermentation.

> 213 Tertio: fermentatio calcis vivae dum aqua adfunditur hac de causa exóritur: in calcis confectione, calor fibras petrae rumpit, poros ampliat, novosque éfficit, interstitia haec, & pori materia subtili, igneisque corpusculis replentur, dum deindè refrigerare íncipit, aër exterior in multos meatus pénetrat, & per alium, atque alium succedentem condensatur; itaque si aqua adfundatur, illa calcem siccissimam violentè pervadit, cujus agitatione igneae particulae, & sal mineralis in poris latens, ac post calcinationem relictus, solvuntur, cárcereque liberantur, unde igniculis majori vi agentibus, ácidis etiam salium particulis, in alkali poros se ingerentibus, partes calcis cédere coactae separantur, disjiciuntur; hinc effervescentia, & calor sensibilis. De hac materia inter alios videri possunt Willis [^75-s3], Boerhaave [^75-s4], Franciscus Bayle [^75-s5] & P. de Lanis [^75-s6].

213 Thirdly: the fermentation of quicklime when water is poured on it arises for this reason. In the making of lime the heat breaks the fibers of the stone, enlarges the pores, and makes new ones; these interstices and pores are filled with subtle matter and fiery corpuscles; then, when the lime begins to cool, the outer air penetrates into its many passages and is condensed by more and more air coming in after it; and so, if water is poured on, it violently pervades the very dry lime, and by its agitation the fiery particles and the mineral salt lying hidden in the pores and left behind after calcination are loosed and freed from their prison; whence, the little fires acting with greater force, and the acid particles of the salts also thrusting themselves into the pores of the alkali, the parts of the lime, forced to yield, are separated and scattered: hence the effervescence and sensible heat. On this matter, among others, Willis (q), Boerhaave (r), François Bayle (s) and Father Lana (t) may be consulted.

> [^75-s3]: De Fermentat.

[^75-s3]: De Fermentatione.

[^75-s4]: Elementa Chemiae, vol. 2, p. 166.

> [^75-s5]: Institut. Physic. tom. 1. p. 455.

[^75-s5]: Institutiones Physicae, vol. 1, p. 455.

> [^75-s6]: Magist. Nat. & Art. tom. 3. p. 50.

[^75-s6]: Magisterium Naturae et Artis, vol. 3, p. 50.

[p. 76]

> 214 Hinc etiam quarto explicari potest phaenómenon *pulveris ardentis*, qui etiam dicitur *pulvis Pyróbola.* Ponatur in disco terreo pulvis aluminis, cum tertia parte sui ponderis mellis, vel farinae, vel sácchari, & posito disco super carbones, diù moveantur hi pulveres, donec probe exsiccentur, & fusci fiant. Tunc contundantur in mortario, & iterum exsiccentur, & hoc donec partes pulveris non amplius uniantur, sed maneant sejunctae. Tunc ponatur hic pulvis in parvo matracio [^76-s1] longi colli, quod sepeliatur usque ad collum in arena, leniter charta obturato matracio, exponatur vas igni per gradus aucto, usque dum inferior pars colli rubeat, nec amplius prodeat fumus: extincto igne ponatur pulvis in phiala probè clausa ne aëri exposita sit, & ad usus servetur.

214 Hence, fourthly, can also be explained the phenomenon of the burning powder, which is also called the pyrophorus powder. Let powdered alum be put in an earthen dish with a third part of its weight of honey, or flour, or sugar, and, the dish being set over coals, let these powders be stirred for a long time until they are thoroughly dried and turn dark. Then let them be pounded in a mortar and dried again, and this until the parts of the powder no longer unite but remain separate. Then let this powder be put in a small long-necked matrass (u), which is buried up to the neck in sand; the matrass being lightly stopped with paper, let the vessel be exposed to a fire increased by degrees, until the lower part of the neck glows red and no more smoke comes forth; when the fire is put out, let the powder be placed in a phial well closed, so that it is not exposed to the air, and kept for use.

> [^76-s1]: Matracium est ampúlla vitrea longo, & recto collo instructa. Aliud est matracium ad adtenuandos lentè igne liquores. Componitur ex phiala vitrea A (Fig. XII.) colli longi, cum alia phiala parva B lutata cum prima: liquor adscendit in B, iterum reddit in A &c. atque per hunc circuitum adtenuatur, & faeces deponit in fundo phialae A.

[^76-s1]: A matrass is a glass flask furnished with a long and straight neck. Another kind of matrass serves for attenuating liquors over a gentle fire. It is composed of a glass phial A (Fig. XII.) with a long neck, with another small phial B luted to the first: the liquor ascends into B, returns again into A, etc., and through this circulation it is attenuated and deposits its dregs at the bottom of phial A.

> 215 Proprietas hujus pulveris est, ut vel minima ejus portio aëri exposita incendatur spontè absque strepitu. Tractu temporis tamèn hanc vim amittit, & quum non citò incenditur saepè eam ore humectando, incenditur. Ratio horum redditur. Quum igni exponitur ut torrefiat; tunc intimè pervaditur ab igne, acquiritque vim detinendi ignem, ut alkali. Statim ac aëri exponitur, ejus humiditatem trahit, atque ita ignis latens compressus acquirit vim se expandendi, & sensibilis redditur, ut calx aqua humectata; hinc tractu temporis vim hanc amittit, quia avolat ignis, & si nimiùm humidum in aëre non fuerit, ore humectata incenditur.

215 The property of this powder is that even the smallest portion of it, exposed to the air, takes fire spontaneously, without noise. In the course of time, however, it loses this force, and when it does not take fire quickly, it often takes fire when it is moistened with the breath. The reason of these things is given. When it is exposed to the fire to be roasted, it is then intimately pervaded by the fire, and acquires the power of retaining fire, as an alkali does. As soon as it is exposed to the air, it draws in the air’s moisture, and so the latent, compressed fire acquires the force of expanding itself and is rendered sensible, as in lime moistened with water; hence in the course of time it loses this force, because the fire flies off; and if there has not been too much moisture in the air, it takes fire when moistened with the breath.

> 216 Preatermittere tamèn non possum hac de re differens vegetationes chymicas. Has inter celebratissimae sunt *arbor Martis*, & *arbor Dianae*, sivè *Philosophica.* Primam exponit Lemery filius in Monumentis Academiae Regiae Parisiensis [^76-s2]. In vase vitreo (Fig. XIII.) in quo sit scobs ferri pone super hanc spiritum nitri, ingens fiet effervescentia, & ebullitio. Spiritus tingetur colore intensè rubro ob ferrum solutum, & plures orientur fumi rubri. Sedáta effervescentia, qua partes ferri adtolluntur ad superiora, prójice in liquorem oleum tartari *per deliquium*, orietur mediocris effervescentia, qua liquor plurimum inflabitur, paulo post ad ejus látera, & labrum innumeri orientur rami, & arbusta, quae absque ulla visibili effervescentia superabunt liquorem, & labrum, atque externè décident, ut exhibetur in figura. In alia vegetatione loco spiritus nitri adhibuit Lemery spiritum productum à vapore rubro, quem emittit spiritus nitri in effervescentia, & hoc usus est in alio experimento ad solvendum ferrum, & vegetatio magis [p. 77] distincta orta est, quia vapor ruber imbibitur sulphure ferri, quod citiùs, & in partes minores ferrum dividit.

216 I cannot, however, pass over the different chemical vegetations that belong to this subject. Among these the most celebrated are the tree of Mars and the tree of Diana, or Philosophical tree. The first is set forth by Lemery the son in the Memoirs of the Royal Academy of Paris (x). Into a glass vessel (Fig. XIII.) in which there are iron filings, pour spirit of niter upon them; a huge effervescence and ebullition will arise. The spirit will be tinged with an intensely red color on account of the dissolved iron, and many red fumes will arise. When the effervescence, by which the parts of the iron are raised to the upper regions, has subsided, throw into the liquor oil of tartar per deliquium; a moderate effervescence will arise, by which the liquor will be greatly swollen; a little after, on its sides and on the lip, countless branches and shrubs will arise, which without any visible effervescence will rise above the liquor and the lip, and fall down on the outside, as is shown in the figure. In another vegetation Lemery employed, in place of the spirit of niter, a spirit produced from the red vapor which spirit of niter gives off in effervescence, and he used this in another experiment to dissolve iron, and a more distinct vegetation [p. 77] arose, because the red vapor is imbibed by the sulphur of the iron, which divides the iron more quickly and into smaller parts.

> [^76-s2]: Memoires de l' Academ. Royal. A. 1706, & 1707.

[^76-s2]: Mémoires de l’Académie Royale, for the years 1706 and 1707.

> 217 Ut haec phaenómena exponantur, observandum est, spiritum nitri dividere ferrum in partes minimas, & cum iis consociari, quae partes eò minores sunt, quò magis spiritus sulphure ferri abundat. Sulphur autem metalla dividere posse incompertò est, accedat modò oleum tartari, quod est alkali terreum; partes accidi nitrosi non adeò cohaerent cum iis ferri, ut non possint cum suis acuminibus ingredi cavitates alkali, hinc oritur effervescentia, quam ostendunt ampullae aëris adsiduè à liquore erumpentes, quum tamen partes acidae cum ferro unitae sint, ideò non maxima vi irruere possunt in alkali, ideoque effervescentia non est sensibilis, ut ea quae oritur, si in simplici spiritu nitri ponatur oleum tartari *per deliquium*; in nostro verò experimento acidae nitri particulae pro parte ingrediuntur álkali, pro parte cohaerent cum ferri particulis.

217 That these phenomena may be explained, it must be observed that spirit of niter divides iron into very small parts and associates itself with them, and these parts are the smaller the more the spirit abounds in the sulphur of the iron. That sulphur, moreover, can divide metals is well established. Now let oil of tartar, which is an earthy alkali, be added: the parts of the nitrous acid do not cohere so closely with those of the iron that they cannot enter with their points into the cavities of the alkali; hence arises the effervescence, which the bubbles of air continually bursting from the liquor display. Since, however, the acid parts are united with the iron, they cannot rush into the alkali with very great force, and therefore the effervescence is not so sensible as that which arises if oil of tartar per deliquium is put into simple spirit of niter; but in our experiment the acid particles of the niter partly enter the alkali, partly cohere with the particles of the iron.

> 218 Ferri verò particulae pressae ab ácido, & álkali magis dividuntur, & sulphur ferri adtenuatur, & magis volátile redditur, ita ut hoc secum deferat, & sursum adtollat maximo impetu versùs superficiem vasis particulas ferri unitas cum salinis, quae quàm primùm expeditae sunt à liquore, determinata ratione coherent, & áridae factae, figuram referunt arbustorum.

218 The particles of the iron, however, pressed by the acid and by the alkali, are divided still more, and the sulphur of the iron is attenuated and rendered more volatile, so that it carries with it and lifts upward with very great impetus toward the surface of the vessel the particles of iron united with the saline ones; and these, as soon as they are freed from the liquor, cohere in a determinate manner and, having become dry, take on the figure of shrubs.

> 219 *Arbor Dianae* facilè & expeditè producitur methodo tradita ab Hombergio in Monumentis Academiae Regiae Parisiensis [^77-s1]. Sume drachmas quatuor scobis argenteae [^77-s2], & amalgáma [^77-s3] fiat absque igne, cum drachmis duobus mercurii. Solve amalgama in quatuor unciis aquae fortis, & projice solutionem in vase cum 18 unciis aquae communis, indè ágita aquam, eamque in phiala benè obturata repóne. Quoties ea uti volueris ad arborem producendam, sume unciam hujus aquae, & repone in alia phiala, in hanc pone amalgama commune auri, aut argenti ad magnitudinem pisi, quod sit semifluidum, seu in consistentia bútyri, post duo, aut tria minuta ex subsidente ad fundum vasis amalgámate prodire incipient fila, quae ramos emittent laterales, & paulatim crescent, & formabuntur in parva arbusta argentea, ut depingitur in Figura XIV, & hoc intra horae quadrantem, & amalgáma, cui inhaerent indurescet, & album fiet. En brevi confecta arbor Dianae, quam prius longa perficiebatur operatione.

219 The tree of Diana is produced easily and expeditiously by the method handed down by Homberg in the Memoirs of the Royal Academy of Paris (y). Take four drachms of silver filings (z), and let an amalgam (a) be made with two drachms of mercury, without fire. Dissolve the amalgam in four ounces of aqua fortis, and throw the solution into a vessel with 18 ounces of common water; then shake the water, and put it away in a well-stopped phial. Whenever you wish to use it to produce the tree, take an ounce of this water and put it in another phial; into this put a common amalgam of gold or of silver of the size of a pea, which should be semifluid, or of the consistency of butter: after two or three minutes threads will begin to come forth from the amalgam that has settled to the bottom of the vessel, which will put out lateral branches, will grow little by little, and will be formed into small silver shrubs, as is depicted in Figure XIV; and within a quarter of an hour this, together with the amalgam to which they adhere, will harden and become white. Behold the tree of Diana made in a short time, which was formerly completed only by a long operation.

> [^77-s1]: Memories de l' Academ. A. 1692.

[^77-s1]: Mémoires de l’Académie, year 1692.

> [^77-s2]: Drachma est octava pars unciae.

[^77-s2]: A drachm is the eighth part of an ounce.

> [^77-s3]: Amalgamatio fit quum aliquod metallum cum alio, vel cum minerali intimè unitur.

[^77-s3]: Amalgamation takes place when some metal is intimately united with another, or with a mineral.

> 220 Ut haec vegatio exponatur, notandum est, aquam nulli ampliùs vegetationi esse posse idoneam, & pisum amalgámae non minui in pondere post operationem. His positis; certum est [p. 78] argentum cum mercurio, & nitro in aqua solutum esse causam vegetationis. Quum solutio dilúta fuerit ab aqua partes nitri non ampliùs maxima vi consociatae sunt cum argenteis, ideòque ponendo in aqua novum amalgama ad hoc feruntur, & relinquunt super amalgama partes argenti, & mercurii, vel rectiùs circa ipsum ramos formant partes nitri cum mercurialibus, & argenteis. Id comprobatur ex diversitate arbustorum: nam si argentum, & mercurius pura fuerint, arbores pulcherrimae oriuntur.

220 That this vegetation may be explained, it must be noted that the water can no longer be fit for any further vegetation, and that the pea of amalgam is not diminished in weight after the operation. These things being laid down, it is certain that the silver [p. 78] dissolved with the mercury and the niter in water is the cause of the vegetation. When the solution has been diluted by the water, the parts of the niter are no longer associated with the silver ones with very great force, and therefore, when a new amalgam is put into the water, they are borne toward it and leave the parts of silver and of mercury upon the amalgam; or, more correctly, the parts of the niter form branches around it together with the mercurial and silver parts. This is confirmed by the diversity of the shrubs: for if the silver and the mercury have been pure, most beautiful trees arise.

> 221 Si solutio sit nimis dilúta lentius producentur arbores, sed rami magis erunt conspicui. Si solutio sit fortior, tunc densiores, minusque perfectè orientur arbores. Si amalgáma positum ad magnitudinem pisi, fuerit durum, resolvetur à solutione, & arbor orietur ut in Fig. XV. Etiam fit vegetatio ope aquae pluviae, quae in sententia nostra optimè explicari potest. Tempore pluvio, & tonitruoso cóllige determinatam quantitatem aquae defluentis à tecto. Hanc serva: post plures dies deponet materiam viridescentem ad altitudinem duarum linearum, quae tempore calido, vel exposita propè camínum, inflabitur, ampullas producet, inde filamenta, & ramos virides, quorum nonnulli usque ad aquae superficiem adscendent, cessante calore iterum deponentur ad fundum, redeunte calore iterum germinabunt.

221 If the solution is too dilute, the trees will be produced more slowly, but the branches will be more conspicuous. If the solution is stronger, then the trees will arise denser and less perfect. If the amalgam put in, of the size of a pea, is hard, it will be dissolved by the solution, and the tree will arise as in Fig. XV. A vegetation is also made by means of rainwater, which can be very well explained on our view. In rainy and thundery weather collect a determinate quantity of water running down from a roof. Keep it: after several days it will deposit a greenish matter to the height of two lines, which in hot weather, or when placed near a fireplace, will swell, will produce bubbles, then filaments and green branches, some of which will rise as far as the surface of the water; when the heat ceases they will settle again to the bottom; when the heat returns they will sprout again.

> 222 Singuli rami habebunt in extremitatibus ampullas aëris veluti esset fructus. Vegetatio haec nisi fortè velis (quod per me licet), verissima semina simul cum aqua in terram decídere; facilè exponitur ope effervescentiae; materia enim primò inflatur, & ob effervescentiam excluditur aër, qui visibilis est, & hic elevat, & distribuit, materiam in ramos, & arbusta, quae ob venustum colorem viridem mirè imittantur naturalem plantarum vegetationem. Haec curiosiora sunt. Plura alia apud Cl. Auctores à me saepius laudatos comperietis.

222 Each branch will have at its extremities bubbles of air, as though they were fruit. This vegetation, unless perhaps you prefer (which I allow) that very true seeds fall to the earth together with the water, is easily explained by means of effervescence; for the matter is first inflated, and on account of the effervescence air is expelled, which is visible, and this raises and distributes the matter into branches and shrubs, which, on account of their charming green color, wonderfully imitate the natural vegetation of plants. These things are rather curious. You will find many others in the celebrated Authors often praised by me.

## CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

> De Tempore.

On Time.

> 223 Perturbatum hìc á nobis fortassè rerum ordinem suspicari quis posset, quòd inter corporum proprietates, temporis quoque ac loci naturam enumeremus, verùm quum concipi non possit corporum motus, nisi temporis etiam, locique natura adcuratè cognita fuerit, iccircò quum plurima de Motu, qui universalis corporum adfectio censeri potest inferiùs dicturi simus, rem instituto nostro [p. 79] satis adcomodam facturi videmur, si antequàm motus naturam, leges, & proprietates omnes explicemus, illa de tempore ac loco (Scholarum subtilitatibus rejectis) brevissimè compléctamur ex quibus pro ceteris oportuniùs explicandis lux quaedam adfulgeat.

erhaps someone might suspect that the order of things has been disturbed 223 P by us here, in that among the properties of bodies we also enumerate the nature of time and of place; but since the motion of bodies cannot be conceived unless the nature of time and of place has also been accurately known, therefore, since we are going to say a great many things below about Motion, which can be considered a universal affection of bodies, we shall seem to be doing something quite [p. 79] in keeping with our plan if, before we explain the nature, the laws, and all the properties of motion, we embrace very briefly (the subtleties of the Schools being set aside) those things concerning time and place from which some light may shine forth for explaining the rest more conveniently.

> 224 Tempus itaque, ut ab illo exordiamur, facillimè quidem concipitur, sed à nobis explicari, vel definiri vix potest. „Quid enim, (*ait Magnus Augustinus*) [^79-s1] Quid enim familiarius, & notiùs in loquendo commemoramus, quàm tempus; & intelligimus quidèm cùm id loquimur, intelligimus etiam cùm aliquo loquente id audimus? Quid est ergo tempus? Si nemo ex me quaerat scio; si querenti explicare velim, nescio: fidenter enim dico scire me, quod si nihil praeteriret, non esset praeteritum tempus; & si nihil esset, non esset praesens tempus.“ Aristoteles autèm tempus definirè volens, ait illud esse *numerum motus secundum prius, & posterius* [^79-s2]. Quae quidem definitio à Recentioribus reprehendi meritò solet, etenim verosimiliùs dici potest, quod motus ipse sit numerus, & mensura temporis; quum certè nos, temporis durationem aliquo motu, ut horologii, vel solis numerare, vel mensurare consuevérimus

224 Time, then, to begin with it, is indeed very easily conceived, but can scarcely be explained or defined by us. “For what,” says the great Augustine (b), “what do we mention more familiarly and more knowingly in speaking than time? And we understand it, surely, when we speak of it; we understand it also when we hear another speaking of it. What, then, is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I wish to explain it to one who asks, I do not know: yet I say confidently that I know that if nothing passed away there would be no past time, and if nothing were, there would be no present time.” Aristotle, however, wishing to define time, says that it is the number of motion according to before and after (c). This definition is deservedly wont to be censured by the Moderns; for it can more probably be said that motion itself is the number and measure of time, since we are certainly accustomed to number or to measure the duration of time by some motion, such as that of a clock or of the sun.

> [^79-s1]: Confess. Lib. 11. n. 17. al. cap. 14.

[^79-s1]: Confessions, bk. 11, no. 17, otherwise ch. 14.

> [^79-s2]: Phys. 5. cap. 16 text. 7.

[^79-s2]: Physics 5, ch. 16, text 7.

> 225 Res etiam non modò quum moventur, sed etiam dum quiescunt, tempori subjiciuntur, atque aliquo tempore continentur, ideoque tempus dici deberet aequaliter numerus, & mensura motus, & quietis, & quemadmodùm tempus dicitur ab Aristotele *numerus cujuscumque motus*, ita quoque dici deberet *numerus cujuscumque quietis.* Quid quòd numerus, sive mensura rerum non est res ipsa numerata, aut mensurata, quemadmodum digiti per quos dies numerantur non sunt dies ipsi, nec ulna qua mensuratur pannus est ipse pannus, ut alia plura omittam, quae videri possunt in Philosophia Sceptica Hispáno idiomate conscripta á Doctore Martinez [^79-s3]. Unde meritò reprehenditur, Aristotelica temporis definitio tanquam vitiosa, vel obscura, vel potius falsa.

225 Things, moreover, are subject to time not only when they are moved but also while they are at rest, and are contained in some time; and therefore time ought to be called equally the number and measure of motion and of rest; and just as time is called by Aristotle the number of any motion whatever, so it ought also to be called the number of any rest whatever. What of the fact that the number or measure of things is not the thing itself numbered or measured, just as the fingers by which days are numbered are not the days themselves, nor is the ell by which cloth is measured the cloth itself? — to omit many other things, which can be seen in the Philosophia Sceptica written in the Spanish language by Doctor Martínez (d). Hence the Aristotelian definition of time is deservedly censured as faulty, or obscure, or rather false.

> [^79-s3]: Dialogo 6. pag. 126. & 127.

[^79-s3]: Dialogue 6, pp. 126 and 127.

> 226 Clariùs itaque describi poterit tempus: *successiva rerum mutabilium duratio*, ex qua definitione intelligitur insigne discrimen inter aeternitatem, & tempus: nam in aeternitate partes aliquae distingui non possunt, nam omnes temporum differentias admirabili modo compléctitur, unde satis adcommodè ab omnibus Theologis cum Boethio definiri solet: *Interminabilis vitae tota simul, & perfecta possessio.* Nos quidem vitam hanc nostram mortalem totam simul haud possidémus: nam quae praeteriit possessa quidem â nobis fuit, & quae futura superst, possidebitur, solumque labile illud instans, quod nobis praesens est, á nobis possidetur, & quemadmodùm sphaéra super aliquod planum revolúta, semper illud [p. 80] in puncto contingit, sic ferè brevis vita nostra, per plura veluti instantia temporis, quibus existit, celerrimè transigitur, nam ut eleganter canit Ovidius [^80-s1].

226 More clearly, then, time can be described as the successive duration of mutable things; from which definition is understood the notable difference between eternity and time: for in eternity no parts can be distinguished, since it embraces all the differences of times in an admirable way; whence it is quite fittingly defined by all Theologians, with Boethius: the whole, simultaneous and perfect possession of interminable life. We, indeed, by no means possess this mortal life of ours all at once: for what has passed was indeed possessed by us, and what remains to come will be possessed, and only that fleeting instant which is present to us is possessed by us; and just as a sphere rolled over some plane always touches it [p. 80] at a point, so our brief life is passed very swiftly through the many instants, as it were, of time in which it exists; for, as Ovid elegantly sings (e),

> [^80-s1]: Metamorph. XV. V. 181.

[^80-s1]: Metamorphoses XV, v. 181.

> *……Velut unda impellitur unda*

……As wave is driven onward by wave,

> *Urgeturque eadem veniens, urgetque priorem,*

And, coming on, is pressed by the next, and presses the one before,

> *Tempora sic fugiunt pariter, pariterque sequuntur.*

So the times flee, and alike they follow.

> 227 Deo autèm immortali tota ejusdem interminabilis vita, ita praesens est, ut ejusdem nihil praeterierit, nihilque unquàm praetéritum sit Aevum quod inter aeternitatem, ac tempus ipsum concipitur, egregiè describitur: *duratio entis creati permanentis, & á Deo dependentis, suaptè natura incorruptibilis.* Talis est duratio Angeli, & animae rationalis.

227 But to the immortal God the whole of His interminable life is so present that nothing of it has passed away, and nothing of it is ever past. Aevum, which is conceived as lying between eternity and time, is excellently described as the duration of a created, permanent being, dependent on God, and by its own nature incorruptible. Such is the duration of an Angel and of the rational soul.

## CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

> Ostenditur quid sit corporum locus.

It is shown what the place of bodies is.

> 228 Aristoteles 4. Phys. *locus est* (inquit) *corporis ambientis terminus immobilis primus*, id est superficies prima & interior corporis aliud corpus continentis. Haec superficies interior, vocatur cóncava, exterior verò convexa. En exemplum: Globus terraqueus undique ab aëre circunscribitur: ubi tria consideranda sunt, & aër ipse, & ejusdem cóncava superficies, & globi terraquei superficies convexa, quae superficiei concavae aëris contigua est: ait itaque Aristoteles: Telluris locum non esse aërem illum ambientem, neque telluris convexam superficiem, sed cóncavam illam aëris superficiem, tellurem ambientem. Aristotelis sententiam Cartesius amplexatus est Expressè namque & ipse docet [^80-s2], externum locum corporis sumi posse pro superficie, quae proximè ambit locatum.

ristotle, in Physics 4: place is (he says) the first immobile boundary of the sur228 A rounding body, that is, the first and interior surface of a body containing another body. This interior surface is called concave, and the exterior convex. Here is an example. The terraqueous globe is circumscribed on every side by the air: here three things are to be considered, the air itself, its concave surface, and the convex surface of the terraqueous globe, which is contiguous to the concave surface of the air. Aristotle therefore says: the place of the Earth is not that surrounding air, nor the convex surface of the earth, but that concave surface of the air which surrounds the earth. Descartes embraced the opinion of Aristotle. For he too expressly teaches (f) that the external place of a body can be taken for the surface which most closely surrounds the thing located.

> [^80-s2]: Part. 2. Princip. num. 15.

[^80-s2]: Pt. 2 of the Principles, no. 15.

> 229 Ambientem hanc superficiem vocat locum externum, ut ipsum discernat ab interno, scilicet à spatio, quod ejus sententia, non re, sed sola cogitatione à locati corporis substantia distinguitur. *Re vera enim*, ait Cartesius [^80-s3] *extensio in longum latum, & profundum, quae spatium constituit, eadem planè est cum illa, quae* [p. 81] *stituit corpus.* Contrà vero Demócrito, & Epicúro adstipulatus olim fuit S. Augustinus [^81-s1] *locus enim*, ait Sanctus Doctor, *in spatio est, quod longitudine, & latitudine, & altitudine corporis occupatur.* Non secùs de loco sentiunt Gassendus [^81-s2], Newtonus [^81-s3], Keil, [^81-s4] iique demùm omnes Recentiores, quibus mihi magis cordi est, quàm in nullius verba jurare Nonnullis itaque positis, quid de loci natura sentiendum putem, brevitèr dicam. Nihil enim hac in re determinari legitimè potest, nisi primò quod certum est, ab incerto discernatur.

229 This surrounding surface he calls the external place, so as to distinguish it from the internal, namely from space, which in his opinion is distinguished from the substance of the located body not in reality but by thought alone. For in truth, says Descartes (g), the extension in length, breadth and depth which constitutes space is plainly the same as that which constitutes body. [p. 81] body. On the other hand, St. Augustine formerly agreed with Democritus and Epicurus (h): for place, says the Holy Doctor, is in space, which is occupied by the length, breadth and height of a body. Not otherwise do Gassendi (i), Newton (j), Keill (k) think about place, and, in short, all the Moderns, to whom nothing is more at heart than to swear by the words of no master. Having laid down these few things, then, I shall say briefly what I think should be held about the nature of place. For nothing can legitimately be determined in this matter unless what is certain is first distinguished from what is uncertain.

> [^80-s3]: Loc. cit. num. 10.

[^80-s3]: Loc. cit., no. 10.

> [^81-s1]: Lib. 83. Quaest. quaest. 20, & lib. 4. sup. Genes. n. 34.

[^81-s1]: Bk. of 83 Questions, q. 20, and bk. 4 on Genesis, no. 34.

> [^81-s2]: Sect. 1. Phys. Lib. 2. cap. 6.

[^81-s2]: Sect. 1 of the Physics, bk. 2, ch. 6.

> [^81-s3]: Princip. Schol. ad Def. 8.

[^81-s3]: Principia, Schol. to Def. 8.

> [^81-s4]: Introduct. ad ver. Philosoph. Lect. 2. & 6.

[^81-s4]: Introductio ad veram Philosophiam, lect. 2 and 6.

> 230 Certum in primis puto: *nullum re ipsa esse corpus, quod aliquo in loco non existat.* An verò Divinitus possit fieri, ut corpus aliquod núllibi existat, vulgares Philosophi, qui *possibilium* philosophia maximè delectantur, ad trúcinam révocent. Pro re comperta itidem habeo, *locum non esse in loco*, atque adeò, *locum non esse ex illis unum, quae in loco existunt.* Si namque ita esset, eadem ratione & *locus loci*, atque ita deinceps in infinitum esset in loco. In comperto etiam est: *nullum eorum haberi posse pro loco corporum, quod localiter movetur.* Id enim duntaxat moveri potest localiter, quod in loco existit. Arbitror postremò: *in eo statuendum esse locum corporum in quo ita singula ipsa corpora existunt, ut unam illius partem repleant, eorum extensioni omninò aequalem, moveantur in ipso prorsùs immobili, ab eoque primo & per se mutuò sese excludant, adeò nempè, ut in eadem simul plura componi naturae viribus nequaquam possint.* Omnes namque fatentur, corpora replére locum, quem singula occupant, ipsum aequare, atque ob id esse *impenetrabilia*, quòd eorum quodlibet ab eo loco, in quo est, aliud excludat. Nomine *spatii* non aliud intelligitur, nisi *negativa, penitusque immobilis secundum trinam dimensionem extensio, in qua existentia corpora modo posita sint, quamque si in nihilum redigerentur, ipsa relinquerent.* Negativa haec extensio dicitur à S. Augustino *spatiosum nihil*, ab aliis *intervallum.* His positis.

230 I hold as certain, in the first place, that no body really exists which does not exist in some place. Whether, however, it can be brought about by Divine power that some body should exist nowhere, let the common Philosophers, who take the greatest delight in the philosophy of possibles, weigh in the scales. I likewise hold as an ascertained matter that place is not in a place, and so that place is not one of those things that exist in a place. For if it were so, by the same reasoning the place of the place also would be in a place, and so on to infinity. It is ascertained also that none of those things which are moved locally can be held for the place of bodies. For only that which exists in a place can be moved locally. I judge, finally, that the place of bodies is to be set in that in which the bodies themselves singly so exist that they fill one part of it altogether equal to their extension, are moved in it while it is itself wholly immobile, and by it, primarily and of themselves, mutually exclude one another, so far, namely, that several cannot by any means be placed together in the same part by the forces of nature. For all admit that bodies fill the place which each occupies, that they equal it, and that they are on that account impenetrable, because each of them excludes another from that place in which it is. By the name of space nothing else is understood but a negative extension, wholly immobile according to its threefold dimension, in which existing bodies are now placed, and which, if they were reduced to nothing, they would leave behind. This negative extension is called by St. Augustine a spacious nothing, by others an interval. These things being laid down:

> 231 Dico 1. admittendum re ipsa est spatium, si illud esse possibile evincatur. Probatur: nam quum spatium non sit aliquod *reale positivum*, sed *purum nihil*, nequit esse terminus actionis productivae: ergo, si non existit, neque profectò potest esse possibile; quum quod non est re ipsa & est possibile, à Deo saltem possit produci. Quamobrem vel possibile non est spatium, vel si est possibile, illud re ipsa existere, necesse est ipsi dicamus.

231 I say 1. Space is really to be admitted, if it is shown to be possible. It is proved: for since space is not something real and positive but a pure nothing, it cannot be the term of a productive action; therefore, if it does not exist, it certainly cannot be possible either, since what does not really exist and is possible can be produced, at least by God. Wherefore either space is not possible, or, if it is possible, we must necessarily say that it really exists.

> 232 Dico 2.: possibile est spatium, in quo nullum planè corpus existat. Prob.: potuit Deus antequam Mundi machinam cónderet, creare duo tantum sphaerica corpora, eaque ita collocare; [p. 82] ut sese mutuò tángerent. In hoc nulla adparet, vel minima repugnantia. Itaque sint duo hujuscemodi corpora A B (Fig. XVI.) quae se tangant in puncto C. Quoniam ergo res est certissima, duarum spherarum contactum in uno duntaxat puncto posse fieri, apertum manet, fore, ut duo corpora A B, non nisi in puncto C. sese mutuò tangant, ac proinde, ut à se mutuò distent convexae eorum superficies, sive ut à puncto *a* ad punctum *b* duci possit recta a b, & sic de aliis. Inter convexas autèm hujuscemodi superficies nullum re ipsa haberetur corpus, quum scilicet positum fuerit duo tantum corpora A & B fuisse à Deo creata: ergo inter illas superficies purum tunc haberetur intervallum, sive spatium, & ideo possibile est spatium, in quo nullum planè corpus existat.

232 I say 2. Space is possible in which no body at all exists. Proof: God could, before He founded the machine of the World, have created only two spherical bodies, and have placed them in such a way [p. 82] that they touched each other. In this no repugnance, not even the least, appears. Let there be, then, two such bodies A, B (Fig. XVI.), which touch each other at the point C. Since, therefore, it is a most certain thing that the contact of two spheres can take place at one point only, it remains evident that the two bodies A, B will touch each other only at the point C, and consequently that their convex surfaces will be distant from each other, or that a straight line can be drawn from the point a to the point b, and so of the others. Between such convex surfaces, however, no body would really be had, since it has been supposed, namely, that only the two bodies A and B were created by God: therefore between those surfaces there would then be a pure interval, or space; and therefore space is possible in which no body at all exists.

> 233 Dico 3. admittendum re ipsa est spatium, negativa scilicet, extensio à corporea substantia omninò diversa. Prob.: re ipsa admittendum est spatium si illud esse possibile evincatur [§. 231.]; sed constat evidenter evidentia mathematica spatium esse possibile: [§. 232.] ergo re ipsa est admittendum. Praeterea existentia spatii non obscurè ex eo etiam colligitur, quod extensio mundi non sit infinita. Nec enim finita esse potest, nisi extra illius fines detur spatium, quod ab aliis corporibus occupari queat. Limitibus porrò minimè carére mundum, eorum omnium sententia est, qui habent pro re comperta, nullum ens praeter Deum esse infinitum Ex dictis manifestum fit, quod omnia corpora in spatio existunt, unam illius partem replent singula, eorum extensioni planè aequalem in eoque moventur prorsùs immobili.

233 I say 3. Space is really to be admitted, namely a negative extension, altogether different from corporeal substance. Proof: space is really to be admitted if it is shown to be possible [§. 231.]; but it is established with mathematical evidence that space is possible [§. 232.]; therefore it is really to be admitted. Moreover, the existence of space is clearly gathered also from the fact that the extension of the world is not infinite. For it cannot be finite unless outside its bounds there is space which could be occupied by other bodies. That the world is by no means without limits is the opinion of all those who hold it for an ascertained matter that no being besides God is infinite. From what has been said it becomes manifest that all bodies exist in space, that each fills one part of it, plainly equal to its extension, and that they are moved in it while it is wholly immobile.

> 234 Constat etiam, quod quum duo quaelibet corpora sibi mutuò re ipsa resistant, videtur aliquid necessariò admitti oportére, in quo dum unum illorum existit, alterum esse naturae viribus minimè possit. Id autèm non esse nisi *spatium*, videtur perspicuum, quum etiam non existente imò repugnante quavis circumambiente superficie, duo quaelibet corpora sint naturaliter impenetrabilia, utpotè quae adhuc sunt corpora. Non inficior *secundariò*, & *per accidens* haud posse duo corpora, quia impenetrabilia una eademque cóncava superficie contineri, sed spatium in quo corpora existunt, illud unicè est à quo ipsa corpora *primò*, & *per se* ratione naturalis suae soliditatis, mutuò sese excludunt.

234 It is established also that, since any two bodies really resist each other, it seems that something must necessarily be admitted in which, while one of them exists, the other can by no means be by the forces of nature. That this, however, is nothing other than space seems perspicuous, since, even if no surrounding surface whatever existed, nay, if one were impossible, any two bodies would be naturally impenetrable, inasmuch as they would still be bodies. I do not deny that secondarily and accidentally two bodies, because they are impenetrable, cannot be contained by one and the same concave surface; but space, in which bodies exist, is the only thing from which the bodies themselves primarily and of themselves, by reason of their natural solidity, mutually exclude each other.

> 235 Dico 4. contra Peripateticos: corpora non idèo sunt in loco, quòd á cóncava alterius corporis superficie circunscribantur. Prob.: si ita esset, núllibi corpus illud existeret quod á nulla circumambiente superficie contineatur: ergo quum ultimum Caelum á nullo externò corpore comprehendatur, illud est re ipsa extra nihil sui quin aliquo in loco existat; sed falsum est existere corpus posse quin sit alicubi [§ 230.] ergo corpora non ideo sunt in loco quod &c. Ultimum porrò Caelum nullibi esse, Aristotelis admissa sententia, inficiari nemo Scholasticorum potest, quin ipsimet Aristoteli apertissimè refragetur. Haec enim habet [p. 83] Peripateticorum Princeps [^83-s1] *Caelum non est alicubi, nec ullo in loco est, siquidem nullum corpus ipsum continet.* Quare, ut ait Clariss. Gassendus [^83-s2]: *mirùm dictu est in quas redigantur angustias Peripatetici, qui dum superficiem desérere nolunt, coguntur locum denegare corpori nobilissimo, eidemque amplissimo, cui ratio suadet principem locum assignare.*

235 I say 4, against the Peripatetics: bodies are not in a place because they are circumscribed by the concave surface of another body. Proof: if it were so, that body which is contained by no circumambient surface would exist nowhere: therefore, since the outermost Heaven is comprehended by no external body, it really is outside its own nothingness without existing in any place; but it is false that a body can exist without being somewhere [§ 230.]: therefore bodies are not in a place because, etc. That the outermost Heaven, moreover, is nowhere, once the opinion of Aristotle is admitted, none of the Scholastics can deny without most openly opposing Aristotle himself. For this is what the Prince of the Peripatetics (l) [p. 83] (l) has: Heaven is not somewhere, nor in any place, since no body contains it. Wherefore, as the most illustrious Gassendi says (m): it is wonderful to tell into what straits the Peripatetics are driven, who, while they are unwilling to abandon the surface, are forced to deny place to the noblest body, and at the same time the most ample, to which reason persuades us to assign the principal place.

> [^83-s1]: Lib. 4 Phys. tex 45.

[^83-s1]: Bk. 4 of the Physics, text 45.

> [^83-s2]: Sect. 1. Phys. Lib. 2. cap. 6.

[^83-s2]: Sect. 1 of the Physics, bk. 2, ch. 6.

> 236 Confirmatur: posita Aristotelis opinione, dicendum est tandiù corpus in eodem loco existere, quandiù ab eadem circumambiente superficie continetur, quod falsum est; ex hoc enim sequitur idem corpus existere simul posse in eodem loco, & localiter moveri, ut patet de aqua vitreo vase contenta. Movetur enim unà cum vase, quum vas ipsum alio transfertur, neque tamen mutatur superficies, qua circunscribitur: ergo corpus non ideo est in loco quod, &c. 2.: etiam concava ambientis corporis superficies, in loco existit, simulque, & ipsa, movetur quum corpus alio transfertur: ergo nequit in ea statui corporum locus quin dicere cogamur, immobilem *localiter* non esse locum, simulque in loco, & ipsum locum existere contra ea quae diximus. [§. 230.]

236 It is confirmed: once the opinion of Aristotle is laid down, it must be said that a body exists in the same place as long as it is contained by the same circumambient surface, which is false; for from this it follows that the same body can at the same time exist in the same place and be moved locally, as is evident in the case of water contained in a glass vessel. For it is moved together with the vessel when the vessel itself is carried elsewhere, and yet the surface by which it is circumscribed is not changed: therefore a body is not in a place because, etc. 2. The concave surface of the surrounding body also exists in a place, and it too is moved at the same time when the body is carried elsewhere: therefore the place of bodies cannot be set in it without our being forced to say that place is not locally immobile, and that place itself at the same time exists in a place, contrary to what we have said [§. 230.]

> 237 Dico 5.: locus corporum est spatium ab ipsis corporibus occupatum. Prob: unumquodque corpus reipsa existit in spatio, unam illius partem replet sibi aequalem, in eoque movetur prorsus immobili [§. 230.] sed nomine loci non aliud intelligitur, nisi id in quo unumquodque corpus hoc modo est [§. 230.]: ergo. Confirmatur: in eo statuendus est locus corporum, in quo corpora ipsa ita existunt, ut unumquodque ab eo in quo est, aliud quodcumque ratione naturalis suae soliditatis primò, & per se excludat [§. 230.]. Id autem non est nisi spatium, quod singula occupant [§§. 233, & 234]: ergo. Secundo: cóncava ambientis corporis superficies haberi nequit pro continentis corporis loco [§. 235]; sed hac rejecta, unum manet spatium, quod pro loco adsumi possit: ergo locus cujusque corporis est ipsum spatium.

237 I say 5. The place of bodies is the space occupied by the bodies themselves. Proof: each body really exists in space, fills one part of it equal to itself, and is moved in it while it is wholly immobile [§. 230.]; but by the name of place nothing else is understood than that in which each body is in this manner [§. 230.]: therefore. It is confirmed: the place of bodies is to be set in that in which the bodies themselves so exist that each, by reason of its natural solidity, primarily and of itself excludes any other whatever from that in which it is [§. 230.]. But this is nothing but the space which each occupies [§§. 233 and 234]: therefore. Secondly: the concave surface of the surrounding body cannot be held for the place of the contained body [§. 235]; but when this is rejected, space alone remains which can be taken for place: therefore the place of each body is space itself.

> Argumenta solvuntur.

THE ARGUMENTS ARE ANSWERED.

> 238 Opp. 1. contra tertiam cum Cartesio: spatium dicitur extensio in longum latum, & profundum; sed haec non distinguitur à corpore: ergo. Disting. maj: spatium dicitur extensio &c., negativa, concedo, positiva, nego, & distinguo min. Extensio positiva non distinguitur &c, concedo, negativa nego, & conseq. Corpus est extensio non qualiscumque, sed positiva, & solida, eaque ratione divisibilis, ut illius partes divelli possint à se mutuò, ac penitùs separari. Spatium autèm dicitur [p. 84] quidem extensio, sed negativa, penetrabilis & omninò indiscerptibilis: corpus namque, & spatium adtributa sibi vindicant, non diversa solùm, sed ita contraria, ut impossibile sit illa, tanquam uni, & eidem inhaerentia subjecto, concipere, maxima itaque corporis à spatio differentia in eo consistit, quod omne corpus tria quidem habet spatiorum (hoc est dimensionum) genera, non tamen quidquid tria habet spatiorum genera, est corpus.

bj. 1, against the third conclusion, with Descartes: space is called exten238 O sion in length, breadth and depth; but this is not distinguished from body: therefore. I distinguish the major: space is called extension, etc., negative, I grant; positive, I deny; and I distinguish the minor: positive extension is not distinguished, etc., I grant; negative, I deny; and the consequence. Body is not any extension whatever, but a positive and solid one, and divisible in such a way that its parts can be torn from one another and entirely separated. Space, on the other hand, is indeed called extension, [p. 84] extension, but negative, penetrable, and altogether indiscerptible: for body and space claim for themselves attributes not only diverse, but so contrary that it is impossible to conceive them as one thing and as inhering in the same subject. The greatest difference of body from space, therefore, consists in this: that every body indeed has the three kinds of spaces (that is, of dimensions), yet not whatever has the three kinds of spaces is body.

> 239 Opp. 2.: Spatium vel est aliquid reale, vel purùm nihil. Si secundum: ergo perperam vocatur extensum, mensurabile &c., quia nihili nullae sunt proprietates Si primùm: ergo aliquid praeter Deum est immensum, interminatum; sed hoc est absurdum: ergo non datur spatium. Respondeo: spatium non esse aliquod reale positivum, sed ut ait S. Augustinus spatiosum nihil. *Reale* dici potest, quatenùs ab intellectu non dependet. Nullo quippè cogitante intellectu, distant à se mutuo puncta a b Fig. XVI. Extensum dicitur spatium, mensurabile &c., eodem planè sensu, quo extensa, & mensurabilis vocatur umbra, quatenùs nempè extensum & mensurabile corpus potest in illo spatio collocari. Nihili autem ut diximus [§. 12] nullae sunt proprietates positivas, negativas multas. Quae quum ita sint, frustra quaeritur, ab Scholasticis: ¿nùm spatium sit substantia, vel accidens? Manifestum est enim, nihil nisi reale positivum esse, quod duntaxat in substantiam, & accidens potest jure distribui. Nec eos juvat, spatium non esse aliquod fictum ab intellectu, etenim neque umbra aliquod hujusmodi est, & tamen Scholasticorum nemo, dicet eam esse substantiam vel accidens. Neque etiam officit *spatium, imaginarium* nuncupari, quatenus ab imaginatione dependeat, nam ideò ita dicitur, quia illius dimensiones instar corporearum dimensionum, quae in sensum cadunt, imaginémur.

239 Obj. 2: Space is either something real or a pure nothing. If the second: then it is wrongly called extended, measurable, etc., because of nothing there are no properties. If the first: then something besides God is immense and unbounded; but this is absurd: therefore there is no space. I reply that space is not something real and positive, but, as St. Augustine says, a spacious nothing. It can be called real inasmuch as it does not depend on the intellect. For with no intellect thinking, the points a, b (Fig. XVI.) are distant from each other. Space is called extended, measurable, etc., in plainly the same sense in which a shadow is called extended and measurable, inasmuch, namely, as an extended and measurable body can be placed in that space. Of nothing, moreover, as we have said [§. 12], there are no positive properties, but many negative ones. Since these things are so, it is vainly asked by the Scholastics whether space is a substance or an accident. For it is manifest that only the real and positive is that which can rightly be divided into substance and accident. Nor does it help them that space is not something feigned by the intellect, for neither is a shadow anything of this kind, and yet none of the Scholastics will say that it is a substance or an accident. Nor does it stand in the way that space is called imaginary, as though it depended on the imagination; for it is so called because we imagine its dimensions after the manner of corporeal dimensions, which fall under the senses.

> 240 Opp. 3. Contra quartam, & quintam: indubia res est locum debere esse aliquod reale, sed hujuscemodi non est spatium: ergo. Disting. maj.: aliquod reale nempè, non fictum ab intellectu, conc. hoc est ens aliquod positivum, quod produci per realem actionem possit, nego, & eadem solut. distincta min., nego conseq. Verùm enim est, locum esse non posse aliquod prorsùs imaginarium, at ex hoc non sequitur debere esse aliquod ens reale positivum: sequeretur enim, vel aliquod ens reale extare posse, quin sit álicubi, vel ipsum quoque locum in loco existere.
