Ea igitur realitas inest spatio, quae loco convenire legitimè potest.

240 Obj. 3. Against the fourth and fifth: it is an undoubted thing that place must be something real, but space is not of this kind: therefore. I distinguish the major: something real, namely not feigned by the intellect, I grant; that is, some positive being which can be produced by a real action, I deny; and, the minor being distinguished by the same solution, I deny the consequence. For it is true that place cannot be something altogether imaginary, but from this it does not follow that it must be some real positive being: for it would follow either that some real being could exist without being anywhere, or that place itself also exists in a place. That reality, therefore, is in space which can legitimately belong to place.

> 241 Opp. 4.: locus dicitur récipere rem locabilem, eam continere, & ab ea repleri, sed haec non conveniunt spatio, sed enti positivo: ergo. Dist. maj. & ab ea repleri, perindè prorsùs, atque vas liquorem recipit, ipsum continet, & ab illo repletur, nego, ita nimirùm, ut sit sensus, quod res existat in loco, & quidem adeò, ut nihil ipsius rei extra locum habeatur, neque sinat loquendo de corporibus, ut ab altera re simul occupetur, conc, & dist. [p. 85] min: haec munera non conveniunt spatio si primo modo sumitur, conc, si sumatur secundo modo, nego, & conseq. Solutio est manifesta.

241 Obj. 4: place is said to receive the locable thing, to contain it, and to be filled by it; but these things do not belong to space, but to a positive being: therefore. I distinguish the major: and to be filled by it exactly as a vessel receives a liquor, contains it, and is filled by it, I deny; in such a way, namely, that the sense is that the thing exists in the place, and indeed so that nothing of the thing itself is had outside the place, and that, speaking of bodies, it does not allow the place to be occupied at the same time by another thing, I grant; and I distinguish the [p. 85] minor: these functions do not belong to space if it is taken in the first way, I grant; if it is taken in the second way, I deny; and the consequence. The solution is manifest.

> 242 Opp. demum: corpus refertur ad ea quae circum ipsum sunt, videlicèt judicamus corpus tandiù esse in eodem loco, quamdiù eandem à circunstantibus corporibus distantiam servat: ergo haec relatio erit corporis locus. Dist. antec.: refertur, ut illius situs definiatur, conc ut certi simus ipsum corpus esse in loco, nego, & conseq. Corporis situs nihil est aliud, nisi respectus quidam ex eo resultans, quod certam positionem corpus ipsum habeat inter illa quibus confertur, quaeque veluti immobilia spectantur, determinatamque distantiam ab illis obtineat; at falsum est referendum esse corpus ad corpora circunstantia, ut certò nobis constet, ipsum in loco existere. Sicuti enim ab illis non dependet, ut sit extra nihil sui, ita iisdem opus non habet ut aliquo in loco existat. Propterea Recentiores dividunt locum in *absolutum*, & *relativum*, primum vocant eam spatii partem, quam corpus occupat. Secundum verò quem modo *situm* diximus etiam adpelant *adparentem*, & *sensibilem.* Ex dictis sequentia Corollaria deducuntur.

242 Obj. finally: a body is referred to the things which are around it; that is, we judge that a body is in the same place as long as it keeps the same distance from the surrounding bodies: therefore this relation will be the place of the body. I distinguish the antecedent: it is referred so that its situation may be defined, I grant; so that we may be certain that the body itself is in a place, I deny; and the consequence. The situation of a body is nothing else but a certain respect resulting from the fact that the body itself has a certain position among those things with which it is compared, and which are regarded as immobile, and holds a determinate distance from them; but it is false that the body must be referred to the surrounding bodies in order that it may be certain to us that it exists in a place. For just as it does not depend on them in order to be outside its own nothingness, so it has no need of them in order to exist in some place. Therefore the Moderns divide place into absolute and relative; the first they call that part of space which the body occupies. The second, which we have just called situation, they also call apparent and sensible. From what has been said the following Corollaries are deduced.

> 243 Primum: *Locus corporum absolutus, nihil est reale positivum.* Spatium quippè nihil hujuscemodi est. Secundum: *Potest corpus mutare locum absolutum, quin mutet relativum.* Homo enim sedens in navi, quae moveatur, eundem in illa, ut patet situm retinet, at simul continuò mutat locum absolutum, quum una cum navi in qua est, diversam spatii partem singulis momentis corpus ipsum occupet. Tertium: *Divisio loci in naturalem, & violentum de loco duntaxat relativo intelligenda est.* Quum enim spatium sit sibi perpetuò uniformè, perindè est corpori quamcumque illius partem teneat, & ideò quilibet locus absolutus, est corpori naturalis. Contra verò est in loco violento, si inter alia corpora eum situm non servet, quem servare debet, ut stet illa eorumdem dispositio, quam initio temporis Deus constituit. Sic terra esset in loco violento, si suprà aquam existeret, quum constitutio mundi requirat, ut infra illam habeatur.

243 First: The absolute place of bodies is nothing real and positive. For space is nothing of this kind. Second: A body can change its absolute place without changing its relative place. For a man sitting in a ship which is moving keeps the same situation in it, as is evident; but at the same time he continually changes his absolute place, since together with the ship in which he is his body occupies a different part of space at each moment. Third: The division of place into natural and violent is to be understood of relative place only. For since space is perpetually uniform with itself, it is all the same to a body whatever part of it it holds, and therefore any absolute place whatever is natural to a body. On the contrary, a body is in a violent place if among other bodies it does not keep that situation which it ought to keep so that that disposition of them may stand which God established at the beginning of time. Thus the earth would be in a violent place if it existed above the water, since the constitution of the world requires that it be held below it.

> CAPUT IV.

CHAPTER IV.

> De Vacuo.

On the Vacuum.

> 244 Loci natura exposita, reliquum est, ut de vacuo non nulla dicamus. Hinc constabit apertiùs, quod superiori capite demonstrabimus, negativam scilicèt extensionem, sive spatium, in quo corpora quaeque sint admitti oportere.

aving set forth the nature of place, it remains for us to say some things 244 H about the vacuum. Hence it will be more openly established, what we demonstrated in the preceding chapter, that a negative extension, namely space, in which each and every body is, must be admitted.

[p. 86]

> 245 Vacuum sive inane propriè sumptum dicitur: *Spatium superficiebus comprehensum, ac veluti terminatum, in quo nullum penitùs corpus, sive fluidum, sive solidum, sive conspicuum, sive inconspicuum à quo repleatur, existat.* Consultò dixi propriè sumptum, etenim, vulgò vacuum etiam vocari solet vas, quod, à nullo corpore nobis conspicuo occupatur, licet repleatur ab inconspicuo. Ex qua definitione sequentia Corollaria deducuntur. Primum. *Nullum est vacuum, si nihil spatii, quod ab aliquo corpore non occupetur, intra universum existat.* Secundum. *Vacuum quoque non satis ex eo evincitur, quod sensibilia quaeque corpora in spatio existere demonstretur.* Possunt enim omnia esse in spatio, quin aliquam illius portionem, quae à nullo corpore occupetur, intercipiant: at vicissim & esto Corollarium tertium. *Evincitur dari spatium, si vacuum existere, aut esse possibile ostendatur* Hoc enim ipso dari extensionem negativam manifestum est.

245 A vacuum or void, taken properly, is called a space comprehended by surfaces and as it were bounded, in which there exists absolutely no body, whether fluid or solid, whether conspicuous or inconspicuous, by which it is filled. I said deliberately taken properly, for in common speech a vessel is also wont to be called empty which is occupied by no body conspicuous to us, although it is filled by an inconspicuous one. From this definition the following Corollaries are deduced. First. There is no vacuum if no space exists within the universe which is not occupied by some body. Second. Nor is a vacuum sufficiently proved from the fact that all sensible bodies whatever are demonstrated to exist in space. For all can be in space without intercepting some portion of it which is occupied by no body: but conversely, and let this be the third Corollary, it is proved that space exists, if a vacuum is shown to exist or to be possible. For by this very fact it is manifest that a negative extension exists.

> 246 Dividi solet vacuum á Philosophis in *coacervatum*, & *disseminatum.* Primum est, *notabile aliquod spatium intra universi ambitum, á nullo penitùs corpore occupatum.* Disseminatum verò dicuntur spatiola corpusculis aquae, aëris ve intercepta, quae jam non aëre, alio ve corpore oppleta, sed penitùs inania, corpore ve omni prorsùs vacua sunt, sive vacuola minima insensibilia inter materiae texturam interclusa, ferè sicut inter plurima tritici grana intérjacent minima spatia in quibus nihil tritici inest. Tria circa vacuum coacervatum ad trutinam revocari solent à Philosophis. Primum: ¿An sit possibile? Secundum, ¿num re ipsa in mundo existat? Tertium ¿an illud possit solius naturae viribus obtineri? Vacuum coacervatum adeò repugnare, ut ne Divina quidem virtute haberi queat, apertissima sententia Cartesi est [^86-s1]. Contrarium verò ii omnes Recentiores sentiunt, quibus solemne est, corpus à spatio distingui.

246 The vacuum is wont to be divided by Philosophers into the coacervate and the disseminate. The first is some notable space within the circuit of the universe, occupied by absolutely no body. Disseminate vacuums, on the other hand, is the name given to the little spaces intercepted by the corpuscles of water or of air, which are no longer filled with air or other body, but are wholly empty, or altogether devoid of every body; or very small, insensible little vacuums shut up within the texture of matter, almost as, between a great many grains of wheat, there lie very small spaces in which there is nothing of wheat. Three questions about the coacervate vacuum are wont to be weighed by Philosophers. First: is it possible? Second: does it really exist in the world? Third: can it be obtained by the forces of nature alone? That the coacervate vacuum is so repugnant that it cannot be had even by Divine power is the most open opinion of Descartes (n). The contrary, however, is held by all those Moderns with whom it is a settled principle that body is distinguished from space.

> [^86-s1]: Part. 2. Princip. n. 16.

[^86-s1]: Pt. 2 of the Principles, no. 16.

> 247 Cl. Newtonus docuisse minimè contentus, *coacervatum vacuum* non repugnare, putat vacuum illud, re ipsa in mundo existere, ut vidére est apud ipsum [^86-s2]. His positis.

247 The celebrated Newton, by no means content with having taught that the coacervate vacuum is not repugnant, thinks that that vacuum really exists in the world, as may be seen in his own works (o). These things being laid down:

> [^86-s2]: Lib. 2. Princip. Sect. 7. Schol. ad prop. 40. pag. 356, Edit. Londin. & pag. 371. Opt.

[^86-s2]: Bk. 2 of the Principia, sect. 7, Schol. to prop. 40, p. 356, London ed., and p. 371 of the Opticks.

> 248 Dico 1.: non adeò repugnat vacuum coacervatum, ut Divina virtute haberi minimè possit. Est contra Cartesium. Prob.: potest Deus corpus omne in vase aliquo contentum rédigere in nihilum, simulque impedire, ne aliud succedat; sed hoc pacto daretur vacuum coacervatum: ergo. Major constat: nullum quippe vas adeò indiget à substantia repleri, ut nisi aliqua substantia in illo sit, existere in rerum natura minimè possit. Praeterea ex duabus rebus realiter entitativè distinctis, potest Deus anihilare unam, & aliam conservare, sic potest anihilare Petrum, conservato Paulo. Sed majorem negat Cartesius, propterea, nimirùm quia tunc [p. 87] necessariò futurum sit, ut latera ipsa non distent à se mutuò, sed planè sese contingant. Contra tamen: Certum enim puto non posse illius vasis látera sese contingere, quin ejusdem figura pereat, ¿quis autem negabit posse Deum O. M. omnem substantiam in vase contentam in nihilum redigere, quin ejusdem vasis figura, vel minimè mutetur, quum á substantia, quae vas replet, nullo planè modo experientia teste, ipsius vasis figura dependeat?

248 I say 1.: the coacervate vacuum is not so repugnant that it can by no means be had by Divine power. This is against Descartes. Proof: God can reduce to nothing every body contained in some vessel, and at the same time prevent another from succeeding; but in this way a coacervate vacuum would be had: therefore. The major is established: for no vessel so needs to be filled by a substance that, unless some substance is in it, it could by no means exist in the nature of things. Moreover, of two things really and entitatively distinct, God can annihilate one and conserve the other, just as He can annihilate Peter while conserving Paul. But Descartes denies the major, for this reason, namely, because then it would necessarily [p. 87] come about that the sides themselves would not be distant from each other, but would plainly touch each other. On the contrary, however: for I hold it certain that the sides of that vessel cannot touch each other without its figure perishing; and who will deny that God, the Best and Greatest, can reduce to nothing all the substance contained in the vessel without the figure of that same vessel being changed in the least, since, as experience witnesses, the figure of the vessel itself depends in no way at all on the substance which fills the vessel?

> 249 Falsum etiam est, ea corpora sese mutuò tangere, quibus nullùm corpus re ipsa interjicitur. Ad physicum enim duorum corporum contactum non solùm requiritur, ut nullum corpus inter illa habeatur, verùm etiam, ut nullum, nè minimum quidem interjici illis posset, quin à suo loco dimoveantur. Id autem, ut constet apertiùs considerate Fig. XVI. Certum est, penitùs repugnare ut illa duo sphaerica corpora A B secundum convexas eorum superficies sese contingant: igitur sibi invicem contigua non erunt puncta a b, e d, m n, x y.; sed tunc nihil reale positivum inter illa haberetur: ergo falsum est duo corpora hoc ipso tangere sese mutuò, quòd nihil reale positivum, sive nullum corpus, re ipsa inter illa existat.

249 It is also false that those bodies touch each other between which no body is really interposed. For the physical contact of two bodies requires not only that no body be had between them, but also that none, not even the smallest, could be interposed between them without their being moved from their place. That this may be more openly evident, consider Fig. XVI. It is certain that it is wholly repugnant that those two spherical bodies A, B should touch each other along their convex surfaces: therefore the points a b, e d, m n, x y will not be contiguous to one another; but then nothing real and positive would be had between them: therefore it is false that two bodies touch each other by the very fact that nothing real and positive, or no body, really exists between them.

> 250 Fallitur ergo Vir Cl. Antonius Le Grand [^87-s1] quum ait: *Substantiam possibilem non posse esse medium actuale dividens, ac séparans corpora*, quum sit perspicuum, puncta a b globorum A B non nisi per substantiam possibilem futurum esse in illa hypothesi, ut re ipsa à se mutuo distent. Neque ipsum juvat, quod opponit, nihil scilicèt, in mundo tunc fore unitum, propterea nimirùm quod *inter partes corporis, quae uniuntur, possibile sit aliquod medium, quod ea separet.* Non juvat inquam, quia ut duo separata re ipsa sint à se mutuò non satis est, ut inter illa possibile sit aliquod medium, sed insupèr requiritur, ut medium aliquod inter ea sit possibile, quin si re ipsa illis interjiciatur, situm suum ea mutare cogantur. Sic distant re ipsa à se mutuò puncta a b globorum A B quia licet superiori facta hypothesi nihil reale interjiciant, intercipere tamen illud possunt, quin diversum ab eo, quem habent situm obtineant. Neque etiam Cartesianos juvat respondere, in proposito casu vasis, adhuc remanere corpus manente nimirùm extensione quae juxta ipsos est corporis essentia. Nam ut jam diximus [§. 4.] haec apertissima est petitio principii, & validissimè ex Tosca [^87-s2] impugnari potest hoc modo.

250 The celebrated Antoine Le Grand (p) is therefore mistaken when he says: A possible substance cannot be an actual medium dividing and separating bodies; since it is perspicuous that in that hypothesis the points a, b of the globes A, B would be really distant from each other only through a possible substance. Nor does what he objects help him, namely that nothing in the world would then be united, for this reason, to be sure, that between the parts of a body which are united some medium is possible which might separate them. It does not help, I say, because for two things to be really separated from each other it is not enough that some medium be possible between them; it is further required that some medium be possible between them such that, if it were really interposed between them, they would not be forced to change their situation. Thus the points a, b of the globes A, B are really distant from each other, because, although in the hypothesis made above they intercept nothing real, they can nevertheless intercept it without obtaining a situation different from the one they have. Nor does it help the Cartesians to reply that in the proposed case of the vessel body still remains, since extension, namely, remains, which according to them is the essence of body. For, as we have already said [§. 4.], this is a most open begging of the question, and it can be very strongly attacked, following Tosca (q), in this way.

> [^87-s1]: Inst. Pilos. P. 4. cap. 13. n. 9.

[^87-s1]: Institutio Philosophiae, pt. 4, ch. 13, no. 9.

> [^87-s2]: Philosoph. Tom. 3. p. 254.

[^87-s2]: Philosoph., vol. 3, p. 254.

> 251 Nam si ut vult Cartesius spatium illud, quod in praedicta hypothesi intra vas necessariò relinqueretur, esset corpus reale, certè vel de novo produceretur quando destrueretur aër, aut aliundè à Deo ibi adduceretur: aut jam ibi erat. Non primum, nec secundum, utrumque enim est contra hypothesim factam, supponitur [p. 88] enim, Deum intra vas, aliud corpus non subrogare: ergo fatendum erit, semper ibidem extitisse, & consequentèr penetratum erat cum aëre; sed penetratio unius corporis cum alio, etiam juxta Cartesium est naturaliter impossibilis: ergo & impossibile erit spatium illud relictum esse corpus reale: ergo est inane.

251 For if, as Descartes would have it, that space which in the aforesaid hypothesis would necessarily be left within the vessel were a real body, certainly it would either be produced anew when the air was destroyed, or be brought there by God from elsewhere, or else it was already there. Not the first, nor the second, for both are against the hypothesis made; for it is supposed [p. 88] that God does not substitute another body within the vessel: therefore it will have to be admitted that it always existed there, and consequently that it was penetrated with the air; but the penetration of one body with another is, even according to Descartes, naturally impossible: therefore it will also be impossible that that space left behind is a real body: therefore it is void.

> 252 Dico 2.: re ipsa non datur in mundo vacuum coacervatum. Prob: existentia vacui coacervati in mundo neque experientia evinci potest: neque ratione demonstrari: ergo re ipsa non datur. Prob. antec.: non experientia: ea etenim experimenta, quae ad id suadendum adferri solent, minimè probant vacui existentiam, ut postea videbimus: neque ratione illius existentia ostenditur: nullius enim roboris sunt, quae censentur precipuae, ut ex solutione argumentorum patebit: ergo.

252 I say 2.: a coacervate vacuum does not really exist in the world. Proof: the existence of a coacervate vacuum in the world can neither be proved by experience nor demonstrated by reason: therefore it does not really exist. Proof of the antecedent: not by experience, for those experiments which are wont to be brought forward to persuade us of it by no means prove the existence of a vacuum, as we shall see later; nor is its existence shown by reason, for the arguments which are reckoned the principal ones are of no strength, as will be evident from the solution of the arguments: therefore.

> 253 Dico 3.: viribus naturae haberi nequit in mundo vacuum coacervatum. Prob.: nam quum ex proximè dictis nullum sit re ipsa intra ambitum universi notabile spatium â nullo corpore occupatum, nequit spatium aliquod notabile omni corpore privari, nisi vel corpus quod in illo erat, redigatur in nihilum, vel fiat, ut idem locus simul á duobus corporibus repleatur; sed manifestum est naturae viribus fieri neutrum posse: ergo naturae viribus haberi nequit in mundo vacuum coaecervatum.

253 I say 3.: a coacervate vacuum cannot be had in the world by the forces of nature. Proof: for since, from what has just been said, there is really no notable space within the circuit of the universe occupied by no body, no notable space can be deprived of every body unless either the body which was in it is reduced to nothing, or it comes about that the same place is filled at the same time by two bodies; but it is manifest that neither can be done by the forces of nature: therefore a coacervate vacuum cannot be had in the world by the forces of nature.

> Argumenta solvuntur.

THE ARGUMENTS ARE ANSWERED.

> 254 Opp. 1. contra primam: nec Divina virtute potest fieri, ut detur vacuum, quando actu datur corpus; sed in casu vasis actu datur corpus: ergo. Prob. min. quod existit, & non est spiritus, ipsum est corpus; atqui spatium in vase existit, & spiritus non est: ergo. Dist. maj. quod existit neque spiritus est, ipsum est corpus, si physicè atque reali existentia existat, conc. Si aequivaleat duntaxat physicè existenti, nego, & conseq. Spatium verò ubi corpore omni vacuum ponitur, tametsi physica existentia corporibus competente non existat, eo tamen pacto existit, ut corpori re ipsa existenti quadam ratione aequivaleat, utpote ad quod recipiendum capacitate donatur.

bj. 1, against the first: not even by Divine power can it come about that 254 O there is a vacuum when there is actually a body; but in the case of the vessel there is actually a body: therefore. Proof of the minor: what exists and is not a spirit is a body; but space in the vessel exists and is not a spirit: therefore. I distinguish the major: what exists and is not a spirit is a body, if it exists by a physical and real existence, I grant; if it is only equivalent to a physically existing thing, I deny; and the consequence. Space, however, where it is posited as empty of every body, although it does not exist by the physical existence that belongs to bodies, nevertheless exists in such a way as to be in a certain manner equivalent to a really existing body, inasmuch as it is endowed with the capacity of receiving one.

> 255 Opp. 2. in illo casu, vasis latera jungerentur: ergo nec Divina virtute daretur vacuum. Prob. antec.: In illo casu nullum reale intervallum intercéderet; sed illa se realiter contingunt, inter quae nullum reale intervallum intérjacet: ergo Dist. maj: nullum intervallum reale intercederet, si hoc nomine intelligatur corpus reale existens, conc., si intelligatur capacitas corporis recipiendi, seu corpus quod interpóni queat, nego, & eisdem terminis distincta minori, nego conseq. Ad hoc ut duo corpora sese non contingant, atque ad invicem distent, satis est, ut ipsis manentibus immotis corpus aliquod interponi possit, quamtumvis nullum reaple [p. 89] intejectum sit, eo namque ipso, illa in remotis, ac distantibus locis existant oportet, ut supra demonstratum á nobis est.

255 Obj. 2. In that case the sides of the vessel would be joined: therefore not even by Divine power would there be a vacuum. Proof of the antecedent: in that case no real interval would intervene; but those things really touch each other between which no real interval lies: therefore. I distinguish the major: no real interval would intervene, if by this name is understood a really existing body, I grant; if there is understood the capacity of receiving a body, or a body which could be interposed, I deny; and, the minor being distinguished in the same terms, I deny the consequence. In order that two bodies should not touch each other and should be distant from one another, it is enough that, while they remain unmoved, some body could be interposed, even though none is actually interposed; [p. 89] for by that very fact they must exist in remote and distant places, as has been demonstrated by us above.

> 256 Opp. 3. contra secundam cum magno Newtono: si actu non datur vacuum coacervatum, tunc caelorum spatia actu deberent esse plena; sed non possunt esse plena, nam sic cometarum, & planetarum motus retardaretur, imò jam inde á mundi principio, quo moventur, languéscere motus deberet: ergo. Nego min. & inclusam: etenim ut astra motum suum jugiter prosequantur, haudquaquam exposcitur aliud, praeter quam quod materia replens caelum planetarium non resistat sensibiliter astris. Adhaec: luminis substantia in qua undequaque per caeli ambitum diffussa, globi planetarum, & cometarum moventur, juxta ipsum eximium Newtonum non efficit, ut perturbentur illorum decursus, neque ut motus ipse paulatim languescat: ergo pari ratione poterunt spatia illa caelorum corpore alio fluidissimo, subtilissimoque repleri, quin perennis siderum motus, vel minimum, vel perturbetur, vel retardetur. Haec autem quae de vacuo coacervao diximus, non impediunt, quominus vacuum disseminatum cum Cl. Gassendo admittamus.

256 Obj. 3, against the second, with the great Newton: if there is not actually a coacervate vacuum, then the spaces of the heavens would have to be actually full; but they cannot be full, for thus the motion of the comets and planets would be retarded; nay, ever since the beginning of the world, from which they have been moving, their motion ought to have been growing languid: therefore. I deny the minor and its included proof: for in order that the stars may continually pursue their motion, nothing else whatever is required than that the matter filling the planetary heaven should not sensibly resist the stars. Moreover, the substance of light, diffused on every side through the circuit of heaven, in which the globes of the planets and comets are moved, does not, according to the excellent Newton himself, bring it about that their courses are disturbed, or that the motion itself grows gradually languid: therefore by the same reasoning those spaces of the heavens could be filled with another body, most fluid and most subtle, without the perennial motion of the stars being either disturbed or retarded even in the least. These things, however, which we have said about the coacervate vacuum do not prevent us from admitting the disseminate vacuum with the celebrated Gassendi.

> 257 Verosimiliùs namque est rebus corporeis spatia exilissima intérseri, quibus vacui disseminati nuncupationem impertímur, quum perspicuum sit subtilissimam ipsam materiam omnia pervadentem inanibus ejusmodi spatiis interrumpi. Etenim quum fluidissima sit, neque perfectè continua, constare debet particulis sese secundum paucissima puncta contingentibus, ac reipsa dissociatis; interstitia verò illa nullo replentur corpore. Si enim subtilior quaedam adstruatur substantia, altérutrum consequatur oportet, scilicèt, vel haec de qua agimus, subtilissima non est futura, vel quoniam hoc subtiliore fluido admisso difficultas eadem recurrit, admittenda erit doctrina materiae in infinitum divissae, & in fluiditate decrescentis. Postremò si nulla essent vacuola corporibus interspersa, nullus in rerum natura fieri posset motus localis. Ad hoc enim ut corpus aliquod moveatur, ex. gr. per aëra, necesse est corpus mobile protrudere aërem anteriorem in alium locum; sed illum non posset in alium locum protrúdere, si nulla essent vacuola corporibus interspersa: ergo. Major patet: neque enim (ut argumentatur Tosca), neque enim corpus moveri potest, quin in locum aëris anterioris subeat: nequit autem in eum subire persistente ibi anteriore aëre: aliter enim daretur naturaliter penetratio: oportet ergo corpus mobile anteriorem aërem protrúdere, ut moveri possit. Min. autem prob.: nam nequit corpus mobile anteriorem aërem in alium locum protrúdere, nisi adsit locus vel antrorsum, vel retrorsum, vel sursum, vel deorsum, vel ad látera occupabilis ab illo aëre protrudendo; sed si nulla dentur vacuola nullus est locus occupabilis, quum omnia sint plena: ergo.

257 For it is more probable that very slender spaces are interspersed among corporeal things, to which we give the name of disseminate vacuum, since it is perspicuous that the most subtle matter itself, which pervades all things, is interrupted by empty spaces of this kind. For since it is most fluid, and not perfectly continuous, it must consist of particles touching one another at very few points and really dissociated; and those interstices are filled by no body. For if some subtler substance is asserted, one of two things must follow: either this matter of which we are treating will not be the most subtle, or, since the same difficulty recurs once this subtler fluid is admitted, the doctrine of matter divided to infinity and decreasing in fluidity will have to be admitted. Finally, if there were no little vacuums interspersed among bodies, no local motion could take place in the nature of things. For in order that some body be moved, e.g. through the air, it is necessary that the moving body push the air in front of it into another place; but it could not push it into another place if there were no little vacuums interspersed among bodies: therefore. The major is evident: for (as Tosca argues) a body cannot be moved without entering into the place of the air in front of it; but it cannot enter into it while the air in front persists there, for otherwise there would naturally be penetration: the moving body must therefore push the air in front of it in order to be able to move. The minor is proved: for the moving body cannot push the air in front of it into another place unless there is a place, forward or backward, upward or downward, or at the sides, that can be occupied by that air which is to be pushed; but if no little vacuums exist, there is no occupiable place, since all are full: therefore.

> 258 Opp. 4. contra tertiam experimentum illud celebre quod [p. 90] Torricellianum adpellatur eo quod *Evangelista Torricellius* omnium primus adseratur hoc experimentum fecisse. Sit canaliculus vitreus A C. (Fig. XVII.) una sui parte hermeticè sigillatus, ejusque longitudo major sit duobus pedibus cùm dimidio; impleatur mercurio, tùm digito obturetur os illud per quod mercurio fuit impletus: invertatur canaliculus sic digito clausus, ac in vas aliquod etiam mercurio satis refertum, ejus extremitas simul cum digito obturante immitatur, post immersionem removeatur digitus, aperiaturque os canaliculi, & statim mercurius ex canaliculo in vas illud descendet, non tamen totus, sed permanebit in ipso canaliculo ad usque altitudinem A E variam, pro varietate temporis, & loci: ergo superior tubi pars E C à mercurio relicta omninò vacua est: ergo dari potest solius naturae viribus vacuum coacervatum.

258 Obj. 4, against the third: that celebrated experiment which is called Torricellian [p. 90] because Evangelista Torricelli is asserted to have been the first of all to perform this experiment. Let there be a little glass tube A C (Fig. XVII.), hermetically sealed at one of its ends, and let its length be greater than two and a half feet; let it be filled with mercury, then let the mouth through which it was filled with mercury be stopped with a finger; let the tube, thus closed by the finger, be inverted, and let its end, together with the stopping finger, be put into some vessel also well filled with mercury; after the immersion let the finger be removed and the mouth of the tube opened, and at once the mercury will descend from the tube into that vessel, not, however, all of it, but it will remain in the tube itself up to the height A E, which varies with the variety of time and place: therefore the upper part of the tube, E C, left by the mercury, is altogether empty: therefore a coacervate vacuum can be had by the forces of nature alone.

> 259 Respondeo falsum esse superiorem tubi partem à mercurio relictam nulla penitùs substantia repleri. Enim verò quum vitrum innumeris porulis, ut jam diximus praeditum sit, nullam tubi partem delérere potest mercurius, quin subtilissima substantia aetherea poros vitri ingressa tubi partem repleat. Certè superior illa pars calorem concipit, si igni admoveatur, lumineque perfunditur, quod minimè contingeret si nulla ibi esset substantia: vacuum enim, quum nihil sit praeter corporis carentiam, non est capax caloris, neque luminis, neque lumen potest propagari, nisi vel substantia, per illud spatium diffunditur, vel quae jam in illo est, secundum rectam lineam validissimè à lucido corpore urgeatur, ut demonstrabimus quum de lumine nobis erit sermo. Caeterum si pars C E vacua omninò est, vellem scire ¿cur totus non depleatur tubus? Non enim adversatur naturae ut totus vacuus fiat, si contrarium legibus naturae non est, ut pars C E planè vacua existat.

259 I reply that it is false that the upper part of the tube left by the mercury is filled with no substance whatever. For since glass is furnished with innumerable little pores, as we have already said, the mercury cannot desert any part of the tube without the most subtle ethereal substance entering the pores of the glass and filling that part of the tube. Certainly that upper part takes on heat if it is brought near a fire, and is suffused with light, which would by no means happen if there were no substance there: for a vacuum, since it is nothing but the absence of body, is not capable of heat or of light; and light cannot be propagated unless either a substance is diffused through that space, or the substance which is already in it is most strongly urged in a straight line by the luminous body, as we shall demonstrate when we come to speak of light. Besides, if the part C E is altogether empty, I should like to know why the whole tube is not emptied? For it is not contrary to nature that the whole should become empty, if it is not contrary to the laws of nature that the part C E should exist plainly empty.

[p. 91]

## DE MOTU. — ON MOTION

## DISSERTATIO I. — DISSERTATION I

> Agitur de Motu locali corporum.

On the local Motion of bodies.

## CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

> De Motus natura, & obiter de Quiete.

On the nature of Motion, and incidentally on Rest.

> 260 De Tempore, Loco, & Vacuo jam satis: nunc motum localem adgredimur, de quo parum sollicita Scholastica Philosophia, ipsum vel cursìm duntaxat spectavit, vel penitùs etiam omisit, ut proindè nemini mirandum sit, si neglecta per tot aetates motûs scientia, nullos pene Physica progressus fecerit. Certè si quid est in rerum natura, quod à Philosophis omnibus maximè inquiri, & adcuratissimè pertractari debuerit, id certè sapientum omnium judicio est motus, cum necessarium sit, ut Aristoteles [^91-s1] fatetur: *ignorato motu, naturam ignorari.* Qua propter mirandum omninò est, quum praedictus Philosophus tanti fecisset motûs notitiam, tam negligenter ab his, qui Aristoteli nomen dedére investigari; quaedam enim in Scholis praevaluit consuetudo, ut non nisi sub aliquibus praecissionibus metaphysicis de motus constitutione, & natura pertractetur, admirandis ejus phaenomenis oblítis, quibus ignoratis omnem ferè Physicam in obscuro versari necesse est. Nos ergo in hac Physices Parte fusius cum Recentioribus Philosophis de motu agemus.

n Time, Place, and the Void we have now said enough: we now approach 260 O local motion, about which the Scholastic philosophy, little concerned, either looked at it only in passing or even omitted it altogether, so that it should therefore be a wonder to no one if, the science of motion having been neglected through so many ages, Physics made almost no progress. Certainly, if there is anything in the nature of things that ought to have been investigated above all by all Philosophers and treated most accurately, that, in the judgment of all the wise, is motion, since, as Aristotle (r) admits, it must be that if motion is unknown, nature is unknown. Wherefore it is altogether to be wondered at that, although the said Philosopher made so much of the knowledge of motion, it was investigated so negligently by those who enrolled themselves under Aristotle’s name; for a custom prevailed in the Schools that the constitution and nature of motion were treated only under certain metaphysical precisions, its admirable phenomena being forgotten, without knowledge of which nearly the whole of Physics must remain in darkness. We, therefore, in this Part of Physics shall treat of motion more fully, together with the Moderns.

> [^91-s1]: 3. Phys. text. 1.

[^91-s1]: 3 Phys., text 1.

> 261 Non defuisse olim, qui motus localis existentiam, non solùm in dubium vérterent, verùm etiam inficiarentur apertè, quales fuere *Parménides*, & *Melissus*, Sextus Empiricus testis est. At verò, motum re ipsa in natura contingere, quum certum adeò sit, [p. 92] tamque evidens, ut ab eo tantum verti queat in dubium, qui loqui potest, quin linguam moveat, piaculum duco in demonstranda motus existentia aliquid vel minimum temporis insúmere, operamque vel levissimam collocare, illum imitatus; qui quum de motu interrogaretur, nihil quidem respondit, sed surgens ambulavit, per ipsam evidentiam sophistae fallaciam irrídens. Existentia, itaque motus localis citra omnem dubitationis aleam posita, illius naturam breviter inquiremus.

261 That there were once some who not only called the existence of local motion into doubt but even openly denied it, such as were Parmenides and Melissus, Sextus Empiricus is witness. But since it is so certain that motion really occurs in nature, and so evident [p. 92] evident that it could be called into doubt only by one who can speak without moving his tongue, I consider it a sin to spend even the least bit of time, and to bestow even the slightest effort, on demonstrating the existence of motion, imitating that man who, when questioned about motion, answered nothing, but rose and walked, mocking the sophist’s fallacy by evidence itself. The existence of local motion being thus placed beyond all hazard of doubt, we shall briefly inquire into its nature.

> 262 Motus ab Aristotele definitur: *actus entis in potentia ad novum locum, pro ut in potentia ad illum.* Clarior verò describi potest: *transitus corporis de loco in locum*, sive: *Status corporis quod actu fertur de loco in locum*, aut *continua loci adquisitio.* Corpus enim dicitur localiter moveri, quum ita ab uno loco in alium transit, ut ideò in uno esse desinat, quia alteri praesens efficitur. Necesse est igitur ad motum localem, ut mobile ex eo desinat esse praesens uni loco, quia praesens alteri efficitur. Dividitur motus localis in *absolutum*, & *relativum.* Absolutus est, migratio corporis ab uno in alium locum absolutum, sive ab una spatii parte in aliam: relativus est migratio corporis ex vicinia eorum, quae circa ipsum sunt, ac veluti immobilia spectantur, in viciniam aliorum quae itidèm considerantur ut penitùs quiescentia.

262 Motion is defined by Aristotle: the act of a being in potency toward a new place, insofar as it is in potency toward it. It can, however, be described more clearly: the passage of a body from place to place, or: the state of a body which is actually carried from place to place, or the continual acquisition of place. For a body is said to be moved locally when it passes from one place into another in such a way that it ceases to be in the one because it is made present to the other. For local motion, therefore, it is necessary that the movable cease to be present to one place from the fact that it is made present to another. Local motion is divided into absolute and relative. Absolute motion is the migration of a body from one absolute place into another, or from one part of space into another; relative motion is the migration of a body from the vicinity of those things which are around it and are regarded as if immovable, into the vicinity of others which are likewise considered as entirely at rest.

> 263 Sic homo sedens in navi, movetur motu absoluto, dum navis à ventis defertur, minimè verò motu relativo, si ad partes navis referatur. Movetur motu absoluto, quum aliam atque aliam spatii partem successivè óccupet, at non movetur motu relativo, quum à partibus navis eandem distantiam servet. Cartesius sicuti non alium admittit locum, nisi relativum, ita non nisi relativum motum agnoscit. At verò praeter relativum, absolutum quoque motum esse admittendum iisdem evincitur rationibus, quibus ostensum est absolutum locum, nempè spatium, praeter relativum admitti oportere.

263 Thus a man sitting in a ship is moved with absolute motion while the ship is carried along by the winds, but not at all with relative motion, if he is referred to the parts of the ship. He is moved with absolute motion, since he successively occupies one part of space after another; but he is not moved with relative motion, since he keeps the same distance from the parts of the ship. Descartes, just as he admits no place other than the relative, so acknowledges no motion but the relative. But besides the relative, an absolute motion too must be admitted, as is proved by the same reasons by which it was shown that, besides the relative place, an absolute place, namely space, must be admitted.

> 264 *Quies* est permanentia corporis in eodem loco, & quidem si corpus permaneat semper in eodem loco relativo, corpus quiescit relativè; sin verò permaneat semper in eodem loco absoluto, corpus quiescit absolutè. Quapropter poterit corpus relativè quiescere, & moveri absolutè, ut accidit homini, qui sedet in navi dum ipsa velis impellitur. Vicissim poterit corpus moveri relativè, quamvis quiescat absolutè; veluti si quis ambulet in navi versùs partem unam, eadem prorsus velocitate, qua navis fertur in oppositam: nam ob duplicem hominis motum aequalem, alterum contrarium proprium, alterum communem, nempè alterum quo homo ambulat, qui est propriùs, alterum quo transfertur, qui est communis, fiet ut is in eodem loco absoluto semper cosistat.

264 Rest is the permanence of a body in the same place; and indeed, if a body remains always in the same relative place, the body rests relatively; but if it remains always in the same absolute place, the body rests absolutely. Wherefore a body can rest relatively and be moved absolutely, as happens to a man who sits in a ship while it is driven by its sails. Conversely, a body can be moved relatively although it rests absolutely: as if someone walks in a ship toward one part with exactly the same velocity with which the ship is carried toward the opposite part; for because of the man’s twofold equal motion, the one contrary and proper, the other common — namely the one by which the man walks, which is proper, and the other by which he is carried along, which is common — it comes about that he always stays in the same absolute place.

[p. 93]

## CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

> De proprietatibus motus, de que illius divisionibus.

On the properties of motion, and on its divisions.

> 265 Tres in motu omni proprietates, è quibus complures ejusdem differentiae derivantur discriminare possumus, scilicet, *determinationem*, *celeritatem*, *& quantitatem*: Determinatio est, *directio corporis quod movetur, in unam potius, quàm aliam partem sivè ad certum terminum.* Etenim quoniam quaquaversùs moveri potest corpus, ut moveatur necesse est dirigatur ad certam plagam. Directionem suam dum persequitur corpus, spatium conficit, quod spactari duplici modo potest: *physicè*, videlicet, ac *mathematicè*: Priori acceptione consideratum est totus locus, quem secundum omnem dimensionem suam, res mobilis succesivè occupat. Sic (Fig. XVIII.) sphaera A perpendiculariter ad lineam B C mota, spatium *physicè* conficit, quod concipitur instar corporis cylindrici recti D E. Posteriori sensu acceptum illud spatium, est *linea directionis* m n, in qua si habeatur ratio longitudinis, adeòque temporis, quo motus perágitur, per ipsam repraesentabitur *spatium percursum.*

265 There are three properties in all motion from which we can discern most of its differences: namely determination, celerity, and quantity. Determination is the direction of a body that is moved toward one part rather than another, or toward a certain term. For since a body can be moved in any direction whatever, in order that it be moved it must be directed toward a certain region. While a body pursues its direction it traverses a space, which can be regarded in two ways: physically, namely, and mathematically. In the former acceptation, what is considered is the whole place which the movable thing successively occupies according to its every dimension. Thus (Fig. XVIII.) the sphere A, moved perpendicularly to the line B C, traverses physically a space which is conceived as a right cylindrical body D E. Taken in the latter sense, that space is the line of direction m n, in which, if account is taken of the length, and so of the time in which the motion is performed, the space traversed will be represented by it.

> 266 Quemadmodùm corpus dicitur movéri *motu simplici*, quando una tantummodò est potentia quae illum ad motum determinat; movéri verò motu composito quum à pluribus simul potentiis & quidem secundum diversas directiones ad motum determinatur: ita directio duplex est; alia *simplex*, alia *composita.* Simplex ab una tantum impressione pendet, ut descensus globi A (Fig. citat) composita proficiscitur à pluribus impressionibus. Ita si globus E (Fig. XIX) simul à globo A directione A F, & à globo B directione B D impellatur, neutram ex his globus E sequetur, sed lineam E G diagonalem insistet.

266 Just as a body is said to be moved with simple motion when there is only one power that determines it to motion, but with compound motion when it is determined to motion by several powers at once, and indeed according to different directions, so direction is twofold: one simple, the other compound. The simple depends on one impression only, as the descent of the globe A (Fig. cited); the compound proceeds from several impressions. Thus if the globe E (Fig. XIX) is impelled at the same time by the globe A in the direction A F and by the globe B in the direction B D, the globe E will follow neither of these, but will keep to the diagonal line E G.

> 267 *Celeritas*, sive velocitas est illa mobilis adfectio qua dato tempore, datum spatium decurrit, unde & spatii, & temporis dimensioni ipsa respondet, adeòque est relatio, quam habet spatium ad tempus. Si enim duo corpora pertranseant idem spatium temporibus diversis, illud majori celeritate procedit, quod minori tempore metam adsequitur; illud verò quod tempore diuturniori ad eandem metam pervenit minori celeritate incédit. Contrà si duo corpora eodem prorsùs tempore emetiantur spatia inaequalia, illud quod majus spatium descripsit, velociùs; quod verò minus spatium peragravit, minus velociter incessisse pronunciamus.

267 Celerity, or velocity, is that affection of a movable by which it runs through a given space in a given time; whence it corresponds to the dimension both of space and of time, and so is the relation which space has to time. For if two bodies pass through the same space in different times, that one proceeds with greater celerity which reaches the goal in less time, while that which arrives at the same goal in a longer time goes with less celerity. Conversely, if two bodies measure out unequal spaces in exactly the same time, we declare that the one which described the greater space went more swiftly, and the one which traversed the smaller space less swiftly.

[p. 94]

> 268 Ex quo facilè intelligitur in conceptu *velocitatis*, duplicem alium conceptum contineri, alterum quidem spatii, alterum verò temporis, in tantum, ut eodem manente tempore, si spatium descriptum augeatur, vel minuatur, etiam velocitas motus proporcionaliter augeatur, vel minuatur, eodem verò manente spatio percurso, si tempus augeatur vel minuatur, vicissim velocitas augeatur vel minuatur in eadem ratione. Quapropter quaerentibus, ¿quid sit velocitas? Respondendum est, esse *relationem quam habet spatium descriptum ad tempus intérea elapsum, adeoque ejus mensuram haberi si spatium descriptum dividatur per tempus in descriptione spatii consumptum*, sive quod idem est. *Quotus spatii quod certo tempore corpus aequabili motu percurrit, per ipsum tempus divisi, valorem celeritatis, qua corpus ipsum eo tempore movetur, optimè designat.*

268 From this it is easily understood that in the concept of velocity two other concepts are contained, the one of space, the other of time, to such an extent that, the time remaining the same, if the space described is increased or diminished, the velocity of the motion is also proportionally increased or diminished; while, the space traversed remaining the same, if the time is increased or diminished, the velocity in turn is diminished or increased in the same ratio. Wherefore to those who ask, what is velocity? the answer must be that it is the relation which the space described has to the time elapsed meanwhile, and so its measure is had if the space described is divided by the time consumed in describing the space; or, what is the same, the quotient of the space which a body runs through with uniform motion in a certain time, divided by that time itself, best designates the value of the celerity with which the body is moved in that time.

> 269 Itaque si mobile A descripsit pedes 20 in tempore 4 minutorum, & mobile B descripsit pedes 40 in tempore 5 minutorum, velocitas mobilis A erit graduum 5, velocitas mibilis B erit gradum 8. Hoc est: spatium descriptum â mobili A in quavis temporis parte, est ad spatium descriptum à mobili B in eadem parte temporis, ut 5, ad 8. Suponamus etiam corpus A percurrisse 20 leucas, 2 horarum spatio, & corpus B 100, 4 horarum spatio: Dico: celeritatem corporis A esse ad celeritatem corporis B, ut est 10, (qui quotus est 20 divisi per 2.) ad 25 (qui quotus est 100 divisi per 4) hoc est: quantum 10 inferior est 25, tantum celeritas corporis A inferior est celeritate corporis B.

269 Thus if the movable A described 20 feet in a time of 4 minutes, and the movable B described 40 feet in a time of 5 minutes, the velocity of the movable A will be of 5 degrees, the velocity of the movable B of 8 degrees. That is: the space described by the movable A in any part of time is to the space described by the movable B in the same part of time as 5 to 8. Let us suppose also that the body A has run through 20 leagues in the space of 2 hours, and the body B 100 in the space of 4 hours: I say that the celerity of the body A is to the celerity of the body B as 10 (which is the quotient of 20 divided by 2) is to 25 (which is the quotient of 100 divided by 4); that is: by as much as 10 is less than 25, by so much is the celerity of the body A less than the celerity of the body B.

> 170 Quod tantum intelligendum est quum corpora moventur aequabiliter, nam si motus sit inaequabilis, quum corpus non moveatur eadem celeritate toto illo tempore, nequit variabilis illa celeritas, per *constantem* quantitatem designari. Corpus autem *aequabiliter* moveri dicitur; *si eadem celeritate continuò moveatur*, nempe, si aequalibus temporibus, aequales spatii partes percurrat. Dicitur verò moveri *inaequabiliter, si non eadem semper sit sui motus celeritas*, videlicèt si temporibus aequalibus, per inaequalia spatia abripiatur. Sic *aequabilis* erit motus corporis A si dum 1o. minuto pedes 5, deinde 2o. pedes 10, tum 3o. pedes 15. atque ita deinceps percurrat. Contrà verò *inaequabilis* erit illius motus si 1o. minuto per spatium pedale, reliquis verò per spatium non pedale, neque constanti semper lege, sed variata semper inaequabiliter spatii magnitudine abripiatur.

270 This is to be understood only when bodies are moved uniformly; for if the motion is non-uniform, since the body is not moved with the same celerity during that whole time, that variable celerity cannot be designated by a constant quantity. A body, moreover, is said to be moved uniformly if it is moved continually with the same celerity, namely, if in equal times it runs through equal parts of space. It is said to be moved non-uniformly if the celerity of its motion is not always the same, namely, if in equal times it is carried through unequal spaces. Thus the motion of the body A will be uniform if it runs through 5 feet in the 1st minute, then 10 feet by the 2nd, then 15 feet by the 3rd, and so on. Conversely, its motion will be non-uniform if in the 1st minute it is carried through the space of a foot, but in the remaining ones through a space not of a foot, and not by a constant law at all times, but with the magnitude of the space always varied non-uniformly.

> 271 *Acceleratus* est, cujus celeritas continuò augetur, *Retardatus*, cujus celeritas continuò minuitur. Si temporibus aequalibus aequalia accedant velocitatis incrementa, motus dicitur *aequabiliter acceleratus*, quemadmodum si ea proportione decedant, *aequabiliter retardatus* nuncupatur. Atque haec sunt praecipuae motus divisiones. Sequitur nunc tertia motus proprietas quae *quantitas* dicitur, sed antequam illam explicemus de Viribus aliquid dicendum est.

271 That motion is accelerated whose celerity is continually increased; retarded, that whose celerity is continually diminished. If in equal times equal increments of velocity are added, the motion is called uniformly accelerated, just as, if they fall away in that proportion, it is named uniformly retarded. And these are the chief divisions of motion. There follows now the third property of motion, which is called quantity; but before we explain it something must be said about Forces.

> 272 *Vis* est *facultas sive potentia, quae vel motum in corpus* [p. 95] *inducit, vel remoto obstaculo induceret*, eamque post doctissimum Leibnitzium dividunt Philosophi in *vivam* & *mortuam.* Vivam adpellant illam, *quae actu inducit motum in corpus*, ut est gravitas in lapide descendente, mortuam verò illam esse dicunt, *quae actu quidem caret effectu, sed quae remoto obstaculo adigeret corpus ad motum*, ut est eadem gravitas in globo, filo sustentato, qui quiescit usque donec sustinetur, at remoto sustentaculo statim déscendere incipit deorsùm. Eadem quoque, *vis initialis*, *conatus* seu *nisus ad motum actualem* compellatur.

272 Force is the faculty or power which either induces motion in a body, [p. 95] or would induce it if an obstacle were removed; and this, following the most learned Leibniz, Philosophers divide into living and dead. They call that force living which actually induces motion in a body, as is gravity in a descending stone; that force, on the other hand, they say is dead which actually lacks its effect, but which, if an obstacle were removed, would drive the body to motion, as is the same gravity in a globe held up by a thread, which rests so long as it is held up, but when the support is removed at once begins to descend downward. This same force is also called initial force, conatus or nisus toward actual motion.

> 273 Per *quantitatem motus* (quam etiam *momentum* adpellant Recentiores) intelligimus, *vim sive impetum, quem corpora extra quietis statum facere possunt contra obstacula objecta*, adeòque ad definiendam quantitatem motus adtendendum est, & ad velocitatem cum qua corpus movetur, & ad massam sive quantitatem materiae ipsius corporis. Sint enim duo corpora A B habentia aequales materiae quantitates, eademque ferantur contra obstaculum oppositum aequali velocitate: utrumque corpus eundem impetum faciet adversus obstaculum, neque enim quidquam causae est, cur unum altero majorem vim facere debeat, quum & massae, & velocitates aequales ponantur; quòd si impetus aequales sunt, aequales pariter erunt motus, sive motuum quantitates.

273 By quantity of motion (which the Moderns also call momentum) we understand the force or impetus which bodies, out of the state of rest, can exert against obstacles set against them; and so, in defining the quantity of motion, attention must be paid both to the velocity with which the body is moved and to the mass, or quantity of matter, of the body itself. For let there be two bodies A B having equal quantities of matter, and let them be carried against an opposed obstacle with equal velocity: each body will exert the same impetus against the obstacle, for there is no cause why the one should exert a greater force than the other, since both the masses and the velocities are supposed equal; and if the impetuses are equal, the motions, or quantities of motions, will likewise be equal.

> 274 At manente massarum aequalitate fac corpus A velociùs ferri, corpus verò B ferri segniùs: tunc impetus corporum A & B facti contra obstaculum, minimè aequales erunt, sed major erit impetus corporis A, quod velocius movetur, eòque major erit, quò major est velocitas cum qua ipsum fertur in obstaculum. Et quoniam impetus, & motus, unum idemque sunt, sequitur, *motus sive quantitatem motuum duorum corporum, A & B, quorum massae sunt aequales, esse inter se, ut sunt velocitates eorumdem corporum.* Quod si manente aequalitate velocitatum ponantur massae corporum A & B inaequales, neque etiam impetus facti ab ipsis contra obstaculum erunt aequales, sed major erit impetus corporis, quod majorem continet materiae quantitatem, eòque major erit, quò major est quantitas materiae, unde *tum impetus, tum motus corporum aeque velocium, erunt in ratione massarum.*

274 But, the equality of the masses remaining, make the body A be carried more swiftly and the body B more sluggishly: then the impetuses of the bodies A and B exerted against the obstacle will by no means be equal, but the impetus of the body A, which is moved more swiftly, will be greater, and the greater, the greater the velocity with which it is carried against the obstacle. And since impetus and motion are one and the same, it follows that the motions, or quantities of motion, of two bodies A and B whose masses are equal are to each other as the velocities of those same bodies. But if, the equality of the velocities remaining, the masses of the bodies A and B are supposed unequal, neither will the impetuses exerted by them against the obstacle be equal, but the impetus of that body will be greater which contains the greater quantity of matter, and the greater, the greater the quantity of matter; whence both the impetuses and the motions of equally swift bodies will be in the ratio of the masses.

> 275 Ex quibus Theorématis consequitur modo tertium, quod ità se hàbet: *momenta sive quantitates motuum corporum, quorum tùm velocitates, tùm massae sunt inaequales, rationem habent compositam ex rationibus simplicibus velocitatum, & massarum* Ut itaque proposito duplici quorumcumque corporum motu, intelligi possit, quisnam ex illis motibus major, aut minor haberi debeat, priùs adcuratè deprehendi debet gravitas, seu massa utriusque corporis, deinde verò velocitas, seu celeritas, qua utrumque movetur, sive spatia, quae ab utroque corpore peraguntur, tùm multiplicata in singulis corporibus per celeritatem corporis massa, productum ex illis exhibebit motus quantitatem, quae singulis corporibus convenit: quod [p. 96] ipsum more Geometrico ita enunciatur. *Quantitas motus, sive momentum corporis, rectè exprimitur per factum ex ductu celeritatis in massam.*

275 From these Theorems there follows directly the third, which runs thus: the momenta, or quantities of motions, of bodies whose velocities as well as masses are unequal have a ratio compounded of the simple ratios of the velocities and of the masses. So that, therefore, when a twofold motion of any bodies whatever is proposed, it may be understood which of those motions must be held the greater or the smaller, first the gravity, or mass, of each body must be accurately ascertained, then the velocity, or celerity, with which each is moved, or the spaces which are traversed by each body; then, the mass of each body being multiplied by the celerity of the body, the product of them will exhibit the quantity of motion which belongs to each body: and this [p. 96] very thing is stated thus in the geometric manner: The quantity of motion, or momentum, of a body is rightly expressed by the product of the celerity multiplied into the mass.

> 276 Quantitas ergò motus non ex sola mobilis celeritate aestimanda est. Quum enim motus, & toti corpori, & singulis ejusdem partibus competat, aliter, ut jam diximus aestimari non poterit, quàm si massam corporis in velocitatem ducamus. Sit enim ex. gr. massa corporis A, 4, velocitas seu celeritas 6. In hoc casu quaelibet pars corporis A, habebit 6 gradus celeritatis, & consequenter 6 item gradus impetus seu motus: impetus ergo seu vis totalis corporis, aequalis erit 6 gradibus impetus quater repetitis, seu quod idem est, si ducatur 4 in 6, quantitas motus in corpore A, erit 24. Similiter sit massa corporis B 3, velocitas 8, ducantur 3 in 8, erit quantitas in corpore B 24. Ex quo facilè intelligi poterit quod in utroque mobili, eadem quantitas motus reperitur. Spectari igitur potest momentum dati corporis veluti rectángulum, cujus basis referat massam ipsius corporis, altitudo verò illius celeritatem. Oritur enim rectangulum ex ductu baseos in altitudinem, ut dictum est in Geometria.

276 The quantity of motion, therefore, is not to be estimated from the celerity of the movable alone. For since motion belongs both to the whole body and to each of its parts, it cannot, as we have already said, be estimated otherwise than by multiplying the mass of the body into the velocity. For let, e.g., the mass of the body A be 4, its velocity or celerity 6. In this case each part of the body A will have 6 degrees of celerity, and consequently also 6 degrees of impetus or motion: the impetus, therefore, or force of the whole body will be equal to 6 degrees of impetus repeated four times; or, what is the same, if 4 is multiplied into 6, the quantity of motion in the body A will be 24. Likewise let the mass of the body B be 3, its velocity 8; let 3 be multiplied into 8: the quantity in the body B will be 24. From which it can easily be understood that the same quantity of motion is found in each movable. The momentum of a given body can therefore be regarded as a rectangle whose base represents the mass of the body itself, and its height the body’s celerity. For a rectangle arises from multiplying the base into the height, as was said in Geometry.

> 277 Quod si gravitas in corpore A sit 4, velocitas 5, massa autem in corpore B sit 3, velocitas 8, quantitas motus in corpore A, erit 20, in corpore B erit 24: unde quantitas motus major erit in B, quàm in A Inde verò facilè deduci potest, quod ipsa quantitas motus virtuti motrici respondére debet, ideòque si certa quaedam vis requiritur, ut corpus 1 librae ad 100 pedum distantiam projiciatur, duplo major virtus requiretur, ut illud eodem tempore ad spatium 200 pedum projici possit. Sicuti eadem ratione manifestissimè adparet, quod si corpus 10 librarum aliquo determinato tempore certa quadam vi ad 30 pedum distantiam projicitur, eadem prorsùs vis, & impetus requiretur, ut corpus 20 librarum per spatium 15 pedum projiciatur.

277 But if the gravity in the body A is 4, the velocity 5, and the mass in the body B is 3, the velocity 8, the quantity of motion in the body A will be 20, in the body B 24: whence the quantity of motion will be greater in B than in A. From this, moreover, it can easily be deduced that the quantity of motion itself must correspond to the motive power; and therefore, if a certain force is required for a body of 1 pound to be thrown to a distance of 100 feet, a power twice as great will be required for it to be thrown in the same time to a space of 200 feet. Just as, by the same reasoning, it appears most manifestly that if a body of 10 pounds is thrown in some determinate time by a certain force to a distance of 30 feet, exactly the same force and impetus will be required for a body of 20 pounds to be thrown through a space of 15 feet.

> 278 Ideòque universaliter tantò major futura est virtus motrix, quantò major est quantitas motus in corpore, quod movetur; quantitas verò motus tantò major erit, quantò major est gravitas seu massa corporis, simulque celeritas qua moveatur. Itaque in priori exemplo, quum eadem sit quantitas motus in utroque corpore, manifestè adparet, quod utrumque ex illis aequali vi, sive potentia movebitur; quod si ut in altero casu contingit, major sit in alterutro corpore quantitas motus, sive ex gravitate, sive potiùs ex celeritate haec inaequalitas oriatur, major quoque vis, sive potentia motrix requiretur. Quae omnia adcuratissimè observanda sunt, quum inde, velut ex uberrimo fonte tota ferè Statica, & Mechanica derivetur, ut in sequentibus data opera ostendemus.

278 And therefore, universally, the motive power will be the greater, the greater the quantity of motion in the body that is moved; and the quantity of motion will be the greater, the greater the gravity or mass of the body, and at the same time the celerity with which it is moved. Thus in the former example, since the quantity of motion is the same in each body, it manifestly appears that each of them will be moved by an equal force or power; but if, as happens in the other case, the quantity of motion is greater in one of the two bodies, whether this inequality arises from the gravity or rather from the celerity, a greater motive force or power is also required. All of which must be observed most accurately, since from this, as from a most abundant source, almost the whole of Statics and Mechanics is derived, as we shall show in what follows when occasion is given.

> 279 Ex dictis fit manifestum, *vim* sive *impetum*, sive *motum*, sive *momentum* (haec enim omnia unum, idemque sunt) alicujus corporis, tripliciter augeri posse. 1. Ex *aucta velocitate*, cujus rei habemus exemplum in globis ferreis, quos tormenta bellica vi [p. 97] pulveris pyrii explodunt contra moenia oppidorum obsessorum, qui globi magno impetu ipsa moenia feriunt, ob magnam velocitatem, cum qua feruntur. 2: *Ex aucta quantitate materiae*; cujus rei habemus exemplum in arietibus, atque aliis machinamentis bellicis, quae apud Veteres obtinebant; ea enim quanquam tardissimè incederent, tamen immensam molem habebant, adeòque ad opugnanda moenia, magnum usum praestabant. 3.: *Ex aucta tum velocitate, tum quantitate materiae*, quo quidem casu impetus evadit immensus, quum incrementum duplici ex causa adveniat momento, ex velocitate scilicet, & ex massa.

279 From what has been said it is manifest that the force or impetus, or motion, or momentum (for all these are one and the same) of any body can be increased in three ways. 1. By increased velocity, an example of which we have in the iron balls which engines of war, by the force of gunpowder, [p. 97] discharge against the walls of besieged towns, which balls strike the walls themselves with great impetus because of the great velocity with which they are carried. 2: By increased quantity of matter; an example of which we have in battering rams and other machines of war which were in use among the Ancients; for these, although they advanced most slowly, yet had an immense mass, and so afforded great use for assaulting walls. 3.: By increased velocity and quantity of matter together, in which case the impetus becomes immense, since the increment comes to the momentum from a double cause, namely from the velocity and from the mass.

> 280 Quoniam autem non nullà quae in hoc capite dicta sunt difficultatem adferre possunt Adolescentibus, iccircò quaedam exempla aequalitatis, & inaequalitatis impetuum, oculis subjicere, & iterum demonstrare juvat, nec non regulas velocitatum, & quantitatis motuum clariùs propónere.

280 But since not a few of the things said in this chapter can cause difficulty for young students, it is helpful to set before their eyes some examples of the equality and inequality of impetuses, and to demonstrate them again, and also to propose more clearly the rules of velocities and of the quantity of motions.

> 281 Ad primum quod adtinet sint duae linae rectae A B, C D, (Fig. XX.) divisae in tot partes aequales, quot volueris, ex. gr. in novem. In prima linea supponatur corpus pedale, in secunda verò corpus aliud pedale priori perfectè homogeneum: tum haec corpora supponantur intra tempus idem, totidem linearum suarum partes percurrere. In hac hypothesi dico, vires motrices, mobilibus illis adplicatas, esse inter se perfectè aequales. Effectus enim producti sunt omninò similes, & consequenter eorum causae productivae judicari debent omninò similes.

281 As to the first, let there be two straight lines A B, C D (Fig. XX.), divided into as many equal parts as you like, e.g. into nine. On the first line let there be supposed a body of one foot, on the second another body of one foot, perfectly homogeneous with the former; then let these bodies be supposed to run through, within the same time, the same number of parts of their lines. In this hypothesis I say that the motive forces applied to those movables are perfectly equal to each other. For the effects produced are altogether alike, and consequently their productive causes must be judged altogether alike.

> 282 Sint rursùs alia duo corpora, per duas alias lineas aequales translata, ità ut corpus trium pedum, quale exhibetur per f g h moveatur per lineam A B, cum tribus gradibus velocitatis; alterum verò pedale, transferatur cum novem gradibus velocitatis per lineam C D.

282 Again, let there be two other bodies carried along two other equal lines, such that the body of three feet, such as is shown by f g h, is moved along the line A B with three degrees of velocity, while the other, of one foot, is carried along the line C D with nine degrees of velocity.

> 283 Dico, impetus corporibus illis adplicatos, esse pariter inter se aequales: quod sic ostendo. Tunc impetus, seu vires seu quantitates motuum sunt inter se aequales, quando eorum effectus sunt aequales: atqui in hoc exemplo effectus sunt aequales. Nam effectus primae virtutis, est transferre corpus trium pedum per tres partes aequales lineae A B, nimirum usque ad punctum 3. Effectus autem secundae virtutis motricis, est per tempus idem transferre corpus pedale per novem partes aequales lineae C D, seu usque ad punctum 9: atqui effectus ii sunt aequales:

283 I say that the impetuses applied to those bodies are likewise equal to each other: which I show thus. Impetuses, or forces, or quantities of motions are equal to each other when their effects are equal: but in this example the effects are equal. For the effect of the first power is to carry the body of three feet through three equal parts of the line A B, namely as far as the point 3; and the effect of the second motive power is to carry, in the same time, the body of one foot through nine equal parts of the line C D, or as far as the point 9: but these effects are equal.

> 284 Nam transferre corpus trium pedum per tres partes aequales lineae A B, est efficere, ut unumquodque corpus pedale componens corpus trium pedum, percurrat tres partes aequales; vel est efficere ut tria corpora pedalia percurrant singula, tres partes aequales illius lineae. Jam verò efficere, ut tria corpora pedalia percurrant singula, tres partes aequales spatii; idem est ac efficere, ut unicum corpus pedale percurrat novem partes aequales spatii; quandoquidem ex utráque parte, novem partes aequales spatii [p. 98] percurruntur à corpore pedali: ergo effectus sunt similes: ergo vires eorum productivae sunt aequales.

284 For to carry a body of three feet through three equal parts of the line A B is to bring it about that each body of one foot composing the body of three feet runs through three equal parts; or it is to bring it about that three bodies of one foot each run through three equal parts of that line. Now to bring it about that three bodies of one foot each run through three equal parts of space is the same as to bring it about that a single body of one foot runs through nine equal parts of space; since on either side nine equal parts of space are traversed [p. 98] by a body of one foot: therefore the effects are alike: therefore their productive forces are equal.

> 285 Sint denique duo alia corpora homogenea, ita ut moles unius sit séxtupla molis alterius, & ambo pari velocitate transferantur. In hac hypothesi, evidens est, ad transferendum corpus séxtupedale, requiri virtutem séxtuplo intensiorem; quàm ad transferendum corpus séxtuplo mole minus. Sed Leges velocitatum, & quantitatis motum supra à nobis propositae, clarius iterum proponantur.

285 Finally, let there be two other homogeneous bodies, such that the bulk of the one is six times the bulk of the other, and let both be carried with equal velocity. In this hypothesis it is evident that, to carry the six-foot body, a power six times more intense is required than to carry the body six times smaller in bulk. But let the Laws of velocities and of the quantity of motions proposed by us above be set out again more clearly.

> *Regulae velocitatum.*

RULES OF VELOCITIES .

> 286 I. Quando spatia á corporibus homogeneis decursa, inter se sunt aequalia, & tempora intra quae fuerunt translata, pariter sunt aequalia; tunc velocitates inter se sunt aequales. II. Quando spatia decursa, inaequalia sunt, tempora verò sunt aequalia, tunc velocitates inter se sunt; ut spatia decursa. III. Quando spatia decursa, aequalia sunt inter se, tempora verò sunt inaequalia; tunc velocitates sunt inter se reciprocè, ut tempora, hoc est, tempus breviùs majorem indicat velocitatem; & majus indicat minorem. IV. Quando spatia decursa inter se sunt inaequalia, & tempora sunt pariter inaequalia; tunc velocitates sunt inter se, ut quoti spatiorum, per tempora divisorum.

286 I.    When the spaces run through by homogeneous bodies are equal to each other, and the times within which they were traversed are likewise equal, then the velocities are equal to each other. II. When the spaces run through are unequal, but the times equal, then the velocities are to each other as the spaces run through. III. When the spaces run through are equal to each other, but the times unequal, then the velocities are to each other reciprocally as the times; that is, the shorter time indicates the greater velocity, and the greater the smaller. IV. When the spaces run through are unequal to each other, and the times likewise unequal, then the velocities are to each other as the quotients of the spaces divided by the times.

> *Regulae pro quantitate motuum.*

RULES FOR THE QUANTITY OF MOTIONS .

> 287 I. Si massae aut moles homogeneae inter se sint aequales, & earum velocitates sint pariter aequales, tunc quantitates impetuum mobilibus illis adplicatorum inter se sunt aequales: quia hoc in casu effectus sunt perfectè similes, sicut probatum fuit. II. Si moles, aut massae homogeneae, inter se sint aequales, & earum velocitates sint inaequales: tunc quantitates motuum, sive impetuum sunt inter se, ut velocitates III Si moles homogeneae, inter se sint inaequales, & earum velocitates sint aequales, tunc quantitates impetuum inter se sunt, ut massae, seu moles. IV. Si moles homogeneae, inter se sunt inaequales, & earum velocitates sint pariter inaequales; tunc quantitates impetuum sunt inter se, ut producta nata, ex multiplicatione cujusque molis per suam velocitatem.

287 I.    If the masses or homogeneous bulks are equal to each other, and their velocities are likewise equal, then the quantities of the impetuses applied to those movables are equal to each other: because in this case the effects are perfectly alike, as was proved. II. If the homogeneous bulks or masses are equal to each other, and their velocities unequal, then the quantities of motions, or of impetuses, are to each other as the velocities. III. If the homogeneous bulks are unequal to each other, and their velocities equal, then the quantities of impetuses are to each other as the masses, or bulks. IV. If the homogeneous bulks are unequal to each other, and their velocities likewise unequal, then the quantities of impetuses are to each other as the products arising from the multiplication of each bulk by its velocity.

> 288 Regulae dudum praescriptae, tùm circa velocitates mobilium, tùm circa quantitates impetuum, spectari debent tanquam fundamenta totius scientiae machinalis, seu illius Philosophiae partis, quae mutuato à Geometria subsidio, variarum machinarum adparatum nobis suppeditat. Quàmverò utilis sit haec Physicae pars, quàmque multum inserviat ad complura naturae phaenomena [p. 99] noscenda, & explananda, tantùm negare poterit, qui planè hospes in Geometria, & Physica sit, ut ea propter necessarium omninò existimarim utilissimam ac jocundissimam hanc Physices partem vobis trádere postquàm de Statica sermonem instituam. Nec vos harum rerum difficultates terreant; difficultas enim utilitate compensabitur. Praeterquam quod in id nervos omnes intendo, ut perexpeditam vobis commonstrem viam, nec scopulum offendetis, si adtenta, & seria meditatione ad veritates contemplandas animum adplicuéritis.

288 The rules just prescribed, both about the velocities of movables and about the quantities of impetuses, must be regarded as the foundations of the whole science of machines, or of that part of Philosophy which, with help borrowed from Geometry, supplies us with the apparatus of various machines. How useful this part of Physics is, and how much it serves for knowing very many phenomena of nature [p. 99] and explaining them, only one who is plainly a stranger to Geometry and Physics could deny; so that for this reason I have judged it altogether necessary to deliver to you this most useful and most delightful part of Physics once I take up the discussion of Statics. Do not let the difficulties of these matters frighten you, for the difficulty will be compensated by the usefulness. Besides which, I bend all my efforts to this, to show you a very easy road; nor will you strike any rock, if you apply your mind attentively and with serious meditation to contemplating the truths.

## CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

> De Naturae legibus Newtonianis.

On the Newtonian laws of Nature. 289

> 289 Naturae legem vocant Philosophi, *regulam universalissimam, quae in omnibus rerum naturalium vicissitudinibus, atque commutationibus locum habet.* Et quoniam omnis naturae vicissitudo proficiscitur à *motu* indè fit, ut naturae legum exercitium praecipuè in motionibus corporum se manifestèt. De his naturae legibus quum multa Philosophi disputassent, tandèm *Newtonus* omnia, quae antea de isto argumento dicta fuerant ad tria praecipua capita revocavit, quae quidem *leges Naturae Newtonianae* hodie passim à Philosophis vocantur.
