Philosophers call a law of nature a most universal rule which has place in all the vicissitudes and changes of natural things. And since every vicissitude of nature proceeds from motion, it comes about that the exercise of the laws of nature shows itself chiefly in the motions of bodies. Since Philosophers had disputed much about these laws of nature, at length Newton reduced everything that had been said before on this argument to three principal heads, which today are commonly called by Philosophers the Newtonian Laws of Nature.

## *Lemma.* — LEMMA

> 290 *Motus quantum est ex se dirigitur per lineam rectam, nec eam deserit, nisi ab aliqua causa extrinseca ab ea detorqueatur.* Ratio est, quia linea recta brevissima est ex his, quae à puncto ad punctum, sive à termino *à quo* ad terminum *ad quem* duci possunt, etiam simplicissima est; non enim quemadmodum linea curva in varias species dividitur: ergo motus per lineam rectam brevior est, ac simplicior; sed natura semper brevitatem, ac simplicitatem in omnibus adfectat, nihil frustra molítur, superflua rejicit, & quo maximo potest compendio cuncta operatur: ergo motus per lineam rectam potiùs quàm per aliam dirigitur. Hoc constituto antequàm Newtonianas motus Leges proponamus, quaedam de *vi inertiae* breviter à nobis dicenda sunt. Hujus nomine intelligimus, *vim eam in unoquoque corpore, qua corpus unumquodque quantum in se est, perseverat in statu suo vel quietis, vel motus, sive vis quaedam materiae insita, qua fit ut unumquodque corpus proprium suum statum tueri, atque conservare nitatur.*

290 Motion, so far as lies in itself, is directed along a straight line, nor does it desert it unless it is turned aside from it by some extrinsic cause. The reason is that the straight line is the shortest of those which can be drawn from point to point, or from the term from which to the term to which, and is also the simplest: for it is not divided into various species, as the curved line is: therefore motion along a straight line is shorter and simpler; but nature in all things affects brevity and simplicity, undertakes nothing in vain, rejects superfluities, and works all things with the greatest possible economy: therefore motion is directed along a straight line rather than along another. This being established, before we propose Newton’s Laws of motion, some things must briefly be said by us about the force of inertia. By this name we understand that force in each body by which every body, so far as lies in it, perseveres in its state either of rest or of motion, or a certain force implanted in matter, by which it comes about that each body strives to maintain and preserve its own state.

[p. 100]

> 291 Nam si corpus quiescit, quies illa in corpore foret in aeternum duratura, si nullus in ipsum impetus fiat. Et similiter corpus semel motum, perpetuò moveretur, si nullam retardationem à resistentia medii pateretur. Etenim omne corpus quod movetur, in medio illi resistente movetur, unde corpus, motum continuare nequit nisi in quantum hanc vincat resistentiam, eam autem vincere non potest, nisi dividendo & separando partes medii, nec potest has partes separare, nisi impendendo contra illas aliquam partem impetus, quem habebat ad se movendum; quum sensim ergo impetus diminuatur in mobili, ejus celeritas minui proportionaliter debet, & tandèm ad nihilum redúci.

291 For if a body rests, that rest in the body would last forever, if no impetus were made upon it. And likewise a body once moved would be moved perpetually, and would suffer no retardation from the resistance of the medium. For every body that is moved is moved in a medium resisting it; whence the body cannot continue its motion except insofar as it overcomes this resistance; and it cannot overcome it except by dividing and separating the parts of the medium, nor can it separate these parts except by spending against them some part of the impetus which it had for moving itself; since, therefore, the impetus is gradually diminished in the movable, its celerity must be diminished proportionally, and at length be reduced to nothing.

> 292 Sed ultra hanc resistentiam medii, datur etiam in corpore alia *Resistentia*, quatenus nempè corpus ad conservandum sibi statum suum, reluctatur vi impressae. Dum enim corpus B quiescens éxcipit ictum à corpore moto A, non movetur corpus B, quin corpus A amittat non nihil de vi sua, quare adest in B vis frangens impetum corporis A, quae vocatur *vis resistentiae.* His suppositis, prima lex Newtoniana ita proponi solet. *Corpus omne perseverat in statu suo quietis, vel motus uniformiter, & in linea recta, nisi ab aliqua vi impressa cogatur statum illum mutare.* Haec lex fundatur in vi inertiae, ob quam fit, ut singula corpora conentur conservare sibi eum statum, quo in statu actu sunt constituta.

292 But beyond this resistance of the medium there is also in the body another Resistance, namely insofar as the body, in order to preserve its own state, struggles against the impressed force. For when the body B at rest receives a blow from the moved body A, the body B is not moved without the body A losing something of its force; wherefore there is in B a force breaking the impetus of the body A, which is called the force of resistance. These things being supposed, the first Newtonian law is usually proposed thus: Every body perseveres in its state of rest, or of moving uniformly and in a straight line, unless it is compelled by some impressed force to change that state. This law is founded on the force of inertia, because of which it comes about that individual bodies strive to preserve for themselves that state in which they are actually placed.

> 293 Corpus quiescens nunquam désinet quiescere ex se ipso, sed ad hoc ut constituatur in motu, necesse est, externam vim intervenire. Contrà corpus quod movetur, nunquam desinet moveri, si omnium circunstantium corporum resistentiam victam, & in nihilum redactam supponamus. Neque hìc audiendi sunt vulgares Peripatetici, qui doceat, *corpora mota suaptè natura quietem adfectare*, sive etiam *ex motu ad quietem tendere*, contra id quod docet eorum Princeps Aristoteles [^100-s1], ea praecipuè inducti ratione, quòd videant lapidum projectorum motum sensim languéscere, ac tandem omninò desinere[?]. Si enim lapides projecti aliquandò desistunt à motu, id quidèm duplici causae imputandum est. Prima quia à gravitate ipsa deorsum propulsi, tandèm in terram impingunt. Secunda quia aër eorum motui obsistit, nam si in vacuo lapis projectus esset, & praetereà si is omni gravitate destitueretur, proculdubiò ejus motus nunquàm languesceret, sed foret in aeternum duraturus.

293 A body at rest will never cease to rest of itself, but in order that it be placed in motion an external force must intervene. Conversely, a body that is moved will never cease to be moved, if we suppose the resistance of all the surrounding bodies overcome and reduced to nothing. Nor are the common Peripatetics to be heard here, who teach that moved bodies by their own nature affect rest, or also tend from motion to rest, contrary to what their Prince Aristotle (a) teaches, led chiefly by this reason, that they see the motion of thrown stones gradually grow languid and at length cease altogether. For if thrown stones at some time desist from motion, this must indeed be imputed to a double cause. The first, because, driven downward by gravity itself, they at length strike against the earth. The second, because the air resists their motion; for if a stone were thrown in a vacuum, and moreover if it were destitute of all gravity, without doubt its motion would never grow languid, but would last forever.

> [^100-s1]: Lib. IV. Phys. text. 69.

[^100-s1]: Bk. IV, Phys., text 69.

> 294 Seposita autèm cùm gravitatis, tùm resistentiae consideratione, projecta non modò moveri debent in aeternum, sed *rectà*, & *aequabiliter* moveantur óportet. Initio enim proculdubiò moventur per lineam rectam [§. 290.], quod si initio, cursus rectilineus est, ob vim *inertiae*, quae facit, ut corpora conservent sibi semper eum statum in quo constituta sunt, projecta corpora perpetuò [p. 101] persistent in eo cursu, neque unquam de semità rectilinea deflectent. Si enim curvam describerent jam mutarent singulis momentis directionem, quod repugnat *inertiae* materiae ob quam non potest sibi ullam determinationem tribuere. Quod autem *aequabiliter* moveri debeant, id fit ex eadem *vi inertiae*, nam ut motus acceleretur, vel retardetur, opus est, novam vim advenire, quae motui illi vel prosit vel officiat, quam tamen nos remotam suppónimus.

294 Setting aside, then, the consideration both of gravity and of resistance, projectiles must not only be moved forever, but must be moved in a straight line and uniformly. For at the beginning they are without doubt moved along a straight line [§. 290.]; and if at the beginning the course is rectilinear, then, because of the force of inertia, which makes bodies always preserve for themselves the state in which they are placed, projected bodies will perpetually persevere [p. 101] in that course, and will never deflect from the rectilinear path. For if they described a curve, they would then be changing their direction at every moment, which conflicts with the inertia of matter, because of which it cannot assign itself any determination. That they must be moved uniformly, moreover, comes from the same force of inertia; for in order that the motion be accelerated or retarded, a new force must come in which either helps or hinders that motion, a force which, however, we suppose removed.

> 295 Adhaec: corpus quàtenùs ex se indifferens est ad motum, & quietem, ut si semel quiescit, in aeternum quiescat, si verò semel positum sit in motu, ut moveatur perpetuò: ergo si semel sit ad motum determinatum, per se solum non redibit ad quietem, aut si quiescit, per se solum ad motum non concitabitur: ergo semel ad motum incitatum nova determinatione indigebit, ut ad quietem revocetur, & è contrariò. Praeterea corpus quod à Deo sphaericum cónditum est, semper sphaericum persevérat, & quod semel quadratum, semper suam figuram tuetur, donec ab aliqua causa haec figura mutetur: ergo similiter corpus quod semel quiescit, semper quiescer.

295 Besides: a body is of itself so indifferent to motion and rest that, if it once rests, it rests forever, but if it has once been placed in motion, it is moved perpetually: therefore, if it has once been determined to motion, it will not return to rest by itself alone; or if it rests, it will not be roused to motion by itself alone: therefore, once incited to motion, it will need a new determination in order to be called back to rest, and conversely. Moreover, a body which was created spherical by God always perseveres spherical, and one that is once square always maintains its figure, until this figure is changed by some cause: therefore likewise a body which once rests will always rest.

> 296 Ex dictis cólliges 1.: corpus intelligi non posse translatum, circa quadratum, pentágonum, aut aliud quodvis polygonum, quin in singulis angulis concipiantur causae occasionales mutatae determinationis ejusmodi corporis. Postquam enim corpus illud descripsit unum latus, per eandem lineam continuatam intelligeretur translatum, nisi foret obex ipsum detorquens per secundum latus; & sic consequenter, sub finem cujusque lateris. Quoniam igitur circulus concipi debet, tanquam polygonum constans lateribus numero indeterminatis, ideò si corpus aliquod circulariter agitetur, cóncipi debent, vel obices perpetui, vel idem continuatus, à quibus determinatio mobilis perpetuò mutetur.

296 From what has been said you will gather, 1.: that a body cannot be understood to be carried around a square, a pentagon, or any other polygon whatever, unless at each angle occasional causes of the changed determination of such a body are conceived. For after that body has described one side, it would be understood to be carried along the same line continued, unless there were an obstacle turning it aside along the second side; and so on consequently at the end of each side. Since, therefore, the circle must be conceived as a polygon consisting of sides indeterminate in number, if some body is moved circularly, there must be conceived either perpetual obstacles, or the same one continued, by which the determination of the movable is perpetually changed.

> 297 Sed ut clariùs intelligatis, circulum cóncipi debére veluti polygonum constantem lateribus infinitis, considerate circuli circunferentiam (& quod de ea dicturi sumus, idem nullo negotio ad reliquas omnes curvas aptari potest), atque in ea intelligite primùm descriptum triangulum, tùm quadratum, postea pentágonum, deinde exágonum denique decágonum omnia tamen regularia.

297 But that you may understand more clearly that the circle must be conceived as a polygon consisting of infinite sides, consider the circumference of a circle (and what we are about to say of it can be applied without any trouble to all the other curves), and understand described in it first a triangle, then a square, afterwards a pentagon, then a hexagon, and finally a decagon, all of them, however, regular.

> 298 Manifestum est omnium jam descriptarum figurarum, triangulum maximè deflectere à circuli ambitu; nam aliquantò plus ad eum accedit quadratum, aliquantò magis pentágonum, adhùc aliquantò magis exágonum, atque multò quidem magis decágonum. Quod si figuram regularem in circulo inscriptam intelligatis ex infinitis, hoc est indeterminatis lateribus constantem, quorum tamen singula sint quàm minima, jam declinatio ejus à circunferentia circuli erit nulla; adeòque circuli, aliarumque curvarum perimetri haberi possunt tanquam figurae rectilineae laterum infinitorum, quorum latera singula sint infinitè parva.

298 It is manifest that of all the figures now described the triangle departs most from the circumference of the circle; for the square comes somewhat nearer to it, the pentagon somewhat more, the hexagon still somewhat more, and the decagon indeed much more. But if you understand a regular figure inscribed in the circle consisting of infinite, that is, indeterminate sides, each of which is nevertheless as small as possible, then its declination from the circumference of the circle will be null; and so the perimeters of the circle and of the other curves can be held as rectilinear figures of infinite sides, each of whose sides is infinitely small.

> 299 Fingite nunc corpus in circuli circunferentia moveri, & [p. 102] jam ipsum re vera movebitur in figura rectilinea infinitorum laterum, quorum singula sunt infinitè parva. Itaque si prima temporis particula corpus describit unum ex istis lateribus, deinceps, omni vi externa sépòsita, moveri aequabiliter debebit, ob vim inertiae, in eodem illo latere ulterius producto, quod latus circulum contingit. Quo circà, si cernimus corpus aliquod revolvi in circuli circunferentia, dicendum est adesse vim aliquam perpetuò agentem in corpus, quae ipsum rétrahit de cursu rectilineo, atque gradatim in reliqua polygoni latera flectit.

299 Imagine now a body moved in the circumference of a circle, and [p. 102] then it will in truth be moved in a rectilinear figure of infinite sides, each of which is infinitely small. Therefore, if in the first particle of time the body describes one of these sides, thereafter, every external force being set aside, it ought, because of the force of inertia, to be moved uniformly along that same side produced further, which side touches the circle. Wherefore, if we see some body revolve in the circumference of a circle, it must be said that there is some force acting perpetually on the body, which draws it back from its rectilinear course and gradually bends it into the remaining sides of the polygon.

> 300 *Vis* haec corporis *recedendi à centro* vocatur *centrifuga*: illa qua corpus centrum petit, *centrípeta*: ambae communi nomine *centrales* adpellantur. Hinc colliges 2. Corpus circulariter motum, & postea sibi relictum, seu remotis obicibus transferendum esse per tangentem circuli, quae sit exiguum latus continuatum; unde deducitur haec regula generalis, quae est totius systématis mundani fundamentum: *Corpus circulariter motum, singulis momentis, nititur à centro sui motus récedere; & quidem eò vehementius, quo vehementius agitatur.* Haec regula confirmatur experientia.

300 This force of a body of receding from the center is called centrifugal; that by which the body seeks the center, centripetal: both are called by the common name central. Hence you will gather 2. that a body moved circularly and afterwards left to itself, or with the obstacles removed, must be carried along the tangent of the circle, which is the small side continued; whence is deduced this general rule, which is the foundation of the whole system of the world: A body moved circularly strives at every moment to recede from the center of its motion; and indeed the more vehemently, the more vehemently it is agitated. This rule is confirmed by experience.

> 301 Si enim lapidem ex. gr. circulariter agitaveris in funda; ubi primum unum fundae funiculum demiseris, elabetur modò sursum, modò deorsum, modò horizontaliter, modò per aliam quamlibet determinationem, pro ut incipit tangens ab ea circunferentiae parte, in qua lapis sibi fuit relictus, & praeterea eò longius excurrit lapis ille, quò vehementius in orbem fuit agitatus. Quod si corpus moveatur in circulo infinito, sive etiam in linea recta, in quam utique migrat circulus infinitus, tunc quia deflèxus tangentis ab ejus circunferentia est nullus ut patet, nullus pariter erit conatus centrifugus, sive vis recendendi á centro.

301 For if you have whirled a stone, e.g., circularly in a sling, as soon as you let go one cord of the sling it will slip away now upward, now downward, now horizontally, now in any other determination, according as the tangent begins from that part of the circumference in which the stone was left to itself; and moreover that stone runs out the farther, the more vehemently it was whirled round. But if a body is moved in an infinite circle, or also in a straight line, into which an infinite circle in any case passes, then, since the deflection of the tangent from its circumference is null, as is plain, there will likewise be no centrifugal conatus, or force of receding from the center.

> 302 Sed *dices*: corpus in aliquo statu semel positum, de se perseverare debet in illo statu, atqui corpus circulariter agitatum, positum fuit in aliquo statu determinato: ergo sibi relictum semper movebitur circulariter. Nego min. Corpus enim, cujus determinatio jugiter mutatur, dici non debet in aliquo statu determinato positum, sed potius dici debet in perpetua mutatione status positum. Porrò determinatio mobilis circulariter agitati, perpetuò mutatur, sicut evidenter adparet, ubi corpus circa polygonum aliquod agitatur.

302 But you will say: a body once placed in some state must of itself persevere in that state; but a body moved circularly was placed in some determinate state: therefore, left to itself, it will always be moved circularly. I deny the minor. For a body whose determination is continually changed should not be said to be placed in some determinate state, but rather should be said to be placed in a perpetual change of state. Now the determination of a movable moved circularly is perpetually changed, as evidently appears when a body is moved around some polygon.

> 303 Instabis: tam determinatio mobilis per lineam circularem, dici debet unicus ejus status, quàm ipsius determinatio per lineam rectam. Nego propositionem: discrimen est, quia initium translationis est linea recta; non autem linea curva. Enimverò initium motus est translatio à puncto ad punctum. Porrò translatio illa fieri potest absque deflectione, adeòque per lineam rectam, sicut fuit probatum.

303 You will insist: the determination of a movable along a circular line should be called its single state just as much as its determination along a straight line. I deny the proposition: the difference is that the beginning of translation is a straight line, but not a curved line. For the beginning of motion is translation from point to point. Now that translation can be made without deflection, and so along a straight line, as was proved.

> 304 Ex dictis sequitur, quod quamvis naturale sit, id est legibus à Deo constitutis consentaneum, ut corpus aliquod translatum, [p. 103] & sibi relictum rectà moveatur, non minus tamen naturale est, corpus idem, linea recta primò translatum, à sua determinatione posteà dimoveri, quoties occurrunt obices ne rectà moveatur. Permanens itaque interturbatio, sive inflectio motus in corpore, qui per lineam circularem movetur, est contra exigentiam naturalem *motus initialis* secundum rectam lineam impressi, secundum quem corpus in unoquoque instanti se movere incipit; at interturbatio, sive inflectio haec, non est contra naturam, quia natura alicujus motus jam incepti non exigit, absolutè non interturbari, sed tantùm non interturbari deficiente obice aliquo qui interturbationem exigat. Sed secundam jam naturae legem proponamus.

304 From what has been said it follows that, although it is natural, that is, consonant with the laws established by God, that some body carried [p. 103] and left to itself be moved in a straight line, it is nevertheless no less natural that the same body, first carried along a straight line, should afterwards be moved away from its determination as often as obstacles occur to prevent its being moved in a straight line. The permanent disturbance, therefore, or inflection of motion in a body which is moved along a circular line, is against the natural requirement of the initial motion impressed along a straight line, according to which the body at each instant begins to move itself; but this disturbance or inflection is not against nature, because the nature of a motion already begun does not require absolutely not to be disturbed, but only not to be disturbed in the absence of some obstacle which requires the disturbance. But let us now propose the second law of nature.

> 305 Secunda lex est: *mutatio motus est semper proportionalis vi motrici impressae, & fit semper secundum rectam lineam, secundum quam vis illa imprimitur.* Quoniam enim à vi motrice generatur motus in corporibus, illud certum est, motum in corpore génitum proportionalem esse ipsi vi motrici, usque adeò, ut si vis aliqua certum motum generet in corpore, dupla vis, duplum, tripla vis, triplum generabit, & generaliter vis una, quae sit ad aliam vim, ut numerus 100 ad 1, generabit motum, qui erit ad motum génitum ab alia vi, ut idem numerus 100 ad 1., sed ut id verum sit postulatur aequalitas temporum. Quod autèm motus fieri debeat per lineam rectam suprà demonstratum jam est.

305 The second law is: the change of motion is always proportional to the motive force impressed, and is always made along the straight line along which that force is impressed. For since motion is generated in bodies by motive force, this is certain, that the motion begotten in a body is proportional to the motive force itself, to such a degree that, if some force generates a certain motion in a body, a double force will generate a double motion, a triple force a triple one; and generally, one force which is to another force as the number 100 to 1 will generate a motion which will be to the motion begotten by the other force as the same number 100 to 1; but for this to be true, equality of the times is postulated. That the motion must be made along a straight line has already been demonstrated above.

> 306 Sequitur regula tertia: *Actioni semper contraria, & aequalis est reactio.* Hoc est, actioni destructae semper contraria & aequalis est resistentia. Ut haec lex intelligatur supponamus equum vim habentem ut 100, trahere lapidem funi adligatum, habentem resistentiam ut 50. Dico: equum non trahere lapidem cùm vi quam habet ut 100, sed cum vi ut 50. Sic intellecta regula, demonstratur: dum enim corpus aliquod in aliud agit, ejus vis eò tendit, ut superet secundi resistentiam. Non itaque vim omnem insúmet corpus agens, sed eam tantum partem, quae requiritur ad superandam[?] resistentiam secundi corporis. Portio vis motricis quam insúmit vocatur *Actio*, & resistentia, quam corpus alterum opponit, dicitur *Reactio.* Actio itaque reactionem habebit contrariam, & aequalem, quae ex lex 3. motus.

306 There follows the third rule: To action reaction is always contrary and equal. That is, to the action destroyed the resistance is always contrary and equal. That this law may be understood, let us suppose a horse having a force as 100 drawing a stone tied to a rope, which has a resistance as 50. I say: the horse does not draw the stone with the force which it has as 100, but with a force as 50. The rule, thus understood, is demonstrated: for while some body acts on another, its force tends to overcome the resistance of the second. The acting body, therefore, will not spend all its force, but only that part which is required for overcoming the resistance of the second body. The portion of the motive force which it spends is called Action, and the resistance which the other body opposes is called Reaction. Action, therefore, will have a contrary and equal reaction, which is the 3rd law of motion.

> 307 Sunt nonnulli qui falsitatem hujus legis indè ostendi posse arbitrantur, quod ea recepta, nullus unquam fieret motus in natura. Moveatur enim corpus A versùs corpus quiescens B. Jam verò si reactio corporis B in A tanta est, quanta est actio ipsius A in B, nullus sequetur motus in B; atqui videmus ipsum moveri; ergo falsum est actioni reactionem aequalem esse & contrariam. Vah putidum sophisma! Enim verò in ejusmodi ratiocinatione nihil est quod improbari non debeat. Isthaec enim naturae lex non vult resistentiam vi *motrici* aequalem esse, & contrariam, sed reactionem *actioni*, quae duo immáne quantùm distant inter se. Vis est omnis ea eficacia quae in corpore datur ad agendum absolutè loquendo. [p. 104] Actio verò est solum ea portiò vis motricis, quam insúmit corpus dum agit. Non ergò semper corpora vim omnem quam habent in effectu producendo insúmunt, sed eam tantùm, quae requiritur ad coaequandam resistentiam corporis in contrarium tendentis; itaque motus fieri utique debet per vim tantam, quantus fuerit excessus actionis supra reactionem, aut resistentiam.

307 There are some who think that the falsity of this law can be shown from this, that, if it were accepted, no motion would ever take place in nature. For let the body A be moved toward the body B at rest. Now, if the reaction of the body B on A is as great as the action of A on B, no motion will follow in B; but we see that it is moved; therefore it is false that reaction is equal and contrary to action. Bah, what a rotten sophism! For in reasoning of this kind there is nothing that ought not to be rejected. For this law of nature does not hold that the resistance is equal and contrary to the motive force, but the reaction to the action, two things which are enormously distant from each other. Force is all the efficacy which there is in a body for acting, speaking absolutely. [p. 104] Action, however, is only that portion of the motive force which the body spends while it acts. Bodies, therefore, do not always spend all the force they have in producing an effect, but only that which is required for equalling the resistance of the body tending in the contrary direction; and so motion must indeed be made through a force as great as the excess of the action over the reaction, or resistance, has been.

> 308 Futilis itaque est objectio. Ut enim duo corpora in se invicèm agentia quiescant, requiritur ne dum, ut *actiones* sint aequales, sed etiam *vires* ab ipsis adhibitae. Tunc nempè quiescent, quum vires aequales habent, & vim omnem ádhibent, quam possident; in hoc enim casu, quum nihil iis supersit virium, & hae ponantur aequales, se mutuò destruent, & nullus orietur motus. Ita si equus trahere velit pondus aequale vi integrae, quam ipse possidet, hic profectò conabitur integra sua vi pondus transferre; quum tamen hoc sit aequale vi equi, eam destruet, & nullus orietur motus. Si verò pondus minus fuerit equi vi, tunc eam tantùm partem vis propriae adhibebit, quae superandam ponderis resistentiam adaequet, atque ita quum adhùc ipsi supersit portio vis, secum deferet pondus.

308 The objection, therefore, is futile. For in order that two bodies acting on each other should rest, it is required not only that the actions be equal, but also the forces applied by them. They will rest, namely, when they have equal forces and apply all the force they possess; for in this case, since nothing of their forces remains to them, and these are supposed equal, they will destroy each other mutually, and no motion will arise. Thus, if a horse wishes to draw a weight equal to the whole force which it possesses, it will certainly strive to move the weight with its whole force; but since this weight is equal to the force of the horse, it will destroy that force, and no motion will arise. But if the weight is less than the horse’s force, then it will apply only that part of its own force which equals the resistance of the weight to be overcome, and thus, since a portion of force still remains to it, it will carry the weight along with it.

> 309 Non incongruum erit hìc animadvertere, quoniam pluribus in locis *elasticitatis* nomen usurpabimus, quod *motus elastici* nomine innuimus eum, quo corpora tensa, compressa, flexa, sublata potentia tendente, comprimente, flectente in priorem figuram & situm restituuntur. Vim hanc sese in nativum statum reducendi: *Elasticitatis*, *virtutis elasticae*, *elaterii* nuncupatione donamus, quae restitutio si perficiatur eádem vi, qua corpus á suo statu dimotum fuit, elasticitas dicitur *perfecta*, secùs, *imperfecta* vocatur.

309 It will not be out of place to note here, since we shall use the name of elasticity in many places, that by the name of elastic motion we mean that by which bodies stretched, compressed or bent are restored to their former figure and situation once the power stretching, compressing or bending them is removed. This force of bringing itself back to its native state we honor with the name of Elasticity, elastic virtue, or elater; and if this restitution is accomplished with the same force by which the body was moved from its state, the elasticity is called perfect; otherwise it is called imperfect.

> CAPUT IV.

CHAPTER IV.

> De Motuum legibus, quae in corporum collisione locum habent.

On the Laws of Motions which have place in the collision of bodies.

> 310 Postquàm ad naturae phaenomena exquirenda seriò Physici animum adverterunt, illicò deprehensum est eam certo itinere, certisque semper legibus prógredi: praecipuè autem naturae constantia adparuit in collisione corporum, utpotè quae perpetuis quibusdam legibus perágitur. Harum legum notitiam, quum ad naturae occultissima arcana pervestiganda adprimè utilem censuisset *Renatus Cartesius*, non mediocre studium in iis perquirendis collocavit. ¡Atque utinam veriores nobis leges ipse dedisset! Stabilioribus enim fundamentis [p. 105] superextruxisset aedificium, quod partìm nutare, partìm corruere, non sine aliquo nominis sui detrimento vidimus. Ejus exemplo admóniti veriora addúcere studebimus.

s soon as Physicists seriously turned their minds to investigating the 310 A phenomena of nature, it was at once discovered that nature proceeds by a certain path and always by certain laws; but the constancy of nature appeared chiefly in the collision of bodies, inasmuch as this is carried on by certain perpetual laws. Since René Descartes had judged the knowledge of these laws exceedingly useful for tracking down the most hidden secrets of nature, he spent no mediocre study in searching them out. And would that he had given us truer laws! For he would have raised on more stable foundations the edifice [p. 105] which we have seen partly totter, partly collapse, not without some detriment to his name. Warned by his example, we shall strive to bring forward truer ones.

> 311 Corpus unum ubi in aliud incurrit, motum huic in collisione impertit: id ipsum quibusdam legibus à natura perficitur, queis *Dynámicae* principia continentur. Advertendum verò collisionem duorum corporum triplici modo fieri posse. *Primò*: si unum in alterum prorsùs immotum incurrat. *Secundò*: si in eandem partem ferantur, sed inaequali velocitate sic, ut illud quod celeriùs movetur, motu suo alterum adsequatur, aut impellat. *Tertiò*: si ex oppositis partibus sibi mutuò occurrant. Jam quum alia sit motuum ratio in corporibus non elásticis, seu inertibus (quo nomine, & perfectè dura, & perfectè mollia comprehenduntur), alia in elasticis, leges utriusque generis in collisione animadversas próponemus. Ac de primis quidem pro triplici casu tres totidem Propositionibus á Nolleto [^105-s1] expressas damus.

311 When one body runs into another, it imparts motion to it in the collision: nature accomplishes this by certain laws, in which the principles of Dynamics are contained. It must be noted, however, that the collision of two bodies can take place in three ways. First: if one runs into the other entirely at rest. Second: if they are carried toward the same part, but with unequal velocity, such that the one which is moved faster overtakes the other with its motion, or impels it. Third: if they meet each other from opposite parts. Now since the ratio of motions is one in non-elastic, or inert, bodies (under which name both perfectly hard and perfectly soft bodies are comprehended), and another in elastic ones, we shall propose the laws of each kind observed in collision. And of the first, indeed, for the threefold case, we give three laws expressed in as many Propositions by Nollet (b).

> [^105-s1]: Leçons de Physique T. 1. Leç. IV. Sect. III.

[^105-s1]: Leçons de Physique, vol. 1, Leç. IV, sect. III.

> Leges motus in collisione corporum elaterii expertium.

LAWS OF MOTION IN THE COLLISION OF BODIES DEVOID OF ELASTICITY.

> Pro primo casu.

FOR THE FIRST CASE .

> 312 *Si corpus quiescens impellitur ab alio, celeritas impingentis dispescitur inter utrumque pro ratione massarum.*

312 If a body at rest is impelled by another, the celerity of the impinging body is divided between both in proportion to the masses.

> 313 Nempè quoniam corpus impellens quiescenti motum impertit ex eo unicè, ut impedimentum sui motus amoliatur: hoc verò ut fiat, necessum sit duntaxat, pro ratione massae utriusque vim dispertiri; si enim intelligantur corpora junctim sumpta in partes aequales, motus item totus in aequales totidem partes divisus, & aequalibus utriusque corporis partibus aequales motus partes tribuantur, patebit hoc pacto fieri, ut partes aequales duorum corporum aequali virium quantitate donatae, eandem directionem, aequali celeritate sint sequuturae, quin aliae aliis motus impedimentùm efficiant. Proinde, si corpus íncurrat in alterum quiescens, & sibi aequale in massa, dimidium velocitatis suae eidem communicabit: si subdúplum fuerit, duas tertias; si duplum, unam tertiam celeritatis partem largítur.

313 Namely, since the impelling body imparts motion to the one at rest solely in order to remove the impediment to its own motion, and since for this to happen it is necessary only to share out the force in proportion to the mass of each — for if the bodies taken together are understood to be divided into equal parts, and the whole motion likewise into as many equal parts, and equal parts of motion are assigned to equal parts of each body, it will be plain that in this way it comes about that equal parts of the two bodies, endowed with an equal quantity of forces, will follow the same direction with equal celerity, without some being an impediment to the motion of others — accordingly, if a body runs into another at rest and equal to it in mass, it will communicate to it half of its velocity; if the other is half as large, two thirds; if double, it bestows on it one third part of its celerity.

## Pro secundo casu. — FOR THE SECOND CASE.

> 314 *Si duo corpora eandem in partem inaequali celeritate ferantur, seu massae sint aequales, seu inaequales, collisione peracta, continuant motum, secundum directionem eandem, celeritate* [p. 106] *communi, quae tamen minor est, atque celeritas impellentis; major autem, quàm corporis impulsi ante impactionem fuerit.*

314 If two bodies are carried toward the same part with unequal celerity, whether their masses are equal or unequal, when the collision is completed they continue their motion along the same direction with a common celerity [p. 106] which, however, is less than the celerity of the impelling body, but greater than that of the impelled body was before the impact.

> 315 Etenim si aequali prorsùs celeritate ferrentur, in eandem partem, atque adeò eandem inter se distantiam haberent, comparatè ad invicem duo corpora, velut quiescentia spectari deberent. Quum itaque celeritatibus inaequalibus ferri ponantur, non secùs haec corpora sese habent, ac si velociùs motum vi celeritatis respectivae, qua excedit alterum, in hoc prorsùs immotum tenderet. Quare idem, quod priori casu, cónsequi necesse est.

315 For if they were carried toward the same part with exactly equal celerity, and so had the same distance between them, the two bodies, compared with each other, would have to be regarded as if at rest. Since, therefore, they are supposed to be carried with unequal celerities, these bodies behave no otherwise than if the one moved faster tended, by the force of the respective celerity by which it exceeds the other, into this one as entirely at rest. Wherefore the same must follow as in the former case.

## Pro tertio casu. — FOR THE THIRD CASE

> 316 *Si duo corpora motu contrario sibi occurrant, motus, aut in utroque aut in uno, ad minimum extinguitur. Si post collisionem pars quaedam motus superstes fuerit, movebitur utrumque in eandem partem, secundum directionem illius, quod majori vi praeditum est, ita ut quantitas motus illis communis, sit aequalis excessui alterutrius ante collisionem.*

316 If two bodies with contrary motion meet each other, the motion is extinguished either in both or at least in one. If after the collision some part of the motion has survived, each will be moved toward the same part, according to the direction of the one which was endowed with the greater force, such that the quantity of motion common to them is equal to the excess of the one over the other before the collision.

> 317 Nimirum si quantitates motus ante collisionem aequentur, quoniam ex diametro eae sibi adversantur, fiet, ut in ictu sese périmant. Eandem hanc regulam P. Regnault in mollibus duntaxat corporibus, at non in duris obtinére arbitràtur, eo quod haec videantur reflecti debere post ictum perindè, atque elastica, quum nulla partium compressio efficiatur. [^106-s1] Verum in utriusque generis corporibus id fieri cum Clariss. â Brixia putamus; [^106-s2] quamvis enim, si corpus perfectè durum in aliud simile prorsùs immotum incurrat, illud post impactum resiliat, ut supra diximus, multò tamen aliud est, quod hìc evenit; planum etenim durum, & immobile solummodo impedit, ne incurrens motum sua directione persequatur, efficitque[?], ut incidentis corporis directio in ictu mutetur; minimè verò impetus quidpiam per contrariam vim in eo extinguit: quemadmodum accidit, quum duo corpora sibi ex adverso occurrentia colliduntur. Si vires ante collisionem inaequales fuerint, earum partes aequales, quia opponuntur invicem, sese destruunt in collisione: idque circo corpus, quod validiùs est, excessu virium suarum in alterum tanquam immotum aget, ac proindè (*per Legem primi casus*) aequâ celeritate progredientur.

317 Namely, if the quantities of motion before the collision are equal, since they are diametrically opposed to each other, it will come about that in the impact they destroy each other. Hence Fr. Regnault thinks that this same rule holds only in soft bodies, but not in hard ones, because these seem to have to be reflected after the impact just like elastic ones, since no compression of the parts is effected. (c) But with the most illustrious Fortunato da Brescia we think that this happens in bodies of both kinds; (d) for although, if a perfectly hard body runs into another similar one entirely at rest, it rebounds after the impact, as we said above, what happens here is yet a very different thing; for a hard and immovable plane only prevents the incurring body from pursuing its motion in its own direction, and brings it about that the direction of the incident body is changed in the impact; but it by no means extinguishes any impetus in it by a contrary force, as happens when two bodies meeting each other from opposite sides collide. If the forces before the collision were unequal, their equal parts, since they are opposed to each other, destroy each other in the collision: and therefore the body which is the stronger will act with the excess of its forces on the other as on one at rest, and accordingly (by the Law of the first case) they will proceed with equal celerity.

> [^106-s1]: Entret. Phys. Tom. I. X. Entret. IV. Regle. & XII. Entret. IV. Regle.

[^106-s1]: Entret. Phys., vol. I, Entret. X, Rule IV, & Entret. XII, Rule IV.

> [^106-s2]: Phys. Gen. P. 1. §. 432.
