## CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

> De Principiis sive Legibus fundamentalibus, & Instrumentis Staticae.

On the Principles, or fundamental Laws, and the Instruments of Statics.

> 357 Exponenda veniunt amplissimi quidem usus, Statices principia, sive Leges, è quibus corporum gravium adpensorum diversa inter se ratio derivatur. Princeps porrò illud, & ad *Geostaticam* juxtà atque *Hydrostaticam* pertinens fundamentum, videlicet: *quantitatem motus dati corporis esse productum ex pondere, sive massa in velocitatem ducta*, jam alias expendimus [§ 276]. Id unum superst, ut eo constituto, evolamus cetera, quae huic seu basi innituntur, & paucis complectamur omnia: eò duntaxat respicientes, ut ad intelligentiam Tironum adcommodatè, & pro Elementorum nostrorum ratione ac brevitate doctrinae summa potissimum capita pertractemus. Sint ergo per ordinem.

ext to be set forth are the principles, or Laws, of Statics, of very 357 N wide use indeed, from which is derived the diverse relation among themselves of heavy bodies hung up. The chief of them, moreover, and the foundation pertaining to Geostatics as well as to Hydrostatics, namely: that the quantity of motion of a given body is the product of the weight, or mass, multiplied into the velocity, we have already weighed elsewhere [§ 276]. One thing alone remains: that, this being established, we unfold the rest, which rest upon it as on a base, and embrace them all in few words, looking only to this, that we treat chiefly the principal heads of the doctrine, in a manner suited to the understanding of Beginners and in keeping with the plan and brevity of our Elements. Let them follow, then, in order.

## Principium Statices I. — PRINCIPLE OF STATICS I

> 358 *Celeritates duorum gravium solidorum, ex ejusdem jugi extremis liberè pendentium, sunt directè inter se, ut eorum distantiae à centro motus.*

358 The velocities of two heavy solid bodies hanging freely from the extremities of the same beam are directly to each other as their distances from the center of motion.

> 359 In comperto quippe est corpus B (Fig. XXIX) moveri per arcum B D non posse, quin eodem ipso tempore corpus A deprimatur per arcum A C. Atqui celeritates duorum corporum motu[?] concitatorum, sunt inter se, ut spatia eodem tempore ab illis percursa. [*Per Leges velocitatum*]: Celeritas igitur corporis A est ad celeritatem corporis B, ut arcus A C ad arcum B D. Arcus autèm prior se habet ad posteriorem, ut distantia A E ad distantiam B E, sive ut radii circulorum, ut notum est ex Geometria: ergo velocitas corporis A est ad velocitatem corporis B, ut A E ad B E, hoc est: ut eorumdem distantiae à centro motus E.

359 For it is well established that body B (Fig. XXIX.) cannot be moved along the arc BD without body A being depressed at the very same time along the arc AC. But the velocities of two bodies set in motion are to each other as the spaces traversed by them in the same time [By the Laws of velocities]: therefore the velocity of body A is to the velocity of body B as the arc AC to the arc BD. But the former arc is to the latter as the distance AE to the distance BE, or as the radii of the circles, as is known from Geometry: therefore the velocity of body A is to the velocity of body B as AE to BE, that is, as their distances from the center of motion E.

## Principium Statices II. — PRINCIPLE OF STATICS II

> 360 *Corpora gravia, quorum pondera aequantur, & ad aequalem distantiam collocantur adpensa, respectivè ad centrum motus; in aequilibrio manent. Si pondera sint inaequalia, & distantiae aequales, non manent in aequilibrio, sed quod pondere majori* [p. 118] *donatum est, deprimetur. Si pondera sint aequalia, & distantiae inaequales, non consistunt aequilibrata, verùm quod à centro motus removetur magis, praeponderat.*

360 Heavy bodies whose weights are equal, and which are placed, hung up, at an equal distance with respect to the center of motion, remain in equilibrium. If the weights are unequal and the distances equal, they do not remain in equilibrium, but the one that is endowed with the greater weight [p. 118] will be depressed. If the weights are equal and the distances unequal, they do not stand balanced, but the one that is removed further from the center of motion preponderates.

> 361 Pars prima patet: quoniam corpora pondere aequalia ponuntur, & aequalis á centro motus distantia habetur, atque adeò aequalis utriusque celeritas (quum enim per Princip. I. celeritates sint, ut distantiae, si haec aequentur, etiam celeritates aequales sint est necesse) iccircò aequalis in utroque est motus quantitas, sive momenta sunt aequalia: immota proindè in aequilibrio consistent (*per Def. aequilib.*) Pars altera ostenditur: quum distantiae corporum ponuntur aequales, aequales itidèm sunt celeritates. Ergo momenta eorum sunt, ut pondera (nam quum pondera corporum sint, ut eorum massae, quantitates autèm motus duorum corporum, aequali celeritate actorum sint ut eorumdem massae; erunt quoque ut pondera ipsorum). Qua propter momentum illius, quod pondere majus est, excedet momentum alterius; & aequilibrio sublato, praeponderabit. Pars tertia quoque claret: quoniam distantia corporis unius major est distantia alterius; celeritas pariter illius, major erit celeritate hujus: Sunt autem corpora pondere aequalia. Majus ergo erit momentum corporis remotioris á centro motus; ac momentum alterius: aequilibrata proindè non persistent, verùm illud, quod removetur magis, magis quoque praeponderabit.

361 The first part is evident: since bodies equal in weight are posited, and an equal distance from the center of motion is had, and so an equal velocity of each (for since, by Princip. I, the velocities are as the distances, if these are equal the velocities too must be equal), therefore the quantity of motion in both is equal, or the momenta are equal: they will therefore stand unmoved in equilibrium (by the Def. of equilib.). The second part is shown: since the distances of the bodies are posited equal, the velocities are likewise equal. Therefore their momenta are as the weights (for since the weights of bodies are as their masses, and the quantities of motion of two bodies driven with equal velocity are as their masses, they will also be as their weights). Wherefore the momentum of the one that is greater in weight will exceed the momentum of the other; and, the equilibrium being removed, it will preponderate. The third part too is clear: since the distance of one body is greater than the distance of the other, the velocity of the former will likewise be greater than the velocity of the latter. But the bodies are equal in weight. Therefore the momentum of the body more remote from the center of motion will be greater than the momentum of the other: they will therefore not persist balanced, but the one that is removed further will also preponderate more.

## Principium Statices III. — PRINCIPLE OF STATICS III

> 362 *Corpora inaequalis ponderis, ex inaequalibus distantiis jugo adpensa, obtinent aequilibrium, si distantiae à centro motus fuerint, ut ipsa pondera reciprocè hoc est: si quod minori pondere donatum est, tantò magis distet à centro motus, quantò magis ponderosum est alterum (quo cum comparatur) minusque distat ab eodem centro.*

362 Bodies of unequal weight, hung on a beam at unequal distances, obtain equilibrium if the distances from the center of motion are reciprocally as the weights themselves, that is: if the one that is endowed with the smaller weight is as much farther from the center of motion as the other (with which it is compared) is heavier and less distant from the same center.

> 363 Sit enim corpus A (Fig. cit.) duplò majoris massae quàm B, sintque hoc pacto adpensa, ut distantia A E sit ad distantiam E B, sicut corpus B ad A, id est: corpus B duplo sit minus altero, sed duplo remotiùs á puncto fixo E absistat: manifestò liquet A, & B in aequilibrio consistere, si quantitas motus in uno aequetur quantitati motus in altero, hoc est: si momenta sint aequalia. Atqui haec aequantur, eo ipso quod eorum distantiae á centro motûs sint in ratione ponderum reciprocâ; quum enim celeritates ponderum A & B sint directè inter se, ut eorumdem distantiae A E, & B E, celeritas corporis B, duplò major est celeritate corporis A. Dicatur illa = 2c haec = c: massa corporis A = 2m, corporis B = m. Ut reciproca indè haec necessariò obtineat proportio 2c : c = 2m : m, quoniam igitur momentum corporis B aequatur facto, quod ex dupla celeritate in simplicem massam ducta [p. 119] consurgit; erit illud = 2c m. Momentum verò corporis A est productum ex multiplicata duplò majore massa per simplicem celeritatem, hoc est: = 2m c. quod evidenter idem est. In aequilibrio igitur corpora perstabunt. Ex his principiis ratio instrumentorum ponderatoriorum, seu Staticorum desumpta est: horum praecipua habentur *Libra*, & *Statéra*.

363 For let body A (Fig. cit.) be of twice greater mass than B, and let them be so hung that the distance AE is to the distance EB as body B to A, that is: let body B be twice smaller than the other, but stand twice as far removed from the fixed point E: it is manifestly clear that A and B stand in equilibrium if the quantity of motion in the one equals the quantity of motion in the other, that is: if the momenta are equal. But these are equal by the very fact that their distances from the center of motion are in the reciprocal ratio of the weights; for since the velocities of the weights A and B are directly to each other as their distances AE and BE, the velocity of body B is twice as great as the velocity of body A. Let the former be called = 2c, the latter = c; the mass of body A = 2m, of body B = m. So that hence this reciprocal proportion necessarily holds, 2c : c = 2m : m; since, therefore, the momentum of body B equals the product that arises from the double velocity multiplied into the simple mass, [p. 119] it will be = 2cm. But the momentum of body A is the product of the mass twice as great multiplied by the simple velocity, that is: = 2mc, which is evidently the same. The bodies will therefore stand in equilibrium. From these principles is taken the rationale of weighing instruments, or Statical ones: the chief of them are held to be the Balance and the Steelyard.

## De Libra. — ON THE BALANCE

> 364 *Libra* seu *bilanx*, notissimum est Staticae instrumentum, quo ignotum dati corporis pondus, altero notae gravitatis adsumpto exploratur. Partes in ea plures distinguuntur. Prima est *jugum* A C (Fig. XXX.) rigida nempè virga, in duas partes A B & C B tum quoad longitudinem, tum quoad pondus, aequales, quae *brachia* dicuntur, divisa. Secunda est *ansa* D B, cui ope axiculi per centrum motûs B, & per foramina ansae transmissi, sic aptatur jugum, ut hoc circa ansae foramina tanquam centrum, liberè moveri possit. Tertia est *lingula* x, quae immobiliter ad angulos rectos medio jugi puncto adplicita est: nuncupatur quoque *trutina, examen, vel argumentum librae* eo, quod jugi vel parallelismum cum plano horizontali, vel inclinationem exhibeat. Quarta sunt lances E & F, quae extremis jugi partibus adpensae, pondera excipiunt.

364 The balance, or scales, is the best-known instrument of Statics, by which the unknown weight of a given body is explored by taking another of known gravity. Several parts are distinguished in it. The first is the beam AC (Fig. XXX.), namely a rigid rod divided into two parts AB and CB, equal both in length and in weight, which are called the arms. The second is the handle DB, to which the beam is so fitted, by means of a small axle passed through the center of motion B and through the holes of the handle, that it can move freely about the holes of the handle as about a center. The third is the tongue x, which is fixed immovably at right angles to the middle point of the beam: it is also called the trutina, examen, or argumentum of the balance, because it shows either the parallelism of the beam with the horizontal plane or its inclination. The fourth are the pans E and F, which, hung from the extreme parts of the beam, receive the weights.

> 365 Totum hoc organum Staticum, ut exactum sit *primò* non brachia solum, sed fila etiam, è quibus hae suspenduntur, pondere aequentur necesse est. *Secundò* lances quoque aequalis sint ponderis, exposcitur. *Tertio* adtritus super jugo, quoad fieri potest, sit exiguus ac propè nullus. Hinc ad minuendum adfrictum, axis trutinae insertus, cylindricus, & forámen in trutina rotundum sit, ut contactus minor evadat. Imò si axis ea parte, qua trutinam tangit[?], in aciem définat, motus jugi pernicior erit. Ad bilancis praeterea perfectionem haec fere pertinent. Brachia sint longiora; ponderum quippe inaequalitas, quae in brevioribus nonnumquam sensu vix discriminatur, in longioribus perfacilè se prodit. Língula pariter longior ob rationem haud absimilem fiat. Lances melius suspenduntur è catenulis metallicis, ac filis, utpote in quae aëris temperies quandoque diversimodè agit.

365 For this whole Statical organ to be exact, it is necessary, first, that not only the arms but also the threads from which the pans are suspended be equal in weight. Secondly, it is required that the pans too be of equal weight. Thirdly, that the friction upon the beam be, as far as can be done, slight and almost none. Hence, to lessen the friction, the axle inserted in the tongue is made cylindrical, and the hole in the tongue round, so that the contact may turn out smaller. Indeed, if the axle ends in an edge on the side where it touches the tongue, the motion of the beam will be quicker. Moreover, the following belong in general to the perfection of the balance. Let the arms be longer; for an inequality of the weights, which in shorter arms is sometimes scarcely discerned by sense, betrays itself very easily in longer ones. Let the tongue likewise be made longer, for a not dissimilar reason. The pans are better suspended from little metal chains than from threads, inasmuch as the temper of the air sometimes acts upon threads in various ways.

> 366 Quod ad praestantiorem adtinet usum ceteris praeferenda est libra, cujus centrum motus sit supra rectam, ex cujus extremis libranda corpora pendent: undè ceteris paribus postulant omnes, ut centrum gravitatis jugi detur paululum infra centrum motus. Usus librae notissimus est, de quo proindè nihil adtinet meminisse. Vitium in libram refundit potissimùm brachiorum inaequalitas; posita enim eorum inaequalitate, non ejusdem, sed inaequalis ponderis erunt corpora, quae lancibus imposita aequilibrantur, uti [p. 120] (é Princip. III.) elúcet. Fraus haec (quin, & omnes) in dolosis libris deteguntur, facta ponderum in lancibus permutatione, docente P. Schotto: *si enim (inquit) illud quod prius aequilibre erat in dextera lance adhuc in sinistra lance positum, servet aequilibrium; signum est libram exactam esse. Quod si contingat, ut ex hac lancium permutatione eadem corpora nunc quidem aequalia, nunc verò inaequalia adpareant; manifestum est, libram dolosam esse, & injustam.* [^120-s1]

366 As regards the more excellent use, that balance is to be preferred to the others whose center of motion is above the straight line from whose extremities the bodies to be weighed hang: whence, other things being equal, all require that the center of gravity of the beam be placed a little below the center of motion. The use of the balance is very well known, so that there is no need to mention anything about it. A defect is brought into the balance chiefly by the inequality of the arms; for, their inequality being posited, the bodies which, placed on the pans, are in equilibrium will be not of the same but of unequal weight, as [p. 120] (from Princip. III.) is clear. This fraud (indeed, every fraud) in deceitful balances is detected by making an exchange of the weights in the pans, as Father Schott teaches: for if (he says) that which was before in equilibrium in the right pan, when now placed in the left pan, preserves the equilibrium, it is a sign that the balance is exact. But if it happens that by this exchange of the pans the same bodies appear now equal, now unequal, it is manifest that the balance is deceitful and unjust. (o)

> [^120-s1]: Mag. Universal. P. 3. Mag. Stat. Syntagm. 3. Prag. 3. sub finem.

[^120-s1]: Magia universalis, pt. 3, Mag. Stat., Syntagm. 3, Pragm. 3, toward the end.

## De Statéra. — ON THE STEELYARD

> 367 *Statéra*, *Stater Romanus*, aut *Sinensis*, est instrumentum ponderatorium brachiis inaequalibus comprehensum (Fig. XXXI.). Quatuor in eo partes numerantur, nimirùm *virga rigida*, sive *jugum* A B, in *brachia* inaequalia B D & A D divisum, ex quibus illud, quod longius est B D, in partes inter se aequales a b, b d, d e, &c. & quae singulae distantiam puncti D, á puncto A, seu longitudinem brachii minoris adaequent, dividitur. Partes hae rursùm in alias minores inter se aequales, pro minutiis determinandis dispescuntur. *Ansa* E D *lingulam* complexa, cui ope *axis* quemadmodum in libra aptatum est *jugum*. *Lanx*, vel *uncus* extremo brachii brevioris adpenditur, ut librandum corpus illi imponi, vel ex hoc suspendi possit. *Aequipondium* N est hùc illùc mobile, propterea *cursor* statérae dictus.

367 The steelyard, the Roman or Chinese Stater, is a weighing instrument comprised of unequal arms (Fig. XXXI.). Four parts are counted in it: namely the rigid rod, or beam, AB, divided into the unequal arms BD and AD, of which the longer, BD, is divided into parts equal among themselves, ab, bd, de, etc., each of which equals the distance of the point D from the point A, or the length of the shorter arm. These parts are divided again into other smaller parts, equal among themselves, for determining minute quantities. The handle ED, enclosing the tongue, to which the beam is fitted by means of an axle, as in the balance. The pan, or hook, is hung from the extremity of the shorter arm, so that the body to be weighed can be placed on it or suspended from it. The counterpoise N is movable hither and thither, and is therefore called the runner of the steelyard.

> 368 Quò instrumentum hoc exactum sit exposcitur, ut brevius brachium unà cum unco adaequet pondus brachii longioris ablato aequipondio: aut si id non fiat, brachium longiùs in partes proportionales dividatur, quae divisio tentando invenitur. Id commodi habent Staterae prae libra, quod pondus magnorum etiam corporum unico eoque satis exiguo pondere per eas explorari queat; quanquam in[?] eo praestent bilances, quòd in his exiguas etiam unciae particulas cognoscere possímus, & commodiùs, & in regionibus nostris plerumque soleamus, secus in statéris. Hac verò lege pondus dati corporis instrumento hoc examinatur: adpenso corpore M, cujus pondus exploratur; aequipondium N eo in loco brachii longioris constituitur, in quo cum librando corpore aequilibrium obtineat; aequilibrio jam posito, corpus adpensum, eam habet rationem ad aequipondium, quàm reciprocè distantia aequipondii á centro motus, ad distantiam corporis adpensi ab eodem, seu ad brachium brevius: scilicet si aequipondium N unius sit librae & distantia ejus D m ad distantiam D A ut 4 ad 1 erit corpus M quatuor librarum.

368 For this instrument to be exact it is required that the shorter arm, together with the hook, equal the weight of the longer arm when the counterpoise is removed: or, if that is not done, that the longer arm be divided into proportional parts, a division that is found by trial. Steelyards have this advantage over the balance, that the weight even of large bodies can be explored by means of them with a single weight, and that a fairly small one; although in this the scales excel, that in them we can discern even small particles of an ounce, and more conveniently, and in our regions we usually do so; not so with steelyards. The weight of a given body is examined with this instrument by the following law: the body M, whose weight is being explored, being hung on, the counterpoise N is set at that place of the longer arm at which it obtains equilibrium with the body to be weighed; equilibrium being now established, the hung body has the same ratio to the counterpoise that, reciprocally, the distance of the counterpoise from the center of motion has to the distance of the hung body from the same, or to the shorter arm: namely, if the counterpoise N is of one pound, and its distance Dm is to the distance DA as 4 to 1, the body M will be of four pounds.

> 369 Ratio hujus liquet adfatim (ex Princip. III. Stat.) Quod [p. 121] si porrò momentum in puncto m augeatur, ut si ea vis constitueretur, quae pondus centenarii exsuperaret, adtolleretur ab eo pondus quatuor centenariorum ex unco F suspensum: si momentum in remotiori parte collocaretur, faciliùs adhùc corpus adpensum extolleretur. Atque hìnc, quoniam potentia ad brachium staterae longius adplicata, eò vi majori pollet, quò longius illud porrigitur, patet, vires hoc pacto in immensum augeri posse: ut ea propter Syracusanus Mathematicus Archimedes, Hieroni, non citra fundamentum Staticae legibus constabilitum, pollicitus fuerit, se tellurem loco suo emoturum, si quis extra eam locus ad consistendum esset.

369 The reason of this is abundantly clear (from Princip. III of Statics). But if [p. 121] if, further, the momentum at the point m is increased, so that, if that force were made such as to exceed the weight of a hundredweight, a weight of four hundredweight suspended from the hook F would be lifted by it: if the momentum were placed in a more remote part, the hung body would be raised more easily still. And hence, since a power applied to the arm of the steelyard is endowed with so much greater force the farther that arm is stretched out, it is plain that forces can in this way be increased without limit: so that for this reason the Syracusan Mathematician Archimedes, not without a foundation established by the laws of Statics, promised Hiero that he would move the earth from its place, if there were some place outside it on which to stand.

> 370 Ceterum plura in stateram vitia irrepere queunt; si enim brachium breviùs cum unco vel lance acceptum, aequilibrium non tueatur cum altero brachio, sublato aequipondio: item si partes, in quas longius brachium dirimitur, sint inaequales, aut debitâ careant dimensione, dolosa semper statera futura est: quin aliis quoque ex capitibus fállere utentes quum possit, nec adeò in promptu sit fallaciam détegere, praestare ait Cl. Wolfius [^121-s1] ut è vita communi proscribatur.

370 Moreover, several defects can creep into the steelyard; for if the shorter arm, taken with the hook or pan, does not keep equilibrium with the other arm when the counterpoise is removed; likewise if the parts into which the longer arm is divided are unequal, or lack the due measure, the steelyard will always be deceitful: indeed, since it can deceive those who use it on other heads as well, and it is not so easy to detect the deceit, the distinguished Wolff says (p) it is better that it be banished from common life.

> [^121-s1]: Elem. Mechan. §. 778.

[^121-s1]: Elem. Mechan., §. 778.

## DISSERTATIO III. — DISSERTATION III

> MECHANICA, sive

MECHANICS, or

> De Machinis doctrina.

The doctrine of Machines.

> 371 *Mechanica*, seu *Machinalis scientia* tradit principia, ac leges, quibus potentia sustinendo, ac movendo corpori ex sese impar, machinarum quarundam adminiculo idonea sive ad sustinendum, sive ad movendum etiam illud reddi possit. Undè *machina mechanica* adpellatur, per quam potentia illi adplicata ad sustinendum vel movendum corpus, quorum neutrum praestare illa possit, apta redditur. Machina alia *simplex* dicitur, alia *composita*. Prior ex pluribus, quarum singulae seorsim ad edendum effectum sufficerent, non coalescit: posterior ex aliis simplicibus certa lege invicem aptatis consurgit.

echanics, or the Machinal science, hands down the principles and laws by 371 M which a power, of itself unequal to sustaining and moving a body, can be rendered fit by the aid of certain machines either to sustain it or even to move it. Whence a mechanical machine is the name for that through which a power applied to it is rendered fit for sustaining or moving a body, neither of which it could accomplish. One machine is called simple, another compound. The former does not coalesce out of several, each of which would separately suffice to produce the effect: the latter arises out of other simple ones fitted to each other by a fixed law.

> 372 Hoc jam loco unicum Machinalis scientiae principium, generale illud quidem, subjiciendum venit, quo uno plura ab aliis isthic constituta, libuit complecti.

372 In this place there now comes to be set down the single principle of the Machinal science, a general one indeed, by which alone it has pleased us to embrace the several principles that others have established here.

[p. 122]

## Principium Mechanices. — PRINCIPLE OF MECHANICS

> 373 *Potentia, & pondus ita machinae adplicentur necesse est, ut simul moveri nequeant, nisi potentia velocius moveatur, quàm pondus: & hac quidem lege, ut celeritas potentiae majorem habeat rationem ad celeritatem ponderis, quàm reciprocè pondus ipsum ad vim potentiae: quae ratio, quò major fuerit, eò facilius potentia exigua corpus ingens dimovebit.*

373 Power and weight must be so applied to a machine that they cannot be moved together unless the power moves more swiftly than the weight: and indeed under this law, that the velocity of the power have a greater ratio to the velocity of the weight than, reciprocally, the weight itself has to the force of the power: and the greater this ratio is, the more easily will a slight power move a huge body.

> 374 Ponatur enim vis potentiae = p & pondus movendum = P celeritas potentiae = C, & celeritas ponderis = c. Si celeritas potentiae majorem habeat rationem ad celeritatem ponderis, quàm reciprocè pondus ad vim potentiae, erit C : c > P : p factum proindè seu momentum potentiae p C, majus, quàm momentum ponderis resistentis P c. Corpus igitur ponderosum a potentia movebitur. Quum porrò productum p C eò majus evadat, quò magis ratio C c excedit rationem P : p consequitur, eò facilius ab exigua etiam potentia, ope machinae, corpus ingens moveri posse, quò ratio celeritatis, quâ potentia pollet, ad celeritatem ponderis major fuerit ratione, quae reciprocè pondus inter, & vim potentiae intercedit. Ex quo quidem elucet actutùm, hoc per machinas pondera levandi compendium cum aliquo temporis dispendio conjunctum esse, quod tamen jure in lucris reponi debet. Hoc constituto, machinas, prout ad Physicae rationem necesse est, tantispèr expendamus.

374 For let the force of the power be = p, and the weight to be moved = P, the velocity of the power = C, and the velocity of the weight = c. If the velocity of the power has a greater ratio to the velocity of the weight than, reciprocally, the weight to the force of the power, it will be C : c > P : p; and therefore the product, or momentum, of the power, pC, will be greater than the momentum of the resisting weight, Pc. The heavy body will therefore be moved by the power. Since, further, the product pC turns out the greater the more the ratio C : c exceeds the ratio P : p, it follows that a huge body can be moved, by means of a machine, the more easily even by a slight power, the greater the ratio of the velocity with which the power is endowed to the velocity of the weight is than the ratio that holds reciprocally between the weight and the force of the power. From which indeed it at once shines out that this saving in lifting weights by machines is joined with some loss of time, which nevertheless ought rightly to be counted among the gains. This being established, let us weigh the machines for a while, so far as is necessary for the purpose of Physics.

## De Vecte. — ON THE LEVER

> 375 *Vectis*, prima Mechanicae machina, est palus oblongus, materia solida constans, qui ad ingentia pondera faciliùs[?] movenda commodè adhibetur. Tria in eo distinguuntur, scilicet: *potentia movens*, sive *momentum*: *resistentia*, sive pondus sustinendum, vel movendum: punctum denique fixum, cui immobili vectis innititur: hoc latinè *fulcrum*, Graecis *hypomochlion*, Vitruvio *pressio* nuncupatur. Quoniam verò tria haec puncta triplici modo disponi in vecte possunt, idcircò triplex genus discriminari solet.

375 The lever, the first machine of Mechanics, is an oblong stake consisting of solid material, which is conveniently employed for moving huge weights more easily. Three things are distinguished in it, namely: the moving power, or momentum; the resistance, or weight to be sustained or moved; and finally the fixed point on which the lever rests, immovable: this is called in Latin fulcrum, by the Greeks hypomochlion, by Vitruvius pressio. But since these three points can be disposed in the lever in a threefold manner, a threefold kind is therefore usually distinguished.

> 376 Primum est, quando fulcrum inter potentiam, & pondus, medium locum tenet, cujus modi est vectis A B, (Fig. XXXII.) ubi inter potentiam B, & pondus A, intermedium est fulcrum C. Secundum genus est, quando fulcrum C, (Fig. XXXIII.) in parte una extrema reperitur, in extremo altero potentia A, & pondus B medium obtinet. Tertium habetur, in quo potentia A (Fig XXXIV) medium inter fulcrum B, & pondus C, occupat. Primi generis vectem *heterodromum*: Secundi *homodromum* adpellant: tertii generis ad *homodromum* révocant.

376 The first is when the fulcrum holds the middle place between the power and the weight, such as the lever AB (Fig. XXXII.), where the fulcrum C is intermediate between the power B and the weight A. The second kind is when the fulcrum C (Fig. XXXIII.) is found at one extremity, the power A at the other extremity, and the weight B holds the middle. The third is had when the power A (Fig. XXXIV.) occupies the middle between the fulcrum B and the weight C. The lever of the first kind they call heterodromous; of the second, homodromous; that of the third kind they refer to the homodromous.

[p. 123]

> 377 In primo vectis genere quantùm distantia C B superat distantiam A C, tantùm potentia B excedit resistentiam corporis A: atque adeò si inter punctum fixum, & potentiam, distantia sit decuplo major, quàm distantia ponderis ab eodem puncto, corpus A verò sit centum librarum; modò potentia B decem libris paulò plus aequivaleat, haec illud adtollet; ea tamen ratione, ut dum potentia spatium ferè decem digitorum descendendo cónficit, pondus unius duntaxat digiti intervallo extollatur. Idem est in vecte secundi generis, quantum enim distantia A C superat distantiam B C, tantò efficacius potentia resistentiam ponderis vincet. In tertio vectis genere id solum commodi est, quod potentia motrix pondus levius movere possit celeritate majori: id quod suâ non caret utilitate, dum temporis compendium quaeritur.

377 In the first kind of lever, by as much as the distance CB exceeds the distance AC, by so much does the power B exceed the resistance of the body A: and so, if the distance between the fixed point and the power is ten times greater than the distance of the weight from the same point, and the body A is of a hundred pounds, then, provided the power B is equivalent to a little more than ten pounds, it will lift it; yet in such a manner that while the power, in descending, covers a space of about ten inches, the weight is raised through an interval of only one inch. The same holds in the lever of the second kind; for by as much as the distance AC exceeds the distance BC, by so much more efficaciously will the power overcome the resistance of the weight. In the third kind of lever there is only this advantage, that the moving power can move a lighter weight with a greater velocity: which is not without its utility when a saving of time is sought.

## De Axe in peritrochio. — ON THE WHEEL AND AXLE

> 378 *Axis in peritrochio*, secunda Mechanicae machina, est instrumentum ponderibus levandis aptum, in quo cylindrus h i (Fig. XXXV) quem axem vocant, fulcris k l utrimque sustentatus, circumpositum habet *tympanum*, m e, quod *peritrochium* compellant: in hujus ambitu baculi teretes, a c, b d, qui *radii*, seu *scytalae* dicuntur, infixi sunt, quibus adplicata potentia peritrochium cum axe versat, & pondus ope funis circumvoluti adtollit. Alias peritrochium dicitur ipsum illud orbiculatum planum, cujus in locum scytalae sufficiuntur. Si axi situm horizontalem obtinenti jungantur scytalae, *Sucula* nuncupatur; si verò ad perpendiculum erectus fuerit, *Ergata* nominatur. Sucularum usus maximus est in metallifodinis. Ergata id commodi habet, quod singulis scytalis plures unà homines adplicari possint, quin sese impediant.

378 The wheel and axle, the second machine of Mechanics, is an instrument suited to lifting weights, in which the cylinder hi (Fig. XXXV.), which they call the axle, sustained on either side by the props k, l, has placed around it a drum, me, which they call the peritrochium: in its circumference are fixed round rods, ac, bd, which are called spokes, or scytalae, by which the power applied turns the peritrochium with the axle, and lifts the weight by means of a rope wound round it. Elsewhere the name peritrochium is given to that circular plane itself, in place of which the scytalae are substituted. If the scytalae are joined to an axle having a horizontal position, it is called a Windlass; but if the axle is set up perpendicularly, it is named a Capstan. The use of windlasses is very great in mines. The capstan has this advantage, that several men together can be applied to each of the scytalae without hindering one another.

> 379 Machina haec ad vectem primi generis revocatur, imò re ipsa est vectis perpetuus. Hypomoclium enim est in medio[?] axis, videlicet in puncto m, vel f, quin per axem totum puncta ejusmodi rectè concipiuntur: potentia motrix in a vel b constituta distantiam a m, vel b m, à puncto fixo habet: resistentia in superficiei axis ipsius puncto è constituitur solaque semidiametro axis e f, à punto fixo f distat. Undè quantum distantia a m, excedit distantiam e f, tantò facilius potentia in a vincit resistentiam in e: quo proindè major futura est scytala, hoc magis vires potentiae crescunt. Atque ex eodem hoc principio deducitur vis & efficientia rotarum, quarum motus calcando exigitur, aut aquae adfluxu, alarum item, quae á vento circumaguntur in móletrinis, aliorumque id genus instrumentorum.

379 This machine is referred to the lever of the first kind; indeed, in reality it is a perpetual lever. For the hypomochlion is in the middle of the axle, namely at the point m, or f; indeed, points of this kind are rightly conceived through the whole axle: the moving power placed at a or b has the distance am, or bm, from the fixed point: the resistance is constituted at the point e of the surface of the axle itself, and is distant from the fixed point f only by the semidiameter of the axle, ef. Whence, by as much as the distance am exceeds the distance ef, by so much more easily does the power at a overcome the resistance at e: and therefore, the greater the scytala is to be, the more the forces of the power increase. And from this same principle are deduced the force and efficiency of wheels whose motion is driven by treading, or by the inflow of water, likewise of the sails that are turned round by the wind in mills, and of other instruments of that kind.

[p. 124]

> De Trochlea.

ON THE PULLEY.

> 380 *Trochlea* tertia Mechanices machina, est instrumentum constans uno, vel pluribus orbiculis, circa axes suos alicubi fixos versatilibus, quibus circumvoluto fune, qui *ductarius* dicitur, pondera adducuntur. Si unus duntaxàt adhibeatur orbiculus adpellatur *trochlea simplex*, & *monospastos*; si è duobus, tribus, quatuor, aut pluribus coalescat; pro eorumdem numero *dispastos*, *trispastos*, *tetraspastos* aut *polyspastos* vocatur.

380 The pulley, the third machine of Mechanics, is an instrument consisting of one or several little wheels revolving about their axles, which are fixed somewhere, by which, with a rope wound round them, which is called the ductarius, weights are drawn in. If only one little wheel is employed, it is called a simple pulley, and monospastos; if it is composed of two, three, four or more, it is called, according to their number, dispastos, trispastos, tetraspastos or polyspastos.

> 381 Trochlea simplex circa axem immobilem volúbilis potentiae motricis vires non auget; quantùm enim ascendit pondus D (Fig. XXXVI.) tantum descendit A, adeòque motus tum ponderis, tum potentiae aequantur. Qua propter emolumentum omne hujus in eo situm est, quod directio potentiae mutetur, dum scilicet adminiculo trochleae illa deorsum movetur, quae alioquin sursum moveri deberet, ut pondus adtolleretur. Adhaec in descensu potentiae, vires ex ipso corporis moventis pondere crescunt. Demum funis circa orbem volutus minus adtéritur.

381 A simple pulley revolving about an immovable axle does not increase the forces of the moving power; for as much as the weight D ascends (Fig. XXXVI.), so much does A descend, and so the motions both of the weight and of the power are equal. Wherefore its whole advantage lies in this, that the direction of the power is changed, while, namely, by the aid of the pulley the power is moved downward which would otherwise have to be moved upward for the weight to be raised. Moreover, in the descent of the power, the forces grow from the very weight of the moving body. Finally, the rope rolled round the wheel is less worn by friction.

> 382 Patet verò trochleam B C vectem esse perpetuum heterodromum; axis quippè fixus L, circa quem revolvitur orbiculus, est instar fulcri, circum quod potentia, & pondus, quae se habent perindè, ac si essent extremis diametri C B adplicata, simul moventur. Si trochlea simplex (Fig. XXXVII.) mobilis fuerit, quoniam A extremum diametri A a D respondens puncto immobili F, est fulcrum, cui funis ope trochleae innititur; potentia in altero extremo diametri D; pondus demùm in medio a, constituuntur; àtque adeò trochlea sic comparata quum sit vectis secundi generis, ac distantia potentiae á fulcro, ad distantiam ponderis ab eodem, nempè D A ad A a[?] sit ut 2 ad 1; liquet (ex superiori Cap.) aequilibrium futurum, si potentia fuerit ad pondus, ut 1 : 2. Movebitur verò â potentia pondus, si illa ad hoc fuerit in majore ratione quam subdúpla; posito enim quod sit ut 4 : 6, quia distantia D A dupla est distantiae A a, deindè quia potentia duplo celerius movetur, quàm pondus (per Princip I. Stat.): celeritas iccircò potentiae majorem habebit rationem ad celeritatem ponderis, quàm reciprocè pondus ipsum ad vim potentiae, scilicet: 2 : 1 > 6 : 4, atque adeò pondus adminiculo trochleae mobilis tum movebitur (per Princip. Mechan.) Trochlea prior *monospastos primi generis*: altera haec *secundi generis monospastos* nuncupatur.

382 It is plain, moreover, that the pulley BC is a perpetual heterodromous lever; for the fixed axle L, about which the little wheel revolves, is like a fulcrum, around which the power and the weight, which behave just as if they were applied to the extremities of the diameter CB, are moved together. If the simple pulley (Fig. XXXVII.) is movable, since A, the extremity of the diameter AaD corresponding to the immovable point F, is the fulcrum on which the rope rests by means of the pulley, the power is placed at the other extremity of the diameter, D, and the weight, finally, in the middle, a; and so, since a pulley so arranged is a lever of the second kind, and the distance of the power from the fulcrum is to the distance of the weight from the same, namely DA to Aa, as 2 to 1, it is clear (from the preceding Chapter) that there will be equilibrium if the power is to the weight as 1 : 2. But the weight will be moved by the power if the latter is to it in a greater ratio than subduple: for supposing it is as 4 : 6, since the distance DA is double the distance Aa, and then since the power moves twice as fast as the weight (by Princip. I of Stat.), the velocity of the power will therefore have a greater ratio to the velocity of the weight than, reciprocally, the weight itself to the force of the power, namely 2 : 1 > 6 : 4, and so the weight will then be moved by the aid of the movable pulley (by the Princip. of Mechan.). The former pulley is called monospastos of the first kind; this other, monospastos of the second kind.

> 383 In *Dispasto* cujus unus orbiculus immobilis, alter mobilis fuerit (Fig. XXXVIII.) duplo celerius movetur potentia P, quàm pondus M; nequit enim inferior orbiculus ex a in D ascendere, nisi potentia P per spatium = D a + b x, hoc est per duplum spatii à pondere confecti descendat. Proindè *dispasti* ope movebit [p. 125] potentia pondus, si fuerit ad ipsum in majore ratione, quam sit 1 : 2, atque adeò dupla redditur per eundem potentia, tantundèmque juvatur, quantùm per *monospastum secundi generis*. Quapropter, quum incrementum omne motricis potentiae ab orbiculis mobilibus ducendum sit, tantùmque vis haec adcrescat quantùm velocitas ejusdem excedit velocitatem ponderis, ea de causâ in *trispasto* (Fig. XXXIX) triplicatur potentia, si quidem orbiculus M N, ex d in b adtolli nequit, nisi potentia P descendendo conficiat spatium altitudinis d b triplum, hoc est: nisi tria funis segmenta altitudini d b aequalia adducantur. Ita in *tetraspasto* quadruplicatur, in *polyspasto* multiplicatur pluries potentia.

383 In the Dispastos, one little wheel of which is immovable and the other movable (Fig. XXXVIII.), the power P moves twice as fast as the weight M; for the lower little wheel cannot ascend from a to D unless the power P descends through a space = Da + bx, that is, through double the space covered by the weight. Therefore, by means of the dispastos, the power will move [p. 125] the weight, if it is to it in a greater ratio than 1 : 2, and so the power is rendered double by it; and it is helped just as much as by the monospastos of the second kind. Wherefore, since all increase of the moving power is to be derived from the movable little wheels, and this force grows by as much as its velocity exceeds the velocity of the weight, for that reason in the trispastos (Fig. XXXIX.) the power is tripled, since indeed the little wheel MN cannot be raised from d to b unless the power P, in descending, covers a space triple the height db, that is: unless three segments of the rope equal to the height db are drawn in. Thus in the tetraspastos the power is quadrupled, in the polyspastos it is multiplied many times over.

> 384 Undè *polyspasti* ope adtolletur ingens pondus, adhibitâ exiguâ potentiâ, si ratio ipsius potentiae fuerit ad pondus major, quàm ratio unitatis ad numerum orbiculorum *polyspastum* constituentium. Quare dato valore potentiae, = 10 numero item orbiculorum = 6. (Fig. XL.) factum exprimet valorem ponderis á potentia huic machinae adplicata sustinendi = 60, sursum autem efferetur hoc pondus, si paulò major potentiae vis addatur. Speciatim pars polyspasti A B, *trochlea superior*; pars verò C D trochlea inferior; utraque *Rechamus* nominatur apud Vitruvium.

384 Whence by means of the polyspastos a huge weight will be lifted with a slight power employed, if the ratio of that power to the weight is greater than the ratio of unity to the number of little wheels constituting the polyspastos. Wherefore, given the value of the power = 10, and the number of little wheels likewise = 6 (Fig. XL.), the product will express the value of the weight to be sustained by the power applied to this machine, = 60; and this weight will be carried upward if a little greater force of the power is added. Specifically, the part AB of the polyspastos is the upper pulley, and the part CD the lower pulley; each is named rechamus in Vitruvius.

> De Prancratio.

ON THE PANCRATIUM .

> 385 *Prancratium* quarta Mechanicae machina, est complexus plurium rotarum dentatarum certo artificio, eaque lege consociatarum, ut unius dentes denticulis alterius rotae circum axem suum volubilis inserantur, quo fiat, ut unâ motâ circa suum axiculum, ceterae omnes in motum cieantur. Machina haec *Glossocomum* â Pappo nuncupatur, [^125-s1] & eodem teste, seu inventa, seu explanata fuit ab Herone Alexandrino, qua de causâ *Heronis Glossocomum* vulgò dicitur. Varia est illius forma, & constructio[?]: suffecerit unam adumbrasse, quò pateat, quantoperè vires rotarum ejuscemodi compositione augeantur. [^125-s2]

385 The Pancratium, the fourth machine of Mechanics, is a complex of several toothed wheels associated by a certain artifice and under such a law that the teeth of one are inserted into the little teeth of another wheel revolving about its own axis, whereby it comes about that, when one is moved about its little axle, all the others are set in motion. This machine is named Glossocomum by Pappus (q), and, on the same witness, it was either invented or explained by Hero of Alexandria, for which reason it is commonly called Hero’s Glossocomum. Its form and construction are various: it will be enough to have sketched one, from which it may appear how greatly the forces are increased by a composition of wheels of this kind (r).

> [^125-s1]: Collect. Mathem. Lib. 8. ad Prop 10.

[^125-s1]: Mathematical Collection, bk. 8, at prop. 10.

> [^125-s2]: P. Schott. Mag. Univers. P 3. Magia Thaumaturga. Cap. 1. diversè constructa Pancrátia exhibet.

[^125-s2]: Father Schott, Magia universalis, pt. 3, Magia Thaumaturga, ch. 1, exhibits Pancratia constructed in various ways.

> 386 Sit (Fig. XLI.) Pancratium é quatuor axibus cum rotis dentatis coalescens. Habeant rotae majores, quoad diametrum, rationem ad minores, ut 10 : 1, eademque sit ratio numeri dentium. Manubrium A B seu radius, cui adplicatur potentia sit decuplo longior radio rotulae C, erit velocitas potentiae ad velocitatem rotae C, ut 10 : 1. In altero axe rota major D, dentibus decuplo pluribus instructa, quàm rotula C, semel convertitur, dum interea C decies revolvitur. Eidem axi commitatur rotula E aequalis [p. 126] priori C, quae eo tempore[?] [?] gyrum[?] absolvit[?], quo rota D circumagitur[?]. Dentes[?] in rota F sint pariter decuplo plures denticulis rotulae E, ut[?] ea[?] decies revolvi debeat, priusquam[?] F semel circa axem feratur[?], secumque[?] rotam adnexam G abripiat[?]. Rota demum H, ipsa[?] quoque dentes plures decuplo habens, vertetur[?] semel cum axe I H, & cylindro K, qui eadem[?] quâ[?] rota C, diametro continetur[?], atque funis ope pondus, revolvendo circa axem I H adtollit[?].

386 Let there be (Fig. XLI.) a Pancratium composed of four axles with toothed wheels. Let the larger wheels have, as to diameter, the ratio to the smaller of 10 : 1, and let the ratio of the number of teeth be the same. Let the handle AB, or radius, to which the power is applied, be ten times longer than the radius of the little wheel C; the velocity of the power will be to the velocity of the wheel C as 10 : 1. On the second axle the greater wheel D, furnished with ten times more teeth than the little wheel C, is turned once while C meanwhile revolves ten times. To the same axle is joined a little wheel E, equal to the former [p. 126] C, which completes its revolution in the time in which the wheel D is turned round. Let the teeth in the wheel F likewise be ten times more numerous than the little teeth of the little wheel E, so that the latter must revolve ten times before F is borne once round its axle and carries off with it the attached wheel G. Finally the wheel H, itself too having ten times more teeth, will turn once with the axle IH and the cylinder K, which is contained by the same diameter as the wheel C, and which, revolving about the axle IH, lifts the weight by means of a rope.

> 387 Posita igitur hac revolutionum serie ac proportione, erit celeritas potentiae A ad celeritatem rotulae C ut 10000 : 1000; hujus[?] ad velocitatem rotulae E, ut 1000 : 100: hujus[?] ad celeritatem G, ut 100 : 10: velocitas tandem G ad celeritatem cylindri, & ponderis L, ut 10 : 1. Quapropter obtinet[?] proportio haec (*ex aequo ordinata*[?]): velocitas potentiae A est ad velocitatem ponderis L, ut 10000 : 1, atque hinc machinae hujus adminiculo vis libram[?] unam potens elevare[?], ad 10000 libras adtollendas idonea redditur. Quin per Glossocomum, potentia tantis incrementis augeri potest[?], ut[?] calculo[?] subducto[?] demonstravit[?] Clariss. P. Schott, machinâ hac ex quatuor & viginti majoribus rotis coagmentatâ, tellurem, etiamsi[?] ex auro conflata foret, in altum extolli[?] suo è loco posse a potentia 125[?] libras ponderante. [^126-s1]

387 This series and proportion of revolutions being posited, the velocity of the power A will be to the velocity of the little wheel C as 10000 : 1000; the velocity of the latter to the velocity of the little wheel E as 1000 : 100; that of this one to the velocity of G as 100 : 10; finally the velocity of G to the velocity of the cylinder, and of the weight L, as 10 : 1. Wherefore this proportion holds (ex aequo ordinata): the velocity of the power A is to the velocity of the weight L as 10000 : 1. And hence, by the aid of this machine, a force able to lift one pound is rendered fit for lifting 10000 pounds. Indeed, by means of the Glossocomum the power can be increased by such increments that, as the most distinguished Father Schott has demonstrated by calculation, with this machine compounded of twenty-four larger wheels the earth, even if it were made wholly of gold, could be raised on high from its place by a power weighing 125 pounds (s).

> [^126-s1]: Loco cit. Mach. 2.

[^126-s1]: Place cited, Mach. 2.

## De Plano inclinato. — ON THE INCLINED PLANE

> 388 *Planum inclinatum* est superficies plana cum plano horizontali, cui insistit[?], angulos inaequales constituens. Recensetur[?] inter Mechanicas machinas eo nomine, quod ingentia in eo pondera faciliùs[?] vel[?] sustineantur[?], vel adtollantur[?]. Quapropter leges, quibus vires corporum moventium, [?] plani[?] hujus[?] augentur[?], paulisper[?] expendendae veniunt; sed ante hoc notetur[?] pondus illud[?], quo corpus plano inclinato superpositum descendere nititur, & superandum est, *pondus respectivum*[?]: integrum verò corporis nulli fulcro innixi pondus *absolutum* nuncupari[?].

388 An inclined plane is a plane surface forming unequal angles with the horizontal plane on which it stands. It is counted among the Mechanical machines on this account, that huge weights are either sustained or lifted on it more easily. Wherefore the laws by which the forces of moving bodies are increased by the aid of this plane come to be weighed a little; but before this let it be noted that the weight with which a body placed on an inclined plane strives to descend, and which must be overcome, is called the respective weight; but the whole weight of a body resting on no prop, the absolute weight.

> 389 Si corpus grave (Fig. XLII.) plano inclinato A B C impositum, sustineatur a potentia quae agit secundum directionem D K plano parallelam, erit potentia ad pondus absolutum corporis, ut altitudo plani A B ad longitudinem A C. Ductis enim lineis, alterâ D E ex centro gravitatis ad punctum contactus plani, alterâ verò D F exprimente directionem gravitatis, seu ponderis absoluti D H, & tandem E F perpendiculari ad lineam D F: tria resultant puncta vectis inflexi, sive *angularis* D E F, cujus hypomochlion est E, potentia D, & pondus F (perinde est quippe, sive in K, sive in D [p. 127] constituta[?] esse potentia, integrum[?] tamen[?] totum[?] pondus cogitetur[?] rectè[?] uno in puncto F lineae directionis D F collectum[?] esse[?]). Quare potentia in D est ad pondus in F, ut F E ad D E, atque ob similitudinem triangulorum D E F, & A B C, est D : F = A B : A C. At si potentia secundum directionem R I (Fig. XLIII.) basi[?] M N parallelam agat, quo ab ea pondus sustineatur[?], necessum[?] est, ut sit[?] potentia ad pondus, ut altitudo plani inclinati ad basim ejusdem[?].

389 If a heavy body (Fig. XLII.) placed on the inclined plane ABC is sustained by a power acting along the direction DK parallel to the plane, the power will be to the absolute weight of the body as the height of the plane AB to its length AC. For let lines be drawn: one, DE, from the center of gravity to the point of contact with the plane; another, DF, expressing the direction of gravity, or of the absolute weight, DH; and finally a third, EF, perpendicular to the line DF: there result the three points of the bent, or angular, lever DEF, whose hypomochlion is E, the power D, and the weight F (for it is all one whether the power at K or at D be [p. 127] be understood to be placed; yet let the whole weight be thought of as rightly collect‐ ed in the one point F of the line of direction D F). Therefore the power in D is to the weight in F as F E to D E, and, on account of the similarity of the triangles D E F and A B C, D : F = A B : A C. But if the power acts along the direction R I (Fig. XLIII.), parallel to the base M N, so that the weight may be sustained by it, it is necessary that the power be to the weight as the height of the inclined plane to its base.

> 390 Erecta enim in directionem R I, perpendiculari Q T, vectis rursum *angularis* T Q S habebitur, ita ut in T potentia I, in S pondus R concipi[?] mente possint[?], iisdem[?] nimirùm[?], quae supra sumpsimus[?], positis. Proinde potentia I erit ad pondus S, ut S Q ad T Q, hoc est ob similia triangula R Q S, S Q O, O P N, & L M N, erit T : S = L M : M N. Unde potentia exigua pondus adtollet per planum inclinatum, si ratio illius[?] ad absolutum corporis pondus fuerit major ea, quae currit[?] inter altitudinem ac longitudinem plani. Atque hinc generatim tanto magis vires potentiae ad sustinendum, vel adducendum corpus grave super planum inclinatum augentur, quanto plani longitudo est[?] quam altitudo major effecta[?]: adeoque si altitudo foret infinitè parva, sive planum horizontale, potentia sustinens infinitè parva [?]. Ex plano inclinato derivantur *Cochlea*, & *Cuneus*.

390 For when the perpendicular Q T has been erected upon the direction R I, the angular lever T Q S will again be had, so that the power I can be conceived to be in T and the weight R in S, the same things, namely, being supposed that we assumed above. Hence the power I will be to the weight S as S Q to T Q; that is, on account of the similar triangles R Q S, S Q O, O P N and L M N, T : S = L M : M N will hold. Hence a slight power will raise a weight along an inclined plane if its ratio to the absolute weight of the body is greater than that which holds between the height and the length of the plane. And hence, in general, the forces of the power for sustaining, or drawing, a heavy body upon an inclined plane are increased the more, the greater the length of the plane is made than its height: and so, if the height were infinitely small, or the plane horizontal, an infinitely small sustaining power is required. From the inclined plane are derived the Screw and the Wedge.

> De Cochlea.

ON THE SCREW.

> 391 *Cochlea* est planum inclinatum circumductum in superficie cylindri, dum nempe cylinder in spiras[?], quas *helices* nuncupamus, aequales, ac parallelas sulcatur[?]. Duplex autem conjungitur[?], alia in exteriore superficie I K (Fig. XLIV.) alia in superficie interiore L M efformata, prior *cochlea mas*, posterior *cochlea foemina*[?] vocatur: utraque hoc modo conficitur[?], ut cavae hujus spirae, eidem incisae[?], prominentibus cylindri interioris spiris exactè[?] congruant, & mutuò helices se excipiant[?]. His porrò legibus continetur ratio, quâ vires, cochleae adminiculo adjuvantur[?].

391 The screw is an inclined plane carried round on the surface of a cylinder, namely when the cylinder is furrowed into equal and parallel spirals, which we call helices. It is joined, moreover, as a double one: one formed on the exterior surface I K (Fig. XLIV.), the other on the interior surface L M; the former is called the male screw, the latter the female screw: each is made in such a way that the hollow spirals of the latter, cut into it, fit exactly the projecting spirals of the inner cylinder, and the helices receive each other mutually. The ratio by which forces are aided by means of the screw is contained in the following laws.

> 392 Quoniam cochlea I K est planum inclinatum, cylindri superficiem ambiens, & potentiae, quae cochleae L M adplicatur, directio in planum[?] inclinatum[?] est basi ipsius cochleae parallela, aequilibrabitur potentia cum pondere, (*per dicta de plano inclin.*[?]) si illa fuerit ad hoc, ut distantia inter duas helices sibi proximas, ad circuitum cochleae, seu peripheriam circuli, quem potentia describit. Quocirca exiguae potentiae viribus cochleae adplicatis movebitur ingens corpus, si peripheria circuli à potentia percursi majorem rationem habeat ad distantiam helicum proximarum, quàm pondus ad potentiam: tum quippe celeritas potentiae majorem obtinebit[?] rationem ad celeritatem ponderis, quàm ipsum[?] pondus habeat[?] ad potentiam: atque adeo momentum potentiae, ponderis, ac [p. 128] resistentiae momentum excedet. Quo fit, ut validiores sint cochleae, quò propiores iis helices inciduntur, eodem cylindri ambitu posito.

392 Since the screw I K is an inclined plane encircling the surface of a cylinder, and the direction of the power applied to the screw L M is parallel to the base of the inclined plane, the power will be in equilibrium with the weight (by what was said on the inclined plane) if the former is to the latter as the distance between two helices nearest each other is to the circuit of the screw, or the periphery of the circle which the power describes. Wherefore a huge body will be moved by the forces of a slight power applied to the screw, if the periphery of the circle run through by the power has a greater ratio to the distance of the nearest helices than the weight to the power: since, namely, the velocity of the power will then have a greater ratio to the velocity of the weight than the weight itself has to the power: and so the momentum of the power will exceed the momentum of the weight and of the resistance. [p. 128] Whence it comes about that screws are the stronger, the closer to one another their helices are cut, the circuit of the cylinder remaining the same.

> 393 Cochlea, si rotae dentatae conjungatur, sic, ut illius revolutione impellantur denticuli rotae, haecque circumagatur, dicitur *cochlea perpetua*, sive *infinita*, quia sine fine gyrari potest. (Fig XLV.) Si potentia adplicetur in A, haec unam cochleae circuitionem perficiet, dum rota F E nonnisi unius dentis intervallo promovetur. Toties igitur revolvi potentia in A adplicata debet, quot dentibus rota F E instructa est, ut integra hujus rotae revolutio obtineatur: adeòque ut axis E H integram revolutionem perficiat, proindè ut pondus G ex eo dependens per spatium aequale peripheriae axiculi adtollatur. Quare si centum dentibus rota F E donata ponatur; peripheria radio A B descripta, decies contineat peripheriam axis H E, erit velocitas potentiae ad ponderis celeritatem; ut centies peripheria circuli radio B A descripti ad peripheriam axis H E semel, hoc est, ut 1000 ad 1. Unde machinae hujus adminiculo vis potens unam libram sustentare, cum pondere mille librarum aequilibrium constituet: adtollet verò, si ad illud majorem sortiatur rationem, ac sit 1 ad 1000.

393 If a screw is joined to a toothed wheel in such a way that by its revolution the little teeth of the wheel are driven and the wheel is turned round, it is called the perpetual or endless screw, because it can be turned without end. (Fig. XLV.) If the power is applied at A, it will complete one circuit of the screw while the wheel F E is advanced by the interval of only one tooth. The power applied at A must therefore be revolved as many times as the wheel F E is furnished with teeth, in order that a complete revolution of this wheel be obtained; and so that the axle E H may complete an entire revolution, and hence that the weight G hanging from it may be raised through a space equal to the periphery of the axle. Wherefore, if the wheel F E is supposed to be furnished with a hundred teeth, and the periphery described by the radius A B contains the periphery of the axle H E ten times, the velocity of the power will be to the speed of the weight as a hundred times the periphery of the circle described by the radius B A to once the periphery of the axle H E, that is, as 1000 to 1. Hence, by means of this machine, a force able to sustain one pound will establish equilibrium with a weight of a thousand pounds; and it will raise it if it obtains a greater ratio to it than 1 to 1000.

> 394 Cochlea demùm peculiaris hoc loco indigitari meretur, quae *Archimedeae* nuncupationem ab eodem illo auctore accepit. (Fig. XLVI.) Definitur ea cylindro A B, cui circumvolvitur spirarum instar tubus, qui opportunius è plumbo conflatur; extrema pars A manubrii ope versari circum axem potest, altera B orificium tubi adjunctum habens, sub aqua demergitur, totusque cylinder ad horizontem sub angulo circiter semirecto inclinatur. His constitutis, ubi cochlea circumagitur, aqua per tubi orificium subiens, ac revolutione ipsius machinae pedetentìm per spiras, veluti per totidem plana inclinata extolletur, tandemque in A profundetur.

394 Finally, a peculiar screw deserves to be pointed out in this place, which received the name Archimedean from that same author. (Fig. XLVI.) It is defined by the cylinder A B, around which a tube is wound in the manner of spirals, a tube more conveniently made of lead; the extreme part A can be turned about the axis by means of a handle; the other, B, having the orifice of the tube attached, is sunk under water, and the whole cylinder is inclined to the horizon at an angle of about half a right angle. These things being set up, when the screw is turned round, the water entering through the orifice of the tube is raised step by step, by the revolution of the machine itself, through the spirals as through so many inclined planes, and is at length poured out at A.

## De Cuneo. — ON THE WEDGE.

> 395 *Cuneus* est pyramis quadrangula in aciem désinens. (Fig. XLVII.) Planum A D F B *basis*, A B *latitudo*, vel *dorsum*, a A vel a B *altitudo*, a C *longitudo*, C E *acies* cunei nuncupantur. Potentia huic machinae adplicari solita, vel est percutiens, vel premens, quae ope cunei findit, divellitque corpora etiam durissima.

395 The wedge is a quadrangular pyramid ending in an edge. (Fig. XLVII.) The plane A D F B is called the base, A B the breadth or back, a A or a B the height, a C the length, C E the edge of the wedge. The power usually applied to this machine is either striking or pressing, and by means of the wedge it splits and tears apart even the hardest bodies.

> 396 Vim cunei ex plano inclinato ducunt plerique (renuente in universum Cl. à Brixia [^128-s1] (de qua nos controversia nihil certi statuemus) spectando eum ceu compositum ex duobus planis inclinatis A C, B C: quumque perinde sit, sive corpus super planum inclinatum moveatur, sive sub corpore movendo planum [p. 129] protrudatur; adhaec directio potentiae, quae ope cunei corpora dispescit, sit ad ejus longitudinem parallela: inferunt propterea potentiam esse ad vim obstaculi, uti est dimidia latitudo sive crassities cunei ad ejus longitudinem, hoc est: ½ A B: a C. Undè quia in acutiore cuneo altitudo minorem habet rationem ad longitudinem, eadem haec si ponatur manere, iccircò acutior validius dirimet partes obstaculi, quàm obtusus.

396 Most derive the force of the wedge from the inclined plane (the illustrious Fortunato da Brescia (t) objecting altogether, a controversy on which we shall settle nothing certain), regarding it as composed of two inclined planes A C, B C: and since it is all the same whether the body is moved over the inclined plane or the plane is thrust forward under the body to be moved and [p. 129] and moreover the direction of the power which drives bodies apart by means of the wedge is parallel to its length, they infer therefore that the power is to the force of the obstacle as half the breadth, or thickness, of the wedge is to its length, that is: ½ A B : a C. Hence, since in a sharper wedge the height has a smaller ratio to the length, if this same is supposed to remain, a sharper wedge will on that account separate the parts of an obstacle more strongly than a blunt one.

> [^128-s1]: Phys. P. 2. §. 2147. Vid. P. Schott. Mag. Mechan. Syntagm. 5.

[^128-s1]: Phys., pt. 2, §. 2147. See Fr. Schott, Mag. Mechan., Syntagm. 5.

> 397 Haec de machinis vulgaribus dicta sint satis. Ex his componuntur innumerae aliae in usus diversos, quarum desiderium si quem teneat deinceps, consulat inter ceteros praecipuè Leupoldum, [^129-s1] Varignonium [^129-s2] & Machinarum ab Academ. Scient. Parisina adprobatarum descriptionem [^129-s3] fusè exaratam. Nostrum est, non artifices, machinarumque fabricatores, verùm Physicos docére ea, quae ab ipsis nec ignorari citra turpitudinem possunt, nec morari nimium properantes ad alia, debent. Paucula solum juverit ad horum cognitionem observare.

397 Let these things said about the common machines suffice. From them innumerable others are composed for various uses; if desire for these should hereafter take hold of anyone, let him consult, among others, chiefly Leupold (u), Varignon (x), and the description, drawn up at length, of the Machines approved by the Paris Academy of Sciences (y). It is our task to teach, not artisans and builders of machines, but Physicists, those things which they can neither be ignorant of without disgrace nor ought to dwell upon too long, hastening on to other matters. It will help only to observe a very few things for the knowledge of these.

[^129-s1]: Theatrum Machinarum.
