> Animadversio in Doctrinam de Machinis.

REMARK ON THE DOCTRINE OF MACHINES .

> 398 Quoniam ubi tria comperiuntur puncta in quorum uno potentia motrix sit adplicata, alteri pondus vincendum respondeat, tertium sit, circa quod motus perficitur, ibi vectem (*seu incurvum* in quo puncta per lineam curvam disponuntur, sive *angularem*, vel *inflexum*, ubi in rectis angulum componentibus puncta constituuntur) congruenter nobis mente sistere possumus, ibique tradita de eo doctrina locum habet; isthaec autèm in rebus multo plurimis quum obtineant, iccircò diversi prorsùs generis motiones ex natura vectis evolvi perspicuè possunt. Borellus certè é vectis cognitione omnes animalium motus explicari ostendit. [^129-s4] Vires profectò instrumentorum complurium hinc derivantur: fórfices, aut forcipes vectem duplicem primi generis referunt, cujus fulcrum est axiculus, potentia extremis brachiorum partibus admovetur, resistentiam corpus scindendum efficit.

398 Since, wherever three points are found, in one of which a moving power is applied, to another of which a weight to be overcome corresponds, while the third is that about which the motion is performed, there we can fittingly set a lever before our minds (either a curved one, in which the points are disposed along a curved line, or an angular or bent one, where the points are set in straight lines composing an angle), and there the doctrine handed down about it has its place; and since this holds in a great many things, motions of quite different kinds can therefore be clearly unfolded from the nature of the lever. Borelli certainly shows that all the motions of animals are explained from the knowledge of the lever (z). Indeed the forces of very many instruments are derived from this: scissors, or pincers, represent a double lever of the first kind, whose fulcrum is the little pin; the power is applied to the extreme parts of the arms; the body to be cut makes the resistance.

> [^129-s4]: Op. de motu animal.

[^129-s4]: Work De motu animal.

> 399 Baculus item super genu facile frangendus duplicem *heterodromum* vectem exhibet, utrique enim extremo manus imprimunt motum; fulcra sunt eae pedis partes, quibus baculus innititur; resistentia vincenda medium haec inter puncta contactus locum occupat. Undè consequitur, eò facilius forficibus discindi [p. 130] corpora, tùm quo brachia manubrii longiora fuerint, tum quò corpus axiculo propiùs accesserit: rursumque baculum hoc promptius frangi, quò partes, quibus adprehenditur, magis protensae. Ratio quoque ex natura vectis *heterodromi* redditur, cur mola vento, vel aquae adfluxu concitata, eo volvatur celerius, quo alae vel radii longius porriguntur? Aëris quippe adlabentis, aut aquae impactus potentias motrices agunt, axis, quem alae, rotaevè ambiunt, hypomochlii vicem subit; lapis oneris rationem habet.

399 Likewise a stick to be easily broken over the knee exhibits a double heterodromous lever. For the hands impress motion on each extremity; the fulcra are those parts of the leg on which the stick rests; the resistance to be overcome occupies the middle place between these points of contact. Whence it follows that bodies are cut apart by scissors the more easily, [p. 130] both the longer the arms of the handle are, and the closer the body comes to the little pin; and again, that this stick is broken the more readily, the farther out the parts by which it is grasped extend. The reason is also given, from the nature of the heterodromous lever, why a mill driven by the wind or by the inflow of water turns the faster, the farther the sails or spokes are stretched out. For the impact of the air flowing against them, or of the water, acts as the moving powers; the axle, which the sails or wheels surround, takes the place of the hypomochlion; the stone has the role of the load.

> 400 Neque absimili lege vectis *homodromus* perspicuam reddit nobis vim remórum; aquae enim ceu fulcro remus innititur, navis promovenda ponderis obtinet partes, manus potentiae: ea de causâ fit, ut faciliùs propellatur navigium quò remotior â scalmo est remigans, & quò scalmus aquae propiùs admovetur, hoc eodem ex principio derivantur guvernaculi vires: item deducitur, cur navis velociùs procurrat, quò altiùs antenna in malo adtollitur? Ventus namque comprimens vela, potentiae loco est, navis pro pondere, ima pars mali pro fulcro. Explicatur quoque, cur clavus tabulae firmiter infixus, bifido malleo excipiente caput illius prominens, facilè revellatur? Vectem namque secundi generis malleus refert, cujus manubrium potentia movens impellit; tabula, cui extremum alterum adprimitur, fulcrum est; clavus oneris adtollendi partes obtinet. Eamdem ob rationem culter una parte mensae adfixus eò scindit validiùs, quo propiùs ad punctum adfixionis res dividenda adplicatur. Similiter dentibus *molaribus* duriores etiam comminuimus cibos fortius, quàm *incisoribus* dictis; illi etenim à fulcro propiùs absunt, quam hi.

400 Nor by a dissimilar law does the homodromous lever make plain to us the force of oars; for the oar rests on the water as on a fulcrum, the ship to be moved forward holds the part of the weight, the hands that of the power: for that reason it happens that the vessel is propelled the more easily, the farther the rower is from the thole-pin and the closer the thole-pin is brought to the water. From this same principle the forces of the rudder are derived: likewise it is deduced why a ship runs forward the more swiftly, the higher the yard is raised on the mast. For the wind filling the sails stands in the place of the power, the ship for the weight, the lowest part of the mast for the fulcrum. It is explained also why a nail firmly fixed in a board is easily pulled out by a forked hammer taking hold of its projecting head. For the hammer represents a lever of the second kind, whose handle the moving power drives; the board, against which its other end is pressed, is the fulcrum; the nail holds the part of the load to be raised. For the same reason a knife fixed at one end to a table cuts the more strongly, the closer to the point of attachment the thing to be divided is applied. Similarly we grind even harder foods more strongly with the molar teeth than with the so-called incisors; for the former are nearer the fulcrum than the latter.

> 401 II. Ad axem in peritrochio referuntur elasticae horologiorum portatilium laminae, & cochlea conica, cui annectitur catena: atque é machinae hujus mechanicae principiis ingeniosè constructio partium automatón animantium excogitata fuit. Hac in compage artificiosa elaterium lamellae chalibeae S (Fig. XLVIII.) in gyrum convolutae, potentiae vices agit, dum illud ope catenulae rotam dentatam, quam in extremitate F, adjunctam habet cochlea A B, & â cujus rotae circuitione pendet reliquarum in horologio motus, impellit: resistentia proindè ab elaterio superanda est rotae E, atque adeò ceterarum revolutio; centrum motus, seu fulcrum in axe ipso A B, reperitur.

401 II. To the wheel and axle are referred the elastic springs of portable clocks, and the conical screw to which the chain is attached; and from the principles of this mechanical machine the construction of the parts of automaton animals was ingeniously devised. In this artful structure the spring of the steel lamina S (Fig. XLVIII.), coiled round in a spiral, plays the part of the power, while by means of the little chain it drives the toothed wheel which it has joined at the extremity F, the screw A B, and the wheel on whose revolution the motions of the rest in the clock depend: the resistance to be overcome by the spring is therefore the revolution of the wheel E, and so of the others; the center of motion, or fulcrum, is found in the axle A B itself.

> 402 Jam, quia lamella elastica plenè convoluta, utpotè validius tensa, quum sese evolvere incipit, vi pollet majore, haec verò continenter ipso evolutionis decursu imminuatur: resistentia ex adverso autem eadem jugiter maneat; (difficultas quippe in movendis horologii rotis non decrescit) iccircò axiculus cochleatus quem ambit catenula, non in cylindrum, sed in conicam formam aptatur, quo fit, ut dum elater sub suae evolutionis initium agit in axiculum, arctiorem hujus partem K L catena complectatur, at progressu evolutionis, catena in ampliorem axis ambitum F vel O [p. 131] pertingat. Quapropter ad eamdem semper vincendam resistentiam, idem jugiter momentum potentia retinet; quum scilicet aequa sit compensatio, sic ut integris elaterii viribus principio, ejus momentum temperetur velocitatis imminutione, dum nempè potentia per catenam adplicata, & agens, initio propiùs admovetur fulcro B: ubi contrà deinceps, amplitudo axiculi efficit, ut, decrescente quidem ex sese potentiâ, haec tamen à fulcro removeatur longiùs, radio videlicèt spirarum F, vel O, atque adeò celeritas augeatur.

402 Now, since the elastic lamina, when fully coiled, being stretched more strongly, has a greater force when it begins to unwind itself, and this force is continually diminished in the very course of the unwinding, while the resistance, on the other hand, remains constantly the same (for the difficulty in moving the wheels of the clock does not decrease), the little screw-shaped axle which the chain surrounds is therefore fashioned not into a cylinder but into a conical form; whereby it comes about that, while the spring acts upon the axle at the beginning of its unwinding, the chain embraces its narrower part K L, but as the unwinding proceeds the chain reaches the wider circuit of the axle, F or O. [p. 131] Therefore, for overcoming the resistance, which is always the same, the power continually retains the same momentum; since, namely, there is an equal compensation, so that, while the forces of the spring are unimpaired at the beginning, its momentum is tempered by a diminution of velocity; while, that is, the power, applied through the chain and acting, is at the beginning brought nearer to the fulcrum B; whereas afterwards, on the contrary, the breadth of the axle brings it about that, though the power indeed decreases of itself, it is nevertheless removed farther from the fulcrum, by the radius, namely, of the spirals F or O, and so its speed is increased.

> 403 Axes in peritrochio haud dubiè sunt etiam claves, quibus utimur ad elateres horologiorum intorquendos, aut pondera eorumdem adtollenda, quae pro vario horologii situ modò *suculam*, modò *ergatam* dabunt. Terebra quoque generis hujus est instrumentum; quanquam hoc ob spíras circum cuspidem contortas, aliquid de cochlea; ob acumen, in quod desinit, quidpiam de cuneo admixtum habet.

403 Wheels and axles, without doubt, are also the keys which we use to wind the springs of clocks or to raise their weights, and which, according to the varying position of the clock, will give now a windlass, now a capstan. The gimlet too is an instrument of this kind; although, on account of the spirals twisted round its point, it has something of the screw mixed in, and on account of the sharpness in which it ends, something of the wedge.

> 404 III. Trochlea, in qua *vectem quaerere ineptum sibi videri*, audacter pronunciavit Cartesius [^131-s1] seorsum usurpata, vires potentiae perparùm quum augeat, consimilibus adjungitur, uti jam docuimus, idque fit ea lege, ut vel aliae aliis immineant, quod schemata superiora exhibuerunt, vel situ ad invicem parallelo juxta se constituantur orbiculi magnitudine aequales (Fig. XLIX.) quae constructio percommoda est, tunc maximè quum angustiae spatii, in quo machina locanda, coordinationem aliam non recipiunt. In usu trochlearum observandum monent, qui de his agunt, ut partes funis ductarii omnes semper sint sibi parallelae. Et quoniam funis in trochleis majoribus minus inflecti debet, quàm in minoribus; iccircò illae his praestant. Verùm quia numerus funium ex amplitudine trochlearum non augetur; adhaec quaedam in majoribus orbiculis sese offerunt incommoda, quae ex pondere eorumdem majori, ex adtritu validiore in axibus &c. oriuntur: iccircò legem illam in universum haud obtinere patescit. Porrò ad minuendam [?] frictionem seu trochleae circa axiculum suum, seu axis in peritrochio intra loculamentum, seu intra foramina, quae *chelonia* dicuntur; oportunum fuerit, foramina orbiculorum, aut loculamenta, non rotunda, sed ex tribùs, quatuorvè arcubus circularibus convexis efformare; has enim superficies arcuatas axiculus sese convertens, in paucioribus punctis continget [^131-s2]. Trochleae cum axe in peritrochio junctae componunt machinam frequentissimi usus, quae *Grus* vocatur, & cujus fabrica commodissima a Musschenbroekio [^131-s3] describitur. Sucula cum polyspasto aliud machinae genus reddit, quam *capram* nuncupant.

404 III. The pulley, in which Descartes boldly declared (a) that it seemed to him foolish to look for a lever, since, used by itself, it increases the forces of the power very little, is joined to similar ones, as we have already taught; and this is done under the law that either some hang over others, as the figures above showed, or the little wheels, equal in size, are set beside one another in a position parallel to each other (Fig. XLIX.), a construction which is very convenient, especially when the narrowness of the space in which the machine is to be placed does not admit another arrangement. In the use of pulleys those who treat of them advise that it be observed that all the parts of the hauling rope always be parallel to one another. And since the rope must be bent less in larger pulleys than in smaller ones, the former are on that account superior to the latter. But since the number of ropes is not increased by the size of the pulleys, and besides certain inconveniences present themselves in larger little wheels, which arise from their greater weight, from the stronger friction on the axles, etc., it is therefore clear that that law does not hold universally. Further, to diminish the friction either of the pulley about its little axle, or of the wheel and axle within its case, or within the holes which are called chelonia, it will be expedient to form the holes of the little wheels, or the cases, not round but out of three or four convex circular arcs; for the little axle, turning round, will touch these arched surfaces in fewer points (b). Pulleys joined with the wheel and axle compose a machine of very frequent use, which is called the Crane, and whose most convenient construction is described by Musschenbroek (c). The windlass with a polyspast yields another kind of machine, which they call the gin.

[^131-s2]: See the illustrious de la Hire, Mechanique, Prop. 63.

[p. 132]

> 405 IV. Rota dentata, si dentes secundum directionem radii promineant, *Stellata*; si ad radium perpendiculares fuerint, & deorsum versi, *pectinata*, si autèm verticales, *coronata* adpellatur.

405 IV. A toothed wheel, if its teeth project along the direction of the radius, is called stellate; if they are perpendicular to the radius and turned downward, pectinate; but if vertical, crowned.

> 406 Axis, qui rotam dentatam saepenumerò circumagit, dentibus, vel incisis, vel insertis, sivè paxillis instruitur, & *laterna*, vel *curriculum rotae* nominatur. Id in hoc instrumento advertendum, quum dentes axeos saepius functionem suam obire debeant, quàm rota dentata, plurium praesertim dentium, magisque propterea adterantur; firmiores illi constituendi sunt, quàm in rota dentata. Curandum praeterea, ne iidem dentes rotae cum eodem semper paxillo, aut dente ipsius axis committantur; sed diversi diversis dum inseruntur, fiat; ut diversimodè inter se adtriti ad aequalitatem motûs eò magis pertingant: id quod efficitur, si dentes in se invicem agentes eo sint numero, quorum unus alterum exactè non contineat, uti si rota 60, axis 7, vel 9, dentes comprehendat. [^132-s1]

406 The axle which often turns a toothed wheel round is furnished with teeth, either cut into it or inserted, that is, with pegs, and is named the lantern, or the runner of the wheel. In this instrument it is to be noted that, since the teeth of the axle must perform their function more often than the toothed wheel, especially one of many teeth, and are on that account worn down more, they must be made firmer than in the toothed wheel. Care must besides be taken that the same teeth of the wheel are not always engaged with the same peg, or tooth of the axle itself; but that, different ones being inserted among different ones, it may come about that, being worn against one another in various ways, they may attain the more nearly to equality of motion: which is effected if the teeth acting on one another are of such a number that one does not exactly contain the other, as if the wheel comprises 60 teeth, the axle 7 or 9. (d)

> [^132-s1]: Vid Krafftius. Praelect. Phys. P. 2. cap. 2. §. 83.

[^132-s1]: See Krafft, Praelect. Phys., pt. 2, ch. 2, §. 83.

> 407 V. Non experimenta modò, sed ratio etiam, antehàc stabilitis principiis nixa, evincit, gravia per planum inclinatum demissa motum accelerare *uniformiter*; nam per planum inclinatum neque gravitantis causae vis, neque motus continuus mobilis ipsius sistitur, proindè momentis singulis novus à fluido gravifico impulsus accedit, quibus celeritas *respectiva* continenter augeatur, eâ proportione, quae intercedit *absolutam* inter & *respectivam* gravitatem [^132-s2]. Undè quemadmodum liberè labentia in fine lapsus eam vim nanciscuntur, quâ ad tantam adtolli possint altitudinem, è qua proruerunt; ita per planum inclinatum descendentia viribus iisdem polleant, necesse est, seclusâ medii, aliorumque corporum resistentiâ; his enim positis quum celeritas in fine lapsûs acquisita, non perimatur in corpore, si corpori deciduo aliud sese non offerat, quàm id duntaxat quod mutet directionem, consectarium est, ut vis in progressu descensûs obtenta in ascensum impendatur.

407 V. Not only experiments but reason too, relying on the principles established before, proves that heavy bodies let down along an inclined plane accelerate their motion uniformly; for along an inclined plane neither the force of the cause of gravitation nor the continued motion of the mobile itself is stopped; hence at each single moment a new impulse from the gravific fluid is added, by which the respective velocity is continually increased in the proportion which holds between the absolute and the respective gravity (f). Hence, just as bodies falling freely acquire at the end of their fall that force by which they could be raised to as great a height as that from which they fell, so it is necessary that bodies descending along an inclined plane possess the same forces, the resistance of the medium and of other bodies being set aside: for, these being supposed, since the velocity acquired at the end of the fall is not destroyed in the body if nothing presents itself to the falling body except that alone which changes its direction, it is a consequence that the force obtained in the progress of the descent is spent upon the ascent.

> [^132-s2]: Vid. Introduct. facil. in doctrin. de motu à P. Erasmo Froelich. cap [?] Prop. 4, & seqq.

[^132-s2]: See Introduct. facil. in doctrin. de motu by Fr. Erasmus Froelich, ch., Prop. 4 ff.

> 408 Hac [?] ex doctrina pendulorum motus, illiusque ratio physica derivatur; arcus etenim, quem funependulum in descensu percurrit, si spectetur ceu complexum ex infinitè parvis lineis rectis, hoc est: tanquàm plana inclinata sibi mutuo contigua C A, A B, (Fig. L.) infinitè parvae longitudinis, & quorum flexus, sive angulus A, directionem solummodò mutet, corpus grave arcum emetiendo, eam adipiscetur celeritatem, cujus vi ad altitudinem eidem aequalem ascendere queat. Frictio equidem fili in puncto suspensionis, ipsiusmet retinaculi partes non omnimodè flexiles, aëris renixus, aliquid sensim de vi motus decerpunt usque: eam ob rem, nisi oscillationum causa quaedam conservatrix accedat, arcus continuè decrescent; neque pondus adpensum ad altitudinem descensus prorsùs, sed, quod ad sensum, aequalem adtolletur.

408 From this doctrine the motion of pendulums, and its physical reason, are derived: for if the arc which a pendulum runs through in its descent is regarded as composed of infinitely small straight lines, that is, as of inclined planes contiguous to one another, C A, A B (Fig. L.), of infinitely small length, whose bend, or angle A, only changes the direction, the heavy body, in traversing the arc, will acquire that velocity by whose force it could ascend to a height equal to it. The friction of the thread at the point of suspension, indeed, the parts of the holder itself, which are not entirely flexible, and the resistance of the air gradually take something away from the force of the motion all the while: for that reason, unless some cause conserving the oscillations is added, the arcs continually decrease; nor is the hung weight raised altogether to the height of its descent, but only to one equal to it so far as the senses can tell.

[p. 133]

> 409 VI. Cochlea; quae multifariam aptari solet, in usus complures adhibetur. Permultùm augentur vires eaurundem ope, eo quidem incremento, ut P. Schottus integras domos ligneas cochlearum adminiculo translatas fuisse ex Munstero referat [^133-s1]. Id praeterea emolumenti in iis deprehenditur, quod pondus, remotâ etiam potentiâ, sustineant per sese, modò helices utriusque mutuò se excipiant, & ad invicem comprimantur; possit proin potentia citrà dispendium interquiescere, ac recreari. Magnus tamen partium hac in machina adtritus, usum ejus minus commodum reddit: cui vitio occurritur pinguedinem spirarum convolutionibus interserendo. Observandum adhaec monet idem Schottus, quò durabilior sit cochlea, matrix plures spiras comprehendat; si enim unicam duntaxat habeat, tunc moles ponderis adtollendi uni illi innixa labem ei facilè infert [^133-s2].

409 VI. The screw, which is usually fitted up in many ways, is employed for a great many uses. Forces are increased very much by its means, and indeed with such an increase that Fr. Schott relates, from Münster, that whole wooden houses were moved by the help of screws (g). This advantage is besides found in them, that they sustain the weight by themselves even when the power is removed, provided the helices of each receive one another mutually and are pressed against each other; so the power can meanwhile rest and recover itself without loss. Yet the great friction of the parts in this machine makes its use less convenient: a defect which is remedied by putting grease between the windings of the spirals. The same Schott advises, besides, that it be observed that, so that the screw may be more durable, the nut should comprise several spirals; for if it has only one, then the mass of the weight to be raised, resting on that one alone, easily causes it damage (h).

> [^133-s1]: Mag. Mechan. Syntag. 6. in Proem.

[^133-s2]: Loc. cit., ch. 2.

> 410 VII. Ad cuneum pertinent artefacta varia: cultri, gladii, forfices, terebrae, aliaque similia; quin efficacia molecularum corpora naturalia componentium ex naturâ hujus machinae mechanicae derivatur: venenorum scilicet acrium, & corrosivorum, qualia sunt mercurius sublimatus, arsenicum, aqua fortis, &c. quae cuneorum instar agunt.

410 VII. To the wedge belong various manufactured things: knives, swords, scissors, gimlets, and others like them; indeed, the efficacy of the molecules composing natural bodies is derived from the nature of this mechanical machine: namely, of acrid and corrosive poisons, such as sublimate of mercury, arsenic, aqua fortis, etc., which act like wedges.

## Adnotatio. — NOTE

> 411 In machinis mechanicis funes multiplici ratione usurpari solent, ac debent: hi uti adminicula sunt ad movendas machinarum ope moles corporum, ita impedimenti saepenumerò non exiguam partem addunt. Pro dignitate auxit hanc Mechanicae Tractationem P. de Lanis [^133-s3] eamdem Cl. Amontons [^133-s4] primus exegit methodo concinna, ostenditque multum interesse, resistentiae hujus mensuram nosse, commonstrans, plerumque ex rigiditate funium unicè augeri posse unâ parte tertiâ resistentiam, à motrice potentia superandam: id quod experimentis [?] commonstravit per sequentia theoremata. I. Resistentiam á funium rigore pendentem crescere in ratione directa ponderum, aut virium, eos tendentium. II. Eandem illam augeri praeterea, ceteris omnibus paribus, ea proportione, qua diameter funium accrescit. III. Funes eò complicari difficiliùs, quò cylindri, vel trochleae, quos ambiunt, sunt minores; quantumvis resistentia haec non augescat eâ ipsa proportione, quâ diametri minuuntur. His Auctoris animadversionibus experimenta, & illustrationes adjecit Clariss. Nolletus. [^133-s5]

411 In mechanical machines ropes are wont to be, and must be, employed in manifold ways: and as they are aids for moving masses of bodies by means of machines, so they very often add no small part of hindrance. Fr. de Lana (i) worthily enlarged this treatment of Mechanics; the illustrious Amontons (j) was the first to work it out by an elegant method, and he showed that it matters greatly to know the measure of this resistance, pointing out that, for the most part, the resistance to be overcome by the moving power can be increased by one third part solely from the stiffness of the ropes: which he demonstrated by experiments through the following theorems. I. That the resistance depending on the stiffness of ropes increases in the direct ratio of the weights, or forces, stretching them. II. That this same resistance is increased besides, all other things being equal, in the proportion in which the diameter of the ropes grows. III. That ropes are folded with the more difficulty, the smaller the cylinders or pulleys which they surround: although this resistance does not grow in that very proportion in which the diameters are diminished. To these remarks of the Author the most illustrious Nollet added experiments and illustrations (k).

## DISSERTATIO IV. — DISSERTATION IV

## HYDROSTATICA. — HYDROSTATICS

> Principia Hydrostaticae.

Principles of Hydrostatics.

> 412 Partem Staticae alteram, Hydrostaticam videlicet, quae de gravium fluidorum viribus agit, scitu dignissimam Physices partem paucis complectemur. Duplici autem spectari modo eorumdem pressio potest: altero dum fluida cum fluidis, altero dum illa cum solidis immersis conferuntur, de utroque adtingendum est aliquid: primum hoc loco, posterius exinde contemplabimur. Unum istic, priusquam rem à principio ordiamur, velut certum constituamus necesse est: fluidi cujuslibet partes superiores gravitare in partes inferiores, quibus illae incumbunt, fundumque vasis premi continenter atque urgeri à fluido contento. Scitum profectò, minimeque controversum habebitur, id, si ad materiae gravificae actionem tantisper mentem revocemus, atque (ut par est) cogitemus, corpus quoad naturam spectatum, aequè comparatum esse ad hunc illumve locum occupandum, neque verò locum ullum enti corporeo *respectivè proprium* [?] dici posse. Coeptum ex ordine prosequamur notionibus anteà expositis.

e shall embrace in a few words the other part of Statics, namely 412 W               Hydrostatics, which treats of the forces of heavy fluids, a part of Physics most worth knowing. Their pressure, moreover, can be regarded in a twofold way: in one, when fluids are compared with fluids; in the other, when they are compared with solids immersed in them; something must be touched upon concerning each: the first we shall contemplate in this place, the second afterwards. One thing we must here lay down as certain before we begin the matter from its beginning: that the upper parts of any fluid gravitate upon the lower parts on which they rest, and that the bottom of the vessel is continually pressed and urged by the fluid contained in it. This will surely be held as known and not at all controverted, if we recall our minds for a little to the action of the gravific matter, and consider (as is right) that a body, regarded as to its nature, is equally disposed to occupy this place or that, and that no place can be called respectively proper to a corporeal being. Let us pursue in order what we have begun, the notions having first been set out.

> 413 Fluidorum pressionem dum hic spectamus, *gravitatem* in iis *specificam* consideramus, quo nomine intelligimus illam, quae corpori competit, quatenus in entium corporeorum certa classe, sive specie reponitur, hoc est: Si materiae duae, ratione ponderis, inter se conferantur, (utraque eodem volumine comprehensa); pondus hoc comparatum *gravitas specifica* nuncupatur. Ita gravitatem aquae, specificam videlicet, ad gravitatem mercurii esse dicimus, ut 1 ad 14, quo innuimus, alterum hoc fluidum (aequali sub volumine) decies, & quater plus appendere, quam illud. *Vas uniforme* dicitur illud cujus omnes sectiones fundo ipsi parallelae sunt figura similes, & amplitudine aequales: cujusmodi habentur vasa cylindrica, & prismatica; secus ex adverso cujus sectiones inaequales erunt *vas difforme* vocatur. Hujus amplitudo, si ad basim minor fuerit quam versus apicem, *divergens* dicitur; si contrà indè ab altiori vertice continuè ad fundum usque amplitudo crescat, *vas convergens* nominatur. *Tubi communicantes* vocitantur, qui eo pacto sunt connexi, ut fluidum immissum ex uno in alium liberè excurrat.

413 While we here regard the pressure of fluids, we consider in them their specific gravity, by which name we understand that which belongs to a body inasmuch as it is placed in a certain class, or species, of corporeal beings; that is: if two matters are compared with each other in respect of weight (each comprised in the same volume), this compared weight is called specific gravity. Thus we say that the gravity of water, namely its specific gravity, is to the gravity of mercury as 1 to 14, by which we indicate that the latter fluid (under an equal volume) weighs fourteen times more than the former. A uniform vessel is said to be one all of whose sections parallel to the bottom itself are similar in figure and equal in breadth: such are cylindrical and prismatic vessels; on the contrary, one whose sections are unequal is called a nonuniform vessel. If its breadth is smaller at the base than toward the top, it is called divergent; if, on the contrary, the breadth grows continually from the higher top down to the bottom, it is named a convergent vessel. Those are called communicating tubes which are so connected that a fluid let in runs freely from one into the other.

[p. 135]

> Leges de pressione fluidorum.

LAWS OF THE PRESSURE OF FLUIDS .

> 414 Lex I. *Fluida vasis comprehensa ea ipsa premunt in ratione altitudinis, quâ super planum horizontale eminent, & latitudinis baseos, quae illorum descensui opponitur: aestimanda est proindè eorundem pressio secundum rationem compositam altitudinis, & baseos.*

414 Law I. Fluids comprised in vessels press them in the ratio of the height by which they stand above a horizontal plane, and of the breadth of the base which is opposed to their descent: their pressure is therefore to be estimated according to the compound ratio of the height and the base.

> 415 *Primò* quippè, fluidum vase uniformi A B C D (Fig. LI.) ad perpendiculum erecto contentum, urgetur secundum directionem horizonti, seu fundo vasis perpendicularem: neque partes duntaxat fundo proximae, sed summa omnium, quae ex amplitudine basis B D, & altitudine a B resultat, vim suam exserit (per §. 412.). Quare pressio in fundum à tota mole, hoc est, ab altitudine in basim ductâ aestimetur, necesse est.

415 Firstly, a fluid contained in a uniform vessel A B C D (Fig. LI.) set up perpendicularly is urged along the direction perpendicular to the horizon, or to the bottom of the vessel: and not only the parts nearest the bottom, but the sum of all, which results from the breadth of the base B D and the height a B, exerts its force (by §. 412.). Therefore it is necessary that the pressure on the bottom be estimated from the whole mass, that is, from the height multiplied into the base.

> 416 *Secundò*: Quod si fluidum vase ad horizontem inclinato M E N O (Fig. cit.) comprehendatur: tametsi major sit massa; quoniam tamen fluidi partes velut incumbunt plano inclinato a N, iccircò gravitatis partem in latus sive longitudinem plani éxserunt. Ea igitur vis duntaxat in fundum E N agit, quae aequalis est altitudini a b, habita ratione basis. Id quod dilucidè menti sistetur, fluidi molem, ductis ad perpendiculum a b parallelis, in columnas dispescendo.

416 Secondly: but if the fluid is comprised in a vessel M E N O inclined to the horizon (Fig. cit.), although the mass is greater, yet, since the parts of the fluid rest as it were upon the inclined plane a N, they therefore exert part of their gravity against the side, or length, of the plane. That force alone, therefore, acts on the bottom E N which is equal to the height a b, account being taken of the base. This is clearly set before the mind by dividing the mass of the fluid into columns, lines parallel to the perpendicular a b being drawn.

> 417 *Tertiò*: In vase divergente (Fig. LII.) basis c d haud aliter premitur, quam si foret cylindro e c d f, fluidum contentum; perspicuum est etenim, columnas m m, l l, &c. vasis ipsius parietibus inniti ceu fulcris, basi verò eas solum incumbere, quae ad perpendiculum eidem impendent. Atqui hae, altitudine e c = f d, ac diametro e f = c d, definiuntur. Fundus itaque vasis divergentis aequè premitur, atque si cylindro aequalis altitudinis, & baseos fluidum committeretur.

417 Thirdly: in a divergent vessel (Fig. LII.) the base c d is pressed no otherwise than if the fluid contained in it were in the cylinder e c d f: for it is clear that the columns m m, l l, etc. rest upon the walls of the vessel itself as on supports, and that only those rest upon the base which hang perpendicularly over it. But these are defined by the height e c = f d and the diameter e f = c d. The bottom of a divergent vessel is therefore pressed just as if the fluid were committed to a cylinder of equal height and base.

> 418 *Quartò*: In convergente demùm vase commonstrandum superest, fundum K H (Fig. LIII.) non minus urgeri ab ipso fluido, quàm si vas aequabilem ubivis amplitudinem K Q T H servaret. Libet praecipuum hoc, Hydrostaticae caput, pereleganti ratiocinio Cl. Varignon [^135-s1] stabilire: Demittantur ex marginibus superioribus, & secundum diametrum oppositis (B & C) ad fundum perpendiculares B M, & C O; tum portio baseos K M in partes aequales, aut minores dimidiae lineae M O dirimatur, ac tali in numero, qui semper aequetur summae terminorum progressionis duplae, incipientis ab unitate ex. gr. in 3, in 7, in 15, in 31, in 63 &c. Nempè K M dividatur, si lubet in K U, U L, L M; acceptisque M N, & O N aequalibus, cuique harum partium, agantur K Q, L R, A N, T H parallelae, & aequales ipsi B M, vel C O.

418 Fourthly: it remains, finally, to be shown that in a convergent vessel the bottom K H (Fig. LIII.) is urged by the fluid itself no less than if the vessel kept everywhere an even breadth K Q T H. I wish to establish this principal head of Hydrostatics by the very elegant reasoning of the illustrious Varignon (l): let the perpendiculars B M and C O be let fall to the bottom from the upper margins (B and C), opposite each other along the diameter; then let the portion K M of the base be divided into parts equal to, or smaller than, half the line M O, and in such a number as is always equal to the sum of the terms of a double progression beginning from unity, e.g. into 3, into 7, into 15, into 31, into 63, etc. Namely, let K M be divided, if you please, into K U, U L, L M; and, M N and O N having been taken equal to each of these parts, let K Q, L R, A N, T H be drawn parallel and equal to B M or C O.

> [^135-s1]: Memoires de l' Academ. 1692. p. 16. edit. Holland.

[^135-s1]: Memoires de l’Academ. 1692, p. 16, Holland ed.

[p. 136]

> 419 His constitutis, columna fluidi B N, libramentum exercebit super fulcro M adversus columnam E M, quae basis margine E D coercetur: exercebit (inquam) perindè ac faceret pondus Z super bilance E X, cujus hypomoclion foret in Y, & brachii extremum E per marginem tubi K E D retineretur. Igitur quoniam hoc pacto onus à fulcro Y sustentatum duplum foret ponderis Z; brachia quippè vectis E X aequantur, aut ab aequalitate parum deerrant, sustineret utique proindè fulcimentum, & pondus, & alioquin simul resistentiam huic aequalem; iccircò punctum M, aut portio L N ipsiusmet fundi, duplo columnae B N praematur, necesse est, seu perindè urgebitur pars L N, atque si R N, columna foret integra fluidi, ac fundo immineret.

419 These things being set up, the column of fluid B N will exert a balancing action upon the fulcrum M against the column E M, which is confined by the margin E D of the base: it will exert it (I say) just as the weight Z would do upon the balance E X, if its hypomochlion were at Y and the extremity E of its arm were held back by the margin of the tube K E D. Since, therefore, in this way the load sustained by the fulcrum Y would be double the weight Z (for the arms of the lever E X are equal, or depart little from equality), the support would accordingly sustain both the weight and, at the same time, a resistance equal to it; therefore it is necessary that the point M, or the portion L N of the bottom itself, be pressed by double the column B N; or the part L N will be urged just as if R N were an entire column of fluid and hung over the bottom.

> 420 Quapropter si spectetur A N L E D tanquàm columna hujuscemodi, comperietur similiter, quod, dum fluidum sese librat super fulcimento L contra fluidi K E L portionem, retentam obstante vasis margine K E, pars fundi K N premenda sit à fluido A N K D B; haud secùs, atque à columna aequali Q N. Pari modo fluidum A N, H, F C, fundi partem N H premet perindè, ac si columna aequalis N T insisteret. Quocirca fluidi tota moles B D K H F C, totum fundum K H ea praecise virium quantitate premet, qua is gravaretur per fluidum Q K H T, paris altitudinis, & latitudinis ubique aequalis basi K H. Atque hoc pressionis fluidorum fundamentum inter alia firmatur experimento, quo tubi plures aequè alti constituuntur, singulorumque fundus aequali apertura pertunditur, aequalibus obturamentis arcenda; eventus namque palam faciet, vim eandem ad sustinenda singulorum obturamenta adhiberi oportere, quamcumque figuram, aut situm vasa haec sortiantur.

420 Wherefore, if A N L E D is regarded as a column of this kind, it will be found similarly that, while the fluid balances itself upon the support L against the portion K E L of the fluid, held back by the margin K E of the vessel standing in its way, the part K N of the bottom must be pressed by the fluid A N K D B no otherwise than by the equal column Q N. In like manner the fluid A N, H, F C will press the part N H of the bottom just as if an equal column N T stood upon it. Wherefore the whole mass of the fluid B D K H F C will press the whole bottom K H with precisely that quantity of forces with which it would be weighed down by the fluid Q K H T, of equal height and of a breadth everywhere equal to the base K H. And this foundation of the pressure of fluids is confirmed, among other things, by an experiment in which several equally high tubes are set up and the bottom of each is pierced with an equal opening, to be closed with equal stoppers; for the outcome will make plain that the same force must be applied to sustain the stoppers of each, whatever figure or position these vessels may have.

> Lex II. *Fluida in omnem partem premunt.*

LAW II. FLUIDS PRESS IN EVERY DIRECTION .

> 421 Fluida deorsum versùs niti, quemadmodum gravia cetera, dubium est [?] nemini. In latera verò conniti, ex ipso pressu, qui secundum gravitatis directionem efficitur, partium habilitate ad motum, earumdem figurâ, exilitate, ac dissociatione répeti perfacilè explicarique potest. Intelligatur enim massa fluidi in columnas, conflatas ex exilissimis sphaerulis, & secundum paucula plana se contingentibus, divisa. (Fig. LIV.) Quoniam partes columnae 3a. impressioni cuivis cedunt promptissimè, & in motum facillimè cientur, dum directione perpendiculari premuntur, locum hunc situmque suum nequaquam servarent, nisi à moleculis columnae ab, & 4c, atque omni ex parte retinerentur. Premuntur igitur sphaerulae minimae secundum latera, & puncta contactuum: id quod de omnibus columnis est concludendum.

421 That fluids strive downward, as do other heavy bodies, no one doubts. But that they also strive against the sides can very easily be traced back to, and explained from, the very pressure which is produced along the direction of gravity, and from the aptness of their parts for motion, their figure, minuteness and disconnection. For let a mass of fluid be understood to be divided into columns composed of most minute spherules touching one another in a very few planes. (Fig. LIV.) Since the parts of the column 3a yield most promptly to any pressure, and are very easily set in motion while they are pressed in a perpendicular direction, they would by no means keep this place and position of theirs unless they were held back by the molecules of the columns ab and 4c, and on every side. The smallest spherules are therefore pressed along their sides and points of contact: which must be concluded of all the columns.

> 422 Demùm ex pressu, quo urgentur vi gravitatis, consequitur, fluida quoque ex imo premere in sublime, dum scilicet aliis prementibus deorsum, adtolluntur, ferè ut in bilance gravius solidum suomet descensu alterum sublevat. Stabiliunt Legem hanc plurima [p. 137] indicia occurrentia phaenomena. Ex vase ad horizontem inclinato liquor non profluèret, si corporum firmorum instar in subjectum duntaxat planum vim suam exsereret: navis è latere hians aquam hoc loco excipit, ac tantò quidem celerius, quò altius circumfusa navigio supra foramen aqua eminet: dolium quacumque parte pertusum liquori exitum praebet.

422 Finally, from the pressure by which they are urged by the force of gravity, it follows that fluids also press from below upward, namely when, others pressing downward, they are raised up, almost as in a balance the heavier solid lifts the other by its descent. Many indications establish this law, phenomena [p. 137] that occur daily. From a vessel inclined to the horizon the liquid would not flow out if, like firm bodies, it exerted its force only on the underlying plane; a ship gaping at the side takes in water at that place, and the more quickly, the higher the water surrounding the vessel stands above the hole: a cask pierced in any part whatever affords an exit to the liquid.

> 423 Uno tentamine omnigenam fluidorum pressionem explorare licebit. Si namque plura inserantur vasi foramina, aliud imminens horizonti ad perpendiculum, aliud verticale eidem, aliud lateri committatur, aperturae obturamentum è subere aptetur, ea lege, ut foramini exactè quidem congruat, leviori tamen impressione queat dimoveri; tunc enim, immisso liquore, observabitur, ab aqua ad altitudinem aperturae pertingente suber protrudi; seu imo, seu laterali, sive in verticem prorrecto foramini, fuerit insertum.

423 By a single trial one may explore the pressure of fluids in every direction. For if several holes are made in a vessel, one looking perpendicularly down toward the horizon, another vertical to it, another let into the side, and a stopper of cork is fitted to each opening under the condition that it fit the hole exactly, yet can be removed by a rather light impression; then, the liquid being let in, it will be observed that the cork is pushed out by the water reaching the height of the opening, whether it was inserted in the bottom hole, the lateral one, or the one stretched out toward the top.

> Lex III. *Fluida homogenea se componunt ad libellam, sive ad eandem horizontalem lineam.*

LAW III. HOMOGENEOUS FLUIDS ARRANGE THEMSELVES AT A LEVEL, OR ALONG THE SAME HORIZONTAL LINE .

> 424 Nimirùm omnes fluidi partes sese mutuò, non secundum perpendiculares lineas tantùm, verùm & secundum obliquas in aequilibrio sustinent. Atque de primo indubium est; scilicet secundum perpendiculares lineas, fluida aequilibrare semet; una quippè è columnis, in quas divisum cogitatur, nequit descendere, quin vicinae, & contingentes ascendant: quemadmodùm pondus in lance una deprimi non potest, quin alterum in altera eodem ipso tempore adtollatur. In homogeneis certè patescit, momenta columnarum fluidi aequari; partium enim ad descensum nisus, ac velocitas est omnium aequalis, massa quoque ejusdem inter eas generis; vis igitur ad motum in singulis par habetur.

424 Namely, all the parts of a fluid sustain one another mutually in equilibrium, not only along perpendicular lines but also along oblique ones. And as to the first there is no doubt, namely that fluids balance themselves along perpendicular lines; for one of the columns into which the fluid is thought to be divided cannot descend unless the neighboring and contiguous ones ascend: just as a weight in one pan cannot be depressed without the other in the other pan being raised at that very same time. In homogeneous fluids, certainly, it is evident that the momenta of the columns of the fluid are equal; for the striving of the parts toward descent, and their velocity, is equal in all, and so also is the mass, being of the same kind among them; the force for motion is therefore held to be equal in each.

> 425 Deindè, quoniam (*per Legem II.*) pressio fluidorum in omnem partem porrigitur, columnae perpendiculares ab obliquis librantur. Quo circa inter omnes fluidi homogenei partes aequilibratio obtinebitur: neque una ejus portio supra horizontalem lineam altius exsurget, quàm altera. Quod quidem experientiae haud adversatur, quâ notum, liquorem ad labia vasis paululum adsurgere: aut, si spatium, quo fluidum comprehenditur protendatur amplius, in convexam abire superficiem eas partes, quae ab extremis versùs medium protenduntur; primum namque ab ipsa liquoris, & laterum vasis proportione, atque adeò adhaesione proficiscitur: alterum ab aequilibrij lege pendet omninò; si quidem telluris superficiei, dum fluida sese adaptant, necessum est, ut quamvis in minore spatio rectam, quoad sensum, lineam tueantur, in majori tamen, superficiem versus centrum suam aequabiliter extrorsum flectant.

425 Next, since (by Law II.) the pressure of fluids extends in every direction, the perpendicular columns are balanced by the oblique ones. Wherefore equilibrium will be obtained among all the parts of a homogeneous fluid; nor will one portion of it rise higher above the horizontal line than another. This indeed is not contrary to experience, by which it is known that a liquid rises a little at the lips of the vessel; or that, if the space in which the fluid is comprised is extended more widely, those parts which stretch from the extremes toward the middle go off into a convex surface; for the first proceeds from the very proportion of the liquid and of the sides of the vessel, and so from adhesion; the second depends entirely on the law of equilibrium, since, while fluids adapt themselves to the surface of the earth, it is necessary that, though in a smaller space they keep a straight line so far as the senses go, yet in a larger one they bend their surface evenly outward with respect to the center.

> 426 Lex IV. *Fluida homogenea in tubis communicantibus* [*quemcumque hi situm obtineant*; & *quâcumque perimetro definiantur*] *ad eandem altitudinem suspensa aequilibrantur.*

426 Law IV. Homogeneous fluids in communicating tubes (whatever position these may hold, and by whatever perimeter they may be defined) are balanced when suspended to the same height.

> 427 In primis si aequali perimetro donentur tubi, & ad perpendiculum erigantur, res in comperto est. Deindè si ad [p. 138] horizontem inclinari ponantur, aequilibrii ratio non minus elucet (ex Lege I.) si demùm perimetri tuborum sint inaequales, ex Geostaticis eruitur principiis, fluida in aequilibrio futura, si obtineat quidem, ut reciproca molis in uno, & in altero velocitatis ratio habeatur. Atqui haec ratio est molis, ac velocitatis in fluido tubis ejusmodi contento. Statuatur enim tubus a b (Fig. LV.) amplitudine alterum C d, centies superare: fieri nequit, ut fluidum in illo deprimatur versus e, altitudine unius pollicis, quin motus in angustiore fiat ad altitudinem centum digitorum.

427 In the first place, if the tubes are endowed with an equal perimeter and are erected perpendicularly, the matter is ascertained. Next, if they are supposed to be inclined to the horizon, [p. 138] the reason of the equilibrium shines out no less (from Law I.). If, finally, the perimeters of the tubes are unequal, it is derived from the principles of Statics that the fluids will be in equilibrium if it holds that the ratio of the mass in the one is reciprocal to the ratio of the velocity in the other. But this ratio of mass and velocity is had in a fluid contained in tubes of this kind. For let the tube a b (Fig. LV.) be supposed to exceed the other, C d, a hundred times in breadth: it cannot happen that the fluid in the former is depressed toward e by the height of one inch without a motion taking place in the narrower one to the height of a hundred digits.

> 428 Est igitur sicuti moles fluidi ampliore tubo comprehensi ad molem in arctiore, ita *reciprocè* velocitas in hoc ad velocitatem in illo: momenta proindè utrinque sunt aequalia; atque hinc aequilibrium fluidi in utroque. Jam verò in homogeneis fluidis id tunc fieri, quum eandem ipsa altitudinem obtinent, patet: quum enim pressio sit in ratione composita altitudinis, & basis (ex Lege I.) si verticalis sectio e f, tanquam basis communis, spectetur & per eam horizontalis linea m n agatur, eriganturque perpendicula m a, n d, erit pressio versùs basim, ceu fundum parte una = e f m a, ex altera = e f n d. Quoniam verò momenta aequantur fluidi (*ex dictis*) & gravitas specifica (*ex hypoth.*) est eadem; ac propterea in mutuae pressionis ad invicèm comparatione hujus, ceu diversa foret, nulla sit ratio habenda: consequitur, pressum in crure utróque versùs e f, secundum directiones oppositas tendentem aequari, hoc est: e f m a = e f n d atque per e f dividendo facta, erit m a = n d, sive altitudines aequales, ac proindè m n, & a d, perpendicula aequalia intercipiunt. Est autem m n (*ex construct.*) horizontalis linea. Ergo a d, sivè superficies geminae fluidi in utroque tubo ad libellam constituuntur.

428 As, therefore, the mass of the fluid comprised in the wider tube is to the mass in the narrower, so reciprocally is the velocity in the latter to the velocity in the former: the momenta are therefore equal on both sides; and hence the equilibrium of the fluid in both. Now, that in homogeneous fluids this comes about when they obtain the same height is clear: for since the pressure is in the compound ratio of height and base (from Law I.), if the vertical section e f is regarded as a common base, and the horizontal line m n is drawn through it, and the perpendiculars m a, n d are erected, the pressure toward the base will be, on the one part, = e f m a, on the other = e f n d. But since the momenta of the fluid are equal (from what has been said), and the specific gravity (by hypothesis) is the same, and therefore in the mutual comparison of the pressure no account need be taken of it as though it were different, it follows that the pressure in each leg toward e f, tending in opposite directions, is equal, that is: e f m a = e f n d; and, division by e f being made, m a = n d will hold, or the heights are equal, and hence m n and a d intercept equal perpendiculars. But m n (by construction) is a horizontal line. Therefore a d, or the twin surface of the fluid in each tube, is settled at a level.

> 429 Lex V. *Fluida heterogenea in tubis communicantibus cujuscumvis [?] figurae atque perimetri, & quomodolibet ad horizontem inclinatis, in aequilibrio persistunt, quum illorum altitudines fuerint reciprocè, ut eorum gravitates specificae.*

429 Law V. Heterogeneous fluids in communicating tubes of any figure and perimeter whatever, and inclined to the horizon in any manner whatever, persist in equilibrium when their heights are reciprocally as their specific gravities.

> 430 Sint enim in tubis fluida hoc modo comparata, ut altitudo a E (Fig. LVI.) sit ad altitudinem b F, sicut est *reciprocè* gravitas specifica fluidi G ad gravitatem fluidi g: futurum assero, ut in aequilibrio conquiescant, quum etenim gravitatis diversae isthic habenda sit ratio, contrà atque in homogeneis momenta utriusque ac pressio versùs communem sectionem B D eo pacto inter sese conferri debent, ut gravitatis discrimen in considerationem adducatur: quamvis ubi seorsim spectantur, & citrà comparationem, pressio (*per Legem I.*) fluidorum duntaxat ex altitudine, & basi aestimetur; iccirco momentorum aequalitas obtinebitur, & aequilibrium consistet, quum eadem fuerit à centro motus distantiarum ratio, quae est *reciprocè* gravitatum (*per Princip. Stat. III.*)

430 For let fluids be so arranged in the tubes that the height a E (Fig. LVI.) is to the height b F as, reciprocally, the specific gravity of the fluid G is to the gravity of the fluid g: I assert that they will rest in equilibrium. For since account must here be taken of the diverse gravity, contrary to what holds in homogeneous fluids, the momenta of each, and the pressure toward the common section B D, must be compared with each other in such a way that the difference of gravity is brought into consideration: although, where they are regarded separately and without comparison, the pressure of fluids (by Law I.) is estimated only from height and base; therefore equality of momenta will be obtained, and the equilibrium will stand, when the ratio of the distances from the center of motion is the same as that which is reciprocally the ratio of the gravities (by Princip. Stat. III.)

> 431 At sectio communis, seu basis, velut centrum motus rectè intelligitur, altitudines verò sunt ipsae ab eodem distantiae; si [p. 139] quidem (*per Legem dictam*) pressio, libramentumque fluidorum, quum ex se expectantur, ab his pendeat, ac repetatur, oportet. Aequilibrium igitur fluida heterogenea component, si altitudines fuerint *reciprocè*, ut specificae ipsorum gravitates.

431 But the common section, or base, is understood as the center of motion; and the heights themselves are the distances from it; since [p. 139] indeed (by the Law cited) the pressure and balancing of fluids, when they are regarded in themselves, must depend upon these and be derived from them. Heterogeneous fluids will therefore compose an equilibrium if their heights are reciprocally as their specific gravities.

> 432 Lex VI. *Fluida actu fluentia, quum ex ampliore spatio in arctiùs transeunt, motum in ipso transfluxu accélerant.*

432 Law VI. Fluids in actual flow, when they pass from a wider space into a narrower one, accelerate their motion in the very passage.

> 433 Ponatur fluidum ex vase profluere hac lege, ut amplitudo spatii ex. gr. cylindri, decuplo sit major, quàm apertura, quae *lumen tubi* vocatur, ex qua fluidum erumpit: dico, fluidum decuplo majori celeritate ad aperturam erupturum, quàm movebatur in spatio latiore. Adigatur enim fluidum cylindro comprehensum vi quadamumcumque versùs angustiorem partem, eo quidem pacto, ut intervallo momenti unius pollicem spatii emetiri debeat. Perspicuum est fluidi massam decuplam, relatè ad diametrum orificii, promoveri non posse hac ratione, quin eodem simul tempore per arctiorem partem, fluidi portio digiti spatium altitudine aequans, & decuplo major latitudine orificii, indè propellatur. Atqui fluidi quantitas pollicem unum alta, & latitudine aperturam decies continens, nequit data temporis intercapedine spatium decuplo minus permeare, quin celeritas decuplo augescat; necessum igitur est, ut decem partes, quas longitudo vel altitudo digiti complectitur, totidem partibus, in quas latitudo foraminis dirimitur, per ordinem respondeant, sive adplicentur momento temporis eodem. Id, quod citra incrementum celeritatis ad decuplum fieri haud potest: quum ad motus celeritatem perindè sit omnino, sive corpus = 1/10 spatii dato tempore percurrat spatium coporis decuplum, seu moles corporea decuplo major, quam sit extensio spatii, eodem tempore per spatium = 1/10 parti corporis feratur.

433 Let a fluid be supposed to flow out of a vessel under this condition, that the breadth of the space, e.g. of a cylinder, is ten times greater than the opening, which is called the lumen of the tube, from which the fluid bursts out: I say that the fluid will burst out at the opening with a velocity ten times greater than that with which it moved in the wider space. For let the fluid comprised in the cylinder be driven by any force whatever toward the narrower part, in such a way that in the interval of one moment it must traverse an inch of space. It is clear that a tenfold mass of fluid, relative to the diameter of the orifice, cannot be moved forward in this way without a portion of the fluid, equaling in height the space of a digit and ten times greater than the breadth of the orifice, being at the same time driven out thence through the narrower part. But a quantity of fluid one inch high, and containing the opening ten times in breadth, cannot pass through a space ten times smaller in the given interval of time unless its velocity grows tenfold; it is therefore necessary that the ten parts which the length or height of the digit comprises correspond in order to as many parts into which the breadth of the hole is divided, or be applied to them in the same moment of time. This cannot be done without an increase of the velocity to tenfold: since, as regards the velocity of motion, it is altogether the same whether a body = 1/10 of the space runs through, in a given time, a space ten times the body, or a corporeal mass ten times greater than the extension of the space is carried in the same time through a space = 1/10 part of the body.

> 434 Deindè res eadem hoc etiam momento nititur, quòd quum fluidum ex latiore spatio transit in arctius, partes laterales constrictos aperturae parietes offendant, atque adeò impedimentum suimet effluxus habeant; à fluido autèm urgente identidem, & liberiùs sese per spatium largius infundente constringantur arctiori tramite: hoc verò pacto fit, ut fluentis liquidi partes per orificium rectà libereque fluxurae, impetum faciant majorem, atque facilem sibi exitum nactae illicò foras profiliant: quam obrem necesse est, ut motus celeritas capiat incrementum.

434 Next, the same thing rests also on this ground, that when a fluid passes from a wider space into a narrower, the lateral parts strike against the narrowed walls of the opening and so meet with a hindrance to their own outflow; but, the fluid continually urging them and pouring itself more freely through the larger space, they are squeezed into the narrower path; and in this way it comes about that the parts of the flowing liquid that are to flow straight and freely through the orifice make a greater impetus and, having found an easy exit, at once leap out: for which reason it is necessary that the velocity of the motion receive an increase.

[p. 140]

> De Fluidorum cum solidis immersis aequilibrii ratione.

ON THE RATIO OF THE EQUILIBRIUM OF FLUIDS WITH IMMERSED SOLIDS .

> 435 Modò fluidorum inter se pressione considerata, explicanda [?] superest eorum cum solidis immersis aequilibrii ratio. De hoc argumento post Archimedem [^140-s1] Galilaeus, Stevinus, Mersennus, Boylius, Varignonius, Mariottus, Newtonus, aliique permulti egerunt: nos rem summatim expendemus, paucis legibus doctrinam complectendo: quas priusquam per ordinem connectamus, immersionis librationisque solidorum in fluidis corporum veluti naturam contemplemur paululum est necesse. Nimirum grave solidum fluido gravi nequit immergi, nisi volumen fluidi par ipsi solido, quod per immersionem recipitur, sua de statione dimoveatur [?].

435 Having just considered the pressure of fluids among themselves, there remains to be explained the ratio of their equilibrium with immersed solids. On this subject, after Archimedes (m), Galileo, Stevin, Mersenne, Boyle, Varignon, Mariotte, Newton and very many others have treated: we shall weigh the matter summarily, embracing the doctrine in a few laws; before we connect these in order, it is necessary to contemplate a little what is, as it were, the nature of the immersion and balancing of solid bodies in fluids. Namely, a heavy solid cannot be immersed in a heavy fluid unless a volume of the fluid equal to the solid itself, which is received by the immersion, is moved from its station.

> [^140-s1]: Libri duo qui vulgò nuncupantur De insidentibus humido, commentariis illustrati à Federico Commandino [?].

[^140-s1]: The two books commonly called De insidentibus humido, illustrated with commentaries by Federico Commandino.

> 436 Excipe tamen, nisi corpus sit spongiosum: tunc enim fluidum magna parte subit poros solidi; aut nisi hoc immersum dissolvatur facilè: eo quippe casu particulae à solido avulsae fluidi poris se insinuabunt. Quamobrem, ut immersio reapse consequatur, solidum pondere suo resistentiam massae fluidi, suo loco excludendae vincat necesse est: unde fit, ut tanta praecisè corporis solidi pars intra fluidum sit recipienda, quantum est volumen seu moles, quam solidum suomet pondere dimovere loco suo potest: atque ut immersio eo usque pergat, donec idem volumen immerso corpori pondere sit aequale [?]. Luculenter ista intelligentur, si fluidum in partes, seu columnas aequales mente dispescatur, unique earum corpus solidum respondere atque incumbere cogitetur. Hoc intellecto consequuntur pro triplici conditione, totidem leges.

436 Except, however, if the body is spongy: for then the fluid in great part enters the pores of the solid; or unless, being immersed, it is easily dissolved; for in that case the particles torn from the solid will insinuate themselves into the pores of the fluid. Wherefore, in order that immersion actually follow, the solid must by its weight overcome the resistance of the mass of fluid to be excluded from its place: whence it comes about that precisely so great a part of the solid body is to be received within the fluid as is the volume, or mass, which the solid can move from its place by its own weight; and that the immersion proceeds until that same volume is equal in weight to the immersed body. These things will be clearly understood if the fluid is divided in the mind into equal parts, or columns, and the solid body is thought to correspond to, and rest upon, one of them. This being understood, there follow, for a threefold condition, as many laws.

> Leges de motu libratorio solidorum fluidis immersorum.

LAWS OF THE BALANCING MOTION OF SOLIDS IMMERSED IN FLUIDS .

> 437 Lex I. *Si corpus solidum ejusdem fuerit gravitatis specificae cum fluido, in quo immergitur, sistet intra fluidi superficiem ubivis, & in quo fuerit constitutum loco, immotum persistet* [?].

437 Law I. If a solid body is of the same specific gravity as the fluid in which it is immersed, it will remain unmoved anywhere within the surface of the fluid, and in the place in which it has been set.

> 438 Quoniam solidum ac fluidum sub aequalibus dimensionibus eadem pollent gravitate, eo prorsus modo se habet solidum, quo illud fluidi volumen, cujus locum illud occupat. Atqui fluidi volumen hoc ante immersionem cum ceteris fluidi partibus suo in loco immotum aequilibrium servaverat. Solidum ergo immersum etiam cum illis in aequilibrio conquiescit. Id clarè percipietur, si fluidum in columnas aequales illi, cui solidum innititur, divisum concipiatur, ac fluidi volumen loco suo expulsum, à reliqua sua mole avelli, substituto illic solido immerso [?].

438 Since the solid and the fluid have the same gravity under equal dimensions, the solid behaves in altogether the same way as that volume of the fluid whose place it occupies. But this volume of the fluid, before the immersion, had kept its equilibrium with the other parts of the fluid, unmoved in its place. Therefore the immersed solid also rests in equilibrium with them. This will be clearly perceived if the fluid is conceived to be divided into columns equal to that on which the solid rests, and the volume of fluid expelled from its place is supposed to be torn away from the rest of its mass, the immersed solid being substituted there.

[p. 141]

> 439 Lex II. *Si corpus solidum specificè sit levius fluido, cum immergitur, illud aliqua solùm parte demergetur.*

439 Law II. If a solid body is specifically lighter than the fluid in which it is immersed, it is sunk in it with only some part of itself.

> 440 Fluidum namque (*ex hypoth.*) est specificè gravius solido. Igitur fluidum, minori sub volumine acceptum pondere adaequat ipsum solidum, sic ut volumen hoc fluidi unam duntaxat solidi partem exaequet. At immersio corporis solidi eo usquè tantùm pertingit, donec fluidi volumen expulsum tanti sit ponderis, quanti est immersum corpus (per §. 435.) ergo solidum specificè levius fluido, aliqua sui parte solum illi immergitur.

440 For the fluid (by hypothesis) is specifically heavier than the solid. Therefore the fluid, taken under a smaller volume, will equal the solid itself in weight, so that this volume of the fluid equals only one part of the solid. But the immersion of the solid body reaches only so far, until the volume of fluid expelled is of as great a weight as the immersed body (by §. 435.); therefore a solid specifically lighter than the fluid is sunk into it with only some part of itself.

> 441 Lex III. *Si corpus solidum specificè sit gravius fluido, huic illud totum immergitur, ejusque fundum petit.*

441 Law III. If a solid body is specifically heavier than the fluid, it is wholly immersed in it and seeks its bottom.

> 442 Solidum eo usque immergitur, donec volumen fluidi loco suo extrusum, illi pondere sit aequale, (per §. 435.) Itaque si volumen expulsum minus ponderis contineat, quàm corpus solidum, hoc totum immergetur. At vero fluidi volumen illud minoris est ponderis, ponitur quippè corpus solidum specificè graviùs: fluidum proindè suo aequali volumine minus ponderis comprehendit. Solidum ergo totum immergetur. Porrò immersum hac lege ubi fuerit, quum in quavis à fundo distantia obtineat, illam fluidi columnam, quae solido est subjecta, majori pondere atque ad pressum majore nisu pollere, quàm ceteras; illa cum his aequilibrium non constituet: proindè fiet, ut nuspiam immotum consistat corpus solidum, sed in vasis fundum praecipitet sese. Hinc

442 The solid is immersed until the volume of fluid thrust out of its place is equal to it in weight (by §. 435.). Therefore, if the expelled volume contains less weight than the solid body, the latter will be wholly immersed. But that volume of fluid is of less weight; for the solid body is supposed to be specifically heavier: the fluid therefore comprises less weight in a volume equal to it. The solid will therefore be wholly immersed. Further, once it is immersed by this law, since at any distance whatever from the bottom it holds that the column of fluid which is placed under the solid has a greater weight, and is able to press with a greater striving than the others, that column will not establish equilibrium with these: hence it will come about that the solid body nowhere stands unmoved, but hurls itself to the bottom of the vessel. Hence

> Corollarium.

COROLLARY. 443

> 443 Quum solidum immersum fluidi volumen loco excludat, hoc autem à ceteris ejusdem partibus suo in situ fuerit sustentatum: necessum est, ut ubi solidum in expulsi voluminis locum succedit, ab iisdem fluidi partibus tantumdem ponderis, quantum in ipso solido est sustentetur, nempè quantum suo de situ dimota fluidi portio continet: ac proindè, ut solidum tanto sui ponderis veluti privetur, quanti est volumen fluidi, quod immersione facta loco suo exclusum fuit. Pondus hoc solidi diminutum *respectiva*, *comparativa*, aut *adparens gravitas* nuncupari adsolet; quum altera, quae corpori in spatio penitùs vacuo competeret, *vera*, & *absoluta* rectè adpelletur.

Since the immersed solid excludes a volume of the fluid from its place, and this had been sustained in its position by the other parts of the same fluid, it is necessary that, where the solid succeeds into the place of the excluded volume, as much weight is sustained in the solid itself by those same parts of the fluid as the portion of the fluid moved from its position contains; and hence that the solid is, as it were, deprived of as much of its weight as is the volume of fluid that was excluded from its place when the immersion was made. This diminished weight of the solid is wont to be called respective, comparative, or apparent gravity; while the other, which belongs to the body in a space altogether void, is rightly called true and absolute.

> 444 Unde quia gravitas haec à sola differentia, quae est inter specificam gravitatem utriusque, hoc est, à densitatis discrimine proficiscitur, iccircò ejusdem solidi immersi respectiva gravitas eadem est, sive immersum corpus fluidi superficiem coaequet, seu profundiùs agatur, posita fluidi ubivis aequabili densitate. Porrò id quod absolutae gravitati decedit, sive jactura ponderis, quam facit idem solidum in diversis fluidis eam rationem habet, quàm gravitates specificae fluidorum. Jacturae verò, quas diversa solida eodem in fluido accipiunt sunt inter se, ut ipsa volumina solidorum.

444 Hence, since this gravity proceeds solely from the difference which exists between the specific gravity of each, that is, from the difference of densities, the respective gravity of the same immersed solid is therefore the same whether the immersed body is level with the surface of the fluid or is driven more deeply, the density of the fluid being supposed everywhere equal. Further, that which departs from the absolute gravity, or the loss of weight which the same solid suffers in different fluids, has the same ratio as the specific gravities of the fluids. But the losses which different solids undergo in the same fluid are to one another as the volumes themselves of the solids.

[p. 142]

> PHYSICES

PHYSICS,

> PARS III.

PART III .

> ELECTROLOGIA seu

ELECTROLOGY, or

> De Virtute Electrica.

ON ELECTRIC VIRTUE .

> 445 Nihil fortassè est, quod nostra hac aetate majus Naturali scientiae studio decus, atque incrementum adtulerit, aut acrius Philosophorum excitarit ingenia, quàm *vis electrica*, ut proindè turpe videatur Naturae arcana inquirentibus pulcherrimam hanc Philosophiae partem aut neglexisse penitùs, quod fecerunt Veteres, aut vix leviter adtigisse, quod & Recentiores plurimi, nescio qua de causa fecére. Quapropter, ne quidquam quod ad rem hanc pertineat praetermittam, Clarissimis ex universa Europa Philosophis, praecipuè verò Cl. *Pauliano* [^142-s1] facem praeferentibus, quaestionem hanc utilissimam sanè ac jocundissimam, primus omnium in America nostra, adcuratiori methodo, majorique quâ possim claritate tradere decrevi.

here is perhaps nothing which in this age of ours has brought 445 T greater honor and increase to the study of Natural science, or has more keenly roused the wits of Philosophers, than the electric force, so that it seems shameful for those who inquire into the secrets of Nature either to have entirely neglected this most beautiful part of Philosophy, as the Ancients did, or to have barely touched it lightly, as very many of the Moderns too have done, for I know not what reason. Wherefore, so as not to pass over anything that pertains to this matter, with the most illustrious Philosophers of all Europe, and especially the illustrious Paulian (n), carrying the torch before me, I have resolved to hand down this question, truly most useful and most pleasant, first of all in our America, by a more accurate method and with the greatest clarity I can.

> [^142-s1]: Grand Dictionnaire de Physique, Verb. Electricité, ex quo, paucis immutatis, universam hanc excerpsimus Dissertat.

[^142-s1]: Grand Dictionnaire de Physique, under the word Electricité, from which, with a few changes, we have excerpted this whole Dissertation.

> 446 In hac ergò de causis electricae virtutis pertractandâ quaestione, de qua maximâ cum animorum contentione ab annis fermè sexaginta disputatur apud Recentiores Physicos, methodum selegimus sequentem. I. Praemittemus definitiones aliquot, quae jure vocantur *primae notiones Electricitatis*. II. Electrica referemus experimenta, quae necessariò debent exponi in qualibet hypothesi physicâ. III. Varias trademus celebriorum Physicorum sententias circa materiam electricam, ipsarumque naevos indicabimus. IV. Sententiam Cl. Pauliani, quae & nostra est, aperiemus, in eaque phaenomena jam relata tentabimus exponere. V denique. Proponemus & solvere conabimur praecipua argumenta, quae contra nostram sententiam fieri ab adversariis solent.

446 In treating, then, this question of the causes of electric virtue, about which there has been dispute, with the greatest contention of minds, among the Modern Physicists for nearly sixty years, we have chosen the following method. I. We shall set down beforehand some definitions, which are rightly called the first notions of Electricity. II. We shall report the electric experiments which must necessarily be explained in any physical hypothesis. III. We shall hand down the various opinions of the more celebrated Physicists concerning electric matter, and shall point out their blemishes. IV. We shall disclose the opinion of the illustrious Paulian, which is ours too, and in it we shall attempt to explain the phenomena already reported. V. Finally, we shall propose, and try to answer, the principal arguments that are usually brought by adversaries against our opinion.

[p. 143]

## CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

> De notionibus ad quaestionem virtutis Electricae praeámbulis.

On the notions preliminary to the question of electric virtue.

> 447 *Notio* I. Componitur Electrica machina *primò*, globo vitreo, cujus diameter potest esse major vel minor: *secundò*, rota lignea, cujus ope motus rotationis imprimitur vitreo globo, quem manus sicca ádfricat: *tertiò*, tubo ferreo, qui per tenuissimas orichalci laméllas cum vitreo globo communicationem habet: *quartò*, funículis sericis, qui ferreum tubum suspensum tenent horizontaliter: *quintò* deniquè, scabéllo resináceo in modum placentae confecto, in quo possit homo suis stans pedibus, facilè, commodèque constitui. Exactè admodum repraesentatur haec machina per Fig LVII.

447 Notion I. An electric machine is composed, first, of a glass globe, whose diameter can be larger or smaller; second, of a wooden wheel, by whose means a rotary motion is impressed on the glass globe, which a dry hand rubs; third, of an iron tube, which has communication with the glass globe through very thin plates of brass; fourth, of silk cords, which hold the iron tube suspended horizontally; fifth, finally, of a stool of resin made in the shape of a cake, on which a man can easily and conveniently be placed standing on his feet. This machine is represented quite exactly by Fig. LVII.

> 448 *Notio* II. Corpus actu electricum, est corpus versus quod eunt, & à quo redeunt corpora quaeque levissima, qualia sunt tabaccum tritum, orichalci folia tenuissima, avium plúmulae &c. Virtus namque electrica manifestari solet per adtractiones, repulsiones, scintillas, inflammationes, motitationes &c. Sese prodit etiam virtus electrica per flammam caeruleam, quae cum crepitu excitatur ex corpore electrico. Lóquimur hìc de hac electricitatis specie, quam in pósterum *totalem*, & *perfectam* adpellabimus. *Notio* III. Ex corporibus alia sunt *per se*, & alia *per communicationem* electrica. Cera obsignatoria (vulgò *lacre*), súccinum, alúmen, ádamas, crystállum, ac praecipuè vitrum sunt córpora *per se* electrica. Metalla autèm & corpora viventia sunt corpora *per communicationem* electrica.

448 Notion II. A body actually electric is a body toward which all very light bodies go, and from which they come back, such as ground tobacco, very thin leaves of brass, the little feathers of birds, etc. For electric virtue is usually manifested by attractions, repulsions, sparks, inflammations, agitations, etc. Electric virtue betrays itself also by a blue flame, which is excited with a crackling from the electric body. We speak here of that species of electricity which we shall hereafter call total and perfect. Notion III. Of bodies, some are electric in themselves, and others by communication. Sealing wax (commonly lacre), amber, alum, diamond, crystal, and especially glass are bodies electric in themselves. Metals, however, and living bodies are bodies electric by communication.

> 449 *Notio* IV. Corpora *per se* electrica virtutem suam manifestant, quotiescumque panno, vel papyro, vel manu sicca fricantur. Corpora autèm *per communicationem* electrica vim electricam perfectam concipiunt, quotiescumque per filum ferreum, aut per funiculum cannábinum communicationem habent cum corporibus *per se*, & actu eléctricis. *Notio* V. Corpora *per se* electrica nullam, aut quasi nullam virtutem electricam per communicationem, & vice versa: corpora *per communicationem* electrica nullam, aut quasi nullam virtutem electricam per frictionem acquirunt. *Notio* VI. Omnia omninò orbis hujus corpora sunt verosimiliter, aut *per se*, aut *per communicationem* electrica.

449 Notion IV. Bodies electric in themselves manifest their virtue whenever they are rubbed with cloth, or paper, or a dry hand. Bodies electric by communication, however, receive a perfect electric force whenever they have communication, through an iron wire or a hempen cord, with bodies electric in themselves and in act. Notion V. Bodies electric in themselves acquire no electric virtue, or as good as none, by communication; and conversely, bodies electric by communication acquire no electric virtue, or as good as none, by friction. Notion VI. All the bodies of this world without exception are, in all likelihood, electric either in themselves or by communication.

[p. 144]

## CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

> De Praecipuis experimentis electricis.

On the principal electric experiments. 450

> 450 Historicè tantùm in hoc Cap. referemus experimenta praecipua, quae fieri solent ope electricae machinae, ipsisque per modum *observationum* subjiciemus experimenta, minus praecipua, & quasi secundaria.

In this Chapter we shall only report, historically, the principal experiments which are usually made by means of the electric machine, and to them we shall subjoin, by way of observations, the less principal and, as it were, secondary experiments.

> 451. Experimentum I. Motus circularis imprimatur ope rotae, globo vitreo, intereadùm adfricatúr manu sicca. Suspendatur horizontaliter funiculorum sericorum ope, tubus ex albo ferro (vulgò *oja de lata*) confectus, qui cum vitreo globo per tenues aliquot orichalci láminas communicationem habeat. Tantam vim electricam cóncipiet ferreus tubus, ut statím flammulam caeruleam ex ipsius sinu cum crépitu prosilientem videas, si ad ipsum admoveas digitum, clavim, uno verbo, corpus quodcumque *per communicationem* electricum.

451 Experiment I. Let a circular motion be impressed by means of the wheel on the glass globe, while meanwhile it is rubbed with a dry hand. Let a tube made of white iron (commonly oja de lata), which has communication with the glass globe through some thin plates of brass, be suspended horizontally by means of silk cords.
