The iron tube will receive so great an electric force that you will at once see a little blue flame leaping out with a crackling from its bosom if you bring near it your finger, or a key, or, in a word, any body electric by communication.

> 452 Observationes I. Tubus idem ferreus funiculorum cannàbinorum ope suspensus vim electricam, vel nullam, vel admodùm exiguam cóncipit, quantòcumque motu rotationis donetur vitreus globus. II. Ex tubo ferreo electrica virtute donato, nullam omninò flammam excitabis, si versùs ipsum admoveas ceram obsignatoriam, túbulum vitreum, vel quodcumque aliud corpus per se electricum. III. Ex tubo ferreo nondùm eléctrica virtute donato pendeant duo fila cannábina sibi invicem parallela, à se invicèm haec duo fila recedent, atque ángulum efficient, statim ut vim electricam concipiet ferreus tubus. Imò quidem eò major erit angulus à duobus filis effectus, quò vividior erit electricitas tubi. Hinc *Electrometri* nomen habent haec duo cannábina fila.

452 Observations. I. The same iron tube, suspended by means of hempen cords, receives either no electric force or very little, however great the motion of rotation with which the glass globe is endowed. II. From an iron tube endowed with electric virtue you will excite no flame at all if you bring near it sealing wax, a little glass tube, or any other body electric in itself. III. If two hempen threads, parallel to each other, hang from an iron tube not yet endowed with electric virtue, these two threads will recede from each other and form an angle as soon as the iron tube receives electric force. Indeed, the angle made by the two threads will be the greater, the livelier the electricity of the tube. Hence these two hempen threads have the name of Electrometer.

> 453 Experimentum II. Super corpus *per se* electricum; qualis est placenta resinácea, collocetur animal quodcumque, & ope fili ferrei communicationem habeat hoc animal cum tubo de quo loquebamur in experimento I: tantam vim electricam quasi subitò concipiet, ut si digitum admoveas, ex ipso cum crepitu prorumpat flamma caerulea, quae tùm tibi, tùm ipsi dolorem pariat adeò sensibilem, ut vos aciculam leviter pupugisse statim credidêritis.

453 Experiment II. Upon a body electric in itself, such as a cake of resin, let any animal be placed, and let this animal have communication, by means of an iron wire, with the tube of which we spoke in experiment I: it will receive so great an electric force, almost suddenly, that if you bring your finger near, a blue flame will burst out from it with a crackling, which will cause both you and it a pain so sensible that you would at once believe you had been lightly pricked with a needle.

> 454 Observationes. I Ad quamcumque distantiam ex tubo ferreo reperiatur placenta resinacea, is qui fuit super illam collocatus, virtutem electricam statim acquiret dummodò per filum ferreum, aut per funiculum cannábinum mádidum cum eléctrico tubo communicationem habeat. II Qui super placentam resinaceam collocatur, is flammam non éxcitat ex electrico tubo quo [p. 145] cum habet communicationem III Si quis humi consistens manu teneat vas aliquod metallicum in quo reperiatur spiritus vini calidus, ipsumque offerat homini super placentam resinaceam collocato, liquorem hunc homo jam electricus inflammabit, quotiescumque ignem ex illo tentabit excitare. IV. Idem prorsùs phaenomenum accidit, quum homo jam electricus vas metallicum manu tenet, & homo electricâ virtute destitutus flammam tentat excitare.

454 Observations. I. At whatever distance from the iron tube the cake of resin is found, he who has been placed upon it will at once acquire electric virtue, provided he has communication with the electric tube through an iron wire or a wet hempen cord. II. He who is placed upon the cake of resin does not excite a flame from the electric tube with which [p. 145] he is in communication. III. If someone standing on the ground holds in his hand some metal vessel containing warm spirit of wine, and offers it to a man placed on the resin cake, this man, now electric, will set the liquor on fire as often as he tries to draw fire from it. IV. Exactly the same phenomenon occurs when the man who is now electric holds the metal vessel in his hand, and a man destitute of electric virtue tries to draw the flame.

> 455 Experimentum III. Corpora quaeque levissima, qualia sunt tabacum tritum, auri vel argenti laminae tenuiores, avium plúmulae, furfur &c. nunc adtrahuntur versus corpus electrica virtute donatum, nùnc repelluntur ab hoc corpore, nùnc adhaerent huic eidem córpori. Imò quidem sese manifestat electrica virtus per itus, & reditus corporum hujusmodi levissimorum.

455 Experiment III. All the lightest bodies, such as ground tobacco, the thinner leaves of gold or silver, small bird feathers, bran, etc., are now attracted toward a body endowed with electric virtue, now repelled from this body, now cling to this same body. Indeed, electric virtue manifests itself by the goings and returnings of bodies of this kind, the lightest ones.

> 456 Observationes. I: electricae máchinae tubo ferreo superimponatur pátera quaedam metallica in qua reperiantur corpora levissima, tubum ferreum fugient haec omnia corpuscula statìm, ut virtutem electricam tubus concipiet. II. Si tubo ferreo subjecta fuisset haec eadem pátera, versùs tubum adtracta fuissent corpora levissima ipsi imposita, statím ut virtutem electricam tubus concepisset.

456 Observations. I. If on the iron tube of the electric machine there is placed some metal dish containing the lightest bodies, all these little bodies will flee the iron tube as soon as the tube receives the electric virtue. II. If this same dish had been placed under the iron tube, the lightest bodies put on it would have been attracted toward the tube as soon as the tube received the electric virtue.

> 457 Experimentum IV. Sit lagéna vitrea aquis semipléna, & folio metallico exteriùs cooperta. Sit in hac lagéna filum ferreum perpendiculariter erectum, quod ad fundum usque protendatur. Filo huic ferreo communicetùr éléctrica virtus; experientia constat, quod si quis lagénam hanc unâ manu per partem ipsius inferiorem sustineat, & alterâ manu flammam éxcitet ex supradicto filo, violentè commovebuntur duo ipsius cúbiti, & pectus (Fig. LVIII.)

457 Experiment IV. Let there be a glass flask half full of water and covered on the outside with metal foil. In this flask let an iron wire be set up perpendicularly, reaching down to the bottom. Let electric virtue be communicated to this iron wire; experience establishes that if someone holds up this flask with one hand by its lower part, and with the other hand draws a flame from the aforesaid wire, both his elbows and his chest will be violently shaken (Fig. LVIII.).

> 458 Observationes. I. Lagéna de qua loquimur, communicationem habeat cum tubo ferreo electrico, & quispiam unâ manu partem inferiorem lagénae tenens, aut etiam tangens, alterâ manu flammam excitet ex tubo, is eandem omninò commotionem experietur. II. Junctis manibus catenam efforment homines non pauci. Primus ex illis, partem inferiorem lagénae manu sustineat; ultimus verò flammam excitet ex electricae machinae tubo, omnes simul, & eodem instanti percutientur eâdem commotione, tùm in cúbitis, tùm in péctore. Ejusmodi experimentum primum Lugduni Batavorum factum fuit ideò vulgò experimentum primum, dicitur *La experiencia de Léyden*.

458 Observations. I. Let the flask of which we speak be in communication with the electric iron tube, and if anyone, holding or even touching the lower part of the flask with one hand, draws a flame from the tube with the other hand, he will feel exactly the same shock. II. Let a good many men form a chain with joined hands. Let the first of them hold up the lower part of the flask with his hand, and the last draw a flame from the tube of the electric machine; all will be struck together, and at the same instant, with the same shock, both in the elbows and in the chest. An experiment of this kind was first made at Leiden; therefore this first experiment is commonly called La experiencia de Léyden [the Leyden experiment].

> 459 Experimentum V. Involvatur chartâ quadam densiori pars aliqua tubi ferrei machinae electricae. Super páteram metallicam collocetur lagéna vitrea cum tubo ferreo communicans. Lagénae fundum inter, & páteram metallicam reperiatur filum ferreum; experientia constat, quod si quis ex eadem hac manu qua filum ferreum tenet, flammam éxcitet ex charta, électrici tubi partem aliquam involvente, maximo cum fragóre perforábitur charta haec densissima.

459 Experiment V. Let some part of the iron tube of the electric machine be wrapped in a rather thick paper. On a metal dish let a glass flask be placed communicating with the iron tube. Between the bottom of the flask and the metal dish let there be an iron wire; experience establishes that if someone, with the same hand with which he holds the iron wire, draws a flame from the paper wrapping some part of the electric tube, this very thick paper will be pierced with a very great crack.

> 460 Observationes. I. Si chartae loco ponatur avis aliqua, [p. 146] mortem ipsi certissimam adferent aliquot scintillae ex ipsius implumi capite excitatae. II. Loco lagénae aquis semiplenae, de qua loquebamur in experimento IV & V possumus uti quadrato vitreo, cujus operiantur pars superior, & pars inferior folio quodam metallico ad extremitates usque vitri vix sese extendente. Notum est hoc experimentum sub nomine *tabellae magicae*, vel *speculi Frankliniani*.

460 Observations. I. If in place of the paper some bird is put, [p. 146] most certain death will be brought upon it by a few sparks drawn from its featherless head. II. In place of the flask half full of water, of which we were speaking in Experiments IV and V, we can use a square of glass whose upper part and lower part are covered with some metal foil, extending, however, scarcely to the edges of the glass. This experiment is known under the name of the magic picture, or of Franklin’s pane.

> 461 Experimentum VI. super tectum alti cujusdam aedificii constituatur placenta resinacea, aut vitrea. Hanc super placentam perpendiculariter erigatur aliqua virga ferrea; experientiâ constat quod si nubes aliqua, fulmen in sinu suo déferens, virgae huic ferreae superimmineat, ex ea excitabuntur scintillae eodem prorsùs modo, ac si virga communicationem habuisset cum vitreo globo actu fricato eximiae cujusdam éléctricae machinae.

461 Experiment VI. On the roof of some high building let a cake of resin, or of glass, be placed. On this cake let some iron rod be set up perpendicularly; experience establishes that if some cloud bearing lightning in its bosom hangs over this iron rod, sparks will be drawn from it in exactly the same way as if the rod had been in communication with the glass globe, actually being rubbed, of some excellent electric machine.

> 462 Experimentum VII. Super placentam resinaceam constituatur globi vitrei Fricator, is non modò vim electricam sensibilem concipiet, sed etiam flammam excitabit ex tubo machinae jam éléctrico ad quem digitum suum admovet. Ex memoria vestra non éxcidat ultimum hoc experimentum.

462 Experiment VII. Let the rubber of the glass globe be placed on a cake of resin: he will not only receive a sensible electric force, but will also draw a flame from the tube of the machine, now electric, to which he brings his finger. Let this last experiment not slip from your memory.

> 463 Observatio. Fricator idem nudo pavimento insistens extra placentam, non concipit vim electricam sensibilem. Haec sunt experimenta praecipua â Viris Clariss. Nolleto, Franklino, Beccaría, Pauliano, & aliis relata, quorum conabimur in sequenti capite explicationem adferre.

463 Observation. The same rubber, standing on the bare floor outside the cake, does not receive a sensible electric force. These are the principal experiments reported by the most distinguished men Nollet, Franklin, Beccaria, Paulian, and others, of which we shall try to give the explanation in the following chapter.

## CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

> De Causis Electricae Virtutis.

On the Causes of Electric Virtue. 464

> 464 Veras electricae virtutis adsignare causas, hoc opus, hic labor semper fuit in Physica quemadmodùm adparebit enumeratione sequenti.

To assign the true causes of electric virtue: this has always been the task, this the toil, in Physics, as will appear from the following enumeration.

> *Sententia Philosophorum Antiquiorum.*

THE OPINION OF THE MORE ANCIENT PHILOSOPHERS .

> 465 Nullum omninò negotium, Philosophis antiquioribus facessebant electrica phaenómena. In promptu enim ipsis erant, vel qualitas quaedam occulta corporibus electricis essentialis, & intrinseca, vel innatus quidam horror vacui. Praevalebat in Scholis haec ultima sententia; plurimi enim apud antiquos adfirmabant aëra per effluvium electricum expelli, & metu vacui adduci corpora quaecumque levissima. Risu potiùs quàm seriis rationibus debet haec sententia confutari.

465 Electric phenomena gave the more ancient Philosophers no trouble at all. For they had ready at hand either some occult quality, essential and intrinsic to electric bodies, or else an innate horror of the vacuum. This last opinion prevailed in the Schools; for very many among the ancients affirmed that the air is expelled by the electric effluvium, and that any of the lightest bodies whatever are drawn in through fear of a vacuum. This opinion ought to be refuted with laughter rather than with serious reasons.

[p. 147]

> *Sententia Cartesii.*

THE OPINION OF DESCARTES .

> 466 De causis electricae virtutis ex instituto egit Cartesius; sic enim loquitur [^147-s1]. „ Ex modo quo vitrum generari dictum est, facilè colligitur praeter illa majuscula intervalla per quae globuli secundi elementi versùs omnes partes transire possunt, multas etiam rimulas oblongas inter ejus particulas reperiri, quae quum sint angustiores, quàm ut istos glóbulos recipiant, soli materiae primi elementi tránsitum praebent, putandumque est hanc materiam primi elementi omnium meatuum quos ingreditur figuras induere assuetam, per rimulas istas transeundo, in quasdam quasi fásciolas tenues, & oblongas efformari, quae quum similes rimulas in aëre circumjacente non inveniant, intra vitrum se continent, vel certè ab eo non multum evagantur, & circa ejus particulas convolútae, motu quodam circulari ex unis ejus rimulis in alias fluunt. Quamvis enim materia primi elementi fluidissima sit, quia tamen constat minutiis inaequaliter agitatis, ratione consentaneum est, ut credamus ex maximè concitatis ejus minutiis, â vitro in aërem assiduè migrare, aliasque ab aëre in vitrum earum loco reverti; sed cùm eae quae revertuntur, non sint aeque concitatae, illas quae minimùm habent agitationis, versùs rimulas, quibus nulli meatus in aëre correspondent, expelli, atque ibi unas aliis adhaerentes, fásciolas istas componere, quae fasciolae iccircò successu temporum figuras acquirunt determinatas, quas non facilè mutare possunt.

466 Descartes treated of the causes of electric virtue expressly; for thus he speaks (o): “From the manner in which glass was said to be generated, it is easily gathered that, besides those larger intervals through which the globules of the second element can pass in all directions, many small oblong chinks are also found between its particles, which, since they are too narrow to receive those globules, afford passage to the matter of the first element alone; and it must be thought that this matter of the first element, being accustomed to put on the shapes of all the passages it enters, is formed, in passing through those chinks, into certain thin and oblong little ribbons, as it were, which, since they do not find similar chinks in the surrounding air, keep themselves within the glass, or at least do not wander far from it, and, wound about its particles, flow with a certain circular motion from some of its chinks into others. For although the matter of the first element is most fluid, yet because it consists of minute parts unequally agitated, it is consonant with reason for us to believe that some of its most strongly agitated minute parts continually migrate from the glass into the air, and that others return from the air into the glass in their place; but that, since those which return are not equally agitated, those which have the least agitation are driven toward the chinks to which no passages in the air correspond, and there, clinging one to another, compose those little ribbons, which ribbons for that reason acquire in the course of time determinate shapes, which they cannot easily change.

> [^147-s1]: Part. 4. Princip. art. 185.

[^147-s1]: Pt. 4, Principles, art. 185.

> 467 „ Undè fit, ut si vitrum satis validè fricetur, ita ut non nihil incalescat, ipsae hoc motu foras excussae, per aërem quidem vicinum se dispergant, aliorumque etiam corporum vicinorum meatus ingrediantur, sed quia non tam faciles ibi vias inveniunt, statim ad vitrum revolvantur, & minutiora corpora quorum meatibus sunt implicitae, secum adducant::::: Quod autem hic de vitro notavimus, de plerisque aliis corporibus etiam credi debet; nempè quod interstitia quaedam inter eorum particulas reperiantur, quae quum nimis angusta sint ad glóbulos secundi elementi admittendos, solam materiam primi recipiunt„. Ex dictis sequitur Cartesium admisisse tanquàm principia totidèm, ea quae sequuntur.

467 “Whence it comes about that if the glass is rubbed strongly enough to grow somewhat warm, they, shaken out by this motion, disperse indeed through the neighboring air, and enter also into the passages of other neighboring bodies; but because they do not find such easy ways there, they at once roll back to the glass, and draw along with them the smaller bodies in whose passages they are entangled … And what we have noted here about glass must also be believed of most other bodies: namely, that certain interstices are found between their particles which, since they are too narrow to admit the globules of the second element, receive only the matter of the first.” From what has been said it follows that Descartes admitted as so many principles the things that follow.

> 468 I. in vitro quolibet éxtant pori majores, & pori minóres. Isti materiae primi elementi, illi verò glóbulis secundi elementi tránsitum praebent. II. Materia primi elementi dificiliùs movetur in aëre, quàm in poris minoribus vitri. III. Propter hanc resistentiam aëris, materia primi elementi citò revertitur in vitrum ex quo [p. 148] fuerat propter frictionem egressa. IV. Materia primi elementi, & materia electrica nullomodo distinguuntur inter se. V. Juxta Cartesium electrica phaenomena pendent à successiva quadam effluentia materiae primi elementi ex poris minoribus vitri, & adfluentia ejusdem materiae versùs poros minores ejusdem vitri, sicca manu fricati.

468 I. In any glass whatever there are larger pores and smaller pores; the latter afford passage to the matter of the first element, the former to the globules of the second element. II. The matter of the first element moves with more difficulty in the air than in the smaller pores of the glass. III. Because of this resistance of the air, the matter of the first element quickly returns into the glass from which it had come [p. 148] come out on account of the friction. IV. The matter of the first element and the electric matter are in no way distinguished from each other. V. According to Descartes, electric phenomena depend on a certain successive outflow of the matter of the first element from the smaller pores of the glass, and inflow of the same matter toward the smaller pores of the same glass, when it is rubbed with a dry hand.

> 469 Adnotationes. I. Gratis, & absque fundamento tanquàm principia ponuntur ea quae fuerunt enunciata numero 1. 2. 3. 4. §. 468. II. Effluentia, & adfluentia materiae electricae videtur esse potius simultanea, quàm successiva, ut adnotabitur inferiùs. III. Peculiaris haec sententia Cartesii circa materiam electricam pendet evidenter ab ipsius systemate generali quod falsum esse, à nobis demonstratum fuit §§. 45, & 46. IV. Eas omnes ob causas nobis esse rejicienda videtur Cartesii sententia circà materiam electricam.

469 Remarks. I. The things that were stated in nos. 1, 2, 3, 4 of §. 468 are laid down as principles gratuitously and without foundation. II. The outflow and inflow of the electric matter seem to be simultaneous rather than successive, as will be noted below. III. This peculiar opinion of Descartes about the electric matter evidently depends on his general system, which we have shown to be false, §§. 45 and 46. IV. For all these reasons the opinion of Descartes about the electric matter seems to us one to be rejected.

> Sententia Honorati Fabri.

THE OPINION OF HONORÉ FABRI .

> 470 Neque profectò sententiam probabiliorem proposuit Honoratus, Fabri qui eodem quo Cartesius aevo floruit. Sic enim loquitur[^148-s1]. ,, Súccinum & cera Hispanica multo igne constant, & pingui succo, quod vel ex filaminibus súccini liquescentis constat: nempè in longum ducuntur illa filámina quorum lentor, & tenacitas ín dubium revocari non possunt :::::: Partes ignis quae súccino ínsunt continuò águnt in humidum illud viscósum, & lentum, quod deindè caloris vi rarescit, ávolatque in hálitum, qui etiam lentus & viscosus est; hinc in filamina ducitur quantumvis insensibilia :::: Porro emittitur praedictus hálitus ad instar jaculi:::::

470 Nor indeed did Honoré Fabri, who flourished in the same age as Descartes, propose a more probable opinion. For thus he speaks (p): “Amber and Spanish wax consist of much fire and of a fat juice, which consists, as it were, of filaments of melting amber: namely, those filaments are drawn out in length, and their viscosity and tenacity cannot be called into doubt … The parts of fire that are in the amber act continually on that viscous and pliant moisture, which then, by the force of heat, is rarefied and flies off in an exhalation, which is itself also pliant and viscous; hence it is drawn out into filaments, however insensible … Further, the aforesaid exhalation is emitted in the manner of a dart …

> [^148-s1]: Tom. 4. Physic.

[^148-s1]: Vol. 4, Physics.

> 471 ,, Quia proptèr lentórem materiae, filum emissum poro adhaeret, indè fit prae impetus violentia, ut filum quod plus aequo in longum ducitur, & valdè adtenuatur, vel tandèm rumpatur circà medium, vel non rumpatur quidèm, sed post validam tensionem ex prima illa emissione derivatam statim redeat etiam cum impetu :::: Analogiam habes in chorda tensa, quae si dimittatur, vel frangatur prae nimia tensione, segmenta reducuntur versùs alteram extremitatem, cui affixa est; hinc si segmentum illud cujus extremitas poro adhaeret, & non sine aliqua vi versùs porum, & succinum reducitur, incidat in minutissima corpuscula, quae facilè moveri possint, en secum rapit & ipsi succino adfigit ,, *Et alibi* ,, Corpus scabrum maleo dúctile vi electrica caret ,,. Sic centum, & triginta ab hinc annis de electricitate sentiebat Honoratus Fabri.

471 “Because, owing to the viscosity of the matter, the emitted thread clings to a pore, it comes about, through the violence of the impulse, that the thread, drawn out in length more than is due and greatly attenuated, either at length breaks about the middle, or indeed does not break, but after the strong tension derived from that first emission at once returns, likewise with impetus … You have an analogy in a stretched string: if it is let go, or breaks from excessive tension, its segments are drawn back toward the other extremity, to which it is fixed; hence if that segment whose extremity clings to the pore, and which is drawn back with some force toward the pore and the amber, falls upon very minute little bodies that can easily be moved, it carries them off with it and fastens them to the amber itself.” And elsewhere: “A rough body that is ductile under the hammer lacks electric force.” So, a hundred and thirty years ago, did Honoré Fabri think about electricity.

> 472 Adnotationes. In hac sententiâ non explicantur [p. 149] phaenomena corporum *per communicationem* electricorum: volebat enim P. Fabri, nullum omninò corpus nequidem metalla fieri posse *per communicationem* electrica, ut ex postremis ipsius verbis jam citatis manifestum fit. II. Non explicatur in hac sententia undenàm oriatur in vitro tanta vis electrica. Adfirmat enim auctor hujus hypotéseos ceram obsignatoriam, & súccinum esse corpora omnium maximè electrica, de vitri autèm electricitate ne verbum quidem ullum fécerat hoc loci. III denique. Non explicantur in hac sententia phaenomena, quorum hâc tempestate tanta est copia, ut stupendum electrica machina spectaculum praebet: ergo rejicienda est sententia Honorati Fabri tanquàm insufficiens ad exponenda electrica phaenomena.

472 Remarks. In this opinion the phenomena of [p. 149] of bodies electric by communication are not explained: for Father Fabri held that no body at all, not even metals, can become electric by communication, as is manifest from his last words, already cited. II. It is not explained in this opinion whence so great an electric force arises in glass. For the author of this hypothesis affirms that sealing wax and amber are the most electric bodies of all, but in this place had not said even a single word about the electricity of glass. III, finally. In this opinion the phenomena are not explained, of which there is in this age so great an abundance that the electric machine affords an astonishing spectacle: therefore the opinion of Honoré Fabri is to be rejected as insufficient for setting forth electric phenomena.

> Sententia D. DuFay.

THE OPINION OF MR. DU FAY.

> 473 Primus fuit in Gallia D. DuFay qui virtutis electricae quaestionem ordine quodam, & methodo perpenderit. Experimenta ipsius praecipua consignantur in Monumentis Academiae scientiarum Paris.[^149-s1] Is adfirmat duplicem esse electricitatem *specificè* diversam, vitream nempè, & recinaceam. Si duplex est electricitas specificè diversa, (inquit ille) duplex erit materia electrica specificè diversa; si autem duplex est materia electrica specificè diversa facilè admodùm exponentur electrica phaenomena per conflictum scilicet duplicis hujus materiae. Vult etiam D. DuFay materiàm electricam omnem vorticosè gyrare circa corpus electricum, tanquam circà centrum proprium.

473 The first in France who weighed the question of electric virtue with a certain order and method was Mr. Du Fay. His principal experiments are recorded in the Memoirs of the Paris Academy of Sciences (q). He affirms that there is a twofold electricity, specifically different, namely vitreous and resinous. If there is a twofold electricity specifically different (he says), there will be a twofold electric matter specifically different; and if there is a twofold electric matter specifically different, electric phenomena will be very easily set forth, namely through the conflict of this twofold matter. Mr. Du Fay also holds that all the electric matter whirls in the manner of a vortex about the electric body, as about its proper center.

> [^149-s1]: Ann. 1733. 1734. 1737.

[^149-s1]: Years 1733, 1734, 1737.

> 474 Adnotationes. I. Vis electrica vitri videtur tantùm intensior esse vi electrica resínae: ergo specificè non disferunt electricitas vitrea, & resinacea electricitas: alioquin dicendum foret specificè differre fervidissimum ignem ab igne minus férvido. II. Nullum est experimentum adsignabile quo probabiliter etiam innuatur motum aliquem vorticosum existere in electrica materia: ergo tanquàm falsa rejicienda est sententia D. DuFay circà materiam electricam.

474 Remarks. I. The electric force of glass seems only to be more intense than the electric force of resin: therefore vitreous electricity and resinous electricity do not differ specifically; otherwise one would have to say that the most fervent fire differs specifically from a less fervent fire. II. There is no assignable experiment by which it is even probably intimated that some vortical motion exists in the electric matter: therefore the opinion of Mr. Du Fay about the electric matter is to be rejected as false.

## Sententia D. de Molieres. — THE OPINION OF MR. DE MOLIÈRES

> 475 Versùs finem Lectionis suae XIV. sententiam suam exposuit D. de Molieres; haec quinque quasi capitibus comprehenditur. I. Non differt electrica materia à vorticulis olei intra quodcumque corpus electricum contentis. II. Per adfrictum manus siccae coguntur ex electrico corpore in aërem égredi oleosi vorticuli, quorum plerique sese per modum atmosphaerae disponunt circà corpus electricum. III. Sese in aëre extendunt [p. 150] oleosi vorticuli atque propter *plenum* perfectum ab initio mundi perseverans in natura, vorticuli similes versùs corpus electricum adfluunt. IV. Plures sunt oleosi vorticuli in metallis, & in aliis corporibus per communicationem electricis, quàm in vitro & in corporibus electricis per *adfrictum*. V denique. Ex corporibus non electricis égreditur insensibilis materia, quae cum atmosphaera corporum electricorum fermentescit, atque ex illa fermentatione oritur scintilla, quàm ex corporibus actu electricis solemus excutere.

475 Toward the end of his Lesson XIV Mr. de Molières set forth his opinion; it is comprised under five heads, as it were. I. The electric matter does not differ from the little vortices of oil contained within any electric body whatever. II. By the rubbing of a dry hand the oily little vortices are forced to go out of the electric body into the air, and most of them dispose themselves in the manner of an atmosphere about the electric body. III. There spread themselves out in the air the [p. 150] the oily little vortices, and, on account of the perfect plenum that has persisted in nature from the beginning of the world, similar little vortices flow toward the electric body. IV. There are more oily little vortices in metals and in other bodies electric by communication than in glass and in bodies electric by rubbing. V, finally. From non-electric bodies there issues an insensible matter which ferments with the atmosphere of electric bodies, and from that fermentation arises the spark which we are accustomed to strike out of bodies actually electric.

> 476 Adnotationes. I. Demonstrabimus inferiùs igneam esse materiam electricam; ergo distinguitur haec materia ab oleo. II. Nihil probat oleum corpus tenax ac lentum in vorticulos adeò rápidos gyrari, & agi posse. III. Probabile non est plùs esse electricae materiae in corporibus *per communicationem* electricis, quàm in corporibus electricis *per se*. Imò quidem indicare videntur experimenta, exiguam admodùm esse electricae materiae quantitatem in corporibus quae sola communicatio potest electrica réddere; haec enim corpora calefacta, & sicciori manu fricata nullum unquam signum praebent electricitatis. IV. Fermentatio de qua loquitur D. de Molieres videtur esse merum commentum: ergo rejicienda est ipsius sententia tanquam hypothesis ex omni fermè parte peccans.

476 Remarks. I. We shall demonstrate below that the electric matter is fiery; therefore this matter is distinguished from oil. II. Nothing proves that oil, a tenacious and viscous body, can be whirled and driven in such rapid little vortices. III. It is not probable that there is more electric matter in bodies electric by communication than in bodies electric per se. Indeed, experiments seem to indicate that the quantity of electric matter is very small in bodies which communication alone can render electric; for these bodies, when heated and rubbed with a rather dry hand, never give any sign of electricity. IV. The fermentation of which Mr. de Molières speaks seems to be a mere fiction: therefore his opinion is to be rejected as a hypothesis faulty in almost every part.

> Sententia D. Jallabert.

THE OPINION OF MR. JALLABERT.

> 477 Haec sibi concedi postulavit D. Jallabert in Opusculo suo de Electricitate.[^150-s1] I. Existit fluidum aliquod elasticum, & tenue, nonmodò replens orbem hunc universum, sed & poros corporum etiam densissimorum. II Partes hujus fluidi, sicut partes fluidorum omnium tendunt ad aequilibrium, ac proindè tendunt ad implenda spatia in quibus derelinquuntur aliqua vacuola. III. Fluidum hoc ab igne elementari prorsùs indistinctum, atque *per adfrictum* ex sinu corporum *per se electricorum* excússum, sese plerumque per modum atmosphaerae disponit circà corpora, quae sunt in statu actuali electricitatis. IV. Fluidum hoc non est homogeneae densitatis; densius enim est in corporibus raris, quàm in densis: densiùs enim est ex. gr. in aëre, quàm in aqua. V. Corpus actu electricum tot accipit ab aëre circumdante particulas igneas, quot ipsi suppeditat. VI denique Ignis elementaris per se ipsum invisibilis secum abripit particulas corporum, ex quibus égredi cogitur, sicque se manifestum reddit.

477 These things Mr. Jallabert asked to be granted him in his little work on Electricity (r). I. There exists a certain elastic and thin fluid, filling not only this whole universe but also the pores of even the densest bodies. II. The parts of this fluid, like the parts of all fluids, tend to equilibrium, and therefore tend to fill the spaces in which some little voids are left. III. This fluid, wholly undistinguished from elemental fire, and shaken out by rubbing from the bosom of bodies electric per se, disposes itself for the most part in the manner of an atmosphere about bodies that are in a state of actual electricity. IV. This fluid is not of homogeneous density: for it is denser in rare bodies than in dense ones; it is denser, e.g., in air than in water. V. A body actually electric receives from the surrounding air as many fiery particles as it supplies to it. VI, finally. Elemental fire, of itself invisible, carries off with it the particles of the bodies from which it is forced to go out, and thus renders itself manifest.

> [^150-s1]: Experiences sur l' Electricitè avec quelques conjectures sur la cause de ses effets.

[^150-s1]: Experiences sur l’Electricité avec quelques conjectures sur la cause de ses effets.

> 478 Adnotationes. Plura sunt in hac hypothesi veritati cónsona, quàm à veritate aliena. Hoc unum falsum est, materiam electricam densiorem esse in corporibus raris, quàm in densis; densior [p. 151] enim est haec materia in súccino, vitro, adamante, quàm in aëre, aqua, &c. Nisi fortè velit Cl. Auct pro *densitate* intelligi majorem materiae electricae copiam, quod non adeò absurdum videtur. Cetera omnia sunt in hac hypothesi aut vera, aut saltèm probabilia; sed haec sententia falso innititur fundamento si pro certo statuit materiam electricam densiorem esse in corporibus raris, quàm in densis; ergo ex hoc capite rejicienda est.

478 Remarks. There are more things in this hypothesis consonant with the truth than foreign to it. This one thing is false, that the electric matter is denser in rare bodies than in dense ones; for this matter is denser in [p. 151] in amber, glass, diamond, than in air, water, etc. Unless perhaps the distinguished Author wishes a greater abundance of electric matter to be understood by density, which does not seem so absurd. All the other things in this hypothesis are either true or at least probable; but this opinion rests on a false foundation if it lays down as certain that the electric matter is denser in rare bodies than in dense ones; therefore on this head it is to be rejected.

## Sententia D. Franklin. — THE OPINION OF MR. FRANKLIN

> 479 In sententia Franklini[^151-s1] haec sunt capita notatu digna. I. Materia electrica non solùm ab igne elementari, sed etiam à materia quacumque communi specificè distinguitur. II. Existit vis repulsiva inter particulas electricae materiae, & vis adtractiva inter particulas materiae electricae, & particulas materiae non electricae. III. Corpus electricum angulósum facilè admodùm per angulos suos materiam electricam amittit. IV. Corpus acuminatum non electricum facilè admodùm electrico corpori 10, aut 12 pollicibus distans, materiam electricam éripit.

479 In the opinion of Franklin (s) these are the heads worth noting. I. The electric matter is specifically distinguished not only from elemental fire but also from any common matter whatever. II. There exists a repulsive force between the particles of the electric matter, and an attractive force between the particles of the electric matter and the particles of non-electric matter. III. An angular electric body very easily loses its electric matter through its angles. IV. A pointed non-electric body very easily snatches the electric matter from an electric body 10 or 15 inches distant.

> [^151-s1]: In Oper. cui titul. Experiences & Observations sur l' Electricitè, faites a Philadelphie, traduites par Mr. d' Alibard.

[^151-s1]: In the work entitled Experiences & Observations sur l’Electricité, faites a Philadelphie, translated by M. d’Alibard.

> 480 Adnotationes. I Nihil probat ignem electricum ab igne elementari specificè distingui. II. Datur evidenter causa physica & immediata phaenomenorum electricorum, quam inferiùs determinabimus: ergo non licet recurrere ad qualitates adtractivas & repulsivas, de quibus in Opúsculo suo Franklinus loquitur.

480 Remarks. I. Nothing proves that electric fire is specifically distinguished from elemental fire. II. There is evidently a physical and immediate cause of electric phenomena, which we shall determine below: therefore it is not permissible to have recourse to the attractive and repulsive qualities of which Franklin speaks in his little work.

> Sententia D. Nollet.

THE OPINION OF MR. NOLLET.

> 481 Hic est proprius sententiae Nolletianae character, *simultanea*, scilicet *effluentia*, & *adfluentia* materiae cujusdam subtilissimae. Sic rem hanc totam exposuit Vir ille Clariss. atque de Electricitate, totaque Physica optimè meritus[^151-s2]. I. Materia electrica nihil est aliud, quàm ignis elementaris, qui plùs, minùsve abundanter reperitur in omnibus omninò corporibus. II Omne corpus electricum sive *per frictionem*, sive *per communicationem* virtutem hanc conceperit, donatur atmosphaerâ quadam igneâ, quae ad majorem minoremvè densitatem sese extendit, prout intensior, vel remissior est corporis electricitas. III. Ex sinu corporis electrici continuò effluunt ignea corpuscula, quibus componitur hujusmodi atmosphaera. IV Non solum ex aëre, sed etiam ex omni circumstanti corpore continuò adfluit versùs corpus [p. 152] electricum, ex. gr. versùs globum vitreum siccâ manu fricatum, ignea materia, quae jacturas abundè réparat, quas ob frictionem vitreus globus patitur. V. Conflictus existit inter materiam electricam effluentem, & materiam electricam adfluentem, atque ex eo conflictu Nolletus deducit phaenomenôn electricorum explicationem, ut videre est in operibus, quae fuerunt ab ipso hanc obrem in lucem édita.

481 This is the proper character of the Nolletian opinion: the simultaneous effluence and affluence, namely, of a certain most subtle matter. Thus did that most distinguished Man, who has deserved excellently of Electricity and of the whole of Physics, set forth this entire matter (t). I. The electric matter is nothing other than elemental fire, which is found more or less abundantly in absolutely all bodies. II. Every electric body, whether it has received this virtue by friction or by communication, is endowed with a certain fiery atmosphere, which extends itself to a greater or lesser density according as the electricity of the body is more intense or more remiss. III. From the bosom of the electric body fiery corpuscles continually flow out, of which an atmosphere of this kind is composed. IV. Not only from the air, but also from every surrounding body, there flows continually toward the electric [p. 152] body, e.g. toward a glass globe rubbed with a dry hand, a fiery matter which abundantly repairs the losses that the glass globe suffers on account of the friction. V. A conflict exists between the effluent electric matter and the affluent electric matter, and from that conflict Nollet deduces the explanation of electric phenomena, as may be seen in the works which he published for this purpose.

> [^151-s2]: Essai sur l' Electricitè, & alibi in variis Opusculis.

[^151-s2]: Essai sur l’Electricité, and elsewhere in various small works.

> 482 Adnotationes. I. Propter resistentiam, & elaterium aëris, pars aliqua, neque sanè exigua, electricae materiae quae per adfrictum & motum rotationis, fuerat ex sinu vitrei globi *effluens*, in ipsummet globum redit, seu fit *adfluens*: vix enim aliter exponi potest, cur tempore frigido & sicco vividior existat electrica virtus, quàm tempore calido & húmido II. In sententia Nolletiana non videtur exponi posse cur homo super placentam resinaceam more solito constitutus, non possit flammulam excitare ex tubo ferreo electrico ad quem digitum ádmovet; tunc enim conflictus maximus existit inter materiam exeuntem ex electrico digito, & materiam effluentem ex tubo pariter electrico: ergo non exponuntur in sententia Nolletiana omnia omninò electrica phaenómena.

482 Remarks. I. On account of the resistance and the elasticity of the air, some part, and that not a very small one, of the electric matter which, through rubbing and the motion of rotation, had been effluent from the bosom of the glass globe returns into the globe itself, or becomes affluent: for scarcely otherwise can it be explained why the electric virtue is livelier in cold and dry weather than in warm and humid weather. II. In the Nolletian opinion it does not seem possible to explain why a man placed in the usual way on a cake of resin cannot draw a little flame from the electric iron tube to which he brings his finger: for then a very great conflict exists between the matter going out of the electric finger and the matter flowing out of the tube, which is likewise electric: therefore not absolutely all electric phenomena are explained in the Nolletian opinion.

## Sententia Clariss. Paulian, quae et nostra est. — THE OPINION OF THE MOST DISTINGUISHED PAULIAN, WHICH IS ALSO OURS .

> 483 Duobus veluti principiorum generibus innititur nostra haec Electricitatis Theoria, quorum alia recipiuntur ab omnibus omninò Physicis, alia verò nobis sunt prorsùs peculiaria. I. Datur materia quaedam electrica. Et verò dantur electrica corpora: ergo datur materia quaedam hanc ipsis virtutem concilians. II. Materia electrica est materia quaedam subtilissima, & fluidissima: pénetrat enim intra corpora densissima, qualia sunt metalla, lapides, &c. III. Materia electrica est materia ignea, quoniàm, materiae hujus ope, inflammatur spiritus vini accenditur candéla, &c. IV. Materia electrica non est homogeneae densitatis; dantur enim corpora quae sunt alia aliis magis electrica. V. Omne corpus electricum, sivè *per frictionem*, sivè per communicationem virtutem hanc concéperit, emittit ex sinu suo ignea corpuscula, quorum plurima in modum atmosphaerae sese disponunt. Et verò eo prorsùs modo formatur atmosphaera corporum electricorum, quo formatur atmosphera corporum odoriferorum, sed atmosphaera corporum odoriferorum per veram emissionem efformatur, ut omnes consentiunt: ergo per veram emissionem pariter efformatur atmosphaera corporum electricorum.

483 Our present Theory of Electricity rests, as it were, on two kinds of principles, of which some are received by absolutely all Physicists, while others are altogether peculiar to us. I. There is a certain electric matter. For indeed there are electric bodies: therefore there is a certain matter that confers this virtue on them. II. The electric matter is a certain most subtle and most fluid matter: for it penetrates within the densest bodies, such as metals, stones, etc. III. The electric matter is a fiery matter, since by the help of this matter spirit of wine is inflamed, a candle is lit, etc. IV. The electric matter is not of homogeneous density; for there are bodies of which some are more electric than others. V. Every electric body, whether it has received this virtue by friction or by communication, emits from its bosom fiery corpuscles, most of which dispose themselves in the manner of an atmosphere. And indeed the atmosphere of electric bodies is formed in exactly the same way in which the atmosphere of odoriferous bodies is formed; but the atmosphere of odoriferous bodies is formed by a true emission, as all agree: therefore the atmosphere of electric bodies is likewise formed by a true emission.

> 484 VI. Tot ignea corpuscula adfluunt versùs corpus electricum, quot effluxerant ex ipsius sinu Suam enim electricitatem non amittit globus vitreus, post frictiones innumeras, & jacturas immensas, [p. 153] quas passus est, ergo jacturas suas evidenter réparat. Non potest autem corpus electricum resarcire jacturas, quin tot ignea corpuscula versùs ipsum adfluant, quot effluxerant ex ipsius sinu: ergo &c. Jam verò quòd spectat ad principia quae nobis sunt hac in re peculiaria, illa sunt numero quinque.

484 VI. As many fiery corpuscles flow toward the electric body as had flowed out of its bosom. For the glass globe does not lose its electricity after innumerable frictions and immense losses, [p. 153] which it has suffered; therefore it evidently repairs its losses. But the electric body cannot make good its losses unless as many fiery corpuscles flow toward it as had flowed out of its bosom: therefore, etc. Now as regards the principles that are peculiar to us in this matter, they are five in number.

> 485 I. Pars aliqua tantùm igneorum corpusculorum ex vitreo globo sicca manu fricato exeuntium, ingreditur ferreum tubum electricae machinae; pars alia verò eorundem corpusculorum sese communicat vel aëri, vel corporibus hinc indè circumstantibus. Constat enim experientiâ non solum Electricae machinae tubum, sed & ipsum vitrei globi Fricatorem vim electricam sensibiliter concipere, dummodò super placentam resinaceam constituatur.

485 I. Only some part of the fiery corpuscles going out of the glass globe rubbed with a dry hand enters the iron tube of the electric machine; another part of the same corpuscles communicates itself either to the air or to the bodies standing round about on every side. For experience establishes that not only the tube of the electric machine, but also the very Rubber of the glass globe sensibly receives electric force, provided he is placed on a cake of resin.

> 486 II. Ignea corpuscula, quae exeunt ex sinu vitrei globi, & quae tubum ferreum electricae machinae non ingrediuntur, reddunt *initialiter* electrica ea omnia corpora, quae machinam hinc indè circumdant, etiamsi super resinam, aut vitrum, aut simile quidpiam non constituantur, dummodò sint haec corpora per communicationem electrica. Et verò Fricator super placentam resinaceam, aut vitream constitutus, *sensibiliter*, seu *perfectè* electricus redditur per ignea corpuscula, quae exeunt ex sinu vitrei globi, & quae tubum ferreum electricae machinae non ingrediuntur: ergo per haec eadem corpuscula *imperfectè*, seu *initialiter* electricus reddi debet Fricator idem in pavimento positus: rétinet enim in hoc situ veram & expedítam potentiam electricitatem recipiendi per viam communicationis. Quod autèm de Fricatore posito in pavimento dicitur, hoc & dicatur proportionaliter de corporibus hinc inde machinam circumdantibus, quae sunt per communicationem electrica, & quae super resinam, aut vitrum non collocantur.

486 II. The fiery corpuscles which go out of the bosom of the glass globe, and which do not enter the iron tube of the electric machine, render initially electric all those bodies which surround the machine on every side, even if they are not placed on resin, or glass, or anything similar, provided these bodies are electric by communication. And indeed the Rubber, placed on a cake of resin or of glass, is rendered sensibly, or perfectly, electric by the fiery corpuscles which go out of the bosom of the glass globe and which do not enter the iron tube of the electric machine: therefore by these same corpuscles the same Rubber, when placed on the floor, must be rendered imperfectly, or initially, electric: for in this situation he retains a true and ready power of receiving electricity by way of communication. And what is said of the Rubber placed on the floor, let it be said proportionally also of the bodies surrounding the machine on every side which are electric by communication and are not set on resin or glass.

> 487 III Circumdantur atmosphaerâ densâ corpora *perfectè*, seu *totaliter* electrica, & atmospaerâ rara, corpora *imperfectè*, seù *initialiter* electrica: dénsitas enim atmospherae electricae est in ratione directa electricitatis corporum IV. Multa ignea corpuscula ex sinu vitrei globi exeuntia in ipsum globum continuò redeunt propter resistentiam & elaterium ambientis aëris. Eam ob causam vividior est vis electrica tempore frigido, & sicco, quàm calido, & humido tempore: eandem etiam ob causam vividior est electricitas in pleno, quàm in vacuo. Hinc sequitur igneorum corpusculorum ex sinu vitrei globi *effluentiae* respondére simultaneam quamdam versùs eundem globum *adfluentiam*, partìm eorundem, partìm similium corpusculorum quae suppedditantur ab aëre, & circumstantibus corporibus. V. Verissima est, quanquàm minimè sensibilis simultanea *affluentia*, & *effluentia* corpusculorum igneorum. Non datur enim etiam in atmosphaera terrestri *plenum* perfectum (§. 257.), quod evidenter requireretur ut physicè sensibiliter patefieret synchrona illa affluentia, & effluentia materiae electricae. His praemissis sit conclusio.

487 III. Bodies perfectly, or totally, electric are surrounded by a dense atmosphere, and bodies imperfectly, or initially, electric by a rare atmosphere: for the density of the electric atmosphere is in the direct ratio of the electricity of the bodies. IV. Many fiery corpuscles going out of the bosom of the glass globe continually return into the globe itself on account of the resistance and the elasticity of the surrounding air. For that reason the electric force is livelier in cold and dry weather than in warm and humid weather; for the same reason, too, electricity is livelier in a plenum than in a vacuum. Hence it follows that to the effluence of the fiery corpuscles from the bosom of the glass globe there corresponds a certain simultaneous affluence toward the same globe, partly of the same corpuscles, partly of similar corpuscles supplied by the air and by the surrounding bodies. V. Most true, although very little sensible, is the simultaneous affluence and effluence of the fiery corpuscles. For not even in the terrestrial atmosphere is there a perfect plenum (§. 257.), which would evidently be required for that synchronous affluence and effluence of the electric matter to become physically and sensibly manifest. These things premised, let this be the conclusion.

[p. 154]

> 488 In sententia nostra rectè exponuntur omnia electricitatis phaenomena. Probatur enumeratione sequenti, revocando scilicèt ad causas suas physicas experimenta praecipua quae fuerunt in cap. II. relata.

488 In our opinion all the phenomena of electricity are rightly explained. This is proved by the following enumeration, namely by referring to their physical causes the principal experiments that were related in ch. II.

> 489 Explicatio Experimenti I Ex globo vitreo siccâ manu fricato, & motu circulari donato exeunt ignea corpuscula, quorum alia ingrediuntur ferreum tubum, funiculorum sericorum ope suspensum horizontaliter, alia verò sese communicant aëri, & corporibus hinc indè circumstantibus Per hanc emissionem, *totaliter* electricus redditur ferreus tubus horizontaliter suspensus, & *initialiter* tantùm electrica redduntur aer, & corpora hinc indè circumstantia. Quo supposito sic ratiócinor. Quum versùs tubum ferreum *totaliter* electricum admoveo digitum *initialiter* duntaxàt electricum, tunc juxta leges aequilibrii, debet atmosphaera electrica densa tubum ferreum circumdans deferri versùs atmosphaeram electricam raram digitum meum ambientem, non secùs atque aer exterior fertur in cubiculum, cujus fuit aër interior igne accenso rarefactus. In ea mixtione, conflictus vehemens existit inter materiam electricam tubum ferreum circumdantem, & materiam electricam ambientem digitum, atque per hunc conflictum excitatur flammula caerulea cum crepitu prosiliens.

489 Explanation of Experiment I. From the glass globe rubbed with a dry hand and endowed with circular motion there go out fiery corpuscles, of which some enter the iron tube suspended horizontally by means of silk cords, while others communicate themselves to the air and to the bodies standing round about on every side. By this emission the iron tube suspended horizontally is rendered totally electric, while the air and the bodies standing round about are rendered only initially electric. This supposed, I reason thus. When I bring my finger, which is only initially electric, toward the totally electric iron tube, then, according to the laws of equilibrium, the dense electric atmosphere surrounding the iron tube must be carried toward the rare electric atmosphere surrounding my finger, just as the outer air is carried into a room whose inner air has been rarefied by a lighted fire. In that mixing a vehement conflict exists between the electric matter surrounding the iron tube and the electric matter surrounding the finger, and through this conflict a little blue flame is excited, leaping forth with a crackle.

> 490 Explicatio Experimenti II. Tubus machinae electricae, filum ferreum quod manu tenetur, & homo super placentam resinaceam collocatus sunt tria corpora *per communicationem* electrica, quorum ultimum separatur ope resinae à reliquo pavimento *per communicationem* tantùm electrico: ergo quum imprimitur globo vitreo sicca manu fricato motus aliquis rotationis, debent tubus, filum ferreum, & homo super placentam resinaceam collocatus vim electricam concipere maximam debet & dolorem sensibilem procreare flamma caerulea ex corpore viventi excitatâ; ¿quis enim non videt flammam hanc caeruleam esse verum, & propriè dictum ignem?

490 Explanation of Experiment II. The tube of the electric machine, the iron wire which is held in the hand, and the man placed on the resin cake are three bodies electric by communication, of which the last is separated by means of the resin from the rest of the floor, which is electric only by communication: therefore, when some motion of rotation is impressed on the glass globe rubbed with a dry hand, the tube, the iron wire and the man placed on the resin cake must receive a very great electric force, and the blue flame drawn from the living body must produce a sensible pain; for who does not see that this blue flame is a true fire, and properly so called?

> 491 Explicatio Experimenti III. Admittimus & nosmetipsi simultaneam quandam *effluentiam* particularum ignearum ex sinu corporum electricorum, & *adfluentiam* particularum ignearum versùs eadem electrica corpora. Per particulas igneas *adfluentes* adtrahuntur corpora quaecumque levissima versùs electrica corpora, & per particulas igneas *effluentes* repelluntur corpora quaecumque levissima ab iisdem corporibus electricis: ergo in nostra sententia rectè exponuntur itus, & reditus levissimorum corporum.

491 Explanation of Experiment III. We ourselves also admit a certain simultaneous effluence of fiery particles from the bosom of electric bodies, and affluence of fiery particles toward the same electric bodies. By the affluent fiery particles any of the lightest bodies whatever are attracted toward the electric bodies, and by the effluent fiery particles any of the lightest bodies whatever are repelled from the same electric bodies: therefore in our opinion the goings and returnings of the lightest bodies are rightly explained.

> 492 Explicatio Experimenti IV. Violenta commotio de qua fit mentio in Experim. IV. óritur à conflictu vehementi duorum profluviorum igneorum, quorum unum ingreditur per manum, quae partem inferiorem lagénae vitreae sustinet, alterum verò per manum quae flammam excitat ex filo ferreo.

492 Explanation of Experiment IV. The violent shock mentioned in Experim. IV arises from the vehement collision of two fiery outflows, one of which enters through the hand that holds up the lower part of the glass flask, and the other through the hand that draws the flame from the iron wire.

> 493 Explicatio Experimenti V. Conflictus vehemens duorum profluviorum igneorum, quorum unum viam habet per filum [p. 155] ferreum, álterum verò per tubum electricum causa est, cur maximo cum fragóre perforetur charta densissima de qua fit mentio in Experim. V.

493 Explanation of Experiment V. The vehement conflict of two fiery outflows, one of which has its way through the iron wire, [p. 155] the other through the electric tube, is the cause why the very thick paper mentioned in Experim. V is pierced with a very great crack.

> 494 Explicatio Experimenti VI. Nubes fulmen in sinu suo deferens est corpus actu electricum, quemadmodùm exponetur inferiùs: ergo scintillae debent excitari ex virga ferrea de qua agitur in Experim. VI.

494 Explanation of Experiment VI. A cloud bearing lightning in its bosom is a body actually electric, as will be set forth below: therefore sparks must be drawn from the iron rod treated of in Experim. VI.

> 495 Explicatio Experimenti VII. Pars aliqua corpusculorum igneorum ex vitreo globo sicca manu fricato exeuntium, sese communicat corporibus machinam electricam circumstantibus: ergo vim electricam sensibilem Fricator concipere debet, dummodò sit super placentam resinaceam constitutus. Debet & Fricator idem flammam excitare ex tubo ferreo ad quem digitum ádmovet: in illo enim vis electrica multò debilior est, quàm in tubo ferreo.

495 Explanation of Experiment VII. Some part of the fiery corpuscles going out of the glass globe rubbed with a dry hand communicates itself to the bodies standing about the electric machine: therefore the Rubber must receive a sensible electric force, provided he is placed on a cake of resin. And the same Rubber must also draw a flame from the iron tube to which he brings his finger: for in him the electric force is much weaker than in the iron tube.

> Solvuntur argumenta, cùm á Cl. Nolleto, tùm ab aliis opposita contra sententiam nostram.

THE ARGUMENTS OPPOSED AGAINST OUR OPINION , BOTH BY THE DISTINGUISHED NOLLET AND BY OTHERS , ARE ANSWERED.

> 496 Opp. I. Explicatio Experim. I non est in hac novâ sententia conformis legibus sanae Physicae: ergo. Prob. antec.: si tubus ferreus per funiculos séricos suspensus vim electricam concipit propter causas adsignatas, pariter & vim electricam concipere debet tubus idem ferreus per funiculos cannábinos suspensus; falsum consequens: ergo & antec. Prob. sequela: tám communicat cum globo vitreo tubus ferreus per funiculos cannábinos suspensus, quàm quum suspenditur per funiculos sericos; ergo si &c.

496 Obj. I. The explanation of Experim. I in this new opinion is not conformable to the laws of sound Physics: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: if the iron tube suspended by silk cords receives electric force on account of the causes assigned, the same iron tube suspended by hempen cords must likewise receive electric force; the consequent is false: therefore the antecedent also. Proof of the sequel: the iron tube suspended by hempen cords communicates with the glass globe just as much as when it is suspended by silk cords; therefore, if, etc.

> 497 Dist. antec.: tam & eodem modo communicat, nego; tam & longè diverso modo communicat tubus ferreus, &c. conc. antec. & neg. conseq. Tubus ferreus per funiculos sericos suspensus, ita concipit vim electricam, ut illam omninò, aut quasi omninò retineat; suspenditur enim ope funiculorum *per se* electricorum; contra verò tubus ferreus per funiculos cannábinos suspensus, ita concipit vim electricam, ut illam magnâ ex parte amittat; suspénditur enim per funículos, qui sunt *per communicationem* electrici.

497 I distinguish the antecedent: it communicates just as much and in the same manner, I deny; just as much, and in a far different manner, the iron tube communicates, etc., I concede the antecedent and deny the consequence. The iron tube suspended by silk cords receives electric force in such a way that it retains it wholly, or almost wholly; for it is suspended by means of cords electric per se; on the contrary, the iron tube suspended by hempen cords receives electric force in such a way that it loses it in great part; for it is suspended by cords that are electric by communication.

> 498 Inst. 1. Si versùs tubum electrica virtute donatum admoveatur obsignatoria cera, nulla omninò excitatur scintilla. Quo supposito sic ratiocinor: ex hac sententia nova sequitur, quod in eo casu flammula cum crépitu debeat excitari ex tubo ferreo; sed hoc est falsum: ergo. Prob. maj.: obsignatoria cera non longè distans ab electrica machina fieri debet *initialiter* electrica: ergo. Prob. antec.: Ferrum quodcumque non longè distans ab electrica machina fit initialiter electricum: ergo pariter obsignatoria cera non longè distans ab electrica machina, fieri debet initialiter electrica. [p. 156] Nego paritatem: Ferrum non longè distans ab electrica machina acquisivit atmosphaeram electricam raram; est enim ferrum per communicationem electricum: contra verò obsignatoria cera per adfrictum duntaxat, electrica nullam acquirit atmosphaeram electricam, quamvis non distet ab electrica machina.

498 Inst. 1. If sealing wax is brought toward the tube endowed with electric virtue, no spark at all is excited. This supposed, I reason thus: from this new opinion it follows that in that case a little flame with a crackle must be drawn from the iron tube: but this is false: therefore. Proof of the major: sealing wax not far distant from the electric machine must become initially electric: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: any iron whatever not far distant from the electric machine becomes initially electric: therefore likewise sealing wax not far distant from the electric machine must become initially electric. [p. 156] I deny the parity: iron not far distant from the electric machine acquires a rare electric atmosphere; for iron is electric by communication: whereas sealing wax, which is electric only by rubbing, acquires no electric atmosphere, although it is not far distant from the electric machine.

> 499 Inst. 2. Ex hac sententia nova saltèm sequitur quod flammula debeat excitari ex tubo ferreo electrico versùs quem admovetur obsignatoria cera sicciori manu fricata, sed hoc est falsum: ergo. Prob. maj.: obsignatoria cera sicciori manu fricata, atmosphaeram electricam acquisivit: ergo. Dist. antec.: atmosphaeram electricam acquisivit, quae aequè densa est, ac atmosphaera tubi ferrei electrici, conc.; quae rarior est, quàm atmosphaera tubi ferrei electrici, nego antec., & consequens. Flammula non excitatur nisi per mixtionem, & consequentem conflictum atmosphaerae densae cum atmosphaera rara: ergo flammula non debet excitari, quum admovetur cera *totaliter* electrica versùs tubum ferreum totaliter electricum.

499 Inst. 2. From this new opinion it at least follows that a little flame must be drawn from the electric iron tube toward which sealing wax rubbed with a rather dry hand is brought; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the major: sealing wax rubbed with a rather dry hand has acquired an electric atmosphere: therefore. I distinguish the antecedent: it has acquired an electric atmosphere which is just as dense as the atmosphere of the electric iron tube, I concede; one which is rarer than the atmosphere of the electric iron tube, I deny the antecedent and the consequent. A little flame is not drawn except through the mixing, and the consequent conflict, of a dense atmosphere with a rare atmosphere: therefore a little flame ought not to be drawn when wax totally electric is brought toward an iron tube totally electric.

> 500 Inst. 3. Saltèm in hac nova sententia non explicatur cur ex tubo ferreo electrico cum crepitu quodam flammula soleat excitari: ergo tanquam insufficiens rejicienda est. Prob. antec.: mixtio materiae electricae tubum ferreum circumdantis, & materiae electricae digitum ambientis, deberet fieri sine crepitu: ergo &c. Prob. antec.: duae flammae contiguae sese immiscent sine crepitu: ergo pariter duae atmosphaerae electricae sese deberent sinè crepitu immiscere. Nego conseq. Duo atmosphaerae electricae de quibus loquimur, expellunt aërem intermedium, vel nullomodo, vel mediocriter duntaxat dilatatum, ac proindè expellunt aërem elasticum, crepitum edendi capacem: contrà vero duae flammae contiguae sese immiscentes expellunt aërem nimis rarefactum, quàm ut crepitum edere queat.

500 Inst. 3. At least in this new opinion it is not explained why a little flame is usually drawn from the electric iron tube with a certain crackle: therefore it is to be rejected as insufficient. Proof of the antecedent: the mixing of the electric matter surrounding the iron tube and of the electric matter surrounding the finger ought to take place without a crackle: therefore, etc. Proof of the antecedent: two contiguous flames mingle with each other without a crackle: therefore likewise two electric atmospheres ought to mingle with each other without a crackle. I deny the consequence. The two electric atmospheres of which we speak expel the intermediate air, which is either not dilated at all or only moderately, and therefore they expel elastic air, capable of producing a crackle: whereas two contiguous flames mingling with each other expel air too much rarefied to be able to produce a crackle.

> 501 Opp. 2. Experimenti II explicatio non videtur esse conformis Physicae legibus: ergo. Prob. antec.: haec explicatio supponit hominem super placentam resinaceam constitutum eodem praecise instanti concipere virtutem electricam, sive placenta resinacea multùm, sive parùm distet ab electrica machina: atqui hoc non videtur conforme Physicae legibus: ergo. Prob. min.: juxta Physicae leges, non debet electrica materia ex globo vitreo exiens, eodem tempore spatia diversa percurrere: ergo. Dist. antec.: eodem tempore reali, & vero, concedo; eodem tempore sensibili & adparente, subdist. supponendo quod spatia differant aliquot millibus leucarum, conc. supponendo quod differant aliquot pedibus, nego, & conseq. Incredibili quadàm velocitate donatur electrica seu ignea materia: debet igitur haec materia eodem sensibiliter tempore ad pedem centesimum, & ad pedem vigesimum pervenire.

501 Obj. 2. The explanation of Experiment II does not seem conformable to the laws of Physics: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: this explanation supposes that a man placed on a resin cake receives electric virtue at precisely the same instant, whether the resin cake is far or but little distant from the electric machine: but this does not seem conformable to the laws of Physics: therefore. Proof of the minor: according to the laws of Physics, the electric matter going out of the glass globe ought not to traverse different spaces in the same time: therefore. I distinguish the antecedent: in the same real and true time, I concede; in the same sensible and apparent time, I subdistinguish: supposing that the spaces differ by some thousands of leagues, I concede; supposing that they differ by some feet, I deny, and I deny the consequence. The electric, or fiery, matter is endowed with a certain incredible velocity: this matter must therefore arrive at the hundredth foot and at the twentieth foot in the same sensible time.

> 502 Inst. ex hac sententia sequitur, quod homo super placentam resinaceam more solito collocatus deberet flammam excitare ex tubo ferreo electrico, quo cum communicationem habet: sed hoc [p. 157] est falsum: ergo. Prob. major.: homo pavimento innixus, flammulam excitat ex tubo ferreo quocum non communicat: ergo à fortiori homo super placentam collocatus deberet &c. Nego conseq: Homo super placentam collocatus aequè electricus est, ac tubus ferreus, ac proindè circúmdatur atmosphaera electrica aequè densa, ac atmosphaera ferrei tubi. Contràverò homo pavimento innixus *initialiter* tantùm est electricus, & consequenter circumdatur atmosphaerâ electrica rara, intereà dùm ferreus tubus cingitur atmosphaera electrica densa: ergo juxta principia superiùs exposita debet hic ex tubo ferreo aliquam, ille verò nullam flammulam excitare. At *inquies*: ¿quonam mechanismo inflammatur spiritus vini, de quo fit mentio in Observatione III experimenti II? Respondeo: eodem prorsùs modo inflammatur spiritus vini, quo ex tubo ferreo flammula quaedam excitatur.

502 Inst. From this opinion it follows that a man placed in the usual way on a resin cake ought to draw a flame from the electric iron tube with which he is in communication: but this [p. 157] is false: therefore. Proof of the major: a man resting on the floor draws a little flame from the iron tube with which he does not communicate: therefore a fortiori a man placed on the cake ought, etc. I deny the consequence. The man placed on the cake is just as electric as the iron tube, and is therefore surrounded by an electric atmosphere just as dense as the atmosphere of the iron tube. Whereas the man resting on the floor is only initially electric, and is consequently surrounded by a rare electric atmosphere, while the iron tube is girded by a dense electric atmosphere: therefore, according to the principles set forth above, the latter must draw some little flame from the iron tube, but the former none. But, you will say, by what mechanism is the spirit of wine inflamed, which is mentioned in Observation III of Experiment II? I reply: the spirit of wine is inflamed in exactly the same way in which a certain little flame is drawn from the iron tube.

> 503 Opp. 3.: non datur in hac nova sententia causa physica *adfluentiae* particularum ignearum versùs corpora actu electrica: ergo admittenda non est explicatio Experimenti. III. Prob. antec: antequàm imprimeretur globo vitreo motus aliquis rotationis, materia electrica, quae reperiebatur in aëre, non adfluebat versùs globum vitreum, aut versùs tubum ferreum: ergo neque adfluere debet, postquàm vitreo globo fuit motus aliquis rotationis impressus. Nego primum antec.: Datur in atmosphaera inferiori plenum sensibile, & aer est elasticus. Quibus praesuppositis sic ratiocinor: Globus vitreus fieri non potest electricus, quin ignea multa corpuscula ex sinu suo emittat, & quin novum motum acquirat materia electrica, quae reperitur in aëre, & in corporibus machinam electricam hinc indè circumstantibus. Haec autem omnia non possunt accidere, quin, propter aërem elasticum, & propter plenum sensibile, effluentiae particularum ignearum ex sinu vitrei globi, correspondeat *adfluentia* earumdem, aut similium particularum ignearum versùs eundem globum vitreum. Quod de globo vitreo dictum est, hoc de tubo ferreo dicatur proportionaliter: ergo in hac sententia datur causa physica adfluentiae particularum ignearum versus electrica corpora.

503 Obj. 3. In this new opinion there is no physical cause of the affluence of fiery particles toward bodies actually electric: therefore the explanation of Experiment III is not to be admitted. I prove the antecedent: before some motion of rotation was impressed on the glass globe, the electric matter which was found in the air did not flow toward the glass globe or toward the iron tube: therefore neither ought it to flow toward them after some motion of rotation has been impressed on the glass globe. I deny the first antecedent: in the lower atmosphere there is a sensible plenum, and the air is elastic. These things presupposed, I reason thus: the glass globe cannot become electric without emitting many fiery corpuscles from its bosom, and without a new motion being acquired by the electric matter which is found in the air and in the bodies standing round the electric machine on every side. But all these things cannot happen without there corresponding, on account of the elastic air and on account of the sensible plenum, to the effluence of fiery particles from the bosom of the glass globe an affluence of the same, or of similar, fiery particles toward the same glass globe. What has been said of the glass globe, let it be said proportionally of the iron tube: therefore in this opinion there is a physical cause of the affluence of fiery particles toward electric bodies.

> 504 Nego ultimam conseq: In primo casu jacturam nullam patiebatur vitreus globus, & novum motum non acceperat electrica materia, quae reperitur in aëre, & in corporibus machinam electricam hinc indè circumstantibus. In 2. autèm casu immensam ferè jacturam particularum ignearum pátitur vitreus globus: & novum motum acquisivit electrica materia, quae reperitur in aëre, & in corporibus machinam electricam hinc indè circumstantibus. At *inquies*: ¿Quaenam est causa physica *effluentiae* particularum ignearum ex sinu vitrei globi sicca manu fricati? Respondeo: *effluentia* haec debetur *frictioni* junctae motui rotationis. *Dices* iterùm: ¿Quanam igitur de causa ex globo metallico sicca manu fricato, & vehementissimo motu rotationis donato non effluunt igneae particulae? Respondeo: existere phaenomeni hujus causam geminam: nam I. multò [p. 158] pauciora sunt ignea corpuscula in metallis, & in corporibus per communicationem electricis, quàm in vitro, & in corporibus electricis per se. II. Habent metalla partes rigidiusculas[?], quibus frictio motum illum non imprimit, ex quo enascitur[?] corpusculorum igneorum effluentia.

504 I deny the last consequence: in the first case the glass globe was suffering no loss, and the electric matter which is found in the air and in the bodies standing round the electric machine on every side had not received a new motion. But in the 2nd case the glass globe suffers an almost immense loss of fiery particles, and the electric matter which is found in the air and in the bodies standing round the electric machine on every side has acquired a new motion. But you will say: what is the physical cause of the effluence of fiery particles from the bosom of the glass globe rubbed with a dry hand? I reply: this effluence is owed to friction joined to the motion of rotation. You will say again: for what cause, then, do no fiery particles flow out of a metal globe rubbed with a dry hand and endowed with a most vehement motion of rotation? I reply that there exists a twofold cause of this phenomenon: for I. there are far fewer [p. 158] fiery corpuscles in metals, and in bodies electric by communication, than in glass and in bodies electric of themselves. II. Metals have somewhat rigid parts, on which friction does not impress that motion from which the effluence of fiery corpuscles arises.

> 505 Opp. 4. Ex nostra sententia sequitur, quod si filum ferreum, de quo fit mentio in Experimento IV includeretur in lagena metallica, commotio foret multò vehementior, quàm quum filum ferreum includitur in lagena vitrea: sed hoc est falsum: ergo. Prob. maj.: si filum ferreum includeretur in lagena metallica, profluvium igneum ingrediens per manum, quae partem inferiorem lagenae metallicae sustinet, multò majus foret, quàm quum experimentum fit ope[?] lagenae vitreae: ergo ex nostra sententia sequitur &c. Prob. antec.: electrica materia multò facilius permeat lagenam metallicam, quàm lagenam vitream: ergo si &c. Nego secundum antec. tanquam falsum supponens. Filum ferreum inclusum in lagena metallica non fieret sensibiliter electricum, per poros enim metalli evaporaretur materia electrica filo ferreo communicata. Hinc concedo ultimum antec. & nego conseq.

505 Obj. 4. From our opinion it follows that if the iron wire mentioned in Experiment IV were enclosed in a metal flask, the shock would be much more vehement than when the iron wire is enclosed in a glass flask; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the major: if the iron wire were enclosed in a metal flask, the fiery outflow entering through the hand that holds up the lower part of the metal flask would be much greater than when the experiment is made by means of a glass flask; therefore from our opinion it follows, etc. Proof of the antecedent: the electric matter permeates a metal flask much more easily than a glass flask: therefore, if, etc. I deny the second antecedent, as supposing something false. The iron wire enclosed in a metal flask would not become sensibly electric; for the electric matter communicated to the iron wire would evaporate through the pores of the metal. Hence I concede the last antecedent and deny the consequence.

> 506 Opp. 5. non datur in sententia nostra causa physica fragóris de quo fit mentio in Experimento V: ergo. Prob. antec.: conflictus vehemens duorum profluviorum electricorum non deberet fragorem tantum excitare: ergo non datur &c. Dist. antec.: conflictus vehemens duorum profluviorum electricorum in loco fere[?] vacuo non deberet fragorem tantum excitare, concedo; conflictus vehemens duorum profluviorum electricorum, quae rarefaciunt, & expellunt aërem intermedium fragorem tantum non deberet excitare, nego & conseq. Quum de sono agemus omnis penitus evanescet difficultas[?].

506 Obj. 5. In our opinion there is no physical cause of the crash mentioned in Experiment V: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: the vehement conflict of two electric outflows ought not to excite so great a crash; therefore there is not, etc. I distinguish the antecedent: the vehement conflict of two electric outflows in an empty place ought not to excite so great a crash, I concede; the vehement conflict of two electric outflows which rarefy and expel the intermediate air ought not to excite so great a crash, I deny, and I deny the consequence. When we treat of sound, every difficulty will vanish entirely.

> 507 Opp. 6. nubes fulmen in sinu suo deferens, non est corpus electricum: ergo non valet explicatio Experimenti VI. Prob. antec.: nubes fulmen in sinu suo deferens est corpus aqueum: ergo non est corpus electricum. Dist. antec.: est corpus aqueum totaliter, nego; partialiter tantum, concedo, & nego conseq. Nubes fulmen deferens, est corpus continens particulas aqueas, sulphureas, bituminosas, nitrosas &c. Exponemus in articulo fulminis, quonam mechanismo nubes haec vim electricam acquirat.

507 Obj. 6. A cloud bearing lightning in its bosom is not an electric body: therefore the explanation of Experiment VI does not hold. Proof of the antecedent: a cloud bearing lightning in its bosom is a watery body: therefore it is not an electric body. I distinguish the antecedent: it is a body totally watery, I deny; partially only, I concede, and I deny the consequence. A cloud bearing lightning is a body containing watery, sulphurous, bituminous, nitrous particles, etc. In the article on lightning we shall set forth by what mechanism this cloud acquires electric force.

> 508 Opp. 7. Ex nostra sententia sequitur, quod Fricator de quo fit mentio in Experimento VII non deberet flammam excitare ex tubo ferreo ad quem digitum suum admovet, sed hoc est falsum: ergo. Prob. maj.: homo super placentam resinaceam more solito collocatus flammam non excitat ex tubo quocum communicat per filum ferreum: ergo pariter Fricator super placentam collocatus non debet flammam excitare ex tubo ferreo quocum per globum vitreum communicationem habet. Nego conseq. Homo super placentam collocatus tam est electricus, quàm tubus ferreus [p. 159] quocum per filum ferreum communicat: contrà verò Fricator multò minus est electricus quàm tubus ferreus, licet constituatur[?] super placentam resinaceam: ergo debet hic ex tubo ferreo aliquam, ille verò nullam flammulam excitare.
