508 Obj. 7. From our opinion it follows that the Rubber mentioned in Experiment VII ought not to draw a flame from the iron tube to which he brings his finger; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the major: a man placed in the usual way on a resin cake does not draw a flame from the tube with which he communicates through the iron wire: therefore likewise the Rubber placed on the cake ought not to draw a flame from the iron tube with which he has communication through the glass globe. I deny the consequence. The man placed on the cake is just as electric as the iron tube with [p. 159] which he communicates through the iron wire: whereas the Rubber is much less electric than the iron tube, even though he is placed on a cake of resin: therefore the former must draw some little flame from the iron tube, but the latter none.

> CAPUT IV.

CHAPTER IV.

> Dubia aliqua circa electricitatem quàm brevissimè explicantur.

Some doubts about electricity are explained very briefly.

> 509 Quaeres I. ¿Quanam de causa vis electrica debilior[?] est humido, aut calido tempore, & vis eadem electrica vividior est tempore sicco, aut frigido? Respondeo: humido, aut calido tempore aërem multò minus esse elasticum, quàm tempore sicco, aut frigido: ergo tempore sicco aut frigido, debent ignea corpuscula ex sinu corporis electrici primùm emissa, meliùs in idem corpus repercuti[?], quàm quum tempus est humidum, aut calidum: ergo vis electrica debet vividior esse tempore sicco, aut frigido, quàm tempore humido, aut calido.

ou will ask, I.: for what cause is the electric force weaker in humid or 509 Y warm weather, and the same electric force livelier in dry or cold weather? I reply: in humid or warm weather the air is much less elastic than in dry or cold weather; therefore in dry or cold weather the fiery corpuscles first emitted from the bosom of the electric body must be better beaten back onto the same body than when the weather is humid or warm: therefore the electric force must be livelier in dry or cold weather than in humid or warm weather.

> 510 Quaeres II. ¿Quanam de causa Homo *initialiter* electricus scintillam vividam excitat ex tubo ferreo ad quem digitum suum ádmovet, & idem Homo flammam debiliorem excitat ex globo vitreo ad quem digitum eundem admovet? Respondeo: quod phaenomenon hoc nobis indicare videtur materiam electricam multò puriorem exire ex globo vitreo, quàm ex tubo ferreo.

510 You will ask, II.: for what cause does a man initially electric draw a lively spark from the iron tube to which he brings his finger, while the same man draws a weaker flame from the glass globe to which he brings the same finger? I reply: this phenomenon seems to indicate to us that a much purer electric matter goes out of the glass globe than out of the iron tube.

> 511 Quaeres III. Utrùm materia electrica possit esse contra paralysim remedium praesens? Narratur enim non modò Paralyticum unum Genevae à D. *Jallabert*[^159-s1], sed etiam Paralyticos multos Monspelii fuisse à D. de *Sauvages* curatos ope electricae machinae. Respondeo affirmative. Et verò juxta Medicos Paralysis est motus animalis, & tactûs in parte quadam corporis abolitio, vel diminutio vehemens, cum ejusdem quandoque atrophia, pulsu debili, aliisque symptomatis, proveniens à partium nervosarum relaxatione propter deficientem spirituum animalium praesentiam, aut activitatem ab oborta obstructione nervorum. Materia electrica est materia quaedam ignea subtilissima, quae motu velocissimo donatur. Debet hic ignis sese insinuare per poros materiae, tubulos [p. 160] nervorum obstruentis, paulatimque obstructionem omnem dissipare, & consequenter praesens esse remedium contra paralysin.

511 You will ask, III.: whether the electric matter can be a present remedy against paralysis? For it is related not only that a Paralytic at Geneva was cured by Mr. Jallabert (u), but also that many Paralytics at Montpellier were cured by Mr. de Sauvages by means of the electric machine. I reply in the affirmative. And indeed, according to the Physicians, Paralysis is the abolition, or vehement diminution, of animal motion and of touch in some part of the body, sometimes with atrophy of the same, a weak pulse and other symptoms, arising from a relaxation of the nervous parts on account of the deficient presence, or activity, of the animal spirits, through an obstruction of the nerves that has arisen. The electric matter is a certain most subtle fiery matter, which is endowed with a most rapid motion. This fire must insinuate itself through the pores of the matter obstructing the tubules of the nerves, [p. 160] and little by little dissipate every obstruction, and consequently be a present remedy against paralysis.

> [^159-s1]: Experiences sur l' electricitè par Mr. *Jallabert*.

[^159-s1]: Experiences sur l’électricité, by Mr. Jallabert.

> 512 Quaeres IV. ¿Ad quam distantiam vapor electricus propagetur? Respondeo: incredibile videri posse maximam distantiam ad quam veluti momento temporis hujusmodi vápor propagatur. Nam Fayus ad pedes 1256, Maffejus ad 2220, Watson ad 8000, ad 10600, ad 12276, pedes in filis ferreis virtutem electricam tanta celeritate propagatam fuisse testantur, ut eodem ferè instanti in altera catenae extremitate succusio perciperetur. At non iccircò putamus instantaneam esse hujusmodi propagationem, quum Beccaria[^160-s1] adcuratissimis experimentis deprehenderit, vaporem electricum in 500 pedibus Parisiens. percurrendis, sensibile aliquod temporis intervallum insúmere.

512 You will ask, IV.: to what distance is the electric vapor propagated? I reply: the very great distance to which a vapor of this kind is propagated, as it were in a moment of time, may seem incredible. For Du Fay at 1256 feet, Maffei at 2220, Watson at 8000, at 10600, at 12276 feet, testify that the electric virtue was propagated along iron wires with such speed that the shock was perceived at the other extremity of the chain at almost the same instant. But we do not on that account think that a propagation of this kind is instantaneous, since Beccaria (x) discovered by most accurate experiments that the electric vapor, in traversing 500 Paris feet, takes up some sensible interval of time.

> [^160-s1]: Dell' Elettricismo Naturale, & Artificiale.

[^160-s1]: Dell’Elettricismo Naturale, & Artificiale.

> 513 Quaeres V. ¿Quid sint *Phosphori*? Respondeo: Phosphoros omnes jure spectari à Recentioribus Physicis tanquàm corpora per adfrictum electrica. Hinc 1. Phosphorus artificiales ex sulphureis, & salinis urinae partibus constans non modò coruscare debet in ténebris, sed & partium adfrictu accendi ac obvia corpora comburere. Hinc 2. mare agitatum, saccharum celeri motu concussum, ligna putrida, squammae piscium, quum putrescere incipiunt &c. scintillas emittere debent. Hinc 3. certa barometra lucent quum agitantur in ténebris. Hinc 4. scintillas habebitis si dorsa felium pilis adversis fricuéritis[^160-s2].

513 You will ask, V.: what are Phosphori? I reply: all phosphori are rightly regarded by the Modern Physicists as bodies electric by rubbing. Hence 1. artificial phosphorus, consisting of the sulphurous and saline parts of urine, must not only glitter in the dark, but also be kindled by the rubbing of its parts and burn the bodies in its way. Hence 2. the agitated sea, sugar shaken with a quick motion, rotten wood, the scales of fish when they begin to putrefy, etc., must emit sparks. Hence 3. certain barometers shine when they are agitated in the dark. Hence 4. you will have sparks if you rub the backs of cats against the lie of the hair (y).

> [^160-s2]: Alii *naturales* sunt *phosphori*, alii *artificiales* reperiuntur. Inter naturales haberi etiam solent lampyrides (vulgò *alumbradores*) oculi catórum, lingua Viperae irritatae, &c. Artificiales arte parantur, suntque vel sicci, vel liquidi. Siccus est inprimis lapis Bononiensis, qui ex monte Paterno propè Bononiam pétitur, hic ubi post calcinationem aëri exponitur lucem ita haurit, ut in obscuriorem locum posteà translatus aliquandiù instàr carbonis accensi luceat. Cl. Homberg, & Lemeri parare norunt phosphoros fluidos, & consistentes. (*Memoires de l'Acad. 1711. & 1715.*) Verùm nobis otium non súppetit, aut methodum conficiendi phosphoros, aut phaenomena plura, eorumque magis distinctam explicationem dandi; pluribus hoc persequuntur Regnault (*Entret. Phys. tom. 2. Ent. 17.*) & Ozanam (*Recreat. Math. & Phys. tom. 4. Lib. 1. 2.*) Id in universùm pro ratione horum phaenomenorum animadvertendum; motum, agitationemque subtilium partium accidere in observationibus phosphóricis: ita phosphorus Bononiensis radiis luminis agitatur, aut potius partes lapidis sulphureae igne evolutae, & exaltatae, nitrosis, aëris, cui exponuntur particulis per potentiores illius meatus ingressis sic agitantur, ut elucescere in tenebris possint.

[^160-s2]: Some phosphori are natural, others are found to be artificial. Among the natural are usually counted also fireflies (commonly alumbradores), the eyes of cats, the tongue of an irritated Viper, etc. The artificial are prepared by art, and are either dry or liquid. Dry, above all, is the Bologna stone, which is fetched from Monte Paterno near Bologna; when, after calcination, it is exposed to the air, it so drinks in the light that, carried afterwards into a darker place, it shines for some while like a lighted coal. The distinguished Homberg and Lemery knew how to prepare fluid and solid phosphori (Memoires de l’Acad. 1711 & 1715.) But we have not the leisure to give either the method of making phosphori, or more of their phenomena and a more distinct explanation of them; several authors pursue this: Regnault (Entret. Phys., vol. 2, Ent. 17.) and Ozanam (Recreat. Math. & Phys., vol. 4, bk. 1, 2.) As the account of these phenomena, this is to be noted in general: that a motion and agitation of subtle parts occurs in phosphoric observations; thus the Bologna phosphorus is agitated by the rays of light, or rather the sulphureous parts of the stone, unfolded and exalted by fire, are so agitated by the nitrous particles of the air to which it is exposed, entering through its more open passages, that they can shine out in the dark.

[p. 161]

> CAPUT V.

CHAPTER V.

> De Tonitru prout electricitati connexo.

On Thunder as connected with electricity.

> 514 Tria distinguimus in tonitru *fulgur* nempè, *fragorem*, & *fulmen*. Repentina coruscatio subitò perstringens oculos, nomen habet *fúlguris*. Sonus quidam hórridus in atmosphaera boans, & reboans dicitur *fragor*. Denique accensa quaedam exhalatio, quae saepè ingenti cum stráge ad terram usquè detrúditur, vocatur *fulmen*. Quaenam sint causae physicae fulgóris, id facile determinabimus, postquàm sedulò perpendérimus, undenam oriatur fulmen.

e distinguish three things in thunder, namely the flash, the crash 514 Wand the lightning. The sudden glitter that suddenly strikes the eyes has the name of flash. A certain horrid sound booming and re-echoing in the atmosphere is called the crash. Finally, a certain kindled exhalation, which is often thrust down even to the earth with huge destruction, is called lightning. What the physical causes of the flash are we shall easily determine after we have carefully weighed whence lightning arises.

> 515 Dico igitur I: materia electrica est causa physica fulminis. Demonstratur experientia sequenti quam in Cap. II retulimus, & quam hìc in probationem adferre necesse est. Super tectum alti cujusdam aedificii constituatur placenta resinacea, aut vitrea. Super hanc erigatur perpendiculariter aliquis ferreus tubus; constat experientiâ, quod si aliqua nubes déferens in sinu suo fulmen superimmineat huic ferreo tubo, ex illo excitabuntur scintillae, eodem prorsùs, modo ac si tubus hic ferreus, horizontaliter suspensus funiculorum sericorum ope, communicationem habuisset cum vitreo globo eximiae cujusdam electricae machinae: ergo materia electrica est causa physica fulminis.

515 I say, therefore, I.: the electric matter is the physical cause of lightning. It is demonstrated by the following experiment, which we related in Ch. II, and which it is necessary to bring forward here as proof. On the roof of some high building let a cake of resin, or of glass, be placed. On it let some iron tube be set up perpendicularly; experience establishes that if some cloud bearing lightning in its bosom hangs over this iron tube, sparks will be drawn from it in exactly the same way as if this iron tube, suspended horizontally by means of silk cords, had been in communication with the glass globe of some excellent electric machine: therefore the electric matter is the physical cause of lightning.

> 516 Dico 2: particulae bituminosae, sulphurae, nitrosae, &c. sunt alimenta fulminis. Demonstratur 1. Ibi fulmen est frequens, ubi reperiuntur fodinae sulphuris, bituminis, nitri, &c: ergo particulae bituminosae; sulphureae, nitrosae sunt alimenta fulminis. 2. Si quis versetur in loco, qui casu quodam misero fuerit fulmine tactus, is bituminis, sulphuris, & nitri tetrum spirabit odórem: ergo particulae bituminosae, sulphureae, nitrosae sunt alimenta fulminis.

516 I say, 2.: bituminous, sulphureous, nitrous particles, etc., are the food of lightning. It is demonstrated 1. Lightning is frequent where mines of sulphur, bitumen, niter, etc., are found: therefore bituminous, sulphureous, nitrous particles are the food of lightning. 2. If anyone is in a place which by some miserable chance has been struck by lightning, he will breathe a foul smell of bitumen, sulphur and niter: therefore bituminous, sulphureous, nitrous particles are the food of lightning.

> Solvuntur argumenta.

THE ARGUMENTS ARE ANSWERED.

> 517 Opp. 1. Si materia electrica foret causa physica fulminis, sequeretur quod nubes fulmen in sinu suo deferens esset actu electrica, sed hoc est falsum: ergo. Prob. maj.: nihil est quod nubem hujusmodi reddat electricam: ergo falsum est quod actu electrica sit nubes fulmen in sinu suo deferens. Nego conseq. Particulae bituminosae, sulphureae, & nitrosae per actionem solis in atmosphaeram elevatae, reddunt electricam nubem, quam videmus fulmen in sinu suo deferentem.

517 Obj. 1. If the electric matter were the physical cause of lightning, it would follow that a cloud bearing lightning in its bosom is actually electric; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the major: there is nothing that renders a cloud of this kind electric: therefore it is false that a cloud bearing lightning in its bosom is actually electric. I deny the consequence. Bituminous, sulphureous and nitrous particles, raised into the atmosphere by the action of the sun, render electric the cloud which we see bearing lightning in its bosom.

[p. 162]

> 518 Inst. Particulae sulphureae, bituminosae, & nitrosae de quibus hìc agitur, non sunt in statu actuali electricitatis: ergo non possunt electricam reddere nubem, quae fulmen defert in sinu suo. Prob. antec: particulae bituminosae &c, quae vólitant in atmosphaera, frictionem nullam patiuntur: ergo non sunt in statu actuali electricitatis. Dist. antec.: frictionem nullam patiuntur, neque patiuntur aliquid, quod aequivaleat frictioni, nego, & patiuntur aliquid, concedo, & nego conseq. Saepè áccidit, ut particulae bituminosae &c. regnantibus ventis contrariis eleventur in atmosphaeram. Hae particulae jam calidae, maximam tunc patiuntur agitationem. Frictioni validissimae aequivalet haec agitatio, sicque facilè pervenitur ad statum actualis electricitatis. Non potest autem nubes aliqua bitumen, sulphur, & nitrum actu electricum in sinu suo continére, quin pars ipsiùs aquea fiat per communicationem electrica. Ea igitur sola nubes fulmen in sinu suo defert, quae est actu electrica; & ea sola nubes est actu electrica, quae continet particulas bituminosas, sulphureas, & nitrosas regnantibus ventis contrariis in atmosphaeram terrestrem elevatas.

518 Inst. The sulphureous, bituminous and nitrous particles treated of here are not in a state of actual electricity; therefore they cannot render electric the cloud which bears lightning in its bosom. Proof of the antecedent: the bituminous particles, etc., which flit about in the atmosphere, undergo no friction: therefore they are not in a state of actual electricity. I distinguish the antecedent: they undergo no friction, nor do they undergo anything equivalent to friction, I deny; they undergo no friction, but they undergo something, I concede, and I deny the consequence. It often happens that bituminous particles, etc., are raised into the atmosphere when contrary winds prevail. These particles, being already warm, then undergo a very great agitation. This agitation is equivalent to a most vigorous friction, and thus they easily arrive at a state of actual electricity. But a cloud cannot contain in its bosom bitumen, sulphur and niter actually electric without its watery part becoming electric by communication. That cloud alone, therefore, bears lightning in its bosom which is actually electric; and that cloud alone is actually electric which contains bituminous, sulphureous and nitrous particles raised into the terrestrial atmosphere when contrary winds prevail.

> 519 Opp. 2. Multa sunt phaenomena fulmen spectantia, quae non possunt exponi in sententia nostra: ergo rejicienda est. Prob. antec: non potest exponi in hac sententiâ quaenam sit causa physica fúlguris: ergo. Prob antec.: non datur in regione nubium, conflictus atmosphaerae electricae densae, cum atmosphaera electrica rara: ergo. Nego secundum antec., & expono phaenomenon propositum: quum nubes minus electrica fertur in nubem magis electricam, tum fulgur habetur eodem prorsùs mechanismo, quo excitatur electrica scintilla, de qua loquebamur in Experimento IV. Cap. II. Nego etiam tertium antec.: nubes fulmen in sinu suo deferens est corpus totaliter electricum, & consequenter corpus atmosphaerâ electricâ densissima circúmdatum, quod redit *initialiter* electricas nubes vicinas, quae fulmen in sinu suo non habent: ergo in sententia nostra datur in regione nubium, conflictus atmosphaerae electricae densae, cum atmosphera electrica rara.

519 Obj. 2. There are many phenomena regarding lightning which cannot be explained in our opinion: therefore it is to be rejected. Proof of the antecedent: it cannot be explained in this opinion what the physical cause of the flash is: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: in the region of the clouds there is no conflict of a dense electric atmosphere with a rare electric atmosphere: therefore. I deny the second antecedent, and I explain the proposed phenomenon: when a less electric cloud is borne into a more electric cloud, then the flash occurs by exactly the same mechanism by which the electric spark is excited of which we spoke in Experiment IV, Ch. II. I deny also the third antecedent: a cloud bearing lightning in its bosom is a body totally electric, and consequently a body surrounded by a very dense electric atmosphere, which renders initially electric the neighboring clouds that do not have lightning in their bosom: therefore in our opinion there is, in the region of the clouds, a conflict of a dense electric atmosphere with a rare electric atmosphere.

> 520 Inst. 1. ex dictis sequitur quod nullum *fulgur* esse deberet, quum nubes *totaliter* electrica habet in vicinia sua nubes *totaliter* electricas, sed hoc repugnare videtur; ergo. Dist. major.: sequitur &c. si nubes omnes eundem habeant gradum *totalis* electricitatis, concedo, si gradum habeant diversum *totalis* electricitatis, nego maj., & conseq Fricator super placentam resinaceam constitutus fit *totaliter* electricus: is tamen scintillam éxcitat ex tubo ferreo *totaliter* etiam electrico, quia scilicet vis electrica multò debilior est in Fricatore, quàm in tubo: ergo pariter ex duabus nubibus *totaliter* electricis scintilla debet excitari, dummodò una sit magis vel minus electrica, quàm altera.

520 Inst. 1. From what has been said it follows that there ought to be no flash when a totally electric cloud has totally electric clouds in its vicinity; but this seems repugnant; therefore. I distinguish the major: it follows, etc., if all the clouds have the same degree of total electricity, I concede; if they have a different degree of total electricity, I deny the major, and the consequence. Let the Rubber placed on a resin cake be totally electric: he nevertheless draws a spark from the iron tube, which is also totally electric, because, namely, the electric force is much weaker in the Rubber than in the tube: therefore likewise a spark must be excited from two totally electric clouds, provided one is more or less electric than the other.

> 521 At inquies ¿Quaenam est in nostra sententia causa physica *fragoris* in atmosphaera boantis, & reboantis? Respondeo: [p. 163] Fulgur dilátat aërem contentum inter nubem magis electricam, & nubem minus electricam, quae sibi mutuo occurrunt. Hic aër subitò dilatatus cómprimit aërem vicinum, aër vicinus eximio elaterio donatus, sese restituit in primam suam figuram, atque sese restituendo fragorem hórridum éxcitat quem audímus in atmosphaera boantem, & reboantem. Ex hac physica explicatione haec necessariò sequuntur 1. Nonnunquam dari debent fulgura, quin fragor audiatur; quum scilicet, vel nimiùm distamus à loco in quo versatur nubes electrica, vel quum aër contentus inter nubem magis electricam, & nubem minus electricam sufficientem non acquisivit dilatationem. II. Nonnunquam audiri debet fragor, quin fulgur habeatur, quod accidit, quum terram inter, & nubem electricam reperitur nubes aliqua crassior; nubes enim hujusmodi, radios luminis absorbet ex quibus fulgura constant.

521 But, you will say, what in our opinion is the physical cause of the crash booming and re-echoing in the atmosphere? I reply: the flash [p. 163] dilates the air contained between the more electric cloud and the less electric cloud which run against each other. This air, suddenly dilated, compresses the neighboring air; the neighboring air, endowed with an excellent elater, restores itself to its first figure, and in restoring itself excites the horrid crash which we hear booming and re-echoing in the atmosphere. From this physical explanation the following necessarily follow: I. There must sometimes be lightning flashes without any crash being heard; namely, when we are too far distant from the place in which the electric cloud is moving, or when the air contained between the more electric cloud and the less electric cloud has not acquired sufficient dilatation. II. Sometimes a crash must be heard without any lightning flash being seen, which happens when some thicker cloud is found between the earth and the electric cloud; for a cloud of this kind absorbs the rays of light of which lightning flashes consist.

> 522 III. Non raro judicare debemus, sonum intra nubium viscera quasi discurrere; sonus enim saepè reflectitur, vel á diversis nubium partibus, vel á diversis montibus, & cautibus, &c. IV. Fragor non auditur ex magna distantia; sonus enim non secùs, ac motus, hoc est per incursum in alia corpora tùm debilior fit, tùm etiam quandoque perit. V. Facilè cognosci potest, quantum distet á nobis nubes, quae fulmen in sinu suo continet. Et verò lumen fulguris ad nos usque intra spatium insensibile temporis, transmittitur; sonus autem intra unum minutum secundum temporis 173 hexapedas parisinas tantummodò percurrit: si igitur fulgur inter, & fragorem numerentur quatuor minuta secunda temporis, inde inferetur evidenter nubem electricam 692 hexapedis Parisinis á nobis esse distantem. VI. Si fragor audiatur eodem instanti praecisè, quo micat fulgur, tùm inferendum erit propiorem esse nubem electricam.

522 III. Not rarely must we judge the sound to be, as it were, running about within the bowels of the clouds; for the sound is often reflected either from different parts of the clouds, or from different mountains and crags, etc. IV. The crash is not heard from a great distance; for sound, no otherwise than motion, that is, through running into other bodies, both becomes weaker and sometimes even perishes. V. It can easily be known how far distant from us is the cloud which holds the thunderbolt in its bosom. And indeed the light of the lightning flash is transmitted all the way to us within an insensible space of time, whereas sound runs through only 173 Paris toises within one second of time: if, therefore, four seconds of time should be counted between the flash and the crash, it will evidently be inferred from this that the electric cloud is 692 Paris toises distant from us. VI. If the crash is heard at precisely the same instant at which the flash gleams, then it will have to be inferred that the electric cloud is nearer.

> 523 Quaeres iterum: ¿Quandonam, & quânam de causa frángitur nubes, fulmen in sinu suo deferens? Respondeo: tùnc frangi nubem fulmen in sinu suo continentem, quum validior est ventus, qui fert nubem minus electricam contra nubem magis electricam, vel quum vividior est electricitas, quae viget intra nubis electricae viscera. Neque profectò ullus erit, qui vim, & efficaciam hujus ultimae causae révocet in dubium; nemo enim nescit propter nimiam electricitatem, hiberno praecipuè tempore, confractos fuisse vitreos globos; ergo á fortiori nimiam propter electricitatem saepius frangi debent electricae nubes.

523 You will ask again: When, and for what cause, is the cloud carrying the thunderbolt in its bosom broken? I reply: the cloud containing the thunderbolt in its bosom is broken then, when the wind which carries the less electric cloud against the more electric cloud is stronger, or when the electricity which thrives within the bowels of the electric cloud is more vigorous. Nor indeed will there be anyone who calls into doubt the force and efficacy of this last cause; for no one is unaware that, on account of excessive electricity, especially in wintertime, glass globes have been shattered; therefore a fortiori electric clouds must more often be broken on account of excessive electricity.

> 524 Ex dictis haec evidenter sequuntur. I. Exhalationes bituminosas, sulphureas, & nitrosas quae reperiuntur intra viscera nubium electricarum, & quae sunt alimenta fulminis accendi debere per ignem electricum. II. Ex his exhalationibus alias esse crassas, alias tenuiores: exhalationes crassae agunt in corpora, quorum ampliores sunt pori; & intacta relinquunt corpora, quorum pori arctiores sunt. Eam ob causam fulmina quaedam nonnunquam vaginam, intacto ense, consumpsére. Tenues autèm exhalationes agunt [p. 164] in sola corpora compacta. Exhalationibus hujus speciei constabant fulmina, quae liquaverunt ensem intacta vagina.

524 From what has been said the following evidently follow. I. The bituminous, sulphureous and nitrous exhalations which are found within the bowels of electric clouds, and which are the fuel of the thunderbolt, must be kindled by the electric fire. II. Of these exhalations some are thick, others thinner: the thick exhalations act on bodies whose pores are wider, and leave untouched bodies whose pores are narrower. For that reason certain thunderbolts have sometimes consumed the scabbard, leaving the sword untouched. Thin exhalations, on the other hand, act only [p. 164] on compact bodies alone. Of exhalations of this species were formed the thunderbolts which melted the sword, leaving the scabbard untouched.

> 525 Quaeres deniquè ¿Undenam oriatur vis stupenda exhalationis accensae? Respondeo: oriri primum ab ipsa velocitate ignis, quam incredibilem esse, norunt omnes; deinde ab ipso elaterio aëris, qui reperitur intra particulas sulphureas, bituminosas, & nitrosas ex quibus exhalatio constat. Hic autem est diligenter adnotandum non omne fulmen, seu non omnem exhalationem accensam in terram décidere. Ea tantum exhalatio cadit, cui nubes superiores resistentiam majorem opponunt, quàm nubes inferiores.

525 You will ask, finally: Whence does the stupendous force of the kindled exhalation arise? I reply: it arises first from the very velocity of fire, which all know to be incredible; then from the very elater of the air which is found within the sulphureous, bituminous and nitrous particles of which the exhalation consists. Here, however, it is to be diligently noted that not every thunderbolt, or not every kindled exhalation, falls to the earth. That exhalation alone falls to which the upper clouds oppose a greater resistance than the lower clouds.

> 526 Opp. deniquè: in sententia nostra exponi non potest, undenam oriatur lapis fulmineus, ergo sunt phaenomena fulmen spectantia quae in hac sententia non possunt exponi. Prob. antec: lapis neque est materia neque alimentum fulminis: ergo. Nego totum argumentum, tanquam falsum supponens. Quaecumque narrantur de lapide fulmineo, haec habentur â Physicis Recentioribus, Viris nempè sanae mentis, tanquam aniles fabulae. Lapis fulmineus nihil est aliud quam lapis existens in loco ad quem fulmen pervenit, & ab accensa exhalatione sensibiliter immutatus. Haec circà tonitru tradenda habuimus. Jam verò postulat naturalis ordo, ut pauca dicamus de terraemotibus, quibus cum tonitru magnam analogiam esse, jure videtur.

526 Obj. finally: in our opinion it cannot be explained whence the thunderstone arises; therefore there are phenomena regarding the thunderbolt which cannot be explained in this opinion. Proof of the antec.: the stone is neither the matter nor the fuel of the thunderbolt: therefore. I deny the whole argument, as supposing what is false. Whatever is related about the thunderstone is held by the more recent Physicists, men, namely, of sound mind, as old wives’ tales. The thunderstone is nothing other than a stone existing in the place to which the thunderbolt has come, and sensibly altered by the kindled exhalation. This is what we had to set forth concerning thunder. Now, however, the natural order demands that we say a few things about earthquakes, with which thunder is rightly seen to have a great analogy.

## CAPUT VI. — CHAPTER VI

> De Terraemotibus prout ab Electricitate pendentibus.

On Earthquakes, as Depending on Electricity.

> 527 Si quis unquam in dubium revocaverit diversos terrae tractus validis aliquandò motibus succuti, is interrogare poterit miseros Olysiponenses, quorum urbs praeclara fuit violentem propter terrae concussionem, die 1 Novembris anni 1755, non solum subversa, sed & quasi absorpta.[^164-s1] Ut autem funesti hujus phaenomeni causas physicas certius, & facilius inveniamus, haec mihi videntur esse necessariò praemittenda. Primo: praeter ignem quem in centro terrae admittunt non pauci Physici, & quem ideo *centralem* adpellant, dantur [p. 165] insuper in ejusdem terrae sinu ignes multi subterranei. Hinc oriuntur flammae, quas évomunt mons Aetna in Sicilia, mons Vesubius in tractu Neapolitano, &c. II. Sine pábulo non servantur ignes isti subterranei. Pábulum autèm ignium istorum commune sunt sulphur, bitumen, nitrum, ceteràque corpora fossilia, quorum plurima sunt per adfrictum electrica. Hinc non mirum est quod frequentes sint sulphuris, & bituminis fodinae in iis terrarum tractibus sub quibus subterranei ignes látitant.

f anyone has ever called into doubt that various tracts of the earth have at 527 I times been shaken by violent motions, he may question the wretched people of Lisbon, whose most illustrious city, on account of a violent concussion of the earth, on the 1st of November of the year 1755, was not only overturned but, as it were, swallowed up. (z) But in order that we may find the physical causes of this deadly phenomenon more surely and more easily, the following seem to me necessarily to be premised. First: besides the fire which not a few Physicists admit at the center of the earth, and which for that reason they call central, there are in addition many [p. 165] many subterranean fires in the bosom of the same earth. Hence arise the flames which Mount Etna in Sicily, Mount Vesuvius in the territory of Naples, etc., vomit forth. II. These subterranean fires are not kept up without fuel. The common fuel of these fires, moreover, is sulphur, bitumen, niter and the other fossil bodies, most of which are electric by friction. Hence it is no wonder that mines of sulphur and of bitumen are frequent in those tracts of land beneath which subterranean fires lie hidden.

> [^164-s1]: Idem infortunium passa est *Guathimala* praeclara Urbs hujus nostrae Americae violentam propter terrae concussionem subversa, die 29 Julii Anni proximè elapsi 1773.

[^164-s1]: The same misfortune was suffered by Guatemala, an illustrious City of this our America, overturned on account of a violent concussion of the earth on the 29th of July of the year just past, 1773.

> 528 III. Accenduntur in ipso terrae sinu particulae sulphureae, bituminosae, & nitrosae jam calidae per motum impressum electricae materiae quam continent. Excitatur autem hic novus motus, seu potiùs aequivalens haec frictio, nùnc à ventis contrariis in intima terrae viscera per ingentes ipsius meatus quos *aerophilacios* vocant penetrantibus, nùnc ab electrica scintilla intùs excitata. Hinc sequitur dari corpora *per se* electrica inflammabilia, & corpora *per se* electrica non inflammabilia. Primi generis sunt materiae omnes sulphureae, secundi generis materiae vitreae. IV. Dantur in sinu terrae specus subterraneae, quibus ut plurimùm ingentes montium moles incumbunt. V. In specubus subtérraneis reperiuntur, ignis, aqua, aër, ita tamen ut ignis, seu potiùs materia combustibilis, nempè sulphurea, bituminosa accensa locum inferiorem occupet, aqua verò locum medium, aër autem locum superiorem. His praemissis, & quasi totidèm principiis positis.

528 III. Within the very bosom of the earth sulphureous, bituminous and nitrous particles, already hot through the motion impressed by the electric matter which they contain, are kindled. This new motion, however, or rather this equivalent friction, is excited now by contrary winds penetrating into the inmost bowels of the earth through its huge passages, which they call aërophylacia, now by an electric spark excited within. Hence it follows that there are bodies electric per se that are inflammable, and bodies electric per se that are not inflammable. Of the first kind are all sulphureous materials, of the second kind vitreous materials. IV. There are in the bosom of the earth subterranean caves, upon which for the most part huge masses of mountains rest. V. In subterranean caves are found fire, water and air, in such a way, however, that the fire, or rather the combustible matter, namely sulphureous and bituminous matter, when kindled, occupies the lowest place, the water the middle place, and the air the uppermost place. These things being premised, and laid down as so many principles,

> 529 Dico: Principiorum mox traditorum ope facilè admodùm exponuntur terreaemotus. Prob. conclusio explicatione sequenti. Sit ingens specus subterranea, cui regio, vel urbs aliqua superincumbat. In inferiori parte hujus specus accendantur per ignem electricum, materiae sulphureae, bituminosae, nitrosae, &c. Partem mediam specus ejusdem occupet aqua, & partem superiorem aër. Quibus suppositis sic ratiocinor. Res in hoc statu esse non possunt, quin ab igne subterraneo incalescant aqua, & aër: incalescere non possunt aqua, & aër, quin mirum in modum rarefiant; rarefieri non possunt, quin majorem locum occupare conentur. Quò faciliùs igitur ab iis angustiis liberentur atque sese expediant, proprium carcerem adtollent, ipsum disrumpent, atque vehementi cum fragóre indè erumpent; ¿quid mirum igitur quòd terra validis tunc succutiatur motibus?

529 I say: By means of the principles just set forth earthquakes are explained very easily. The conclusion is proved by the following explanation. Let there be a huge subterranean cave over which some region or city lies. In the lower part of this cave let sulphureous, bituminous, nitrous materials, etc., be kindled by electric fire. Let water occupy the middle part of the same cave, and air the upper part. These things supposed, I reason thus. Things cannot be in this state without the water and the air growing hot from the subterranean fire: the water and the air cannot grow hot without being rarefied in a wonderful manner; they cannot be rarefied without striving to occupy a greater space. Therefore, in order to free themselves from those straits and extricate themselves the more easily, they will lift up their own prison, burst it asunder, and break out from it with a violent crash: what wonder, then, that the earth is at that time shaken by violent motions?

> 530 Ea fuit probabiliter causa physica non solum violentae hujus concussionis qua subversa fuit Urbs Olysiponensis, & Guathimalensis, sed etiam omnium omninò terraemotuum de quibus ampla fit apud Historicos mentio. Funesti hujus phaenomeni sensibilem vobis praebent imagines cuniculi militares. Et verò si pulvere pyrio selecto cuniculum instruas, & probè majores omnes meatus obstruas; pulvis pyrius accensus certum terrae tractum non movebit modò, sed penitùs subvertet:[^165-s1] ergo principiorum traditorum ope rectè, & facilè admodum exponitur, quidquid ad terraemotus adtinet.

530 This was probably the physical cause not only of the violent concussion by which the City of Lisbon was overturned, and that of Guatemala, but also of absolutely all the earthquakes of which ample mention is made among the Historians. Military mines afford you sensible images of this deadly phenomenon. And indeed, if you furnish a mine with choice gunpowder and duly stop up all the larger passages, the kindled gunpowder will not merely move a certain tract of earth but will utterly overturn it: (*) therefore by means of the principles set forth, whatever pertains to earthquakes is explained rightly and very easily.

> [^165-s1]: Vid. Memoir. de l' Academ. Royal, ad ann. 1700.

[^165-s1]: See Memoir. de l’Academ. Royal, for the year 1700.

[p. 166]

> Solvuntur argumenta.

THE ARGUMENTS ARE ANSWERED.

> 531 Opp. 1. Tota haec explicatio terraemotuum falsum supponit: ergo & ipsa falsa est. Prob. antec.: Supponit ignes accensos existere in fundo subterranearum specuum; sed hoc est falsum: ergo. Prob. minor.: si existerent ignes accensi, existeret, & aer in eodem fundo, atqui ibi non existit: ergo. Prob. minor: aër occupat partem superiorem specus: ergo non existit in ejus fundo. Dist. ultimum antec.: omnis aër subterraneus occupat &c, nego, maxima pars illius, concedo & nego conseq. Quemadmodùm in excipulo machinae pneumaticae ex quo fuit aër exhaustus, existere non potest accensus ignis, ita similiter non existerent ignes accensi in fundo subterranearum specuum, si fundum hoc esset prorsùs aëre vacuum. Quamvis igitur maxima pars aëris subterranei reperiatur in parte superiori specus, non dubium est, quin multus aër existat in ejus fundo.

bj. 1. This whole explanation of earthquakes supposes what is false: 531 O therefore it is itself false as well. Proof of the antec.: It supposes that kindled fires exist at the bottom of subterranean caves; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the minor: if kindled fires existed, air also would exist at the same bottom; but it does not exist there: therefore. Proof of the minor: air occupies the upper part of the cave: therefore it does not exist at its bottom. I distinguish the last antecedent: all subterranean air occupies, etc., I deny; the greatest part of it, I grant, and I deny the consequence. Just as kindled fire cannot exist in the receiver of the pneumatic machine from which the air has been exhausted, so likewise kindled fires would not exist at the bottom of subterranean caves if this bottom were altogether empty of air. Although, therefore, the greatest part of the subterranean air is found in the upper part of the cave, there is no doubt that much air exists at its bottom.

> 532 Opp. 2. Si terraemotus pendérent à causis superiùs adsignatis, sequeretur quod loca maritima non deberent esse terraemotibus magis obnoxia, quàm loca non maritima, sed hoc est falsum: ergo. Prob. maj.: in nostra sententia, maris proximitas non fuit adsignata tanquam una ex causis physicis terraemotuum: ergo loca maritima non deberent esse magis obnoxia terraemotibus, quàm loca mediterranea. Dist. antec.: non fuit adsignata directè, concedo antec.: indirectè, nego, & conseq. Mare suppeditat ignibus subterraneis materiam combustibilem: ergo loca maritima debent esse magis obnoxia terraemotibus, quàm loca non maritima.

532 Obj. 2. If earthquakes depended on the causes assigned above, it would follow that maritime places ought not to be more subject to earthquakes than places not maritime; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the maj.: in our opinion the nearness of the sea was not assigned as one of the physical causes of earthquakes: therefore maritime places ought not to be more subject to earthquakes than inland places. I distinguish the antec.: it was not assigned directly, I grant the antec.; indirectly, I deny, and the conseq. The sea supplies combustible matter to the subterranean fires: therefore maritime places must be more subject to earthquakes than places not maritime.

> 533 At *inquies*, ¿quomodo fieri potest, ut quum terra tremit, tùm saepè mare intumescat? Respondeo: Quum terra tremit, saepè maris fundum elevatur. Non mirum est igitur, quod mare tunc intumescat; non mirum est etiam quod ipsius aquae hùc illùc in utramque partem non sine quodam terrarum diluvio excurrant. Hinc explicabis I. Cur in terraemotu tractus maris absorptis undis, siccus aliquandò remanserit; tunc enim apertis quae sub mari erant subterraneis specubus, tanta voragine aquae exhaustae sunt, ut tractus siccus remanserit. Explicatur II. Cur intumescentia, & inundatio fluminum saepè fuerit terraemotuum effectus. Et verò quoties habemus magnum aliquem terraemotum, totiès fundum maris adtollitur, & ipsius aquae intumescunt; quoties fundum maris adtollitur, totiès fluminum aquae non possunt maris alveum ingredi, quod quum accidit, tum aquae fluviatiles necessariò hùc illùc in utramque partem non sine terrarum diluvio excurrunt.

533 But you will say: how can it come about that, when the earth trembles, the sea then often swells? I reply: When the earth trembles, the bottom of the sea is often raised. It is no wonder, therefore, that the sea then swells; no wonder, too, that its waters run out hither and thither in both directions, not without a certain deluge of the land. Hence you will explain I. Why in an earthquake a tract of the sea, its waves swallowed up, has sometimes remained dry; for then, the subterranean caves which were under the sea being opened, the waters were drained off by so great an abyss that the tract remained dry. There is explained II. Why the swelling and flooding of rivers has often been an effect of earthquakes. And indeed, as often as we have some great earthquake, so often the bottom of the sea is raised and its waters swell; as often as the bottom of the sea is raised, so often the waters of the rivers cannot enter the bed of the sea; and when this happens, then the river waters necessarily run out hither and thither in both directions, not without a deluge of the land.

> 534 Explicabis III: cur in quibusdam terraemotibus adsurrexerint insulae novae. Tunc enim aër per ignes subterraneos dilatatus, ita terram sub aquis delitescentem adtollit, ut haec eadem terra [p. 167] sublimior evadat aquarum superficie. Ea fuit probabiliter origo certarum insularum quae in Archipelago, & in Oceano Atlantico adsurrexerunt.

534 You will explain III: why in certain earthquakes new islands have risen up. For then the air, dilated by the subterranean fires, so lifts up the land lying hidden under the waters that this same land comes out higher [p. 167] than the surface of the waters. This was probably the origin of certain islands which have risen up in the Archipelago and in the Atlantic Ocean.

> 535 Inst. 1. Si terraemotus penderent à solis causis superiùs memoratis, sequeretur quod loca montuosa frequentiores terraemotus pati non deberent, quàm loca non montuosa; sed hoc est falsum: ergo. Prob. major.: in sententia nostra montes non adnumerantur inter causas terraemotuum: ergo. Dist. antec.: non adnumerantur directè, concedo; indirectè, nego, & conseq. Ideo loca montuosa frequentiores motus patiuntur, quia ut plurimùm sub montibus specus reperiuntur, ut superiùs diximus. Hinc explicatur facilè cur tremat, nunc major, nunc minor terrae tractus. Id enim pendet ceteris paribus á majore, vel minore cavernae profunditate, & latitudine, quò profundior enim, & latior est subterranea caverna, eò majus evidenter debet esse spatium terrae quod adtollitur.

535 You will insist 1. If earthquakes depended on the causes mentioned above alone, it would follow that mountainous places ought not to suffer more frequent earthquakes than places not mountainous; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the major: in our opinion mountains are not numbered among the causes of earthquakes: therefore. I distinguish the antec.: they are not numbered directly, I grant; indirectly, I deny, and the conseq. Mountainous places suffer more frequent motions for this reason, that for the most part caves are found under mountains, as we said above. Hence it is easily explained why now a greater, now a lesser tract of earth trembles. For this depends, other things being equal, on the greater or lesser depth and breadth of the cavern; for the deeper and broader the subterranean cavern is, the greater, evidently, must be the space of earth which is lifted up.

> 536 Inst. 2. Ex dictis sequitur quod idem terraemotus non posset duas urbes concútere, quin & concúteret omnia loca intermedia, sed hoc est falsum, nam ultimus terraemotus, quem *Olysiponensem* vocare possumus, plurimas Europae urbes, aut concussit, aut subvertit; nec tamèn omnia loca intermedia detrimentum aliquod passa fuerunt: ergo. Dist. majorem: quin & concúteret omnia loca intermedia, supponendo quod hic terraemotus pendeat ab unico igne in unica specu subterranea accenso, concedo; supponendo quod pendeat à pluribus ignibus accensis, nego, & conseq. Ultimus terraemotus pendebat evidenter á pluribus ignibus accensis in diversis specubus subterraneis, quae per venas sulphureas inter se communicabant.

536 You will insist 2. From what has been said it follows that the same earthquake could not shake two cities without also shaking all the places in between; but this is false, for the last earthquake, which we can call that of Lisbon, either shook or overturned very many cities of Europe; and yet not all the places in between suffered some damage: therefore. I distinguish the major: without also shaking all the places in between, supposing that this earthquake depends on a single fire kindled in a single subterranean cave, I grant; supposing that it depends on several kindled fires, I deny, and the conseq. The last earthquake evidently depended on several fires kindled in different subterranean caves, which communicated with one another through sulphureous veins.

> 537 Opp. 3. multa sunt phaenomena ad terraemotus pertinentia quae non possunt exponi in sententia nostra: ergo insufficiens est. Prob. antec. enumeratione sequenti. In nostra sententia non videtur exponi posse phaenomenum sequens: visi sunt terraemotus[?] per quos novae scaturigines apertae sunt, & antiquae scaturigines siccatae fuerunt: ergo &c. Nego antec., & expono phaenomenon propositum. Terraemotus per quos rupti fuerunt ággeres, qui prius aquas quasi inclusas detinebant, novas scaturigines aperire debuerunt. Contrà verò terraemotus per quos novi ággeres fluentibus aquis oppositi fuerunt, antiquas debuerunt siccare scaturigines, ipsasque à pristinâ via, apertis aliis meatibus avértere; ergo in nostra sententia rectè exponitur phaenomenum propositum.

537 Obj. 3. There are many phenomena pertaining to earthquakes which cannot be explained in our opinion: therefore it is insufficient. Proof of the antec. by the following enumeration. In our opinion the following phenomenon does not seem able to be explained: earthquakes have been seen through which new springs were opened, and old springs were dried up: therefore, etc. I deny the antec., and I explain the phenomenon proposed. Earthquakes through which dikes were broken which formerly held back the waters as though shut in must have opened new springs. On the other hand, earthquakes through which new dikes were set against the flowing waters must have dried up the old springs, and turned the waters themselves aside from their former course, other passages being opened: therefore in our opinion the phenomenon proposed is rightly explained.

> 538 At *inquies*: quomodo fieri potuit, ut in quibusdam terraemotibus aquae prius frigidae, evaserint calidae, in aliis verò aquae prius calidae frigefactae fuerint? Respondeo: motus omnes, qui juxta látices aliquot novum ignem accendunt, debent aquas calefacere quae prius erant frigidae, nemo autem dubitat, quin per motum accendi possint materiae combustibiles. Quotiescumque verò per aliquem terraemotum extinguuntur ignes antiqui, sive per [p. 168] evaporationem, sive per aliam quamcumquè causam extinguantur, toties frigescere debent aquae quas prius calefaciebant ignes recens extincti. *Dices* iterum. ¿Quomodo ex certis terraemotibus pestilentia procedere potuit? Respondeo. In quibusdam terraemotibus exeunt ex ipso terrae sinu exhalationes bituminosae, sulphureae, nitrosae &c., quae inficiunt aërem: ergo ex certis terraemotibus debuit procedere pestilentia.

538 But you will say: how could it come about that in certain earthquakes waters formerly cold became hot, while in others waters formerly hot were made cold? I reply: all motions which kindle a new fire near some springs must heat the waters which were formerly cold; and no one doubts that combustible materials can be kindled by motion. But as often as the old fires are extinguished through some earthquake, whether they are extinguished through evaporation [p. 168] or through any other cause whatever, so often must the waters grow cold which the fires lately extinguished used to heat. You will say again: How could pestilence proceed from certain earthquakes? I reply. In certain earthquakes bituminous, sulphureous, nitrous exhalations, etc., come forth from the very bosom of the earth, which infect the air: therefore pestilence must have proceeded from certain earthquakes.

## CAPUT VII. — CHAPTER VII

> De Fluiditate corporum prout electricitati connexa.

On the Fluidity of Bodies, as Connected with Electricity.

> 539 Ea sunt corpora fluida, quae partium suarum sensibilium divisioni non resistunt, & quorum partes insensibiles sunt in motu continuo, & perturbato. Ex hac descriptione haec videntur necessario sequi. Primò. Corpora fluida constare particulis exiguis. Si enim partes ipsorum essent majusculae, & crassiores, non possent hùc illùc facilè moveri. Secundò: Plerumque rotunda est figura particularum ex quibus fluida constant. Et verò particulae hujusmodi facilè separantur aliaé ab aliis: ergo aut parum, aut nihil inter se cohaerent: ergo illas plerumque rotundas esse adfirmari potest. Dixi *plerumque*; non enim negaverim nonnullas, ex his partibus oblongas esse, conicas nonnullas, nonnullas cylindricas, aut alterius cujuscumque figurae. Tertiò: Fluida communia penetrantur á fluido subtiliori, quod ab igne electrico indistinctum esse credimus. His praemissis.

hose bodies are fluid which do not resist the division of their sensi539 T ble parts, and whose insensible parts are in continual and disordered motion. From this description the following seem necessarily to follow. First: Fluid bodies consist of tiny particles. For if their parts were rather large and rather thick, they could not easily be moved hither and thither. Second: For the most part the figure of the particles of which fluids consist is round. And indeed particles of this kind are easily separated one from another: therefore they cohere among themselves either little or not at all: therefore it can be affirmed that they are for the most part round. I said for the most part; for I would not deny that some of these parts are oblong, some conical, some cylindrical, or of any other figure whatever. Third: Common fluids are penetrated by a subtler fluid, which we believe to be not distinct from the electric fire. These things premised,

> 540 Dico: I. Partes insensibiles corporum fluidorum sunt semper in motu perturbato. Prob: sublato motu continuo, & perturbato in partibus insensibilibus corporum fluidorum, explicari non possunt pléraque naturae phaenomena; admisso autem hoc motu, facilè admodùm explicantur haec eadem phaenomena: ergo partes insensibiles corporum fluidorum sunt semper in motu perturbato. Prob. antec.: sublato motu continuò, & perturbato in partibus insensibilibus corporum fluidorum, explicari non potest ex. gr. cur sales exsolvantur in aqua frigida; cur metalla dissolvantur in aquis stygiis &c; admisso autèm hoc motu, negotium nullum facessit horum effectuum explicatio, quemadmodùm vel leviter consideranti patebit: ergo.

540 I say I: The insensible parts of fluid bodies are always in disordered motion. Proof: if continual and disordered motion in the insensible parts of fluid bodies is taken away, most of the phenomena of nature cannot be explained; but if this motion is admitted, these same phenomena are explained very easily: therefore the insensible parts of fluid bodies are always in disordered motion. Proof of the antec.: if continual and disordered motion in the insensible parts of fluid bodies is taken away, it cannot be explained, for example, why salts are dissolved in cold water, why metals are dissolved in Stygian waters, etc.; but if this motion is admitted, the explanation of these effects gives no trouble at all, as will be plain to anyone considering it even lightly: therefore.

> 541 Dico 2: Ignis intra fluida látitans est causa motus continui, & perturbati, quò agitantur partes insensibiles corporum [p. 169] fluidorum. Prob.: motus continuus & perturbatus quò agitantur partes insensibiles corporum fluidorum repetendus est ab illo corpore, cujus partes sunt semper in motu perturbato, ut fatentur omnes Physici: ergo repetendus est ab igne intra hujusmodi corpora latitante.

541 I say 2: The fire lying hidden within fluids is the cause of the continual and disordered motion by which the insensible parts of fluid bodies are agitated. [p. 169] Proof: the continual and disordered motion by which the insensible parts of fluid bodies are agitated is to be traced back to that body whose parts are always in disordered motion, as all Physicists acknowledge: therefore it is to be traced back to the fire lying hidden within bodies of this kind.

> 542 Dico 3: Ignis producens motum continuum, & perturbatum in partibus insensibilibus corporum fluidorum non videtur esse distinctus ab igne electrico. Probatur: Ignis augens fluiditatem corporum, non videtur esse distinctus ab igne hanc eandem fluiditatem producente, sed ignis electricus est ignis augens fluiditatem corporum: ergo ignis electricus est ignis hanc eandem fluiditatem producens. Prob. min.: sint duo vasa perfectè aequalia A, & B (Fig. LIX.) quae adimpleantur eâdem aquâ. Electrica fiat aqua in vase A contenta, remaneatque nonelectrica aqua in vase B comprehensa. Duobus istis vasis succesivè adplicetur idem *sipho capillaris* experientia constat, quod aqua electrica multò velocius fluet, quàm aqua non electrica, seu quod idem est, experientiâ constat, quod aqua electrica fluidior erit, quàm aqua non electrica; ergo ignis electricus, est ignis augens fluiditatem corporum.

542 I say 3: The fire producing the continual and disordered motion in the insensible parts of fluid bodies does not seem to be distinct from the electric fire. Proof: The fire increasing the fluidity of bodies does not seem to be distinct from the fire producing this same fluidity; but the electric fire is a fire increasing the fluidity of bodies: therefore the electric fire is the fire producing this same fluidity. Proof of the min.: let there be two perfectly equal vessels, A and B (Fig. LIX.), which are filled with the same water. Let the water contained in vessel A be made electric, and let the water held in vessel B remain non-electric. To these two vessels let the same capillary siphon be applied in succession: experience establishes that the electric water will flow much more swiftly than the non-electric water, or, what is the same, experience establishes that the electric water will be more fluid than the non-electric water: therefore the electric fire is a fire increasing the fluidity of bodies.

> Solvuntur argumenta.

THE ARGUMENTS ARE ANSWERED.

> 543 Opp. I. Si corpora fluida semper essent in motu perturbato sequeretur quod omnia fluida, forent sensibiliter calida, sed hoc est falsum: ergo. Prob. maj.: natura caloris sensibilis consistit in motu perturbato partium corporis calidi: ergo si &c. Antec. rotundè negari debet â nobis, qui ut Dissertatione sequenti videbimus oppositam sententiam contra Cartesium defendimus. Sed claritatis gratia dist. antec.: in motu perturbato partium sensibilium, ut postea, explicabimus, concedo; partium duntaxat insensibilium corporis calidi, nego, & conseq. Solutio melius explicabitur quum de calore agemus. Sed dices: hoc posito nunquam dici potest fluida esse in quiete. Dist. esse in quiete partium earundem insensibilium, concedo; sensibilium, nego. Ea fluida quiescere dicuntur, quorum pártes sensibiles existunt in quiete respectivâ, hoc est quoad sensum nostrum.

bj. I. If fluid bodies were always in disordered motion, it would follow 543 O that all fluids would be sensibly hot; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the maj.: the nature of sensible heat consists in the disordered motion of the parts of the hot body: therefore if, etc. The antec. must be roundly denied by us, who, as we shall see in the following Dissertation, defend the opposite opinion against Descartes. But for clarity’s sake I distinguish the antec.: in the disordered motion of the sensible parts, as we shall explain afterwards, I grant; of the insensible parts only of the hot body, I deny, and the conseq. The solution will be better explained when we treat of heat. But you will say: this being supposed, it can never be said that fluids are at rest. I distinguish: that they are at rest as to those same insensible parts, I grant; as to the sensible parts, I deny. Those fluids are said to be at rest whose sensible parts exist in respective rest, that is, as far as our sense is concerned.

> 544 Opp. 2. Ignis non est in motu continuo: ergo non est causa fluiditatis corporum. Prob. antec.: motus perpetuus non existit in rerum natura: ergo. Dist. antec.: non existit in rerum natura; hoc est, non existit, motus semel impressus, qui constanter idem, & in eodem praecisè gradu perseveret, concedo; hoc est, non existunt in rerum natura corpora quae semper sint in aliquo motu nunc majore, nec minore, nego, & conseq. Sic autem explicamus, & ad Mechanicae leges redúcimus motum ignis quem liberum supponimus. Primò. Dantur in rerum natura moleculae infinitè parvae, aut quasi infinitè parvae primi, secundi, tertii ordinis &c. à Geometris representari solent hujusmodi moleculae per hos characteres [?]

544 Obj. 2. Fire is not in continual motion: therefore it is not the cause of the fluidity of bodies. Proof of the antec.: perpetual motion does not exist in the nature of things: therefore. I distinguish the antec.: it does not exist in the nature of things, that is, there does not exist a motion, once impressed, which perseveres constantly the same and in precisely the same degree, I grant; that is, there do not exist in the nature of things bodies which are always in some motion, now greater, now lesser, I deny, and the conseq. Thus, moreover, we explain the motion of fire, which we suppose free, and reduce it to the laws of Mechanics. First. There exist in the nature of things molecules infinitely small, or as it were infinitely small, of the first, second, third order, etc. Molecules of this kind are customarily represented by Geometers by these characters:

[p. 170]

> 545 Secundò: Molecula infinitè parva primi ordinis est infinitè major, quàm molecula infinitè parva secundi ordinis; item molecula infinitè parva secundi ordinis est infinitè, aut quasi infinitè major, quàm molecula infinitè parva tertii ordinis &c: molecula A ex. gr. vorticosè gyrabit versùs moleculam B (Fig. LX.) si donetur eodem tempore, & perseveranter motu perpendiculari, seu *centrípeto*, juxta lineam A B, & motu horizontali seu projectionis, juxta lineam A C. Non alio mechanismo Luna gyrat circa terram, & planétae circa Solem periodicè moventur.

545 Second: A molecule infinitely small of the first order is infinitely greater than a molecule infinitely small of the second order; likewise a molecule infinitely small of the second order is infinitely, or as it were infinitely, greater than a molecule infinitely small of the third order, etc.: the molecule A, for example, will whirl round in a vortex toward the molecule B (Fig. LX.) if it is endowed at the same time, and perseveringly, with a perpendicular or centripetal motion along the line A B, and with a horizontal motion, or motion of projection, along the line A C. By no other mechanism does the Moon revolve about the earth, and the planets move periodically about the Sun.

> 546 Centrípeta vis juxta eximium Newtonum [^170-s1] est quâ corpora versùs punctum aliquod tanquàm ad centrum undique trahuntur, impelluntur, vel utcumque tendunt. Demonstravit itaque Cl. Newtonus quod molecula A. infinitè parva secundi ordinis sensibiliter tendet, seu motum centrípetum habebit in moleculam B infinitè parvam primi ordinis, dummodò istae duae moleculae non multum distent à se invicèm. Sic igitur expono motum continuum & vorticosum elementaris ignis. Ignis elementaris seu igneus quicumque vorticulus componitur ex molecula infinitè parva ordinis superioris, circà quam vorticosè gyrant moleculae infinitè parvae inferioris ordinis, simul & perseveranter donatae vi projectionis, & vi centrípeta. Si moleculà centralis sit quantitas infinitè parva primi ordinis, moleculae gyrantes erunt quantitates infinitè parvae secundi ordinis. Si molecula centralis sit quantitas infinitè parva secundi ordinis, moleculae gyrantes erunt quantitates infinitè parvae tertii ordinis &c.

546 Centripetal force, according to the eminent Newton (a), is that by which bodies are drawn, impelled, or in any way tend from all sides toward some point as toward a center. The celebrated Newton has accordingly demonstrated that a molecule A, infinitely small of the second order, will sensibly tend, or will have a centripetal motion, toward a molecule B, infinitely small of the first order, provided these two molecules are not far distant from each other. Thus, therefore, I explain the continual and vortical motion of elementary fire. Elementary fire, or any fiery little vortex whatever, is composed of a molecule infinitely small of a higher order, about which molecules infinitely small of a lower order whirl round in a vortex, endowed simultaneously and perseveringly with the force of projection and with centripetal force. If the central molecule is a quantity infinitely small of the first order, the whirling molecules will be quantities infinitely small of the second order. If the central molecule is a quantity infinitely small of the second order, the whirling molecules will be quantities infinitely small of the third order, etc.

> [^170-s1]: Princip. Lib. 1. Def. [?]

[^170-s1]: Principia, bk. 1, Def. 5.

> 547 Opp. denique: Si per electricitatem fluidior fieret aqua jam fluida, pariter per electricitatem augeretur mercurii fluiditas; sed hoc est falsum: ergo. Prob. minor.: Si per electricitatem augeretur mercurii fluiditas, sequeretur quod mercurius altior esse deberet in thermometro (de quo cum de frigore agemus) cui communicata fuit vividior electricitas, quàm in simili thermometro, quod nullam acquisivit electricitatem, sed hoc est falsum ut experientiâ constat: ergo. Prob. major.: si per electricitatem augetur mercurii fluiditas, sequitur quod major ipsi communicatur ignis quantitas; sed si mercurio thermometri communicatur major ignis quantitas, profectò altior debet esse in thermometro mercurius: ergo si &c.

547 Obj. finally: If water already fluid were made more fluid through electricity, the fluidity of mercury would likewise be increased through electricity; but this is false: therefore. Proof of the minor: if the fluidity of mercury were increased through electricity, it would follow that the mercury ought to stand higher in a thermometer (of which we shall speak when we treat of cold) to which a livelier electricity has been communicated than in a similar thermometer which has acquired no electricity; but this is false, as experience establishes: therefore. Proof of the major: if the fluidity of mercury is increased through electricity, it follows that a greater quantity of fire is communicated to it; but if a greater quantity of fire is communicated to the mercury of the thermometer, the mercury must surely stand higher in the thermometer: therefore if, etc.

> 548 Dist. majorem, si per electricitatem augetur mercurii fluiditas, sequitur quod major ipsi communicatur quantitas ignis electrici & quasi elementaris, concedo, ignis mixti, & quasi usualis, nego, & dist. minorem: si mercurio thermometri communicatur major quantitas ignis mixti, & quasi usualis, profectò altior esse debet in thermometro mercurius, concedo minorem: major quantitas ignis electrici, & quasi elementaris, altior esse debet &c., nego, & conseq. Ignis elementaris constituitur à vorticulis: usualis verò [p. 171] efformatur ab iisdem vorticulis, qui secum abripnerunt particulas bituminosas, sulphureas, oleosas, nitrosas &c. A majori vel minori dilatatione pendet altitudo mercurii in thermometro. Haec autem dilatatio, effectus est ignis mixti, & quasi usualis, non verò ignis electrici, & quasi elementaris; ergo mercurius altior esse non debet in thermometro, cui communicata fuit vividior electricitas, quàm in simili thermometro, quod nullam acquisivit electricitatem. Atque hactenùs de Electricitate.

548 I distinguish the major: if the fluidity of mercury is increased through electricity, it follows that a greater quantity of electric and, as it were, elementary fire is communicated to it, I grant; of mixed and, as it were, usual fire, I deny; and I distinguish the minor: if a greater quantity of mixed and, as it were, usual fire is communicated to the mercury of the thermometer, the mercury must surely stand higher in the thermometer, I grant the minor; if a greater quantity of electric and, as it were, elementary fire, it must stand higher, etc., I deny, and the conseq. Elementary fire is constituted by little vortices; usual fire, on the other hand, [p. 171] is formed by those same little vortices, which have swept along with them bituminous, sulphureous, oily, nitrous particles, etc. On the greater or lesser dilatation depends the height of the mercury in the thermometer. This dilatation, moreover, is an effect of mixed and, as it were, usual fire, not of electric and, as it were, elementary fire: therefore the mercury ought not to stand higher in a thermometer to which a livelier electricity has been communicated than in a similar thermometer which has acquired no electricity. And so much for Electricity.

## PHYSICES — PHYSICS

> PARS IV.

PART IV.

> DE QUALITATIBUS CORPORUM.

ON THE QUALITIES OF BODIES.

## DISSERTATIO I. — DISSERTATION I

> De Physica natura qualitatis sensibilis.

On the Physical Nature of Sensible Quality.

## CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

> Notiones necessariae praemittuntur.

The Necessary Notions Are Set Forth First.

> 549 Suas corpus quodcumque habere *qualitates*, quibus formaliter, ut Scholae verbo utar, sensibile redditur, nescius nemo est: at quae sit physica illarum natura, inter Philosophos acriter disputatur. Scholastici namque, sive Peripatetici, quos vocant *rigidiores* ratum fixumque habent, eas esse, entitates talis naturae, quae à corporea substantia cui insunt, quamque nobis sensibilem reddunt, separari divinitùs possint, & sine illa existere, illas iccircò *accidentia absoluta* adpellant, contrà verò Recentioribus persuasum est, nullam sensibilem qualitatem esse *accidens absolutum* prout illud sumunt Scholastici, sed ex magnitudine, figura, motu, quiete, atque textura corpusculorum; quibus sensibilia quaeque corpora componuntur eas omnes immediatè provenire. Ut verò ordine quo possit magis adcuratiori procedamus, definitiones aliquot praemittendae sunt.

hat every body has qualities by which, formally, to use the word of the 549 T          Schools, it is rendered sensible, no one is unaware: but what their physical nature is, is keenly disputed among Philosophers. For the Scholastics, or Peripatetics, those whom they call the stricter, hold it settled and fixed that they are entities of such a nature that they can be separated by divine power from the bodily substance in which they inhere and which they render sensible to us, and can exist without it; for that reason they call them absolute accidents. The Moderns, on the contrary, are persuaded that no sensible quality is an absolute accident as the Scholastics take it, but that all of them proceed immediately from the magnitude, figure, motion, rest and texture of the corpuscles of which all sensible bodies are composed. But in order that we may proceed in the more accurate order possible, some definitions must be set out first.

[p. 172]

> 550 *Sensibile* dicitur, *quod quia tale formaliter, ita nostra[?] sensoria [?] afficit, ut sensum in nobis excitet*. Sic lignum quia durum est, vel coloratum, dicitur sensibile, quia si sensoriis nostris adplicetur, ita ea afficit, quatenus tale, ut hinc animus sentiat. Ex quo infertur, quod corpus per id formaliter est sensibile, per quod formaliter ejusmodi est, ut adplicatum externis sensoriis, ita ipsa afficiat, ut hinc animus ad sentiendum determinetur. Nomine *sensibilis qualitatis* ea corporis adfectio intelligitur, *per quam formaliter corpus est sensibile*, sic color, sapor &c. dicuntur qualitates sensibiles corporum, quatenùs per illas formaliter habet corpus, ut externorum sensuum ministerio à nobis percipiatur. Ex quo infertur, quod qualitas sensibilis in eo physicè posita est, per quod formaliter habet corpus, ut eam in organo sensorio, cui adplicatur immutationem faciat, ad quam in anima sensatio quaedam determinata, consequitur, quae in cogitatione consistit.

550 That is called sensible which, because it is formally such, so affects our sense organs as to excite sensation in us. Thus wood, because it is hard or colored, is called sensible, because, if it is applied to our sense organs, it so affects them, inasmuch as it is such, that the mind thereupon feels. From this it is inferred that a body is formally sensible by that through which it is formally of such a kind that, when applied to the external sense organs, it so affects them that the mind is thereupon determined to feel. By the name of sensible quality is understood that affection of a body by which the body is formally sensible; thus color, taste, etc., are called sensible qualities of bodies, inasmuch as through them a body formally has it that it is perceived by us through the ministry of the external senses. From this it is inferred that a sensible quality is physically placed in that by which a body formally has it that it produces in the sense organ to which it is applied a change upon which there follows in the soul a certain determinate sensation, which consists in thought.

> 551 Existentia sensibilium qualitatum in corporibus certissima est. Qui negant accidentia absoluta in sensu Scholastico, qualitatum sensibilium existentiam non iccircò inficiantur: & ipsi namque fatentur, id verè esse in corporibus per quod habent formaliter, ut externorum sensuum organa pro sensationis negotio immutent, certoque modo afficiant. *Nervi sunt tenuissimi quidam veluti funiculi, qui ex intima cerebri substantia, tum etiam ex membranis cerebrum circumdantibus, tanquam ex radice prodeuntes, per totam animalis machinam praecipuè sensationis gratia[?] diffunduntur*. Filamenta ex quibus nervi componuntur non omnino solida sunt: sed (ut demonstrat Cl. Heister) intùs cava, ut proindè tanquam vera vascula haberi possint.

551 The existence of sensible qualities in bodies is most certain. Those who deny absolute accidents in the Scholastic sense do not on that account deny the existence of sensible qualities: for they too acknowledge that there truly is in bodies that by which they formally have it that they change the organs of the external senses for the business of sensation and affect them in a certain way. Nerves are certain very slender little cords, as it were, which, proceeding as from a root out of the inmost substance of the brain, and also out of the membranes surrounding the brain, are spread through the whole machine of the animal, chiefly for the service of sensation. The filaments of which the nerves are composed are not altogether solid, but (as the celebrated Heister demonstrates) hollow within, so that they can accordingly be regarded as true little vessels.

> 552 *Spirituum animalium* nomine intelligitur *substantia summè fluida, & maximè mobilis in cerebro secreta*. Ex his quae in Logica, & in Metaphysica dicta sunt persuasum nobis est: ex immutatione, quae ex rei sensibilis adpulsu in organo sensorio efficitur, nullam in nobis sensationem contingere, nisi immutatio ipsa cerebro communicetur. Certum itidem est, organum externi cujusque sensus positum esse in tenuissimis quibusdam nervorum fibris, dissimili artificio pro specifico sensuum discrimine simul intextis, eisque nostri corporis parti *exteriori* insertis, quae dum ab re sensibili adficitur, sensatio in animo contingit. Positum est itaque ex. gr. organum visûs in ea oculi membrana, quae opticorum nervorum expansio est, & vulgo *retina* nuncupatur. His positis, veluti principium fundamentale sequens adsertio haberi debet.

552 By the name of animal spirits is understood a substance supremely fluid and most mobile, secreted in the brain. From what was said in the Logic and in the Metaphysics we are persuaded that from the change which is produced in the sense organ by the impulse of a sensible thing no sensation occurs in us unless that change is communicated to the brain. It is likewise certain that the organ of each external sense is placed in certain very slender fibers of the nerves, interwoven with a dissimilar artifice according to the specific difference of the senses, and inserted in the outer part of our body; while this part is affected by the sensible thing, sensation occurs in the mind. Thus, for example, the organ of sight is placed in that membrane of the eye which is the expansion of the optic nerves and is commonly called the retina. These things being laid down, the following assertion must be held as a fundamental principle, as it were.

> 553 Immutatio externi sensorii ex sensibilis rei adpulsu proveniens, quam sensatio ipsius rei in anima consequitur, non est physicè loquendo, nisi certa quaedam motio in iis nervorum fibris, quae externum sensorium constituunt, ex rei ipsius adpulsu excitata. Agens namque corporeum non agit, nisi per motum localem, videlicet nonnisi quatenùs localiter movet id, in quod agit. Nulla certè corporea actio est, quae partium motu, (ut patebit consideranti) [p. 173] non absolvatur. Ergo nullum quoque corpus pátitur aliquid ab agente corporeo, nisi quatenùs ab illo movetur. Patiuntur autem sensoria à rebus sensibilibus, dum illa ab hisce pro sensationis negotio excitantur: ergo in sola motione fibrarum nervearum, ex quibus ipsa sensoria composita sunt, illorum passio consistit.

553 The change of the external sense organ arising from the impulse of a sensible thing, upon which the sensation of that thing follows in the soul, is nothing else, physically speaking, than a certain motion in those fibers of the nerves which constitute the external sense organ, excited by the impulse of the thing itself. For a bodily agent does not act except through local motion, namely, only insofar as it locally moves that on which it acts. Certainly there is no bodily action which by the motion of its parts (as will be plain to anyone who considers it) is [p. 173] not accomplished. Therefore no body, either, undergoes anything from a bodily agent except insofar as it is moved by it. But the sense organs undergo something from sensible things while they are excited by them for the business of sensation: therefore their undergoing consists in the motion alone of the nervous fibers of which the sense organs themselves are composed.

> Objectiones diluuntur.

THE OBJECTIONS ARE DISPELLED.

> 554 Opp. 1. Ex nostra adsertione sequitur: organum illud, cujus est omnes impressiones discernere, nempè cérebrum, praeditum esse tactu exquisitissimo; sed tantum abest, ut cérebrum gaudeat exquisito tactu, quin potius sit penè stupidum: ergo impressiones sensibilium non sunt merè locales motiones. Argumentum ab ipsis Peripateticis responderi etiam debet: nam juxta ipsos: sensus communis in cérebro résidet. Dist. major. tactu exquisitissimo, si hoc vult dicere quod medullaris illius substantia ejus, sit naturae, ut valeat externorum omnium sensuum motiones recipere, concedo; si vult dicere quod tota ejus substantia capax sit sensûs, si vel levissimè à re externa tangatur, nego, & dist. minor.: cérebrum caret tactu, hoc est, intima illius substantia nequit omnium sensuum impressiones recipere, nego, hoc est nullus fit sensus, si tantum pars illius éxtima, hoc est cérebri cortex in quo nulli sunt nervi, tangatur, concedo minor., & nego conseq.

bj. 1. From our assertion it follows that that organ whose office it is 554 Oto discern all impressions, namely the brain, is endowed with a most exquisite touch; but so far is the brain from enjoying an exquisite touch that it is rather almost insensible: therefore the impressions of sensible things are not merely local motions. The argument must be answered by the Peripatetics themselves as well: for according to them the common sense resides in the brain. I distinguish the major: with a most exquisite touch, if this means that its medullary substance is of such a nature that it is able to receive the motions of all the external senses, I grant; if it means that its whole substance is capable of sensation if it is touched even very lightly by an external thing, I deny; and I distinguish the minor: the brain lacks touch, that is, its inmost substance cannot receive the impressions of all the senses, I deny; that is, there is no sensation if only its outermost part, that is, the cortex of the brain, in which there are no nerves, is touched, I grant the minor, and I deny the conseq.

> 555 Praeterea argumentum peccat fallacia *dictionis*. Est nempè error in voce *tactus*, quae dupliciter sumi potest 1 pro sensu qui ex contactu nervi sensorii à re sensibili á nobis excitatur. 2 pro sensu quo *calida*, *frigida*, *humida* *&c.* à nobis percipiuntur. 1. modo sumpta vox illa tactus ad quemlibet sensationis speciem referri potest, quia omnis sensus contactu perficitur, ut expressè docet magnus Boerhaavius [^173-s1]: secundo modò sumpta: tactus pecularis sensus est, id tantum commune habens cum sensibus reliquis, ut quemadmodùm illi, ita etiam ipse in nobis non excitetur, nisi nervi, qui ei peragendo inserviunt à proprio objecto contingantur.
