Quâ distinctione posita, non est cur Peripatetici vitio vertant Recentioribus quod omnes sensus externos ad unum tactum révocent, quasi nempè, ipsi tunc sumant tactum, pro eo speciali sensu quo calor & frigus &c. percipiuntur, quod falsum omninò est.

555 Moreover, the argument sins by the fallacy of diction. There is, namely, an error in the word touch, which can be taken in two ways: 1. for the sensation which is excited in us by the contact of a sensory nerve with a sensible thing; 2. for the sense by which hot, cold, moist, etc. things are perceived by us. Taken in the first way, that word touch can be referred to any species of sensation whatever, because every sensation is accomplished by contact, as the great Boerhaave expressly teaches (b); taken in the second way, touch is a particular sense, having only this in common with the other senses, that, just like them, it too is not excited in us unless the nerves which serve it in performing its office are touched by their proper object. This distinction laid down, there is no reason why the Peripatetics should turn it into a fault in the Moderns that they reduce all the external senses to touch alone, as if, namely, they then took touch for that special sense by which heat and cold, etc., are perceived, which is altogether false.

> [^173-s1]: Praelect. in suas Inst. Med. ad n. 566.

[^173-s1]: Praelect. in suas Inst. Med., at no. 566.

> 556 Opp. 2. Si immutatio externorum organorum, id est, sensuum ex contactu oritur, frustranea est specifica organorum diversitas, sed Deus Opt. M. nihil egit frustrà: ergo. Argumentum contra ipsum Aristotelem urgeri potest. Pluribus enim locis tradit apertissimè, gustum esse speciem *tactus*. Lib. 2. de anima ait; [p. 174] *Sapor unum quid est rerum, quae tactu percipiuntur*. Directè ad argumentum respondeo, quod quum maximè inter se differant sensibilia ea corpora, à quibus externa sensoria immutantur, & planè dissimilis sit modus, quo sensoria ipsa ab illis adficiuntur, factum non est frustra, sed summo Divini Opificis consilio, maximáque necessitate naturae, ut notabiliter quoque diversa sit externorum ipsorum sensoriorum structura, ex quo sequitur ad omnes rerum sensibilium impressiones suscipiendas, & cérebro communicandas, unum tactus organum, sumpto tactu pro speciali sensu nequaquàm sufficere.

556 Obj. 2. If the change of the external organs, that is, of the senses, arises from contact, the specific diversity of the organs is in vain; but God, Best and Greatest, did nothing in vain: therefore. The argument can be pressed against Aristotle himself. For in many places he teaches most openly that taste is a species of touch. In bk. 2 On the Soul he says: Taste is [p. 174] is one of the things which are perceived by touch. To the argument I reply directly that, since the sensible bodies by which the external sense organs are changed differ very greatly among themselves, and the manner in which the sense organs themselves are affected by them is plainly dissimilar, it was not done in vain, but by the supreme counsel of the Divine Maker, and by the greatest necessity of nature, that the structure of the external sense organs themselves should also be notably diverse; from which it follows that for receiving the impressions of all sensible things and communicating them to the brain, a single organ of touch, touch being taken for a special sense, would by no means suffice.

> 557 Opp. 3. instando: quaecumque diversitas contingit in impressionibus rerum sensibilium, communicatur cerebro per nervos, fibras nerveas, & spiritus animales; sed in omni corporis parte hae res omnes reperiuntur & quidem ejusdem rationis: ergo in omni corporis parte extant organa quae possunt recipere sensibilium rerum impressionem, seu mutationem: ergo nostra opinione posita in solo tactu sensitiva vis consistit, & hoc uno sensu lucem, saporem, &c. percipiemus: ergo superflua erunt reliqua organa humani corporis. Nego min. argumenti: etenim humani corporis partes, quae sensationibus instrumentaliter peragendis inserviunt maximè differunt inter se, quamvis ex nervorum filamentis singulae componantur: non potest ergo dici, eas esse ejusdem rationis, hoc est, nullum planè essentiale discrimen inter eas interesse. Nego itaque fibras in omnibus corporis partibus eodem artificio simul esse intextas: hoc enim artificium, ipsâ teste experientia planè dissimile est pro specifico ipsarum partium discrimine.

557 Obj. 3, by insisting: whatever diversity occurs in the impressions of sensible things is communicated to the brain through the nerves, the nervous fibers and the animal spirits; but in every part of the body all these things are found, and indeed of the same nature: therefore in every part of the body there exist organs which can receive the impression, or change, of sensible things: therefore, our opinion being laid down, the sensitive power consists in touch alone, and by this one sense we perceive light, taste, etc.: therefore the remaining organs of the human body would be superfluous. I deny the min. of the argument: for the parts of the human body which serve instrumentally for performing sensations differ greatly among themselves, although each of them is composed of filaments of nerves: it cannot, therefore, be said that they are of the same nature, that is, that there is no essential difference whatever between them. I deny, therefore, that the fibers are interwoven with the same artifice in all parts of the body: for this artifice, as experience itself attests, is plainly dissimilar according to the specific difference of those parts.

> 558 Hinc enim fit, ut corpuscula solùm, ex quibus species colorum constant penetrare possint per visum, ipsumque sensorium commovere, non item verò corpuscula, quae sola, ac solummodò subire possunt, ac movere auditum, atque ita de ceteris Itaque etsi omnia externa organa ex nervorum fibris componantur, verumtamèn quia illorum structura planè diversa est, fit ut non nisi à rebus dissimilibus immutari pro sensatione ipsa possint, videlicèt, ut à lucis radiis eae tantum nervorum fibrae valeant commoveri, quae reticularem oculi membranam constituunt. Immeritò ergo interrogat P. de Benedictis, quamobrem quum in pede, ut in membris reliquis sint nervi, & fibrae, non propterea sensibilia quaeque, unius pedis ministerio à nobis discernantur? Supervacanea namque est istaec interrogatio, cui hac alterâ interrogatione responderi optimè potest. si manu ex gr. tantas, tamque mirabiles operationes facimus, ut scribere, pingere, sculpere, &c. quia manus instructa est digitis, musculis, nervis, & fibris, eccur easdem operationes nequeunt fieri pede in quo etiam digiti, musculi, nervi, & fibrae reperiuntur?

558 For hence it comes about that only the corpuscles of which the species of colors consist can penetrate through the sight and move its sense organ, but not likewise the corpuscles which alone, and only they, can strike and move the hearing, and so of the rest. Therefore, although all the external organs are composed of nerve fibers, nevertheless, because their structure is plainly different, it comes about that they cannot be changed for sensation except by dissimilar things; namely, that only those nerve fibers which constitute the reticular membrane of the eye can be set in motion by the rays of light. Wrongly, therefore, does Father de Benedictis ask why, since there are nerves and fibers in the foot as in the other members, not every sensible thing is therefore discerned by us through the ministry of the foot alone. For this question is superfluous, and can best be answered by this other question: if with the hand, for example, we perform so many and such wonderful operations, such as writing, painting, sculpting, etc., because the hand is furnished with digits, muscles, nerves and fibers, why can the same operations not be done with the foot, in which digits, muscles, nerves and fibers are also found?

> 559 Opp. 4. Si nulla sensatio potest sine motu pércipi, sequitur nullam esse memoriam aut sensationem in dormientibus, quum [p. 175] nulla detur impressio facta ab objectis tunc absentibus; sed hoc est contra experientiam: ergo. Dist. maj.: nullam esse sensationem ab occasione externa (de qua procedit quaestiò), concedo; mere internam, nego, & conseq.

559 Obj. 4. If no sensation can be perceived without motion, it follows that there is no memory or sensation in those who are asleep, since [p. 175] no impression is made by objects then absent: but this is contrary to experience: therefore. I distinguish the maj.: that there is no sensation on an external occasion (which is what the question concerns), I grant; a merely internal one, I deny, and the conseq.

> 560 Opp. 5. Si adsertio nostra vera est, anima sentit eo ipso temporis puncto, quo in organo sensorio mutatio aliqua producitur; sed hoc esse non potest, si motus nervis sensoriis impressus ad cérebrum usque propagari debeat, ut anima percipiat: ergo, &c. Major constat. Nam si arbori oculos clausos obvertas, dum eosdem aperis, illicò lumen oculos ingreditur, & illicò vides, nec minima quidem mórula inter mutationem oculi, & animae perceptionem intercedit. Minor verò patet, quia quum motus in tempore fiat, aliquod temporis intervallum necessarium est, ut motus retinae fibrillis impressus ad cerebrum usque propagetur: ergo &c. Resp. disting. maj.: anima sentit eo ipso temporis puncto quo mutatio fit in organo sensorio, hoc est, inter motum nervis sensoriis impressum, & animae perceptionem nulla intercedit mora *observabilis*, conc. Nulla *absolutè*, nego maj., & sic distinct. min. neg. conseq. Si motus per exiguum spatium magna celeritate propagetur, tempus, quo per illud spatium propagatur, á nobis non percipitur seu non distinguitur. Sic quamvis certum sit, (ut postea videbimus) sonum *successivè* propagari, non verò in *instanti*; nullam tamèn possumus observare moram inter momentum, quo quis nobis proximus loquitur, & momentum, quo vox ipsius ad aures nostras pérvenit. Idem quoquè patet in propagatione lucis; statim ac accenditur candela in tenebroso loco, illicò objecta omnia etiam remota, lumine videntur perfusa, quamvis lux in instanti propagari non possit. Igitur experimentum, quod nobis objicitur, id unum probat, motum à nervis sensoriis ad cerebrum usquè magna celeritate transmitti.

560 Obj. 5. If our assertion is true, the soul feels at the very point of time at which some change is produced in the sense organ; but this cannot be, if the motion impressed on the sensory nerves must be propagated all the way to the brain in order that the soul may perceive: therefore, etc. The major is evident. For if you turn your closed eyes toward a tree, while you open them the light at once enters the eyes, and at once you see, nor does even the least little delay intervene between the change of the eye and the perception of the soul. The minor, however, is plain, because, since motion takes place in time, some interval of time is necessary for the motion impressed on the little fibers of the retina to be propagated all the way to the brain: therefore, etc. Reply: I distinguish the maj.: the soul feels at the very point of time at which the change takes place in the sense organ, that is, between the motion impressed on the sensory nerves and the perception of the soul no observable delay intervenes, I grant. None absolutely, I deny the maj., and, the min. being distinguished in the same way, I deny the conseq. If motion is propagated through a very small space with great velocity, the time in which it is propagated through that space is not perceived, or is not distinguished, by us. Thus, although it is certain (as we shall see afterwards) that sound is propagated successively and not in an instant, we can nevertheless observe no delay between the moment at which someone very near us speaks and the moment at which his voice reaches our ears. The same is also plain in the propagation of light: as soon as a candle is lit in a dark place, all objects, even distant ones, are at once seen bathed in light, although light cannot be propagated in an instant. Therefore the experiment which is objected to us proves this one thing only, that the motion is transmitted from the sensory nerves to the brain with great velocity.

> 561 Inst. 1. Motus ad cerebrum non propagatur per nervos, qui ad cerebrum non pertingunt; sed sensorii nervi complures, nimirum 6[?], qui ex medulla spinali prodeunt ad cerebrum non protenduntur: ergo &c. Respondeo, conc. maj. neg. min. Nam medulla spinalis est cerebri ipsius, seu medullae oblongatae productio, & nervis constat ad cerebrum usque protensis, undè fit, ut in vertebrarum [^175-s1] dorsi luxationibus, membra corporis infra luxationem posita, & motum, & sensibilitatem, quae à nervis infra luxationem constitutis pendent, amittant. Sunt itaque nervi, veluti cerebrum in omnes corporis partes diffusum.

561 You will insist 1. Motion is not propagated to the brain through nerves which do not reach the brain; but several sensory nerves, namely 60, which come out of the spinal marrow, do not extend to the brain: therefore, etc. I reply: I grant the maj., I deny the min. For the spinal marrow is a prolongation of the brain itself, or of the medulla oblongata, and consists of nerves extended all the way to the brain; whence it comes about that in dislocations of the vertebrae (a) of the back, the members of the body placed below the dislocation lose both the motion and the sensibility which depend on the nerves situated below the dislocation. The nerves are thus, as it were, the brain diffused into all parts of the body.

> [^175-s1]: Vertebrae dicuntur ossa intus excavata, superius, & inferius plana, exterius variis processibus donata, quorum in collo septem, dorso, duodecim, lumbis, quinque, numerant Anatomici. Dicuntur vertebrae, quia per eas corpus variè inflectitur, vertiturque.

[^175-s1]: Vertebrae is the name given to bones hollowed within, flat above and below, and furnished on the outside with various processes, of which Anatomists count seven in the neck, twelve in the back, and five in the loins. They are called vertebrae because through them the body is variously bent and turned.

[p. 176]

> 562 Inst. 2. Reperti sunt homines, qui sine cerebro vivebant, ac sentiebant: ergo ad animae sensationem necesse non est, ut motus nervis sensoriis impressus ad cerebrum usque propagetur. Respond. dist. antec. Vivebant, & sentiebant sine maxima cerebri parte, conc. prorsùs sine illa tota parte, nego antec. & conseq. In illis erat spinalis medulla, & in ipsius principio potuit esse specialis quaedam structura, qua pars illa apta[?] redderetur[?], ut cerebri munere aliquatenùs fungeretur. Ceterùm verisimile est, homines illos stupidos admodum, atque hebetes fuisse. Si autem in aliquibus etiam deesset spinalis medulla, necessariò hujus partis vices gerere debuit pars alia quaecumque fuerit. Tandem partes has suppletorias adfuisse, ex ipsa cadaverum sectione, & observatione anatomica innotuit; fieri autem potuit, ut partes illae vi ipsius morbi corruptae, & obliteratae perierint.

562 You will insist 2. Men have been found who lived and felt without a brain: therefore for the sensation of the soul it is not necessary that the motion impressed on the sensory nerves be propagated all the way to the brain. Reply: I distinguish the antec.: they lived and felt without the greatest part of the brain, I grant; altogether without that whole part, I deny the antec. and the conseq. In them there was the spinal marrow, and at its beginning there could have been some special structure by which that part was fitted to discharge in some measure the office of the brain. For the rest, it is likely that those men were very stupid and dull. If, however, in some the spinal marrow too was lacking, some other part, whatever it may have been, must necessarily have taken the place of this part. Finally, that these supplementary parts were present became known from the very dissection of the corpses and from anatomical observation; it could also have happened, however, that those parts, corrupted and obliterated by the force of the disease itself, perished.

> 563 Inst. 3. Si serpentes, lacerti, aliaque animalia, quae circularibus incisuris distinguuntur, transversim secentur, singulae illorum partes ad acûs puncturam, aut aliam quamcumque irritationem variis modis torquentur, & agitantur: ac proindè adhuc sentiunt sine cerebro: ergo per analogiam, quae est inter corpora hominis, & bruti, idem dicendum est de homine. Respondeo, nego conseq. & parit. Alia enim est corporis humani structura, alia serpentum, & lacertorum, in quibus medullae spinalis partes considerari possunt tanquam totidem minora cerebra. Hinc fit, ut partes corporis humani resectae, post brevissimum tempus omni motu destituantur.

563 You will insist 3. If serpents, lizards and other animals which are marked by circular incisions are cut crosswise, the single parts of them are twisted and agitated in various ways at the prick of a needle or any other irritation whatever: and accordingly they still feel without a brain: therefore, by the analogy which exists between the bodies of man and of brute, the same must be said of man. I reply: I deny the conseq. and the parity. For the structure of the human body is one thing, that of serpents and lizards another; in these the parts of the spinal marrow can be considered as so many smaller brains. Hence it comes about that parts of the human body, when cut off, are deprived of all motion after a very short time.

> 564 Inst. 4. Incertum omninò est, an motus ex organo sensorio ad cerebrum propagetur fibrillarum nervearum oscillatione, an fluidi nervei, aut spirituum animalium ope, aut alio quocumque modo: ergo &c. Respond. permitto antec. & nego conseq. Etsi non investigemus modum, quo illa motus propagatio absolvitur, satis est ratione, atque experientia constare in organo sensorio motum quemdam excitari, qui ad cerebrum usque nervorum auxilio propagatur, dum anima sentit. Eodem modo respondendum est, si quis objiciat, à nobis intelligi non posse, qua ratione fieri queat, ut propter motum nervis impressum anima, quae est substantia simplex, & spiritualis percipiat objectum sensibile: factum hic statuimus, rationem facti non quaerimus. Porrò adversus facta indubitata, objectiones quaecumque nihil valent.

564 You will insist 4. It is altogether uncertain whether motion is propagated from the sense organ to the brain by the oscillation of the nervous fibrils, or by means of the nervous fluid or the animal spirits, or in any other way whatever: therefore, etc. Reply: I allow the antec. and deny the conseq. Even if we do not investigate the manner in which that propagation of motion is accomplished, it is enough that it is established by reason and experience that some motion is excited in the sense organ which is propagated all the way to the brain by the help of the nerves while the soul feels. In the same way one must reply if anyone objects that it cannot be understood by us how it can come about that, on account of the motion impressed on the nerves, the soul, which is a simple and spiritual substance, perceives the sensible object: here we establish the fact; we do not seek the reason of the fact. Moreover, against indubitable facts objections of whatever kind have no force.

> 565 Inst. 5. Qui organo sensorio destituuntur, sentiunt tamen, & contrà sensatione carent aliqui, in quorum nervis sensoriis motus etiam validus producitur. Ergo ut anima sentiat, necesse non est, motum nervis sensoriis imprimi. Prob. antec. ii, quibus abscissa sunt membra, dolorem aliquando in iisdem membris sentire sibi videntur, ut contigit puellae de qua Cartesius meminit [^176-s1] [p. 177] Furiosi, & delirantes homines objecta sibi videri videntur, quae praesentia non sunt, quaeque proinde nullam, in eorum organis sensoriis mutationem producunt. S. Augustinus [^177-s1] hoc factum narrat: *Presbyter quidam fuit nomine Restitutus, qui quando ei placebat ita se auferebat à sensibus, & jacebat simillimus mortuo, ut non solum vellicantes, atque pungentes minimè sentiret, sed aliquando igne ureretur admoto sine ullo doloris sensu*. Respondeo: his observationibus conclusionem adprimè confirmari. Nam in omni sensatione quatuor ut diximus in Log. sunt accuratè distinguenda; duo quae pertinent ad nostrum corpus, scilicet, motus organo sensorio ab objecto sensibili impressus, & motus inde ad cerebrum propagatus; ac tertium, quod animae est nempè, his motibus respondens objecti sensibilis perceptio. Si motus organo sensorio impressus ad cerebrum usque non propagetur, anima non sentit, ut accidit in nobis dormientibus, & contingebat in Presbytero Restituto, qui mortuo simillimus jacebat.

565 You will insist 5. Those who are deprived of a sense organ nevertheless feel, and, on the contrary, some lack sensation in whose sensory nerves even a strong motion is produced. Therefore, in order that the soul may feel, it is not necessary that motion be impressed on the sensory nerves. Proof of the antec.: those whose limbs have been cut off sometimes seem to themselves to feel pain in those same limbs, as happened to the girl whom Descartes mentions (c). [p. 177] Madmen and delirious persons seem to themselves to see objects which are not present, and which accordingly produce no change in their sense organs. St. Augustine (e) relates this fact: There was a certain priest named Restitutus who, whenever it pleased him, so withdrew himself from his senses, and lay so very like a dead man, that he not only felt nothing at all of those who plucked and pricked him, but was sometimes even burned with fire applied to him without any sense of pain. I reply: by these observations our conclusion is confirmed most excellently. For in every sensation four things, as we said in the Logic, are to be accurately distinguished; two which pertain to our body, namely, the motion impressed on the sense organ by the sensible object, and the motion thence propagated to the brain; and a third, which belongs to the soul, namely, the perception of the sensible object corresponding to these motions. If the motion impressed on the sense organ is not propagated all the way to the brain, the soul does not feel, as happens in us when we sleep, and as happened in the priest Restitutus, who lay most like a dead man.

> [^176-s1]: Princip. P. [?]

[^176-s1]: Principles, pt. IV.

> [^177-s1]: Lib. XIV. de Civ. Dei, cap. 24.

[^177-s1]: Bk. XIV of The City of God, ch. 24.

> 566 Si verò sine actione objecti sensibilis externi, fibrae cerebri à causis internis eodem prorsùs modo agitentur; quo moventur, ubi objectum sensibile sua in organum extrinsecum actione eosdem motus producit, tum anima easdem habet perceptiones, quas haberet objecto sensibili in organum extrinsecum agente, & perceptiones suas vi imaginationis productas, à sensationibus non distingueret; uti accidit furiosis, & delirantibus hominibus, in quorum cerebro irregulares, ac vehementiores motus excitantur: & hoc pacto, quae sibi imaginantur confundunt cum his quae vident. Simili modo explicatur, cur ii, quibus membrum aliquod abscissum est, dolorem in eodem membro aliquandiu sentire sibi videantur; nimirùm in nervis illis, qui ad partem corporis amputatam pertingebant iidem aliquando à causis extrinsecis motus oriuntur, quos objecta externa excitarent, si nulla pars fuisset resecta.

566 But if, without the action of an external sensible object, the fibers of the brain are agitated by internal causes in exactly the same way in which they are moved when a sensible object by its action on the external organ produces the same motions, then the soul has the same perceptions which it would have if the sensible object were acting on the external organ, and it does not distinguish its perceptions, produced by force of imagination, from sensations; as happens to madmen and delirious men, in whose brain irregular and more vehement motions are excited: and in this way they confuse what they imagine with what they see. In the same way it is explained why those whose limb has been cut off sometimes seem to themselves to feel pain in that same limb for a while; namely, because in those nerves which reached the amputated part of the body the same motions sometimes arise from extrinsic causes which external objects would excite if no part had been cut off.

## CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

> Stabilitur physica natura qualitatis sensibilis.

The Physical Nature of Sensible Quality Is Established.

> 567 His suppositis quae à nobis dicta sunt in Logica: adsero: Qualitates sensibiles corporis naturalis, ex mechanicis adfectionibus particularum materiae, ex quibus illud compositum est, unicè provenire. Prob. In eo posita est sensibilis corporis qualitas, per quod [p. 178] formaliter habet corpus aptum, ut sit sensibile [§. 550], sed à mechanicis adfectionibus particularum materiae, quibus compositum est, habet corpus ut *specificè*, (quemadmodùm ab illarum *soliditate*, ut *genericè*) sit sensibile: ergo. Prob. min.: Naturale quodcumque corpus per id formaliter est sensibile, per quod habet formaliter, ut externis sensoriis adplicatum nerveas illorum fibras movere certa ratione valeat [§. 550.] sed hóc praestare potest quodcumque corpus, hoc ipso, quod ex solidis corpusculis certâ magnitudine, & figurâ praeditis, certo artificio simul intextis intrinsecus componatur.

hese things being supposed which were said by us in the Logic, I assert: 567 T          The sensible qualities of a natural body arise solely from the mechanical affections of the particles of matter of which that composite consists. Proof. The quality of a sensible body is placed in that by which [p. 178] a body formally has it that it is fit to be sensible [§. 550]; but from the mechanical affections of the particles of matter of which it is composed a body has it that it is specifically sensible (just as from their solidity it is so generically): therefore. Proof of the min.: Any natural body whatever is formally sensible by that through which it formally has it that, applied to the external sense organs, it is able to move their nervous fibers in a certain manner [§. 550.]; but any body whatever can achieve this by the very fact that it is intrinsically composed of solid corpuscles endowed with a certain magnitude and figure and interwoven together with a certain artifice.

> 568 Et certè hoc ipsum adfirmare debent Peripatetici, nisi dicere velint eodem eos adfici modo eandem prorsùs qualitatem sensibilem haberi in lapide ex altitudine pedis unius, & ex apice turris praealtae in caput delapso, ubi lapis idem est, mechanica solum adfectio, *motus*, nempè, diversus est. In fine adverte, quod an *Gratia*, *lumen gloriae* atque id genus aliae *spirituales* animae *qualitates* sint accidentia *absoluta* in sensu Peripatetico, viderint Theologi. Moneo tantùm, etsi qualitates istae pro hujusmodi accidentibus habeantur, id ipsum non propterea de qualitatibus sensibilibus (de quibus tota quaestio est) dici oportere. Sunt enim genere diversae. Falli iccircò eos putò, qui ut evincant qualitates *sensibiles* corporum esse entitates absolutas, ad *spirituales* animae qualitates confugiunt, easque hujus esse naturae demonstrare nituntur; ut optimè advertit Clarissim. à Brixia.

568 And certainly the Peripatetics must affirm this very thing, unless they wish to say that we are affected in the same way, and that exactly the same sensible quality is found in a stone that has fallen on the head from a height of one foot and from the top of a very high tower, where the stone is the same and only the mechanical affection, namely the motion, is different. Finally, note that whether Grace, the light of glory, and other spiritual qualities of the soul of that kind are absolute accidents in the Peripatetic sense, let the Theologians see. I only point out that, even if these qualities are held to be accidents of this kind, it does not on that account follow that the same must be said of sensible qualities (which the whole question concerns). For they are diverse in genus. I therefore think those are mistaken who, in order to prove that the sensible qualities of bodies are absolute entities, take refuge in the spiritual qualities of the soul and strive to demonstrate that these are of this nature; as the most celebrated Fortunato da Brescia excellently observes.

## DISSERTATIO II. — DISSERTATION II

> De Qualitatibus tactilibus.

On Tactile Qualities.

## CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

> De Calore.

On Heat.

> 569 Partes corporis dicuntur *perturbatè* moveri, *quum ita moventur singulae, ut nulla sit loci differentia, secundum quam non abripiantur*. Dicuntur verò moveri *motu expansivo*, *quum tendunt motu suo ab ipsius corporis centro ad illius circumferentiam, adeò nimirùm ut illius tendentiae causâ, corporis extensio secundum omnem dimensionem, nisi impedimentum adsit, augeatur*. Hinc veluti Principium fundamentale sequens propositio haberi debet. Dilatatio corporis, motusque perturbatus, qui in [p. 179] partibus illius internis, quum calorem concipit, excitatur sunt caloris effectus principes, ejusque veluti charactéres. Expansivus quippè ille, perturbatusque motus partium corporis incalescentis, ita á calore, quo adficitur corpus dependet, eaque ratione ipsum consequitur, ut non secùs dependeat effectus á sua efficiente causa, illumque consequatur. Posito enim calore in corpore, in eodem ponitur, & ipse motus, illo aucto, & hic augetur, sublato verò, aut imminuto, motus quoque tollitur penitùs vel sensim decrescit, atque imminuitur.

he parts of a body are said to be moved in a disordered way when they are 569 T moved singly in such a way that there is no difference of place toward which they are not carried away. They are said to be moved with an expansive motion when they tend with their motion from the center of the body itself toward its circumference, so that, by reason of that tendency of theirs, the extension of the body is increased in every dimension unless an impediment is present. Hence the following proposition must be held as a fundamental Principle, as it were. The dilatation of a body, and the disordered motion which is excited in the parts [p. 179] within it when it conceives heat, are the principal effects of heat, and, as it were, its characteristics. For that expansive and disordered motion of the parts of a body growing hot so depends on the heat by which the body is affected, and follows it in such a way, that it depends on it and follows it no otherwise than an effect depends on its efficient cause and follows it. For when heat is posited in a body, the motion itself is also posited in it; when the former is increased, the latter too is increased; but when it is taken away or diminished, the motion also is either taken away entirely or gradually decreases and is diminished.

> 570 Calor itaque in ea entitate positus formaliter est, cujus vi dilatantur corpora quaeque, eorumque internae partes perturbatè agitantur. Deinceps itaque, ut loquar cum Doctissimo Boerhaavio [^179-s1] calorem, sive ignem adpellabo illam rem, quae istam in se proprietatem habet, ut corpora omnia consistentia, & fluentia penetret atque eò ipsò eadem dilatet in spatia majora. Non placet ergo nobis ea *caloris* definitio quae à Peripateticis traditur, calorem scilicet, esse, id, *quo congregantur homogenea*, *& heterogenea disgregantur*. Ut enim egregiè observat Mallebranchius [^179-s2] calor partes aquae non congregat, illas potius in vapores dissipat. Non congregat partes vini, imò nec partes argenti vivi. Contrà, omnia corpora solida, & fluida homogenea, & heterogenea resolvit, & disgregat. Ac si quaedam sint quorum partes, ignis non possit dissipare, id non fit quod sint ejusdem naturae, sed quia sunt crassiores, & solidiores, quàm ut possint ábripi motu partium. Adhaec: massam ex auro, argento, & aere conflatam nullus calor ita segregare poterit ut metalla etiam imperfecta seorsim ab auro & argento remaneant, imò si diversae auri, argenti, & aeris portiones in vase contineantur, ignique subjiciantur, post aliquod tempus vi caloris in unam congregantur massam. His positis.

570 Heat, therefore, is formally placed in that entity by force of which all bodies are dilated and their internal parts are agitated in a disordered way. Henceforth, then, to speak with the most learned Boerhaave (f), I shall call heat, or fire, that thing which has in itself this property, that it penetrates all bodies, solid and fluid, and by that very fact dilates them into greater spaces. We are not pleased, therefore, with the definition of heat which is handed down by the Peripatetics, namely that heat is that by which homogeneous things are gathered together and heterogeneous things separated. For, as Malebranche excellently observes (g), heat does not gather together the parts of water; rather it dissipates them into vapors. It does not gather together the parts of wine, nor even the parts of quicksilver. On the contrary, it resolves and separates all bodies, solid and fluid, homogeneous and heterogeneous. And if there are some whose parts fire cannot dissipate, this does not happen because they are of the same nature, but because they are too thick and too solid to be carried away by the motion of the parts. Moreover, no heat will be able so to segregate a mass melted together from gold, silver and copper that even the imperfect metals remain apart from the gold and silver; nay, if different portions of gold, silver and copper are contained in a vessel and placed over the fire, after some time they are gathered by the force of heat into one mass. These things laid down,

> [^179-s1]: Elem. Chem. tom. 1. p. 69.

[^179-s1]: Elem. Chem., vol. 1, p. 69.

> [^179-s2]: Recherche de la Verité. Cap. 5.

[^179-s2]: Recherche de la Verité, ch. 5.

> 571 Dico 1. Calor non consistit in motu céleri, perturbato, & expansivo partium corporis incalescentis. Est contra Cartesium. Probatur: In eo non consistit calor, quod caloris effectus est; sed motus celer, perturbatus, & expansivus partium corporis, quum calorem concipit est caloris effectus [§. 569.] ergo. Confirmatur: certum omninò est, calorem esse omninò aliud ab ea sensorii passione, quam ipsius caloris sensatio in animo consequitur; sed passio sensorii, non est nisi dilatatio quaedam fibrarum nervearum quibus illud constat, & perturbata motio spirituum animalium quibus illae turgent: ergo calor est aliud ab illo celeri, perturbato, expansivoque motu, qui in particulis corporis quum calorem concipit excitatur.

571 I say 1. Heat does not consist in the swift, disordered and expansive motion of the parts of the body growing hot. This is against Descartes. Proof: Heat does not consist in that which is an effect of heat; but the swift, disordered and expansive motion of the parts of a body, when it conceives heat, is an effect of heat [§. 569.]: therefore. It is confirmed: it is altogether certain that heat is something entirely other than that undergoing of the sense organ upon which the sensation of heat itself follows in the mind; but the undergoing of the sense organ is nothing but a certain dilatation of the nervous fibers of which it consists, and a disordered motion of the animal spirits with which they swell: therefore heat is something other than that swift, disordered and expansive motion which is excited in the particles of a body when it conceives heat.

> 572 Dico 2: Calor in actu primo, sive prout est in corporibus, aptissimè constituitur in corpusculis mole exilissimis, celerrimo, expansivo perturbatoque motu adfectis, in fibras corporis animalis [p. 180] irruentibus, similique illas motu incitantibus. Prob. per partes: 1. Certum est, calorem esse corpus, & ejus conditionis, ut pervadere queat corpora omnia: sed nequit calor, si corpus est, pervadere omnia corpora, nisi quatenùs subeat illorum poros; neque potest poros subire, & per totam ipsorum corporum molem sese diffundere, nisi quatenùs calor nihil sit diversum à corpusculis, ut est perspicuum: ergo. *Secundò*: nullum penitus in rerum natura existit corpus adeò compactum, ut illius poros calor subire minimè possit, ut testatur magnus Boerhaave [^180-s1]: ergo adeò exilia sunt caloris corpuscula, ut jure dixerit idem ille Auctor, modò laudatus, illorum subtilitatem si ad imaginationem nostram referatur, esse infinitam.

572 I say 2: Heat in first act, or as it is in bodies, is most fitly constituted in corpuscles extremely slight in bulk, endowed with a most rapid, expansive and disordered motion, which into the fibers of the animal body [p. 180] rush, and stir them up with a similar motion. Proof by parts: 1. It is certain that heat is a body, and of such a condition that it can pervade all bodies; but heat, if it is a body, cannot pervade all bodies except insofar as it enters their pores; nor can it enter the pores and diffuse itself through the whole mass of those bodies unless heat is nothing different from corpuscles, as is evident: therefore. Second: there exists absolutely no body in the nature of things so compact that heat cannot enter its pores, as the great Boerhaave testifies (h): therefore the corpuscles of heat are so slight that the same Author, just praised, has rightly said that their subtlety, if it is referred to our imagination, is infinite.

> [^180-s1]: Elem. Chem. Tractat. de Igne.

[^180-s1]: Elem. Chem., Tract. de Igne.

> 573 *Tertiò*: Necesse est ut caloris particulae moveantur celerrimè motu perturbato, & expansivo. Certum est enim, fieri nullatenùs posse ut vi caloris omnia corpora dilatentur, ebulliant fluida, dura liquescant, omniumque demùm minimae partes expansivum, perturbatumque motum quum incalescunt concipiant, nisi particulae exilissimae in quibus calor consistit, urgeant parietes pororum corporis, quos subeunt, vincant momentum, quo illius moleculae adhaerent sibi mutuò, easque iccircò divellant, propellantque multiplici directione, simulque impediant, quandiu cum illis permixtae sunt, ne ad pristinum contactum partes ipsae corporis revertantur; sed hoc non possunt praestare caloris particulae, nisi expansivo, perturbatoque motu praeditae sint, ut per se patet: ergo.

573 Third: It is necessary that the particles of heat be moved most swiftly with a disordered and expansive motion. For it is certain that it can in no way come about that by force of heat all bodies are dilated, fluids boil, hard things liquefy, and finally the smallest parts of all things conceive an expansive and disordered motion when they grow hot, unless the extremely slight particles in which heat consists press upon the walls of the pores of the body which they enter, overcome the momentum by which its molecules adhere to one another, and therefore tear them apart and drive them in manifold directions, and at the same time prevent, as long as they are mixed with them, the parts of the body itself from returning to their former contact; but the particles of heat cannot accomplish this unless they are endowed with an expansive and disordered motion, as is self-evident: therefore.

> 574 Ad haec: motum esse celerrimum constat, quum enim dictae particulae sint mole exilissimae, nec agant nisi per motum, certumque sit ex dictis, vim quâ moventur seu quantitatem motus earum, aequare factum ex ductu massae singularum in celeritatem earumdem: apertum manet vim illarum particularum non posse esse maximam (qualis necessaria est quum valeant etiam corpora durissima dilatare), nisi maxima sit celeritas, qua motum suum perficiunt. Confirmatur adsertio: Hac caloris naturâ posita, omnes illius effectus ac phaenomena aptè explicantur. Explicatur enim *primò*. Cur calor non aequè facilè corpora dura pervadat ac fluida; quum enim particulae fluidi corporis solutae sint, atque ad motum magis expeditae, exigua resistentia á caloris corpusculis superanda est, ut in fluidum corpus sese insinuent, & per totam illius molem dispergantur: oppositum est de duris sentiendum.

574 Moreover: it is established that the motion is most swift; for since the said particles are extremely slight in bulk and do not act except through motion, and it is certain from what has been said that the force with which they are moved, or their quantity of motion, equals the product of the mass of each into their celerity, it remains plain that the force of those particles cannot be the greatest (such as is necessary, since they are able to dilate even the hardest bodies) unless the celerity with which they perform their motion is the greatest. The assertion is confirmed: This nature of heat being laid down, all its effects and phenomena are fitly explained. For there is explained first why heat does not pervade hard bodies as easily as fluids; for since the particles of a fluid body are loose and more ready for motion, a slight resistance has to be overcome by the corpuscles of heat in order that they may insinuate themselves into a fluid body and be dispersed through its whole mass: the opposite is to be thought of hard bodies.

> 575 *Secundò*: Rarefactio corporum cur per calorem fiat ratio redditur, quia quum caloris particulae motu expansivo praeditae sint; eae corporum poros subire nequeunt, quin contra illorum parietes vim faciant, partes urgeant, easque cogant ad recedendum á se mutuò, atque adeò ad majus spatium occupandum. *Tertiò* exponitur induratio, & exsiccatio luti, contra verò emollitio cerae eodem calore effecta: ibi enim partes aqueae, ac fluidiores, quae tractabilem [p. 181] limum reddiderant, avolantes, faciunt ut aliae terrestres, tenaciores, & graviores propius coeant, & implicentur: in cera verò particulae viscosae, minusque evaporationi obnoxiae á vehementi motu ac vario deducuntur, hinc minus inter se compactae, minus resistunt manui prementi. Ex his autèm complura alia cognoscere poteritis, & facilè explanare.

575 Second: The reason why the rarefaction of bodies takes place through heat is given because, since the particles of heat are endowed with expansive motion, they cannot enter the pores of bodies without exerting force against their walls, pressing upon the parts and compelling them to recede from one another, and so to occupy a greater space. Third, the hardening and drying of mud, and on the other hand the softening of wax, by the same effect of heat, is explained: for in mud the watery and more fluid parts, which [p. 181] had made it tractable, fly off and cause the other parts, earthy, more tenacious and heavier, to come closer together and become entangled; in wax, on the other hand, the viscous particles, less liable to evaporation, are drawn apart by the vehement and varied motion; hence, being less compacted with one another, they resist less the hand that presses them. From these things, moreover, you will be able to understand and easily explain many others.

> Solvuntur argumenta.

THE ARGUMENTS ARE ANSWERED.

> 576 Opp. 1. Calor consistit in motu celerrimo perturbato, & expansivo corporis incalescentis, ergo Prob. antec.: illo motu posito, & aucto in corpore, in eodem ponitur, & augetur calor, & vicissim, eo motu sublato vel imminuto ipse quoque calor tollitur penitus, vel sensim decrescit: ergo. Dist. antec.: & hoc tantùm probat motum perturbatum, & expansivum corporis incalescentis esse caloris effectum principem, ac illius veluti charactérem, concedo; & probat aliquid contra adsertionem nostram, nego. Profectò verò: motio quoque similis in fibrillis sensorii *tactus*, quum *caloris* sensus in nobis fit, excitata, hac ipsâ proportione calori respondet, neque tamen in illa motione statuendus calor est, nisi velímus de nomine, ut ajunt Scholastici, disputare.

576 Obj. 1. Heat consists in a very swift, perturbed and expansive motion of the body growing hot: therefore. Prob. antec.: when that motion is posited and increased in a body, heat is posited and increased in it, and conversely, when that motion is removed or diminished, the heat itself too is either wholly removed or gradually decreases: therefore. Dist. antec.: and this proves only that the perturbed and expansive motion of the body growing hot is the principal effect of heat, and as it were its character, I grant; and it proves anything against our assertion, I deny. And indeed a similar motion too, excited in the fibrils of the sensorium of touch when the sensation of heat arises in us, answers to heat in this very proportion, and yet heat is not to be placed in that motion, unless we wish to dispute about a name, as the Scholastics say.

> 577 Opp. 2.: Ignis sive calor saepè donatur motu recto: ergo non donatur motu perturbato, aut vorticoso. Prob. antec.: Ignis saepè lucet, ergo donatur motu recto. Dist. antec.: motu recto inconjungibili cum motu perturbato, aut vorticoso, nego; conjungibili cum motu perturbato, conc. Vorticulus idem igneus eodem tempore motu recto, motuque perturbato donari poterit. Dum enim vel centrum vorticuli, vel etiam totalis vorticulus feretur per lineam rectam, perturbatè, necessariò gyrabunt moleculae quae constituuntur in ipsius circumferentia. ¿Nonne globus idem super planum quodcumque volutus, donatur eodem tempore, & motu per lineam rectam, & motu rotationis circa centrum suum? Ergo motus rectus non est inconjungibilis cum motu perturbato. Caloris motum varium esse posse penès pabuli, aut subjecti in quod vim suam exerit varietatem, aut juxta obices, & impedimenta, quae illius motum inhibent, fatentur omnes. Sic fieri potest, ut motus caloris sit vorticosus, aut rotationis, sed hoc non impedit quo minus perturbatus dicatur. Dum enim sulphureae particulae vertigine abreptae circa se gyrant, & aliae alias impellunt, fit quidam motus perturbatus, ut omnes consentiunt.

577 Obj. 2. Fire, or heat, is often endowed with a straight motion: therefore it is not endowed with a perturbed or vortical motion. Prob. antec.: fire often shines; therefore it is endowed with a straight motion. Dist. antec.: with a straight motion incompatible with a perturbed or vortical motion, I deny; with one compatible with a perturbed motion, I grant. The same small fiery vortex can be endowed at the same time with a straight motion and with a perturbed motion. For while either the center of the small vortex, or even the whole small vortex, is carried along a straight line, the molecules placed at its circumference will necessarily whirl in a perturbed way. Is not the same globe, rolled upon any plane whatever, endowed at the same time both with motion along a straight line and with a motion of rotation about its center? Therefore straight motion is not incompatible with perturbed motion. All admit that the motion of heat can be varied according to the variety of the fuel, or of the subject on which it exerts its force, or according to the obstacles and impediments that check its motion. Thus it may happen that the motion of heat is vortical, or rotatory, but this does not prevent its being called perturbed. For while the sulphureous particles, carried off in a whirl, spin about themselves, and some drive others, there arises a certain perturbed motion, as all agree.

> 578 Opp. 3: Fluida quaeque corpora, cujus generis sunt aqua, aër, mercurius &c, partes habent motu vario, & indeterminato agitatas, nec tamen sunt actu calida: ergo. Respondeo 1. Nullum fluidum esse omnis caloris expers, licet fortè cum corpore nostro comparatum frigidum videatur: quum scilicet partes sanguinis, aut spirituum celeriùs agitantur, quàm corporis fluidi particulae. [p. 182] Respondeo 2: non satis esse ad calorem sensibilem, ut motus partium corporis sit varius, & perturbatus sed praeterea necessè est, ut sit celerrimus. Hinc fit ut partes aquae leni motu agitatae frigus potiùs quàm calorem in corporibus nostris procreent: nam ingenitum nobis calorem, aut motum magis minuunt, quàm augeant

578 Obj. 3. All fluid bodies, of which kind are water, air, mercury, etc., have their parts agitated with a varied and indeterminate motion, and yet they are not actually hot: therefore. I reply 1. that no fluid is wholly devoid of heat, although perhaps, compared with our body, it seems cold: namely, since the parts of the blood or of the spirits are agitated more swiftly than the particles of the fluid body. I reply [p. 182] 2.: that for sensible heat it is not enough that the motion of the parts of the body be varied and perturbed, but it is necessary besides that it be very swift. Hence it comes about that the parts of water, agitated with a gentle motion, produce cold rather than heat in our bodies: for they rather diminish our innate heat, or motion, than increase it.

> 579 Inst. Multa sunt ad motum proclivia, quae in calidorum censu non habentur, ut nitrosi, & acidi liquores qui copioso abundant spiritu, & fermentationem multum promovent: ergo. Resp. non solum motum, sed & varium, & perturbatum, & celerrimum ad caloris naturam pertinere. Hinc liquores acidi licet fermentationem promoveant, tamen soli, calorem vix procreant, quod motu illo perturbato eorum particulae non agitentur, nisi quum salibus alkalicis permiscentur: ut quum spiritus nitri sali fixo alkalico adfunditur. Sic aër tenui ore vibratus frigidior est, sed patulo ore erumpens est calidior: quum enim ore contracto expellitur, céleri quidem motu, sed directo, & non perturbato emittitur.

579 Inst.: There are many things prone to motion which are not held in the number of hot things, such as nitrous things and acid liquors, which abound in copious spirit and greatly promote fermentation: therefore. Resp.: not motion alone, but a varied, perturbed and very swift motion belongs to the nature of heat. Hence acid liquors, although they promote fermentation, yet by themselves scarcely produce heat, because their particles are not agitated with that perturbed motion except when they are mixed with alkaline salts: as when spirit of niter is poured onto a fixed alkaline salt. Thus air blown out with a narrow mouth is colder, but bursting out of a wide-open mouth is hotter: for when it is expelled with the mouth contracted, it is emitted with a swift motion indeed, but a direct and not a perturbed one.

> 580 Opp. 4: dantur fermentationes in quibus conspicua est perturbata partium motio sine ullo calore, imò cum ingenti frigore, ut testantur Viri Clariss. Muschembroekius, Slare, Amontonsius, Gulielminus, Geoffroy, aliique plurimi Physici: ergo expansivus, perturbatusque motus partium corporis non est adeò proprius caloris effectus, ut calor ipse statui in eo legitimè possit, cujus vi, & energia ille motus in corporibus excitatur. Nego conseq.: ebullitio namque, sive perturbata etiam partium motio in frigidis fermentationibus, non sine calore est, licet propter magnam salinae substantiae copiam, quae in illis exsolvitur, calor ipsae non sit conspicuus. Observatum hoc est in fermentatione quadam ex qua teste Clariss. Muschembroek fumi adeò calidi erumpebant, ut liquor thermometri ad fumos adplicati per plures gradus ascenderet; intereadùm thermometri alterius liquor in ipsum liquidum fermentans immersum, deprimeretur.

580 Obj. 4.: There are fermentations in which a perturbed motion of the parts is conspicuous without any heat, nay, with intense cold, as the most distinguished men Musschenbroek, Slare, Amontons, Guglielmini, Geoffroy and very many other physicists testify: therefore the expansive and perturbed motion of the parts of a body is not so proper an effect of heat that heat itself can legitimately be placed in it, by whose force and energy that motion is excited in bodies. I deny the conseq.: for the ebullition, or perturbed motion of the parts, even in cold fermentations, is not without heat, although, on account of the great quantity of saline substance that is dissolved in them, their heat is not conspicuous. This was observed in a certain fermentation from which, as the most distinguished Musschenbroek testifies, fumes so hot burst forth that the liquor of a thermometer applied to the fumes rose through several degrees, while meanwhile the liquor of another thermometer, immersed in the fermenting liquid itself, was depressed.

> 581 Observandum est igitur, duo esse fermentationum genera, alterum scilicet earum in quibus praevalet substantia sulphurea, earum verò alterum in quibus salina praedominatur. Fermentationes primi generis dicuntur calidae, quia ob sulphuris praedominium ea in illis praevalent corpuscula in quibus calor consistit. Fermentationes secundi generis frigidae nuncupantur, quatenùs ob praedominium *salinarum* particularum quae in illis exsolvuntur principem in ipsis locum tenent corpuscula in quibus, ut dicemus, frigus résidet. Fermentationes frigidas esse omninò *salinas*, vel maximam partem salis complecti, experimenta ipsa frigidarum fermentationum luculentissimè demonstrant observante Cl. Gulielmino.

581 It is to be observed, then, that there are two kinds of fermentations: the one, namely, of those in which a sulphureous substance prevails, the other of those in which a saline one predominates. Fermentations of the first kind are called hot, because, owing to the predominance of sulphur, the corpuscles in which heat consists prevail in them. Fermentations of the second kind are named cold, inasmuch as, owing to the predominance of the saline particles that are dissolved in them, the chief place in them is held by the corpuscles in which, as we shall say, cold resides. That cold fermentations are wholly saline, or contain for the most part salt, the very experiments on cold fermentations most clearly demonstrate, as the distinguished Guglielmini observes.

> 582 Opp. 5. manifestum est, experientiâ, excitari posse calorem sine ullo motu partium perturbato, & expansivo, ut testatur auctor supra laudatus: ergo: Dist. antec.: sine motu, &c. partium insensibilium, nego, Sensibilium, conc. & nego conseq. Potest haberi calor in [p. 183] corpore, quin aliquis sensibilis motus in illo adpareat, quia potest contingere, ut in ipso corpore ea non exsolvatur copia corpusculorum *caloris*, quae ad sensibiles illius partes perturbatè agitandas sufficiat. Verùm in corpore nequit esse calor sine ullo prorsùs partium insensibilium motu, quia calor in illo esse non potest, quin ea corpuscula in ipso sint, & moveantur in quibus calor consistit, & sanè quum liquor thermometri in illas fermentationes de quibus auctor loquitur immissi, per plures gradus ascendat, apertum manet, in ipsis tenuissima corpuscula existere, quae acta in motum vitri poros subeant, contentumque liquorem expansivo, perturbatoque motu exagitent, nisi velimus liquorem ipsum dilatari, quin aliquid existat cui illa dilatatio accepta referatur.

582 Obj. 5.: It is manifest from experience that heat can be excited without any perturbed and expansive motion of the parts, as the author praised above testifies: therefore. Dist. antec.: without motion etc. of the insensible parts, I deny; of the sensible parts, I grant; and I deny the conseq. Heat can be present in a body [p. 183] without any sensible motion appearing in it, because it can happen that there is not released in that body such a quantity of corpuscles of heat as suffices to agitate its sensible parts in a perturbed way. But there cannot be heat in a body without any motion whatever of the insensible parts, because heat cannot be in it unless those corpuscles in which heat consists are in it and are moved; and surely, since the liquor of a thermometer immersed in those fermentations of which the author speaks rises through several degrees, it remains plain that very fine corpuscles exist in them which, driven into motion, enter the pores of the glass and agitate the contained liquor with an expansive and perturbed motion; unless we wish the liquor itself to be dilated without anything existing to which that dilatation may be ascribed.

> 583 Opp. 6. boreas vehementi motu fertur & tamèn frigidus est: ergo. *Secundò*: aquae in fluminum gurgitibus perturbato, & celeri motu praecipitantur; sed nullum in iis calorem observamus: ergo. Ad primum respondeo, quod licet boreas vehementi motu feratur, quia tamen recto agitur frigidus est, praesertim quum è partibus septentrionalibus particulas, quae partium insensibilium motum concitatum sistere queunt advehat. Ad secundum dico: ideo non observari calorem in aquae gurgitibus, quia partes aquae sensibiles hoc motu abripiuntur, ad caloris autem naturam, non solum motus vehemens, ac perturbatus quarumcunque partium, sed agitatio requiritur tenuissimarum, & insensibilium: quae à particulis potissimum igneis abreptae, alia corpora, fibrasque penetrare similique motu incitare queant.

583 Obj. 6. The north wind is carried with a vehement motion, and yet it is cold: therefore. Secondly: waters in the whirlpools of rivers rush headlong with a perturbed and swift motion; but we observe no heat in them: therefore. To the first I reply that, although the north wind is carried with a vehement motion, yet because it is driven in a straight line it is cold, especially since it brings from the northern regions particles which can check the excited motion of the insensible parts. To the second I say: heat is not observed in the whirlpools of water because the sensible parts of the water are carried off by this motion; but for the nature of heat there is required not merely a vehement and perturbed motion of any parts whatever, but an agitation of very fine and insensible parts, which, carried off above all by the fiery particles, can penetrate other bodies and fibers and stir them with a similar motion.

> 584 Opp. 7: Metalla aliaque dura corpora quandoque calent, quin corpuscula tumultuario motu adfecta in illis existant: ergo. Nego antec.: Ut enim omittam nullum corpus, quantumvis durum *calorem* posse concipere, quin illius extensio augeatur; manifestum est, metalla, si quum summè calent, frigidae aquae immergantur, insignem in illa ebullitionem cum strepitu excitare: ergo in illorum poris tenuissima corpuscula existunt, quae particulis aquae tumultuarium illum motum communicant, unde non dissimili motu ipsa pollére, videtur perspicuum.

584 Obj. 7: Metals and other hard bodies are sometimes hot without corpuscles affected with a tumultuous motion existing in them: therefore. I deny the antec.: For, to pass over the fact that no body, however hard, can take on heat without its extension being increased, it is manifest that metals, if they are immersed in cold water when they are extremely hot, excite in it a notable ebullition with a hissing noise: therefore very fine corpuscles exist in their pores which communicate that tumultuous motion to the particles of the water; whence it seems evident that they themselves are possessed of a not dissimilar motion.

> 585 Opp. denique ovi albúmen in consistentem massam, caloris actione concrescit: ergo calor non consistit in corpusculis motu celerrimo, perturbato, & expansivo adfectis: concipi enim nullatenus potest, quomodo ab eo, quod celerrime movetur, consistentia, atque adeò partium quies oriri possit. Dist. antec.: concrescit ita ut illa consistentia sit caloris effectus per se nego; ita ut sit caloris effectus per accidens, conc. & nego conseq. Consistentiam acquirit albúmen ovi, non quia caloris natura per se valeat consistentiam corporibus tribuere, sed quia corporum quorundam partes ejus sunt magnitudinis, & figurae, eoque artificio intextae, ut moveri nequeant á caloris corpusculis, quin implicentur inter se, & in duram massam concrescant. Profectò ipsum ovi [p. 184] albúmen, quod primò caloris actione durescit, planè dissolvitur si calor ipse augeatur, maximo sanè argumento, illius consistentiam, non directè, & per sese, sed per accidens à calore provenire.

585 Obj. finally: the white of an egg congeals into a consistent mass by the action of heat: therefore heat does not consist in corpuscles affected with a very swift, perturbed and expansive motion; for it can in no way be conceived how consistency, and hence rest of the parts, could arise from that which is moved most swiftly. Dist. antec.: it congeals in such a way that that consistency is an effect of heat per se, I deny; in such a way that it is an effect of heat per accidens, I grant; and I deny the conseq. The white of an egg acquires consistency not because the nature of heat is of itself able to bestow consistency on bodies, but because the parts of certain bodies are of such a size and figure, and woven together with such artifice, that they cannot be moved by the corpuscles of heat without becoming entangled with one another and congealing into a hard mass. Indeed the very white of the egg, [p. 184] which at first hardens by the action of heat, is wholly dissolved if the heat itself is increased: a very strong argument indeed that its consistency comes from heat not directly and of itself, but by accident.

## CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

> De Frigore.

On Cold.

> 586 Proprium *frigoris est densare corpora, dura reddere quae mollia sunt, liquores plurimos, in consistentem massam mutare, motumque perturbatum, & expansivum internarum partium corporis tardare, atque etiam planè sistere*[?]. Necesse est enim ut contrarii sint effectus caloris, & frigoris. Hinc necessariò sequitur, quod frigus in eo formaliter consistat, cujus causâ constringuntur corpora, rigescunt mollia, liquores plurimi in duram abeunt massam, motusque perturbatus, & expansivus partium internarum corporis retardatur, & sistitur. In eo enim statuendum est frigus, à quo effectus qui vulgo frigori tribuuntur, proveniunt. Hinc frigus non optimè definitur à Peripateticis, *qualitas quae congregat, tum homogenea, & heterogenea*[?]. Certum enim est, non esse constantem frigoris effectum, ut heterogenea congreget. Si enim vehementiori frigori subjiciantur vinum, acetum, spiritus vini, separantur atque dissolvuntur liquores illi, pars vini aquea in glaciem concrescit, spiritus suam fluiditatem retinet, & tartarum praecipitatur. His positis.

t is proper to cold to condense bodies, to make hard those that are soft, to 586 I change very many liquors into a consistent mass, and to retard, and even wholly to stop, the perturbed and expansive motion of the internal parts of a body. For it is necessary that the effects of heat and of cold be contrary. Hence it necessarily follows that cold formally consists in that by whose agency bodies are constricted, soft things stiffen, very many liquors pass into a hard mass, and the perturbed and expansive motion of the internal parts of a body is retarded and stopped. For cold must be placed in that from which the effects commonly attributed to cold proceed. Hence cold is not well defined by the Peripatetics as a quality that gathers together both homogeneous and heterogeneous things. For it is certain that it is not a constant effect of cold to gather heterogeneous things together. For if wine, vinegar and spirit of wine are subjected to a rather intense cold, those liquors are separated and dissolved: the watery part of the wine congeals into ice, the spirit retains its fluidity, and the tartar is precipitated. These things being laid down,

> 587 Dico 1: Frigus in partium quiete haud rectè collocatur. Est contra Cartesium. Prob.: non rectè explicatur calor, per motum partium corporis incalescentis [§. 573.] ergo neque frigus per partium quietem rectè exponitur. *Secundò*: In eo quod frigoris effectus est, statui frigus rectè non potest: sed quies partium est frigoris effectus [§. 586.] ergo non nisi perperam potest frigus in partium quiete consistere. Confirmatur: Ratum enim est, frigus ab ea distingui realiter organi tactus passione, quam frigoris sensatio in anima consequitur; sed passio organi tactus non est nisi privatio motus in iis nervorum fibris, quae organum ipsum constituunt: ergo. *Tertiò*: Si frigus nihil esset à partium quiete diversum, nullum haberi posset corpus *vel minimè frigidum*[?], nisi ejus partes quoad sensum quiescerent: sed hoc est, prorsùs falsum, ut ex fermentationibus frigidis constat: ergo. Adhaec: illud corpus erit frigidissimum, cujus partes nulla prorsùs ratione moventur: ergo corpora quaeque durissima erunt frigidissima, glaciesque ipsa ex qua frigidus halitus cumulatim erumpit. intestinoque partium motu donata est, [p. 185] [?]

587 I say 1: Cold is not rightly placed in the rest of the parts. This is against Descartes. Prob.: heat is not rightly explained by the motion of the parts of the body growing hot [§. 573.]; therefore neither is cold rightly expounded by the rest of the parts. Secondly: Cold cannot rightly be placed in that which is an effect of cold: but the rest of the parts is an effect of cold [§. 586.]: therefore only wrongly can cold be made to consist in the rest of the parts. It is confirmed: It is settled that cold is really distinguished from that passion of the organ of touch which the sensation of cold in the soul follows; but the passion of the organ of touch is nothing but a privation of motion in those fibers of the nerves which constitute the organ itself: therefore. Thirdly: If cold were nothing different from the rest of the parts, no body could be had that is in the least cold unless its parts were at rest as far as sense can tell: but this is altogether false, as is clear from cold fermentations: therefore. Moreover: that body will be the coldest whose parts are moved in no way at all: therefore all the hardest bodies will be the coldest, and ice itself, from which a cold exhalation bursts forth abundantly, and which is endowed with an intestine motion of its parts, [p. 185] would not be a supremely cold body. Although, therefore, a body whose parts are at rest is not hot, it is not on that account, by this very fact, to be judged cold.

> 588 Dico secundò[?] cum magno Boerhaavio [^185-s1] [?]

588 I say secondly, with the great Boerhaave (i): cold by no means consists in the mere privation of heat. This is against very many of the Moderns, among whom the distinguished ’s Gravesande is numbered. Prob.: Since water is dilated in congelation [§. 571. ff.], if it passed into ice on account of the withdrawal of heat, the water would be dilated solely on account of that withdrawal; and hence, conversely, it would be condensed by heat, as the hypothesis of our adversaries supposes; we should have to say that water has from the efficient cause by which it is condensed that very thing, namely that it is fluid: but it is against the nature of heat that water affected by it should be reduced to a smaller space than it possesses of itself [§. 567.]: therefore water is not changed into ice for this cause alone, that it is deprived of heat; but it is converted into ice when something is added to it: therefore it does not grow cold through the mere withdrawal of heat, and consequently cold does not consist in the mere privation of heat. Hence, by the very fact that a body is not hot, it cannot be judged cold, unless other things are equal.

> [^185-s1]: Elem. Chem. Tom. 1. p. 73.

[^185-s1]: Elem. Chem., vol. 1, p. 73.

> 589 Dico 3: [?] C. s' Gravesande [^185-s2] [?]

589 I say 3: Cold, even in its cause, is something real and positive. Prob.: For if cold is neither motion nor the privation of heat, as we have already demonstrated, it certainly remains that, since it is opposed to heat, it too, just as heat does, consists in a positive entity. Secondly: It is proved from an observation of the distinguished ’s Gravesande (k). Let snow be taken, mixed in equal parts with sea salt, contained in a vessel, and surrounding a glass filled with water. If this mixture is placed on the fire, at the moment at which it melts, that is, at which its heat is increased, it does not, as other bodies do, communicate heat to the water, but the water is converted into ice. No other reason can be given for this phenomenon except that the corpuscles of heat which penetrate that vessel and dissolve the snow drive something positive out of the snow into the water, which makes the water change into ice: therefore cold consists in something positive.

> [^185-s2]: Elem. Phy[?]. §. 2460, & seq.

[^185-s2]: Elem. Phys., §. 2460 ff.

> 590 Dico 4: [?] [p. 186] ipsa esse corpuscula in quibus diximus frigus consistere. Quod autem nitrosae particulae principem locum teneant argumento est frigus illud intensissimum quod nitri ope producitur. Thermometro si quidem ex mercurio confecto in nivem immisso, cum nitri spiritus adfusus fuerat, deprehendit toties laudatus Muschembroek, tubi mercurium infra terminum, qui glaciei frigus indicat, descendisse. Invenit quoque fortissimum aceti spiritum in eandem nivem immersum abiisse in glaciem. Quod autem aqua non habeat in glaciem, etiam si nitrum illi admisceatur, causa est, quia ut hoc accideret, nitrum deberet in sua primitiva corpuscula resolvi, ita autem ab aqua solvi nequit, ut omnes fatentur. Ex hoc ergo non sequitur nitrum non esse congelationis causam, neque in illius potissimum particulis frigus residere; quippè non in quibuscumque, sed in primitivis salium corpusculis frigus collocavimus.

590 I say 4: Cold in first act consists in corpuscles extremely slender in bulk, and these slender corpuscles are the most subtle primitive particles of salts, but chiefly of niter. The first part can be proved aptly enough from what we have said about heat. The second part is established by experience; for the most subtle particles of every salt contribute to producing cold in bodies, and cold increases or decreases according to the greater or smaller quantity of them, as the Florentine Academicians testify; for all salts placed round a vessel containing water assist its congelation. The most subtle parts of salt, therefore, even though they are few, seem to penetrate through the pores of vessels, to put the fire to flight, to fix the parts of the water, and hence to be those very [p. 186] corpuscles in which we have said that cold consists. That the nitrous particles hold the chief place is argued by that very intense cold which is produced by means of niter. For the often-praised Musschenbroek found that, when a thermometer made with mercury was immersed in snow onto which spirit of niter had been poured, the mercury descended below the mark that indicates the cold of ice. He found also that very strong spirit of vinegar, immersed in the same snow, passed into ice. But that water does not pass into ice even if niter is added to it, the cause is that, for this to happen, the niter would have to be resolved into its primitive corpuscles; but it cannot be so dissolved by water, as all admit. From this, therefore, it does not follow that niter is not the cause of congelation, nor that cold does not reside chiefly in its particles; since we have placed cold not in any corpuscles whatever, but in the primitive corpuscles of salts.

> 591 Neque silentio praeterire possum celebre experimentum ab Accademicis Florentinis peractum: quemadmodum nempe calor ignis, aut solis in speculo collectus, & ad proximum thermometrum reflexus, ejusdem thermometri liquorem rarefacit, & altius illum cogit ascendere; ita si loco solis, glacies substituatur, thermometri liquor descendit, & condensatur; sed in primo casu etiam juxta adversarios corpuscula quaedam egrediuntur ab igne, quae spiritum vini thermometro inclusum rarefaciunt: ergo corpuscula quaedam ex glacie prodire debent, quae à speculo collecta in thermometrum reflectantur, ejusque liquorem condensent, ac propterea frigus non in caloris absentia tantummodò constitui debet, ut inter alios ostendere conatur D. de Ratte [^186-s1] non animadvertens contra ipsum probare experimenta, quae adfert ut nostram sententiam infirmet.

591 Nor can I pass over in silence the celebrated experiment performed by the Florentine Academicians: namely, that just as the heat of a fire, or of the sun, collected in a mirror and reflected onto a nearby thermometer, rarefies the liquor of that same thermometer and forces it to rise higher, so, if ice is substituted in place of the sun, the liquor of the thermometer descends and is condensed; but in the first case, even according to our adversaries, certain corpuscles come out from the fire which rarefy the spirit of wine enclosed in the thermometer: therefore certain corpuscles must come out of the ice which, collected by the mirror, are reflected onto the thermometer and condense its liquor; and consequently cold must not be made to consist only in the absence of heat, as, among others, Mr. de Ratte (l) tries to show, not noticing that the experiments he brings forward to weaken our opinion prove against himself.

> [^186-s1]: L' Encyclopedie, verb. Froid.

[^186-s1]: L’Encyclopédie, s.v. Froid.

> 592 Quid quòd in sententia nostra optimè exponuntur frigoris phaenomena. Referunt Scriptores in Ukrania Poloniae Provincia esse acerrimum frigus, longèque intensius, quàm in Normanna Galliae Provincia; cum tamen in globo terrestri idem sit respectivus locorum situs. Fluvius qui Regiam Sinarum Urbem Pekin alluit, circa mensem Novembris tanta vi frigoris intra diem unum concrescit, & induratur, ut quatuor mensium spatio currus, & ingentia pondera sustineat, illae tamen Sinensis fluvius eandem habet respectivam in globo terrestri positionem, quàm obtinet Romae Tyberis, in quo non viget haec frigoris vis.

592 What of the fact that on our opinion the phenomena of cold are explained excellently? Writers report that in the Ukraine, a province of Poland, the cold is very keen, and far more intense than in Normandy, a province of France, although the respective situation of the places on the terrestrial globe is the same. The river that washes Peking, the royal city of the Chinese, congeals about the month of November within a single day with such force of cold, and hardens so, that for the space of four months it sustains carriages and huge weights; yet that Chinese river has the same respective position on the terrestrial globe as the Tiber at Rome holds, in which this force of cold does not prevail.

> 593 Hinc dicendum est, ventos quosdam aliis frigidiores esse, qui salinos, nitrosos halitus secum deferant, & ipsis referti, ac permixti corporum poros pervadant, praedictosque effectus producant. In nostrâ sententiâ intelligitur etiam, cur rivuli quidam hiberno tempore liberrimè fluant, tempore autem aestivo in durissimam glaciem concrescant: Observatum enim est, rivulorum illorum litora, plurimis nitri, salisque particulis abundare, quae quidem particulae [p. 187] aestivo calore solvuntur, & in rivuli aquas defluunt, iisque permiscentur. Ultra ea quae diximus [§ 201] de glacie, dicendum nunc etiam est aquam dum in glaciem abit dilatari, quia primitivae aquae partes ejus sunt texturae, ut corpuscula itidem primitiva nitri, aliorumque salium à quibus congelatio peragitur, nequeant cum illis intimè misceri, quemadmodùm ad indurandam aquam requiritur, quin magna effervescentia contingat. *Glaciei ergo expansiva virtus*, ait toties laudatus Musschembroek [^187-s1], *oritur à corpusculis subtilissimis in atmosphaera volitantibus, aquae admixtis, cum ea effervescentibus, eamque figentibus in firmam solidamque massam*.

593 Hence it must be said that certain winds are colder than others, which carry saline and nitrous exhalations with them and, filled with them and mixed with them, pervade the pores of bodies and produce the aforesaid effects. On our opinion one understands also why certain streams flow most freely in wintertime, but in summertime congeal into the hardest ice: for it has been observed that the banks of those streams abound in a great deal of niter and in saline particles, which particles indeed [p. 187] are dissolved by the summer heat and flow down into the waters of the stream and are mixed with them. Besides what we have said [§. 201] about ice, it must now also be said that water is dilated while it passes into ice because the primitive parts of water are of such a texture that the likewise primitive corpuscles of niter, and of the other salts by which congelation is effected, cannot be mixed intimately with them, as is required for hardening water, without a great effervescence taking place. The expansive force of ice, therefore, says the often-praised Musschenbroek (m), arises from very subtle corpuscles flitting in the atmosphere, mixed with the water, effervescing with it, and fixing it into a firm and solid mass.

> [^187-s1]: Comment. in Experim. Acad. del Cimento. P. 1. p. 137.

[^187-s1]: Comment. in Experim. Acad. del Cimento, pt. 1, p. 137.

> 594 Adversus sententiam nostram plurima opponi solent argumenta, quae facilè solvuntur. Unum tantummodò vobis proponam. Experientia constat, frigidam sentiri aquam, si ab eo calore quo sensorium nostrum adfectum est, ipsius aquae calor deficiat: ergo frigus non consistit in corpusculis frigorificis, sed in caloris tantummodò diminutione. Nego conseq.: Frigida enim nobis ea aqua adparet, quae minus quàm tactus organum calida est, quia quum motus in aquae partibus à caloris corpusculis, quae in illa sunt, productus, sit illo remissior, quo tunc pollent nerveae tactus fibrae; aqueae ipsae particulae illis fibris adplicatae, earum motum retardant, & sistunt, simulque eas densant, atque constringunt, uno verbo, eam passionem in illis excitant, quàm frigoris sensatio in anima comitatur.

594 Against our opinion very many arguments are usually opposed, which are easily answered. I shall propose to you only one. Experience shows that water is felt as cold if the heat of the water falls short of that heat by which our sensorium is affected: therefore cold does not consist in frigorific corpuscles, but only in a diminution of heat. I deny the conseq.: For that water appears cold to us which is less hot than the organ of touch, because, since the motion produced in the parts of the water by the corpuscles of heat that are in it is more remiss than that with which the nervous fibers of touch are then endowed, the watery particles themselves, applied to those fibers, retard and stop their motion, and at the same time condense and constrict them; in a word, they excite in them that passion which the sensation of cold in the soul accompanies.

> 595 Ceterum haec objectio, vel nulla est, vel certè probat etiam calorem in sola frigoris diminutione consistere. Enim verò: quemadmodum frigidum nobis adparet corpus, quod minus quàm sensorium nostrum calidum est; ita experientiâ teste, corpus illud nobis *calidum* se prodit, quod debiliore, quàm ipsum sensorium, est *frigore* adfectum. *Tepidum, dicimus*, (inquit Cl. Boerhaavius) [^187-s2] *quod eodem cum corpore humano calore gaudet; calidum quando calorem corporis nostri superat, frigidum, quod minus calidum est.*

595 Moreover, this objection either is worthless or certainly proves that heat too consists in the mere diminution of cold. For indeed, just as that body appears cold to us which is less hot than our sensorium, so, as experience witnesses, that body shows itself hot to us which is affected with a weaker cold than the sensorium itself. We call tepid (says the distinguished Boerhaave) (n) that which enjoys the same heat as the human body; hot, when it exceeds the heat of our body; cold, what is less hot.

> [^187-s2]: Praelect. Acad. in suas Instit. sup. sens. tact. n. 483.

[^187-s2]: Praelect. Academ. in suas Instit., on the sense of touch, no. 483.

> 596 Non superfluum erit hic data occasione in vestram utilitatem animadvertere *perniciosissimum* atque *saluberrimum* esse posse frigidi potus usum pro diversâ corporis nostri conditione. Si vehementiori exercitatione, & qualibet alia corporis agitatione aliquis aestuaverit, id summoperè vitare debet, quod refrigerationem interius, vel exterius adferre possit. Ex imprudenti in his casibus balneorum frigidorum usu subitaneam mortem non raròoriginem, habuisse, Doctissimus Medicus Lancissi [^187-s3] testatur.
