Etenim frigoris impressio, solidas corporis animalis partes constringit, fluidas autem condensat, atque talis esse potest effectus, ut partium solidarum actio, fluidarum autem motus nimis minuatur. Hinc maximè turbari potest tota corporis machina. Hinc nascuntur in canalibus obstructiones, & [p. 188] frequentissima in humorum secretionibus impedimenta, & ex imminuta, aut penitùs sublatâ transpiratione inuumera morborum genera, tum ipsa mors eveniat.

596 It will not be superfluous here, the occasion being given, to point out for your benefit that the use of cold drink can be most pernicious and most wholesome according to the diverse condition of our body. If anyone has grown heated by rather vehement exercise, or by any other agitation of the body, he must avoid above all whatever could bring on a cooling, inwardly or outwardly. That sudden death has not rarely had its origin in the imprudent use of cold baths in these cases, the most learned physician Lancisi (o) testifies. For cold, when impressed, constricts the solid parts of the animal body and condenses the fluid ones, and the effect can be such that the action of the solid parts and the motion of the fluids are too greatly diminished. Hence the whole machine of the body can be thrown into the greatest disorder. Hence arise obstructions in the canals, and [p. 188] very frequent impediments in the secretions of the humors, and from diminished or wholly suppressed transpiration there ensue innumerable kinds of diseases, and even death itself.

> [^187-s3]: Lib. 2. de mortis subitaneis.

[^187-s3]: Bk. 2, De mortibus subitaneis.

> 597 Ex potionis frigidioris abusu intelligitur quoque illius usus. Si nempè nimia sit in fibris extensio, relaxatio, nervorumque *atonia*, in his casibus utilissimè adhibentur potiones frigidae. Quae quum ita sit, mirum esse non debet, quod Vir Clariss. Hoffmannus duo ediderit opuscula, quorum unum inscribitur. *De frigido potu vitae, & sanitati hominum inimicissimo*: alterum verò *de aquae frigidae potu salutari*.

597 From the abuse of cold drink its use too is understood. Namely, if there is excessive extension and relaxation in the fibers, and atony of the nerves, in these cases cold drinks are most usefully applied. This being so, it ought not to be a wonder that the most distinguished Hoffmann published two little works, of which one is entitled On Cold Drink, Most Hostile to the Life and Health of Men; the other, however, On the Wholesome Drinking of Cold Water.

## CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

> DE CALORIS ET FRIGORIS CRITERIO.

ON THE CRITERION OF HEAT AND COLD.

> Et obiter de criterio humiditatis, & siccitatis, nec non de Barometro gravitatis aëris criterio.

AND INCIDENTALLY ON THE CRITERION OF HUMIDITY AND DRYNESS , AND ALSO ON THE BAROMETER, THE CRITERION OF THE WEIGHT OF THE AIR .

> 598 Ut tactûs vitio in explorando corporum calore, & frigore occurrerent Recentiores Philosophi instrumentum illud invenere, quod vulgò *Thermometrum*, aut *thermoscopium* adpellatur, quo utimur veluti criterio ad discernendum in corporibus gradum caloris ac frigoris. Hujus plures sunt formae, ac veluti species. Prima ejus inventio tribuitur Cornelio Drebbel, Bátavo, eum ad meliorem conditionem reduxit postea Sanctorius, majorem perfectionem addiderunt Academici Florentini, â quibus thermometra Florentina nuncupantur. Hi omnes constructi sunt cum spiritu vini rectificatissimo. Thermometrum mercuriale inventum est â Daniele *Fahrenheyt*, dictum propterea *Thermometrum Fahrenheytianum*. Clariss. *Reaumurius* invenit methodum conficiendi thermometra ex vini spiritu, quae ea constanti lege sibi mutuò respondeant, ut in eodem loco posita eundem caloris gradum designent. In explicanda constructione thermometri nollumus immorari. Eam quam clarissimè explicavit in suis foliis Periodicis [^188-s1] American. noster D. Joseph. Ignatius Bartolache, Medicinae Doct., atque in Reg. Pont. Mex. Acad. Primariae Medicinae Cathedrae ad quadrienium Moderat. &c. Vir de Mathematica totaque Medicinâ optimè meritus, Scientiarum, Bonarumque Artium Cultor egregius. Fig. LXI. exactè repraesentat thermomentrum *Fahrenheyt*.

o remedy the defect of touch in exploring the heat and cold of bodies, 598 T the more recent Philosophers invented that instrument which is commonly called the Thermometer, or thermoscope, which we use as a criterion for discerning the degree of heat and cold in bodies. There are several forms of it, and as it were species. Its first invention is attributed to Cornelis Drebbel, a Dutchman; Sanctorius afterwards brought it to a better condition; the Florentine Academicians added greater perfection, after whom they are named Florentine thermometers. All these are constructed with most highly rectified spirit of wine. The mercurial thermometer was invented by Daniel Fahrenheit, and is therefore called the Fahrenheit Thermometer. The most distinguished Réaumur found a method of making thermometers of spirit of wine which correspond to one another by so constant a law that, placed in the same spot, they mark the same degree of heat. We do not wish to dwell on explaining the construction of the thermometer. It has been explained most clearly in his periodical sheets (p) by our fellow American Don José Ignacio Bartolache, Doctor of Medicine, and for a four-year term Holder of the Principal Chair of Medicine in the Royal and Pontifical Academy of Mexico, etc., a man who has deserved excellently of Mathematics and of the whole of Medicine, an outstanding cultivator of the Sciences and of the Liberal Arts. Fig. LXI exactly represents the Fahrenheit thermometer.

> [^188-s1]: Mercurio Volante sobre asuntos de Fisica y Medicina n. 3.

[^188-s1]: Mercurio Volante sobre asuntos de Física y Medicina, no. 3.

[p. 189]

> 599 Ne vobis aliquid utilitatis deesit, aliqua de *Hygroscopio* & *Barometro* subjungam. *Hygroscopium* quod & *Hygrometrum* dici solet, est instrumentum, quo aëris humiditas, atque siccitas explorantur, earumque incrementa, & decrementa palam fiunt. Hoc autèm modo construi solet. Cannábinus funis, aut nervea chorda A B (Fig. LXII.), cujus alterum extremum A sit muro infixum, extendatur super rotulam B ex altero chordae extremo, pondus D pendeat cum annexo indice E. Eidem parieti adfixa sit lamina a b in partes aequales divisa cui index ille respondeat: quum teste experientiâ minuatur longitudo funis cannábini, & nerveae chordeae dum humorem contrahunt, contrà verò dum exsiccantur, longiores fiant, altius ascendet index D auctâ aëris humiditate, ea verò iminutâ, descendet. Hoc itaque ascensu & descensu incrementum, & decrementum humiditatis, & siccitatis, quibus aër adficitur, nobis innotescent.

599 That nothing of use may be lacking to you, I shall add something on the Hygroscope and the Barometer. The Hygroscope, which is also usually called the Hygrometer, is an instrument by which the humidity and dryness of the air are explored, and their increases and decreases are made manifest. It is usually constructed in this way. Let a hempen rope, or a gut string A B (Fig. LXII), whose one end A is fixed in the wall, be stretched over the small wheel B; from the other end of the string let a weight D hang, with an attached index E. To the same wall let there be fixed a plate a b divided into equal parts, to which that index corresponds: since, as experience testifies, the length of a hempen rope and of gut strings is diminished while they take up moisture, and on the contrary they become longer while they are dried out, the index D will rise higher when the humidity of the air is increased, and will descend when it is diminished. By this ascent and descent, therefore, the increase and decrease of the humidity and dryness by which the air is affected will become known to us.

> 600 Aërem ponderosum esse, nemo prorsùs Recentiorum est qui vel minimùm dubitet. Nimis enim videtur apertum suspensionem mercurii in Torricellanis tubis ab externo premente aëre provenire. Accedit: certissimè constare globum vitreum ex. gr. aëre plenum, se ipso aëre vacuo esse graviorem. Neque ab hac opinione Aristoteles ipse abhorruit. Dixerat enim *Lib. 4. de Caelo text. 29. Omnia gravitatem habere praeter ignem*, & ibid. *textu 30, cuncta in sua regione, etiam aërem ipsum gravitare*. Erit fortassé qui putet ponderosum esse aërem propter vapores, & exhalationes quibus aër ipse abundat. Verùm animadvertat is velim, si vapores, exhalationesque graves sunt, debere etiam aërem esse ponderosum, ut nempè vapores ipsi atque exhalationes in eo suspendi, illique innatare liberrimè possint. Non enim potest fluidum, quod omni caret pondere, solida graviaque corpora sustinére.

600 There is no one at all among the Moderns who doubts even in the least that air is heavy. For it seems all too plain that the suspension of mercury in Torricellian tubes comes from the external pressing air. Add that it is most certainly established that a glass globe, for example, full of air, is heavier than itself emptied of air. Nor did Aristotle himself shrink from this opinion. For he had said, bk. 4 On the Heavens, text 29: all things have gravity except fire; and ibid., text 30: all things in their own region, even the air itself, gravitate. There will perhaps be someone who thinks that the air is heavy on account of the vapors and exhalations with which the air itself abounds. But I should like him to notice that, if vapors and exhalations are heavy, the air too must be heavy, so that, namely, the vapors themselves and the exhalations can be suspended in it and float in it most freely. For a fluid which lacks all weight cannot sustain solid and heavy bodies.

> 601 Ex aëris itaque pondere originem suam sumpsit *Barómetrum*, instrumentum scilicet, quo ad mutationes gravitatis aëris explorandas velut criterio uti solémus. Constat autem Barómetrum tubo inflexo A C D (Fig. LXIII.) mercurio pleno, planaeque tabulae A D immobiliter adfixo. Ad tubi latus habetur scala, cujus una portio est E F in pollices divisa, sumpto initio divisionis â superficie a b mercurii stagnantis in aperto tubi orificio inferiori C D. Hinc enim altitudo illa comparatur, ad quam vi pressionis, quam in stagnantis mercurii superficiem b externus aër exercet, mercurius ipse per tubum ad tractum A C sustinetur. Singuli porrò scalae pollices in suas lineas subdividi solent, ut exiguae etiam mutationes, quas mercurii altitudo patitur, exactius discernantur.

601 From the weight of the air, therefore, the Barometer took its origin: that is, an instrument which we are accustomed to use as a criterion for exploring the changes in the gravity of the air. The Barometer consists of an inflected tube A C D (Fig. LXIII) full of mercury and immovably fixed to a flat board A D. At the side of the tube there is a scale, of which one portion E F is divided into inches, the beginning of the division being taken from the surface a b of the mercury standing in the open lower orifice C D of the tube. For from here is reckoned that height to which, by the force of the pressure which the external air exerts on the surface b of the standing mercury, the mercury itself is sustained through the tube up to the stretch A C. Further, the single inches of the scale are usually subdivided into their lines, so that even the small changes which the height of the mercury undergoes may be discerned more exactly.

> 602 *Barometri* usus in eo totus est, ut quanta sit incumbentis atmosphaerae gravitas quotidiè dignoscatur. Quo itaque altius in *Barometro* haeserit mercurius, eò gravior atmosphaera censenda est, eò autem levior, quò depressior in illo mercurius fuerit. Eritque hodierna atmosphaerae gravitas ad externam ejusdem gravitatem, quemadmodùm ad hesternam mercurii in Barometro [p. 190] altitudinem, hodierna se habuerit, ut si ex. gr. heri suspensus manserit mercurius in Barometri tubo A C (Ead. Fig.) ad altitudinem a e, hodie verò ad altitudinem a B in illo suspensus existat, gravitas hodierna atmosphaerae erit ad externam, quemadmodùm se habet altitudo a e, ad altitudinem a B. Sed de his hactenùs.

602 The use of the Barometer lies wholly in this, that it may be recognized day by day how great the gravity of the incumbent atmosphere is. Therefore the higher the mercury has stood in the Barometer, the heavier the atmosphere is to be judged, and the lighter, the lower the mercury has been in it. And today’s gravity of the atmosphere will be to its yesterday’s gravity as today’s height of the mercury in the Barometer is to yesterday’s [p. 190] height; so that if, for example, yesterday the mercury remained suspended in the tube A C of the Barometer (same Fig.) at the height a e, but today it stands suspended in it at the height a B, today’s gravity of the atmosphere will be to yesterday’s as the height a e is to the height a B. But enough of these things.

## DISSERTATIO III. — DISSERTATION III

> De Qualitatibus olfactilibus, gustabilibus, & audibilibus.

On the Qualities perceived by Smell, Taste, and Hearing.

## CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

> ¿In quonam consistat odor corporum?

In what does the smell of bodies consist?

> 603 His supositis, quae de odoribus dicta sunt [§. 158. & seq.] Dico: odor in actu primo, seu prout est in corporibus, in substantiali subtilissimo odori corporis efluvio consistit, & hoc efluvium sunt particulae volatilis substantiae sulphureo-mercurialis corporis odori, quae certo modo configuratae, ac determinatae atque â corporibus odoratis avulsae, cum aëre tanquam vehiculo narium cavitates dum inspiramus subeunt, fibrillasque nerveas per organum olfactus distributas variè impellunt, ac cómmovent. Prob. per partes. Prima constat ex eo, quod concipi nequeat, quomodo organum corporeum, sine reali partium contactu possit adfici, & commoveri; sed fibrae nervorum irritantur, premuntur, & vellicantur ab odoribus: ergo. *Feminae* etenim (ut ait Boerhaavius [^190-s1] *ad solum odorem moschi, ambrae, continuò animo linquuntur. Eadem odorata in epilepticis exacervationes faciunt.* Clariss. Boyle [^190-s2] refert se novisse hominem firmae valetudinis, sed perquàm sanguineae temperiéi, qui violentos ex odore moschi percipiebat capitis dolores, alium qui haud dissimile incommodum patiebatur, ob suavem damascenarum [p. 191] rosarum fragrantium [^191-s1] haec autem, & alia plurima explicari néqueunt nisi per substantiale odori corporis effluvium.

hese things being supposed which have been said about smells [§. 158. 603 T ff.], I say: smell in first act, or as it is in bodies, consists in a substantial and most subtle effluvium of the odorous body, and this effluvium is the particles of the volatile sulphureo-mercurial substance of the odorous body, which, configured and determined in a certain manner and torn away from odorous bodies, enter the cavities of the nostrils with the air as their vehicle while we breathe in, and variously push and stir the nervous fibrils distributed through the organ of smell. Prob. by parts. The first is established from this, that it cannot be conceived how a bodily organ could be affected and stirred without a real contact of parts: but the fibers of the nerves are irritated, pressed and plucked by smells: therefore. For women (as Boerhaave says (q)) at the mere smell of musk and amber at once fall into a faint. The same odorous things cause exacerbations in epileptics. The most distinguished Boyle (r) reports that he knew a man of firm health, but of a very sanguine temperament, who felt violent headaches from the smell of musk; another who suffered a not dissimilar discomfort from the sweet fragrance of damask roses (s). [p. 191] (s). These things, however, and very many others cannot be explained except through a substantial effluvium of the odorous body.

[^190-s1]: Praelect. Academ., on smell.

> [^190-s2]: De insig. efficacia effluvior. cap. 6.

[^190-s2]: De insig. efficacia effluvior., ch. 6.

> [^191-s1]: Plura alia tradit Clariss. P. de Lanis in *Magisterio Naturae, & Artis* (ex quo velut thesauro suam haud pauci Physicorum absterserunt inopiam quàm faciles ad usurpanda aliena, tàm officiosi utinam ad reddendum auctori meritum honorem!)

Lana Terzi reports many other things in the Magisterium Naturae et Artis (from which, as from a treasury, not a few Physicists have relieved their own poverty: would that they were as dutiful in rendering the author his deserved honor as they are ready to appropriate what belongs to others!)

> 604 Secunda pars probatur: nam ex experimentis chymicis constat ea tantum corpora esse odora quae volátili sulphureo-mercuriali substantia praedita sunt, eaque olére intensiùs, quae hujuscemodi substantia magis abundant: ergo. Tertia pars, nempè has particulas configuratas esse, constat apertissimè. Certum enim omninò est, corpuscula odori efluvii per id formaliter esse odora, per quód nerveas olfactus fibras titillare possunt; constat autem nerveas has fibras non moveri â corpusculis odoriferi effluvii, nisi quatenùs ipsa corpuscula magnitudine certa donata sunt, certâque figurâ adfectâ, ratione demonstrante, effectum purè mechanicum, cujusmodi est illa fibrarum motio, nonnisi mechanicae causae posse acceptum referri: ergo.

604 The second part is proved: for it is established from chemical experiments that only those bodies are odorous which are endowed with a volatile sulphureo-mercurial substance, and that those smell more intensely which abound more in a substance of this kind: therefore. The third part, namely that these particles are configured, is most plainly established. For it is altogether certain that the corpuscles of the odorous effluvium are formally odorous through that by which they can tickle the nervous fibers of smell; but it is established that these nervous fibers are not moved by the corpuscles of the odoriferous effluvium except inasmuch as the corpuscles themselves are endowed with a certain size and affected with a certain figure, since reason demonstrates that a purely mechanical effect, such as that motion of the fibers is, can be ascribed only to a mechanical cause: therefore.

> 605 Postrema pars probatur: nullus enim odor percipitur, nisi aër naribus adtrahatur. *Spiritus salis ammoniaci, qui validissimè nares nostras adficit*, (inquit laudatus Boerhaavius [^191-s2] *adpositus naso nihil omninò faciet, quandiu, vel exspiramus, vel certè non inspiramus*. Nisi enim aër naribus adtrahatur nequeunt odoriferi effluvii corpuscula, quae per aërem dispersa sunt, eique innatant, in nerveas narium fibras incurrere easque prout ad excitandum sensum olfactus requiritur, titillare. Praeterea in nostra sententiâ clarissimè explicantur odorum phaenomena. Primo: *calor odorem in corporibus excitat, frigus prohibet*. Calore enim separatur â crassioribus particulis *sulphureo-mercurialis* substantia, qua corpus constat, & plurimum adtenuatur. Dilatantur itidem pori corporis, unde quae in illo est volatilis substantiae portio facilè erumpit, & quoquoversùs diffunditur. Contra verò frigus poros corporis constringit, motumque intestinum partium retardat, & prohibet.

605 The last part is proved: for no smell is perceived unless air is drawn in through the nostrils. Spirit of sal ammoniac, which most powerfully affects our nostrils, (says the praised Boerhaave (t)) placed at the nose will do nothing at all as long as we either breathe out, or at any rate do not breathe in. For unless air is drawn in through the nostrils, the corpuscles of the odoriferous effluvium, which are dispersed through the air and float in it, cannot run into the nervous fibers of the nostrils and tickle them as is required for exciting the sense of smell. Moreover, on our opinion the phenomena of smells are explained most clearly. First: heat excites smell in bodies, cold prevents it. For by heat the sulphureo-mercurial substance of which the body consists is separated from the coarser particles and is very greatly attenuated. The pores of the body are likewise dilated, whence the portion of volatile substance that is in it easily bursts out and is diffused in every direction. On the contrary, cold constricts the pores of the body and retards and prevents the intestine motion of the parts.

> [^191-s2]: Loco citat.

[^191-s2]: Loc. cit.

> 606 Secundò: *Confricatione atque adtritu ea dura corpora fiunt odora, quae inodóra videntur, quae verò odora sunt, intensiorem odorem spargunt*. Confricatione enim laxatur corporis textura, ejusque pori dilatantur, quaeque in illis est *sulphureo-mercurialis* substantia ad magnum sanè motum concitatur. Tertio: *Quamplura quae divisim sumpta minimè olent, validum, si misceantur odorem diffundunt*, Sal ammoniacus. & sal alkalinus inodórus uterque, in ipsa commistione odorem validissimum spirant. Ex mistione enim sequitur fermentatio, atque hinc subtilium illarum particularum dissolutio, & evaporatio in quibus odor consistit. Sic etiam auripigmentum, & calx viva utrumq̃ inodórum corpus in aqua permixta, & cocta tetrum atque adversum odorem spirant. Ut autem [p. 192] paucis dicamus de specifico odorum discrimine, duo tantum genera distingui possunt, suave nempè, & molestum.

606 Secondly: By rubbing and friction those hard bodies become odorous which seem inodorous; and those which are odorous breathe out a more intense smell. For by rubbing the texture of the body is loosened and its pores are dilated, and the sulphureo-mercurial substance that is in them is stirred to a truly great motion. Thirdly: Very many things which, taken separately, smell very little, give off a powerful smell if they are mixed. Sal ammoniac and alkaline salt, each of them inodorous, breathe out a most powerful smell in the very mixing. For from the mixture there follows a fermentation, and hence the dissolution and evaporation of those subtle particles in which smell consists. So also orpiment and quicklime, each an inodorous body, when mixed in water and boiled, breathe out a foul and repugnant smell. But, to say a few words [p. 192] about the specific difference of smells, only two kinds can be distinguished, namely the pleasant and the troublesome.

> 607 Suavis est odor, si odori effluvii corpuscula ita respondeant olfactus organo, ut ejus fibrae ordinatè, placidèque ab illis moveantur. Contra verò odor est *molestus*, si nerveae olfactus fibrae perturbatè ab odori effluvii corpusculis vexentur, & distorqueantur. Hinc non nisi ex diversa dispositione organi olfactus repetenda videtur ratio, cur idem odor uni gratus sit, alteri ingratus, sicuti etiam cur idem odor nobis nec placeat semper, neque semper displiceat. Dubium non est enim, quin mutatâ temperie vel texturâ nervearum fibrarum olfactus, fieri necessario debeat, ut ex eorumdem corpusculorum adpulsu [?] fibrae ipsae non eodem semper modo moveantur.

607 A smell is pleasant if the corpuscles of the odorous effluvium so answer to the organ of smell that its fibers are moved by them in an orderly and gentle way. On the contrary, a smell is troublesome if the nervous fibers of smell are harassed and twisted in a perturbed way by the corpuscles of the odorous effluvium. Hence the reason why the same smell is agreeable to one person and disagreeable to another, as also why the same smell neither always pleases us nor always displeases us, seems to be sought only in the different disposition of the organ of smell. For there is no doubt that, when the temper or texture of the nervous fibers of smell is changed, it must necessarily come about that the fibers themselves are not always moved in the same way by the impact of the same corpuscles.

> 608 Sed *dices* contra nostram conclusionem: si odor consistit in profluvio substantiali, &c., pondus corporis longa odoris emissione continuè minueretur; sed hoc experientiae adversatur: ergo. Nego min.: quia ipsa teste experientiâ pondus odori corporis camphorae ex. gr. sensibiliter etiam decrescit ut observavimus cum Clariss. Boyle [§. 185.]. Neque decrescere potest pondus odori corporis odorae evaporationis causâ, nisi corporis materia hanc ob causam minuatur, ac proinde nisi odor corporis in substantiali illius effluvio consistat. Ceterùm posse odorem, quem corpus spargit in effluvio consistere, quin ipsius pondus sensibiliter decrescat, inficias ibit nemo, cui perspecta fuerit subtilitas illorum corpusculorum ex quibus sensibilia quaeque corpora primo consurgunt. Plurima hac de re à nobis dicta sunt §§. 158. & seqq. & §. 185.

608 But you will say against our conclusion: if smell consists in a substantial outflow, etc., the weight of a body would be continually diminished by a long emission of smell; but this is contrary to experience: therefore. I deny the min.: because, as experience itself testifies, the weight of an odorous body, of camphor for example, does decrease even sensibly, as we have observed with the most distinguished Boyle [§. 185.]. Nor can the weight of an odorous body decrease on account of the odorous evaporation unless the matter of the body is diminished for this cause, and consequently unless the smell of the body consists in a substantial effluvium of it. For the rest, no one will deny that the smell which a body spreads can consist in an effluvium without its weight decreasing sensibly, if he has clearly seen the subtlety of those corpuscles from which all sensible bodies first arise. Very many things on this matter have been said by us in §§. 158 ff. and §. 185.

## CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

> ¿In quonam consistat sapor corporum?

In what does the taste of bodies consist?

> 609 *Observatio prima*. Ea corpora sapida sunt, quae sale abundant, & quo majorem salis copiam continent, eò sunt sapidiora. Contra verò planè insipida sunt illa quae nihil planè, aut ferme nihil salinae substantiae complectuntur. Comprobare id vel ex eo licet, quod sapidum nihil sit, ex quo extrahere sal non detur, quod extracto sale non reddatur insipidum, nihil itidem insipidum, quod commixto sale sapidum non fiat. *Observatio secunda*: nullius solidi corporis sapor percipitur, nisi corpus ipsum dentibus conteratur, & salivae beneficio dissolvatur. Hinc insipida planè sunt, quae dentibus conteri nequeunt, & saliva dissolvi, ut metalla, lapides, &c. [p. 193] *Observatio tertia*: solidorum corporum etsi sapida ea sint, nullus planè sapor percipitur, si lingua vel nimis arida fuerit, vel nimio humore túrgida. *Observatio quarta*: sapida corpora calore fiunt sapidiora, contra verò insipida planè evadunt, si nimiè frigescant. Quae frigidissima sunt, inquit Doctiss. Boerhaavius, ea non gustantur, neque gustus ullus superest, quando lingua exquisitè friget. His positis.

bservation first. Those bodies are savory which abound in salt, and the 609 O greater the quantity of salt they contain, the more savory they are. On the contrary, those are altogether insipid which contain nothing at all, or almost nothing, of saline substance. This can be confirmed even from the fact that there is nothing savory from which salt cannot be extracted and which, once the salt is extracted, is not rendered insipid; likewise nothing insipid which does not become savory when salt is mixed in. Observation second. The taste of no solid body is perceived unless the body itself is ground by the teeth and dissolved by the help of the saliva. Hence those things are altogether insipid which the teeth cannot grind and the saliva cannot dissolve, such as metals, stones, etc. Observation [p. 193] third: although solid bodies are savory, no taste at all is perceived if the tongue is either too dry or swollen with too much moisture. Observation fourth: savory bodies become more savory with heat, but on the contrary become altogether insipid if they grow excessively cold. Things that are very cold, says the most learned Boerhaave, are not tasted, nor does any taste remain when the tongue is exquisitely cold. These things being laid down,

> 610 Dico: Sapores in actu primo, & prout in corpore existunt consistunt primariò in salinis sapidi corporis particulis certâ magnitudine ac figurâ adfectis, quae â saliva dissolvi, cuticulam gustatus organum vestientem pervádere, nerveàs papillas sub ea protuberantes agitare varia ratione, vellicare, stringere, compungere, aut demulcere pro varia modificatione possint. Prob. per partes. Prima, ex *observatione prima*: nam si corporum sapor â salinis particulis non oriretur, neque insipida ea essent corpora quae sale destituta sunt, neque illa essent sapida quae sale abundant. Dixi *primario* consistere sapores in salinis particulis. Dubium enim non est, quin etiam sulphurea substantia ad sapores plurimum conferat, experientiâ demonstrante salinarum particularum vim non parùm â sulphure minui: proinde ab illo effici, ut gustus organum non eodem semper modo â salinis corpusculis immutetur

610 I say: Tastes in first act, and as they exist in the body, consist primarily in saline particles of the savory body, affected with a certain size and figure, which, dissolved by the saliva, can pervade the cuticle that clothes the organ of taste and agitate in various ways the nervous papillae protruding beneath it, and pluck, squeeze, prick or soothe them according to their various modification. Prob. by parts. The first, from observation first: for if the taste of bodies did not arise from saline particles, neither would those bodies be insipid which are destitute of salt, nor would those be savory which abound in salt. I said that tastes consist primarily in particles of salt. For there is no doubt that a sulphureous substance too contributes very much to tastes, since experience demonstrates that the force of the saline particles is diminished not a little by sulphur: hence it is brought about by it that the organ of taste is not always changed in the same way by the saline corpuscles.

> 611 Quod autem certam magnitudinem, ac figuram habere debeant. Prob. Etenim non nisi ratione magnitudinis, & figurae quibus donata sunt, linguae pórulos subire possunt illa corpuscula, easque nervorum fibras vellicare, quae gustatus organum immediatè constituunt. Mechanici siquidem effectus non nisi mechanicam esse causam, manifestum est; constat autem salina corpuscula ab eo habere formaliter, ut sint sapida, â quo habent formaliter, ut nerveas gustatus fibras titillare possint: ergo. Quod autem sint hujusmodi ut salivâ dissolvi possint constat ex *observatione secunda*. Saporum varietates gemino hoc carmine comprehenduntur.

611 But that they must have a certain size and figure, Prob. For only by reason of the size and figure with which they are endowed can those corpuscles enter the little pores of the tongue and pluck those fibers of the nerves which immediately constitute the organ of taste. It is manifest indeed that a mechanical effect has only a mechanical cause; but it is established that the saline corpuscles have formally that they are savory from that from which they have formally that they can tickle the nervous fibers of taste: therefore. But that they are of such a kind as to be able to be dissolved by the saliva is established from observation second. The varieties of tastes are comprised in this pair of lines:

> Sunt *Salsus*, *Pinguis*; *Dulcisque*, *Acidusque* sapores:

The tastes are Salty, Fatty, Sweet and Acid;

> *Acer*, & *Insipidus*, *Austerus*, *Acerbus*, *Amarus*.

Sharp, and Insipid, Austere, Harsh, Bitter.

> Aliqui volunt, Insipidum propriè non esse saporem, sed saporis negationem.

Some hold that Insipid is not properly a taste, but the negation of taste.

> 612 Confirmatur conclusio: in nostra sententia ratio redditur eorum quae de saporibus in limine observavimus. Primo: Sapor consistentis corporis non percipitur, nisi corpus ipsum conteratur dentibus, & saliva dissolvatur. Salinae siquidem cujus [?] corporis particulae immutare non possunt gustus organum, nisi ab iis, quibus in ipso corpore permixtae sunt sejunctae fuerint, atque ita saliva dissolutae, ut linguae poros subire queant. Secundo: nullius solidi corporis sentitur sapor, si lingua nimis arida fuerit, vel nimio humore turgida. Humore siquidem deficiente deest menstruum, quo salina corporis [p. 194] substantia dissolvatur, & ad gustus organum deducatur. Nimius verò humor minuit rationem corporis soluti ad vehiculum solvens, ideoque parva, aut propè nulla fit organi sensorii immutatio. Praeterea si nerveae linguae papillae nimio humore turgescant ineptae sunt, ut ex salinarum particularum adpulsu motum concipiant, atque hinc, ut gustus sensatio in nobis excitetur.

612 The conclusion is confirmed: on our opinion a reason is given for those things which we observed about tastes at the threshold. First: the taste of a consistent body is not perceived unless the body itself is ground by the teeth and dissolved by the saliva. For the saline particles of a body cannot change the organ of taste unless they are separated from those with which they are mixed in the body itself, and are so dissolved by the saliva that they can enter the pores of the tongue. Secondly: the taste of no solid body is felt if the tongue is too dry or swollen with too much moisture. For when moisture is lacking, the menstruum is wanting by which the saline substance of the body [p. 194] may be dissolved and conducted to the organ of taste. But excessive moisture diminishes the ratio of the dissolved body to the dissolving vehicle, and therefore little or almost no change of the sense organ takes place. Moreover, if the nervous papillae of the tongue swell with excessive moisture, they are unfit to take on motion from the impact of the saline particles, and hence for the sensation of taste to be excited in us.

> 613 Redditur etiam ratio *observationis quartae*. Calor enim efficit ut non solum dissolvantur particulae salinae, verùm etiam ut fortiùs irruant in gustus sensorium, idque validiùs moveant. Contra verò frigus non solum prohibet dissolutionem salinarum particularum, verùm etiam motum earum, quae solutae sunt, retardat, & etiam sistit, constrictisque linguae porulis, impedit insupèr, ne illae porulos ipsos subeant, nerveasque gustatus fibras premant, & vellicent. Advertendum est in fine, quod sapor agit pro ratione variae dispositionis organi. Proindè quia non omnium eadem est temperies hominum, nec eadem in omnibus nervearum fibrillarum textura, idem sapor neque omnibus grátus est, neque omnibus molestus. Similiter ob mutatam organi dispositionem fit, ut sapor, qui gratus nobis antea fuerat, non amplius placeat. Undè obtinuit hispanica pároemia: *sobre gustos no hai disputas*.

613 A reason is also given for observation fourth. For heat brings it about not only that the saline particles are dissolved, but also that they rush more strongly into the sensorium of taste and move it more powerfully. On the contrary, cold not only prevents the dissolution of the saline particles, but also retards and even stops the motion of those which have been dissolved, and, by constricting the little pores of the tongue, prevents them moreover from entering those very pores and pressing and plucking the nervous fibers of taste. It is to be noted at the end that taste acts according to the various disposition of the organ. Hence, because not all men have the same temperament, nor is the texture of the nervous fibrils the same in all, the same taste is neither agreeable to all nor troublesome to all. Similarly, because of a changed disposition of the organ, it happens that a taste which had been agreeable to us before pleases no longer. Whence the Spanish proverb has gained currency: sobre gustos no hai disputas [there is no disputing about tastes].

## CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

> De Sono, & ejus praecipuis adfectionibus.

On Sound, and its principal affections.

> 614 Qui clarè soni naturam explicare cupiunt, sonum alium in corpore sonóro, alium in medio per quod transmittitur considerant. Priorem *sonum primitivum*, secundum *derivativum* adpellant. *Centrum soni* dicitur illud punctum, ex quo sonus diffunditur, atque ad aures pérvenit. *Sonus directus* est ille qui â corpore sonoro rectâ fertur ad auditum. *Sonus reflexus*, vocatur ille, qui ab obstaculo, in quod incurrit, regéritur, atque ex illo ad aures pérvenit. Certum est, ea tantùm corpora sonora esse, quae tremorem concipiunt, si percutiantur. Motus hicce tremulus extra omne dubium est in chordis, ex quibus agitatione tremula, sonus elicitur. In campanis majoribus, & in multis aliis corporibus motus hicce tremulus admodùm sensibilis est. Sublato aëre nullum percipi sonum, tametsi corpus sonorum validis percusionibus urgeatur, dictum jam â nobis est in Logica (§. 107). His constitutis.

hose who wish to explain clearly the nature of sound consider one sound 614 Tin the sonorous body, another in the medium through which it is transmitted. The former they call primitive sound, the latter derivative. The center of sound is said to be that point from which the sound is diffused and reaches the ears. Direct sound is that which is carried straight from the sonorous body to the hearing. Reflected sound is called that which is thrown back from an obstacle into which it runs, and from it reaches the ears. It is certain that only those bodies are sonorous which take on a tremor if they are struck. This tremulous motion is beyond all doubt in strings, from which sound is drawn out by a tremulous agitation. In larger bells, and in many other bodies, this tremulous motion is quite sensible. That when the air is removed no sound is perceived, although the sonorous body be plied with strong blows, has already been said by us in the Logic (§. 107). These things being established,

> 615 Dico: Sonus prout spectatur in corpore sonóro, sive *primitivus*, consistit in motu tremulo minimarum corporis sonori [p. 195] partium: ut autem est in medio, per quod transmittitur, adeòque sonus *derivativus*, potissimum in tremulo aëris motu, qui â tremóre & fremitu corporum sonantium oritur, & ad auditus usque organum propagatur, positus est. Pars prima demonstratur. Ea tantùm corpora sonora sunt, quae percussa, aut vibrata tremorem concipiunt, atque adeò quae partibus elasticis atque aptis ad celerrimas vibrationes peragendas constant; sed eo ipso sonus primitivus consistit in motu tremulo minimarum corporis sonori partium: ergo. Major constat, si quidem experimentis compertum habemus, ea corpora quae sunt magis elastica, adeòque ad motum tremulum aptiora, etiam esse magis sonóra. Sic quia stannum praeplumbo riget, argentum magis quàm aurum, chalybs prae ferro, iccircò alterum altero magis est sonorum; & nimiùm flexilibus partibus constantia corpora, sono destituta esse, vulgò notum est. Adhaec: novimus campanas solo contactu manûs, dum sonant admotae, sonum reddere diminutum, quia motus trémulus aliquo ex parte impeditur.

615 I say: Sound as it is regarded in the sonorous body, or primitive, consists in a tremulous motion of the smallest parts of the sonorous body; [p. 195] but as it is in the medium through which it is transmitted, and hence derivative sound, it is placed chiefly in a tremulous motion of the air, which arises from the tremor and quivering of sounding bodies and is propagated all the way to the organ of hearing. The first part is demonstrated. Only those bodies are sonorous which, when struck or vibrated, take on a tremor, and hence which consist of elastic parts fit for performing very swift vibrations; but by that very fact primitive sound consists in a tremulous motion of the smallest parts of the sonorous body: therefore. The major is established, since we have found by experiments that those bodies which are more elastic, and hence fitter for tremulous motion, are also more sonorous. Thus, because tin is stiffer than lead, silver more than gold, steel than iron, for that reason the one is more sonorous than the other; and it is commonly known that bodies consisting of excessively flexible parts are destitute of sound. Moreover: we know that bells, by the mere contact of a hand applied while they are sounding, give back a diminished sound, because the tremulous motion is in some part impeded.

> 616 Prob. altera pars: scilicet corpora non esse sonora per tremorem, seu vibrationes totales, sed particulares, id est, per motum tremulum exiguarum partium, id quód detexerunt Viri Cl. Perrault [^195-s1] Carrè [^195-s2] & de La Hire [^195-s3], quum antea corpora per vibratione totales sonora esse putarentur. Res vulgaribus experimentis comprobata est. Duo tantùm adhibeam. Si fides musica plectro sebo uncto vehementiùs percutiatur, tametsi vibrationes totales futurae sint, sonum non edit, plectrum verò pice vel resina asperum si per eamdem ducatur, sonus clarè percipitur; sed hujus reddi ália ratio nequit, quàm quod plectrum resinâ obductum exasperetur, & denticulos velut obtineat, quibus minimas partes chordae cónfricet, & ágitet, quas perstringere non potest plectrum sebo lúbricum: ergo. Secundo: Forcipis focariae flexilis, elasticae si extrema digitis compressa repentè dimittantur, aut nullus auditur sonus, aut modicus, etsi elasticitate sua in motum vibratorium concitentur forcipis brachia, clarum tamen sonant, si corpore duro percutiantur: ergo exiguarum partium motus tremulus sonum efficit primitivum.

616 The second part is proved: namely, that bodies are not sonorous through a tremor, or vibrations, that are total, but through particular ones, that is, through a tremulous motion of small parts; which the distinguished men Perrault (u), Carré (x) and de La Hire (y) discovered, whereas formerly bodies were thought to be sonorous through total vibrations. The thing is proved by common experiments. I shall use only two. If a musical string is struck rather vehemently with a bow greased with tallow, even though total vibrations are bound to occur, it gives no sound; but if a bow made rough with pitch or resin is drawn over the same string, a sound is clearly perceived: but no other reason can be given for this than that the bow coated with resin is roughened and as it were obtains little teeth, with which it rubs and agitates the smallest parts of the string, which the bow made slippery with tallow cannot graze: therefore. Secondly: if the ends of a pair of flexible, elastic fire tongs, pressed together by the fingers, are suddenly released, either no sound is heard or a moderate one, although the arms of the tongs are set into a vibratory motion by their elasticity; yet they sound clearly if they are struck with a hard body: therefore the tremulous motion of small parts produces primitive sound.

> [^195-s1]: Essai de Physique.

[^195-s1]: Essai de Physique.

> [^195-s2]: Memoir de l' Academ. 1709 [?].

[^195-s2]: Mémoires de l’Académie, 1709.

> [^195-s3]: Memoir de l' Academ. 1716.

[^195-s3]: Mémoires de l’Académie, 1716.

> 617 Prob. 3. pars: per motum derivativum intelligimus id quod aptum est ad percellendum organum auditus: sed talis est motus tremulus medii, potissimùm autem aërearum particularum: ergo. Major constat: quum enim soni sensatio in nobis non fiat, nisi auditus organum á corpore sonante immutetur, immutari autèm immediatè ab eo nequeat, quum ab illo immediatè non tangatur, iccircò immutari debet per interjectum medium. Medium verò [p. 196] hoc esse in primis aërem, patet primò ex natura ejus, qui quoniam insigni est elasticitate praeditus aptitudine gaudet, ut ejus particulae corpori sonoro proximae â vibratis hujus partibus exiguis repellantur, hae alias, & alias remotiores urgeant, dum tandem impressio fiat in ipsum organum ac sonus percipiatur; deinde liquet id ipsum ex eo, quod nullus sonus sublato aëre percipiatur: ergo sonus derivativus, &c.

617 The 3rd part is proved: by derivative motion we understand that which is apt to strike the organ of hearing: but such is the tremulous motion of the medium, and chiefly of the aerial particles: therefore. The major is established: for since the sensation of sound does not arise in us unless the organ of hearing is changed by the sounding body, and it cannot be changed by it immediately, since it is not immediately touched by it, for that reason it must be changed through an interposed medium. But that this medium [p. 196] is above all the air is plain, first, from its nature: for since it is endowed with a notable elasticity, it has the aptitude that its particles nearest the sonorous body are repelled by the small vibrated parts of that body, and these urge others, and still others more remote, until at length an impression is made on the organ itself and the sound is perceived; next, the same is clear from the fact that no sound is perceived when the air is removed: therefore derivative sound, etc.

> 618 Diximus sonum derivativum in motu tremulo aërearum *potissimum* particularum positum esse: aërem enim non esse unicum medium per quod sonus transferatur experimenta plurima â D. Nollet [^196-s1], aliisque capta, planè evincunt. Sic aqua aptum satis videtur corpus ad motum tremulum concipiendum, experientiâ testante pisces campanae sonitu saepe saepius in piscinis ad escam paratam convocari.

618 We have said that derivative sound is placed in the tremulous motion chiefly of aerial particles: for that air is not the only medium through which sound is transferred, very many experiments made by Mr. Nollet (z) and others clearly prove. Thus water seems a body quite fit for taking on a tremulous motion, since experience testifies that fish in fishponds are very often called together by the sound of a bell to food prepared for them.

> [^196-s1]: Leçons de Physique Tom. 3. Leç. 11. Exp. 4.

[^196-s1]: Leçons de Physique, vol. 3, lesson 11, exp. 4.

> 619 Naturâ soni perspectâ, adfectiones principes, quoad licet expendamus. *Celeritas* soni, *diffusio* illius determinato tempore per certum spatium, inter adfectiones praecipuas meritò referuntur. Hanc Eruditi diversi studiosè observare conati sunt, ut videre est apud Muschembroekium [^196-s2] Tandèm juxta celebriores observationes, 180 perticarum Gallicarum, intervallo unius minuti secundi constituta fuit; quia tamen de hoc ipso producto adhùc controversia erat, iccircò ab Academia Regia Scientiarum Parisina, rei hujus exactior inquisitio commissa fuit ann. 1738. Viris Clariss. De *Tury*, *Maraldi*, & *de la Caille*. Hi itaque lineam pro suis operationibus delegeruut 14636 perticas, sive hexapedas longam, expertique sunt primò.

619 The nature of sound having been examined, let us weigh its principal affections, as far as we may. The celerity of sound, or its diffusion through a certain space in a determinate time, is rightly reckoned among its principal affections. Various learned men have tried to observe it carefully, as can be seen in Musschenbroek (a). At length, according to the more celebrated observations, it was fixed at 180 French perches in the interval of one second; but because there was still controversy about this very result, a more exact inquiry into this matter was for that reason entrusted by the Royal Academy of Sciences of Paris, in the year 1738, to the most distinguished men de Thury, Maraldi and de La Caille. These, then, chose for their operations a line 14636 perches, or toises, long, and found, first:

> [^196-s2]: Comment. Acad. del Cimento P. 3. p. 113.

[^196-s2]: Comment. Acad. del Cimento, pt. 3, p. 113.

> 620 *Sonum* spatio 1 minut. 2di, tam interdiù, quàm noctu, pluvio aeque, ac sereno tempore conficere 173 perticas sive Hexapedas, ut alibi diximus. 2: quod ventus secundum eadem lineam, quam sonus percurrit, spirans, vel retardet, vel acceleret eum pro ratione suae celeritatis, hoc est; ventus adversus retardat, secundus promovet sonum. 3: celeritatem soni ea semper lege comparatam esse, ut is aequalibus temporibus, aequalia spatia percurrat. 4: quod intensio soni, sive ejus vis nihil de celeritate mutet; ut enim vehementior sonus longius diffundatur, quàm debilior; iste tamèn per 1 minut. 2dum perindè, atque alter 173 perticas percurrit. [^196-s3]

620 That sound, in the space of 1 second, both by day and by night, in rainy as in clear weather, covers 173 perches or toises, as we have said elsewhere. 2: that a wind blowing along the same line which the sound runs through either retards or accelerates it in proportion to its own celerity, that is: a contrary wind retards the sound, a following wind furthers it. 3: that the celerity of sound is always constituted by such a law that it runs through equal spaces in equal times. 4: that the intensity of sound, or its force, changes nothing in its celerity; for although a more vehement sound is diffused farther than a weaker one, the latter nevertheless runs through 173 perches in 1 second just as the other does (b).

> [^196-s3]: Memoir. de l' Acadm. 1738.

[^196-s3]: Mémoires de l’Académie, 1738.

> 621 Cujus ratio haec esse videtur, quod quum impressio ex. gr. á tormento bellico validior sit, proximae aëreae particulae ob majorem vim ad vicinas magis accedendo, majus quidem conficiunt spatium, adtamen ut se suis locis iterum restituant, necesse sit, tantundèm spatii habeant rursum: at aëris particulae á sclopo pugillari minus impulsae, sicut minus spatium ob vim minorem progrediendo faciunt, ita regrediendo minus percurrunt. Ex his jam sequitur.

621 The reason of which seems to be this: that since the impression, e.g., from a cannon, is stronger, the nearest aerial particles, by approaching the neighboring ones more on account of the greater force, do indeed cover a greater space; yet in order to restore themselves to their places again, they must have just as much space once more: but the particles of air less impelled by a pistol, just as they make less space in going forward on account of the smaller force, so in going back they run through less. From these things it now follows:

[p. 197]

> 622 Celeritatis aequabilis, quâ sonus fertur, perutilem cognitionem esse ad distantias locorum definiendas, ubi operationes Geometricae adhiberi nequeunt, videlicèt: ad mensuranda freta marium, ostia fluminum, distantiam fossae obsidionariae â propugnaculo &c. Nempè si inter tormenti, vel sclopi exonerationem, & sonum auditum numerentur minuta secunda; quum singula respondeant distantiae 173 perticarum, atque hae per numerum minutorum secundorum multiplicentur, habebitur distantia loci (intelligendo distantiam in linea recta, secundum quam sonus diffunditur) in quo tormentum exoneratum est; ita si 10 minut. 2d. elabantur inter visum ignem, & sonum perceptum: distantia erit 1730 perticarum. Ad haec, dimetiri etiam licebit venti celeritatem; quum enim ventus secundus promoveat sonum, si â celeritate per ventum adaucta 173 perticas, singulis minutis secundis respondentes subtraxeris, residuum celeritatem venti exhibebit.

622 The knowledge of the uniform celerity with which sound is carried is very useful for determining the distances of places where geometrical operations cannot be applied: namely, for measuring straits of the seas, mouths of rivers, the distance of a siege trench from a bulwark, etc. That is, if between the discharge of a cannon or of a musket and the hearing of the sound the seconds are counted, then, since each corresponds to a distance of 173 perches, and these are multiplied by the number of seconds, the distance of the place in which the cannon was discharged will be had (understanding the distance along the straight line along which the sound is diffused); thus, if 10 seconds elapse between the fire seen and the sound perceived, the distance will be 1730 perches. Moreover, it will also be possible to measure the celerity of the wind; for since a following wind furthers the sound, if from the celerity increased by the wind you subtract the 173 perches corresponding to each second, the remainder will show the celerity of the wind.

> 623 *Reflexio* est singularis soni adfectio. Nempè sonus non secùs, ac motus alius, directionem suam, ubi in obstaculum impingit, mutat, & juxta motus legem generalem sic reflectitur ut angulus reflexionis aequalis sit angulo incidentiae. Nihil autem admirabilius in soni reflexione est quàm *resonantia*, quae *Echo* dicitur, tumque habetur, quum aër variè agitatus á corpore sonante, in oppositum corpus incidens eádem prorsùs modificatione regeritur, ut auribus eundem ferè sonum exhibeat haec repercussio, quàm directi radii sonori efficiunt. Verùm non omnis sonus reflexus, & ab obice in aurem remissus id praestat, ut *Echo* sistatur: certae scilicèt, conditiones adsint necesse est.

623 Reflection is a singular affection of sound. That is, sound, no otherwise than any other motion, changes its direction when it strikes an obstacle, and according to the general law of motion is so reflected that the angle of reflection is equal to the angle of incidence. But nothing is more admirable in the reflection of sound than the resonance which is called Echo, and which takes place when the air, variously agitated by the sounding body and falling on an opposite body, is thrown back with exactly the same modification, so that this repercussion presents to the ears almost the same sound as the direct sonorous rays produce. But not every reflected sound, sent back from an obstacle into the ear, brings it about that an Echo is formed: certain conditions, namely, must be present.

> 624 Ac primo quidem exposcitur, ut ea sit distantia audientis ab obstaculo, ex quo sonus redit, ut antecedenter ab sono directo auditus organum perfectè immutetur, priusquàm sonus reflexus ad illud perveniat: cujus quidem ratio est, quia si non sit discretum tempus, quod inter adpulsum soni directi, & soni reflexi intercedit, una tantum motio, & immutatio organi excitabitur ab utroque sono, vel certè consequens, priorem tanta festinatione excipiet, ut discriminari minimè possint, adeòque etiam unus tantùm â nobis percipietur sonus, facit tamen haec coincidentia soni directi, & soni reflexi, ut melius corpus sonans exaudiatur.

624 And first, indeed, it is required that the distance of the hearer from the obstacle from which the sound returns be such that the organ of hearing is perfectly changed beforehand by the direct sound before the reflected sound reaches it: the reason of which is that, if the time which intervenes between the impact of the direct sound and that of the reflected sound is not distinct, only one motion and change of the organ will be excited by both sounds, or at least the subsequent one will follow the prior with such haste that they can by no means be discriminated; and hence also only one sound will be perceived by us. This coincidence of the direct sound and the reflected sound nevertheless makes the sounding body heard better.

> 625 Requiritur secundo: non solum reflexio vocis, & sonantis corporis ex debita distantia, sed etiam ut sit reflexio ejusmodi, vi cujus vox resiliat, ex quibusdam quasi concameratis meatibus, anfractibus, & cavernosis antris, ita, ut vibrationes sonorae per ejusmodi obstacula collectae, perveniant ad aurem, postquàm priores, quae aërem primo commoverant, jam cessarint: cujus iterùm ratio est, quia si qualiscumque & omnis omninò reflexio sufficeret ad hanc resonantiam, *Echo* semper existeret; at experientiâ constat, tunc solum fieri repercusionem, quum vox directa fertur in obices variis meatibus, ductibus, & anfractibus horridos. Memorabilis est [p. 198] *Echo* Villae Simonettae propè Mediolanum, ubi vox è fenestra in oppositum parallelè murum, passibus 33. distantem emissa, quater, & vigesies, imò etiam trigesies repetitur. Haec adnotare placuit ex P Klaus. Celebria per orbem terrarum de *Echo* exempla referunt P. Kirker [^198-s1], Sturmius [^198-s2], aliique.

625 It is required, secondly, not only that there be a reflection of the voice and of the sounding body from a due distance, but also that the reflection be of such a kind that by its force the voice leaps back from certain as it were vaulted passages, windings and cavernous grottoes, so that the sonorous vibrations, collected through obstacles of this kind, reach the ear after the prior ones, which first set the air in motion, have already ceased: the reason of which again is that, if any reflection whatsoever, and every one at all, sufficed for this resonance, an Echo would always exist; but it is established by experience that a repercussion occurs only when the direct voice is carried into obstacles bristling with various passages, ducts and windings. Memorable is the [p. 198] Echo of the Villa Simonetta near Milan, where a voice sent from a window against the opposite parallel wall, 33 paces distant, is repeated twenty-four times, nay even thirty times. It has pleased me to note these things from Fr. Klaus. Celebrated examples of Echo throughout the world are reported by Fr. Kircher (c), Sturm (d) and others.

> [^198-s1]: In Phonurgia.

[^198-s1]: In the Phonurgia.

> [^198-s2]: Phys. Elect. tom. 1. p. 659. & seqq.

[^198-s2]: Phys. Elect., vol. 1, p. 659 ff.

> Solvuntur argumenta.

THE ARGUMENTS ARE ANSWERED.

> 626 Opp. 1: Tubae sonus ex plusquam centum passibus auditur; quum tamen aëris motus â tuba commoti vix ex duobus passibus percipiatur: ergo sonus eò usque diffunditur, quo usque motus aëris pervenire non potest. Respondeo negando conseq. & dico: insonante tuba, aëris tremorem ad eandem distantiam pervenire ad quam ejusdem sonus extenditur: hic autem aëris motus quum tremulus tantùm sit, & ex minutissimis vibrationibus componatur, sensui tactus est omninò imperceptibilis, neque enim ad eum immutandum ob ejus tenuitatem sufficit, percipitur tamen ab auditus sensorio, ob exquisitam ad idque proportionatam texturam, quam habet, ratione cujus â tam tenuibus percusionibus adficitur.

626 Obj. 1: The sound of a trumpet is heard from more than a hundred paces, although the motion of the air stirred by the trumpet is scarcely perceived from two paces: therefore sound is diffused as far as the motion of the air cannot reach. I reply by denying the conseq., and I say: when a trumpet sounds, the tremor of the air reaches the same distance to which its sound extends; but this motion of the air, since it is only tremulous and composed of very minute vibrations, is altogether imperceptible to the sense of touch, for on account of its tenuity it does not suffice to change that sense; it is perceived, however, by the sensorium of hearing, on account of the exquisite texture, proportioned to this, which it has, by reason of which it is affected by such slight percussions.

> 627 Quod autèm aëris tremor ad eandem distantiam excurrat, ad quam pérvenit sonus, experientiâ patet; quum enim tormentum bellicum exploditur, fenestrae praesertim vitreae, etiam mille, aut bis mille passus distantes, tremunt, nec antè tremunt, quàm explosionis sonus audiatur; quumque talis tremor, nonnisi ab aëre impellente possit provenire, perspicuum fit, aëris tremorem esse â sono inséparabilem & ad eandem distantiam cum ipso pervenire.

627 But that the tremor of the air runs out to the same distance which the sound reaches is plain from experience; for when a cannon is fired, windows, especially glass ones, even a thousand or two thousand paces distant, tremble, and they do not tremble before the sound of the explosion is heard; and since such a tremor can only come from air impelling them, it becomes evident that the tremor of the air is inseparable from sound and reaches the same distance with it.

> 628 Opp. 2: Si intra ampullam vitream hermeticè sigillatàm tintinnabulum aliquo artificio pulsetur, sonus percipitur; sed hoc néquaquam ita eveniret, si sonus in aëris motu vibratorio consisteret: nam aër intra ampullam inclusus, vitrum pertransire nequit ut aërem externum ad aurem usque impellat: ergo. Respondeo: quod quoties sonus aliquis excitatur, non modò aërem, verùm & cetera corpora motu quodam trémulo cieri: frequenter enim experímur sonantibus crassioribus chordis instrumenti musici, ac canentibus majoribus orgáni pneumatici fistulis, ábacos, sedilia, imò & solum ipsum, cui dicta instrumenta insistunt, trémere. Quid ergo mirum si in casu objectionis, vibrante aëre in ampulla incluso vitrum ipsum simili tremore concitetur, quod experientia testatur: nam si ampulla manu stringatur, quasi surdus, & valde obtusus sonus auditur eò scilicet, quod vitri vibrationes ab adplicata manu ex parte prohibeantur.

628 Obj. 2: If, inside a glass phial hermetically sealed, a little bell is struck by some artifice, the sound is perceived; but this would by no means happen if sound consisted in a vibratory motion of the air: for the air enclosed within the phial cannot pass through the glass so as to drive the external air all the way to the ear: therefore. I reply that whenever any sound is excited, not only the air but also the other bodies are stirred with a certain tremulous motion: for we frequently experience that, when the thicker strings of a musical instrument sound and the larger pipes of a pneumatic organ sing, the tables, the seats, nay even the very floor on which the said instruments stand, tremble. What wonder, then, if, in the case of the objection, when the air enclosed in the phial vibrates, the glass itself is stirred with a similar tremor, as experience testifies? For if the phial is gripped by the hand, a deaf, as it were, and very dull sound is heard, namely because the vibrations of the glass are in part prevented by the applied hand.

> 629 Opp. 3: Si vera esset nostra opinio, non possémus simul, & [p. 199] eodem tempore diversos sonos percipere, ut vocum, campanarum &c sed hoc est contra experientiam: ergo. Prob. maj.: Nam aër nequit eodem tempore simul diversis motibus concitari, idemque dicendum de auriculari tympano. Respondeo negando propositionem: Nam motus aëris tremulus suis etiam constat mótulis, undè alternantibus percusionibus diversorum corporum, eidem organo communicatis, potest ipsum diversis motibus eodem sensibili tempore cieri, quod idem dicendum est de tympano auris, & consequenter possunt diversi soni eodem tempore sensibili percipi.

629 Obj. 3: If our opinion were true, we could not at once and at the same time [p. 199] time perceive different sounds, as of voices, bells, etc.; but this is contrary to experience: therefore. Proof of the major: the air cannot be set in motion at the same time by different motions together; and the same must be said of the drum of the ear. I reply by denying the proposition. For the tremulous motion of the air also consists of its own small motions; hence, when the alternating percussions of different bodies are communicated to the same organ, the air can be stirred by different motions in the same sensible time; and the same must be said of the drum of the ear, and consequently different sounds can be perceived in the same sensible time.

> 630 Exemplum habetis in stagnante aqua, cui si lapillos in diversis ejus partibus simul injiciatis, profectò videbitis totam in protuberantes undulas in circuli morem crispari, qui continuò sese dilatantes, invicem intersecantur absque ulla prorsùs perturbatione: similiter ergo in nostro casu vibrationes â diversis corporibus per sonum concitatae absque ulla perturbatione ad aurem usque excurrunt, eamque diversimodè adficiunt, quo fit ut simul diversi soni percipiantur.

630 You have an example in standing water: if you throw little stones into different parts of it at the same time, you will surely see the whole of it ruffled into swelling ripples in the manner of a circle, which, continually spreading themselves out, intersect one another without any disturbance whatever. Likewise, therefore, in our case the vibrations excited by different sounding bodies run all the way to the ear without any disturbance, and affect it in different ways, whence it comes about that different sounds are perceived at the same time.

> 631 Opp. 4. Si sonus in praefatis vibrationibus consisteret non possemus per auditum, corporis sonantis distantiam emetiri: ergo. Respondeo: quod vibrationes in aëre in modum circuli efformantur, & aër undulatim crispatur quaquaversus, in cujus circuli centro corpus sonans existit: hinc, quò plus hujusmodi vibrationes â centro recedunt, eo majores peripherias efficiunt, & consequenter minor illarum portio, seu minor arcus aërem remotiorem adficit, quàm propiorem; hinc particulae aëris ferientes pauciores sunt, simulque minus unitae, minorem ergo adfectionem imprimunt sensui, remotiùs â corpore sonante existenti, & ope hujus majoris, aut minoris adfectionis, objecti sonantis distantia percipitur.

631 Obj. 4. If sound consisted in the aforesaid vibrations, we could not measure the distance of a sounding body by hearing: therefore. I reply: since the vibrations in the air are formed in the manner of a circle, and the air is rippled in waves in every direction, at the center of which circle the sounding body stands, hence the farther vibrations of this kind recede from the center, the greater the circumferences they make, and consequently a smaller portion of them, or a smaller arc, affects the more remote air than the nearer; hence the particles of air that strike are fewer, and at the same time less united; they therefore impress a smaller affection on the sense the farther one stands from the sounding body; and by means of this greater or smaller affection the distance of the sounding object is perceived.

> 632 Opp. tandem: juxta probabiliorem sententiam: sonus gravis in tardioribus, acutus verò in velocioribus vibrationibus consistit; sed vibrationes tympani auris debent esse Isochronae, seu ejusdem durationis, ut sunt vibrationes ejusdem chordae aequè tensae: ergo semper audiretur idem sonus in ratione gravis, vel acuti, quod experientiae repugnat, praesertim quum idem corpus eadem servatâ tensione non possit modò in tardiores, modò in velociores vibrationes concitari. Resp. negando suppositum nempè, quod auris tympanum eamdem semper servet tensionem. Auriculare namque typanum id fermè muneris praestat auditui, quod lens crystallina visui.

632 Obj. finally: according to the more probable opinion, a low sound consists in slower vibrations, a high one in swifter vibrations; but the vibrations of the drum of the ear must be isochronous, or of the same duration, as are the vibrations of the same string equally stretched: therefore the same sound would always be heard as to low or high, which is contrary to experience, especially since the same body, keeping the same tension, cannot be set now into slower, now into swifter vibrations. Reply: by denying the supposition, namely that the drum of the ear always keeps the same tension. For the drum of the ear performs for hearing nearly the same office that the crystalline lens performs for sight.

> 633 Quemadmodum enim crystallina lens ita luminis radios excipit, ut vi suae convexitatis eos in basim retíneae debita distinctione projiciat, quod ut efficiat, convexitatem suam in majorem, aut minorem mutat, pro diverso radiorum illapsu, diversaque incidentia; ita & tympanum auris ita constitutum est, ut pro diverso aëris vibrantis illapsu, modò tensionem augeat, modò minuat; ita ut quemadmodum crystallina lens convexitatem auget, aut minuit [p. 200] sese explicando, aut contrahendo, operâ delicatissimi musculi, ita & tympanum auriculare suam tensionem auget, aut minuit operâ gemini musculi, quo typanum vel adducitur, vel laxatur: analogiam habetis in militari tympano, cujus membrana funiculorum operâ magis tenditur, aut làxatur.

633 For just as the crystalline lens receives the rays of light in such a way that by the force of its convexity it projects them onto the base of the retina with due distinctness, and to accomplish this changes its convexity to greater or smaller according to the different falling-in and different incidence of the rays: so also the drum of the ear is so constituted that, according to the different falling-in of the vibrating air, it now increases its tension, now diminishes it; so that, just as the crystalline lens increases or diminishes its convexity by [p. 200] or contracting itself through the action of a most delicate muscle, so also the drum of the ear increases or diminishes its tension through the action of a twin muscle, by which the drum is either drawn tight or slackened: you have an analogy in the military drum, whose membrane is stretched more or less by means of cords.

> 634 Praeterea quemadmodùm crystállina lens ad majorem, aut minorem contractionem determinatur â primâ radiorum projectione, quibus suscipiendis, & intus projiciendis confestim aptatur; ita auris tympanum ad tensionem augendam, aut minuendam á primis aëris impulsionibus determinatur, quo fit ut facillimè celerioribus, aut diuturnioribus sese adcommodet, sonorumque differentias in ratione etiam gravis, & acuti percipiat.

634 Moreover, just as the crystalline lens is determined to a greater or smaller contraction by the first projection of the rays, to receiving which and to projecting them inward it straightway adapts itself, so the drum of the ear is determined to increasing or diminishing its tension by the first impulses of the air; whence it comes about that it very easily accommodates itself to swifter or longer-lasting ones, and perceives the differences of sounds also as to low and high.

## DISSERTATIO IV. — DISSERTATION IV

> De Qualitatibus visibilibus, sive de Luce & ejus proprietatibus.

On visible Qualities, or on Light and its properties.

## CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

> Lucis tàm primitivae, quàm derivativae natura inquiritur.

The nature of light, both primitive and derivative, is inquired into.

> 635 *Corpus lucidum* dicitur illud, quod ipsâ suâ naturâ tale est, ut lumen emittat. Illud verò *illuminatum* vocatur, quod lumen, quo fulget non habet ex se, sed illud totum ab extrinseco recipit. Sic flamma ex. gr., carbones accensi & praecipuè Sol sunt corpora lucida. *Illuminata* verò ea omnia, quae praesente sole aut flammâ nobis conspicua sunt; inconspicua, luminoso aut sublato aut extincto. *Lux primitiva* est illa adfectio, per quam formaliter corpus est luminosum. Lux *derivativa* est adfectio illa quae per medium â lucido corpore diffusa, atque ad oculos usque propagata, efficit ut circumstantia corpora, alioquin inconspicua, videantur. His explicatis.

luminous body is said to be that which is such by its own nature that it 635 A emits light. That, on the other hand, is called illuminated which does not have from itself the light with which it shines, but receives it wholly from without. Thus flame, for example, burning coals, and above all the Sun are luminous bodies. Illuminated, on the other hand, are all those things which are visible to us when the sun or a flame is present, invisible when the luminous body is taken away or extinguished. Primitive light is that affection through which a body is formally luminous. Derivative light is that affection which, diffused through a medium from a luminous body and propagated all the way to the eyes, brings it about that surrounding bodies, otherwise invisible, are seen. These things explained,

> 636 Dico primo: Lux prout spectatur in corpore lucido, seu *primitiva* in concitatissimo quodam motu subtilium partium ejusdem rectè constituitur. Prob.: Lux primitiva rectè constituitur in eo, [p. 201] quod cum ipsa luce semper in corpore conjunctum est, & â quo lux sic dependet, ut illo posito in corporibus, ipsa illicò in iis habeatur, eaque lucida efficiantur, quo contra sublato, lux statim pereat; sed cum luce semper conjunctus est subtilium corporis partium concitatissimus motus, sic ut nullum sit corpus lucidum, in quo motus ejusmodi non deprehendatur, & quàmprimum subtiliores corporum partes in motum concitatum aguntur, lux ab eis emittitur, ea verò extinguitur simul ac partes agitatae ad quietem rediguntur: ergo Lux primitiva in concitatissimo quodam motu subtilium corporis partium consistit. Minor per partes apertissimè demonstratur.

636 I say first: light as it is regarded in a luminous body, or primitive light, is rightly made to consist in a certain most agitated motion of the subtle parts of that body. Proof: primitive light is rightly made to consist in that [p. 201] which is always joined with light itself in a body, and on which light so depends that, when it is posited in bodies, light is at once had in them and they are made luminous, whereas when it is taken away light straightway perishes; but always joined with light is a most agitated motion of the subtle parts of the body, so that there is no luminous body in which a motion of this kind is not detected; and as soon as the subtler parts of bodies are driven into agitated motion, light is emitted by them, but it is extinguished as soon as the agitated parts are brought back to rest: therefore primitive light consists in a certain most agitated motion of the subtle parts of a body. The minor is demonstrated part by part most plainly.

> 637 Et ad primam quod adtinet, scilicet, corpora omnia lucicida tali motu donari, certissimum omninò est. In flamma enim, & carbonibus accensis vehemens partium motio conspicua est, corpora item putrescentia, pisces putridi, ligna putredine corrupta, lucem emittentia intestino partium motu agitari ex alibi dictis manifestum est, quum fermentatio, & putrefactio sine partium motu & agitatione explicari nequeat. Pars quoque altera liquet, videlicèt: corpora lucem emittere, quàmprimum subtiliores particulae ad motum concitantur.

637 And as to the first part, namely that all luminous bodies are endowed with such a motion, it is altogether most certain. For in flame and in burning coals a vehement motion of the parts is visible; likewise that putrefying bodies, putrid fish, wood corrupted by rot, which emit light, are agitated by an intestine motion of the parts is manifest from what has been said elsewhere, since fermentation and putrefaction cannot be explained without motion and agitation of the parts. The other part too is clear, namely that bodies emit light as soon as their subtler particles are set in motion.

> 638 „¿An non corpora omnia, (*inquit Clariss. Newtonus* [^201-s1] quae partibus abundant terrestribus, & praesertim sulphurosis lumen emittunt; quotiescumque partes istae satis sint agitatae, sive id calore fiat, sive adtritu, sive percussu, sive putrescendo, sive motu aliquo vitali, sive alia quavis de causâ? Ut aqua marina, felis dorsum manu obliquè in loco tenebricoso affrictum, ligna, carnes, & pisces dum putrescunt, vapores ex aquis putridis, qui ignes fatui vulgò appellantur, cicindelae, & animalium quorundam oculi, motu quodam vitali, phosphorus Bononiensis radiis luminis agitatus, & certi liquores inter se permixti, quorum particulae cum impetu concurrunt, ut oleum vitrioli, á nitro pari pondere destillatum, dein dupla portione mixtum cum oleo garyophillorum, sive anisi?„

638 “Do not all bodies (says the most distinguished Newton (e)) which abound with terrestrial parts, and especially with sulphureous ones, emit light as often as those parts are sufficiently agitated, whether this be done by heat, or by friction, or by percussion, or by putrefying, or by some vital motion, or by any other cause whatever? As sea water, the back of a cat stroked obliquely with the hand in a dark place, wood, flesh and fish while they putrefy, the vapors from putrid waters which are commonly called ignes fatui, glowworms and the eyes of certain animals by a certain vital motion, the Bononian phosphorus agitated by the rays of light, and certain liquors mixed with one another whose particles come together with an impetus, as oil of vitriol distilled from an equal weight of niter, and then mixed with a double portion of oil of cloves or of aniseed?”

> [^201-s1]: Optic. quaest. 9.

[^201-s1]: Opticks, query 9.

> 639 Sed infinita sunt, quae veritatem hanc manifestam reddunt, & phaenomenorum electricorum consideratio ad evidentiam demonstrat. Postrema pars facilè admodùm ostenditur: motu nempè partium cessante, lucem á corporibus non spargi, nemo quippè ignorat, flammam extingui dum inflammatum corpus comprimitur, lucem in accensis corporibus carbonibus ex. gr. ignitoque ferro disperire, dum aquae immerguntur, quâ partium agitatio sistitur.

639 But there are countless things that make this truth manifest, and the consideration of electrical phenomena demonstrates it to evidence. The last part is shown quite easily: for no one is unaware that, when the motion of the parts ceases, light is not spread from bodies; that flame is extinguished when the inflamed body is compressed; that light in burning bodies, for example in coals and in red-hot iron, vanishes when they are plunged into water, by which the agitation of the parts is stopped.

> 640 Dico secundo: lux derivativa sive lumen est substantia subtilissima, motu celerrimo secundum rectam lineam adfecta. Prob. per partes. Et in primis lumen esse corpoream substantiam, ex eo [p. 202] redditur perspicuum, quod adfectiones corporis participet: nam primò dum ex uno in alium medium transit, refringitur. Secundo: in superficiem opacam incidens in adversam partem reflectitur. Tertio: lux propagata colligi in unum punctum ac quasi condensari potest, si concavo speculo, vel convexa lente exceptum fuerit in puncto quod *focum* vocant, in quo intensum adeò calorem producit, ut combustibilia quaeque corpora eo in loco posita post pauca minuta incendat, metalla, omniaque liquabilia fundat, dissolvat; quae liquefactioni minimè obnoxia sunt, quaeque sale abundant in vitrum mutet, ut videre est in Actis Eruditorum Lipsiae [^202-s1], ubi plurima referuntur de *concavo speculo* quod ab illius inventore D. Tschirnhause, Tschirnhausianum vocatur. [^202-s2]

640 I say second: derivative light, or lumen, is a most subtle substance, affected with a very swift motion along a straight line. Proof, part by part. And first, that light is a corporeal substance is made [p. 202] evident from this, that it shares in the affections of a body: for, first, while it passes from one medium into another, it is refracted. Second: falling upon an opaque surface, it is reflected toward the opposite side. Third: propagated light can be gathered and, as it were, condensed into one point, if it is received by a concave mirror or a convex lens, in the point which they call the focus, in which it produces a heat so intense that it sets on fire, after a few minutes, any combustible bodies placed in that spot, melts and dissolves metals and all fusible things, and turns into glass those which are least liable to liquefaction and abound in salt, as may be seen in the Acta Eruditorum of Leipzig (f), where a great many things are related of the concave mirror which, from its inventor D. Tschirnhaus, is called the Tschirnhausian. (g)

> [^202-s1]: Ad ann. 1687. Mens. Jan. pag. 53.

[^202-s1]: For the year 1687, month of January, p. 53.

> [^202-s2]: Quoniam verò radiorum collectio, atque adeò vires speculorum subsidio auctae, pendent â figura eorundem cóncava, iccircò materia quaevis speculo caustico opportuna est, modò poliri exactè queat. Hinc Wolfio teste celeber Dresdae artifex *Gaertnerus* magna specula ustoria ex ligno construxit, quae efficiendi habilitate Tschirnhausianis superaria [?] dicebantur. Quin *Zannius* [?] [*apud Wolf. Elem. Catoptr.* §. 223.] refert confectum fuisse â *Neumanno* speculum, quo metalla fluida reddebantur ex charta duriore, & stramine ei adglutinato. Adtamen complexus matériae ex qua parantur specula comparatus ea lege sit oportet, ut luminis radios regerat non vero absorbeat, ut fit in corporibus nigris. Ea de causa Cl. *Boyle*, ope speculi, quod in formam caustici ex nigro marmore confecit, lignum in *foco* adstitutum, sole etiam diutiùs in speculum illapso comburere non potuit, ut refert Muschenbroeck [*Essai de Physique* §. 975.].

[^202-s2]: But since the gathering of the rays, and hence the powers of mirrors, increased by their aid, depend on their concave figure, therefore any material whatever is suitable for a burning mirror, provided it can be polished exactly.
