Hence, on Wolff’s testimony, the celebrated Dresden craftsman Gärtner constructed great burning mirrors of wood, which were said to surpass the Tschirnhausian ones in effectiveness. Indeed Zahn [in Wolff, Elem. Catoptr. §. 223.] relates that a mirror was made by Neumann by which metals were rendered fluid, out of rather hard paper with straw glued onto it. Nevertheless, the texture of the material from which mirrors are prepared must be so constituted that it sends back the rays of light and does not absorb them, as happens in black bodies. For that reason the distinguished Boyle, by means of a mirror which he made in the form of a burning glass out of black marble, could not burn wood set in the focus, even though the sun had fallen upon the mirror for quite a long time, as Musschenbroek relates [Essai de Physique §. 975.].

> 641 Quarto organum visus perstringit lumen, illudque copia sua, aut vehementia (non secus ac nimius fragor aurem offendit) disturbat, imò laedit magnoperè, sed haec omnia manifestè arguunt substantiam corpoream, sive impenetrabilem: ergo. Et sanè ut optimè argumentatur Cl. Gassendus [^202-s3] sicuti impacta in parietem pila, ab ea resilit, quia corpus quum sit, transire per locum â corpore occupatum non potest; ita lucis radius in corpus impactus ab ipso repercutitur, quia illud suâ corpulentiâ locum occupat, nam effectuum naturalium ejusdem generis easdem esse causas regula constans est, ut diximus [§. 22.]. Deinde substantiam esse subtilissimam ex eo patescit, quod vitri poros subeat facillimè. Quid quod structura exilissimorum animalculorum luminis exilitatem demonstret? Si enim animalcula ipsa, ut diximus jam [§. 164.] tantae sint exilitatis, si tam exiguae molis sunt oculi, & eorum pupillae, quàm longè minor debet esse luminis materia, ut in oculos ac pupillam illabatur, facilèque haec organa permeet?

641 Fourth: light strikes the organ of sight, and by its abundance or vehemence (just as an excessive crash offends the ear) it disturbs it, nay hurts it greatly; but all these things manifestly prove a corporeal, or impenetrable, substance: therefore. And indeed, as the distinguished Gassendi argues very well (h), just as a ball driven against a wall rebounds from it, because, since it is a body, it cannot pass through a place occupied by a body, so a ray of light driven against a body is struck back by it, because that body occupies the place with its bulk; for it is a constant rule that natural effects of the same kind have the same causes, as we have said [§. 22.]. Next, that it is a most subtle substance is evident from this, that it enters the pores of glass most easily. What of the fact that the structure of the tiniest animalcules demonstrates the tenuity of light? For if the animalcules themselves, as we have already said [§. 164.], are of such tenuity, if their eyes and the pupils of them are of so slight a bulk, how much smaller must the matter of light be, so that it may glide into the eyes and the pupil and easily permeate these organs?

> [^202-s3]: Sect. 1. Phys. Lib. 6. cap. 2.

[^202-s3]: Sect. 1, Phys., bk. 6, ch. 2.

[p. 203]

> 642 Quod verò celerrimus sit motus illorum corpusculorum evincitur. Primò ex celerrima luminis diffusione. Secundò: demonstratur ex stupenda vi illa speculi caustici ut diximus [§. 640.]; quum enim vis hujusmodi sit ea ipsa, quâ illa corpuscula moventur, & haec oriatur ex ductu massae in celeritatem [§. 275.]; exilissima nequit esse, ut re verá est massa singulorum illorum corpusculorum, nisi ut eorum vis sit tanta, quantam esse vidimus, atque adeò celeritate maxima moveantur necesse est. Denique motum hunc rectilineum esse experimento compertum habemus, radius enim luminosus per exiguum forámen in cámeram obscuram immissus jugiter lineâ rectâ propagatur, & in punctum foraminulo juxta rectam lineam oppositum, incidit: ergo lumen est substantia subtilissima, motu celerrimo secundum rectam lineam adfecta.

642 That the motion of those corpuscles is very swift is proved, first, from the very swift diffusion of light. Second, it is demonstrated from that astonishing force of the burning mirror of which we have spoken [§. 640.]: for since a force of this kind is that very force by which those corpuscles are moved, and this arises from the product of the mass into the celerity [§. 275.], the mass of each of those corpuscles, being most slight, as indeed it is, cannot give them a force as great as we have seen it to be unless they are moved with the greatest celerity; and so it is necessary that they be moved with the greatest celerity. Finally, we have it ascertained by experiment that this motion is rectilinear: a luminous ray let in through a very small hole into a dark chamber is always propagated in a straight line, and falls upon the point opposite the little hole along a straight line: therefore light is a most subtle substance, affected with a very swift motion along a straight line.

> 643 Dico 3: Lucis propagatio seu lux derivativa, sive lumen non rectè explicatur per igneum profluvium ex corporibus lucidis dimanans. Est contra Cl. Gassendum, & Newtonum. Prob.: Si ita esset, medium semel illustratum etiam sublato lucido corpore, illuminatum manéret. Non enim luminis corpuscula lucidi corporis praesentia indigent, ut in ipso medio conserventur, etsi lucidum corpus â quo emissa fuere non amplius illi praesens existat; sed falsum est illuminatum manere medium sublato lucido corpore â quo illustratur: ergo. Deinde, lumen sparsum â candela in cubiculo vel â sole per aërem eò intensiùs fieri deberet, quò longiore tempore corpus illic praesens est; quum enim corpus lucidum nova luminis corpuscula singulis momentis emittat, necesse est, ut in eadem parte medii per quod lumen diffunditur, corpuscula semper fiant copiosiora, ac proindè lumen intensiùs, quod tamen utrumque cum experientia pugnat.

643 I say 3: the propagation of light, or derivative light, or lumen, is not rightly explained by a fiery outflow emanating from luminous bodies. This is against the distinguished Gassendi and Newton. Proof: if it were so, a medium once lit up would remain illuminated even when the luminous body was taken away. For the corpuscles of light do not need the presence of the luminous body in order to be preserved in the medium itself, even though the luminous body from which they were emitted is no longer present to it; but it is false that the medium remains illuminated when the luminous body by which it is lit up is taken away: therefore. Next, the light spread by a candle in a small room, or by the sun through the air, ought to become the more intense the longer the body is present there; for since the luminous body emits new corpuscles of light at every moment, it is necessary that in the same part of the medium through which the light is diffused the corpuscles always become more abundant, and therefore the light more intense; yet each of these conflicts with experience.

> 644 Utraque haec ratio firmatur similitudine, quâ utitur Cl. Gassendus ad explicandam suam de lumine opinionem: ait enim, lumen produci non secùs atque odores, emissione videlicèt exilium corpusculorum; sed certum est odorem conservari sublato etiam corpore, odoras moleculas spargente; certum item est, odorem intensiorem vividioremque reddi continuò in eadem medii parte, quò diuturnior est praesentia eorum corporum á quibus odorata corpuscula emanant: ergo in substantiali lucidi corporis effluvio lumen non rectè collocatur.

644 Each of these reasons is strengthened by the comparison that the distinguished Gassendi uses to explain his opinion about light: for he says that light is produced just as odors are, namely by the emission of slender corpuscles; but it is certain that an odor is preserved even when the body spreading the odorous molecules is taken away; it is likewise certain that an odor is made continually more intense and more lively in the same part of the medium the longer the presence of the bodies from which the odorous corpuscles emanate lasts: therefore light is not rightly placed in a substantial effluvium of the luminous body.

> 645 Dicunt Newtoniani: illuminatum non manere medium, quod semel illustratum est, lucido corpore sublato: quia licet luminis corpuscula non indigeant praesentiâ corporis lucidi, ut in medio, per quod diffusa sunt conserventur; ea tamen indigent, ut in illo moveri non cessent; ac proindè, ut ipsum medium nobis illustratum exhibeant.

645 The Newtonians say that the medium, once lit up, does not remain illuminated when the luminous body is taken away: because, although the corpuscles of light do not need the presence of the luminous body in order to be preserved in the medium through which they have been diffused, they do need it in order not to cease being moved in it, and therefore in order to show the medium itself lit up to us.

> 646 Contra tamen, arguit Clariss. Fort. â Brixia: etenim nullum corpus projectum indiget praesentiâ projicientis, ut in motu quem ab illo recepit perseveret; sed pergit moveri, & si [p. 204] ciens post impressum illi motum deficiat: ergo neque luminis corpuscula non [?] indigent praesentiâ corporis lucidi, ne motus quem ab illo receperunt [?] in ipsis pereat. Praeterea neque *soni*, neque *odoris* corpuscula ita dependent â sonoro, aut odoro corpore, ex quo emanant, ut nonnisi illius praesentiâ moveri queant, & sensationem in nobis excitare: ergo neque corpuscula luminis ita dependent [?] â lucido corpore, ut in motu sistantur [?], atque ad *luminis* sensationem in nobis excitandam planè inepta evadant, statim ac lucidum corpus non amplius nobis praesens existit.

646 But against this, argues the most distinguished Fortunato da Brescia: for no projected body needs the presence of the projector in order to persevere in the motion that it received from it; but it goes on being moved even if the projector [p. 204] fails after impressing the motion on it: therefore neither do the corpuscles of light need the presence of the luminous body, lest the motion which they received from it should perish in them. Moreover, neither the corpuscles of sound nor those of odor so depend on the sounding or odorous body from which they emanate that they can be moved, and excite sensation in us, only in its presence: therefore neither do the corpuscles of light so depend on the luminous body that they should come to a halt in their motion and be rendered wholly unfit for exciting the sensation of light in us as soon as the luminous body is no longer present to us.

> 647 Quod si quis dicat *soni* corpuscula moveri posse etiam absente sonoro corpore â quo emissa fuere, quia illorum motus *perturbatus* est, & per aërem quaquaversus diffunditur [?], non nisi praesente lucido, â quo fuerint [?] vibrata, moveri posse corpuscula *luminis*, quia illorum motus est *rectilineus*: contra est, quod sicut *perturbatus* corpusculorum motus non indiget ut conservetur, praesentiâ corporis perturbatè moventis, ita neque motus corpusculorum *rectilineus* opus habere deberet, ne pereat, praesentiâ corporis vibrantis secundum rectam lineam. Utriusque namque motus eadem omninò ratio est, independentia [?] scilicet corporis moti â movente, ut eum, quem semel accepit, quemcumque motum retineat. Imò tantum abest durationem motus *rectilinei* semel corpori impressi, â moventis duratione dependere, ut inter naturae leges ea sit una, *omne corpus semel in motum concitatum semper moveri secundum rectam lineam, quamdiu non cogitur â causa externa directionem suam mutare* [§. 294.].

647 But if someone should say that the corpuscles of sound can be moved even when the sounding body from which they were emitted is absent, because their motion is perturbed and spreads through the air in every direction, whereas the corpuscles of light can be moved only when the luminous body by which they were darted forth is present, because their motion is rectilinear: against this it is urged that, just as the perturbed motion of corpuscles does not need, in order to be preserved, the presence of a body moving them in a perturbed way, so neither should the rectilinear motion of corpuscles need, lest it perish, the presence of a body vibrating them along a straight line. For the reason of each motion is altogether the same, namely the independence of the body moved from the mover, so that it retains the motion it has once received, whatever that motion may be. Nay, so far is the duration of a rectilinear motion once impressed on a body from depending on the duration of the mover, that among the laws of nature this is one: every body once set in motion is always moved along a straight line, so long as it is not compelled by some external cause to change its direction [§. 294.].

> 648 At hinc nemo eorum, qui pro certo habent, substantiale lucidi corporis *effluvium* in quo lumen constituunt, notabili aliquo temporis intervallo indigere, ut â sole, ceterisque astris ad nos perveniat, inficiari poterit [?], fore, ut *lumen* maneat in medio, per quod diffusum est, etiam lucido sublato corpore, â quo producitur. Evidens est enim in hac hypothesi, *lumen independenter* â corpore lucido in medio conservari toto illo temporis spatio, quod labitur [?] dum transit [?] â lucido ipso corpore ad nos perveniens [?]. Nam si ponatur unam horam requiri, ut *lumen* â Sole S ad terram T (Fig. 117.), propagetur, evidens est lumen â S diffusum manere per spatium â S ad T, etiamsi intra illud unius horae intervallum, Sol S, â quo lumen ipsum emissum, non amplius existat.

648 But hence none of those who hold for certain that the substantial effluvium of the luminous body, in which they make light consist, needs some notable interval of time in order to reach us from the sun and the other stars, can deny that it will come about that light remains in the medium through which it has been diffused, even when the luminous body by which it is produced is taken away. For it is evident on this hypothesis that light is preserved in the medium independently of the luminous body for that whole time which elapses while it travels from the luminous body itself to us. For if it is supposed that one hour is required for light to be propagated from the Sun S to the earth T (Fig. 117.), it is evident that the light diffused from S remains in the space from S to T even if, within that interval of one hour, the Sun S, which emitted that light, ceases to exist.

> 649 Quum igitur Vir Cl. Newtonus [^204-s1], *s' Gravesandius* [^204-s2], Musschenbroekius [^204-s3], aliique praeterea multi ponunt, *lumen* spatio septem, vel octo *minutorum primorum* â sole ad terram venire, [p. 205] adeoque indigere spatio aliquot *horarum*, ut à sole ad Saturnum, tum à Saturno ad nos perveniat, spatio vero aliquot *mensium*, ut à fixis stellis ad terram usque propagetur; arbitror, hos omnes facile concessuros, in substantiali corporis effluvio minimè posse lumen constitui, quum simul ab illis detur, quod experientiae apertè contrarium est, fore scilicet, ut lumen ipsum notabili temporis spatio conservetur in medio, per quod semel diffusum est, etiam lucido absente corpore, à quo fuit productum.

649 Since, then, the distinguished Newton (i), ’s Gravesande (k), Musschenbroek (l) and many others besides hold that light comes from the sun to the earth in the space of seven or eight minutes, and hence [p. 205] that it needs the space of some hours in order to reach Saturn from the sun, and then us from Saturn, and the space of some months in order to be propagated from the fixed stars all the way to the earth, I think that all these will readily grant that light can by no means be made to consist in a substantial effluvium of a body, since at the same time it would be granted by them, what is plainly contrary to experience, namely that light itself is preserved for a notable space of time in the medium through which it has once been diffused, even when the luminous body by which it was produced is absent.

> [^204-s1]: Princip. Philosoph. Mathem. Lib. 1. Schol. ad prop. 96, nec non Optic. Lib. 2. Prop. 11.

[^204-s1]: Princip. Philosoph. Mathem., bk. 1, Schol. to prop. 96, and also Optic., bk. 2, prop. 11.

> [^204-s2]: Elem. Phys. §. 2155 [?].

[^204-s2]: Elem. Phys. §. 2155.

> [^204-s3]: Comment. in Exp. Acad. del Cimento Part. 2. p. 184 [?].

[^204-s3]: Comment. in Exp. Acad. del Cimento, pt. 2, p. 184.

> 650 Dico quarto: Luminis propagatio explicanda videtur per aethereae substantiae, motu vibratorio donatae pressionem rectilineam à corporis lucidi motu profectam, & visus organum impellentem. Prob. Materia namque aetherea corporeae substantiae affectiones sibi vendicat, & frangi, reflecti, movere organum potest, & subtilissima quum sit, motum recipere à lucidi corporis particulis potest; quumque ubivis diffusa habeatur, motus propagatio per eam quàm optime explicatur. Praeterea constat à solo tremulo motu aëris, aurium cavitatem subeuntis ita affici organum auditus, ut in nobis fiat soni sensatio; sed juxta omnes inter lumen, & sonum maxima analogia habetur: ergo à solo motu vibratorio aethereae subtilissimae substantiae, quae oculi pupillam penetret, potest visus organum ita immutari, ut sensatio luminis in nobis excitetur.

650 I say fourth: the propagation of light seems to be explained by a rectilinear pressure of an ethereal substance endowed with vibratory motion, a pressure proceeding from the motion of the luminous body and impelling the organ of sight. Proof: for the ethereal matter claims for itself the affections of a corporeal substance, and can be refracted, reflected and move the organ; and since it is most subtle, it can receive motion from the particles of the luminous body; and since it is had diffused everywhere, the propagation of motion through it is explained in the best possible way. Moreover, it is established that the organ of hearing is so affected by the tremulous motion of the air alone, entering the cavity of the ears, that the sensation of sound arises in us; but among all things there is the greatest analogy between light and sound: therefore by the vibratory motion alone of a most subtle ethereal substance, which penetrates the pupil of the eye, the organ of sight can be so altered that the sensation of light is excited in us.

> Solvuntur argumenta.

THE ARGUMENTS ARE ANSWERED.

> 651 Opp. 1. contra primam: rationes quibus conclusio nostra innititur, nihil aliud evincunt, nisi lucem primitivam à motu partium corporis lucidi, tamquam à necessaria conditione dependere: ergo lux primitiva tantum veluti à conditione, non tamquam à formali sua ratione dependet à agitatissimo[?] motu subtilium partium corporis lucidi. Nego totum argumentum: quoniam nihil prorsus praeter tremorem communicatur corpori sonoro dum percutitur, & sonum edit, nullo [?] ex Philosophorum repugnante, tremor hujusmodi, non conditio ad sonum praerequisita, sed ipse sonus est: ergo eadem ratione si dum corpus efficitur lucidum, nihil aliud, praeter motum in subtilioribus ejus partibus excitatur, motus ipse non mera est conditio ad primitivae lucis productionem necessariò requisita, sed ipsa lux.

bj. 1 against the first: the reasons on which our conclusion rests prove 651 O nothing else than that primitive light depends on the motion of the parts of the luminous body as on a necessary condition: therefore primitive light depends on the most agitated motion of the subtle parts of the luminous body only as on a condition, not as on its formal reason. I deny the whole argument: since nothing whatever except a tremor is communicated to a sounding body while it is struck and gives forth a sound, therefore, with none of the Philosophers objecting, a tremor of this kind is not a condition prerequired for sound, but is sound itself: therefore by the same reason, if, while a body is made luminous, nothing else is excited but motion in its subtler parts, that motion is not a mere condition necessarily required for the production of primitive light, but is light itself.

> 652 Opp. 2. contra 2. non bene probatur ex reflexione luminis, ipsam esse corpus: ergo. Prob. antec. Nam reflexio luminis non est sicut pilae reflexio, nam reflexio dicitur de luce metaphoricè, & impropriè: ergo. Nego antec. probationem: nam ut evincatur, eo modo non resilire lumen, quemadmodum requiritur, ut corpus idcirco dicatur, satis non est ostendere ipsum, non sicut pilam ex speculo reflecti. Etenim neque sonus resilit ut pila, quum fit Echo, & tamen corporeae sunt aereae illae particulae in quarum tremore [p. 206] consistit sonus[?], etiam juxta Peripateticos, corporeae sunt, & certum est ideo[?] reflecti sonum[?], quia corporeae sunt illae particulae[?]: ergo & lumen non metaphoricè, sed verè, & propriè reflectitur, quamvis non ut pila â pariete resiliat.

652 Obj. 2 against the 2nd: it is not well proved from the reflection of light that it is a body: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: for the reflection of light is not like the reflection of a ball, since reflection is said of light metaphorically and improperly: therefore. I deny the proof of the antecedent: for in order to prove that light does not rebound in the way that is required for it therefore to be called a body, it is not enough to show that it is not reflected from a mirror like a ball. For neither does sound rebound like a ball when an Echo occurs, and yet those aerial particles in whose tremor [p. 206] sound consists, even according to the Peripatetics, are corporeal, and it is certain that sound is reflected because those particles are corporeal: therefore light too is reflected not metaphorically, but truly and properly, even though it does not rebound like a ball from a wall.

> 653 Opp. 3. Luminis particulae sunt tenuissimae: ergo non possunt [?] resistentiam[?], ut reflecti, & refringi possint: [?] lux [?] in [?]: ergo refractio de luce dicitur tantùm[?] metaphoricè. Nego conseq.[?] [?] tenuitas[?] particularum luminis[?] [?] motu [?] & reflecti[?] [?] quàm à lucido corpore impelluntur[?] [?]. Quum enim[?] illae particulae sint corporeae, [?] nemo non videt in iis esse posse texturam, in qua corporum [?] posita est, & ex qua [?] dependet.

653 Obj. 3: the particles of light are most tenuous: therefore they cannot meet with [such resistance] that they can be reflected and refracted: for since light […] in […]: therefore refraction is said of light only metaphorically. I deny the consequence. For just as […] the tenuity of the particles of light, and […] by motion […], since among them they can […] and be reflected, since […] than they are impelled by the luminous body […]. For since those particles are corporeal, […] no one fails to see that there can be in them the texture in which the […] of bodies is placed, and on which their […] depends.

> 654 Opp. 4. Corpora quae refringuntur ex raro in densum medium transeuntia[?], recedunt â perpendiculari, quoniam eorum motus ex duobus componitur, ex perpendiculari scilicet[?], qui â gravitate oritur[?], & ex horizontali extrinsecus impresso; sed lux non ita refringitur, quum[?] ad perpendicularem accedat: ergo non est corpus. Nego conseq.[?] Nam quamvis globus plumbeus ex. gr.[?] ita refringatur[?] in transitu ex aëre in aquam, quia corpus est, non rectè inde infertur[?], lumen ideo non esse corpus, quia non eodem modo, quo plumbeus globulus, refringitur[?]; sed dicendum est, lucem non in eamdem partem refringi[?], ac globum illum, non quia ille globus est corpus, sed quia lux refringitur non cum recessu, sed cum accessu ad perpendicularem, sive ob rationem allatam jam â nobis [§. 3[?]], sive quia fortius ab aqua quam ab aëre attrahatur, ut Cl. Newtonus censuit. Ut ergo evincant Peripatetici non bene â Recentioribus probari luminis corporeitatem ex ipsius refractione, demonstrare deberent[?] eam solam[?] refractionem ex corporeitate oriri, quae in transitu ex medio rariori in densius cum recessu â perpendiculari perficitur.

654 Obj. 4: bodies which are refracted in passing from a rare medium into a dense one recede from the perpendicular, because their motion is compounded of two, namely of the perpendicular one, which arises from gravity, and of a horizontal one impressed from without; but light is not so refracted, since it approaches the perpendicular: therefore it is not a body. I deny the consequence. For although a leaden ball, for example, is refracted in this way in passing from air into water because it is a body, it is not rightly inferred from this that light is not a body because it is not refracted in the same way as a leaden ball; but it must be said that light is not refracted toward the same side as that ball, not because the ball is a body, but because light is refracted not with a recession from, but with an approach to, the perpendicular, either for the reason already brought forward by us [§. 3…], or because it is attracted more strongly by water than by air, as the most distinguished Newton held. In order, then, to prove that the corporeality of light is not well proved by the Moderns from its refraction, the Peripatetics ought to demonstrate that only such a refraction arises from corporeality as is performed, in the passage from a rarer medium into a denser one, with a recession from the perpendicular.

> 655 Neque valet dicere, lumen non refringi ex se, sed ratione subjecti, aëris scilicet[?] in quo producitur. Primò etenim explicare Peripatetici deberent, quamobrem aër illuminatus, licet sit corpus, non tamen ut corpora solida, nempe[?] cum recessu â perpendiculari, dum aquam subire cogitur, refringatur. 2. Danda ab eis causa est, cur aër lumine perfusus vitrum possit subire[?], non possit lumine carens[?]: ergo stat[?] â Recentioribus firmissimè[?] corporeitatem luminis ex illius reflexione, & refractione contra Peripateticos demonstrari.

655 Nor does it avail to say that light is not refracted of itself, but by reason of its subject, namely the air in which it is produced. For, first, the Peripatetics ought now to explain why illuminated air, although it is a body, is nevertheless not refracted as solid bodies are, namely with a recession from the perpendicular, while it is forced to enter water. 2. They must give the cause why air suffused with light can enter glass, while air lacking light cannot. It stands, then, that the corporeality of light is most firmly demonstrated by the Moderns against the Peripatetics from its reflection and refraction.

> 656 Opp. 5. Lux compenetratur[?] cum toto corpore diaphano; sed corpora nequeunt naturaliter compenetrari[?]: ergo lux non est substantia [p. 207] corporea. Dist. maj.[?] [?]

656 Obj. 5: light is compenetrated with the whole diaphanous body; but bodies cannot be naturally compenetrated: therefore light is not a corporeal substance. Dist. [p. 207] I distinguish the major: it is compenetrated in such a way that it truly enters and passes through the solid particles of that body, I deny the major; inasmuch as it enters its pores and runs freely through them, I grant the major, and I deny the consequence: for the pores with which a diaphanous body abounds are set in a straight line and communicate with one another, so that light is diffused through them in such a way that it passes through the body itself and runs freely beyond it. The whole body, moreover, seems to be occupied by light, that is, there seems to be no part at all in it which is not suffused with light, because the pores of that body are not only innumerable, but also so close to one another that we ourselves can discern no interval whatever between them. And just as […] it does not follow that glass is compenetrated with water, so must it be said of light […] illuminating the glass.

> 657 Inst.[?] [?]

657 Inst.: those parts of the glass which exist between the pores are either opaque or diaphanous. Not the first, because then the whole glass would be opaque, since the pores are not glass but empty spaces, which are nothing. But if those parts are diaphanous, they are then receptive of light: therefore light is received not only in the pores of the glass, but also in the very body of the glass. I reply that those parts are opaque, and I deny that it will therefore come about that the whole glass is opaque. For although the pores are nothing but empty spaces, yet if they are so disposed as to be set in a straight line and to communicate with one another, they constitute a diaphanous body, although they do not constitute the light which falls into it, but make the free passage of the rays. The Peripatetics themselves […] two bodies […]. A body, then, is porous, and is rightly called a body, although its pores are not a body but the empty spaces of a body, which are nothing: therefore by the same reason a body is rightly called diaphanous, although the pores, from whose right disposition its diaphaneity is derived, are not a body.

> 658 [?]

658 Moreover, although the particles which bound the pores of a body are entirely solid and the pores are not a body, the Peripatetics do not on that account infer that the body is altogether solid: therefore by the same reason a body can be diaphanous although those particles of it are not diaphanous, but opaque. […] it is necessary that the particles be solid from whose position and mutual adhesion we call a body solid […]. A body, then, can truly be, and be called, fluid, although the particles which constitute it are solid: therefore it can also be, and be called, a diaphanous body, although the particles of which it is composed are opaque; and just as from this alone, that the component particles of a body are solid, it cannot be inferred that the whole body is solid, so from this alone, that the particles of which a body is made up are opaque, it is not rightly deduced that it is opaque.

> 659 [?] [p. 208] [?]

659 You will say: these reasons have no weight, since it is certain that no body is wholly porous, that none can […] [p. 208] […] be called, just as on the contrary the whole body is called diaphanous […]. But against this: for it is asserted gratuitously and without foundation that the whole glass is diaphanous. For since, as every new experiment plainly demonstrates, […] light […] innumerable […] it is evident that light does not so pervade the whole glass that nothing […] to which light denies passage.

> 660 [?]

660 You will say: the whole glass is denominated luminous, just as the whole […] is said to receive light, which is by no means affirmed of a sieve pierced with very small holes, whose parts are not diaphanous, but receive light only through the holes. But I reply very easily: the whole glass is called luminous because both its pores, through which light passes, and the very particles which bound them and […] reflect it, are of so small a magnitude that they altogether escape the senses. But in a sieve the matter stands the other way. For however many the holes may be which […] light in it, and give it passage, they are nevertheless far […], just as also the parts in it […] by which the incident rays of light are sent back to us.

> 661 [?] [^208-s1] [?]

661 Obj. 6: if what has been said were true, light, being a most subtle substance, […] through the pores […] of the substance would fly away and vanish; but light […]: therefore light is not a most subtle substance. […] since […] is let in only through the pores […] water […] with a varied and diverse motion […] is refraction. For from this, that light is constantly propagated along a straight line, […] passes through the pores […] in the bodies […] in a straight line […] communicate […]. And this reply is that of […] Newton (m), […]

> [^208-s1]: Lib. [?] quaest. [?]

[^208-s1]: Bk. 2, […] quaest. […].

> 662 [?]

662 To the second it is said that […] because the motion […] is varied and diverse, […] since […] in the same straight line […] communicated […]. And although water also is agitated with a varied and diverse motion […] the Peripatetics […] in which its diaphaneity consists […] nothing hinders […] in a most subtle substance affected with a rectilinear motion […].

[p. 209]

## CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

> De Luminis reflexione[?], & refractione[?].

On the reflection and refraction of light.

> 663 R[?]

he reflection of light is its going back from the surface of the opaque body 663 Ton which it falls. Thus light is said to be reflected when it goes back from the surface of a mirror toward the opposite side. The incident ray of light is the straight line along which light is propagated in falling; the reflected ray, on the other hand, is the straight line along which it is propagated in being reflected: so that, if light falls on the surface A B (Fig. LXV.) along the straight line a b, and rebounds along the straight line b d, the straight line a b will be the direct ray of light, and the straight line b d the reflected ray. Recall to memory what we said when we spoke of the reflection of motion.

> 664 [?]

664 A ray of light falling on the polished surface of an opaque body is reflected by this constant law, that the angle of reflection is equal to the angle of incidence. For it is most evidently established that light let in through a very small hole of a darkened room, if it is received on the polished surface of a mirror, always rebounds from it in such a way that the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence; and this proposition is so certain that it is assumed as an axiom in Catoptrics by common consent. Light falling obliquely on the polished surface of an opaque body makes the angles of inclination of the direct and the reflected ray equal. So, if light falls from the radiant point a (same Fig.) on the point b, and rebounds to d, then, the perpendicular z b being erected, the angles a b z and d b z will be equal. For since the angles z b A and z b B are equal, being right angles, the angles of reflection and incidence, a b A and d b B, cannot be equal unless the angles of inclination a b z and d b z are also equal.

> 665 [?]

665 Light itself is reflected […], keeping after reflection the [celerity] with which it fell. For if it were otherwise, the angle of reflection would not be equal to the angle of incidence. Nor does the heat which is communicated by the incident light to the bodies from which it is reflected stand in the way. For since those bodies are heated more which […] a greater quantity of light, […] the heat arises not from that part of the light which is reflected, but from the other part which is refracted, it is also easily understood that […] the reflected light is propagated not with a different [celerity], and that hence, in a perfect reflection of light, the angles of incidence and of reflection are equal to each other.

> 666 [?] [p. 210] diversa media transeuntis, à directione quam habuerat abscessio detorsioque[?]. Haec deviatio locum non habet ubi radius ad perpendiculum illabitur, verùm requiritur obliquitas incidentiae. Recólere juvat, quae de refractione motùs à nobis dicta sunt. Principium universale refractionis radiorum luminis hujusmodi est: *Lumen obliquè transiens ex medio rariore in densius, ex aëre nempè in aquam, vel vitrum, refringitur accedendo ad perpendicularem: at ex medio densiore in rarius, ex vitro nimirum, aut aqua in aërem commeans, refringitur à perpendiculari linea recedendo.*

666 The refraction of light is the departure and deflection of a luminous ray, passing through different [p. 210] media, from the direction which it had. This deviation has no place where the ray falls along the perpendicular; rather, obliquity of incidence is required. It is helpful to recall what we have said of the refraction of motion. The universal principle of the refraction of the rays of light is this: Light passing obliquely from a rarer medium into a denser one, namely from air into water or glass, is refracted by approaching the perpendicular: but passing from a denser medium into a rarer one, namely from glass or water into air, it is refracted by receding from the perpendicular line.

> 667 Prob. prima pars. Esto vas vitreum plani fundi D F H E (Fig. LXVI) opacâ laminâ tenuissimè in B perforata coopertum. Fiat ut luminis radius A B per foramen B vas ipsum subeat. Compertum experientiâ est, dùm vas solo repletur aëre, radium A B rectâ prógredi in b, contra verò pergere in a, si eodem penitùs manente vasis situ, vas ipsum aqua repleatur. Igitur ad perpendicularem B e accedit radiùs A B dum ab aëre in aquam obliquè transit. Quod ad secundam partem spectat, vulgatissima res est, nummum A (Fig. LXVII.) positum in fundo vasis C A B videri ex loco a si vas aqua repleatur, conspici vero eodem ex loco non posse si solo aëre vas ipsum plenum fuerit. Radius ergo A B erumpens è vase aquâ pleno, declinat à recto tramite ac proindè refringitur recedendo à perpendiculari B E dum ab aqua in aërem transit: ergo lumen &c.

667 Proof of the first part. Let there be a glass vessel with a flat bottom D F H E (Fig. LXVI), covered with an opaque plate very finely perforated at B. Let a ray of light A B enter the vessel itself through the hole B. It is ascertained by experience that, while the vessel is filled with air alone, the ray A B proceeds straight to b, but on the contrary goes on to a if, the position of the vessel remaining entirely the same, the vessel itself is filled with water. Therefore the ray A B approaches the perpendicular B e while it passes obliquely from air into water. As to the second part, the matter is very well known: a coin A (Fig. LXVII.) placed on the bottom of the vessel C A B is seen from the spot a if the vessel is filled with water, but cannot be seen from the same spot if the vessel itself is full of air alone. The ray A B, therefore, breaking out of the vessel full of water, turns aside from the straight path and is therefore refracted by receding from the perpendicular B E while it passes from water into air: therefore light, etc.

> 668 Sed animadversione dignum est, quod licet verissimum sit, lumen hac ratione refringi, dum ex aëre in aquam aut vitrum, & vicissim dum ex aqua, aut vitro in aërem obliquè transit: non propterea verum est, quod vulgò dici solet, nempe universaliter refringi lumen, accedendo, ad perpendicularem, vel ab ea recedendo, dum ex uno medio in aliud diversae densitatis obliquè progreditur; neque est universaliter verum, refringi lumen accedendo ad perpendicularem, dum transit obliquè ex quocumque medio *rariore* in quodcumque *densius*: contra verò frangi recedendo a perpendiculari, dum ex quocumque medio *densiore* in quodcumque *rarius* itidèm obliquè transit: contrarium enim observavit certoque deprehendit solertissimus S Gravesandus [^210-s1].

668 But it is worth noting that, although it is most true that light is refracted in this way while it passes obliquely from air into water or glass, and conversely from water or glass into air, it is not therefore true, as is commonly said, that light is universally refracted by approaching the perpendicular, or by receding from it, while it proceeds obliquely from one medium into another of different density; nor is it universally true that light is refracted by approaching the perpendicular whenever it passes obliquely from any rarer medium into any denser one, or on the contrary is refracted by receding from the perpendicular whenever it likewise passes obliquely from any denser medium into any rarer one: for the most ingenious ’s Gravesande observed and certainly detected the contrary (n).

> [^210-s1]: Elem. Phys. §. 2644. & seqq.

[^210-s1]: Elem. Phys. §. 2644 ff.

> 669 Observavit namque lumen nullam prorsùs refractionem pati, sed transire tramite recto, ex *oleo olivarum* in *boracem*, & ex *borace* in *oleum olivarum* licet hujusmodi corpora densitate differant. Densitas siquidem olei olivarum est ad densitatem bóracis, ut 6 ad 2. Lumen refringi perpendicularem versùs in transitu ex *alumine* in *vitriolum Gedanense*[?] quamvis eadem planè sit horum corporum *densitas*. Lumen refringi accedendo itidèm ad perpendicularem in transitu ex *aqua* in *spiritum Terebinthinae*, adeòque ex medio *densiore* in *rarius*. Est enim densitas aquae ad densitatem spiritus Terebinthinae ut 8 ad 7.

669 For he observed that light suffers no refraction at all, but passes in a straight path, from olive oil into borax, and from borax into olive oil, although bodies of this kind differ in density. For the density of olive oil is to the density of borax as 6 to 2. That light is refracted toward the perpendicular in the passage from alum into Danzig vitriol, although the density of these bodies is entirely the same. That light is likewise refracted by approaching the perpendicular in the passage from water into spirit of turpentine, and hence from a denser medium into a rarer one. For the density of water is to the density of spirit of turpentine as 8 to 7.

[p. 211]

## CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

> Nonnulla ad Opticam, Catoptricam, & Dioptricam spectantia quam brevissimè exponuntur.

Some things pertaining to Optics, Catoptrics and Dioptrics are set forth as briefly as possible.

> 670 Complura hunc in locum referenda forent instrumenta, quae vel utilitate sua, vel jucunditate spectaculi, quod praebent, sese commendant: adtamen, quia; per angustias temporis, diffusioribus exindè nobis esse haud licet, iccircò admonitione hac, uti nostrum isthaec persequendi desiderium exprimimus, ita, quod jure debemus, tempus causamur. Quaedam igitur delibabimus duntaxat.

ery many instruments ought to be brought into this place which com670 V mend themselves either by their usefulness or by the pleasure of the spectacle they afford; nevertheless, since the narrowness of time does not allow us to be more expansive about them, by this notice, just as we express our desire to go through these things, so too, as we rightly ought, we plead the lack of time. We shall therefore merely touch on some of them.

> 671 *Optica*, est scientia visionis directae, sive scientia Physico-Mathematica qua docemur, quo mechanismo objecta quae ex omnibus punctis radios lucis ad oculum mittunt, à nobis videantur. *Catoptrica* est scientia visionis reflexae. Principium universale reflexionis radiorum ex superficiebus politis, minime diversum est à lege illa, quam cetera corpora in reflexione servant, scilicèt ut angulus reflexionis sit angulo incidentiae aequalis. Porrò superficies ejusmodi, in quibus regularis isthaec luminis reflexio deprehenditur, *Specula* adpellantur. Dividuntur autèm specula potissimùm in *plana*, *convexa*, & *concava*: planum vocatur quod *plana*, convexum, quod *convexa*; concavum, quod *concava* superficie terminatur.

671 Optics is the science of direct vision, or the Physico-Mathematical science by which we are taught by what mechanism objects which send rays of light from all their points to the eye are seen by us. Catoptrics is the science of reflected vision. The universal principle of the reflection of rays from polished surfaces is not at all different from the law which other bodies keep in reflection, namely that the angle of reflection is equal to the angle of incidence. Further, surfaces of this kind, in which this regular reflection of light is detected, are called mirrors. Mirrors, moreover, are divided chiefly into plane, convex and concave: that is called plane which is bounded by a plane surface, convex that which is bounded by a convex one, concave that which is bounded by a concave one.

> 672 Ut aequalitas angulorum incidentiae, ac *reflexionis* in speculis seu concavis, sive convexis innotescat, ducenda est per punctum in quod radius luminosus incidit, recta linea tangens superficiem curvam. Hujusmodi est (Fig. LXVIII., & LXIX.) linea F C ducta per punctum D, in quod radius directus I D, perpendiculariter illapsus, in se ipsum reddit: radius verò A D obliquè in idem punctum incidens sic reflectitur in E, ut angulus *incidentiae* C D A aequetur angulo reflexionis F D E. Idem de ceteris radis intelligendum est.

672 In order that the equality of the angles of incidence and of reflection in mirrors, whether concave or convex, may become known, a straight line tangent to the curved surface must be drawn through the point on which the luminous ray falls. Such (Fig. LXVIII. and LXIX.) is the line F C drawn through the point D, on which the direct ray I D, falling perpendicularly, returns into itself; but the ray A D, falling obliquely on the same point, is so reflected to E that the angle of incidence C D A equals the angle of reflection F D E. The same is to be understood of the other rays.

> 673 *Dioptrica* est scientia visionis refractae, quae radiorum luminosorum flexionem in vitris praecipuè considerat. Dispesci verò adsolent vitra in classes varias, à diversâ eorumdem figura discretas. Vitrum planum superficiebus planis inter se parallelis terminatur. *Lens* est vitrum formae lenticularis: haec alia est *convexo-convexa*, quae nempè convexâ sphaericâ superficie duplici comprehenditur, alia *plano-convexa*, quae una superficie planâ, altera convexâ definitur. Vitrum *concavo-concavum* est, cujus utraque superficies [p. 212] cavitatem [?]

673 Dioptrics is the science of refracted vision, which considers chiefly the bending of luminous rays in glasses. Glasses, moreover, are usually divided into various classes, distinguished by their different figure. A plane glass is bounded by plane surfaces parallel to each other. A lens is a glass of lenticular form: one is convexo-convex, namely that which is enclosed by a double convex spherical surface; another plano-convex, which is bounded by one plane surface and the other convex. A concavo-concave glass is that each of whose surfaces shows a cavity; [p. 212] a plano-concave one, one of whose surfaces is plane, while the other presents a cavity. Finally, a glass concave on one side and convex on the other is called a meniscus.

> 674 [?]

674 It is the task of Dioptrics to contemplate all these things distinctly, to examine the properties of the different media, and to form from glasses, having obtained either a convex or a concave form, telescopes, microscopes and spectacles, by all of which our sight is wonderfully helped, whether for the viewing of remote things, or for detecting the more minute secrets of nature, or for discerning more easily and better any new bodies whatever. We shall touch on a few things.

> 675 [?] [^212-s1] [?]

675 Glasses, or spectacles, for the eyes are most useful to the myopic, or those who […] see distant things confusedly; for since, owing to the too convex conformation of the eye, […] they need light with diverging rays, they therefore use concave glasses, which render parallel rays diverging: on the contrary, to presbyopes, or those who see distant things more clearly and distinctly and near things confusedly, convex glasses are of great help: for the rays from […] near objects […] are fixed in their […]; for which reason they fittingly use glasses of this kind, which gather the rays, or at least promote their convergence. The distinguished Redi (o) affirms that the [invention] of these spectacles is owed to Alessandro della Spina, and […] about the year […].

> [^212-s1]: [?] ad Falconerium[?].

[^212-s1]: Letter to Falconieri.

> 676 [?]

676 Further, from the combination of both kinds of glass the Telescope came forth, its author being (as seems to most) Zacharias Jansen, toward the end of the sixteenth century. It was constructed on this plan: that a convex glass should be turned toward the objects and a concave one toward the eye […]. This telescope is also called the Galilean, because […] for observing the phenomena of the heavens by Galileo. […] first perfected this instrument […]; the Astronomical telescope derived its origin from the same source, consisting of two glasses convex on both sides; but since it seemed somewhat inconvenient that […] the object […] inverted, […] added two further glasses, which should set upright what the former had inverted; and then, for viewing terrestrial objects, a telescope […] with four convex glasses […].

> 677 [?] [^212-s2] [?] [p. 213] Grew, [?]

677 Finally, from glasses which swell out with a convex surface […], since they enlarge the images of minute objects, microscopes, or engyscopes, are constructed by the fit composition of various glasses […]. The first of those who […] this instrument is said to be, as Musschenbroek (p) [relates], Francesco Stelluti, who in the year […] published a description of the parts of the […] which he discovered with this aid. Then followed Power, Hooke, Grew, [p. 213] Malpighi, Leeuwenhoek, Bonanni, Hartsoeker, Joblot, Réaumur and very many others, who have shown, as it were, a new world of minute things. A microscope consisting of only one lens is called simple; one of several is called compound, whose inventor is said to be Cornelis Drebbel, in the year […], as Huygens relates in his Dioptrics.

> [^212-s2]: Essai de Physique §. [?]

[^212-s2]: Essai de Physique §. […].

> 678 [?] [^213-s1] [?]

678 James Gregory in the year 1663 invented and described a catadioptric telescope composed of lenses and mirrors. A few years afterwards the most distinguished Newton (q) published a catadioptric telescope of a somewhat different structure, very well suited to celestial observations, called Newtonian from the name of its author, just as the former was named Gregorian. Both, however, at length, after an interval of some years, […] namely John Hadley brought them to perfection.

> 679 [?]

679 From the combination of a lens and a mirror the Polemoscope was likewise made: namely an instrument by whose aid one can view objects while looking in another direction. Its chief part is a plane mirror […] inclined, from which the image of the object is sent back toward the eye of the beholder, since he himself cannot have it along a straight line. In this way it will be possible to observe without danger the movements of the enemy, […] behind the defenses of bulwarks, […] and to […] who […], etc.

> 680 [?]

680 Here too belongs the camera obscura, which represents on a flat ground external objects expressed in their own colors, so that they can conveniently be drawn. The Magic Lantern, too, is reckoned among these instruments, in which, by the aid of a concave mirror, minute things are enlarged to […] form.

## DISSERTATIO V. — DISSERTATION V

> De Qualitatibus insensibilibus.

On insensible Qualities.

## CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

> De Sympathia, Antipathia, Idiosyncrasia, & Antiperístasi.

On Sympathy, Antipathy, Idiosyncrasy and Antiperistasis.

> 682 Qualitates *insensibiles*, sive *occultae* vocantur illae, quae non agunt ipsae immediatè in sensus nostros, sed ex effectibus, & ratione cognoscuntur, quibus tamen immeritò *occultarum* nomen tribui existimant Recentiores Philosophi, qui rectam philosophandi rationem insequuntur, nec abstractis pèrperam vocibus, quibus summoperè Peripatetici delectantur, *facultatis* nempè, aut *qualitatis*, aut *formae* aliisque similibus contenti sunt, verùm causas inquirunt rerum, quas non oculis quidem, sed animo complecti licet. Inter hujusmodi qualitates recensentur Sympathia, Antipathia, & aliae omnes supra memoratae, de quibus hoc loco acturi sumus.

hose qualities are called insensible, or occult, which do not themselves act 682 T immediately on our senses, but are known from their effects and by reason; the name of occult, however, is held to be undeservedly given to them by the Modern Philosophers, who follow the right method of philosophizing and are not content with abstract words wrongly used, in which the Peripatetics delight exceedingly, namely faculty, or quality, or form, and others like them, but they inquire into the causes of things, which can be grasped not indeed with the eyes, but with the mind. Among qualities of this kind are reckoned Sympathy, Antipathy and all the others mentioned above, of which we are to treat in this place.

> 683 *Simpathia* autem dicitur illa rerum consensio, quá fit, ut una adfectâ, sentiente, motâ, patiente, adficiatur, sentiat, moveatur, patiatur etiam altera. Quo pariter refertur amicitia quaedam aut potius cônvenientia inter homines, & amor quidam naturalis. *Antipathiam* ex adverso vocant repugnantiam, & quandam velut inimicitiam inter res, ita, ut una alteram respuat, & aversetur *Idiosyncrasiam* dicunt quando vel res innoxias, imò salutares aversamur, & ferre non possumus, vel res noxias, & adversas ceteròqui adpetimus, facilèque toleramus. *Antiperistasis* deffinitur in Scholis *resistentia unius corporis adversus corpus contrariu à quo circumquaque obsidetur, invalescentis, & intensio qualitatis propter qualitatem contrariam*.

683 Sympathy, then, is the name for that agreement of things by which it comes about that, when one is affected, feels, is moved or suffers, the other too is affected, feels, is moved and suffers. To this likewise is referred a certain friendship, or rather fitness, between men, and a certain natural love. Antipathy, on the contrary, is the name they give to a repugnance and, as it were, a certain enmity between things, such that one rejects and turns away from the other. They speak of idiosyncrasy when we either turn away from harmless, nay salutary, things and cannot bear them, or seek and easily tolerate things harmful and otherwise adverse. Antiperistasis is defined in the Schools as the resistance of one body against a contrary body by which it is besieged on every side, growing in strength, and the intensification of a quality on account of the contrary quality.

> 684 Qualitatum harum explanatio Physicis Recentioribus tam recondita haud videtur, ut si ad omnes quae circumstant, conditiones animum maturè ac circunspecto judicio advertamus, eae ex genuinis, claris, verisque principiis exponi non possint, advertendo tamen, dandam esse operam, ut de re ipsa certiores facti, illud in primis adcuratè inquiramus, num quidquid narratur, ita re vera, sub iis circunstantiis & conditionibus se habeat. Plurimae enim sublestae fidei observationes, & fabulae hic se ingerunt, plurimaque [p. 215] narrantur quae si experientiam consulamus, & adcuratissimè omnia pervestigemus, vel prorsùs non ita se habere, pro certo comperiemus, vel eo quo perhibentur modo, nunquam contingere. Hoc animadverso.

684 The explanation of these qualities does not seem so recondite to the Modern Physicists that, if we turn our mind with mature and circumspect judgment to all the attendant conditions, they cannot be set forth from genuine, clear and true principles; observing, however, that care must be taken that, in order to be made more certain of the thing itself, we first of all inquire accurately whether whatever is narrated is really so under those circumstances and conditions. For very many observations of doubtful credit, and fables, intrude themselves here, and very many things are narrated [p. 215] which, if we consult experience and investigate everything most accurately, we shall find for certain either not to be so at all, or never to happen in the way in which they are reported. This having been noted,

> 685 Dico primo: Sympathia, Antipathia, Idiosyncrasia, & Antiperistasis, profluviis substantialibus, & motui, quieti, figurae, situi partium, aliisque mechanicis adfectionibus, item consuetudini, moribus, temperamento, aut imaginationi rectè tribuuntur. Prob. per partes. Primò effectus sympathicos ex dictis principiis quámclarissimè exponendo. Sic ex. gr. pulvis ex vitriolo calcinato, qui sympathicus dicitur, injectusque in sanguinem recens emissum è vulnere, fluxum hujus sistere, & vulneri, mederi deprehenditur: non aliter hunc effectum praestare concipietur, quàm per vitrioli corpuscula, quae calentibus adhùc sanguinis particulis admixta, & cum iisdem in fermentationem concitata, ad vulnus unde expressus est sanguis, feruntur (non secùs, ac transpiratio contingit) & quidem tanquam cunei apertos meatus, quibus sanguis profluit, penitùs obstruunt.

685 I say first: Sympathy, Antipathy, Idiosyncrasy and Antiperistasis are rightly attributed to substantial outflows, and to the motion, rest, figure and situation of the parts, and to other mechanical affections; likewise to custom, to manners, to temperament, or to imagination. Proof, part by part. First, by explaining sympathetic effects most clearly from the said principles. Thus, for example, the powder from calcined vitriol which is called sympathetic, and which, when thrown into blood freshly let out of a wound, is found to stop its flow and to heal the wound, will be conceived to produce this effect in no other way than through the corpuscles of the vitriol, which, mixed with the still warm particles of the blood and set into fermentation together with them, are carried to the wound from which the blood was pressed out (just as transpiration takes place), and indeed, like wedges, entirely block up the open passages through which the blood flows forth.

> 686 Effectuum id genus aliorum item in hominibus, & animalibus ratio redditur ex conclusione nostra. Sic quod oscitante uno, oscitet alter, cane uno latrante, latret & alter, canentibus aviculis aliis. incitentur aliae ad modulandum, ex eo est, quod homines, & animalia quae idoneam habent corporis dispositionem ad ea facilè excitentur, quae ab aliis geruntur, excitatis quippè certis ideis, conspirant corporis membra, facilèque motibus secundum certam ideam determinatis incitantur. Multum quoque ad effectus sympathicos confert vis consuetudinis, quando per eam peculiaris dispositiò & habilitas corporibus inducitur. Denique propensio unius hominis erga alium enascitur ex morum in primis convenientia, temperamenti congruentia, ex elegantiis item in sermone, corpore, vita, moribusque. Ista quippè amorem próvocant, & conciliant, tacitisque velut vinculis adstringunt. Effectus *antipathici* oppositam suo modo causam habent. Sic aversionis inter homines causae facilè sunt detegendae: etenim in vultu, moribus, vita, sermone, aut actionibus, reperitur semper aliquid, quo unus alteri non potest esse non adversus. Effectus quoque hujusmodi in animalibus congruè ex stabilitis jam principiis ducuntur. Sic agni fugam, praesente lupo; hujus impetum in agnum; gallinarum clangórem praetervolante milvo, à quibusdam impressionibus duci, quis negaverit?

686 The reason of other effects of this kind, likewise in men and animals, is given from our conclusion. Thus, that when one yawns another yawns, that when one dog barks another barks too, that when some little birds sing others are stirred to warble, comes from this, that men and animals which have a fit disposition of body are easily stirred to the things that are done by others: for when certain ideas are excited, the members of the body conspire, and are easily stirred to motions determined according to a certain idea. The force of custom also contributes much to sympathetic effects, when through it a particular disposition and aptitude is induced in bodies. Finally, the inclination of one man toward another arises above all from the agreement of manners, the congruence of temperament, and likewise from elegance in speech, body, life and manners. For these provoke and win love, and bind men as with silent chains. Antipathetic effects have, in their own way, the opposite cause. Thus the causes of aversion between men are easily detected: for in the face, manners, life, speech or actions something is always found by which the one cannot but be averse to the other. Effects of this kind in animals too are fittingly derived from the principles already established. Thus who will deny that the flight of the lamb when the wolf is present, the wolf ’s rush upon the lamb, and the clucking of hens when the kite flies past, are brought about by certain impressions?

> 687 Ex structura & dispositione partium mira phaenomena herbae *mimosae*, vel pudicae (*vulgò* la vergonzosa) manu adpropinquante expallescentis, folia contrahentis, & velut se substrahentis contactui, manumque aversantis, eleganter deduxit Cl. *Camerarius* [^215-s1] [p. 216] Praeviè[?] scilicet posita anatomia hujuscemodi plantae, animadversa foliorum ex varii generis fibris, utriculis, vasculis, & vésiculis aëre turgidis reticulari compositione, vasculorum succiferorum, & trachearum aequilibrio expenso, rem illustrat: nempè, manu adpropinquante ab emissis calidis halitibus aër in vesiculis contentus rarefit, atque expanditur, hinc vascula succifera aliquo modo comprimuntur, his compressis uberior influxus succi, à quo folia vigorem, & extensionem obtinebant, reprimitur, unde folia expallescunt, flaccida redduntur, & contrahuntur. Manu deindè retractâ, non mirum est, herbae vigorem restitui, quando cessante expansionis, causâ aëris rarefactio à succo per vascula influente superatur.

687 From the structure and disposition of the parts the distinguished Camerarius (t) has elegantly deduced the wonderful phenomena of the herb mimosa, or pudica (commonly la vergonzosa), which grows pale when a hand approaches, contracts its leaves and, as it were, withdraws itself from contact and shuns the hand, [p. 216] having, namely, first set out the anatomy of this kind of plant, having noted the reticular composition of the leaves out of fibers, utricles, small vessels and little vesicles swollen with air of various kinds, and having weighed the equilibrium of the sap-bearing vessels and of the tracheae, he illustrates the matter: namely, when a hand approaches, the air contained in the vesicles is rarefied and expanded by the warm exhalations emitted, hence the sap-bearing vessels are in some measure compressed; when these are compressed, the more abundant inflow of the sap, from which the leaves obtained their vigor and extension, is checked, whence the leaves grow pale, become flaccid and contract. When the hand is then withdrawn, it is no wonder that the vigor of the herb is restored, since, the cause of the expansion ceasing, the rarefaction of the air is overcome by the sap flowing in through the vessels.

> [^215-s1]: In Diss. peculiar. de herba mimosâ.

[^215-s1]: In a special dissertation on the herb mimosa.

> 688 *Idiosyncrasiarum* ratio potissima in eo est, quod ob singularem organum dispositionem, constitutionem, similitudinem, cùm primis vero fibrarum nervearum, vel teneriorem, molliorem, laxiorem, vel rigidiorem &c. constitutionem, certae impressiones animum adficiant, & prout illae menti, vel gratae sunt, vel adversae, ea variis modis adficiatur, vel placidè, vel ingratè, aut impetuosè: unde communis sensorii & nervorum, qui indè ad partes, & per eas protensi, ac distributi sunt, determinati motus sequuntur. Explicatur proindè cur quidam homines timeant feles, canes, mures, aliaque animalia horreant, abominentur atque ad nomen etiam illorum expallescant, & contremiscant.

688 The chief reason of idiosyncrasies lies in this, that, owing to a singular disposition, constitution and likeness of the organs, and above all a more tender, softer, looser or more rigid etc. constitution of the nervous fibers, certain impressions affect the mind, and according as they are either agreeable or adverse to the mind, it is affected in various ways, either calmly, or unpleasantly, or impetuously; whence there follow determinate motions of the common sensorium and of the nerves which are stretched out and distributed from there to the parts and through them. It is accordingly explained why certain men fear cats, dogs, mice, and shudder at and abominate other animals, and grow pale and tremble even at their name.

> 689 Si enim infantes rebus ejusmodi à vetulis imperitis terrefacti, & offensi fuerint, (ut saepius contingit non sine magno salutis detrimento, imò etiam vitae periculo), quum fibrae cerebri in infante adhuc tenellae, vehementi impressione fuerint nimis exagitatae, & labefactatae, iccircò per reliquam deinceps vitam reducta, ac denuo exorta simili idea *materiali*, sive imaginatione, impressio, & agitatio in fibris labefactatis est justò vehementior; in mente verò idea *immaterialis* ingratissima, & adversa existit. Atque è dictis ferè fundamentis redditur ratio Idiosyncrasiarum haereditariarum, adventitiarum, seu quae post nativitatem vario modo contrahuntur, & consuetudine acquisitarum.

689 For if infants have been frightened and offended by things of this kind by ignorant old women (as happens very often, not without great harm to health, nay even with danger to life), since the fibers of the brain, still tender in the infant, have been too much agitated and weakened by the vehement impression, therefore, through the rest of life thereafter, when a similar material idea, or imagination, is brought back and arises anew, the impression and agitation in the weakened fibers is more vehement than is right; and in the mind an immaterial idea arises that is most disagreeable and adverse. And from the foundations stated, more or less, the reason is given of idiosyncrasies that are hereditary, adventitious, or contracted in various ways after birth, and acquired by custom.

> 690 Similiter si advertatur ad diversos modos, quibus ab objectis variis organa nostra, & per nervos diffusi spiritus animales adficiuntur, hosque spiritus ope imaginationis tàm in brutis, quàm hominibus celerrimè per totum corpus moveri posse, difficile non erit illos effectus exponere, qui per matris nervos ob vivam imaginationem in tenellum, atque adeò facilè mutabile fetus corpusculum propagantur.

690 Likewise, if attention is paid to the different ways in which our organs, and the animal spirits diffused through the nerves, are affected by various objects, and to the fact that these spirits, by the aid of the imagination, can be moved very swiftly through the whole body, in brutes as well as in men, it will not be difficult to explain those effects which, through the nerves of the mother, on account of a lively imagination, are propagated into the tender, and hence easily changeable, little body of the fetus.

> 691 Effectus illi, qui *Antiperistasi* tanquam qualitati occultae tribuuntur à Peripateticis, sine metaphorica illa qualitatum pugna per mechanicas adfectiones explicari non secus possunt, ut quòd loca subterranea aestivo tempore frigidiora sint, quàm hiemali, & profectò experimenta, quae ad *occultae* hujus *qualitatis* [p. 217] probationem adferuntur, vel ex sensuum fallacia oriuntur, vel insufficientia sunt ad eam qualitatem adstruendam. Siquidem idem locus temperatus pro diversa sensorii constitutione, modò calidus, modò frigidus sensu judice videtur, ut in Logica explanatum à nobis fuit.

691 Those effects which are attributed by the Peripatetics to Antiperistasis as to an occult quality can just as well be explained by mechanical affections, without that metaphorical battle of qualities: as, for instance, that underground places are colder in summer than in winter. And indeed the experiments which, for the proof of this occult quality, [p. 217] are adduced either arise from the deception of the senses or are insufficient to establish that quality. For the same place, though equally tempered, seems to the judgment of sense now hot, now cold, according to the different constitution of the sensorium, as was explained by us in the Logic.

> 692 Unde quando hieme ex aëre frigidiore sensorio jam frigoris vi occupato, in minus frigidum, qualis est in locis subterraneis (in quibus causis frigorificis minus liber accessus patet) transimus, calidus hic judicatur; contrà verò ubi ex calidiore per aestatem, organo calore jam occupato in minus calidum, qualis est caverna (quae solaribus radiis non illustratur) frigoris sensus nobis obrépere videtur. Sensuum quippè judicium fallax esse circa calorem & frigus, quis non novit?

692 Hence, when in winter we pass from the colder air, the sensorium being already taken over by the force of cold, into a less cold one, such as there is in subterranean places (into which a less free access lies open to the causes producing cold), the place is here judged hot; but contrariwise, when in summer we pass from a hotter place, the organ being already taken over by heat, into a less hot one, such as is a cave (which is not lit by the rays of the sun), a sensation of cold seems to steal over us. For who does not know that the judgment of the senses about heat and cold is deceptive?

> 693 Diffusius hujus capitis argumenta exsequuntur Verulamius [^217-s1], Kircherus. [^217-s2] P. de Lanis [^217-s3], Schott [^217-s4] aliique Recentiores, quos consulere potestis. De Viribus medicamentorum pauca dicamus.

693 The arguments of this chapter are pursued more at length by Bacon (u), Kircher (x), Fr. de Lana (y), Schott (z) and other Moderns, whom you may consult. Let us say a few things about the Powers of medicines.

[^217-s1]: In Hist. Nat.

[^217-s2]: In Art. Magnet.
