Ut quae pro immobili terrae stabilitate jactantur, ea de firmitate duntaxat, consistentia, perduratione, localem motum nequaquam excludente, intelligantur: namque & Caelos, seu *Aethera firmasse sursum* Divina Sapientia dicitur *Proverb.* 8. cùm tamen ab ea caelorum firmitate motus juxta Ptolomaei Systema nequaquam abhorreat: Quae verò pro Solis mobilitate ex Sacris Literis proferuntur, haec non ex rei veritate, sed ex vulgi opinione, communique more loquendi sint dicta; ut ad rudis populi sensum sese accommodarent Scriptores Sacri: quod aliis tàm multis exemplis dedimus manifestum: atque in hoc ipso, quod de Josue praesertim objicitur, certissimum est; ex vulgi scilicèt opinione id esse dictum, si tota rei gestae narratio diligentius adtendatur. *Sol*, inquit Josue, *contra Gabaon ne movearis*: & tamen cùm tellus Solis comparatione exigua moles sit, & Gabaon in eodem terrae globo veluti minutissimum punctum; quid quaeso Soli praecipitur, ne moveatur contra Gabaon? ¿Ita ne huic puncto respondere potuit ingens Solis globus, ut contra illud aut moveretur aut staret? Ad vulgare igitur oculorum judicium allusit Josue: nostris enim oculis Sol apparet veluti discus duobus ad summum palmis dimetiendus, ac super exiguum caeli spatium decurrens„.

746 The distinguished Theologian Hyacinthe Serry too, after adducing the testimonies of Sacred Letters cited above, rises up thus against the adversary of the Copernican hypothesis (l): “Do you wield the censor’s rod on account of those few little words of Scripture? Why not rather, if you are a Theologian, until the Church condemns the ingenious System, bend the words of Scripture cited to a convenient sense? So that those words which are paraded in favor of the immobile stability of the earth may be understood only of firmness, consistency and duration, in no way excluding local motion: for Divine Wisdom is also said to have established the Heavens, or the sky above, Prov. 8, though motion according to Ptolemy’s System is in no way at odds with that firmness of the heavens: while those which are brought forward from Sacred Letters in favor of the mobility of the Sun were said not according to the truth of the thing, but according to the opinion of the common people and the common manner of speaking, so that the Sacred Writers might accommodate themselves to the understanding of an unlearned people: which we have made manifest by so many other examples; and in this very one which is especially objected, about Josue, it is most certain, namely that it was said according to the opinion of the common people, if the whole narration of the deed is attended to more diligently. Move not, O sun, says Josue, toward Gabaon: and yet, since the earth is a small mass in comparison with the Sun, and Gabaon on that same globe of the earth is as a most minute point, what, I ask, is the Sun commanded, that it should not move toward Gabaon? Could the huge globe of the Sun so correspond to this point as either to move or to stand still over against it? Josue therefore alluded to the common judgment of the eyes, for to our eyes the Sun appears as a disk to be measured by two palms at most, running over a small space of the sky.

> [^232-s2]: Loco supra citat.

[^232-s2]: In the place cited above.

> 747 „Additur in historica narratione: *Stetit itaque Sol in medio caeli*: at caelestes orbes, utpotè sphaerici (si exactè loqui velimus) ut extremis, ita quoque medio carent; nullumque in [p. 233] semita, aut linea circulari excogitari medium potest. Illud itaque ad vulgi sensum interpretari necesse est; quòd illi medius videatur caelorum locus, qui ab Oriente, & Occidente aequaliter distat. Clauditur tandem narratio his verbis: *non fuit antea, nec postea tam longa dies*. Ita ne verò nulla unquam in toto terrarum orbe longior dies illuxit? At regiones sub utroque Polo sitas peragrantibus exploratum est, Solem illic lucere diutiùs, longioresque contingere dies: imo hoc ipsum demonstrativa, & evidentissima ratione ab Astronomicae Scientiae peritis probari, certissimum est. Judaici itaque populi, cui Solis effectus in polaribus regionibus erant ignoti, accommodata narratio fuit.

747 “It is added in the historical narration: So the sun stood still in the midst of heaven: but the celestial orbs, being spherical (if we wish to speak exactly), as they lack extremities, so also they lack a middle; and no middle can be devised in a circular path [p. 233] or line. That, therefore, must be interpreted according to the understanding of the common people: that that place of the heavens seems to them the middle which is equally distant from the East and the West. The narration is finally closed with these words: there was not before nor after so long a day. Has then no longer day ever shone in the whole world? But it is well ascertained by those who travel through the regions situated under either Pole that the Sun shines longer there and that longer days occur: nay, it is most certain that this very thing is proved by a demonstrative and most evident reasoning by those skilled in Astronomical Science. The narration, therefore, was accommodated to the Jewish people, to whom the effects of the Sun in the polar regions were unknown.

> 748 „Id ni dicamus, Sacrosque Scriptores in his de Solis motu, Terraeque stabilitate loquendi formulis non ex vulgi more locutos fateamur, periculum est, ne & pari licentiâ, parique Divinarum Scripturarum abusu hoc ipsum Copernici, & Galilaei de Terrae mobilitate systema, quod suis inconsideratè censuris inúrunt plerique Theologi Recentiores, demonstrare aggrediatur morosus quidam Sacrorum Verborum exactor. Cùm enim tam saepè Sacris in Literis orbis terrae cardinibus dicatur impositus, *Regum.* 1. *cap.* 2. *Domini sunt cardines terrae*; *Proverb.* 8. *Adhuc terram non fecerat, & flumina, & cardines orbis terrae*; cárdines verò, si pressè loqui velimus, rem versatilem, mobilemque impositam sonent, quae super iis volvatur, vertaturque; quid indè, rogo vos, consequetur, nisi mobilem esse tellurem, atque versátilem, quae suis imposita cardinibus certâ lege volvitur, agiturque? Eo vel maximè, quòd & *Job.* Cap. 9. ℣. 6. Deus terram de loco suo commovere dicatur; quòd citra figuram & *Katàlexim* (certum morem loquendi vulgò adcommodatum) dictum volet morosus verborum exactor„. Hactenùs Cl. Serry.

748 “Unless we say this, and confess that the Sacred Writers, in these formulas of speech concerning the motion of the Sun and the stability of the Earth, spoke according to the custom of the common people, there is danger lest, with equal license and an equal abuse of the Divine Scriptures, some morose exactor of the Sacred Words should set about demonstrating this very system of Copernicus and Galileo on the mobility of the Earth, which most of the more recent Theologians brand with their inconsiderate censures. For since the world is so often said in Sacred Letters to be set upon its cardines [poles, hinges]: 1 Kings ch. 2: For the poles of the earth are the Lord’s; Proverbs 8: He had not yet made the earth, nor the rivers, nor the poles of the world; and since cardines, if we wish to speak strictly, denote a turning and movable thing set upon them, which is revolved and turned upon them: what, I ask you, will follow from this, except that the earth is movable and turning, which, set upon its hinges, is revolved and driven by a fixed law? All the more because in Job ch. 9, v. 6, God is said to move the earth out of its place; which the morose exactor of words will want to have been said without figure and katalexis (a certain manner of speaking accommodated to the common people).” Thus far the distinguished Serry.

> 749 Sed sint haec obiter dicta, non ut Copernici, & Galilaei systema velut ratum fixumque habeamus, quum jam indè á principio dixerimus, velut meram hypothesin ad explicanda phaenomena illum tantùm nos adoptare.

749 But let these things be said in passing, not so that we may hold the system of Copernicus and Galileo as ratified and fixed, since we said from the very beginning that we adopt it only as a mere hypothesis for explaining the phenomena.

## ADPENDIX. — APPENDIX

> Quid de Astrorum influxu sentiendum sit?

What is to be thought of the influence of the Stars?

> 750 Pervulgata est quaestio: an sidera ad productionem effectuum in tellure observatorum concurrant, sive, ut vulgò proponitur, in sublunaria influant. Sol praecipuè, & Luna effluviorum cum tellure nostra communionem sortiri videntur quibusdam: quod argumentum á duobus his Astris ad reliqua proferunt; neque contenti sunt dicere, sidera per calorem, & lucem agere in sublunaria, sed diversos alios [p. 234] influxus in tellurem praestari putant, dum Astris diversas proprietates specificas tribunt: Lunam adprime humidam, humores in tellure excitare; Saturnum frigidum; Martem siccum, & calidum, &c. ut proinde quorumdam ortus pluviam concitet, aliorum siccitatem inducat &c. Haec & plura id genus persequi porrò non libet: compendio nostrum de influxu Astrorum sensum proferemus. Quo circa sequitur conclusio.

ublicly debated is the question whether the stars concur in producing the 750 P effects observed on the earth, or, as it is commonly put, whether they influence sublunary things. The Sun chiefly, and the Moon, seem to some to share a communion of effluvia with our earth: an argument which they extend from these two Stars to the rest; nor are they content to say that the stars act on sublunary things through heat and light, but they think that various other influences [p. 234] are exerted upon the earth, while they attribute different specific properties to the Stars: that the Moon, being exceedingly moist, excites the humors on the earth; that Saturn is cold; Mars dry and hot, etc.; so that, accordingly, the rising of some brings on rain, that of others induces drought, etc. It is not our pleasure to pursue these and more things of the kind any further: we shall set forth our view of the influence of the Stars in brief. Wherefore the conclusion follows.

> 751 Praeter actionem lucis nullum alium influxum astrorum in tellurem agnoscimus: excipe tamen Solem qui calore suo satis sensibili terram nostram fovet, tum etiam Lunam quae sinminus calore, frigoreve, at certè pondere suo in subjectam atmosphaeram pro vario situ, variè nostrum globum premere potest. In primis enim effluvia quaedam substantialia humida, sicca &c. in terram ab astris transmitti nequeunt; ¿quae enim causa proferri potest, à qua ejusmodi effluvia ultrà sui astri atmosphaeram ad aliquod solum milliaria porrectam per longissima spatia propellatur? Certè de effluviis terrestribus inter omnes convenit, ea minimè ultra atmosphaeram in Lunae regionem excurrere; deindè tametsi effluvia extruderentur, ¿quid tamen fingi potest, quod ea ad nostram potius tellurem, quàm ad aliud spatium & corpus caeleste determinet? Deniquè si Luna in qua adversarii vim maximam reponunt, effluvia sua sphaericè spárgeret, qnum haec, quò ampliùs recedunt à corpore lunari, eò magis divergant ab invicem, & in tanta distantia, quantam Luna à tellure habet, divaricari possint, ac debeant plurimum, minimè possunt hoc tam avaro & exiguo effluviorum rore effectus ii produci, qui lunae influxui tribuuntur.

751 Apart from the action of light we acknowledge no other influence of the stars upon the earth: except, however, the Sun, which by its heat, sensible enough, warms our earth, and also the Moon, which, if not by heat or cold, yet certainly by its weight upon the atmosphere beneath it, can press upon our globe variously according to its varying position. For, in the first place, certain substantial effluvia, moist, dry, etc., cannot be transmitted from the stars to the earth; for what cause can be adduced by which such effluvia should be propelled through the longest spaces beyond the atmosphere of their star, which extends only some miles? Certainly about terrestrial effluvia all agree that they by no means run out beyond the atmosphere into the region of the Moon: then, even if effluvia were thrust out, what can be imagined that would direct them to our earth rather than to some other space and celestial body? Finally, if the Moon, in which our adversaries place the greatest force, scattered its effluvia spherically, then, since these diverge from one another the more, the further they recede from the lunar body, and at so great a distance as the Moon has from the earth can and must be spread very far apart, those effects which are attributed to the influence of the moon can by no means be produced by so stingy and meager a dew of effluvia.

> 752 Ostenditur secundò. Luminis actio causa esse potest omnium effectuum; lumen enim consistit in presione rectilinea aethereae substantiae ad nos usque propagata. Ergo alius potest excitari motus particularum minimarum, vehemens nempè, varius, ac perturbatus, hoc autem motu posito, alius sequi effectus, hoc cessante, rursus alius, absque eo, ut ad noctium humiditatem explicandam, ad Lunae, nescio, quae profluvia recurratur. Quapropter dùm totam naturam foveri, ac propagari, plantas adolescere, frumentum flavescere, fructus maturescere, verbo promoveri, generationes, alterationes, augmentationes cernimus, dùm tempestates anni certo moderamine recurrere, magis peculiares aëris mutationes saepè multum diversas pro aliarum causarum concursu fieri experimur, Solis actioni tribuamus haec necesse est, sed non alia ratione agentis, quàm luce sua, atque hinc consequente calore.

752 It is shown, secondly. The action of light can be the cause of all the effects; for light consists in the rectilinear pressure of the ethereal substance, propagated all the way to us. Therefore a different motion of the smallest particles can be excited, namely a vehement, varied and perturbed one; and once this motion is posited, one effect follows, and when it ceases, again another, without any need to have recourse, in order to explain the moisture of the nights, to I know not what outflowings of the Moon. Wherefore, when we see the whole of nature cherished and propagated, plants growing up, grain turning yellow, fruits ripening, in a word, generations, alterations and augmentations promoted; when we experience the seasons of the year recurring with a fixed regulation, and more particular changes of the air, often very diverse, taking place according to the concurrence of other causes, it is necessary that we attribute these things to the action of the Sun; but to the Sun acting in no other way than by its light and the heat consequent upon it.

> 753 Unde licet sideribus ceteris vis insit, exigua nervorum opticorum capillamenta concutiendi, & agitandi, atque adeo, quum his capillamentis tenuiores & ad motum aptiores in aëre, aqua, & terra particulae contineantur, vis agitandi movendique has particulas, ac proindè effectus aliquos (quantum vero sub sensum casuros, quisque arbitrabitur ex distantia ferè immensa fixarum, ex [p. 235] lumine languido Planetarum) edendi, iis tamen nullus omninò adscribendus est, nisi pro luminis ratione, cujus actio pro demonstrata haberi debet. Et quoniàm siderum universorum lumine fortius est, lumen Solis unius, ideò ei horum effectuum omnium, causa praecipuè est tribuenda. Quod si fortè observatum fuerit, non eandem esse temperationem aëris quotiescumque Sol eodem modo radios in tellurem vibrat: id non in reliquo Astra, sed peculiarem tùm aëris aut terrae habitudinem refundendum est. Ex his manat.

753 Hence, although there is in the other stars a force of striking and agitating the slender fibrils of the optic nerves, and so, since particles thinner than these fibrils and more apt for motion are contained in the air, water and earth, a force of agitating and moving these particles, and consequently of producing some effects (how far these will fall under sense, each will judge from the almost immense distance of the fixed stars, and from the [p. 235] faint light of the planets), nevertheless none at all is to be ascribed to them except in proportion to their light, whose action must be held as demonstrated. And since the light of the Sun alone is stronger than the light of all the stars together, therefore the cause of all these effects is chiefly to be attributed to it. But if it should perhaps be observed that the temper of the air is not the same whenever the Sun darts its rays upon the earth in the same way, this is to be referred not to the other heavenly bodies, but to some peculiar condition, at that time, of the air or of the earth. From these things it follows:

> Corollarium I.

COROLLARY I .

> 754 *Astrologiam Judiciariam* tanquam imposturam vanissimam, & Philosopho indignam repudiandam esse, tùm quod á Sacris Litteris reprobetur, damnetur á Conciliis Bràcarensi, & Toletano, reprehendatur á Patribus, Summorum Pontificum auctoritate, legibus Canonicis, & Civilibus interdicatur; tùm quòd â sapientibus omnibus risu explodatur. Certè divisio illa Caeli in 12 domos, in qua fundatur horoscopus, sive figura constitutionis caelestis, quae in momento nativitatis existit, commentitia est. Praeterea nec eadem fata eveniunt omnibus, qui eodem sidere nati sunt, ut patet exemplo geminorum Esau, & Jacob, qui & propensionem, & fortunam habuerunt diversissimam: nec eodem gaudent horoscopo, qui similia fata experiuntur, pro ut manifestum est; quia multi simul pereunt naufragio, incendio, peste, pugnâ, quum tamen diversissimis temporibus in lucem editi sint. Ut nihil dicam suppositum totum artis hujus, adsumptum â numero septenario Planetarum, & â situ domorum caelestium, falsum esse. Primum ostenditur â Satellitibus Jovis, & Saturui, imò, & Veneris uno; alterum, quia Constellationes quae tribuerunt nomen 12 Signis Zodiaci, juxta quorum ordinem 12 domos suas reperiri in Caelo ponunt, dudùm â pristino loco jam 30 gradibus recesserunt. Sed nugis immorari non vacat.

754 Judicial astrology is to be repudiated as a most empty imposture, unworthy of a Philosopher, both because it is reproved by the Sacred Scriptures, condemned by the Councils of Braga and Toledo, censured by the Fathers, and forbidden by the authority of the Supreme Pontiffs and by the canon and civil laws, and because it is hissed off with laughter by all the wise. Certainly that division of the Heaven into 12 houses, on which the horoscope is founded, or the figure of the celestial configuration that exists at the moment of birth, is a fiction. Moreover, neither do the same fates befall all who are born under the same star, as is plain from the example of the twins Esau and Jacob, who had the most different propensity and fortune; nor do those who experience similar fates enjoy the same horoscope, as is manifest: since many perish together by shipwreck, fire, plague, or battle, although they were brought into the light at the most different times. Not to mention that the whole supposition of this art, taken from the septenary number of the planets and from the situation of the celestial houses, is false. The first is shown by the satellites of Jupiter and Saturn, indeed even by the single one of Venus; the second, because the constellations to which they gave the name of the 12 Signs of the Zodiac, in whose order they hold that their 12 houses are found in the Heaven, have long since already receded 30 degrees from their original place. But there is no leisure to dwell on trifles.

> Corollarium II.

COROLLARY II .

> 755 *Astrologiam Aëroscopicam*, seu quae tempestates, & aëris mutationes ex Astris vaticinatur, Philosopho respuendam esse; neque enim ars haec vel ratione ulla, aut experientia firmatur, etenim quasdam ponunt Planetis inesse proprietates, hujusmodi vaticinatores: Saturnum frigidum, & siccum, Venerem Planetam calidum, & humidum, &c., quae suppositiones, non conjecturae sunt philosophicae, sed fabulosae; ¿cur enim unus calidus sit, humidus alter, quando omnes sunt massa opaca, â tellure nostra non multum abludentes? Experientiâ suam artem [p. 236] stabilire nequeunt; haec enim nititur repetita saepius observatione, Astrologi vero nec habent, nec habere possunt observationem, ubi ex simili stellarum positu similis fuerit secutus eventus in rebus sublunaribus: quando per Astronomos certum est; eorundem siderum aspectum in compluribus annorum millionibus non redire; etsi positio etiam ejusmodi rediisset, ea quoad omnia sidera ignota fuisset imperitis illis, quum ii antè praeteritum saeculum Planetas secundarios ignoraverint.

755 Aeroscopic astrology, or that which foretells storms and changes of the air from the stars, is to be rejected by the Philosopher: for this art is confirmed neither by any reason nor by experience; for soothsayers of this kind posit certain properties in the planets: Saturn cold and dry, Venus a hot and moist planet, etc., which suppositions are not philosophical conjectures but fabulous ones; for why should one be hot, another moist, when all are opaque masses not much unlike our earth? By experience they cannot establish their art; [p. 236] for this rests on frequently repeated observation, whereas the astrologers neither have nor can have an observation in which, from a similar position of the stars, a similar event has followed in sublunary things: since it is certain from the astronomers that the same aspect of the same stars does not return within many millions of years; and even if such a position had returned, it would have been unknown, as regards all the stars, to those unskilled men, since until the past century they were ignorant of the secondary planets.

> 756 Neque faciunt pro veritatis praesumptione quidpiam praedictiones quandoque verae: quis est enim, inquit Cicero, qui totum diem jaculans non aliquando collimet, praeterquam quod longè plures falsae ad derogandam Astrologis fidem plurimùm momenti habeant, innumera ejus rei sunt exempla. Sic anno 1524 ob magnas Planetarum Conjunctiones in Aquario praedicebantur integra, ac certa diluvia, annus tamen erat serenissimus, anno 1586 venti & procellae propter Conjunctiones omnium Planetarum, quum tamen annus totus pacatè exactus sit. Ipsi certè Astrologi non conveniunt inter se suis in praedictionibus: hinc Gallus quidam sibi coemit tot Calendaria, ut singulis diebus potuerit unum seligere conforme Caelo, quo factum, ut diceret, suum Calendarium toto anno esse conforme Caelo, ac licet vaticinia haec nonnumquam Calendariis inserantur, minimè tamen evincitur sapientum consilio ista fieri, aut ab iis fidem his ineptiis tribui, quando nullum facile quis in toto Orbe doctum Astronomum reperiet, qui non simplicitatem hanc indignanter respuat indignam docto, ut ait Amort. [^236-s1]

756 Nor do predictions that sometimes come true do anything for a presumption of truth; for who is there, says Cicero, who, hurling darts all day long, does not sometimes hit the mark? Besides the fact that the far more numerous false ones carry very great weight toward detracting from the astrologers’ credit, there are innumerable examples of this. Thus in the year 1524, on account of great conjunctions of the planets in Aquarius, entire and certain deluges were predicted, yet the year was most serene; in the year 1586, winds and storms on account of conjunctions of all the planets, although the whole year was passed in calm. Certainly the astrologers themselves do not agree among themselves in their predictions: hence a certain Frenchman bought himself so many calendars that for each single day he could choose one conformable to the heavens, whereby it came about that he said his calendar was conformable to the heavens the whole year round; and although these prophecies are sometimes inserted in calendars, it is by no means proved that this is done by the counsel of the wise, or that credence is given by them to these follies, since one will hardly find in the whole world a learned astronomer who does not indignantly reject this simplicity, unworthy of a learned man, as Amort says. (m)

> [^236-s1]: Phys. Partic. P. 1. q. 10.

[^236-s1]: Phys. Partic., pt. 1, q. 10.

> 757 Fiunt nempe haec, ut consuetudini serviatur non aliter, ac dum medici ipsi tabulae phlebotomicae se accommodant, cujus fundamentum non aliud est, quàm ordo numericus dierum à novilunio computatorum, qui nullam vim habet. Certè Amort ait: tabula pro sectione venae, quae solet esse in Calendariis est tantum pro pueris, rusticis, & simplici plebe. Ob eandem inefficacem numerorum relationem de diebus criticis, annis climactericis opiniones fabulis accensendae sunt.

757 These things, namely, are done so that custom may be served, not otherwise than as physicians themselves accommodate themselves to the phlebotomic table, whose foundation is nothing other than the numerical order of the days counted from the new moon, which has no force at all. Certainly Amort says: the table for the letting of a vein, which is usually in calendars, is only for boys, rustics, and the simple common people. On account of the same inefficacious relation of numbers, the opinions about critical days and climacteric years are to be counted among fables.

> Corollarium III.

COROLLARY III .

> 758 *Effectus Lunae* falsò, nimiaque credulitate adtribui. Ita creditur Luna lapides vi quadam peculiari corrodere, animalium ossa crescente Luna medullae plena, senescente autem medulla vacua, & sanguine ferè repleta esse putantur. Astaci, ostrea, multique alii pisces pleniores esse nova aut plena Luna, quàm dimidiata existimantur. Verùm haec inter temere vulgata meritò reponantur; veri enim simillimum est, ait Cl. [p. 237] Rohaultius [^237-s1] solis calorem plurium annorum spatio haec, & saxa torrere, & conficere posse, quae igne paucis horis conficiuntur, quod quum contingit, minimè mirum videri debet, si aëris humor tam saxa haec quàm calcem in pulverem redigit. Similiter, prosequitur ille, falsò existimatur, animalium ossa crescente Luna medullae plena esse, vacua senescente, hanc enim rem quum amplius 25 annos observaverit ille, alia ossa medullae plena, alia vacua crescente Luna atque senescente semper comperuit.

758 Effects are falsely, and with excessive credulity, attributed to the Moon. Thus the Moon is believed to corrode stones by a certain peculiar force; the bones of animals are thought to be full of marrow while the Moon is waxing, but empty of marrow while it is waning, and almost filled with blood. Lobsters, oysters, and many other fish are judged to be fuller at the new or the full moon than at the half moon. But these things are deservedly placed among things rashly spread abroad; for it is most likely, says the distinguished Rohault (n) [p. 237] (n), that the heat of the sun in the space of many years can torrefy and consume these stones, which are consumed by fire in a few hours; and when this happens, it ought to seem no wonder at all if the moisture of the air reduces these stones, just as it does lime, to powder. Similarly, he continues, it is falsely thought that the bones of animals are full of marrow while the Moon waxes and empty while it wanes; for when he had observed this for more than 25 years, he always found some bones full of marrow and others empty, both while the Moon was waxing and while it was waning.

> [^237-s1]: Phys. Part. II. c. 27.

[^237-s1]: Phys., pt. II, ch. 27.

> 759 Quamobrèm alia adsignanda causa: illud verisimillimum quorundam animalium ossa medulla vacua esse, vel quia alimento defecerint, vel quia labore defessa fuerint: Falsò quoque, & omninò adversante experientia creditum est, astacos, ostrea &c. se pro varia Lunae acie implere, aut extenuare. Quod si piscium corpora aliquandò minui videantur, hoc evenit vel ob alimenti defectum, vel undis tempestate commotis, aut etiam propria contentione nimium agitati, id quod iis verosimillimum videbitur, qui norint pisces in freto Caletensi, ubi aqua maximè agitatur, captos, plerumque minus plenos esse, quàm eos, qui propè Bononiam, ubi mare paulò magis tranquillum conquiescit, capiuntur. Ceteri demùm effectus non humido Lunae influxui, sed praesenti tunc atmosphaerae constitutioni, nempè, vel nimio humore vel noxiis aliis effluviis refertae, tribuendi sunt.

759 Wherefore another cause is to be assigned: it is most likely that the bones of certain animals are empty of marrow either because the animals have lacked nourishment or because they have been worn out by labor. Falsely too, and wholly against experience, has it been believed that the Moon, according to her various phases, fills out or thins lobsters, oysters, etc. If the bodies of fish sometimes seem diminished, this happens either from a lack of nourishment, or because they are too much agitated, the waves being stirred up by a storm, or even by their own exertion; which will seem most likely to those who know that the fish caught in the Strait of Calais, where the water is most agitated, are generally less full than those caught near Boulogne, where the sea rests somewhat more tranquil. Finally, the other effects are to be attributed not to a moist influence of the Moon, but to the constitution of the atmosphere present at the time, filled, namely, either with excessive moisture or with other noxious effluvia.

## DISSERTATIO II. — DISSERTATION II

> De Terra elementari.

ON THE ELEMENTAL EARTH .

## CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

> De Natura Terrae.

On the Nature of the Earth.

> 760 De natura Elementorum tractaturi primò nobis occurrit Terra; ea est enim, quae, ut ait Plinius, nos nascentes excipit, natos alit, semelque editos sustinet. Quare sit conclusio.

760 As we are about to treat of the nature of the Elements, the Earth first presents itself to us; for it is she that, as Pliny says, receives us when we are born, nourishes us once born, and, once we are brought forth, sustains us. Let the conclusion therefore be:

> 761 Terra verosimiliter est corpus compositum ex crassioribus, atque ad motum minus aptis particulis, irregulari potissimùm figurâ adfectis. Prob. ex eo quia hoc optimè congruere videtur inertiae, [p. 238] gravitati, soliditati terrae. Adhaec: quum ignis vi difficillimè solvatur terra, nec particulae ejus in auram difflari possint, crassiores eae sint, est necesse: quumque simul unitae massam consistentem fixamque efficiant, atque lumini transitum intercludant, irregularis figurae verosimiliter sunt, quae variè inter se impliceantur, & anfractuosos meatus forment. Quum demùm terra reliquorum miscibilium velut basis & fundamentum habeatur, necnon durities, fixitas, soliditas, gravitas corporum magna ex parte, à terra ducatur, non tantum crassiores illius particulas esse cónvenit, magisque invicem implexas, sed minus etiam ad motum aptas.

761 The earth is in all likelihood a body composed of coarser particles, less apt for motion, affected for the most part with an irregular figure. Proof: from the fact that this seems to agree best with the inertia, gravity, and [p. 238] and solidity of the earth. Further: since the earth is dissolved with the greatest difficulty by the force of fire, and its particles cannot be blown off into the air, they must be coarser; and since, united together, they make a consistent and fixed mass and shut off the passage of light, they are in all likelihood of an irregular figure, such as to be variously entangled with one another and to form winding passages. Finally, since the earth is held to be, as it were, the basis and foundation of the other miscible bodies, and since the hardness, fixity, solidity, and gravity of bodies is derived in great part from the earth, it is fitting that its particles be not only coarser and more entangled with one another, but also less apt for motion.

## *Adnotatio.* — REMARK

> 762 Cartesius terram ex tertii elementi partibus, corpusculis nempè striatis inter sé implexis, & invicem contortis componit [§. 44.]. Gassendus cum Epicureis ex anlulis, & atomis hamatis, sibique mutuò adhaerentibus, ut reliqua corpora firma & arida, constare vult. P. Regnault ramosas esse terrae particulas adserit, quae lucem non transmittant, massamque consistentem efficiant. Cl. à Brixia ait, cujus figurae sint corpuscula terrae primitiva divinare certò non possumus. Probabile est, subdit deindè, primitivas particulas affectas esse figura cubica: quòd haec, ut ait Plato, firmissimas, tutissimasque bases possideat, ac propterea maximè propria illorum corpusculorum videatur, quae ad aridum, iners, fixumque constituendum corpus, sunt à natura destinata. De hoc verò nos nihil certi constituimus.

762 Descartes composes the earth from parts of the third element, namely from striated corpuscles entangled among themselves and twisted together [§. 44.]. Gassendi, with the Epicureans, would have it made up, like the other firm and dry bodies, of little rings and hooked atoms mutually adhering to one another. Fr. Regnault asserts that the particles of earth are branching, such as do not transmit light and make a consistent mass. The distinguished da Brescia says that we cannot divine with certainty of what figure the primitive corpuscles of earth are. It is probable, he then adds, that the primitive particles are affected with a cubic figure: since this, as Plato says, possesses the firmest and safest bases, and therefore seems most proper to those corpuscles which are destined by nature to constitute a dry, inert, and fixed body. On this, however, we determine nothing certain.

## CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

> De figura, situ, & magnitudine, globi terraquei.

On the Figure, Situation, and Magnitude of the Terraqueous Globe. 763

> 763 Tellurem tanquam corpus mundanum, quod *orbis*, vel *globus terraqueus* dici solet, hic contemplamur. *Tellus* igitur est, *corpus mundanum ex terra & aqua, sparsim interjecto fluido igneo, in vastam molem compactum, aëre undique cinctum, hominum ac brutorum commune habitaculum*. Terrae nomine imprimis hìc venit congeries varii generis corporum solidorum crassiorum sabuli, argillae, terrarum pinguium diversi colorum, lapidum, salium, &c.: quam congeriem in [p. 239] tellure reperiri, nemo, nisi ignarus, & historiae, & narrationum negaverit. Aqua intelligitur substantia illa fluida, & humida, quam Deus O. M. in prima creatione á solido, ac sicco separavit, atque in mare, magnam superficiei terrestris partem occupans congessit.

We here contemplate the Earth as a mundane body, which is usually called the orb, or the terraqueous globe. The Earth, then, is a mundane body compacted of earth and water, with a fiery fluid interspersed here and there, into a vast mass, surrounded on every side by air, the common habitation of men and of brutes. Under the name of earth there comes here first of all the heap of solid and coarser bodies of various kinds: sand, clay, fat earths of diverse colors, stones, salts, etc.: a heap which is found in the Earth, [p. 239] as no one, unless he were ignorant both of history and of narratives, would deny. By water is understood that fluid and moist substance which God, Best and Greatest, in the first creation separated from the solid and dry, and gathered into the sea, which occupies a great part of the terrestrial surface.

> 764 Ignem per interiores terrae partes diffundi patet, tùm ex eo, quod in mixtis corporibus comprehendatur, tùm ex thermis, calore fodinarum, exhalationibus variis, montibus ignivomis. Compactum esse in molem vastam corpus telluris, nemo nescit; suam autem compactionem, & firmitatem á causa gravitatis habet, quâ nempe partes circumquaque comprimuntur, & compelluntur. Illud verò difficilius resolvitur, in quam figuram moles haec compacta sit: an videlicèt sphaericam contineat? Vel sphaeroidicam, atque hanc, an ad polos depressam, & ad aequatorem elevatam, num contrà ad polos adsurgentem, subsidentem in aequatore.

764 That fire is diffused through the interior parts of the earth is plain, both from the fact that it is contained in mixed bodies, and from hot springs, the heat of mines, various exhalations, and fire-vomiting mountains. That the body of the Earth is compacted into a vast mass, no one is unaware; and it has its compaction and firmness from the cause of gravity, by which, namely, its parts are compressed and driven together on every side. But this is more difficult to resolve: into what figure this mass has been compacted: whether, namely, it holds a spherical one? Or a spheroidal one; and this, whether depressed at the poles and raised at the equator, or, on the contrary, rising at the poles and sinking at the equator.

> 765 Tellurem esse quoad sensum, & physicè sphaericam commonstrare nituntur Physici. *Primò* ex ipsis Lunae eclipsibus, haec enim eclipsim patitur, quia telluris umbram ingreditur, eamque sic dividit, perindè, atque si esset planum basi ipsius umbrae parallelum: quum nempè circa tellurem Luna revolvatur. Atqui umbra terrae in omnibus eclipsibus lunaribus hucusque per tot secula observatis, semper adparuit rotunda: ergo. *Secundò* quia omnes adparentiae tàm caelestes, quàm terrestres aptissimè, ac citra errorem sub figura telluris Sphericâ explicantur, ut patet in globis & Sphaeris artefactis. *Tertio* quia iter facientes vident priùs, & quidem aequaliter versùs omnem partem, montium culmina, & turrium apices, quàm bases. Diximus *Physico* sensu, non *Mathematico* rotundam esse tellurem. Figurae verò *quoad sensum* sphericae nequaquam officiunt praealti montes, nam terra ut ait Seneca, se habet ad montes, sicut ingens pila ad pilum. Neque obstat etiam camporum planities, dum terra nobis in planum excurrere videtur: id enim provenit partim ab ejus magnitudine, partim ab horizonte viso, qui relatè ad totum globum, est pars valdè exigua, neque sensibilem curvaturam habet.

765 Physicists endeavor to demonstrate that the Earth is spherical as regards sense, and physically. First, from the very eclipses of the Moon; for she suffers an eclipse because she enters the shadow of the Earth, and divides it just as if she were a plane parallel to the base of that shadow: since, namely, the Moon revolves around the Earth. But the shadow of the earth in all the lunar eclipses observed hitherto through so many centuries has always appeared round: therefore. Secondly, because all appearances, celestial as well as terrestrial, are explained most aptly and without error under a spherical figure of the Earth, as is plain in artificial globes and spheres. Thirdly, because those who travel see the summits of mountains and the tops of towers sooner than their bases, and that equally in every direction. We have said that the Earth is round in the physical sense, not the mathematical. Very high mountains in no way hinder its figure from being spherical as regards sense, for the earth, as Seneca says, is to the mountains as a huge ball to a hair. Nor does the flatness of the plains stand in the way, when the earth seems to us to stretch out into a plane: for this comes partly from its magnitude, partly from the visible horizon, which, relative to the whole globe, is a very small part and has no sensible curvature.

> 766 Hinc telluris figurae quoad sensum sphaericae non officit neque Newtoni, Hugenii, S Gravesandi, aliorumque opinionem, existimantium terraqueam molem non sphaerae instar conformatam, sed sphaeroidis sub aequatore turgescentis, ad polos autem subsidentis figuram referre; neque Cassini utriusque, Maraldi, Mairani, Eisenschmidii, ac plurium hypothesim, quâ telluri oblonga versus polos, depressa sub aequatore figura tribuitur. Nam praeterquàm quod argumenta supra exposita Figuram telluri rotundam sensu physico adstruant, certum est, neutram harum opinionum physicae, ac sensibili telluris rotunditati magnopere adversari.

766 Hence the figure of the Earth, spherical as regards sense, is not hindered either by the opinion of Newton, Huygens, ’s Gravesande, and others, who think that the terraqueous mass is not formed like a sphere but presents the figure of a spheroid swelling under the equator and sinking at the poles; or by the hypothesis of both Cassinis, of Maraldi, Mairan, Eisenschmidt, and many more, by which a figure oblong toward the poles and depressed under the equator is attributed to the Earth. For besides the fact that the arguments set out above establish a round figure for the Earth in the physical sense, it is certain that neither of these opinions is greatly opposed to the physical and sensible roundness of the Earth.

> 767 Etenim excessus ille majoris diámetri supra minorem tam est exiguus, ut nihil impediat, quominus habeantur pro diámetris physicè aequalibus, adeòque terraquea moles pro physicae sphaerica. Newtonus [p. 240] quippe majorem telluris diametrum, ad minorem esse ponit, ut 230 ad 229, adeoque terra sub aequatore altior foret, quam sub polis 17 milliaribus & [?] parte. Hugenius verò eandem fere diametrorum rationem statuit, quae est numeri 578 ad 577: quae si deindè ratio, ut solet, per regulas proportionum in milliaribus investigetur, patebit, excessum majoris semidiametri telluris supra minorem, nec 7 quidem milliaria aequare; quae tam exigua differentia tellurem utique quoad sensum sphaericam relinquit.

767 For that excess of the greater diameter over the lesser is so slight that nothing prevents their being held as physically equal diameters, and hence the terraqueous mass as physically spherical. Newton [p. 240] indeed holds that the greater diameter of the Earth is to the lesser as 230 to 229, and hence that the earth would be higher under the equator than under the poles by 17 miles and a sixth part. Huygens, on the other hand, establishes almost the same ratio of the diameters, namely that of the number 578 to 577; and if this ratio is then worked out in miles by the rules of proportion, as is usually done, it will be plain that the excess of the greater semidiameter of the Earth over the lesser does not equal even 7 miles; and so slight a difference leaves the Earth, at any rate as regards sense, spherical.

> 768 Neque argumentum pro prima opinione, à telluris diurno motu desumptum, evincit quidpiam, ex qua revolutione consequi putant Patroni hujus hypotheseos, ut partes per vim centrifugam sub aequatore majorem, quàm versus polos, longius à telluris axe recedant, atque adeò elevatiores sint sub aequatore, quàm sub polis, molemque sphaeroidicam telluris efforment. Non, inquam, evincit quidpiam: posito enim telluris circa axem motu, non sequitur evidenter, partes circa aequatorem turgescere, versus polos comprimi: massa quippe telluris non mollis, sed firmiter compacta est, nec conforme experientiae videtur, Sphaeram circa axem circumvolutam in sphaeroidem ad cardines revolutionis compressum mutari, quantacumque celeritate convertatur.

768 Nor does the argument for the first opinion, taken from the daily motion of the Earth, prove anything; from this revolution the patrons of this hypothesis think it follows that the parts, by a greater centrifugal force under the equator than toward the poles, recede farther from the axis of the Earth, and so are more elevated under the equator than under the poles, and form the spheroidal mass of the Earth. It does not, I say, prove anything: for, granting the motion of the Earth about its axis, it does not evidently follow that the parts about the equator swell out and are compressed toward the poles: for the mass of the Earth is not soft but firmly compacted, nor does it seem conformable to experience that a sphere revolved about its axis should be changed into a spheroid compressed at the poles of the revolution, with whatever speed it be turned.

> 769 *Situm* telluris quod adtinet, communis opinio est, eam in ipso universi centro minimum quoad sensum, collocatam esse. Quamvis enim per Copernicanam hypothesim Sol in universi centro constituatur, tellus autem in orbe magno circa Solem convertatur; ex mente tamen Astronomorum semidiameter orbis magni, si ad semidiametrum caeli stelliferi referatur, veluti evanescit, efficitque, ut tellus à centro universi nullo sensibili intervallo distet.

769 As regards the situation of the Earth, the common opinion is that it is placed in the very center of the universe, at least as regards sense. For although, by the Copernican hypothesis, the Sun is set in the center of the universe and the Earth is turned in the great orb around the Sun, yet in the judgment of the astronomers the semidiameter of the great orb, if it is compared with the semidiameter of the starry heaven, as it were vanishes, and brings it about that the Earth is distant from the center of the universe by no sensible interval.

> 770 Rationes porro situm hunc telluris evincentes sunt. *Prima* quia in utroque aequinoctio tempus, quo Sol supra horizontem moratur, *penitus* adaequat tempus, quo is sub aequatore moratur. *Secunda* quia nobis in telluris superficie existentibus quamcunque demum regionem incolamus, Stellae semper sub eadem magnitudine seu in ortu, seu in occasu, seu in medio Caeli adparent, dummodo absint vapores, nebulae, atque exhalationes, visum impedientes, & figuram corporum mutantes. *Tertia*, quia in quacunque terrae parte seclusis montium & vallium impedimentis semper videmus Caeli dimidium: ita ex 12 Zodiaci signis, 6 supra horizontem perpetuo conspiciuntur, & ex Stellis diametraliter oppositis, quales ferè sunt oculus Tauri, & cor Scorpii, quando una in horizonte orientali ascendit, altera in occidentali descendit.

770 The reasons, moreover, that establish this situation of the Earth are these. The first, because at either equinox the time during which the Sun stays above the horizon exactly equals the time during which it stays below the horizon. The second, because to us who exist on the surface of the Earth, whatever region at last we may inhabit, the stars always appear of the same magnitude, whether at their rising, or at their setting, or in the middle of the heaven, provided there are absent vapors, mists, and exhalations, which impede the sight and change the figure of bodies. The third, because in whatever part of the earth, setting aside the hindrances of mountains and valleys, we always see half of the heaven: thus of the 12 signs of the Zodiac, 6 are perpetually seen above the horizon, and of stars diametrically opposite, such as are, more or less, the Eye of the Bull and the Heart of the Scorpion, when one rises on the eastern horizon, the other sets on the western.

> 771 *Magnitudo* telluris si cum Caelo stellifero comparetur, adeò exigua est, ut perinde, ac punctum ad illud se habeat. Absoluta verò ejus magnitudo incerta est omnino. Profectò in definienda magnitudine unius gradus è maximis circulis orbis terraquei, plurimum inter se discrepant Auctores. Unde mirum non est, si in telluris magnitudine stabilienda dissentiant: ex valore siquidem unius [p. 241] gradus colligitur valor peripheriae circuli maximi, atque hinc quantitas diametri, & semidiametri, tùm convexae superficiéi, ac demùm soliditas, ut Geómetrae norunt. Plurium hic mensuras adferre non licet; unam & alteram ad communiorem ferè calculum exactam subjicio. Telluris diameter continet milliaria germanica ferè 1720. Superficies, milliaria quadrata ferè 92,880,000. Soliditas, ferè 26,563,680,000. Gradus unus caelestis continet 25 leucas communes Galliae: leuca autem communis continet 2400 passus geometricos.

771 The magnitude of the Earth, if it is compared with the starry heaven, is so slight that it stands to it just as a point. Its absolute magnitude, however, is altogether uncertain. Indeed, in determining the magnitude of one degree of the great circles of the terraqueous orb, authors disagree very much among themselves. Hence it is no wonder if they dissent in establishing the magnitude of the Earth: since from the value of one degree [p. 241] is gathered the value of the periphery of a great circle, and hence the quantity of the diameter and of the semidiameter, as well as of the convex surface, and finally the solidity, as geometers know. It is not possible to bring forward many measures here; I submit one or two, worked out, nearly, to the more common calculation. The diameter of the Earth contains nearly 1720 German miles. The surface, nearly 92,880,000 square miles. The solidity, nearly 26,563,680,000. One celestial degree contains 25 common leagues of France: and a common league contains 2400 geometric paces.

## CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

> De nonnullis corporibus terrestribus, ac primum de petrificationibus.

On Certain Terrestrial Bodies, and First on Petrifications.

> 772 Non possum mentionem non facere de certo corporum terrestrium genere, scilicèt de conchis, óstreis, aliisque testaceis corporibus, quae inter quorundam montium strata occurrunt. De horum origine triplex est Physicorum opinio. Wooduardus ex diluvio universali hoc phaenomenon derivat, scilicèt: quando aquis operiebantur omnes terrae; tùm quidem petrae, marmora, metalla, corpora omnia, in minutas particulas, & moleculas dividebantur, divisa confusim in illa aquarum vi ferebantur hùc illùc, sub finem autem corpora haec aquae immixta secundum gravitatis leges praecipitabantur: hinc factum, ut corpora ista marina testacea conchilia, utpotè non nihil graviora, eam partem peterent, quae petris, lapidibus, & aliis convenit, inter quae ea etiam hodie inveniuntur ipsam hanc ob causam. Altera hypothesis, quam nuper Leibnitzius propugnavit, adserit in omnibus illis locis olim mare fuisse, in quibus conchae, ostreae reperiuntur, ab illis locis verò mare ipsum in praesens recessisse corporibus ibidem relictis.

cannot fail to make mention of a certain kind of terrestrial bodies, 772 I namely of shells, oysters, and other testaceous bodies, which occur among the strata of certain mountains. On their origin the opinion of physicists is threefold. Woodward derives this phenomenon from the universal deluge, namely: when all the lands were covered by the waters, then indeed rocks, marbles, metals, all bodies were divided into minute particles and molecules; thus divided, they were carried confusedly hither and thither by that force of the waters, but toward the end these bodies, immersed in the water, were precipitated according to the laws of gravity: hence it came about that those marine testaceous shells, being somewhat heavier, sought the part that belongs to rocks, stones, and the like, among which they are found even today for this very reason. The second hypothesis, which Leibniz recently defended, asserts that the sea was once in all those places in which shells and oysters are found, but that the sea itself has at present receded from those places, leaving the bodies there.

> 773 Tertia statuit cum Lazaro Moro, ideò testacea corpora inter montium strata haberi, quod montes ipsi unà cum corporibus illis ejecti olim è maris fundo actione ignis subterranei fuerint. Hypotheses has excutere, & expendere non libet in praesens, uberiorem disceptationem exposcentes. Hoc unum innuere juverit: non unam eandemque in universum causam, & originem ostreorum, testaceorumque ejusmodi corporum in montibus locisque prominentioribus repertorum esse. A verisimilitudine profectò abludere haud videtur, exuvias illas marinas, quas in superficiebus montium aut profunditate non magna hinc inde reperiunt Naturae [p. 242] scrutatores potissimum à diluvio maribusque aliquando illis in locis, quod Historiae, & Geographiae cognitio docebit, diffusis repetendas esse.

773 The third holds, with Lazzaro Moro, that testaceous bodies are found among the strata of mountains because the mountains themselves, together with those bodies, were once cast up from the bottom of the sea by the action of subterranean fire. It is not my pleasure at present to sift and weigh these hypotheses, which demand a fuller discussion. It will be enough to hint at this one thing: that there is not one and the same cause and origin, universally, of the oysters and testaceous bodies of this kind found in mountains and in more prominent places. It does not seem, indeed, to stray from likelihood that those marine spoils which the investigators of Nature find here and there on the surfaces of mountains, or at no great depth, [p. 242] are to be traced chiefly to the deluge, and to seas at some time spread over those places, as a knowledge of History and Geography will show.

> 774 Illas verò, quae profundioribus in cavernis non raró deprehenduntur, existimo terraemotibus saepè vehementibus ibidem deponi: hac enim ratione, terra exagitata, montibus disruptis, & absorptis animalium exuviae una simul consepeliri poterant, & tractu diuturno temporis in petras converti, hoc est *petrificari*. Si autem ex genere marinarum exuviarum sint, hae unà cum maris parte per subterraneos meatus in motibus his terrae effectos, & excavatos eò delatae sunt ubi diuturnitate temporis aquâ exsiccatâ, & in stratis terrae diffusa in vapores coacta, ejusmodi exuvias deposuit.

774 But those which are not rarely discovered in deeper caverns were, I think, deposited there by earthquakes, often violent ones: for in this way, the earth being shaken, the mountains burst asunder, and swallowed up, the spoils of animals could be buried together, and in the course of a long time be converted into stones, that is, be petrified. But if they are of the kind of marine spoils, these were carried there, together with a part of the sea, through subterranean passages made and hollowed out in these motions of the earth, where the water, having dried away in the length of time, and having been diffused into the strata of the earth or driven off into vapors, deposited spoils of this kind.

> 775 Demum quod ejusdem generis in uno, alterius in altero reperiantur monte, id non praeciso sensu accipiendum judico; neque ideò, quod unius generis potissimum uno in loco hucusque repertae sint exuviae, dicendum est alterius generis non latère, aut reperiri posse. His in universum breviter inspectis, aliqua de magnete dicamus oportet. Lapis enim hic ob praecelentem suam virtutem, utilitatemque, & in admiratione est, & in pretio habetur; ut proinde turpe videri posset, naturae arcana inquirentibus nullam prorsus de eo mentionem facere. Sit itaque.

775 Finally, that spoils of one kind are found in one mountain and those of another kind in another, I judge is not to be taken in a precise sense; nor, because spoils of one kind have hitherto been found chiefly in one place, must it be said that those of another kind do not lie hidden there or cannot be found. These things having been briefly surveyed in general, we must say something about the magnet. For this stone, on account of its excellent virtue and utility, is both held in admiration and valued at a high price; so that it might accordingly seem shameful for those who inquire into the secrets of nature to make no mention of it at all. Let it, then, be:

> CAPUT IV.

CHAPTER IV.

> ¿Quid de Magnetis vi sentiendum sit?

What Is to Be Thought of the Force of the Magnet?

> 776 *Magnes* nomen & ortum suum à Magnesia Macedoniae Provincia, ubi effoditur, habet: juxta quosdam autem à Magnete pastore, qui primus in Ida monte, ex baculi ferrea cuspide lapidi ejusmodi, qui magnes nunc dicitur, adhaerente illum detexisse fertur. Est is lapidi subnigrum colorem praeferenti haud absimilis, gravis, ferro praegnans; siquidem igni subjectus chalybem exstillat, & praeterea è ferri fodinis eruitur. Vis ejus, quae *magnetica* dicitur, & multis adhuc difficultatibus involuta est, ad tria praecipue capita revocatur: ad illius *directionem*, magnetis vel ferri *adtractionem*, & virtutis suae *communicationem*. Vis *directrix* in eo sita est, quod magnes in aëre suspensus sese ad meridianum loci componat, ac polum suum australem, ad borealem telluris convertat, uti etiam in acu magnetica accidit. Adtamen haec versùs polum directio non est ubivis constans; nunc quippè pluribus, nunc paucioribus gradibus pro regionum diversitate plus minusve nunc hùc nunc illùc (hoc est nunc [p. 243] orientem versus, nunc versus occidentem) declinant acus nanticae quin post notabile tempus in eodem quandoque loco directionem mutant, quae *adfectio declinatio* adpellatur.

he magnet has its name and origin from Magnesia, a province of 776 T          Macedonia, where it is dug up; but according to some, from Magnes, a shepherd, who is said to have first discovered it on Mount Ida, when the iron tip of his staff adhered to a stone of this kind, which is now called a magnet. It is a stone not unlike iron, showing a blackish color, heavy, pregnant with iron; since indeed, when subjected to fire, it exudes steel, and moreover it is dug out of iron mines. Its force, which is called magnetic and is still wrapped in many difficulties, is reduced chiefly to three heads: to its direction, to the attraction of a magnet or of iron, and to the communication of its virtue. The directive force consists in this, that a magnet suspended in the air sets itself toward the meridian of the place and turns its southern pole toward the northern pole of the Earth, as also happens in the magnetic needle. However, this direction toward the pole is not constant everywhere; for now by more, now by fewer degrees, according to the diversity of regions, more or less, now hither now thither (that is, now toward the east, [p. 243] now toward the west) the nautical needles decline; indeed, after a notable time they sometimes change their direction in the same place; and this affection is called declination.

> 777 Hùc quoque pertinet alia ejusdem adfectio, quae *inclinatio* nuncupatur, varia quidem, sed constans, vi cujus magnes, vel acus magnetica in aequilibrio liberè suspensa, versus unam partem praeponderat, ac inclinatur, ea lege ut inclinatio sit magis vel minus notabilis, quo terrae tractus vel remotior vel vicinior est aequatori; sub hoc namque perfectum habetur equilibrium. Vis *adtractrix* est, qua magnes vel alterum magnetem, vel ferrum ad se trahit; hoc tamen discrimine, ut ferrum ex utrâque sui parte ad se magnes rapiat: magnetem verò ex una parte ad se ducat, ex altera repellat. Vis demùm *magnetica sui communicatrix* est, qua chalybem vel ferrum eâdem, qua ipse pollet, virtute imbuit: directrice nempe, & adtractrice. His expositis causam horum phaenomenorum inquirimus: qua in re omninò obscura, constituemus illud, quod verisimilitudinis speciem habeat, dictosque effectus ad captum aliqua ratione exponat. Id priusquam exigamus, praevia constituitur hypothesis.

777 To this also pertains another affection of the same, which is called inclination, various indeed, but constant, by virtue of which a magnet, or a magnetic needle freely suspended in equilibrium, preponderates toward one side and is inclined, by this law: that the inclination is more or less notable according as the tract of the earth is more remote from or nearer to the equator; for under it a perfect equilibrium is had. The attractive force is that by which a magnet draws to itself either another magnet or iron; with this difference, however, that a magnet snatches iron to itself by either of its sides, but draws a magnet to itself by one side and repels it by the other. Finally, the force communicative of itself is that by which it imbues steel or iron with the same virtue in which it is itself strong: namely, the directive and the attractive. These things set out, we inquire into the cause of these phenomena: in which altogether obscure matter we shall lay down whatever may have an appearance of likelihood and may in some fashion expound the said effects to the understanding. Before we carry this out, a preliminary hypothesis is laid down.

> 778 Haud incongruum existimamus dicere, vel cum Gilberto, quod totus ipse globus terraqueus sit ingens quidàm magnes, qui Auctor propterea magnetem terrenum adpellavit: vel, ut cum pluribus aliis P. Zuchius sentit, quod nucleus ipsius telluris verus sit magnes.

778 We think it not incongruous to say either, with Gilbert, that the whole terraqueous globe itself is a certain huge magnet, which that author therefore called the terrestrial magnet; or, as Fr. Zucchi holds with many others, that the nucleus of the earth itself is a true magnet.

> 779 Declaratur 1: quia ferramenta ex solo contactu, & adplicatione ad terram, vim sortiuntur magneticam: praesertim, si erecta super terram diutius constiterint. Unde forcipes, & similia ferrea instrumenta, quae ad ignem tractandum juxta focos erecta retineri solent, vim comparant ad adtrahendas aciculas chalybeas. Sic etiam virgae ferreae, quae diuturno tempore praesertim in lineae meridianae plani constitutae haeserunt, vim conversivam ad polum acquirunt. Secundo, quia acus magneticae filo suspensae, inclinantur versus globum terrae perindè, atque inclinari observantur ad magnetem.

779 This is explained, 1: because iron implements acquire a magnetic force from mere contact and application to the earth: especially if they have stood erect upon the earth for a rather long time. Hence tongs and similar iron instruments, which are usually kept standing erect beside hearths for handling the fire, acquire a force for attracting little steel needles. So too iron rods which have remained a long time, especially in the line of the meridian plane, acquire a conversive force toward the pole. Secondly, because magnetic needles suspended by a thread are inclined toward the globe of the earth just as they are observed to be inclined toward a magnet.

> 780 Ut ea propter nisus *tonicus* magnetis seu verticitatis non sit versus polos caelestes, sed versus terrestres: proindè vis magnetica terrestri globo insit. Tertio in fodinis, rupibus, lapicidinis adparent inter media immania saxa descriptae lineae, quasi fibrae, longissimè protensae ab austro in boream, & dispositae parellelè ad axem terrestrem. Ex quo conficitur verosimiliter, magneticam vim per effluvia illapsam illis tractibus, determinare dispositionem eam á polo in polum. Ex his jam ducitur.

780 So that for this reason the tonic nisus of the magnet, or of verticity, is not toward the celestial poles but toward the terrestrial ones: hence the magnetic force resides in the terrestrial globe. Thirdly, in mines, rocks, and quarries there appear, amid huge stones, lines traced like fibers, extended very far from south to north and disposed parallel to the terrestrial axis. From this it is gathered, in all likelihood, that the magnetic force, having slipped into those tracts through effluvia, determines that disposition from pole to pole. From these, now, is deduced:

[p. 244]

> Corollarium.

COROLLARY.

> 781 Ex magnetismo globi terraquei concluditur, quod effluvia quaedam ab uno polo telluris egressa, versus alterum ejus polum circa tellurem proficiscantur, ibique rursus in eundem ingressa per alterum mundi polum egrediantur, sicque perpetua cieatur in tellure effluviorum hujusmodi circulatio non secus, ac perpetua aquae subterranae cum superficie terrestri á polo in polum circulatio péragi dicitur: quanquam causa, qua fiat, ut fluidum ê terrae visceribus erumpens feratur ab uno alium polum versus, industriam, & intelligentiam Physicorum adhuc effugiat, oportunè aliàs ê mechanicis principiis deducenda. Porrò effluvia haec communicantur quidem etiam corporibus aliis in hoc globo existentibus, sed praecipuè iis quae maximè terrea sunt, ut magneti, & ferro, in quibus apta particularum, & pororum dispositio tùm ad recipienda, tùm ad emittenda illa sese praebet.

781 From the magnetism of the terraqueous globe it is concluded that certain effluvia, having gone out from one pole of the Earth, travel around the Earth toward its other pole, and there, entering into it again, go out through the other pole of the world; and thus a perpetual circulation of effluvia of this kind is set up in the Earth, not otherwise than a perpetual circulation of subterranean water, together with the terrestrial surface, is said to be carried on from pole to pole: although the cause by which it comes about that the fluid bursting forth from the bowels of the earth is borne from one pole toward the other still escapes the industry and intelligence of physicists, and must be deduced elsewhere, at the proper time, from mechanical principles. Moreover, these effluvia are indeed communicated also to other bodies existing in this globe, but chiefly to those which are most earthy, such as the magnet and iron, in which an apt disposition of the particles and pores offers itself both for receiving and for emitting them.

> 782 Et quemadmodum in ipso globo terraqueo effluvia dicta ab uno polo constanter egrediuntur, & circum tellurem lata, in alterum rursùs polum ingrediuntur, ita etiam magnes, velut parvus orbis, sua habet effluvia, atmospheram nempè vorticosam, quae in uno ipsius polo ingrediuntur, egrediuntur ex altero, & eadem quidem semper lege; id quod scobs ferri, cui immergitur magnes, adprimè declarat, quae versùs polos erecta est; in locis à polo remotioribus, inclinata: deindè ipsa particularum magnetis dispositio hoc evincere potest, quae in unam partem magis quàm in alteram inclinatae sint, adeòque ita dispositae, ut ingressum per unam praebere possint, non verò vicissim egressum, quam dispositionem partium fieri posse patet ex eo, quod dum in ipsa fodina magnes formaretur, magnetica materia terram ab uno polo ad alterum secundum lineas axi parallelas trajiciens, & perpetuo circuitu remeans magnetis meatus aptare potuerit, eo pacto, ut interiores eorum villos illam in partem, ad quam ferebatur, depresserit.

782 And just as in the terraqueous globe itself the said effluvia constantly go out from one pole and, carried around the Earth, enter again into the other pole, so too the magnet, like a little orb, has its effluvia, namely a vortical atmosphere, which enter at one of its poles and go out from the other, and indeed always by the same law; this is shown excellently by the iron filings into which a magnet is plunged, which stand erect toward the poles and, in places more remote from the pole, are inclined. Then the very disposition of the particles of the magnet can prove this, since they are inclined more to one side than to the other, and are so disposed that they can afford ingress through one side but not, in turn, egress; that such a disposition of the parts can come about is plain from this, that while the magnet was being formed in its mine, the magnetic matter, crossing the earth from one pole to the other along lines parallel to the axis and returning in a perpetual circuit, could fit the passages of the magnet in such a way as to press down their interior little hairs toward that side to which it was carried.

> 783 Ponit cum D. DuFay Cl. Helvetius, magnetum poros intus esse villis ornatos, & illos ita esse prostratos, & inflexos, ut eorum mucrones vergant versùs polos boreales magnetum. Illi itaque villi motum magneticae materiae à *polo ingressus*, seu quem effluvia subeunt, ad *polum egressus*, sivè per quem erumpunt non remorantur, quum eam in partem sint inflexi: at ejusdem materiae per eosdem meatus regressui obsistunt; siquidem in partem oppositam difficillimè, aut omninò non inclinantur. His positis, sit conclusio.

783 The distinguished Helvétius holds, with Mr. Du Fay, that the pores of magnets are furnished within with little hairs, and that these are so laid down and bent that their points incline toward the north poles of the magnets. Those little hairs, therefore, do not delay the motion of the magnetic matter from the pole of ingress, that is, the one which the effluvia enter, to the pole of egress, that is, the one through which they burst out, since they are bent toward that side; but they resist the return of the same matter through the same passages, since they are inclined toward the opposite side with the greatest difficulty, or not at all. These things laid down, let the conclusion be:

> 784 Dico 1. Vis magnetis directrix à subtilissimis effluviis è telluris polo uno erumpentibus, & per alterum irrumpentibus repetenda videtur. Nimirùm vis directrix magnetis est, qua magnes sese ad utrumque mundi polum convertit. Atqui haec congruè [p. 245] repetitur à profluviis dicto modo expositis; ea quippè per eosdem magnetis meatus, quos sibi in fodina fecerat, deinceps moventur, magnetem proinde in sui motus normam secundum lineas axi terrae parallelas componunt, ut ex paulò prius dictis colligitur. Equidem in propatulo quum sit, nullum corpus posse perenniter vergere versùs debitum punctum, nisi contactu alterius corporis acti versùs idem punctum, uti rectè Helvetius, perspectum est, dari fluida proximè tellurem circumfusa qua directione sui motus aguntur ex australi polo versùs borealem.

784 I say 1. The directive force of the magnet seems to be traced to most subtle effluvia bursting out from one pole of the Earth and breaking in through the other. The directive force of the magnet is, namely, that by which the magnet turns itself toward each pole of the world. But this is fittingly traced [p. 245] to the effluxes set forth in the said manner; for these, moving thereafter through the same passages of the magnet which they had made for themselves in the mine, accordingly set the magnet, by the rule of their own motion, along lines parallel to the axis of the earth, as is gathered from what was said a little before. Indeed, since it is plain that no body can perpetually incline toward its due point except by the contact of another body driven toward the same point, as Helvétius rightly says, it is evident that there are fluids spread closely around the Earth which are driven, in the direction of their motion, from the southern pole toward the northern.

> 785 Certè id manifestè etiam ex eo ostenditur, quod si in pyxide nautica acus ferrea, magnetica vi nondum imbuta, fulcro imponatur, haec in aequilibrio horizonti parallela videbitur; ubi verò acus magneti adfricta fuerit, & directricem vim obtinuerit, in Septentrionalibus quidem locis pars acus in Septentrionem directa aliquantum infra horizontem deprimetur, ut addendus sit cuspidi australi ipsius acus globulus cereus, quo aequilibrium restituatur. In Aequatore, seu aequali à polo utroque distantia nihil acus deprimitur. Aequatore transmisso versùs austrum elevatur borealis cuspidis pars, & Australis deprimitur. Quae certè omnia effluxum, atque influxum circulationemque effluviorum circa telluris superficiem non vanè comprobant.

785 Certainly this is shown manifestly also from the fact that if an iron needle, not yet imbued with magnetic force, is placed on a pivot in a nautical box, it will be seen in equilibrium, parallel to the horizon; but when the needle has been rubbed on a magnet and has obtained the directive force, then in northern places the part of the needle directed toward the north is depressed somewhat below the horizon, so that a little ball of wax must be added to the southern point of the needle to restore the equilibrium. At the Equator, or at an equal distance from either pole, the needle is not depressed at all. Once the Equator is crossed toward the south, the northern part of the point is raised and the southern is depressed. All of which certainly confirm, not in vain, the efflux and the influx, and the circulation, of the effluvia around the surface of the Earth.

## *Scholion I.* — SCHOLIUM I.

> 786 Declinationis magneticae phaenomenon in Hypothesi nostra congruè exponitur. Nempè certum est, partes globi terrestris esse plurimum heterogeneas, & varias subindè ferri venas occurrere; quin in eodem non solum montes, sed etiam scopuli, & partes aliae sub terra vel mari latentes, magneticis venis nunc copiosius praeditae sunt, nunc, sivè plaga quadam motu terrae concussa, ac partium situ mutato, sivè effossionibus, aliavè ratione, parcè venis ejusmodi sunt interstinctae. Quid? quod in terrarum visceribus magnetes alicubi profundè sub terra delitescant, alibi in montium cacuminibus, visceribus, radicibus, haereant, quod vel á terraemotibus, vel ab ignibus subterraneis, vel ab aquarum subterranearum alluvionibus, vel à fossoribus, ferri venae praedictae frequenter alterentur, minuantur, detorqueantur, quin aër ipse, & diffusa in eo corpuscula aliquantulum à motu recto effluvia magnetica fortassè depellant.

786 The   phenomenon    of  magnetic    declination is fittingly expounded in our Hypothesis. For it is certain that the parts of the terrestrial globe are very heterogeneous, and that various veins of iron occur here and there; indeed, in the same place not only the mountains, but also the rocks and the other parts lying hid under the earth or the sea, are now more copiously endowed with magnetic veins, now, whether because a certain tract has been shaken by a motion of the earth and the situation of its parts changed, or by excavations, or in some other way, are sparsely interspersed with veins of this kind. What of the fact that in the bowels of the lands magnets in some places lie hidden deep under the earth, and elsewhere cling in the summits, the bowels, and the roots of mountains; that the said veins of iron are frequently altered, diminished, and twisted, either by earthquakes, or by subterranean fires, or by floods of subterranean waters, or by diggers; and indeed that the air itself and the corpuscles diffused in it perhaps drive the magnetic effluvia somewhat out of their straight motion?

> 787 Igitur ex his causis varia ejusdem acus, & magnetis in eodem etiam loco contingere potest declinatio, ita ut in locis quoque haud longè dissitis, sit valdè notabilis, & in uno quidem vergat ad Orientem, in altero ad Occidentem. In quorum confirmationem facit experimentum à Kirchero, & Jansonio relatum: quod nempè Neapoli post insignem montis Vesuvii conflagrationem continuò notabilis magneticae declinationis mutatio fuerit observata.

787 Therefore from these causes a varied declination of the same needle and magnet can occur even in the same place, so that in places not far distant from each other it is very notable, and in one it inclines toward the East, in another toward the West. In confirmation of this there serves the experiment reported by Kircher and Jansonius: namely, that at Naples, after the notable conflagration of Mount Vesuvius, a notable change of the magnetic declination was continually observed.

[p. 246]

## *Scholion II.* — SCHOLIUM II

> 788 Inclinationis phaenomenon explicatur quoque: positis enim magneticis effluviis è terra prorumpentibus, nil mirùm, quod acus inclinetur versùs globum terrestrem secundum eam partem, secundum quam validiora, & copiosiora dimanant effluvia, nimirùm in partibus borealibus secundum unam sui partem, in australibus secundum alteram, & eò quidem magis, quò regiones polo boreali, aut australi viciniores sunt. Nihil etiam mirùm, quod acus sub Aequatore, ubi videlicet neutra praevalent effluvia, & à polis aequa intercapedine locus absistit, perfectum servet aequilibrium omnis expers inclinationis.

788 The phenomenon of inclination is also explained: for, magnetic effluvia being supposed to burst forth from the earth, it is no wonder that the needle inclines toward the terrestrial globe along that part along which the stronger and more copious effluvia flow out, namely in the northern parts along one of its parts, in the southern along the other, and this the more, the nearer the regions are to the north or to the south pole. Nor is it any wonder that the needle under the Equator, where, namely, neither effluvia prevail and the place stands off from the poles by an equal interval, keeps a perfect equilibrium, free of all inclination.

## *Scholion III.* — SCHOLIUM III

> 789 His è principiis illustratur, cur magnes situm contrarium situi, quem in fodina obtinuit, extra eam in superficie telluris habeat; etenim si profluvia magnetica per polum terrae australem ingredi concipiantur, ea australem quoque magnetis polum eidem terrae parti obversum, dum adhuc in fodina est, subire debent: sed quum effluvia ab austro in boream per lineas axi parallelas in terrae meditullio fluentia, in superficie ejus á boreali ad australem revertantur, magnes è terra eductus, contrario situ ad ea profluvia recipienda disponi debet; ac polus ejus australis ad borealem telluris, undè effluvia erumpere ponuntur, obverti.

789 From these principles it is illustrated why the magnet, outside the mine, on the surface of the Earth, has a situation contrary to the situation which it held in the mine; for if the magnetic outflows are conceived to enter through the southern pole of the earth, they must also enter the southern pole of the magnet turned toward the same part of the earth while it is still in the mine: but since the effluvia flowing from south to north along lines parallel to the axis in the interior of the earth return on its surface from the northern pole to the southern, the magnet, drawn out of the earth, must be disposed in a contrary situation for receiving those outflows, and its southern pole must be turned toward the northern pole of the Earth, whence the effluvia are supposed to burst out.

> 790 Dico 2. Vis magnetis adtractrix non ab aëris retrosubeuntis impulsu; verùm à motu atmosphaerae magnetem ambientis, verosimiliter, eadem mechanicâ agendi ratione, qua accessus corporum homogeneorum, derivatur. Pars prima patet. In vacuo, & adtractio ferri ad magnetem, & adhaesio illius contingit: quin citius ferrum á magnete adripitur, recipiente exhausto. Igitur vis adtractrix ab aëris actione repeti nequit. Ad haec si effluvia magnetica hac pollent vi, ut aërem inter ferrum, & magnetem expellant, sicque aequilibrium illius columnae cum reliquis aëreis columnis interturbent, ¿qui fieri posse putem, ut in spatio illo intermedio minor sit resistentia, comparatè ad aërem à tergò urgentem ferrum, & magnetem? Siquidem in aëris locum validiùs corpus, (effluvia nempe aërem excludentia) succedit.

790 I say 2. The attractive force of the magnet is derived not from the impulse of air coming in behind, but from the motion of the atmosphere surrounding the magnet, in all likelihood by the same mechanical manner of acting as the approach of homogeneous bodies. The first part is plain. In a vacuum both the attraction of iron to the magnet and its adhesion take place: indeed, iron is seized more quickly by the magnet when the receiver has been exhausted. Therefore the attractive force cannot be traced to the action of the air. Besides, if the magnetic effluvia have such force as to expel the air between the iron and the magnet, and so to disturb the equilibrium of that column with the other columns of air, how should I think it can happen that in that intermediate space there is a lesser resistance, compared with the air pressing on the iron and the magnet from behind? Since into the place of the air there succeeds a stronger body (namely, the effluvia excluding the air).

> 791 Pars secunda commonstratur. Ad explicandam vim adtractricem magnetis necesse est, ut ratio detur, cur poli cognomines sive australis unus, & alter, aut duo boreales se invicem repellant [p. 247] non in magnete solum, sed acu etiam magneticâ; deinde cur poli non cognomines australis unus nempè, & alter borealis ad sese accedant: denique cur ferrum à magnete ex utrâque parte rapiatur. Atqui haec commodè explicantur per vim atmosphaerae magneticae. Etenim si ut supra [§. 781, & seqq.] posuimus, magnetum configuratio interna, & pororum structura sit ejusmodi, ut moleculae minimae villorum instar prostratae, & inflexae, vergant suis apicibus versus unum magnetici corporis polum ex. gr. borealem, fiet, hoc partium contextu posito, ut fluidum incurrens in polum australem, hunc liberè pervadere, ac super villorum superficie fluenter ferri possit, nulla ipsis vi illata; contrà in polum borealem illapsae tenuioris fluidi partes, obtinentibus villorum tramites vestientium apicibus vim inferent.
