Qua propter si magnes ea lege ad alterum constituatur, ut polus borealis illius australem hujus spectet, quoniam fluidum atmosphaericum unius agitur secundum eam directionem, quam villorum inflexio sortitur in altero, subtilissimae fluidi partes per ipsam villorum superficiem nulla, aut minima in ipsos vi atque impressione facta commeabunt.

791 The second part is demonstrated. To explain the attractive force of the magnet it is necessary that a reason be given why poles of the same name, whether one southern and the other southern, or two northern, repel each other [p. 247] not only in the magnet but also in the magnetic needle; then why poles not of the same name, namely one southern and the other northern, approach each other; and finally why iron is snatched by a magnet from either side. But these things are conveniently explained by the force of the magnetic atmosphere. For if, as we laid down above [§. 781 ff.], the internal configuration of magnets and the structure of their pores is such that the smallest molecules, laid down and bent like little hairs, incline with their tips toward one pole of the magnetic body, e.g. the northern, it will come about, this contexture of the parts being supposed, that the fluid running into the southern pole can freely pervade it and be carried flowingly over the surface of the little hairs, no force being brought upon them; whereas the parts of the subtler fluid that have slipped into the northern pole will bring force upon the tips which occupy and line the paths of the little hairs. Wherefore, if one magnet is placed toward another in such a way that the northern pole of the former faces the southern pole of the latter, then, since the atmospheric fluid of the one is driven in the direction which the inflection of the little hairs has in the other, the most subtle parts of the fluid will pass along the very surface of the little hairs with no force and impression, or the least, made upon them.

> 792 At verò, ubi magnetum poli illi conjunguntur, é quibus prorrumpit subtilior atmosphaerae torrens, tum quidem fluidi hujus moleculae ex unius polo effluentes, poli consimilis in altero magnete subire poros haud poterunt villorum porrectis, atque adeò obsistentibus cuspidibus: proindè, vi tramitibus his illata, magnetem, in quem, irruunt, repellere connitentur. Quod si autem haud longè ab invicem locentur magnetum ii poli, in quorum utrumque circumfussum fluidum irrumpit, praeterquamquod fluidi magnetici directiones sibi adversentur, repulsio consequatur oportet, ex eo, quod átmosphaerae geminae in unam non coalescant hoc pacto, ut fluidum aliud interfusum omne removeatur, atque adeò accessus consequatur; ac tametsi per unum, & alterum horum polorum pateat effluviis aditus, quia tamen uterque ponitur ejusmodi pororum habitudine donari, ut per eos ingredi duntaxat fluidum magneticum possit, iccircò atmosphaerarum commixtio, & in unum quodammodò vorticem conjunctio, (exclusis aliis heterogeneis fluidis) impeditur: proindè fiet, ut magnetes ad sese invicem non accedant, sed oppositis utrinque effluviorum directionibus repellantur. Idem de acu magnetica sentiendum.

792 But when those poles of the magnets are joined from which the subtler torrent of atmosphere bursts forth, then indeed the molecules of this fluid flowing out of the pole of the one will be unable to enter the pores of the like pole in the other magnet, since the points of the little hairs are stretched out and so resist: hence, force being brought upon these paths, they will strive to repel the magnet into which they rush. But if those poles of the magnets into each of which the surrounding fluid breaks in are placed not far from each other, then, besides the fact that the directions of the magnetic fluid oppose each other, repulsion must follow from this, that the twin atmospheres do not coalesce into one in such a way that all the other fluid interposed is removed and so an approach follows; and although an entrance lies open to the effluvia through each of these poles, yet because each is supposed to be endowed with such a habit of pores that only the magnetic fluid can enter through them, the commingling of the atmospheres and their conjunction, in a manner, into one vortex (other heterogeneous fluids being excluded) is for that reason impeded: hence it will come about that the magnets do not approach each other, but are repelled by the opposite directions of the effluvia on either side. The same is to be thought of the magnetic needle.

> 793 Ferrum denique nondum magnetica ut ajunt, virtute imbutum, ad magnetem rapi, cuivis polo adstitutum, eo nomine adserimus, quod metalli hujus structura, & tramitum conformatio videatur adcommodata, ad magnetica effluvia recipienda ea transmitenda, eo quidem pacto, ut haec per interiorem ejus superficiem liberius se penetrare, ac fluenter deferri, nulla vi ipsis pororum parietibus illata, possint: quo efficietur, ut é spatio magnetem inter & ferrum fluida cetera interfusa removeantur, quibus dimotis, quoniam circumfuso corporibus fluido subtilissimo secundum eam [p. 248] partem nihil obnititur, consectarium est, ut presu ejus ferrum ad magnetem urgeatur

793 Finally, that iron not yet imbued, as they say, with magnetic virtue is snatched to the magnet, at whatever pole it is placed, we assert on this ground: that the structure of this metal and the conformation of its paths seem adapted for receiving and transmitting the magnetic effluvia, in such a way indeed that these can penetrate more freely through its interior surface and be carried flowingly along, no force being brought upon the walls of the pores: whereby it will be brought about that the other fluids interposed in the space between the magnet and the iron are removed; and these being moved away, since, the most subtle fluid being spread around the bodies, along that part [p. 248] nothing resists, it follows that by its pressure the iron is urged toward the magnet.

> 794 Firmatur adsertio expositione phaenomenorum ac primo quidem redditur ratio, cur praeter ferrum aut chalybem, non alia etiam corpora trahantur á magnete: quia nempè ea pororum est dispositio in ferro, partiumque configuratio tamquam in corpore cum magnete homogeneo, ut effluvia illud facilius penetrent, quàm corpora reliqua: hinc dum copia majori torrens effluviorum trajicit ferri poros, renixus intermedio in spatio minuitur, quo sublato viribus prementis fluidi haec corpora junguntur.

794 The assertion is confirmed by an exposition of the phenomena; and first a reason is given why, besides iron or steel, no other bodies are drawn by the magnet: namely, because such is the disposition of the pores in iron, and the configuration of its parts, as in a body homogeneous with the magnet, that the effluvia penetrate it more easily than the other bodies: hence, while the torrent of effluvia crosses the pores of the iron in greater abundance, the resistance in the intermediate space is diminished, and, this being removed, these bodies are joined by the forces of the pressing fluid.

> 795 Ex quo pariter ratio eruitur, cur magnes si chalybe vel ferro vestiatur, sivè, ut ajunt, *armetur*, circumpositis chalybeis probè laevigatis laminis, longe validius adtrahat, adtractumque sustineat: videatur namque effluvia per chalybem facilius fluere, quàm per aërem, adeòque uberior illorum copia tunc in ferrum adtrahendum irrumpit, quae antea circum latera magnetis liberius evagabantur, minusque collecta fuerunt, secundo: explicatur aptius in nostra sententia: cur minores non nunquam magnetes majora pondera sustineant, ubi majores saepè sunt infirmiores, imò cur portentosam aliqui vim habeant; saepè enim magnetes partibus notabiliter constant heterogeneis, per quas effluvia tàm copiosè non trajiciantur, qui exigua proindè atmosphaera polleant, cujus ope adpulsio consequatur: contra evenire potest, ut exiguus quamtumvis magnes, purioribus compactus partibus, pro mole sua grandem circumfusam habeat atmosphaeram.

795 From this likewise the reason is drawn why a magnet, if it is clothed with steel or iron, or, as they say, armed, with well-polished steel plates placed around it, attracts far more strongly and holds fast what it has attracted: for the effluvia seem to flow more easily through steel than through air, and therefore a more abundant supply of them then bursts into the iron that is to be attracted, which before wandered more freely around the sides of the magnet and were less collected. Secondly: our opinion explains more aptly why smaller magnets sometimes sustain greater weights, whereas larger ones are often weaker, indeed why some have a portentous force; for magnets often consist of notably heterogeneous parts, through which the effluvia are not transmitted so copiously, and which accordingly possess a slight atmosphere, by whose help the attraction is effected; on the contrary it can happen that a magnet, however small, compacted of purer parts, has for its bulk a great surrounding atmosphere.

> 795 Tertio: nostrâ opinione posita magis adcommodatè ad Physicam exponitur motus *fugae*, & repulsio, quàm in ceterorum sententia, qui hunc ad vortices oppositos referunt, adtractionem verò aëri adtribuunt. Concipi profectò vix potest, ac dici, quod aër inter duos polos egressus non extrudatur, quum duo magnetes in vicinia constituuntur; neque tamen hanc aëris repulsionem adtractio consequitur, quam quidem fieri dicunt aëre intermedio expulso ad latera, & à tergo subeunte, atque duo haec corpora magnetica ad invicem, ubi minor est resistentia, impellente.

795 Thirdly: on our opinion being laid down, the motion of flight and repulsion is expounded more fittingly for Physics than in the opinion of the others, who refer this to opposite vortices but attribute attraction to the air. It can scarcely be conceived, indeed, or said, that the air between two poles of egress is not driven out when two magnets are set near each other; and yet attraction does not follow this repulsion of the air, the attraction which they say comes about when the intermediate air is expelled to the sides, and the air coming in from behind drives these two magnetic bodies toward each other, where the resistance is less.

> 797 Dico tertio: Vis magnetica ferro, aut chalybi communicata, à profluviis magneticis ducenda est. Tum quippè magnetica vis ferro, aut chalybi communicatur, quando haec corpora vel magnetis polo vel ipsius armaturae adfricantur, aut adplicantur, quae in eo consistit, quod ferrum vel chalybs se ad mundi polos dirigat, aliudque ferrum trahat. At vis haec à magneticis profluviis haud dubiè proficiscitur; nam dum aut acus nautica polo magnetis, vel ejus armaturae adfricatur, profluvia illa in acum irrunt, fibrillasque, seu villos in unam partem, pro ut ferri juxta magnetem ductus sit, inclinant, ut duos sibi polos, alterum ingressus, egressus alterum in ferro, vel acu, non secùs, quàm in magnete ipso sint, efforment; id, quod ex eo verosimilitudinem nanciscitur, quod pori hi contrario magnetis ductu commutentur: ergo.

797 I say thirdly: The magnetic force communicated to iron or steel is to be derived from magnetic outflows. For magnetic force is communicated to iron or steel when these bodies are rubbed on, or applied to, the pole of a magnet or of its armature; and it consists in this, that the iron or steel directs itself toward the poles of the world and attracts other iron. But this force without doubt proceeds from magnetic outflows; for while a nautical needle is rubbed on the pole of a magnet or of its armature, those outflows rush into the needle and incline its little fibers, or hairs, to one side, according as the iron has been drawn along the magnet, so that they form for themselves two poles in the iron or the needle, one of ingress and the other of egress, not otherwise than they are in the magnet itself; which gains likelihood from the fact that these pores are interchanged by drawing the magnet in the contrary direction: therefore.

[p. 249]

> 798 Profectò fieri hoc effluviorum ope posse, congruè ostenditur; ex eo in primis, quod molliores sint ferri, quàm magnetis fibrillae, magisque flexiles, id, quod diversitas texturae suadet. Deindè analogiâ mercurii subeuntis in virgam auream, id ipsum explicatur; tàm facile quippè intelligitur minerale effluvium magnetis subire in ferrum, eique magnetismum conferre, quàm effluvium mercurii in aurum, illudque inalbare. Quid? quod sicut per ignem separatur imbibitus ab auro mercurius, ita à ferro magnetico, per ignem vis magnetica tolli dicatur.

798 That this can come about by the help of effluvia is fittingly shown; first of all from the fact that the little fibers of iron are softer and more flexible than those of the magnet, as the diversity of their texture suggests. Then this very thing is explained by the analogy of mercury entering into a rod of gold; for it is understood just as easily that the mineral effluvium of the magnet enters into iron and confers magnetism on it, as that the effluvium of mercury enters into gold and whitens it. What of the fact that, just as the mercury imbibed by gold is separated from it by fire, so the magnetic force is said to be removed from magnetic iron by fire?

## *Adnotatio.* — REMARK

> 799 Minimè fictitia est effluviorum magneticorum circa tellurem circulatio & ab uno ejus polo egressus, in alium ingressus; id enim, quod accommodè ad explicanda naturae phaenomena dicitur, non illicò fictitium est censendum, si fundamentis verisimilitudinem praebentibus non destituatur. Certè non alia de causa pyxis nautica in locis polo proximis nullius est usus, quàm, quod profluvia magnetica è polo erumpentia ferè ad perpendiculum, non in unam potius, quàm in aliam partem dirigant acum ipsam; quod Bátavi in suo itinerario se expertos referunt.

799 By no means fictitious is the circulation of the magnetic effluvia around the Earth, and their egress from one of its poles and ingress into the other: for what is said fittingly for explaining the phenomena of nature is not forthwith to be deemed fictitious, if it is not destitute of foundations that afford likelihood. Certainly for no other reason is the nautical box of no use in the places nearest the pole than because the magnetic outflows, bursting from the pole almost perpendicularly, direct the needle itself no more to one side than to another; which the Dutch report that they experienced on their voyage.

> 800 Neque fictitia est similis gyratio circa ipsum magnetem; nam si ceteris omnibus corporibus atmosphaeram adscribimus, magneti profectò hanc praeposterè denegamus. Ceterùm effluvia ad jugem motum compelluntur à fluido universali subtilissimo; verùm quo mechanismo id perficiatur, docendum superest, ad hunc verò circa magnetem circuitum ab ipsa pororum, partiumque in magnete dispositione velut determinantur, qui aptiores sunt ad ea recipienda, quàm quaevis alia corpora, & quidem una parte accommodati magis ad immitenda, secundum alteram ad emittenda. Utrumque analogia succorum in plantis per fibras se insinuantium, nec per easdem regredientium, eorumque per canaliculos perennis circulatio suadet, & exponit. Plura de magnere tradunt Kyrcherus, Gaspar Schottus, de Lanis, Wolfius, Muschenbroeckius, aliique plures.

800 Nor is a similar gyration around the magnet itself fictitious; for if we ascribe an atmosphere to all other bodies, we should surely deny it preposterously to the magnet. However, the effluvia are driven to perpetual motion by a most subtle universal fluid; but by what mechanism this is accomplished remains to be taught; and toward this circuit around the magnet they are, as it were, determined by the very disposition of the pores and parts in the magnet, which are apter for receiving them than any other bodies whatever, and indeed on one side better accommodated for letting them in, on the other for emitting them. Both points are suggested and expounded by the analogy of the juices in plants, which insinuate themselves through fibers and do not return through the same, and by their perennial circulation through little canals. Many more things about the magnet are handed down by Kircher, Gaspar Schott, Lana Terzi, Wolff, Musschenbroek, and many others.

[p. 250]

## DISSERTATIO III. — DISSERTATION III

> De Aquae Elemento.

ON WATER AS AN ELEMENT.

## CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

> De Natura Aquae.

On the Nature of Water.

> 801 Naturam aquae Gassendus cum Epicureis in particulis laevigatis, ac rotundis, quae lubricae sint, & crebris vacuolis discretae constituunt. Alii cubicas aquae atomos esse praetendunt, eo quod aqua vix comprimi possit. Cartesius oblongas esse, & téretes existimat.

he nature of water is made by Gassendi, with the Epicureans, to consist 801 Tin smooth and round particles, which are slippery and separated by frequent little voids. Others claim that the atoms of water are cubic, because water can scarcely be compressed. Descartes thinks they are oblong and rounded.

> 802 Dico: Aqua verosimilius est substantia partibus oblongis, teretibus, flexilibus, lubricis, volubilibus, sibi minus implexis, atque ovalibus, sive ovata figurâ donatis, constans.

802 I say: Water is more probably a substance consisting of parts that are oblong, rounded, flexible, slippery, voluble, little entangled with one another, and oval, that is, endowed with an egg-shaped figure.

> 803 Etenim hac positâ naturâ aquae, phaenomena, omnesque proprietates, aquae competentes expediri congruè possunt. Sic fluiditas deducitur ex lubricitate, & volubilitate; ex qua pariter vis solvendi corpora laxius cohaerentia derivatur. Vis humectandi ex flexilitate, & figurâ oblongâ ac téreti fluit; sic enim & porulis corporum se facilè insinuant, & eminentioribus in eorum superficie partibus circumvolvuntur, iisdemque adhaerescunt. Vis abluendi sordes ex his quoque intelligitur, quae ablutio fit commodius, ubi lenta materia, uti sapone, corpus abluendum praeparatur, sordes etenim plerumque pingues, lentae materiae facilius adhaerescunt, tum aquae sordes unà, & viscosam materiam expurgat.

803 For, this nature of water being supposed, the phenomena and all the properties belonging to water can be fittingly accounted for. Thus fluidity is deduced from slipperiness and volubility; from which likewise is derived the force of dissolving bodies that cohere more loosely. The force of moistening flows from flexibility and from the oblong and rounded figure; for thus the particles easily insinuate themselves into the little pores of bodies, roll around the more prominent parts on their surface, and adhere to them. The force of washing off dirt is also understood from these things; and this washing is done more conveniently when the body to be washed is prepared with a viscous matter, such as soap: for since dirt is generally fatty, it adheres more easily to the viscous matter, and then the water purges away the dirt together with the viscous matter.

> 804 Vis lubricandi ac diffluendi ex glabritie, teretique figurâ pendet, ob quam ex corporibus politis ac tersis, uti sunt vitra, aut ex pinguibus, prout évenit in avium plumis, facilè decurrit. Evaporatio cita, & velox à minus implexis particulis ducitur. Gravitas ex densitate &c. ex qua etiam habilitas in glaciem abeundi prae aliis liquoribus, qui tenuioribus particulis componuntur, oritur: hinc quoque est, quod mirùm in modum rarefieri, comprimi verò vix possit aqua, partes scilicèt *immediatè* se contingentes, & super se invicèm provolutae, conjungi propius nequeunt. Demum odoris juxta ac saporis defectus, in aqua ex flexilitate volubilitateque proficiscitur; flexiles enim ac volubiles particulae seu moleculae, leni motu super organum gustus, & olfactus decurrunt, nec acie sua papillas & fibrillas feriunt. Ceterarum quoque proprietatum ratio ex partium illa fructura, & conformatione facilè deducetur.

804 The force of lubricating and of flowing off depends on smoothness and on the rounded figure, on account of which water runs off easily from polished and clean bodies, such as glass, or from fatty ones, as happens with the feathers of birds. Quick and swift evaporation is derived from particles little entangled. Gravity, from density, etc.; from which also arises its aptitude for passing into ice, beyond other liquors which are composed of finer particles: hence too it is that water is rarefied in a wonderful manner, but can scarcely be compressed, since its parts, touching one another immediately and rolled over one another, cannot be joined more closely. Finally, the lack of odor as well as of taste in water proceeds from its flexibility and volubility; for flexible and voluble particles, or molecules, run over the organ of taste and of smell with a gentle motion, and do not strike its papillae and fibrils with any edge. The reason of the other properties too will easily be deduced from that structure and conformation of the parts.

[p. 251]

## *Scholion.* — SCHOLIUM

> 805 Ad constituendam aquae naturam, pro ut ea substantia est fluida, in primis requiritur, uti (ex dictis de fluiditate) constat, ut partes inter se divisae, ac dissociatae sint, atque in paucis sese planis contingant. Cl. Helvetius ovatam molecularum aquearum figuram magis congruere effectibus omnibus, quos edunt, censet; nam illae, ait „sese non contingent nisi secundum minimas superficies ac proinde poterunt minima vi fluenter ferri; & tamen in glaciem concrescent, eo quod interstitia ipsis interjecta minora sint his, quae darentur, si partes aquae sphaericâ gauderent figurâ. Praeterea aquae partes hac figurâ donatae poterunt solutionem corporum faciliùs peragere, eo quod earum extrema sunt tenuiora, media earum parte. Tandem insipidam, & inodoram esse debere aquam, eo quod hebetiora sint ejus partium extrema.„ Haec ille.

805 In order to constitute the nature of water, insofar as it is a fluid substance, it is first of all required, as is clear (from what was said on fluidity), that its parts be divided and dissociated from one another and touch one another in few planes. The distinguished Helvétius judges that an oval figure of the aqueous molecules agrees better with all the effects which they produce; for these, he says, “will not touch one another except along the smallest surfaces, and accordingly they can be carried flowingly by the least force; and yet they will congeal into ice, because the interstices placed between them are smaller than those which would be given if the parts of water enjoyed a spherical figure. Moreover, the parts of water endowed with this figure can accomplish the dissolution of bodies more easily, because their extremities are finer than their middle part. Finally, water must be insipid and odorless, because the extremities of its parts are blunter.” Thus he.

## CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

> De Fontibus, fluminibus, ac ceteris aquis.

On Springs, Rivers, and the Other Waters. 806

> 806 Fontium hic fluminumque originem praecipuè expendemus, de qua duplex est sententia. Recentiores alii, à mari, alii à pluviis, nivibusque solutis originem répetunt. Primi docent maris aquas per subterraneos meatus in montes, & cetera loca, in quibus fontium scaturigines reperiuntur, deferri, suamque in illis salsedinem, & amarorem, depónere, subindè per occultos meatus & fissuras prosilire. Posteriores contendunt aquarum partem, quae per pluvias delabitur, & à terra combibitur, per fissuras, rimasque rupium, & montium penetrare, recipi, & colligi in quibusdam eorum cavitatibus, & hydrophylaciis, ex quibus deinceps per angusta quaedam ostiola, sensim defluant, & fontibus originem praebeant, è quibus flumina derivantur. Quid hac in controversiâ sentiendum sit, statuit nostra conclusio.

The origin of springs and rivers is what we chiefly weigh here, and on it there is a twofold opinion. Of the Moderns, some trace their origin from the sea, others from rains and melted snows. The first teach that the waters of the sea are carried through subterranean passages into the mountains and the other places in which the sources of springs are found, and that, having deposited in them their saltness and bitterness, they then leap forth through hidden passages and fissures. The latter contend that the part of the waters which falls down in rains and is drunk in by the earth penetrates through the fissures and chinks of rocks and of mountains, is received and collected in certain cavities of them and in reservoirs, from which the waters then flow down little by little through certain narrow outlets and give origin to springs, from which rivers are derived. What is to be thought in this controversy our conclusion establishes.

> 807 Fontes, & flumina non ex mari, occulto itinere terram penetrante, & indè, facta velut via, scaturiente: sed ex pluviis, nivibus solutis, & vaporibus oriuntur. Prob. prima pars. Si fontes orirentur ex mari, aquae marinae deberent salsedinem suam & amaritudinem deponere, & ad eam altitudinem supra montes, in [p. 252] quibus fontes scaturire observamus, sua velut spontè ascendere. Atqui neutrum sustineri posse videtur: hoc namque modo aqua maris salsedinem, & amarulentiam amitteret, quatenus in illis anfractibus, quos statuunt adversarii, particulas sallas, & amarulentas deponeret, sive relinqueret; sed hoc fieri haud potest: nam vel hoc sequâtur, necesse est, ut tandem lapsu temporis viae illae, & meatus ab adhaerente sale obstruantur, vel hoc alterum, ut ab aqua superveniente abradantur, & abripiantur atque adeò potentiore sale, sivè majore ejus copia refertae è fontibus aquae prorrumpant.

807 Springs and rivers arise not from the sea, by a hidden route penetrating the earth and thence welling out, as if by a road made for it, but from rains, melted snows, and vapors. The first part is proved. If springs arose from the sea, the sea waters would have to deposit their saltness and bitterness, and to ascend, as it were of their own accord, to that height above the mountains at which [p. 252] we observe springs welling forth. But neither seems capable of being maintained; for in this way the sea water would lose its saltness and bitterness insofar as it deposited, or left behind, its salty and bitter particles in those windings which the adversaries posit; but this cannot happen: for one of two things must follow: either that at length, in the course of time, those ways and passages are obstructed by the adhering salt, or this other, that the salt is scraped off and carried away by the water coming upon it, and so the waters burst forth from the springs filled with a more potent salt, or with a greater quantity of it.

> 808 Alterùm conciliari nequit cum principiis Hydrostaticis: ex his enim certum habemus, aquàm in tubis communicantibus, cujuscumque demum figurae, & perimetri, non tueri aequilibrium, nisi eandem in iis altitudinem obtinuerit, hoc est: superficiem in utroque tubo lineae horizontali physicè parallelam constituerit. Atqui plurimorum fontium loca altiora sunt, quàm maris superficies. Igitur maris aqua eam ad altitudinem, ex qua fontes scaturiunt, ascendere nequit.

808 The other cannot be reconciled with the principles of Hydrostatics: for from these we hold it as certain that water in communicating tubes, of whatever figure and perimeter at last, does not keep equilibrium unless it has obtained the same height in them, that is, has set its surface in each tube physically parallel to a horizontal line. But the places of very many springs are higher than the surface of the sea. Therefore the sea water cannot ascend to the height from which springs well forth.

> 809 Secunda pars prob.: Fontes & flumina positis vaporibus, pluviis, nivibus solutis, habentur, iis sublatis pereunt, auctis vel imminutis augentur vel imminuuntur. Nempè constanti experientia probatur, eas regiones fontibus abundare, in quibus saepè pluit, & ningit; contra verò paucissima in iis flumina interfundi, in quibus rarus imber: nulla in iis, in quibus nullae unquam pluviae, & nix decidit. Dein experientiâ compertum est, durantibus diutius pluviis, fontes intumescere, & cessantibus etiam pluviis flumina tamen adhuc manere altiora, tempore sicco fontes imminui, & diuturna siccitate penitus disparere,

809 The second part is proved: Springs and rivers are had when vapors, rains, and melted snows are given; when these are taken away, they perish; when these are increased or diminished, they are increased or diminished. For it is proved by constant experience that those regions abound in springs in which it often rains and snows; whereas very few rivers are interspersed in those in which rain is rare; none in those on which no rain and snow ever falls. Then it has been found by experience that when rains last rather long the springs swell, and even after the rains have ceased the rivers still remain higher; that in dry weather springs are diminished, and in a long drought they disappear entirely.

> 810 Sic testatur Cl. Mariotte anno 1681, qui siccissimus in Gallia fuerat, exsiccatas fuisse plurimorum fontium aquas: qui se didicisse experientiâ, & observatione suamet fatetur, quod post longam siccitatem ingruentibus pluviis, prius putei minus profundi, tardius profundiores aquam receperint, & adcreverint, indicio evidente, quod pluvia moderata primis restaurandis sufficiens, non sufficiat secundis.

810 Thus the distinguished Mariotte attests that in the year 1681, which had been very dry in France, the waters of very many springs were dried up: and he confesses that he learned by his own experience and observation that after a long drought, when the rains came on, the less deep wells received water and rose first, the deeper ones more slowly: an evident indication that a moderate rain, sufficient for replenishing the first, does not suffice for the second.

> 811 Accedit testimonium ejusdem Mariotti, tum & Halleji, quorum ille inito calculo deprehendit, longè majorem esse aquae copiam, in locis Séquanae [^252-s1] circumpositis, è caelo decidentis, quàm quae ex ipso fluvio eodem tempore in mare labitur. Hallejus verò circà quantitatem vaporum, qui Solis praesertim vi ex Mediterraneo mari, (idem de aquis aliis) quotidiè ascendunt, invenit, facto periculo, tantam illorum esse copiam, ut, quae ex Ibero, Tiberi, Nilo, ceterisque fluminibus in illud quotidiè aquae illabuntur, vix unam tertiam partem adaequent illius, quae singulis itidèm diebus in vapores ex ipso mari adtollitur.

811 There is added the testimony of the same Mariotte, and also of Halley; the former of whom, having made a calculation, found that the quantity of water falling from the heavens in the places lying around the Seine (*) is far greater than that which flows from that river into the sea in the same time. Halley, on the other hand, concerning the quantity of the vapors which, chiefly by the force of the Sun, ascend daily from the Mediterranean Sea (the same is true of other waters), found, having made the trial, that their quantity is so great that the waters which daily flow into it from the Ebro, the Tiber, the Nile, and the other rivers scarcely equal one third part of that which is likewise raised into vapors from the sea itself each single day.

> [^252-s1]: Sequana Galliae fluvius.

[^252-s1]: The Seine, a river of France.

[p. 253]

> 812 Narrat praeterea in Insula S. Helenae saepè se nocte in vertice montis, maris superficiem 2400 pedibus superante tantam condensationem vaporum suda etiam tempestate expertum esse, ut intra non multa minuta eo pacto madefecerint vitra optica, ut essent abstergenda, observationibus alias Astronomicis minus idonea futura. Charta etiam in qua scribebat, tam brevi tempore madefiebat, rore deciduo, ut atramentum rore dilueretur: unde intelligere est, quanta vaporum copia in amplissimis montium cacuminibus densetur.

812 He relates, moreover, that on the island of St. Helena, often at night on the summit of a mountain exceeding the surface of the sea by 2400 feet, he experienced so great a condensation of vapors even in clear weather that within not many minutes it had so wetted the optical glasses that they had to be wiped, and were otherwise little fit for astronomical observations. The paper, too, on which he was writing was so quickly wetted by the falling dew that the ink was diluted by the dew: whence one may understand how great a quantity of vapors is condensed on the very lofty summits of mountains.

> 813 Qua propter si condensatos vapores pluviis, & nivibus solutis conjungamus, satis aquarum erit ad fontes omnes alendos. Ad haec: experientiâ sua fossores testantur, receptacula ingentia aquarum pluviarum, & nivialium infra terram diffundi: talium hydrophylaciorum Kircherus quatuor prorsus memorabilia enumerat; unum Asiae praecipuum in Regno Mogolis, alterum Europae sub alpibus Rheticis, tertium in Africa sub montibus Lunae, quartum ex Americanis inter Peruviam, & Regnum Chyli. Neque officit illud Ecclesiast. Cap. 1. *omnia flumina intrant in mare.... unde exeunt flumina revertuntur.* Sufficit namque aquas marinas in vapores condensari, in pluviam, seu nivem resolvi, ut verè adfirmetur flumina exire ex mare.

813 Wherefore, if we join the condensed vapors with rains and melted snows, there will be water enough to feed all springs. Besides, diggers testify from their own experience that huge reservoirs of rain and snow waters are spread out beneath the earth: of such hydrophylacia Kircher enumerates four altogether memorable: one, the chief of Asia, in the Kingdom of the Mogul; another, of Europe, under the Rhaetian Alps; the third in Africa, under the Mountains of the Moon; the fourth, among the American ones, between Peru and the Kingdom of Chile. Nor does that text of Ecclesiastes, ch. 1, stand in the way: all the rivers run into the sea . . . unto the place from whence the rivers come, they return. For it suffices that the sea waters are condensed into vapors and resolved into rain or snow for it to be truly affirmed that the rivers go out from the sea.

> 814 Aquarum diversae sunt species, ac proprietates, juxta illud Plinii: tales sunt aquae qualis est terra, per quam transit, intelligendo non solum terram strictè sic dictam, sed succos etiam, & mineralia, ac universum subterranea omnia, ex quibus aqua interfluens delibare aliquid potest. Hinc fontium calidorum, thermarum, aliarumque aquarum salutarium origo. Ex similibus causis aquae nonnullae, & fontes metalliferi sunt. Fluviique plurimi lotoribus arenae aurum suppeditant, dum ii per venas, & canales auro foetas praeterlapsi moleculas minimas devehunt.

814 Of waters there are diverse species and properties, according to that saying of Pliny: waters are such as the earth through which they pass, understanding not only earth strictly so called, but also juices, and minerals, and in general all subterranean things from which the water flowing through can take up something. Hence the origin of hot springs, of thermal baths, and of other healthful waters. From similar causes some waters and springs are metal-bearing; and very many rivers furnish gold to the washers of their sand, while, having flowed past veins and channels teeming with gold, they carry down very minute particles.

[p. 254]

## DISSERTATIO IV. — DISSERTATION IV

> De Elementis Aëris, & Ignis, atque corporibus sublimibus, seu meteoris, nec non de plantis.

ON THE ELEMENTS OF AIR AND FIRE, AND ON THE SUBLIME BODIES, OR METEORS, AND ALSO ON PLANTS

## CAPUT I. — CHAPTER I

> De Natura Aëris.

On the Nature of Air.

> 815 Telluri circumfusum esse fluidum subtile jam supra dictum est, quod ut ut invisibile, ex variis tamen effectibus percipitur, & ad plurimas in natura motiones, ac mutationes producendas, ad vitam animalem prorogandam necessarium, *aëris* nomine insignimus. Multa de eo per decursum Physicae innuimus, ex quibus ejus proprietates, vires, satis superque intelliguntur, hic ceu loco proprio in illius naturam breviter inquirimus. Quare sit conclusio.

hat a subtle fluid is spread round the Earth has already been said 815 T above; this fluid, though invisible, is nevertheless perceived from various effects, and is necessary for producing very many motions and changes in nature and for prolonging animal life; we designate it by the name of air. Many things about it we have indicated in the course of the Physics, from which its properties and forces are more than sufficiently understood; here, as in its proper place, we briefly inquire into its nature. Let the conclusion therefore be:

> 816 Aër est congeries particularum subtilium laxè cohaerentium, cum quadam rigiditate flexilium, quae fluidum, à congerie vaporum, atque exhalationum terrestrium omninò diversum, componunt.

816 Air is an aggregate of subtle particles loosely cohering, flexible with a certain rigidity, which compose a fluid altogether different from the aggregate of vapors and terrestrial exhalations.

> 817 *Subtiles*, & *exiguas* esse aëris moleculas ex eo adparet, quod in poros corporum promptè se insinuent, id, quod potissimum ii advertunt, qui ope antliae pneumaticae experimenta tentant. Laxè eas cohaerere, adeòque aërem porosum esse docet fluiditas; deindè impuritas, dum se particulis aliorum corporum saturat quodammodo quas in poros recipit, & ob quas persaepè malignum se praebet animali corpori. *Flexilitas* cum rigiditate ex ejus elasticitate, qua constanti, & maxima pollet, patet: hinc Cartesius aërem esse corpus valde rarum instar mollium plumularum conjecit [?]: Gulielmini [?] congeriem spirarum sphaericè contortarum, & aethere repletarum esse putat, cui tantum per angustas convolutionum aperturas in earum cavitatem penetrare possit.

817 That the molecules of air are subtle and minute appears from this, that they readily insinuate themselves into the pores of bodies, which is chiefly noticed by those who attempt experiments by means of the air pump. That they cohere loosely, and hence that air is porous, is taught by its fluidity; then by its impurity, since it in some manner saturates itself with the particles of other bodies, which it receives into its pores, and on account of which it very often shows itself malignant to the animal body. Its flexibility together with rigidity is evident from its elasticity, in which it is constantly and very greatly powerful: hence Descartes conjectured that air is a very rare body, like soft little feathers; Guglielmini thinks it is an aggregate of spirals twisted spherically and filled with ether, which can penetrate into their cavity only through the narrow openings of the convolutions.

> 818 Fluidum aëreum *diversum esse à vaporibus atque exhalationibus terrestribus*, atque adeò sui, & proprii generis particulis aërem [p. 255] constare, ex eo elucescit in primis, quod constet vapores, & exhalationes ascendere, illi verò adtolli non possent nisi á graviori corpore extrudantur: ut proindè circa telluris globum necessariò corpus aliud à vaporibus, & exhalationibus distinctum, quod aër sit, admitti debeat. Adhaec: in comperto est aërem metallico vase inclusum, & validissimè etiam compressum, immutatum persistere, id quod de vaporibus minimè verum est. Denique elasticitas ejusdem densitati proportionalis est, occupatque spatia, quae ponderibus comprimentibus sunt reciprocè proportionalia, id quod vaporibus, & exhalationibus non competit.

818 That the aërial fluid is different from vapors and terrestrial exhalations, and hence that air consists of particles of its own proper kind, [p. 255] is evident above all from this, that it is established that vapors and exhalations ascend, but that they cannot be raised unless they are thrust out by a heavier body; so that accordingly around the globe of the Earth some other body, distinct from vapors and exhalations, which is air, must necessarily be admitted. Moreover, it is ascertained that air enclosed in a metal vessel, and even very strongly compressed, persists unchanged, which is not at all true of vapors. Finally, its elasticity is proportional to its density, and it occupies spaces which are reciprocally proportional to the compressing weights, which does not belong to vapors and exhalations.

> 819. Aëris proprietates sunt *fluiditas*, *gravitas*, *compressibilitas*, ac demum *elasticitas*. Atque hanc, quod adtinet, certum est, quod aër compressus eam exerceat secundum quasmcumque directionem; in quocumque enim loco vas aëre compresso plenum, pertundatur, erumpet continuò, erumpit autem quatenus se ad omnem partem dilatare nititur. Observandum porrò, quod elater compressi aëris vim adaequet, quae comprimitur, eousque enim comprimitur, donec vis qua pressioni resistit, fuerit vi comprimenti aequalis: tunc quippe propter aequilibrium compressio sistitur, adeòque vis elastica inferioris adaequat pondus superioris aëris in atmosphaera.

819 The properties of air are fluidity, gravity, compressibility, and finally elasticity. And as regards this last, it is certain that compressed air exerts it in any directions whatever; for in whatever place a vessel full of compressed air is pierced, the air will burst out continuously; and it bursts out inasmuch as it strives to dilate itself in every direction. It is further to be observed that the spring of compressed air equals the force by which it is compressed; for it is compressed until the force by which it resists the pressure has become equal to the compressing force: for then, on account of the equilibrium, the compression is ended; and therefore the elastic force of the lower air equals the weight of the upper air in the atmosphere.

> 820 Aër cum terrestribus vaporibus, & exhalationibus telluri circumfusus *atmosphaera* terrae dicitur: circa altitudinem hujus inter Philosophos non convenit. Nolletus expensis omnibus, quae barometri ope facta sunt, tentamina, ait, terrestris atmosphaerae altitudinem minorem esse non posse 6 leucis Gallicis, neque 15 aut 20 leucas posse superare, adeòque inter has mensuras atmosphaerae altitudinem consistere.

820 Air, together with the terrestrial vapors and exhalations spread round the Earth, is called the atmosphere of the Earth; about its height there is no agreement among Philosophers. Nollet, having weighed all the trials that have been made by means of the barometer, says that the height of the terrestrial atmosphere cannot be less than 6 French leagues, nor can it exceed 15 or 20 leagues, and hence that the height of the atmosphere lies between these measures.

> 821 Aërem omnem veteres Philosophi in tres sphaeras sive regiones diviserunt: *primam*, & *supremam* dicebant illam, quae lunari orbitae proxima sit, nullis prorsus, aut subtilissimis halitibus repleta; *infima* illa ponebatur, quae terraqueum globum proximè cingens à crassioribus, & gravioribus halitibus occupatur: unde reliquis densior est magisque caliginosa, atque insuper modò calida, modò frigida, pro ut nunc rectè, nunc obliquè à sole respicitur: *media* est quae inter utramque sita concipitur. Hinc deducitur.

821 The ancient Philosophers divided the whole air into three spheres, or regions; the first and supreme they called that which is nearest to the lunar orbit, filled with no exhalations at all, or with very subtle ones; the lowest was held to be that which, girding the terraqueous globe most closely, is occupied by thicker and heavier exhalations: whence it is denser than the rest and more misty, and moreover now hot, now cold, according as it is regarded by the Sun now directly, now obliquely: the middle is that which is conceived as situated between the two. Hence it is deduced:

> Corollarium.

COROLLARY.

> 822 Ventorum hic natura, & origo inquirenda, cum ii nihil esse videantur aliud, quàm aër fluens impetu, aut vis ejus in unam partem currentis, aut concitatior motus, sic ut inter ventum, & aërem, quod Seneca ait, nihil aliud intersit, quàm inter lacum, & flumen. Origo eorum est varia. Sol imprimis agens in aërem, ventum excitat, quatenus nempè efficit calore suo, ut aër illi directè subjectus, adprimè rarescat, rarior [p. 256] effectus hoc ipso fiat levior, ac proindè à ceteris gravioribus & densioribus protrudatur, sicque aequilibrio aëris turbato ventus exoriatur.

he nature and origin of the winds are to be inquired into here, since they 822 T seem to be nothing other than air flowing with force, or its force running toward one quarter, or a more agitated motion, so that between wind and air, as Seneca says, there is no other difference than between a lake and a river. Their origin is various. The Sun, first of all, acting on the air, excites wind, inasmuch, namely, as it brings about by its heat that the air directly beneath it is greatly rarefied, and, having become rarer, [p. 256] by that very fact becomes lighter, and hence is thrust out by the rest, which are heavier and denser, and thus, the equilibrium of the air being disturbed, wind arises.

> 823 Deindè Sol vapores calore suo rarefaciendo, ventos excitat, similiter, dum ejusdem actione nives, quibus obducta sunt montium cacumina, liquescunt, tùm enim particulae exsolutae aërem urgent, & versùs eam plagam ipsum propellunt, quae soli subjecta est, utpotè quae rarior minus earum dilatationi resistat, hinc verè adventante frequentes valdè sunt venti septentrionales, australes apropinquante autumno, eò, quod accedente sole ad tropicum Cancri, liquescere incipiant nives montibus borealibus insidentes: contra verò Sole ad tropicum Capricorni propinquante nives montibus australibus incumbentes dissolvantur: quò refertur alia etiam causa ventorum, nempè admixtio halituum qui in atmosphaera copiosius sparsi sunt, & exorta indè effervescentia.

823 Next, the Sun excites winds by rarefying vapors with its heat; similarly while, by its action, the snows with which the summits of mountains are covered melt; for then the released particles press on the air and propel it toward that very region which lies beneath the Sun, since, being rarer, it resists their dilatation less; hence at the approach of spring north winds are very frequent, and south winds at the approach of autumn, because, as the Sun draws near the tropic of Cancer, the snows lying on the northern mountains begin to melt; but on the contrary, as the Sun draws near the tropic of Capricorn, the snows lying on the southern mountains are dissolved: to which is referred another cause of the winds as well, namely the admixture of the exhalations which are rather copiously scattered in the atmosphere, and the effervescence arising thence.

> 824 Denique venti in terrae visceribus suam habere originem possunt, atque ex illis non secus ac ex imo maris erumpere, quorum subterraneorum ventorum causae probabilius sunt ignes subterranei, halitus copiosi &c. Ventorum celeritatem quod adtinet ea varia est. Muschenbroeckius ex Derhami observationibus ait colligi, ventos impetuosissimos tanta rapiditate promotos esse ut 66 pedes Britannicos minuto 2do. & 45 milliaria horae spatio absolverint, quo eodem teste tantarum virium illi fuerunt, ut lapideam statuam 12 pedes altam 5 latam & 2 crassam diffregerint.

824 Finally, winds can have their origin in the bowels of the earth, and burst forth from them no otherwise than from the bottom of the sea; the more probable causes of these subterranean winds are subterranean fires, copious exhalations, etc. As regards the velocity of the winds, it is various. Musschenbroek says that it is gathered from Derham’s observations that the most violent winds were driven with such rapidity that they covered 66 English feet in a second, and 45 miles in the space of an hour; and, by the same witness, they had such great force that they tore apart a stone statue 12 feet high, 5 wide and 2 thick.

> 825 Diversae sunt eorum proprietates ac qualitates, quae è diversis vaporibus & exhalationibus, quas secum venti devehunt, & incursu suo reperiunt, secumque abripiunt, oriuntur, ita, ut Septentrionalis frigidus; quia particulas nitrosas, & frigidas magna secum copia devehit: australes tepidi, & humidi, quia ex Zona torrida, aut partibus illi vicinioribus exhalationes calidas & simul ex Mediterraneo mari humidos vapores advehunt.

825 Diverse are their properties and qualities, which arise from the diverse vapors and exhalations which the winds carry down with them, and meet in their course, and snatch away with them; so that the north wind is cold, because it carries down with it a great quantity of nitrous and cold particles; the south winds tepid and humid, because they bring hot exhalations from the torrid Zone, or from the parts nearer to it, and at the same time humid vapors from the Mediterranean Sea.

> 826 Diversitas ventorum est multiplex; praeter ventos etiam, qui variè dividuntur ob plagas varias, unde spirant, datur insuper varietas alia relatè ad tempus spirationis: similiter alii sunt venti provinciales dicti, qui in certis quibusdam locis, & provinciis dominantur; alii ab impetu, & celeritate, aut contrà placido spiramine diversitatem habent, illi procellosi, hi placidi dicuntur, quorum nomina & conditionem persequi non vacat.

826 The diversity of the winds is manifold: besides the winds, too, which are divided variously by reason of the various quarters from which they blow, there is besides another variety, relative to the time of blowing; similarly some winds are called provincial, which prevail in certain particular places or provinces; others have their diversity from their force and swiftness, or on the contrary from a gentle breath; the former are called stormy, the latter gentle; whose names and condition there is no leisure to pursue.

[p. 257]

## CAPUT II. — CHAPTER II

> De Natura ignis.

On the Nature of Fire.

> 827 Dico: Ignis est fluidum subtilissimis, ac durissimis, summe mobilibus particulis constans. Commonstratur expositione. Ignem corpus esse fluidum patet ex eo, quod aliis corporibus fluiditatem communicet, ut metallis, in aliis etiam conservet fluiditatem, se reducat ad aequilibrium, ut observamus in cubiculo, ubi calor tandem aequabiliter difunditur. Subtilissimas ac durissimas esse ignis moleculas exinde colligimus, quod corpora omnia quantumcunque compacta, pervadat, quum tamen fluida cetera etiam summè volatilia in vitris vel vasis aliis conservari possint, deindè quòd corpora ferè omnia, velut dissolvens universale, sic discerpat, & dissolvat, ut nulla industriâ nostrâ in pristinum statum reponi queant, undè mobilitas maxima igni inesse evincitur: necesse est etiam ut ad rarefactionis dissolutionis, combustionis &c. motus efficiendos, quantitas motus in igne sit maxima.

say: Fire is a fluid consisting of most subtle, most hard, supremely 827 I mobile particles. It is demonstrated by exposition. That fire is a fluid body is plain from this, that it communicates fluidity to other bodies, as to metals, and in others also preserves their fluidity, and brings itself back to equilibrium, as we observe in a room, where the heat is at length evenly diffused. That the molecules of fire are most subtle and most hard we gather from this, that it pervades all bodies, however compact, whereas the other fluids, even supremely volatile ones, can be kept in glasses or other vessels; then from this, that, as a universal solvent, it so tears apart and dissolves almost all bodies that by no industry of ours can they be restored to their former state; whence it is proven that the greatest mobility is in fire: it is necessary too that, to effect the motions of rarefaction, dissolution, combustion, etc., the quantity of motion in fire be very great.

## *Scholion.* — SCHOLIUM

> 828 Ignis non consistit in particulis sulphureis & nitrosis á materia subtili agitatis, ut Cartesiani opinantur, ut enim praeteream plura, patet hoc ex eo, quod in foco speculi caustici, ubi tantus est ignis, ut metalla saltem imperfecta brevi in vitrum abeant nihil sulphuris aut nitri reperiatur, nec ad aërem his corpusculis impraegnatum refugere licet; quum in exhausto recipiente idem eveniat; nec effugium in metallis quaeratur, quia per chymicos, ex auro, silice, adamante, sulphur nullum extrahitur.

828 Fire does not consist in sulphurous and nitrous particles agitated by the subtle matter, as the Cartesians suppose; for, to pass over many things, this is plain from this, that in the focus of a burning mirror, where the fire is so great that the imperfect metals at least turn in a short time into glass, nothing of sulphur or nitre is found; nor may one take refuge in air impregnated with these corpuscles, since the same thing happens in an exhausted receiver; nor let an escape be sought in the metals, since no sulphur is extracted by the chemists from gold, flint or diamond.

> Corollarium.

COROLLARY.

> 829 Flamma est congeries bullularum sive particularum sulphurearum, terrearum, salinarum, rigidarum, & acuminatarum á fluido subtilissimo igneo, motu vehementi, & confuso exagitatarum, atque ab aëre circumfuso, ne continuò dissipentur, condensatarum. Flamma enim respectivè ad alia corpora ignita parum urit, quòd minus ignis, & multum alienae materiae relatè ad ista corpora ignita complectatur. Figura ejus conica ex [p. 258] eo nascitur quod in unico loco aërem findat: ibi nempè ubi aër debilius resistit, & flamma magis est activa, siquidem partes subtilissimae illùc extruduntur.

829 Flame is an aggregate of little bubbles, or of sulphurous, earthy, saline, rigid and pointed particles, agitated with a vehement and confused motion by the most subtle igneous fluid, and condensed by the surrounding air, so that they are not continually dissipated. For flame, relatively to other ignited bodies, burns little, because it embraces less fire, and much foreign matter, relatively to those ignited bodies. Its conical figure arises from [p. 258] this, that it cleaves the air in a single place: namely, there where the air resists more weakly and the flame is more active, since the most subtle parts are thrust out thither.

> 830 Colores flammae à materia ejus diversa oriuntur, caeruleus circa basim ex humore oleagino non dum benè execocto, & dissipato; flamma enim quò est purior & in majori copia igniculos continet, eò candidior est; in medio rubrum colorem paticulae multae terreae igni permixtae efficiunt, si enim lamella mediam in flammam ingeratur, multa fuligine inficitur, non ita in basi & apice. Quod apex flammae albescat, ex depurata flammae materia habetur: adhaec lanugo veluti circa flammam adparet, quae nihil esse aliud videtur, nisi humor adtenuatus & non benè accensus atque adeo aëri, ex parte autem igni admixtus, non secus, ac ex. gr. gutta vini aquae immixta, velut in filamina quaedam sese dispergit. Nullus hactenùs (quod viderim) melius de igne tractavit, quàm toties & nunquam satis laudatus Boerhaave, in Elementis Chemiae. Ipsum consulite si plura vultis.

830 The colors of flame arise from its diverse matter: the blue around the base, from an oily humor not yet well concocted and dissipated; for the purer the flame is, and the greater the quantity of little fires it contains, the whiter it is; in the middle, many earthy particles mixed with the fire produce the red color, for if a small plate is thrust into the middle of the flame, it is stained with much soot, not so at the base and the tip. That the tip of the flame whitens is owing to the purified matter of the flame: besides, a kind of down appears, as it were, round the flame, which seems to be nothing else but an attenuated humor, not well kindled, and hence mixed partly with the air, partly with the fire, no otherwise than, e.g., a drop of wine mixed with water disperses itself, as it were, into certain filaments. No one hitherto (that I have seen) has treated of fire better than Boerhaave, so often and never sufficiently praised, in the Elementa Chemiae. Consult him, if you want more.

## CAPUT III. — CHAPTER III

> De Meteoris in universum.

On Meteors in General.

> 831 Meteorum idem notat, ac in sublimi adparens, unde quae à Graecis meteora seu pressius *metarsia* dicuntur, ea latinè communiter *sublimia* vocantur. Dispescuntur commodè in tria genera sive classes. Primam aërea vel aquea obtinet, in quibus nempè aër vel aqua exsuperat. Secunda complectitur ignita, in quibus praevalent halitus subtilissimi ac spirituosi. Tertia classis meteora lucida seu emphatica sunt, in quibus vel unicè vel saltem potiori parte lux, & splendor sub considerationem cadunt. Universim meteorum dicitur mixtum imperfectum ex halitibus quibusdam adtenuatis seu ut Chymici loquuntur sublimatis constans & in superiori aëre formatum. De singulis pauca delibabimus, & generalem hanc definitionem ac naturam meteori singillatim ostendemus.

eteor means the same as appearing on high; whence the things that 831 Mare called by the Greeks meteora, or more precisely metarsia, are commonly called in Latin sublimia [lofty things]. They are conveniently divided into three kinds, or classes. The first contains the aërial or aqueous ones, in which, namely, air or water predominates. The second embraces the fiery ones, in which most subtle and spirituous exhalations prevail. The third class are the luminous or emphatic meteors, in which either solely, or at least for the greater part, light and splendor fall under consideration. A meteor, universally, is said to be an imperfect mixture consisting of certain attenuated (or, as the Chemists speak, sublimated) exhalations, and formed in the upper air. Of each we shall touch on a few things, and we shall show this general definition and nature of a meteor in each one singly.

> 832 Nubes est congeries vaporum in sublimi suspensa. Oritur ex vaporibus, qui in principio ita sunt tenues, ut non sint sensibiles, deinde verò accessu aliarum ad alias particulas mutua conjunctione moleculas majores constituunt, & hae aliis adhaerentes nubem vastissimam efformant, ut adeò nubes, congeries quaedam exiguarum bullularum in quibus aquei vapores consistunt, dicenda sit. A nube nebula non nisi densitatis gradu & loco differt; utraque enim ex [p. 259] humidorum halituum bullulis simul in magna copia adglomeratis nascitur: in illo tamen discrepant, quod bullulae nubem constituentes longè latiores adeòque respectu ad aërem leviores sint iis, quae nebulam efficiunt, ut illi veluti incumbant: mutatur nebula in nubes, hoc ipso quod inferior aër eas rarefactas ac propterea leviores redditas dissipatasque extrudat: hinc patet cur sole ad meridianum accedente, nebulae in nubes plerumque transeant.

832 A cloud is an aggregate of vapors suspended on high. It arises from vapors which at the beginning are so tenuous that they are not sensible, but which then, by the accession of some particles to others, constitute larger molecules by mutual conjunction; and these, adhering to others, form a very vast cloud, so that a cloud is accordingly to be called an aggregate of minute little bubbles in which aqueous vapors consist. Mist differs from a cloud only in its degree of density and in place; for each arises from little bubbles of humid [p. 259] exhalations agglomerated together in great quantity: they differ, however, in this, that the little bubbles constituting a cloud are far wider, and hence lighter with respect to the air, than those which make a mist, so that they lie, as it were, upon them: mist is changed into clouds by the very fact that the lower air thrusts out the bubbles, rarefied and therefore made lighter and dissipated: hence it is plain why, as the Sun approaches the meridian, mists for the most part pass into clouds.

> 833 Pluvia ex diffractis nubium bullulis oritur, quae diffringuntur pluribus è causis, nempè, vel ob nimium solis calorem, per quem plurimum dilatantur, vel si contrariorum ventorum impetu inter se collidantur, vel si contra montium latera urgeantur, vel demum si ab intenso aëris frigore nimis constringantur. Aura Seròtina, est humor quidam instar pluviae subtilissimae, & insensibilis, ingruente nocte ex alto deciduus, oriturque ex tenuissimis aqueis bullulis, quae in altum evectae diffringuntur, abeuntque in guttas insensibiles, quamprimùm aër post Solis occasum frigore aliquo corripitur: hinc nulla est hiemis tempore, sed aestate tantum ac potissimum vere, & autumno, nulla quoque flante vento Caeloque nimboso, & pluvio, hieme etiam crassiores illae guttuleae à ventis dissipantur, aut in tam exiguas per rarefactionem non dilatantur.

833 Rain arises from the broken little bubbles of the clouds, which are broken from several causes: namely, either on account of the excessive heat of the Sun, by which they are very greatly dilated; or if they collide with one another by the force of contrary winds; or if they are pressed against the sides of mountains; or, finally, if they are too much constricted by an intense cold of the air. The evening damp is a certain humor, like a most subtle and insensible rain, falling from on high as night comes on; and it arises from most tenuous aqueous little bubbles, which, carried on high, are broken and turn into insensible drops as soon as the air, after sunset, is seized by some cold: hence there is none in wintertime, but only in summer, and chiefly in spring and autumn, when, moreover, no wind is blowing. And when the sky is stormy and rainy, and in winter too, those thicker droplets are dissipated by the winds, or are not dilated by rarefaction into such minute ones.

> 834 Ros matutinus ratione temporis differt solum: labitur enim paulò ante ortum Solis, eo quod humidior tunc aër sit, proindè halitus illi concrescant, qui in aëre supererant, quare minus vera est illorum sententia, qui censent, quod ros nihil sit aliud quam plantarum sudor ex vasculorum orificio continuò exspirans & frigoris vi concretus; etsi etenim hanc transpirationem non negemus, aliud tamen de rore adfirmandum est, quum constet lineos laneosque pannos ceteraque corpora, vitrum item quae nihil hujusmodi sudoris transmittunt, si tempore roris decidui aperto aëri exponantur, sensibiliter madefieri. Pruina nihil est aliud, quàm ros acriori frigore gelatus, decoquit illa & exsugit teneriores fruges, & folia, uti gemmas vitium, imo non raro vites ipsas, nam alimentitius succus qui è terra extrusus ac diffusus in omnes plantae fibras est, frigore pruinae densatur: hinc textura fibrillarum constringitur ac mutatur.

834 The morning dew differs only in respect of time: for it falls a little before the rising of the Sun, because the air is then more humid, and hence those exhalations which remained over in the air concrete; wherefore the opinion of those is less true who think that dew is nothing else than the sweat of plants, continually breathing out from the orifice of their little vessels and congealed by the force of cold; for although we do not deny this transpiration, yet something else must be affirmed of dew, since it is established that linen and woolen cloths and other bodies, glass likewise, which transmit nothing of a sweat of this kind, are sensibly wetted if they are exposed to the open air at the time when the dew is falling. Hoarfrost is nothing other than dew frozen by a sharper cold; it scorches and sucks out the tenderer crops and leaves, such as the buds of vines, indeed not seldom the vines themselves; for the nutritive juice, which, thrust out from the earth, is diffused into all the fibers of the plant, is condensed by the cold of the hoarfrost: hence the texture of the little fibers is constricted and changed.

> 835 Grando est pluvia congelata à frigidissima aëris regione: fit tunc, quando tenues vaporum flocci ab aëre calido in minimas liquaefacti guttas, & deorsum jam nitentes alteri frigido occurrunt, & ab eo confestim coagulati durantur, accedentibus subindè novis quasi tunicis ob vapores, quos in lapsu contingunt. Hinc patet cur hieme non grandinet, nàm tunc sunt nubes telluri viciniores, quàm ut plurimae ex illis mininis guttulis, in quas primae ille abeunt, coire in unam possint; priusquam à frigore corripiantur, item cur quò altior fuerit nubes, ex qua resoluta grando formatur, eò grana grandinis sint majora.

835 Hail is rain congealed by the very cold region of the air: it is made when thin flakes of vapors, liquefied by warm air into very small drops and already tending downward, meet another, cold air, and are at once coagulated and hardened by it, new coats, as it were, being thereupon added on account of the vapors which they touch in falling. Hence it is plain why it does not hail in winter: for then the clouds are too near the Earth for very many of those very minute droplets, into which the first ones turn, to be able to come together into one before they are seized by the cold; likewise why, the higher the cloud from whose resolution the hail is formed, the larger the grains of hail are.

> 836 Nix efficitur si dum bullulae humidi halitus in pluviam [p. 260] abeuntes frigore glacientur; flocci enim nivium nihil aliud sunt, quàm tenuissimae aquae guttulae, quae frigore correptae uniuntur. Primum inter se filorum instar, tum diversa ratione sibi in descensu implicantur. Figura nivis quandoque regularis est, nonnunquam irregularis, saepè stellam hexagonam, interdum lilium, nec raro rosam si microscopio inspiciatur, exhibet, quae figurae pendere videntur ex diversis exhalationibus conglaciatis. Ex his facilè intelligitur quìd mel, manna, capillitium Veneris seu fila virginea, quae velut fila aranearum super saepes, & gramina adparent sint, & unde originem ducant.

836 Snow is produced if the little bubbles of a humid exhalation, while turning into rain, [p. 260] are frozen by cold; for the flakes of snow are nothing else than most tenuous droplets of water, which, seized by cold, are united first among themselves like threads, when they become entangled with one another in diverse ways in their descent. The figure of snow is sometimes regular, sometimes irregular; often, if it is examined with a microscope, it shows a hexagonal star, at times a lily, and not seldom a rose; which figures seem to depend on the diverse exhalations frozen together. From these things it is easily understood what honeydew, manna, and the hair of Venus, or virgin threads, which appear like spiders’ threads over hedges and grasses, are, and whence they draw their origin.

> 837 Meteora ignita sunt *primò* fulgur, *secundò* tonitru, *tertiò* fulmen, de quibus satis dictum in Electrologia est, *quartò* Helena, Pollux, sunt ignes, qui navigantibus adparent in infima aëris regione, & ex spirituosis fumis, quos mare tempestatibus agitatum transpirat, paululùm evecti, coadunatis atque succensis formatur. Si unus adparuit, Helena, dum duo videbantur, Castor & Pollux dicebantur. *Quintò*: stellae cadentes, & discurrentes sunt ignei quidam globuli in sublimi aëre accensi, & ita per illum moti, ut interdum rectà incedere, quandoque praecipite de caelo labi nobis adpareant. *Sextò*: ignis lambens, & fatuus, est pinguis ex hominum vel corporum carne, & pinguiori materia exsudans halitus, qui ex compressione vel adtritu accenditur, & equis vel hominibus adhaeret citra damnum.

837 The fiery meteors are, first, the flash; second, thunder; third, lightning, of which enough has been said in the Electrology; fourth, Helen and Pollux, which are fires that appear to those sailing, in the lowest region of the air, and are formed from spirituous fumes, which the sea, agitated by storms, transpires, carried up little by little, gathered together and kindled. If one appeared, it was called Helen; when two were seen, Castor and Pollux. Fifth: falling and shooting stars are certain fiery globules kindled in the upper air, and so moved through it that at times they appear to us to proceed straight, at other times to glide headlong from the sky. Sixth: the licking fire, and the foolish fire, is a fat exhalation sweating out from the flesh of men or of bodies, and from fattier matter, which is kindled by compression or friction, and clings to horses or men without harm.

> 838 Ignis fatuus est halitus quidam uliginosus ex putrefactis plantis, cadaveribus aliisque oleaginosis dissolutis corporibus diurno solis calore praeparatus, qui accedente adtritione, vel fermentatione accenditur, lucet, & ac velut ardet. Fatui dicuntur ignes, quòd non solum huc illucque more fatui hominis nullâ certa lege discurrant, verum etiam quod sequantur, qui eos fugiunt, & ex adverso fugiant, qui illos sequuntur, unde à simplicibus metuuntur, non intelligentibus scilicet, ea causa id fieri, quod qui ignem insequitur, tum motu sui corporis, tum halitu suo aërem ante se, & cum hoc ignem fatuum impellat, qui verò ab igne fugit aërem post se, & cum aëre ignem fatuum adducat, dum locum à suo corpore relictum aëri implendum cedit.

838 The foolish fire is a certain marshy exhalation from putrefied plants, corpses and other oily dissolved bodies, prepared by the daily heat of the Sun, which, upon the onset of friction or fermentation, is kindled, shines, and, as it were, burns. They are called foolish fires because not only do they run hither and thither by no certain law, in the manner of a foolish man, but also because they follow those who flee them, and in turn flee those who follow them; whence they are feared by simple folk, who do not understand, namely, that this happens for the reason that he who pursues the fire, both by the motion of his body and by his breath, drives the air before him, and with it the foolish fire; while he who flees from the fire draws the air after him, and with the air the foolish fire, while he yields the place left by his body to be filled by the air.

> 839 *Septimo*: eadem est ratio, quae ferè praedictorum meteororum, phaenomenorum, quae sola diversa figura inter se discriminantur; si enim uliginosus, aut bituminosus halitus unà cum nitrosis spiritibus collectus, & in sublimi aëre fermentationis, adtritionis, aut compressionis ope repentè accensus, globi ignei speciem referat, habeatque penès se pensiles quasi floccos, ac saltatorio motu feratur, Capra saltans dicitur: si oblonga, & horizonti parallela, Trabs: si in sui medio intumescat, Draco: si sit rotunda, & plana, Clypeus: si teres, & cylindrica, columna: si desinat in mucronem, Pyramis si latè dispersa sit, & incensas veluti paleas ostendat, Stipula nuncupatur. *Octavo*: Aurora Borealis sive lux septentrionalis est [p. 261] fulgor ille, qui nocturno tempore in Septentrionali caeli plaga ita nobis interdum adparet, ut caelum ipsum ea in parte velut ardere videatur. Hujus phaenomeni historia diffusa est, quae passim apud Recentiores quum reperiatur, brevitatis causâ necessaria solum adduco.

839 Seventh: nearly the same is the account of the phenomena of the aforesaid meteors, which are distinguished among themselves only by their diverse figure; for if a marshy or bituminous exhalation, gathered together with nitrous spirits and suddenly kindled in the upper air by means of fermentation, friction or compression, presents the appearance of a fiery globe, and has about it hanging flakes, as it were, and is borne with a leaping motion, it is called the Leaping Goat; if it is oblong and parallel to the horizon, the Beam; if it swells in its middle, the Dragon; if it is round and flat, the Shield; if smooth and cylindrical, the Column; if it ends in a point, the Pyramid; if it is widely dispersed and shows, as it were, kindled straws, it is named the Stubble. Eighth: the Aurora Borealis, or northern light, is [p. 261] that glow which in the nighttime at times appears to us in the northern quarter of the sky in such a way that the sky itself seems, as it were, to burn in that part. The history of this phenomenon is extensive; since it is found everywhere among the Moderns, for brevity’s sake I adduce only what is necessary.

> 840 In primis in telluris atmosphaera, ut cetera ignita meteora, suam habet sedem, in eaque producitur; nam infra nubes interdum visa haec lux fuit, testante Mayero: deinde si ultra atmosphaeram porrigeretur, ea foret altissima, adeòque conspiceretur è locis etiam aequatori vicinis, quod tamen est contra experientiam, praesertim quum contingat saepè, ut in uno loco videatur, in alio paucis milliaribus dissito non observetur. Quapropter ex halitu, & vapore in altum è terra delatis sive ex materia fulminum, ac fulgurum nondum benè matura, ut ita dicam, & ad fulmineos fulgurisque effectus nondum praeparata lucem hanc, uti reliqua meteora ignita, provenire existimamus.

840 In the first place, it has its seat in the atmosphere of the Earth, like the other fiery meteors, and is produced in it; for this light has at times been seen below the clouds, as Mayer testifies: then, if it extended beyond the atmosphere, it would be very high, and hence would be seen even from places near the equator, which, however, is contrary to experience, especially since it often happens that it is seen in one place and is not observed in another a few miles distant. Wherefore we think that this light, like the remaining fiery meteors, comes from an exhalation and vapor carried on high from the earth, or from the matter of lightning and of flashes not yet well ripened, so to speak, and not yet prepared for the effects of lightning and of flashes.

> 841 Meteora lucida seu Emphatica sunt. *Primo* Iris quae est arcus multicolor in nube rorida ex oppositi solis refractione reflexioneque formatus, unde vel devehit, vel naturaliter indicat pluviam, sed sine magna aquarum eluvione, nubes enim nimium gravidae ad reflectendos sicque refringendos solis radios non sunt idoneae. Colores iridis magis conspicui sunt: ruber seu puniceus, flavus, viridis, caeruleus, ac demum purpureus seu violaceus, & hi quidem in Iride primaria ordinem memoratum obtinent, & vivaciores sunt; in secundaria verò conversum, sic ut extima illius parte reluceat purpureus, deinde caeruleus &c. Qui etiam debiliores magisque diluti conspiciuntur.

841 The luminous or Emphatic meteors are: first, the Rainbow, which is a many-colored arc formed in a dewy cloud by the refraction and reflection of the Sun opposite; whence it either brings down or naturally indicates rain, but without a great flood of waters; for clouds too heavily laden are not fit for reflecting and thus refracting the rays of the Sun. The more conspicuous colors of the rainbow are: red or crimson, yellow, green, blue, and finally purple or violet; and these in the primary rainbow hold the order mentioned and are more vivid; but in the secondary the reverse, so that in its outermost part the purple shines, then the blue, etc.; which are also seen weaker and more diluted.

> 842 Dicitur autem Iris primaria, quae post duas radiorum refractiones, & unam reflexionem ad oculum pervenit, ac ferè sub angulo circiter 42 gradum videtur. Secundaria verò quae post duas refractiones totidemque reflexiones sub angulo circiter 52 graduum in oculum incidit. Illud advertendum Iridem non videri, nisi visus inter Solem & nubem roridam intermediet, sic quando ad lucem per fenestras immissam ex ore aquam spargis, & medius inter Solem, & guttas consistis, Iridem conspicis, cujus alias etiam analogias in fonticulis salientibus, in telis aranearum, in collo columbae, floribus vel herbis sub Solis ortum rore conspersis ac debito situ locoque aspectis habes.

842 That rainbow, moreover, is called primary which reaches the eye after two refractions of the rays and one reflection, and is seen at an angle of about 42 degrees; and the secondary, that which falls into the eye after two refractions and as many reflections, at an angle of about 52 degrees. It is to be noticed that the rainbow is not seen unless the sight is between the Sun and the dewy cloud; so when you sprinkle water from your mouth toward the light let in through windows, and stand between the Sun and the drops, you behold a rainbow, of which you also have other analogies in little leaping fountains, in spiders’ webs, on the neck of a dove, in flowers or grasses sprinkled with dew about sunrise and viewed in the due situation and place.

> 843 Porrò cur idem colores semper esse, & permanere videantur, ex eo est, quod continuò aliae atque aliae nubis roridae partes, seu novae identidem guttulae eodem situ ac dispositione prioribus succedant, non secus ac in ardente cereo eadem flamma perdurare creditur, ob alias, & alias ignis particulas continuò succedentes. *Secundo* Halo sive corona, vel area est circulus coloratus, & communius subalbicans, quandoque tamen colores Iridis, sed obscuriores referens, qui non nunquam circa Solem, crebrius circa Lunam adparet, formatur in nube rorida inter astrum, & oculum [p. 262] interjecta cum plexu ad duplicem refractionem idoneo vi cujus radii cum axe seu linea per centrum sideris, & oculum ducta angulum fere 23 graduum efficiunt.

843 Further, why the same colors seem always to be and to remain is from this, that continually other and other parts of the dewy cloud, or new droplets again and again, succeed the earlier ones in the same situation and disposition, no otherwise than in a burning taper the same flame is believed to endure, on account of other and other particles of fire continually succeeding. Second: the Halo, or crown, or area, is a colored circle, more commonly whitish, sometimes however showing the colors of the rainbow, but more obscure, which appears now and then around the Sun, more often around the Moon; it is formed in a dewy cloud placed between the star and the eye, [p. 262] with a texture suited to a double refraction, by virtue of which the rays make with the axis, or the line drawn through the center of the star and the eye, an angle of nearly 23 degrees.

> 844 Si Halo semper major, ac major addensetur, pluviam praesagit, quia sensim in imbrem nubes concrescunt: si à multis, vel etiam ab una parte dissipetur, ventos, vel à pluribus, vel una ex parte exortos indicat, si totus evanescat, serenitatem praenunciat, tum enim vi caloris nubes dissipantur. Tertiò: *Parhelium*, & *Paraselene* sunt meteora lucida juxta Solem, vel Lunam consistentia, horumque astrorum imagines exhibentia; quoties enim Soli non infra versus terram neque è regione, sed ad latera, & ex obliquo sive ad boream sive ad austrum nubes adcurrit proximè in aquas resolvi apta, & versus solem etiam diaphana, ex altera verò parte instar speculi terminata, toties suam ipsi imaginem imprimit, quae indè ad oculos nostros reflexa nobis solem in nube repraesentat, ut ita geminos lucere Soles ignari arbitrentur. Insuper fieri potest ut imago Solis simili ratione in unam nubem impressa aliam rursus imaginem in nubem alteram inducat, & haec rursus in aliam, idem de Luna cum proportione sentiendum.

844 If the Halo is condensed ever larger and larger, it presages rain, because the clouds gradually concrete into a shower; if it is dissipated on many sides, or even on one side, it indicates winds arising either from several quarters or from one; if it vanishes wholly, it foretells fair weather, for then the clouds are dissipated by the force of heat. Third: the Parhelion and Paraselene are luminous meteors standing beside the Sun or the Moon and showing the images of those stars; for as often as a cloud apt to be resolved very soon into waters, diaphanous, too, toward the Sun, but terminated on the other side like a mirror, runs up to the Sun, not below it toward the earth, nor directly opposite, but at the sides and obliquely, either toward the north or toward the south, so often the Sun impresses its own image upon it, which, reflected thence to our eyes, represents the Sun to us in the cloud, so that the ignorant judge that twin Suns are shining. Moreover, it can happen that the image of the Sun, impressed in like manner on one cloud, induces again another image on a second cloud, and this again on another; the same is to be thought, proportionally, of the Moon.

> 845 Quarto: *Virgae* formantur in aëre, quum vel rectus nubium tractus diversos exhibet colores eam ob causam, ob quam in iride vel corona formantur.
