Quinto: *Voraginem*, *hiatum*, vel *foveam* adpellamus, quando serena nocte exhalationes sursum evectae in medio quidem densiores, reliqua parte rariores inter astrorum lucem & oculum nostrum sunt collocatae, si enim multae fuerint, voraginem, si pauciores, hiatum, si in longum protensae, foveam, vel lacum exhibent; siquidem propter densitatem in medio minus illustrantur, omne verò obscurum licet aequè vicinum, & in eadem superficie positum, semper remotius videtur, ac depressius, nitidum verò propinquius magisque elevatum. Haec de uberrima materia compendio dixisse sufficiat.

845 Fourth: Rods are formed in the air when a straight tract of clouds shows diverse colors, for the same cause for which these are formed in the rainbow or the crown. Fifth: we call it a Chasm, a Gap, or a Pit, when on a clear night exhalations carried upward, denser in the middle and rarer in the remaining part, are placed between the light of the stars and our eye; for if they are many, they show a chasm; if fewer, a gap; if extended lengthwise, a pit or lake; since on account of the density in the middle they are less illuminated, and everything dark, although equally near and placed in the same surface, always seems more remote and more depressed, while what is bright seems nearer and more elevated. Let it suffice to have said this, in compendium, on a most copious matter.

> CAPUT POSTREMUM.

CHAPTER THE LAST.

> Quid de Plantis dicendum sit.

What is to be said of Plants.

> 846 Plantae, quo nomine stirpium omne genus, quod ex terra erumpit, intelligitur: sunt corpora organica vario partium organicarum sapientissimè coordinatarum, & conjunctarum adparatu constantia, radicibus suis terrae inhaerentia, atque succi convenientis in orbem euntis ac redeuntis influxu animata. Adparatum mirabilem organicorum horum corporum [p. 263] perquisivére, & explicuere *Malpighius* Italus, & *Grevius* Anglus. Vita quodammodo, & actiones in plantis absolvuntur fluidi vitalis per organa solida sapientissimè disposita jugi & in orbem redeunte motu, quem aetheris aërisque agitatio, impulsus, pressio mediante simul vi elastica efficiunt, ut ea propter rectè dicantur machinae Hydraulico-Pneumaticae, quae ut penitius intelligantur breviculam earum Anatomen subdo.

lants, by which name every kind of growth that bursts forth from the 846 P earth is understood, are organic bodies consisting of a varied apparatus of organic parts most wisely co-ordinated and joined together, adhering to the earth by their roots, and animated by the influx of a suitable juice going round and returning in a circuit. The wonderful apparatus of these organic bodies was investigated [p. 263] and explained by Malpighi the Italian and Grew the Englishman. Life, in a manner, and its actions are accomplished in plants by the continual motion, returning in a circuit, of the vital fluid through solid organs most wisely disposed; which motion the agitation, impulse and pressure of the ether and the air bring about, the elastic force mediating at the same time; so that on that account they are rightly called Hydraulic-Pneumatic machines; and that these may be understood more deeply, I subjoin a very brief Anatomy of them.

> 847 Plantarum partes aliae sunt fluidae, aliae solidae. Fluida pars est humor ille vel succus, qui instar sanguinis in homine, per solidas plantae partes diffunditur. Succum hunc, & verum ac genuinum plantarum nutrimentum, probabilissimè dicunt esse partes salinas, terreas, oleosas, quae in succo aqueo praeparatae, extenuatae, subactae, & cum hoc succo tanquàm vehiculo in plantarum totam structuram distributae circumferuntur, sic ut singulae partes, quod earum substantiae nutriendae, & augendae idoneum est, recipere possint. Partes solidae organicum ipsarum corpus constituunt & sunt: truncus, radices, rami, folia, flores, fructus. Truncus qui in arboribus caudex & stipes, in floribus & herbis caulis, scapus, & thyrsus in tritico, & similibus calmus, vel culmus, dicitur, est veluti corpus plantae quod è terra erumpens ei supereminet, atque in ramos frondes &c. se explicat. Radix est ea plantae pars, quae tota infra terram posita, ei adhaerescens suum plantae alimentum trahit. Rami quemadmodum ortus ex corpore animalis, ita ex plantae corpore sive trunco plerumque inordinatè, quandoque eleganti ordine erumpunt, & quaquaversus se difundunt; ejus prorsùs naturae, cujus truncus, ex quo nascuntur, cortice uti ille muniti, medullam continent in medio iisdemque vasculis, fibris nempè, utriculis atque tracheis componuntur. Folia duas praecipuè partes complectuntur: pediculum nempè quo folium est plantae annexum, & ipsum folii corpus.

847 Of the parts of plants, some are fluid, others solid. The fluid part is that humor or juice which, like the blood in man, is diffused through the solid parts of the plant. This juice, and the true and genuine nourishment of plants, they say most probably to be saline, earthy and oily parts, which, prepared in the aqueous juice, attenuated, worked up, and distributed with this juice, as with a vehicle, into the whole structure of the plants, are carried round, so that the single parts can receive what is suitable for nourishing and increasing their substance. The solid parts constitute their organic body, and are: the trunk, roots, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits. The trunk, which in trees is called the bole and stock, in flowers and herbs the stalk, scape and thyrsus, in wheat and the like the straw or haulm, is, as it were, the body of the plant, which, bursting forth from the earth, rises above it and unfolds itself into branches, fronds, etc. The root is that part of the plant which, placed wholly below the earth and adhering to it, draws its nourishment for the plant. The branches, just as the limbs from the body of an animal, so burst forth from the body, or trunk, of the plant, for the most part without order, sometimes in an elegant order, and spread themselves in every direction; being of altogether the same nature as the trunk from which they arise, and furnished like it with bark, they contain pith in the middle, and are composed of the same little vessels, namely fibers, utricles and tracheae. The leaves embrace chiefly two parts: namely, the petiole, by which the leaf is attached to the plant, and the very body of the leaf.

> 848 Flores sunt velut primus plantae partus, in iis quatuor partes distinguntur, nempè, calix qui est floris basis & fulcimentum: foliola quae supra calicem adsurgunt à dilatato caule propagata, constant ex lignosis fistulis sivè fibris, tracheis quoque, & simul multiplici utriculorum ordine; stamina ex imâ floris parte erumpunt varia numero atque figura: constant pedunculo, & adpensa capsula, quae lignosis fistulis tracheis atque utriculis per longum locatis integratur: stylus demum est ea floris pars, quae illius centrum occupans plantae semen cavitate sua recondit, & fovet. Fructus est ultimum plantarum opus, cui producendo, & perficiendo reliquae omnes partes sunt destinatae, constat autem involúcro atque semine, illud pro specifico fructuum discrimine differt; & multiplex est, ac diversae consistentiae, & firmitatis in fructibus diversis; semen ad ortum plantarum pertinet: de quo breviter.

848 The flowers are, as it were, the first offspring of the plant; in them four parts are distinguished, namely: the calyx, which is the base and support of the flower; the petals, which rise above the calyx, propagated from the dilated stalk, and consist of woody tubes, or fibers, of tracheae too, and at the same time of a manifold order of utricles; the stamens burst forth from the lowest part of the flower, various in number and figure: they consist of a filament and an attached capsule, which is made up of woody tubes, tracheae and utricles placed lengthwise: the style, finally, is that part of the flower which, occupying its center, hides and cherishes the seed of the plant in its cavity. The fruit is the last work of plants, to the producing and perfecting of which all the remaining parts are destined; it consists, moreover, of an envelope and the seed; the former differs according to the specific difference of the fruits, and is manifold, and of diverse consistency and firmness in diverse fruits; the seed pertains to the origin of plants: of which briefly.

> 849 Semen dicitur illud granulum seu nucleus, ex quo veluti ex ovo planta progerminat, quatuor in eo distinguuntur involúcra; [p. 264] primum sive omnium extimum ceteris duriùs est, eo detracto duae occurrunt pelliculae, quatum exterior crassa, ac fermè cartilaginosa est, interior valdè subtilis, sic ut in exsiccato semine vix ab exteriori sejungi possit. Post haec integumenta, quae secundinae vocantur, duo vel etiam plures lobi in conspectum veniunt tenui admodum pellucidaque membrana, quae ordine quarta est, comprehensi, complectuntur autem in quadam veluti fossula utrinque in lobis excavata germen futurae plantae, quod nihil est aliud quàm ipsa tota planta ex semine nascitura partibus omnibus, trunco nempè, caule, radicibus, ramis, &c. absoluta adeò, ut seminalis plantula in germine delitescens, non nisi penès partium magnitudinem ab adulta differat.

849 That little grain, or kernel, is called the seed, from which, as from an egg, the plant germinates; four things are distinguished in it: the envelopes; [p. 264] the first, or outermost of all, is harder than the rest; when it is removed, two little skins are met, of which the exterior is thick and almost cartilaginous, the interior very subtle, so that in a dried seed it can scarcely be separated from the exterior. After these integuments, which are called secundines, two or even more lobes come into view, enclosed in a certain thin and pellucid membrane, which is fourth in order; and they embrace, in a kind of little ditch, as it were, hollowed out on either side in the lobes, the germ of the future plant; which is nothing else than the whole plant itself that is to arise from the seed, complete in all its parts, namely trunk, or stalk, roots, branches, etc., so that the seminal plantlet lying hidden in the germ does not differ from the adult except in the size of its parts.

> 850 Ortus porrò ex semine hac ratione peragitur; semine idoneo terrae commisso, ejus, & Solis calore leniter laxantur fibrae membranarum earumque meatus dilatantur, quo fit ut humor, quo terra abundat, eos paulatim subeat, in illis variè percoletur, fermentet, aptusque nutritioni efficiatur: nutritius succus in membranis percolatus loborum substantiam ingreditur, ubi cum specifico succo plantulae miscetur, fermentescit ac novas partes adsciscit: is debita ratione in lobis praeparatus, radiculae ipsius germinis subtilissimos poros subit, & in ejus fibrillas se insinuat, quae hoc succo nutrita, & aucta extra prorrumpit, capillitium spargit, & terrae illorum filamentorum ope inseritur, aucta sufficienter radice vividior nutritii liquoris portio in reliquam germinis partem transit, ejusque partes irradians, & impellens motum ipsis communicat: hinc evolvuntur, & explicantur partes futurae plantae, quae in germine inter se convolutae complicataeque delitescunt, tum sensim eaedem ipsae augentur, & suo ordine in conspectum veniunt: ut adeò ex prima hac seminis evolutione reliqua plantae adcretio facilè intelligatur.

850 The rising from the seed, further, is accomplished in this way: when the seed is committed to suitable earth, the fibers of its membranes are gently loosened by the heat of the earth and of the Sun, and their passages are dilated; whence it comes about that the humor in which the earth abounds gradually enters them, is variously strained in them, ferments, and is made apt for nutrition: the nutritive juice, strained in the membranes, enters the substance of the lobes, where it is mixed with the specific juice of the plantlet, ferments, and takes on new parts; this juice, prepared in due manner in the lobes, enters the most subtle pores of the radicle of the germ itself and insinuates itself into its little fibers; and the radicle, nourished and increased by this juice, bursts forth outward, spreads out its hair, and by means of those filaments is inserted into the earth; the root being sufficiently increased, a more lively portion of the nutritive liquor passes into the remaining part of the germ, and, irradiating and impelling its parts, communicates motion to them; hence are evolved and unfolded the parts of the future plant, which lie hidden in the germ, rolled up and folded together among themselves; then by degrees these same parts are increased and come into view in their order: so that from this first evolution of the seed the remaining growth of the plant is easily understood.

> Corollarium.

COROLLARY.

> 851 Nullae adeò plantae sunt quae ex semine non generentur. Certè peculiaris plantarum dispositio miro ordine, & distinctione partium collocatio, vénulae, utriculi, tracheae, ad flores fructus ejusdem speciei producendos manifestum faciunt, non ex fortuito elementorum concursu aut ex putri plantas enasci. Id ipsum Malpighii experimento ostenditur, qui terram ex profundiore voragine érutam vasi ita incluserat, ut superiorem partem telis delicatissimis obduceret sic ut aëri pluviaeque ingressus in vas pateret, non vero aliis minimis corpusculis per aërem delatis; atque ita Solis radiis exposuit. Reperit post longissimum tempus nullam herbam, aut plantae indicium adparere; ut ea propter intulerit, quod quum nullum semen vel antea in terra [p. 265] profundius eruta latuerit vel per aerem in vas incidere potuerit, plantae suam genesim ex semine habeant.

851 There are therefore no plants that are not generated from seed. Certainly the peculiar disposition of plants, the collocation of their parts in wonderful order and distinction, the little veins, utricles and tracheae, for producing flowers and fruits of the same species, make it manifest that plants are not born from a fortuitous concourse of the elements, or from putrid matter. This very thing is shown by an experiment of Malpighi, who had enclosed earth dug out of a rather deep pit in a vessel in such a way as to cover its upper part with very delicate cloths, so that entrance into the vessel lay open to the air and the rain, but not to other very minute corpuscles carried through the air; and so he exposed it to the rays of the Sun. He found that after a very long time no herb, or sign of a plant, appeared; so that on that account he inferred that, since no seed had either lain hidden before in the earth [p. 265] dug out from deeper down, or could have fallen into the vessel through the air, plants have their genesis from seed.

> 852 Nutritionem & augmentum plantarum quod adtinet, ea convenientis succi admissione, elaboratione, depuratione, & ejus per organa plantae jugi circulatione absolvitur; radices enim humorem adtrahunt, is receptus per lignosas plantae fistulas ascendit eo, quod ab altero â dilatatione, & constructione trachearum, quae lignosis fistulis interseruntur, sursum indesinenter urgeatur; è quibus in ceteras partes dispensatur. Circulari verò succum alimentitium ostenditur imprimis, quia non nisi hâc ratione videtur absolvi posse plantarum nutritionem; si quidem haec fieri nequit, nisi utile & quod conveniens plantae alimentum est, ab inutili secernatur, hocque ad eas iterùm partes retrudatur, ut idoneum nutritioni per novam depurationem, & elaborationem reddatur: deinde patet experientia; Malpighius enim cortice in orbem secto avulsaque annulari portione deprehendit, superioris corticis limbum notabiliter intumescere atque etiam augeri, inferioris verò nullum obtinuisse incrementum, sed gemmas duntaxat suo tempore praetulisse. Atque haec, quae ex P. Klaus excerpta sunt dicta sufficiant, ut Physicae cùm Generali tum Particulari supremam manum imponamus.

852 As regards the nutrition and growth of plants, it is accomplished by the admission, elaboration and purification of a suitable juice, and by its continual circulation through the organs of the plant; for the roots draw in moisture; this, once received, ascends through the woody tubes of the plant, because it is urged upward unceasingly by the alternate dilatation and constriction of the tracheae which are interspersed among the woody tubes; and from these it is dispersed into the other parts. That the nutritive juice circulates is shown, first of all, because only in this way does it seem that the nutrition of plants can be accomplished; since indeed this cannot take place unless that which is useful, and is suitable nourishment for the plant, is separated from the useless, and this is thrust back again to those parts, so that it may be rendered fit for nutrition through a new purification and elaboration; and then it is plain from experience; for Malpighi, when the bark had been cut round in a circle and a ring-shaped portion torn away, found that the edge of the upper bark swelled notably and also increased, but that the lower obtained no increase, but only put forth buds in their season. And let these things, which have been excerpted from Fr. Klaus, suffice to have been said, so that we may put the finishing hand to the Physics, both General and Particular.

> 853 Quod si cui fortassè aliqua, quae in hisce *Recentioris Philosophiae Elementis* adtuli breviora quàm oporteret videantur, eum cogitare velim, me solis Adolescentibus scripsisse. Prostant in aliorum commodum eruditi multorum, longèque ampliora volumina. Nec tamen propterea muneri meo defuisse putem, qui utilius judicarem quidquid negotium tironibus facessere posset, planum facere, atque *Elementis* hisce Americanos Juvenes juvare potius, quàm majore mole disputationum ipsos onerare. Philosophia namque, & meditatione & experimentis acquirenda est, nec magni commodi quicquam in prolixitate situm habet.

853 But if to anyone perhaps some of the things which I have brought forward in these Elements of the Newer Philosophy should seem briefer than was fitting, I would wish him to consider that I have written for Young Men alone. Many large volumes of learned men, far fuller ones, are available for the convenience of others. Nor yet would I think on that account that I have failed in my office, since I judged it more useful to make plain whatever could cause trouble to beginners, and with these Elements rather to help the American Youth than to burden them with a greater mass of disputations. For Philosophy is to be acquired both by meditation and by experiments, and it has nothing of great advantage placed in prolixity.
